Chapter Nine: The Awakening of Radiance At that time,
the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from the wheels on the soles of his two feet,
illuminating this trichiliocosm— ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Pūrvavidehas, and ten billion Aparagoyānīs.
One billion bhikṣuṇīs; one billion Uttarakurus; one billion great oceans; one billion Cakravāḍa mountains;
one billion bodhisattvas taking birth; one billion bodhisattvas leaving the household life; one billion Tathāgatas attaining perfect enlightenment;
one billion Tathāgatas turning the wheel of Dharma; one billion Tathāgatas entering parinirvāṇa; one billion Sumerus...
Mount Sumeru, ten billion assemblies of the gods of the Four Great Kings, ten billion Trāyastriṃśa heavens,
ten billion Yāma heavens, ten billion Tuṣita heavens, ten billion Nirmāṇarati heavens, ten billion Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens,
ten billion Brahmakāyika heavens, ten billion Ābhāsvara heavens, and ten billion Śubhakṛtsna heavens.
The Śuddhāvāsa heavens, ten billion Bṛhatphala heavens, and ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens—
all that exists therein was clearly manifested.
Just as here, one saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.
Within those ten billion Jambudvīpas, ten billion Tathāgatas were likewise seated.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great Bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
Their names were:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Bodhyaṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Dhanaṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Ratnāṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Guṇāṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Netrāṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Vīryāṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Dharmāṅgadhara Bodhisattva, Jñānāṅgadhara Bodhisattva, and Bhadrajyotirbodhisattva.
The lands from which these bodhisattvas have come are as follows:

the Golden World, the World of Sublime Color, the Lotus-Color World, the Campaka-Flower-Color World, the Utpala-Flower-Color World, the Gold-Color World, the Jewel-Color World, the Vajra-Color World, the Crystal-Color World, and the World of Equal Color.
These bodhisattvas each cultivated the pure conduct of brahmacarya under various buddhas, namely:

Akṣobhyajñāna Buddha, Asaṅgajñāna Buddha, Vimuktijñāna Buddha, Īryāpathajñāna Buddha, Lakṣaṇajñāna Buddha, Niṣṭhajñāna Buddha, Paramajñāna Buddha, Vaśitājñāna Buddha, Brahmajñāna Buddha, and Vipaśyanājñāna Buddha.
At that time, in every location, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
“If one sees the Perfectly Awakened One, Who is liberated and free from all outflows,
And remains unattached to any world— That person has not yet realized the Eye of the Path.”
If there is one who knows that the Tathāgata’s essence and marks are non-existent,
and through cultivation attains clear realization, this person will swiftly become a Buddha.
Able to see this world, their mind remains unshaken.
It is likewise with the Buddha’s body; one shall become a supreme knower.
If, regarding both the Buddha and the Dharma, the mind realizes their equality and dualistic thoughts do not arise, one shall tread upon the inconceivable stage.
If one perceives the Buddha and one’s own body as abiding in equality, without dwelling and without entering anywhere, one shall become a rare and difficult-to-meet being.
Form and sensation are beyond numbering; so too are perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If one can know in this way, one shall become a Great Muni.
Transcending all views of both the mundane and the supramundane,
and being able to thoroughly know the Dharma, one shall become a Great Radiance.
If one generates the mind of dedication toward all-knowledge,
And perceives that the mind has no arising, One shall obtain great renown.
Sentient beings have no birth, Nor do they undergo destruction.
If one attains such wisdom, one shall accomplish the unsurpassed path.
Understanding the infinite within the one, and the one within the infinite,
and comprehending their mutual arising, one shall become fearless.
At that time, the light passed beyond this world and illuminated ten Buddha-lands in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
In each and every one of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In this place, one sees the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
in each of those individual worlds, there are likewise hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas and hundreds of millions of Tathāgatas, all seated in the same manner.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas were, namely,
Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely,
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
“Sentient beings lack wisdom and are wounded by the poison of the thorns of craving;
for their sake, I seek enlightenment—such is the nature of all Buddhas’ Dharma.”
Universally perceiving all phenomena, He abandons both extremes;
having perfected the Path, he never regresses, And turns this peerless wheel.
Throughout inconceivable eons, He has cultivated all practices with diligence.
To deliver all sentient beings—this is the power of the Great Sage.
The Guide subdues the hosts of Māras; valiant and invincible, he expounds the wondrous meaning within his radiance, acting thus out of compassion.
With that wisdom-mind, he shatters all afflictive obstructions;
in a single thought-moment, he perceives all things—this is the Buddha’s spiritual power.
He beats the drum of the True Dharma, awakening all lands in the ten directions.
Causing all to turn toward Bodhi—such is the power of their mastery.
Without destroying the boundless realm, they travel through billions of lands;
unattached to existence, they possess a mastery like that of a Buddha.
The Buddhas are like space, Ultimately and eternally pure;
Recalling them brings forth joy, And those vows are fully fulfilled.
Within each and every hell, Passing through immeasurable kalpas,
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, they are able to endure such suffering.
Without sparing their own bodies or lives, they constantly protect all Buddha-dharmas.
With a selfless mind that is disciplined and supple, they are able to attain the Way of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the light passed beyond ten worlds and illuminated a hundred worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Within those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In each and every Jambudvīpa therein, he saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas, namely Mañjuśrī and others,
and the lands from which they had come, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely:
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, in every location, simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
“The Buddha realizes that all phenomena are like illusions; He has attained unimpeded penetration.
With a pure mind free from all attachments, He tames all living beings.”
Some see him at birth, with a wondrous form like a mountain of gold;
dwelling in his final body, he forever becomes a moon among men.
Others see him when he walks in meditation, endowed with immeasurable merit.
Mindfulness and wisdom are both skillful; the Great Being walks with the stride of a lion.
Sometimes his deep blue eyes are seen surveying the ten directions;
at times he manifests playful laughter to accord with the desires of sentient beings.
Some see the Lion’s Roar, his peerless and most excellent body, manifesting his final birth; whatever he speaks is nothing but truth.
Others see him renounce the world, liberated from all bonds.
Cultivating the practices of all Buddhas, they always joyfully contemplate tranquil extinction.
Or they see them seated at the site of enlightenment, awakening to all phenomena and reaching the further shore of merit.
The darkness of delusion and afflictions are exhausted;
one may behold the Supreme Being, who, endowed with great compassion,
turns the wondrous Wheel of Dharma and delivers immeasurable sentient beings.
In some places he is seen roaring like a lion, his majestic radiance most extraordinary,
transcending all worlds with peerless power of supernormal faculties;
in others he is seen with a mind utterly tranquil, like a worldly lamp forever extinguished.
"Manifesting various supernatural powers, the One of Ten Powers is able to act thus.
At that time, the light passed beyond a hundred worlds and illuminated a thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
In each and every one of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In each and every Jambudvīpa, he saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas were, namely,
Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely,
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
“The Buddha has attained a profound Dharma, Unrivaled in its thorough penetration;
Sentient beings cannot comprehend it, So he reveals it to them step by step.”
The nature of the self has never existed, and that which belongs to the self is likewise empty and quiescent;
how then can the Tathāgatas possess a body?
Those who practice the clear conduct of liberation are infinite and beyond compare.
The various causes and measures of the world, when sought for faults, cannot be found.
The Buddha is not comprised of the worldly aggregates, nor is he a phenomenon of the elements, sense-bases, or the cycle of birth and death;
since he cannot be established by numerical categories, he is called the Lion among Men.
Its nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent; Both internally and externally, it is liberated.
Free from all deluded thoughts, Such is the peerless Dharma.
Its essence is eternally unmoving; Without self, there is no coming or going.
Able to awaken the world, they bring all infinite beings to complete subdual.
Always delighting in the contemplation of quiescent extinction, they perceive the single mark as being without duality;
their minds neither increase nor decrease as they manifest immeasurable spiritual powers.
Without performing the karmic actions that cause the retribution of all sentient beings,
yet being able to understand them without obstruction— such is the Dharma of the Sugata.
Sentient beings of various kinds wander and transmigrate throughout the ten directions.
The Tathāgata makes no discriminations, yet delivers infinite beings.
The true golden color of all Buddhas is neither existent nor non-existent, pervading all realms of existence;
according to the inclinations of sentient beings' minds, he preaches the Dharma of quiescent extinction.
At that time, the light passed beyond a thousand worlds and illuminated ten thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as in the four intermediate points, above, and below.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In each and every Jambudvīpa therein, he saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas were, namely,
Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely:
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses at the presence of each Buddha:
“Arouse the mind of great compassion To rescue and protect all sentient beings;
To forever deliver them from the realms of humans and devas— Such is the deed one ought to perform.”
Always with a mind that trusts and delights in the Buddha, his heart never regresses;
drawing near to all Tathāgatas, such deeds as these he should perform.
Taking joy in the virtues of the Buddha, his mind never ever recedes.
Abiding in the wisdom of cool serenity, one should perform such deeds.
In all modes of conduct, one should constantly recollect the Buddha’s virtues without interruption, day and night; thus should one perform such deeds.
Contemplating the boundless three periods of time, one should study the virtues of those Buddhas with a mind forever free from weariness; such is the karma that should be performed.
Contemplating the body according to its true nature, one sees that all things are utterly quiescent.
Free from attachment to self and non-self, one should perform such actions.
Observing the minds of sentient beings with equanimity, without giving rise to any conceptual discriminations,
and entering the realm of reality, one should perform such actions.
Lifting up all boundless realms and drinking from all oceans—such is the power of their supernormal knowledge; such is the work they should perform.
Contemplating all lands and their characteristics, both material and immaterial,
One can know them all, and thus one should perform such deeds.
As for the dust motes in the lands of the ten directions, taking each mote to represent a Buddha,
one can know their total number, and thus one should perform such deeds.
At that time, the light passed beyond ten thousand worlds and illuminated a hundred thousand worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so in the south, west, and north, as well as in the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In each and every Jambudvīpa therein, he saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas were, namely,
Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely:
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
“If one perceives the Teacher of Men through his majestic power, physical form, or lineage, This is the distorted vision of diseased eyes; such a person cannot know the most supreme Dharma.”
The Tathāgata’s physical form, features, and all such marks cannot be fathomed by any in the world;
even if they were to contemplate them together for billions of nayutas of eons, his physical marks and majestic virtue would only become more boundless.
The Tathāgata does not take marks as his essence; he is merely the markless, quiescent Dharma.
Yet, with all physical marks and dignified deportment fully perfected, he is seen by those in the world according to their inclinations.
The Buddha-dharma is subtle and profound, difficult to measure; no words or expressions can reach it.
It is neither a combination nor a separation; its essential nature is quiescent and devoid of all marks.
The Buddha’s body is unborn and transcends conceptual proliferation; it is not a phenomenon consisting of an aggregation of aggregates.
Having attained the power of mastery, one sees with certainty that his conduct is fearless and beyond the reach of words.
Body and mind are entirely equal; both internally and externally, one is liberated.
Abiding in right mindfulness for eternal kalpas, one is without attachment and has nothing to bind.
For one whose mind is pure and luminous, there is no defilement or clinging in their conduct.
The eye of wisdom reaches everywhere, extensively benefiting sentient beings.
One body becomes immeasurable, and the immeasurable returns to one.
Thoroughly understanding all worlds, they manifest forms throughout everything.
This body has no origin, nor does it have any accumulation;
yet because sentient beings engage in conceptual discrimination, they perceive the Buddha’s manifold bodies.
The mind discriminates the world, yet this mind itself has no inherent existence.
"The Tathāgata knows this Dharma; thus he perceives the Buddha-body.
At that time, the light passed beyond hundreds of thousands of worlds and illuminated a million worlds in the eastern direction;
likewise it did so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifest.
In each and every Jambudvīpa, he saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, there was a great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, who came to where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas were, namely,
Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely:
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
“The Tathāgata is most sovereign, Transcending the world with nothing upon which to rely;
Possessing all merits and virtues, He delivers beings from all states of existence.”
Untainted and unattached, Without conceptualization and without dependence, Your essential nature is immeasurable; All who behold you offer praise.
Your radiance is universally pure, Completely washing away all defilements and burdens.
Immovable and free from the two extremes— this is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If one perceives the Tathāgata such that body and mind are free from conceptual discrimination,
then regarding all phenomena, one will forever transcend all doubts and obstructions.
Throughout all worlds, in every place, he turns the wheel of Dharma;
yet there is no intrinsic nature and nothing to be turned—this is the skillful teaching of the Guide.
Regarding these dharmas, there is no doubt; forever severed are all conceptual proliferations.
Not giving rise to conceptualizing thoughts— this is mindfulness of the Buddha’s awakening.
Thoroughly understanding differentiated phenomena without clinging to verbal expressions,
and realizing there is neither one nor many— this is called following the Buddha’s teaching.
Within the many there is no single nature, and within the one there is no multiplicity;
by relinquishing both of these, one universally enters the merit of the Buddha.
Sentient beings and their lands—everything is utterly quiescent.
Without dependence and without conceptual discrimination, one can enter the Buddha’s bodhi.
Sentient beings and their lands—neither identity nor difference can be apprehended.
To observe thus with skill is called knowing the meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the light passed beyond a million worlds and illuminated a billion worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In each and every Jambudvīpa therein, they each saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.
The great bodhisattvas were, namely,
Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely,
the Tathāgata Immovable Wisdom and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses in the presence of each Buddha:
"Wisdom is peerless and phenomena are boundless; Transcending the ocean of existence, he has reached the other shore.
His lifespan and radiance are both beyond compare; Such merit is the power of his skillful means."

All Buddha-dharmas are clearly understood; Constantly observing the three periods of time without weariness, Though engaging with objective realms, no discrimination arises— This is the power of skillful means of the inconceivable one.

Delighting in observing sentient beings without the notion of "beings," Universally seeing all realms of existence without the notion of "realms," Constantly abiding in meditative stillness with an unattached mind— This is the power of skillful means of unimpeded wisdom.
Skillfully penetrating all phenomena, Diligently cultivating the path to nirvana with right mindfulness,
Delighting in liberation and departing from all that is uneven— Such is the power of skillful means of this person of tranquil extinction.
There are those who can encourage others toward the Buddha’s bodhi, Leading them toward the omniscience that accords with the dharma-realm;
Skillfully transforming sentient beings so they enter the truths— This is the power of skillful means of abiding in the Buddha-mind.
They enter into all the teachings spoken by the Buddha; Their vast wisdom is unimpeded in every respect.
Having reached the perfection of conduct in all places, This is the power of their mastery in practicing skillful means.
Constantly abiding in nirvāṇa like space, manifesting transformations according to the mind without exception;
this taking of the signless as a sign is the power of skillful means for those who have reached what is difficult to reach.
Days and nights, days and months, years and eons, as well as the signs of the world’s beginning, end, formation, and destruction—he fully knows all such recollections;
this is the power of his skillful means in the knowledge of temporal calculation.

All sentient beings undergo birth and death; whether they possess form or are formless, whether they have perception or are non-percipient—knowing all their names completely, this is the dwelling in the power of inconceivable skillful means.

All speech throughout the past, present, and future worlds they can fully comprehend, yet they know that the three periods of time are entirely equal; this is the peerless power of their skillful means.
At that time, the light passed beyond one hundred million worlds and illuminated ten billion worlds in the eastern direction;
it was likewise so in the south, west, and north, as well as in the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Within each of those worlds, there were ten billion Jambudvīpas, up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha Heavens;
everything contained therein was clearly manifested.
In each and every Jambudvīpa therein, he saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne within a lotus treasury, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions there came a great bodhisattva, each accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, arriving at the place where the Buddha was.

Mañjuśrī and others; the lands from which they had come were, namely:
The Golden World and others;
the Buddhas whom he originally served, namely:
Akṣobhyajñāna Tathāgata and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously raised his voice before each Buddha and spoke these verses:
“He has cultivated all vast ascetic practices, Diligent day and night without weariness or indolence;
Having crossed over what is difficult to cross with a lion’s roar, Universally transforming sentient beings—this is his conduct.”
Sentient beings wander in the ocean of craving and desire, Enmeshed in the net of ignorance and oppressed by great sorrow;
The Benevolent One, with valorous courage, completely severs them all— I vow likewise to practice this very deed.
The world is heedless and attached to the five desires; through unreal conceptualization, it undergoes manifold sufferings.
To practice the Buddha’s teachings and always restrain the mind, vowing to deliver such beings—this is their conduct.
Sentient beings, attached to a self, enter the cycle of birth and death; though they seek its limit, it cannot be found.
By serving the Tathāgatas everywhere, they obtain the wondrous Dharma; to proclaim this for their sake is their practice.
Sentient beings are without refuge, entangled by illness; Constantly sinking into evil realms, they give rise to the three poisons.
The fierce flames of a great fire perpetually burn and scorch them; To deliver them with a pure mind—this is their practice.
Sentient beings are deluded and lose the right path; constantly traversing deviant ways, they enter the dark abode.
To light the great lamp of the True Dharma for them, and to provide eternal illumination—this is their practice.
Sentient beings drift and drown in the ocean of existence, Amidst boundless sorrows and hardships, unable to find rest;
For their sake, he constructs the great Dharma-ship, Causing them all to cross over—this is his practice.

Sentient beings, lacking knowledge, do not see the source; deluded and crazed within the midst of perilous difficulties, the Buddha takes pity on them and builds a bridge of Dharma, causing them to ascend by means of right mindfulness—this is his practice.

Seeing all sentient beings in perilous paths, constantly oppressed by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, they cultivate immeasurable skillful means; their practice is the vow to deliver them all.
Hearing the Dharma, they believe and understand it without doubt; realizing that nature is empty and quiescent, they are not startled or terrified.
Following forms throughout the six realms across the ten directions, they universally instruct the deluded masses—this is their practice.

At that time, the light passed beyond ten billion worlds and pervasively illuminated hundreds of billions, thousands of billions, hundreds of thousands of billions, nayuta-billions, hundreds of nayuta-billions, thousands of nayuta-billions, and hundreds of thousands of nayuta-billions of worlds in the eastern direction; likewise, it reached as far as all worlds throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space—incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, uncountable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable—and it was the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

everything contained therein was clearly manifested.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously uttered these verses before each Buddha:

"In a single thought, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; Without going, without coming, and without abiding— Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, One transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the Ten Powers."
With incomparable and virtuous renown throughout the ten directions, forever free from all calamities and always joyful,
they travel everywhere to all lands and extensively proclaim this Dharma.
Making offerings to the Buddhas for the benefit of sentient beings, they obtain corresponding fruits according to their intentions;
they fully understand all phenomena in accordance with reality, and manifest spiritual powers throughout the ten directions.
From the first making offerings to the Buddhas with a mind of gentleness and patience, entering deep meditative concentration to contemplate the nature of phenomena,
universally exhorting sentient beings to resolve upon the Way— by these means, one swiftly accomplishes the unsurpassed fruit.
Seeking the Dharma throughout the ten directions with undifferentiated intent, they cultivate merit until it is fully perfected;
having utterly eliminated both existence and non-existence, such a person is one who truly sees the Buddha.
Universally proceeding to all lands throughout the ten directions, Extensively expounding the sublime Dharma to bring forth benefit and merit,
Abiding immovably in the limit of reality— The merit of such a person is equal to that of a Buddha.
The sublime wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata is entirely composed of the factors of enlightenment;
if one can awaken to the nature of phenomena upon hearing it, such a person constantly beholds the Buddha.
One does not see the Ten Powers as empty and like an illusion; though one sees them, it is not seeing, like a blind man looking.
By discriminating and grasping at signs, one does not see the Buddha; only by ultimately abandoning all attachment can one truly see.
Sentient beings differ according to their various karmas; Throughout the ten directions, both within and without, they are difficult to see exhaustively.
The Buddha-body is unimpeded and pervades the ten directions; That it cannot be seen exhaustively is likewise so.
Just as immeasurable lands in space, Neither coming nor going, pervade the ten directions, Arising, abiding,
and perishing without dependence, So too does the Buddha pervade all of space.
Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Buddhabhadra, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
The nature of the mind is one.
How is it that various distinctions are perceived? Namely:
Rebirth in the happy realms or the miserable realms;
the completeness or deficiency of the sense faculties;
and the similarity or difference of the mode of birth.
The handsome and the ugly;
suffering and pleasure are distinct;
karma does not know the mind, and the mind does not know karma.
Feeling does not know retribution, and retribution does not know feeling;
the mind does not know feeling, and feeling does not know the mind;
the cause does not know the condition, and the condition does not know the cause.
"Wisdom does not know the object, and the object does not know wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Awakening Head (Jue-shou) replied in verse:
"You now ask about this meaning / To bring enlightenment to the ignorant masses."
I shall answer according to their true nature; may you, O Benevolent One, listen with careful attention.
All phenomena are devoid of activity and possess no intrinsic essence;
therefore, they are all entirely unaware of one another.
Just as the waters in a river, Rushing and competing in their swift current,
Each unaware of the others, So too are all phenomena.
Also like a great mass of fire, Whose fierce flames break out simultaneously.
Each is unaware of the other; so too are all phenomena.
Again, like a long wind that arises and encounters objects to fan them all, each is unaware of the other; so too are all phenomena.
Furthermore, just as the various elements of earth Abide by depending on one another in succession,
Yet each is unaware of the others, So too are all phenomena. The eyes, ears, nose,
tongue, body, And the mind— the various faculties of perception— Are likewise.
By this, there is constant transmigration, yet there is no one who transmigrates.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally unborn, yet it manifests as being born;
herein there is no one who manifests, nor is there any object manifested.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties— All are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature;
they exist only through the conceptualization of the deluded mind.
When observed according to reality, all are found to be without intrinsic nature.
The Dharma-eye is inconceivable; this vision is not inverted.
Whether real or unreal, whether false or non-false, mundane or supramundane—all are merely provisional designations.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Vasumitra:
"O Son of the Buddha!
All sentient beings are not sentient beings."

How does the Tathāgata, according to their time, their lifespan, their bodies, their conduct, their understanding, their speech, their inclinations, their skillful means, their reflections, and their observations, manifest his body among such sentient beings to teach and discipline them?
Then, the Bodhisattva Wealth Chief replied in verse:
"This is the realm of those who delight in quiescence and possess great learning;
I shall proclaim it for you, so you should now listen and receive it."
Contemplate the internal body analytically: "Who herein is the self?
If one can understand in this way, they will realize the existence or non-existence of the self.
This body is a provisional designation; its dwelling place has no fixed location.
One who thoroughly understands this body has no attachment within it.
By skillfully observing the body, one clearly perceives all things;
knowing that all phenomena are empty and false, one does not give rise to the mind of conceptual discrimination.
By whom is life-span caused to arise, and by whom does it subsequently decline and cease?
Like a whirling firebrand, its beginning and end cannot be known.
The wise are able to observe that all existence is impermanent.
All phenomena are empty and without self, forever free from all marks.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī:

The Buddha has taught that there is no creator;

Just as the nature of the earth is one, yet sentient beings each dwell upon it separately,

Water has no various distinctions; the Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise.
Just as the nature of wind is one, capable of blowing upon all things, yet the wind has no thought of oneness or difference—the Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise.
Just as a great cloud and thunder Rain everywhere upon all lands,

Also like the single element of earth, Which can produce various kinds of sprouts.
The earth has no distinctions; such is the nature of all Buddhas’ teachings.

Like the Great Brahmā King, he manifests throughout the three thousandfold world system.
"Their bodies have no distinction; such is the nature of all Buddhas.

Just as a tiny spark is quickly extinguished by damp firewood,

Without practicing the Dharma, even great learning is just like that.

it is as if a blind man were painting various images; he shows them to others but cannot see them himself.
One who does not practice the Dharma, though they have heard much, is just like this.

so too is one who hears much but does not practice the Dharma.
Like one standing at a crossroads who speaks extensively of many fine things, [yet remains there].

Within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is the foremost.

throughout the past and future ages, and among all the Teachers of the present,

It is like first establishing a foundation and thereafter constructing a palace.
Generosity and ethical discipline are likewise the foundation of all the practices of a bodhisattva.
Just as one constructs city walls to protect the multitude of people,
so too are patience and diligence used to guard and protect all bodhisattvas.
Just as a powerful king is venerated by all the land,
so too are concentration and wisdom that upon which bodhisattvas rely.
And just as a wheel-turning monarch is able to bestow all happiness, [so too are concentration and wisdom].
"The four immeasurables are likewise; they grant joy to all bodhisattvas.

there are differences in the world-systems, the realms of sentient beings, the teaching and its discipline, the lifespan, the radiance, the supernormal powers, the assemblies, the pedagogical methods, and the duration of the Dharma.

All those who are unimpeded, follow the One Path to transcend birth and death.
The bodies of all Buddhas are but the single Dharma-body;
they share one mind and one wisdom, and likewise their powers and fearlessnesses.

may such buddha-fields be attained, along with their assemblies and the preaching of the Dharma.
May all the buddha-fields be perfectly adorned and complete in every way.
According to the differing conduct of sentient beings, their visions likewise differ.

such dharmas of the Buddhas cannot be seen by sentient beings.
With minds already purified and all vows fully accomplished,
such persons of clear realization are able to behold it here.

It is solely according to the minds of sentient beings that such differences in vision appear.

it is not the fault of all the Tathāgatas, the Great Sages.
It is according to those who are to be transformed within all the worlds.
"One constantly beholds the Hero among Men; such is the Dharma of all Buddhas.

What is the teaching of the Buddha’s realm?
What is the knowledge of the Buddha’s realm?

even if one were to proclaim them for billions of eons, they could never be fully exhausted.
According to their minds and wisdom, they guide and inspire them all to benefit;
thus do they deliver sentient beings—this is the realm of the Buddhas.
All the various lands in the world, they enter into them all accordingly.
The body of wisdom has no form; it cannot be seen by them.

such is the realm of insight, equal and vast as space.
The realm of phenomena and the realm of sentient beings, Ultimately without distinction, To fully comprehend them all—

The Buddha’s wisdom comprehends all things accordingly, yet remains free from discrimination.

Neither karma nor afflictions, Without substance and without abode,

Chapter Eleven: On Pure Conduct.

may all beings find delight in the Dharma and realize that such entertainments are not real.
When in palaces and mansions, may all beings...
Entering the sacred ground, may they forever eliminate defiled desires.
When putting on necklaces and ornaments, they should wish that all sentient beings cast off all artificial adornments and reach the realm of ultimate reality.
Ascending the multi-storied pavilion, may all sentient beings ascend the tower of the True Dharma and see all things clearly.
If there is anything given in charity, may all sentient beings:
Able to relinquish all things, with a mind free from attachment;
when gathered in a great assembly, may all beings:
relinquish the phenomena of congregating and achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
If encountering hardship and distress, one should wish that all beings may attain mastery according to their will, so that their actions are unimpeded.
When leaving the household life, one should wish that all beings:
Leaving the household life without hindrance, may the mind attain liberation.
Upon entering a saṃghārāma, one should wish that all sentient beings may expound various teachings free from discord and contention.
When approaching teachers, great and small,
may all beings skillfully serve their elders and superiors, practicing and cultivating wholesome dharmas.
When requesting permission to leave the household life, may all beings:
Having attained the dharma of non-retrogression, their minds are free from obstruction.
Upon casting off their secular robes, they should wish that all sentient beings:
diligently cultivate roots of goodness and abandon all burdens of transgression.
When shaving off hair and beard, one should wish that all sentient beings:
forever leave afflictions behind and ultimately attain tranquil extinction.
When donning the kāṣāya robe, one should wish that all sentient beings:
With a mind free from defilement, one is endowed with the Great Sage’s Way.
At the time of right renunciation, one should wish that all sentient beings:
renounce the world together with the Buddha, to rescue and protect all.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all beings perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and resolve upon the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all beings...
Entering deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom is like the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, they should wish that all sentient beings preside over great assemblies, free from all hindrances.
When receiving the precepts for training, one should wish that all beings:
skillfully learn the precepts and commit no evil.
When receiving the instructions of the ācārya, one should wish that all beings:
Perfecting in dignified deportment, their conduct is true and real.
Receiving the instructions of the preceptor, they should wish that all beings enter the wisdom of non-arising and reach the state of no dependence.
Upon receiving full ordination, one should wish that all beings be endowed with all skillful means and attain the most supreme Dharma.
When entering a hall or building, one should wish that all beings:
Ascending the Unsurpassed Hall, dwelling in immovable stability.
When arranging a seat, may all sentient beings cause the wholesome dharmas to blossom and perceive the true mark of reality.
Sitting upright with body straight, one should wish that all beings sit upon the seat of enlightenment with minds free from attachment.
Sitting in the full lotus posture, one should wish that all beings...
With roots of goodness firm and stable, one attains the Immovable Ground.
Practicing meditative concentration, one should wish that all sentient beings subdue their minds through concentration until nothing remains.
When practicing contemplation, one should wish that all beings perceive reality as it is and never engage in discord or strife.
When relinquishing the full-lotus posture, one should wish that all beings:
Contemplating all conditioned phenomena, which all return to dispersal and extinction;
when placing the foot down and coming to rest,
may all sentient beings attain liberation of mind and dwell in unshakable stability.
When lifting the foot, one should wish that all beings emerge from the sea of birth and death and be endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
When putting on the lower garment, one should wish that all beings:
Wearing all roots of goodness and being fully endowed with shame and remorse, they adjust their robes and fasten their belts; at that time, they should wish for all sentient beings:
may they restrain and gather their roots of goodness so as not to let them be lost or scattered.
When putting on the upper robe, one should wish that all sentient beings attain supreme roots of goodness and reach the further shore of the Dharma.
When putting on the saṃghāṭī, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Entering the first stage, one attains the state of immovability.
Holding a willow branch in hand, one should wish that all sentient beings may attain the sublime Dharma and achieve ultimate purity.
When chewing on a tooth-stick, one should wish that all sentient beings:
may their minds be harmonious and pure, and may they devour all afflictions.
When defecating or urinating, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminating sinful states;
having finished one's business, one approaches the water.
May all sentient beings swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma.
When washing away physical impurities, one should wish that all sentient beings be pure,
harmonious, and ultimately free from defilement.
When rinsing the hands with water, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Having obtained clean hands, one receives and upholds the Buddha-dharma.
Washing the face with water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the pure Dharma-gate and be forever free from defilement.
Holding the mendicant’s staff, one should wish that all beings:
establish great assemblies of giving and reveal the path of reality.
Holding the alms bowl, one should wish that all beings:
Having become a vessel of the Dharma, receiving the offerings of devas and humans;
setting out toward the Way, one should wish that all beings:
follow the conduct of the Buddhas and enter the state of non-reliance.
If one is on the road, one should wish that all beings:
be able to practice the Buddha-way and turn toward the Dharma of no-remainder.
When traveling along the path, one should wish that all beings:
Treading upon the pure Dharma-realm, the mind is free from obstruction.
Seeing the path ascending to heights, one should wish that all beings forever transcend the three realms, their minds free from timidity or weakness.
Seeing a downward path, one should wish that all beings:
with minds humble and lowly, may they ever increase the Buddha’s roots of goodness.
Seeing a crooked and winding path, one should wish that all beings:
Abandoning the wrong path and forever eliminating evil views,
if one sees the direct road, one should wish that all sentient beings have upright minds, free from flattery and deception.
Seeing a road with much dust, one should wish that all beings:
remain far removed from defilement and attain the pure Dharma.
Seeing a road free of dust, one should wish that all beings:
Constantly practicing great compassion, their minds are moist and supple.
If they see a perilous path, they should wish that all beings:
dwell within the realm of the True Dharma and be free from all calamities and transgressions.
If one sees a gathering of people, one should wish that all sentient beings may preach the most profound Dharma and be in complete harmony.
If one sees a great pillar, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Free from the mind of contention, without anger or resentment;
if seeing a grove, one should wish that all beings be honored and paid homage by gods and humans alike.
If one sees a high mountain, one should wish that sentient beings:
may their roots of goodness surpass all others, such that none can reach their summit.
If one sees a thorny tree, one should wish that sentient beings:
May they swiftly cut away the thorns of the three poisons.
Seeing the lush foliage of the tree, may all sentient beings wish:
through meditative concentration and liberation, to provide shade and protection.
If one sees flowers blooming, one should wish that all sentient beings:
may their supernormal powers and other dharmas be like these blossoming flowers.
If one sees tree blossoms, one should wish that all sentient beings:
The various marks are like flowers, complete with the thirty-two [major characteristics].
Upon seeing the fruit, one should wish that all sentient beings:
obtain the most supreme Dharma and realize the path to Bodhi.
If one sees a great river, one should wish that all beings:
enter the stream of the Dharma and plunge into the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
If one sees a marsh or a pond, one should wish that all beings:
May they swiftly awaken to the single-flavored Dharma of all Buddhas.
Upon seeing a pond, they should wish that all sentient beings:
may their verbal karma be perfected, skillfully able to expound the teachings.
If one sees someone drawing water from a well, one should wish that all sentient beings be endowed with eloquence to expound all dharmas.
If one sees a spring gushing forth, one should wish that all sentient beings...
May skillful means increase, and may roots of goodness be inexhaustible.
If one sees a bridge or a path, one should wish that all sentient beings may extensively deliver all others, just like a bridge.
If one sees flowing water, one should wish that all sentient beings attain noble intentions and wash away the defilements of delusion.
If one sees the cultivation of gardens and orchards, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Within the garden of the five desires, one must weed out the grass of craving.
Seeing the Forest of No-Sorrow, one should wish that all sentient beings forever leave behind greed and attachment, and give rise to no sorrow or fear.
If they see a garden or grove, they should wish that all beings diligently cultivate all practices and proceed toward the Bodhi of the Buddha.
If they see a person adorned with ornaments, they should wish that all beings:
With the thirty-two marks as his adornment,
yet appearing without any ornamentation, he should wish that all beings:
abandon all finery and ornaments, and fully accomplish the dhūta practices.
Seeing those who delight in and are attached to worldly pleasures, one should wish that all beings:
may find joy in the Dharma themselves, and cherish it without ever forsaking it.
Seeing those who have no such delight or attachment, one should wish that all beings:
Amidst conditioned phenomena, the mind finds no delight.
Seeing those who rejoice, one should wish for all sentient beings:
that they may always attain peace and happiness, and joyfully make offerings to the Buddha.
Seeing those afflicted by suffering, one should wish that all beings attain fundamental wisdom and extinguish all forms of misery.
Seeing those who are not ill, one should wish that all beings:
Entering true wisdom, one is forever free from illness and affliction.
Upon seeing those who are diseased, one should wish that all beings realize the body is empty and quiescent,
and remain free from the dharma of discord and strife.
Seeing a person of handsome appearance, one should wish that all beings:
may they always give rise to pure faith in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Seeing a person of ugly appearance, one should wish that all beings:
Regarding unwholesome matters, do not give rise to attachment or delight.
Upon seeing one who returns kindness, one should wish for all sentient beings:
that they may recognize the grace and virtue of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Upon seeing one who has betrayed their kindness,
one should wish that all beings do not retaliate against those who are evil.
If one sees a śramaṇa, one should wish that all beings:
Tranquil and serene, ultimately supreme;
seeing a Brahmin, one should wish that all beings forever maintain pure conduct and remain free from all evil.
Seeing one who practices asceticism,
may all beings rely upon ascetic practice and reach the ultimate state.
Seeing one who practices self-restraint, may all beings...
Firmly maintaining their vows and conduct, they do not abandon the Buddha-way.
Seeing those clad in armor, one should wish that all beings always wear the armor of goodness and advance toward the teacherless Dharma.
Seeing those without armor or weapons, one should wish that all beings forever leave behind all unwholesome karma.
Seeing those engaged in debate, one should wish that all beings:
Regarding all heterodox doctrines, he is able to utterly subdue them.
Upon seeing one who lives by right livelihood, he should wish for all sentient beings:
May they obtain a pure livelihood and refrain from feigning dignified deportment.
If one sees a king, one should wish that all beings:
become Dharma-kings and constantly turn the True Dharma.
If one sees a prince, one should wish that all beings:
Born through transformation from the Dharma, they become children of the Buddha.
Upon seeing an elder, they should wish that all beings may skillfully discern and judge, and never practice unwholesome dharmas.
If you see a great minister, you should wish that all beings:
always maintain right mindfulness and practice all manner of goodness.
If you see a city wall, you should wish that all beings:
May they attain a firm and solid body, with a mind that never yields.
If they see a royal capital, they should wish that all sentient beings may gather their merits together, and that their minds be ever joyful.
When seeing forests and thickets, one should wish that all beings:
be praised and looked up to by devas and humans.
When entering a village to beg for food, one should wish that all beings:
Entering the profound realm of phenomena, with a mind free from obstruction;
entering the gates of others' homes, may all beings wish:
to enter the gates of all the Buddha-dharma.
Having entered their home, they should wish that all beings enter the Buddha-vehicle and attain equality throughout the three periods of time.
Upon seeing those who do not abandon others, they should wish that all beings:
May they never abandon the dharmas of supreme merit.
Seeing those who are able to renounce, may all beings forever attain liberation from the sufferings of the three evil realms.
If one sees an empty bowl, one should wish that all beings have pure minds, empty and free from afflictions.
If one sees a full bowl, one should wish that all beings:
Fully accomplishing and perfecting all wholesome dharmas;
if one receives honor and respect, one should wish that all sentient beings respectfully practice all Buddha-dharmas.
When encountering those who do not show respect, one should wish that all sentient beings do not practice any unwholesome dharmas.
When seeing those who feel shame and modesty, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Possessing the practice of shame and modesty, they conceal and protect their sense faculties.
Upon seeing those who lack shame and modesty, they should wish that all beings:
abandon shamelessness and abide in the path of great compassion.
If one obtains fine food, one should wish that all sentient beings:
have their aspirations fulfilled, and their minds be free from covetous desire.
If one obtains coarse food, one should wish that all sentient beings:
There is none who does not obtain the flavor of all samādhis.
Having obtained this soft food, they should wish that all sentient beings be permeated by great compassion, so that their minds and intentions become supple.
When obtaining coarse and astringent food,
one should wish that all beings have minds free from attachment and sever worldly craving and love.
When eating a meal, one should wish that all beings:
Taking the joy of dhyāna as food, filled with the delight of the Dharma:
when receiving its flavor, may all sentient beings attain the supreme flavor of the Buddha and be fully satisfied by the nectar of immortality.
When the meal is finished, may all sentient beings accomplish all that they have to do and be endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
When preaching the Dharma, may all sentient beings:
Attaining inexhaustible eloquence, they widely proclaim the essentials of the Dharma.
When departing from their homes, they should wish that all sentient beings:
enter deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom and forever transcend the triple world.
When entering the water, may all beings enter into omniscience and know the equality of the three periods of time.
When bathing the body, may all beings:
Body and mind are free from defilement, radiant and pure within and without.
Amidst the scorching heat and toxic vapors of the intense summer,
may all sentient beings abandon all afflictions until they are entirely exhausted.
When the heat has subsided and the coolness first arrives,
may all sentient beings realize the unsurpassed Dharma and attain ultimate, refreshing purity.
When reciting the sutras, may all sentient beings:
In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, may they uphold this dhāraṇī without forgetting it.
If they should behold the Buddha, they should make this vow for all sentient beings:
"May they attain unobstructed eyes and see all Buddhas."
When contemplating the Buddha, may all sentient beings be as Samantabhadra, upright and magnificent.
When seeing a stupa of the Buddha, may all sentient beings:
Revering it as a stūpa, receiving offerings from devas and humans;
observing the stūpa with a respectful mind, one should wish that all sentient beings be gazed upon by both devas and humans.
Prostrating before the stūpa, one should wish that all sentient beings:
among all devas and humans, none shall be able to see their crown.
Circumambulating the stūpa to the right, one should wish that all sentient beings:
Their conduct is without opposition, and they achieve all-encompassing wisdom.
Circumambulating the stupa three times, they should wish that all sentient beings diligently seek the Buddha-way with minds free from weariness.
In praising the Buddha’s merit, may all beings be fully endowed with all virtues, their praises never-ending.
In praising the Buddha’s marks and signs, may all beings...
Accomplishing the Buddha-body and realizing the signless Dharma.
When washing the feet, one should wish that all beings possess the power of the divine feet, so that their actions are unimpeded.
When resting and sleeping at the proper time,
may all beings attain peace and stability of body, and have minds free from agitation and confusion.
Upon first awakening from sleep, may all beings:
The awakening of all-knowledge surveys the ten directions.
"O Son of the Buddha!
If bodhisattvas employ their minds in this way, they will attain all supreme and wondrous merits."
It cannot be shaken by any in all the worlds—gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth—nor by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

12. The Chapter on Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha) At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had finished expounding the great merit of the pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion, he wished to reveal the merit of the bodhicitta. Thus, he addressed Bhadramukha Bodhisattva in verse, saying:
"I have now, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, Expounded the pure conduct practiced by the Buddha in the past;
You, too, should within this assembly Proclaim the supreme merit of his practice."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied in verse:
“Excellent! O virtuous one, you should listen attentively. Those various merits are immeasurable;
I shall now describe a small portion according to my ability, just like a single drop of water from the great ocean.”
If there is a bodhisattva who first resolves their mind, Vowing to seek the realization of Buddha-enlightenment,
Their merit shall be boundless, Incalculable and beyond compare.
How much more so for those who, throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, have fully cultivated all the virtues of the stages and the perfections;
even if all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions were to praise them together, they could not exhaustively describe them.
Such are his boundless great merits; I now describe but a small fraction of them, like the space traversed by a bird's feet, or like a single mote of dust upon the great earth.
When a bodhisattva resolves to seek awakening, it is not without cause and without conditions;
by generating pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, they give rise to this vast and great mind.
Seeking neither the five desires nor royal sovereignty, nor wealth, nor personal pleasure, nor great renown,
but solely for the sake of forever extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings and benefiting the world, they resolve their minds [upon awakening].
Constantly desiring to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings, Adorning buddha-fields and making offerings to the Buddhas,
Upholding the True Dharma and cultivating all forms of wisdom, They resolve their minds for the sake of realizing Bodhi.
With a profound mind of faith and understanding ever pure, They revere and honor all Buddhas;
Toward the Dharma and the Sangha they act likewise, Making offerings with utmost sincerity as they resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
With deep faith in the Buddha and the Buddha’s Dharma, and likewise faith in the path practiced by the sons of the Buddha,
as well as faith in unsurpassed, great Bodhi— by these means, a bodhisattva first arouses the mind.
Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of all merit;
it nurtures all wholesome dharmas, cuts through the net of doubt, and leads one out of the stream of craving, revealing the unsurpassed path to Nirvana.
Faith is a mind free from defilement and pure; it eradicates arrogance and is the root of reverence.
It is also the foremost treasure within the Dharma-treasury, serving as the pure hand that receives all practices.
Faith enables one to practice giving with a heart free from stinginess; Faith enables one to enter the Buddha-dharma with joy;
Faith enables the growth of wisdom and merit; Faith enables one to surely reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Faith causes all the faculties to be pure, bright, and sharp; The power of faith is firm and indestructible;
Faith can forever extinguish the root of afflictions; Faith can single-mindedly direct one toward the Buddha’s merits.
Faith is unattached to sense objects; it distances one from all perils and brings about the attainment of the state beyond peril.
Faith enables one to transcend the paths of all Māras, manifesting the unsurpassed path of liberation.
Faith is the indestructible seed of merit; faith can grow the tree of Bodhi;
faith can increase the most supreme wisdom; faith can manifest all Buddhas.
Therefore, following the sequence of practice, it is said that faith and delight are most excellent and extremely difficult to find;
they are like a wondrous wish-fulfilling jewel existing within the entire world.
If one constantly places faith in all Buddhas, one will be able to uphold the precepts and cultivate the points of training;
if one constantly upholds the precepts and cultivates the points of training, one will be able to be fully endowed with all meritorious virtues.
Precepts can develop the root of bodhi; training is the ground for diligently cultivating merit.
Those who always act in accordance with the precepts and training are praised by all Tathāgatas.
If one constantly places faith in all Buddhas, one will be able to assemble great offerings;
if one can assemble great offerings, that person’s faith in the Buddha is inconceivable.
If one constantly places faith in the Honored Dharma, then one will never grow weary of hearing the Buddha’s teachings;
if one never grows weary of hearing the Buddha’s teachings, that person’s faith in the Dharma is inconceivable.
If one always reveres and places faith in the pure Sangha, one will attain a confidence that does not regress;
having attained such non-regressive confidence, the power of that person’s faith cannot be shaken.
If one attains the power of faith that cannot be shaken, then one will attain the purity, clarity, and sharpness of the faculties;
if one attains the purity, clarity, and sharpness of the faculties, then one will be able to distance oneself from evil associates.
If one can distance oneself from evil associates, one will gain proximity to virtuous friends;
if one gains proximity to virtuous friends, one will be able to cultivate and accumulate vast goodness.
If one can cultivate and accumulate vast goodness, that person will achieve the power of great causes;
if a person achieves the power of great causes, they will attain supreme and certain understanding.
If one attains a sublime and resolute understanding, one will be protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
if one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas, one will be able to give rise to the bodhicitta.
If one can give rise to the bodhicitta, Then one can diligently cultivate the Buddha’s virtues;
If one can diligently cultivate the Buddha’s virtues, Then one will be born into the family of the Tathāgata.
If one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, Then one skillfully practices expedient means;
If one skillfully practices expedient means, Then one attains pure faith and joy.
If one attains a mind of faith and joy that is pure, then one attains the superior and most excellent mind;
if one attains the superior and most excellent mind, then one constantly cultivates the pāramitās.
If one constantly cultivates the pāramitās, one will be able to fulfill the Mahāyāna;
if one can fulfill the Mahāyāna, one will be able to make offerings to the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma.
If one can make offerings to the Buddha according to the Dharma, then the mind that recollects the Buddha will remain unmoving;
if the mind that recollects the Buddha remains unmoving, then one will constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas.
If one constantly beholds immeasurable Buddhas, then one sees that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding;
if one sees that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding, then one can know that the Dharma is forever indestructible.
If one can know that phenomena are forever imperishable, Then one will attain unimpeded eloquence;
If one attains unimpeded eloquence, Then one can expound the boundless Dharma.
If one can expound the boundless Dharma, then one can compassionately deliver sentient beings;
if one can compassionately deliver sentient beings, then one attains a firm and steadfast heart of great compassion.
If one attains a firm and resolute mind of great compassion, one will be able to delight in the most profound Dharma;
if one can delight in the most profound Dharma, one will be able to abandon the faults of conditioned existence.
If one can abandon the faults of the conditioned, then one will be free from arrogance and heedlessness;
if one is free from arrogance and heedlessness, then one can benefit all beings both for oneself and others.
If one can benefit all sentient beings simultaneously, then one will dwell in birth and death without weariness;
if one dwells in birth and death without weariness, then one will be courageous and invincible.
If one is courageous and invincible, then one can give rise to great supernormal powers;
if one can give rise to great supernormal powers, then one knows the conduct of all sentient beings.
If one knows the conduct of all sentient beings, one can bring all beings to fulfillment;
if one can bring all beings to fulfillment, one attains the wisdom that skillfully gathers sentient beings.
If one attains the wisdom that skillfully gathers sentient beings, Then one can accomplish the four methods of attraction;
If one can accomplish the four methods of attraction, Then one brings infinite benefit to sentient beings.
If one bestows infinite benefit upon sentient beings, Then one possesses the most supreme wisdom and skillful means;
If one possesses the most supreme wisdom and skillful means, Then one abides in the courageous, unsurpassed path.
If one abides in the courageous, unsurpassed path, one can utterly destroy all demonic powers;
if one can utterly destroy all demonic powers, one can transcend the realms of the four Māras.
If one can transcend the realms of the four māras, then one shall reach the stage of non-retrogression;
if one reaches the stage of non-retrogression, then one shall attain the profound dharma-patience of non-arising.
If one attains the profound dharma-patience of non-arising, one will receive the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas;
if one receives the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas, then all Buddhas will appear before one.
If all Buddhas appear before one, then one will understand the profound and secret functions of supernormal powers;
if one understands the profound and secret functions of supernormal powers, then one will be remembered by all Buddhas.
If one is remembered by all Buddhas, one will then adorn oneself with the virtues of a Buddha;
if one adorns oneself with the virtues of a Buddha, one will obtain a body of sublime merit and dignified majesty.
If one attains a wondrous merit and a dignified body, then that body will radiate brilliance like a mountain of gold;
if the body radiates brilliance like a mountain of gold, then it will be adorned with the thirty-two marks.
If one is adorned with the thirty-two marks, then one is further embellished by the secondary characteristics;
if one is embellished by the secondary characteristics, then the radiance of one’s body is immeasurable.
If the radiance of the body is immeasurable, then it is adorned with inconceivable light;
if it is adorned with inconceivable light, then from that light emerge various lotus flowers.
When light issues forth from those lotus flowers, immeasurable Buddhas sit upon them;
manifesting throughout the ten directions without exception, they are able to tame and transform all sentient beings.
If one can thus discipline sentient beings, Then one manifests immeasurable supernormal powers.
If one manifests immeasurable supernormal powers, Then one dwells in inconceivable lands,
Expounding inconceivable teachings, Causing inconceivable multitudes to rejoice.
If one preaches the inconceivable Dharma, causing the inconceivable multitude to rejoice,
then by the power of wisdom and eloquence, one transforms and guides them according to the minds of sentient beings.
If, by the power of wisdom and eloquence, one transforms and guides according to the minds of sentient beings,
then taking wisdom as the precursor, the actions of body, speech, and mind will never falter.
If one takes wisdom as the precursor, such that the actions of body, speech, and mind are ever without fault,
then the power of one's vows will attain mastery, manifesting bodies everywhere in accordance with the various realms of existence.
If the power of one's vows attains mastery, manifesting bodies throughout all realms of existence according to their needs,
then when preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes, the sounds will accord with each type in ways that are inconceivable.
When they are able to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, their voices adapt to each type in ways inconceivable;
thus, within a single thought-moment, they fully know the minds of all sentient beings without exception.
If one can, in a single thought-moment, fully know the minds of all sentient beings without exception,
then one will know that afflictions do not arise, and shall never again sink into the cycle of birth and death.
If one knows that afflictions do not arise, one will never sink into the cycle of birth and death;
then, having attained the body of the dharma-nature endowed with merit, one manifests in the world through the power of the Dharma.
If one attains the body of the Dharma-nature of merit, And manifests in the world through the power of the Dharma,
Then one attains the ten stages and the ten masteries, Practicing the perfections and supreme liberation.
If one attains the ten stages and the ten masteries, and practices the supreme liberations of the various perfections,
then one obtains the great supernormal powers of consecration and abides in the most excellent samādhis.
If one attains the great supernormal powers of empowerment and abides in the most excellent samādhis,
then before all the Buddhas of the ten directions, one shall receive empowerment and ascend to the rank of Buddhahood.
If one is to receive empowerment and ascend to the rank of a Buddha among the Buddhas of the ten directions,
then all the Buddhas of the ten directions shall, with their own hands, sprinkle the nectar of immortality upon one’s crown.
If one is graced by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, who pour the nectar of immortality upon the crown of one's head,
then the body will pervade everywhere like space, abiding immovably and filling the ten directions.
If his body pervades everywhere like space, Abiding immovably and filling the ten directions, Then his conduct is beyond compare; Neither gods nor people of the world can know it.
The Bodhisattva diligently cultivates the practice of great compassion; His vow to deliver all beings shall surely bear fruit.
Whether they see, hear, or receive his teachings, or offer him worship, There are none among them who do not attain peace and happiness.
By the majestic spiritual power of those great beings, their Dharma-eye is ever whole and without deficiency;
they cause all paths, such as the ten virtuous actions, and all supreme, unsurpassed jewels to manifest.
Just as the great ocean, a mass of vajras, produces various jewels through its majestic power—
neither decreasing, nor increasing, nor ever exhausted— so too is the mass of merit of a bodhisattva.
In some lands where there is no Buddha, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
in some realms where the Dharma is unknown, he proclaims for them the treasury of the sublime Dharma.
Free from conceptual discrimination and effortless, In a single moment, they pervade the ten directions;
Like the moonlight’s reflection reaching everywhere, They transform all living beings through immeasurable skillful means.
Throughout those worlds of the ten directions, in every thought-moment he manifests the attainment of the Buddha-way,
turns the wheel of the true Dharma, enters into nirvana, and even widely distributes his relics.
Sometimes manifesting the paths of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, Or manifesting the universal adornment of attaining buddhahood,
Thus expounding the teachings of the three vehicles, Universally delivering sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Sometimes manifesting in the forms of boys or girls, or as devas, nāgas, and asuras,
even down to mahoragas and others— he causes all to see him according to their respective inclinations.
The forms and appearances of sentient beings are each different, and their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable;
that all such things can be manifested is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi.
They purify inconceivable buddha-fields, making offerings to all Tathāgatas;
they radiate boundless great light, delivering and liberating sentient beings without limit.
Mastery of wisdom is inconceivable; in preaching the Dharma, his speech is unimpeded.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, as well as wisdom, skillful means, and the supernormal powers—[all these he possesses].
All these are sovereign through the power of the Buddha’s Flower Adornment Samādhi;
entering samādhi within a single atom, they accomplish the meditative concentrations of all atoms,
yet that atom does not increase, as they universally manifest inconceivable lands therein.
Within a single atom are many lands; some have Buddhas, some are without Buddhas;
some are defiled, some are pure; some are vast, some are narrow;
some are in the process of formation, some are in the process of destruction; some stand upright, some stand sideways.
Sometimes like a mirage in a vast wilderness during the heat of the day, sometimes like Indra’s net in the heavens;
as it is manifested within a single atom, so it is in every atom without exception.
These sages of great renown, through the power of their samādhi, liberation, and supernormal faculties,
if they wish to make offerings to all Buddhas, enter into samādhi and manifest miraculous transformations;
with a single hand they pervade the trichiliocosm, universally making offerings to all Tathāgatas.
All the most excellent and wondrous flowers, unguents, powdered incense, and priceless jewels throughout the ten directions—
all these emerge from their hands, as offerings to the Most Victorious Ones beneath the Bodhi tree.
Priceless precious robes mixed with exquisite incense, Jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies, all magnificent and fine;
Flowers of pure gold and curtains of jewels— All of these rain down from within his palms.
Whatever exquisite objects exist throughout the ten directions, all worthy of being offered to the Unsurpassed Honored One—
may they rain down from his palms in full abundance, as he makes offerings before the Bodhi tree.
All manner of musical instruments throughout the ten directions— bells, drums, lutes, and harps of every kind—
all produce harmonious, elegant, and wondrous sounds, none of which fail to emerge from within his palms.
All the hymns of praise existing throughout the ten directions, extolling the Tathāgata’s true merits—
such various and wondrous words as these are all manifested and proclaimed from within his palms.

The Bodhisattva releases pure light from his right hand; From within that light, fragrant water rains down from the sky, Universally sprinkling all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, As an offering to all the Lamps that Illuminate the World.
Again, he emits a light of wondrous adornment, Which gives birth to immeasurable jewel lotuses;
The colors and forms of these flowers are all exquisite, And with them he makes offerings to all Buddhas.
Again, they emit a light adorned with flowers, A canopy formed by gathering various wondrous blossoms;
They scatter them everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, As an offering to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, they emit a light adorned with fragrance, With various exquisite scents gathered into canopies;
They scatter them everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, As an offering to all the Honored Ones of Great Virtue.

Again, they emit a light of exquisite powdered incense; Various kinds of powdered incense gather to form canopies, Scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, As an offering to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, he emits a light called "Adorned with Garments," Which gathers various famous robes to form canopies;
These are scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions As an offering to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, they emit light adorned with jewels, forming canopies composed of various exquisite gems;
these are scattered throughout all lands in the ten directions as an offering to all Honored Ones of Great Virtue.
Again, he emits a light adorned with lotuses, With various lotus flowers gathered into canopies,
Scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, As an offering to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones.

Again, they emit a light adorned with necklaces; various exquisite necklaces gather to form canopies, which are scattered throughout all lands in the ten directions as an offering to all the Great Virtuous Honored Ones.
Again, he emits the light called "Banner Adornment," Its banners brilliant and radiant, complete with every color;
