Diverse and immeasurable, all exquisitely beautiful, With which he adorns all Buddha-lands.
Canopies adorned with various kinds of miscellaneous jewels, With many exquisite silk banners hanging together as ornaments;
Maṇi-jewel bells proclaiming the Buddha’s voice— Holding these up, they make offerings to all Tathāgatas.

From his hands emerge inconceivable offering implements; thus he makes offerings to a single Guide, and does so likewise before all Buddhas— such is the power of the Great Being’s samādhi and supernormal faculties.
The Bodhisattva, dwelling within samādhi, Gathers in sentient beings through manifold masteries;
By means of all the dharmas of merit practiced, He guides and inspires them through immeasurable skillful means.
Either by the gate of making offerings to the Tathāgata, or by the gate of inconceivable generosity,
or by the gate of asceticism and upholding the precepts, or by the gate of immovable patience.
Some enter by the gate of ascetic diligence, some by the gate of tranquil meditative concentration,
some by the gate of definitive wisdom, and some by the gate of practiced skillful means.
Either through the gateway of Brahma-abodes and supernormal powers, or through the gateway of benefiting others by means of the four integrative methods,
or through the gateway of the adornments of merit and wisdom, or through the gateway of liberation via causes and conditions.
Some enter by way of the faculties, powers, and the path; some by way of the liberation of the śrāvakas;
some by way of the purity of the pratyekabuddhas; and some by way of the mastery of the Mahāyāna.
Either by way of impermanence and manifold suffering, or by way of non-self and the absence of a life-principle,
or by way of impurity and detachment from desire, or by way of the samādhi of cessation.
According to the differing illnesses of sentient beings, he treats them all with the medicine of the Dharma;
according to the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, he satisfies them all through skillful means;
according to the distinctions in the conduct of sentient beings, he brings them all to fulfillment through his expertise.
Such are the characteristics of this samādhi and its supernormal powers, which no devas or humans can fathom.
There is a wondrous samādhi called "Following Joy"; when Bodhisattvas abide in it, they observe all things universally.
They manifest according to what is appropriate to deliver sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice and be transformed by the Dharma.
During times of famine and calamity within the kalpa, they provide all the requisites for worldly happiness to the world;
fulfilling every desire according to what is wished for, they universally bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Whether it be food and drink of exquisite flavor, precious garments, ornaments, and various wonderful objects,
or even the throne of a king— he is able to relinquish them all, causing those who delight in giving to be completely transformed by his example.
Some adorn their bodies with the marks and signs of excellence, with exquisite garments and precious necklaces;
decorated with flower garlands and anointed with fragrant perfumes, they possess perfect dignified conduct as they deliver sentient beings.

Whatever is cherished and esteemed by all the world—be it physical form, countenance, or attire—he manifests universally according to what is appropriate to satisfy their hearts; even those who delight in sensual beauty are led thereby to the Way.
With the exquisite voice of the kalaviṅka bird and the wondrous sounds of the cuckoo and others,
possessing every kind of Brahma-voice, he preaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of their hearts.
The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates—by these all Buddhas deliver sentient beings;
they too, according to those various distinct dharmas, transform and deliver them as is appropriate for the world.
The suffering and joy, gain and loss, and all other phenomena enacted within the world of sentient beings—
He is able to manifest in accordance with them and participate in those very affairs, thereby universally delivering all living beings.
All the various sufferings and afflictions of the world are as deep, vast, and boundless as the great ocean;
yet one can endure them all while acting in concert with others, thereby bringing them benefit and peace.
If there are those who do not recognize the Dharma of renunciation, who do not seek liberation from worldly clamor and distraction,
the Bodhisattva manifests for them the abandonment of kingdom and wealth, always delighting in the tranquility of the mind through leaving the home life.

The household is a place bound by craving and attachment; desiring to cause all sentient beings to be entirely free from it, he demonstrates that leaving home leads to liberation, wherein one receives no part in any sensual pleasures.
The Bodhisattva manifests the practice of ten kinds of conduct, And also practices all the dharmas of great beings;
All the practices of the sages, without exception, Are undertaken for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings whose lifespans are immeasurable, whose afflictions are subtle, and who are fully endowed with pleasures,
the Bodhisattva attains mastery therein and manifests the experience of the various sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.
Some possess greed, hatred, and delusion, with the fierce fires of affliction constantly blazing;
for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests old age, sickness, and death, so that those sentient beings may all be tamed.
The Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessnesses, As well as the eighteen unique qualities—
All these immeasurable virtues he manifests To deliver all sentient beings.
Mind-reading, instruction, and supernormal powers— All these are the sovereign applications of the Tathāgata;
Those great beings manifest them all, Able to bring all sentient beings to complete subdual.
Through various skillful means, the Bodhisattvas accord with worldly dharmas to deliver sentient beings;
like a lotus flower that is unstained by water, they dwell in the world in this manner, causing others to have deep faith.
Of profound learning and vast talent, a king among those skilled in composition; his song, dance, and discourse are a joy to all.
Regarding all the various arts and crafts of the world, he manifests them all, like a master illusionist.
Sometimes he is a householder or a leader of a town; sometimes he is a guide for merchants and traders;
sometimes he is a king or a high minister; and sometimes he acts as a skilled physician well-versed in all treatises.
Sometimes appearing as great trees in the wilderness, sometimes becoming excellent medicines or treasuries of various jewels;
sometimes manifesting as wish-fulfilling gems according to what is sought, or showing the right path to sentient beings.
If he sees the world first coming into being, when sentient beings have not yet acquired the necessities for sustaining their bodies,
at that time the Bodhisattva acts as a craftsman and manifests various types of work for them.
He does not perform acts that harm living beings, but speaks only of matters that benefit the world;
regarding incantations, medicinal herbs, and all such treatises, he is able to expound upon them all.
The supreme practices of all the ṛṣis, which humans, devas, and other classes alike revere—
such difficult and ascetic dharmas, the Bodhisattva is able to perform them all as appropriate.
Some become renunciants of non-Buddhist paths, or dwell in mountain forests practicing self-mortification;
some go naked without clothing, acting as teachers and leaders among those multitudes.
Sometimes they manifest various modes of wrong livelihood, practicing unrighteousness as if it were supreme;
sometimes they manifest the various dignified demeanors of a brahmin, acting as the leader among that assembly.
Some undergo the practice of five fires while turning with the sun; some observe the precepts of oxen, dogs, or deer;
some wear tattered rags and serve the sacrificial fire—for the sake of transforming such as these, he acts as their guide.
Sometimes he visits the temples of various deities, and at other times he shows himself entering the waters of the Ganges;
he displays the practice of eating roots, fruits, and the like, while constantly contemplating the Dharma that is already supreme.
Sometimes they appear squatting or standing on one foot; sometimes they lie upon grass, thorns, or ashes;
or again, they lie upon pestles seeking liberation, acting as the foremost teachers among those multitudes.
Regarding such various types of non-Buddhists, he observed their inclinations and engaged in their activities;
the ascetic practices he displayed were such that the world could not endure them, causing those who saw them to be all tamed and subdued.
Sentient beings are deluded, following false teachings; dwelling in evil views, they undergo manifold sufferings.
For their sake, I preach the sublime Dharma as an expedient means, so that all may attain liberation through the true reality.
Some explain the Four Truths through borderland mantras; some explain the Four Truths through skillful secret words;
some explain the Four Truths through human direct speech; some explain the Four Truths through celestial secret words;
some explain the Four Truths by analyzing written characters; and some explain the Four Truths by determining their definitive meaning.
Skillfully refuting the claims of others, he proclaims the Four Noble Truths; Unmoved by outsiders, he proclaims the Four Noble Truths;

Whether speaking in the eight classes of languages or in every possible tongue, He proclaims the Four Noble Truths according to the linguistic sounds through which they may understand, Teaching the Four Noble Truths so that they may attain liberation.
All the teachings of all Buddhas are thus expounded without exception;
knowing that the realm of speech is inconceivable—this is called the power of the Samādhi of Expounding the Dharma.
The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sutra, Scroll Ten;
The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sutra, Scroll Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Shikshananda of Khotan, by Imperial Command.
The Twelfth Chapter on the Two Worthy Leaders, Part Two:
"There is a supreme samādhi named 'Peaceful Bliss,' Which can universally rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
It emits great, inconceivable radiance, Causing all who behold it to be fully tamed."

The light he emits is named "Excellent Manifestation"; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they will certainly obtain benefit that is not in vain, and by means of this, they shall achieve unsurpassed wisdom.
That light manifests all Buddhas, Manifests the Dharma, manifests the Saṅgha, and manifests the True Path;
It also manifests Buddha-stūpas and images, And for this reason, it has attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Illumination," which eclipses all the radiance of the devas;
there is no darkness or obstruction that it does not dispel, universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
This light awakens all beings, causing them to hold lamps as an offering to the Buddha;
by offering lamps to the Buddhas, they shall attain the state of the unsurpassed lamp within the world.
Yet all oil lamps and butter lamps, as well as various other kinds of bright torches,
fragrant incense, wondrous medicinal herbs, and supreme jewel candles— by making these offerings to the Buddha, one obtains this light.
Again, he emits a light named "Deliverance," which can awaken all beings,
causing them universally to give rise to the mind of great vows, so as to rescue and liberate all sentient beings from the sea of desire.
If one can universally give rise to the great vow-mind to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of desire,
then one can cross over the four torrents and show the way to the city of liberation free from sorrow.
At places where great waters obstruct the paths of beings, he constructed bridges and rafts;
he disparaged the conditioned and praised tranquility—thereby he attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Extinction of Craving";
this light awakens all beings, causing them to abandon the five desires and focus their thoughts on the wondrous flavor of the Dharma of liberation.
If one can renounce the five desires and single-mindedly contemplate the wondrous flavor of the Dharma of liberation,
then by means of the Buddha’s rain of ambrosia, one may universally extinguish all the thirst and craving of the world.
By generously bestowing ponds, wells, springs, and flowing streams, and single-mindedly seeking the path of unsurpassed bodhi,
by disparaging the five desires and praising meditative concentration, he has therefore attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Joy," which can awaken all sentient beings,
causing them to cherish and long for the Buddha’s Bodhi, and to resolve to realize the Teacherless Way.

Having fashioned an image of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, adorned with all marks and seated upon a lotus throne, he constantly extolled the most supreme merits; therefore, he has attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Affectionate Joy"; this light awakens all beings, causing their hearts to delight in the Buddhas, as well as in the Dharma and the Sangha.
If one’s mind always delights in the Buddhas, And likewise delights in the Dharma and the Sangha,
Then, within the assemblies of the Tathāgatas, One shall attain the unsurpassed, profound *dharmakṣānti*.
Awakening immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to mindfully recollect the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
and demonstrating the meritorious practices of generating the bodhicitta— thereby this radiance is attained.
Again, he emits a light named "Accumulation of Merit";
this light awakens all beings, causing them to practice various kinds of immeasurable giving, and through this, they seek the unsurpassed path.

He established great assemblies of giving without restriction; all who came seeking were fully satisfied, never allowed to feel their hearts lacked anything—it is for this reason that he attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Possessing Wisdom," which can awaken all beings,
causing them within a single dharma and a single thought-moment to fully understand immeasurable gateways to the Dharma.
For the sake of all sentient beings, you have analyzed the teachings and definitively realized their true meaning;
because you skillfully expound the Dharma and its significance without deficiency, you have attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Wisdom Lamp"; this light can awaken all beings, causing them to know that the nature of sentient beings is empty and quiescent, and that all phenomena are non-existent.

He expounds that all phenomena are empty and without a master, Like illusions, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, And even like dreams or reflections; Therefore, he has attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named Dharma-Sovereignty; this light can awaken all beings, enabling them to attain inexhaustible dhāraṇīs and to uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas.
By reverently making offerings to those who uphold the Dharma, serving and protecting all the worthy sages,
and bestowing various teachings upon sentient beings, one thereby attains this radiance.

Again, he emits a light named "Able to Renounce"; this light awakens stingy sentient beings, causing them to know that wealth and treasures are all impermanent, so that they constantly delight in giving while their minds remain free from attachment.

The stingy mind is difficult to tame, yet he has tamed it; Understanding that wealth is like a dream or a floating cloud, He increases his pure heart of generous giving; Therefore, he has attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Dispelling Heat," which can awaken those who have violated the prohibitions,
causing them everywhere to receive and uphold the pure precepts and resolve their minds to realize the teacherless Way.
Exhorting and guiding sentient beings to uphold the precepts, so that the ten paths of wholesome action are entirely purified,
and further causing them to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment— for this reason, he has attained this radiance.

Again, he emits a light named "Adorned with Patience"; this light awakens those who harbor anger, causing them to eliminate hatred and abandon pride, so that they may always delight in the dharma of patience and gentleness.
Sentient beings are violent and evil, difficult to endure; yet for the sake of Bodhi, his mind remains unshakable.
Always delighting in praising the merit of patience, he has therefore attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Valiant," which awakens those who are indolent,
causing them to always pay respect and make offerings within the Triple Gem without weariness.
If one constantly pays respect and makes offerings to the Triple Gem without weariness,
one will be able to transcend the realms of the four māras and swiftly attain the unsurpassed Bodhi of a Buddha.
Exhorting and transforming sentient beings to advance in their resolve, Constantly and diligently making offerings to the Triple Gem,
Dedicating oneself to protect the Dharma when it is about to perish— For these reasons, this radiance was attained.

Again, he emits a light named "Tranquility"; this light awakens those with distracted minds, causing them to distance themselves from greed, hatred, and delusion, so that their minds become unshakable and enter right concentration.
Having abandoned all evil associates, Discourse on meaningless matters, and defiled conduct, They praised meditative concentration and forest hermitages; Therefore, they have attained this radiance.

Again, he emits a light named "Wisdom Adornment"; this light awakens those who are ignorant and deluded, causing them to realize the Truths and understand dependent origination, so that their faculties and wisdom are all fully penetrated.
If one can realize the Truths and understand dependent origination, And fully penetrate all faculties and wisdoms,
Then one will attain the Dharma of the Sun-Lamp Samādhi, And through the light of wisdom, achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.
They were able to relinquish both national wealth and their own persons;
for the sake of Bodhi, they sought the True Dharma, and having heard it, they diligently expounded it for the multitude. Therefore, they have attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Buddha-Wisdom"; this light awakens all sentient beings, causing them to see immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, each seated upon a precious lotus flower.
Praising the Buddha’s majestic virtue and liberation, Explaining the Buddha’s immeasurable sovereignty,
Revealing the Buddha’s powers and supernormal faculties— Therefore, this radiance has been attained.
Furthermore, he emits a light named Fearlessness; when this light touches those who are terrified, all poisons and harms inflicted by non-human beings are swiftly extinguished.
Able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings, Whenever encountering harm or affliction, they urge them to desist;
Rescuing those in distress and aiding the orphaned and destitute— By these means, this radiance was attained.

Again, he emits a light named "Peaceful Security"; this light can illuminate those who are ill, causing them to eliminate all suffering and pain, so that they all attain the bliss of the samādhi of right concentration.
Bestowing excellent medicines to save the multitude from affliction, Applying life-prolonging fragrant jewels to their bodies,
And providing butter, oil, milk, and honey for food and drink— By these means, this radiance was attained.

Again, he emits a light named "Beholding the Buddha"; this light awakens those who are about to pass away, causing them to see the Tathāgata through recollection, so that at the end of life they may be born in his pure land.
Seeing those at the point of death, they urge them to recite the Buddha’s name;
They further display sacred images for them to behold and revere, Causing them to develop profound faith and devotion toward the Buddha; For this reason, they have attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Delight in the Dharma"; this light awakens all beings, causing them to always rejoice in the True Dharma, and to listen to its exposition, recite it, and write it down.
When the Dharma was about to perish, he was able to expound it, causing those who sought the Dharma to have their minds fulfilled;
through his love for the Dharma and diligent practice, he attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Exquisite Sound"; this light awakens all bodhisattvas and enables every sound throughout the three realms to be heard by all as the voice of the Tathāgata.
By praising the Buddha with a great voice, And by offering bells and various musical instruments,
Causing the sound of the Buddha to be heard throughout the world, He has therefore attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named Bestowing Ambrosia;
this light awakens all beings, causing them to abandon all heedless conduct and to fully cultivate all meritorious virtues.
He taught that conditioned phenomena are not secure, being entirely pervaded by immeasurable suffering and affliction;
he constantly delighted in praising the bliss of nirvāṇa, and for this reason, he attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Most Supreme," which awakens all beings,
causing them to universally hear from the Buddha the sublime Dharma of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Constantly delighting in praising all Buddhas— their supreme precepts, supreme concentration, and transcendent wisdom—
for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed path, they have therefore attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named Jewel Adornment; this light can awaken all beings, enabling them to obtain inexhaustible treasuries of jewels, with which they make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
By offering various kinds of supreme and wondrous jewels to the Buddha and his stupas,
and by bestowing gifts upon the poor and destitute, he has attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Fragrant Adornment";
this light can awaken all beings, causing those who hear it to find joy and satisfaction, so that they will certainly attain the merit of Buddhahood.
With exquisite celestial and human incense they anointed the ground, making offerings to the Sovereign of All Most Victorious Ones;
they also constructed stupas and images of the Buddha, and for this reason they have attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Variegated Adornment," with countless jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies;
incense is burned, flowers are scattered, and various music is played, filling the city both inside and out.

Originally, with the sounds of subtle and exquisite music, And various adornments such as fragrant incense, wonderful flowers, banners, and canopies, I made offerings to the Buddha; Therefore, I have attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Pure Adornment," which makes the earth level like the palm of a hand and adorns the Buddha-stūpas and their sites; for this reason, he has attained this light.
Again, he emits a light named Great Cloud, Which can raise fragrant clouds and rain scented water;
By sprinkling this water upon the stūpa and its courtyard, He has thus attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Ornament," which causes those who are naked to obtain fine garments;
by bestowing exquisite objects for adorning the body, he has thus accomplished this light.
Again, he emits a light named "Supreme Flavor," Which enables the hungry to obtain fine food;
By bestowing various kinds of precious delicacies, He has therefore accomplished this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named Great Wealth, Causing those who are destitute to obtain treasuries of jewels;
By bestowing inexhaustible goods upon the Triple Gem, He therefore succeeds in accomplishing this light.
Furthermore, he emits a light named "Purity of the Eye," Which enables the blind to see all forms;
Because he offered lamps to the Buddha and the Buddha-stūpas, He has thus attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of Hearing," Which enables the deaf to hear clearly;
By playing music to delight the Buddha and his stūpas, He has therefore attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purification of the Nose," by which all fragrances never before heard are now perceived;
because he offered incense to the Buddha and the Buddha-stūpas, he has thus attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of the Tongue," which can praise the Buddha with beautiful sounds;
having forever eliminated coarse, evil, and unwholesome speech, he therefore achieves this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of the Body," which causes those with impaired faculties to become complete;
because they prostrated their bodies before the Buddha and his stūpas, they have attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of Mind," which causes those who have lost their minds to regain right mindfulness;
through the practice of samādhi, they all attain mastery, and for this reason, he has accomplished this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of Form," which causes one to behold the inconceivable forms of all Buddhas;
because he adorned stupas with various exquisite colors, he has attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Pure Sound," which causes one to know that the nature of sound is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
by contemplating the dependent origination of sound as being like an echo, this radiance is thereby accomplished.
Again, he emits a light named "Pure Fragrance," which causes all foul odors to become fragrant and clean;
having washed the stupas and the Bodhi tree with scented water, he therefore attained this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Pure Flavor," Which can eliminate all poisons within flavors;
By constantly making offerings to the Buddha, the Sangha, and one's parents, One therefore attains this radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of Touch," which can cause all harsh sensations to become soft and supple;
even spears, lances, swords, and halberds raining down from the sky are all transformed into exquisite flower garlands.

Because in the past, while on a road, you offered scented ointments, scattered flowers, and spread garments, welcoming and escorting the Tathāgata so that he might tread upon them; for this reason, you have now obtained such radiance.
Again, he emits a light named "Purity of Dharma," Which causes every single pore to proclaim The inconceivable, wondrous Dharma; All sentient beings who hear it rejoice and attain awakening.
That which arises from causes and conditions has no true birth; the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is not a body.
The nature of phenomena is eternally abiding like space; such is the light of explaining its meaning.

Such gateways of light as these, as infinite in number as the sands of the Ganges, all issue forth from the pores of the Great Sage; each performs its respective activity with distinct differentiation.
The light emitted from a single pore is immeasurable and incalculable, like the sands of the Ganges;
it is the same for every single pore—this is the power of the Great Sage’s samādhi.
The light obtained through his original practices, Accordant with those who shared his past conditions, Is now emitted as such;
This is the sovereign mastery of the Great Sage’s wisdom.
Those who in the past practiced meritorious deeds together, And who possessed the joy of sympathetic rejoicing (anumodanā),
Seeing their actions likewise performed, They all behold this light.
If there are those who personally cultivate various meritorious deeds,
making offerings to countless Buddhas and constantly aspiring for the Buddha’s virtues, it is they whom this light awakens.
For example, though one born blind does not see the sun, it is not that the sun has not arisen in the world;
all those with eyes see it clearly, each according to their own tasks, cultivating their respective labors.
The radiance of the Great Being is likewise: those possessed of wisdom all behold it, while ordinary people of false faith and inferior understanding cannot perceive this radiance at all.
Mani palaces and celestial carriages, polished and adorned with exquisite jewels and divine incense, are spontaneously provided for those possessed of merit;
they cannot be the dwelling place of those lacking virtue.

The radiance of the Great Being is likewise: those with profound wisdom are all touched by its illumination, yet among the deluded and ignorant commoners of false faith and inferior understanding, none are able to see this light.
If there are those who hear of these distinctions of light, And are able to give rise to pure, profound faith and understanding,
They will forever sever all nets of doubt And swiftly perfect the banner of unsurpassed merit.
There is a supreme samādhi capable of manifesting, wherein the retinue and adornments are all sovereign;
throughout all lands in the ten directions, the assembly of the Buddha’s sons is without peer.
There is a wondrous lotus flower adorned with light, Its size equal to the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system;
His body sits upright, completely filling it— This is the supernatural power of this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are as many exquisite lotus flowers as there are atoms in ten lands surrounding [the assembly];
within them sit the sons of the Buddhas, abiding by the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi.

Having accomplished virtuous causes and conditions in past lives, and being fully endowed with the practice of the Buddha’s merits, these beings surround the Bodhisattva; all together they join their palms and gaze upon him without weariness.
Just as the bright moon stands out among the stars, so too does the Bodhisattva dwell amidst the assembly;
such is the practice of the Great Being, entered through the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi.
Just as they are manifested in one direction, surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons, so it is in every direction;
this is through the majestic spiritual power of abiding in this samādhi.

There is a supreme samādhi called "Square Net"; dwelling within this, the Bodhisattva extensively reveals it, manifesting their body everywhere throughout all directions, sometimes appearing to enter meditative absorption and sometimes emerging from it.
Sometimes entering right concentration in the east, they emerge from concentration in the west;
sometimes entering right concentration in the west, they emerge from concentration in the east;
or entering right concentration in another direction, they emerge from concentration in yet another direction.
Thus entering and emerging throughout the ten directions— this is called the power of a bodhisattva’s samādhi.
Reaching to the end of all lands in the eastern quarter,
he manifests before all the countless Tathāgatas and approaches them all universally, yet remains unmoving in the stillness of samādhi.
And throughout all the worlds of the western quarter, in the presence of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
he manifests arising from samādhi and extensively performs immeasurable offerings.
Throughout all the lands of the western direction, All the Tathāgatas, beyond measure, appear before him;
He approaches them all universally, Abiding in samādhi, tranquil and unmoving.
And throughout all the worlds in the eastern direction, at the abodes of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas,
he manifests arising from samādhi and extensively performs immeasurable offerings.
In this way, throughout all worlds of the ten directions, Bodhisattvas enter them all without exception;
some manifest in the stillness and immobility of samādhi, while others manifest in reverent worship of the Buddhas.
Entering right concentration within the eye-faculty, emerging from that concentration amidst the objects of form,
he manifests the inconceivable nature of form, which no devas or humans can comprehend.
Entering right concentration within the sphere of form, Arising from concentration with an undisturbed mind regarding the eye,
He teaches that the eye is unarisen and without origination, Its nature being empty, quiescent, and without activity.
Entering right concentration within the faculty of the ear, emerging from that concentration amidst the objects of sound,
they discern all spoken languages and sounds, such that neither gods nor worldly beings can comprehend it.

Entering right concentration amidst the object of sound, Arising from concentration in the ear with an undisturbed mind, He teaches that the ear is unborn and has no arising; Its nature is empty, quiescent, and without activity.
Entering right concentration within the faculty of the nose, he emerges from that concentration amidst the objects of fragrance;
he universally perceives all supreme and wondrous scents, which neither gods nor worldlings can know.

Entering right concentration within the sensory object of fragrance, Emerging from that concentration with an undisturbed mind, he taught that the nose is unborn and has no arising; Its nature is empty, quiescent, and without activity.
Entering right concentration within the faculty of the tongue, he emerges from that concentration amidst the objects of taste;
he universally attains all supreme flavors, such that neither gods nor worldly people can know it.

Entering right concentration amidst the objects of taste, Arising from concentration with a mind undisturbed, He teaches that the tongue is unborn and has no arising; Its nature is empty, quiescent, and inactive.
Entering right concentration within the body-faculty, Emerging from concentration within the object of touch,
He skillfully discerns all tactile sensations, Such that neither gods nor worldlings can know it.
Entering right concentration within the object of touch, Arising from concentration in the body with an undisturbed mind,
He teaches that the body is unborn and without arising, Its nature being empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.

Entering right concentration within the faculty of mind, emerging from that concentration amidst mental objects, he discerns the characteristics of all phenomena; neither gods nor men are able to know this.
Entering right concentration within the objects of the mind, he arises from that mental absorption with an undisturbed mind;
he teaches that the mind is unborn and without arising, its nature being empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Entering right concentration within the body of a youth, he emerges from concentration within the body of a man in his prime;
entering right concentration within the body of a man in his prime, he emerges from concentration within the body of an old man;
entering right concentration within the body of an old man, he emerges from concentration within the body of a virtuous woman.
Entering right concentration within the body of a virtuous woman, he emerges from concentration within the body of a virtuous man;
entering right concentration within the body of a virtuous man, he emerges from concentration within the body of a bhikṣuṇī;
entering right concentration within the body of a bhikṣuṇī, he emerges from concentration within the body of a bhikṣu.
The body of a bhikṣu enters right concentration, and from that concentration emerges the body of one in training or one beyond training;
the body of one in training or one beyond training enters right concentration, and from that concentration emerges the body of a pratyekabuddha;
the body of a pratyekabuddha enters right concentration, and from that concentration emerges the manifested body of a Tathāgata.
Entering right concentration within the body of a Tathāgata, he emerges from concentration within the bodies of devas;
entering right concentration within the bodies of devas, he emerges from concentration within the bodies of great nāgas;
entering right concentration within the bodies of great nāgas, he emerges from concentration within the bodies of yakṣas.
Entering right concentration within the body of a yakṣa, one emerges from concentration within the body of a spirit;
entering right concentration within the body of a spirit, one emerges from concentration within a single pore;
entering right concentration within a single pore, one emerges from concentration within all pores.
Entering right concentration from all pores, one emerges from concentration at the tip of a single hair;
entering right concentration at the tip of a single hair, one emerges from concentration within a single atom;
entering right concentration within a single atom, one emerges from concentration within all atoms.
Entering right concentration within all atoms, Emerging from concentration upon the vajra-ground;
Entering right concentration upon the vajra-ground, Emerging from concentration atop mani-trees;
Entering right concentration atop mani-trees, Emerging from concentration within the Buddha’s radiance.
Entering right concentration within the Buddha’s radiance, he emerges from it within rivers and seas;
entering right concentration within rivers and seas, he emerges from it within the element of fire;
entering right concentration within the element of fire, he emerges from it within the element of wind with an undisturbed mind.
Entering right concentration within the great element of wind, he emerges from concentration within the great element of earth;
entering right concentration within the great element of earth, he emerges from concentration within the celestial palaces;
entering right concentration within the celestial palaces, he rises from concentration within space with an undisturbed mind.
This is called one of immeasurable merit; The mastery of samādhi is inconceivable.
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions Could not exhaustively describe it even in immeasurable kalpas.
All Tathāgatas together proclaim: the karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable;
the transformations of the nāgas and the mastery of Buddhas are likewise, and the supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas are also beyond thought.
I wish to reveal this through analogies, yet there is ultimately no analogy capable of illustrating it;
nevertheless, those of wise and discerning intellect understand its meaning by means of these metaphors.
The minds of the śrāvakas abide in the eight liberations; all their transformations are sovereign:
they can manifest many bodies from a single body, and again manifest a single body from many bodies.
Entering the fire-concentration in the midst of empty space, he walks, stands, sits, and lies down entirely within it;
water issues from his upper body while fire issues from his lower body, and fire issues from his upper body while water issues from his lower body.
Thus, within a single thought-moment, there are various kinds of sovereign powers beyond measure.

Even those who do not possess great compassion, nor seek the path of the Buddha for the sake of sentient beings, can still manifest such inconceivable deeds; how much more so, then, those with the sovereign power of great benefit?
Just as the sun and moon travel through the void, their reflections pervade the ten directions;
in springs, ponds, marshes, and the water within vessels, as well as in rivers, seas, and all precious waters, there is nowhere they do not appear.
The physical form of the Bodhisattva is likewise so: universally manifesting throughout the ten directions in an inconceivable manner.
All of these are the dharmas of mastery in samādhi, which only the Tathāgata can fully realize and comprehend.
Just as the images of the fourfold army appear in clear water, each distinct and without intermixture—
swords, halberds, bows, and arrows being of many kinds, and armor, helmets, chariots, and carriages not of a single sort.
According to all their various characteristics and distinctions, there are none that do not appear within the water;
yet the water itself is fundamentally without discrimination. The samādhi of the bodhisattva is also like this.
In the ocean there is a deity named Good Sound; its voice universally accords with all beings of the sea, making all their speech clear and eloquent, causing them all to rejoice.
That deity, though possessing greed, anger, and delusion, is still able to skillfully understand all sounds;
how much more so, then, could one with the sovereign power of dhāraṇī fail to bring joy to the multitude!
There was a woman named Prajñā (Eloquence), whom her parents obtained through prayers to the gods;
if there is one who abandons evil and delights in the truth, wondrous eloquence shall enter their very being.
If even those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can still provide benefit and eloquence to others according to their conduct,
how much more so for a Bodhisattva endowed with wisdom— who could not bring benefit to sentient beings!
Just as a master of illusion, knowing the arts of illusion, can manifest all manner of immeasurable things,
showing in an instant the creation of days, months, and years, and cities, towns, and abundant great peace and happiness.
Even a magician who possesses greed, hatred, and delusion can delight the world through the power of illusion;
how much more so, then, could those with the powers of meditative concentration and liberation fail to bring joy to the multitude!
When the devas and asuras fought in battle, the asuras were defeated and fled;
their weapons, chariots, and followers all vanished at once, unable to be seen.
If those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion can still manifest inconceivable transformations,
how much more so for one who dwells in the dharmas of supernatural powers and fearlessness— how could they not manifest sovereign mastery!
Śakra Devānām-indra has an elephant king; when he knows the Lord of Devas intends to travel, he transforms himself into thirty-three heads, each fully endowed with six tusks.
Upon every tusk are seven pools of water, pure, fragrant, and brimming to the brim.
Within each of the pure ponds, there are seven exquisite lotus flowers as adornments;
upon each of these adorned lotuses dwell seven celestial jade maidens,
all skilled in the arts, who perform various music and entertain Śakra.
That elephant may again cast off its original form, transforming its body to become identical to those of the devas;
in its majestic deportment and every movement, it is entirely equal to them—such is the power of its manifested supernormal transformations.
If those who possess greed, hatred, and delusion can still manifest such supernatural powers,
how much more so for one who is fully endowed with the wisdom of skillful means— how could they not be masterful in all meditative concentrations!
Just as when an asura manifests a transformed body, standing upon the diamond-limit within the ocean,
the seawater reaches only half his height, and his head stands level with Mount Sumeru.
If even those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can manifest such great supernormal powers,
how much more so for the Lamp that Illumines the World, who has subdued the enmity of Māra— could he lack sovereign spiritual power?
When the devas and asuras wage war together, Śakra’s supernatural power is inconceivable;
according to the number of the asura hosts, he manifests bodies equal to theirs to oppose them.
The asuras gave rise to this thought:
"Śakra Devānām Indra is coming toward us; he will surely bind my body with the fivefold fetters.
Because of this, that host was entirely distressed and withered.
Śakra manifests his body with a thousand eyes, holding a vajra that emits flames;
clad in armor and wielding a staff, he is most majestic and awe-inspiring, so that upon seeing him, the asuras all retreat and submit.
If even one with such a meager force of merit can still crush great enemies,
how much more so for the Savior of All, who possesses perfect virtue and sovereign power!
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is a celestial drum, produced through the karmic retribution of the gods;
when it perceives that the host of devas is becoming heedless, this sound spontaneously issues forth from the air.
All five desires are entirely impermanent; Like a mass of foam on water, their nature is false and deceptive.
All conditioned things are like dreams or mirages, And also like floating clouds or the moon reflected in water.
Heedlessness is an enemy and a source of suffering; it is not the path to the Deathless, but the track of birth and death.
If one engages in various acts of heedlessness, one enters the mouth of the great fish of death and extinction.
The root of all suffering in the world, which all noble ones loathe and abhor, is the nature of the five sensory pleasures—perishable and subject to decay; you should take delight in the true Dharma.
When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard this sound, they all ascended together to the Sudharma Hall;
there Śakra preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma, causing them all to accord with tranquility and eliminate craving and attachment.
That sound is formless and invisible, yet it can still benefit the multitudes of devas;
how much more so when the physical body manifests according to their mental inclinations—how could it fail to deliver all living beings!
When the devas and asuras were engaged in battle, by the power of the devas' superior merit and virtue,
the celestial drum emitted a sound to inform their hosts:
"You all should not feel anxiety or fear!"
When the devas heard these words of proclamation, their grief and fear were entirely dispelled and their strength increased.
At that time, the heart of the asura trembled with dread, and the troops he had led all retreated in flight.
The wondrous samādhi of ambrosia is like a celestial drum, Constantly producing the tranquil sound that subdues Māra;
With great compassion and pity, it rescues all beings, Universally causing sentient beings to extinguish their afflictions.
Śakra, universally responding to all the celestial maidens— ninety-two nayutas of them—
caused each of them to think in her own mind:
"The Heavenly King is sporting with me alone."
Just as their bodies universally respond among the celestial maidens, so too is it within the Hall of Good Dharma;
able to manifest spiritual powers in a single thought-moment, they appear before everyone to preach the Dharma for them.
Even Śakra, who possesses greed, anger, and delusion, can cause his own retinue to be entirely joyful;
how much more so could one with great skillful means and supernormal powers fail to gladden all beings!
The six celestial kings of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Attain mastery within the realm of desire;
With karma, delusion, and suffering as their snare, They bind all ordinary beings.
If those possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion can still attain mastery over sentient beings,
how much more so for one endowed with the ten kinds of sovereign power— who could not cause all beings to practice together?
The Great Brahmā King of the trichiliocosm, in all the abodes where Brahmās dwell,
is able to manifest his body seated therein, proclaiming the subtle and wondrous sound of Brahmā.
While dwelling in the worldly path of Brahmā, his meditative concentration and supernormal powers were already as he wished;
how much more so for one who has transcended the world and is unsurpassed—could he possibly lack mastery over dhyāna and liberation?
Maheśvara, sovereign in wisdom, when the Dragon King of the Great Ocean sends down rain,
is able to distinguish and count every single drop, discerning them all within a single thought-moment.
Having diligently practiced and studied for immeasurable billions of eons, you have attained this supreme wisdom of Bodhi;
why then, in a single thought-moment, do you not universally know the minds of all sentient beings?

The karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable; by the power of a great wind, the world is raised up—vast oceans, all the mountains, celestial palaces, and the myriad seeds of things, radiant with many jewels.
It can also raise clouds and send down great rain; it can also disperse and extinguish all vapors;
it can also bring all grains to maturity; and it can bring peace and happiness to all living beings.
Even the wind cannot learn the *pāramitās*, nor can it learn the various merits of the Buddhas;
yet it still accomplishes inconceivable deeds—how much more so for one who has fulfilled all vows!
The various voices of men and women, all the sounds of birds and beasts,
and the roars of thunder from the great oceans and flowing rivers— all these can satisfy the minds of sentient beings.
How much more so for one who knows the nature of sound is like an echo, who has attained unimpeded and wondrous eloquence,
and who preaches the Dharma in universal response to sentient beings— how could such a one fail to bring joy to the world?
The ocean possesses a rare and extraordinary quality: it can serve as the seal of equality for all things.
Whether they be sentient beings, precious treasures, or flowing rivers, it universally encompasses them all without refusal.
Those who possess inexhaustible meditative concentration and liberation, Are likewise sealed by the seal of equality;
Regarding all sublime practices of merit and wisdom, They cultivate them all universally without weariness or satiety.
When the Dragon King of the Great Ocean sports, he attains mastery over all places;
he raises clouds that pervade the four continents, their variously adorned colors being such that in the sixth heaven,
the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, the hue of those clouds is like pure gold.
On the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, it is the color of red pearls;
on the Tuṣita Heaven, the color of frost and snow;
and on the Yāma Heaven, the color of lapis lazuli.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the color of agate;
the Cāturmahārājakāyika Heaven is the color of crystal;
and the surface of the great ocean is the color of vajra.
Among the kinnaras, it has the color of exquisite fragrance;
in the abodes of the nāgas, the color of a lotus;
and in the abodes of the yakṣas, the color of a white goose.
In the realm of the asuras, it has the color of mountain rock;
in the land of Uttarakuru, the color of golden flames;
and in Jambudvīpa, the color of blue gemstone.
The remaining two continents are adorned with various ornaments, responding to the inclinations of the beings therein.
Furthermore, in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, lightning flashes like sunlight amidst the clouds;
in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, it is like moonlight.
On the Tuṣita Heaven it is Jambūnada gold;
on the Yāma Heaven it is the color of snow-white jade;
on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven it is the color of golden flames.
The color of various jewels in the heavens of the Four Great Kings;
the color of red pearls within the great ocean;
and the color of lapis lazuli in the realm of the kiṃnaras.
The color of the jewel-treasury where the dragon kings dwell;
the color of crystal where the yakṣas dwell;
and the color of agate among the asuras.
The realm of Uttarakuru has the color of fire-pearls;
Jambudvīpa is the color of indranīla;
the other two continents are variously adorned, like the appearance of clouds and likewise the lightning.
The thunderous roar of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is like the voice of Brahmā;
the sound of the great drums in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
and the sound of singing in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The voices of the goddesses in the Yāma Heaven;
in that Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, like the various sounds of the kinnaras;
in the abodes of the gods of the Four World-Protecting Kings, like the sounds produced by the gandharvas;
The sound of two mountains colliding in the ocean;
the sound of flutes and pipes among the kiṃnaras;
the sound of kalaviṅkas in the cities of the nāgas;
The sound of nāga maidens in the abodes of yakṣas;
the sound of celestial drums among the asuras;
and the sound of ocean tides in the realm of humans.
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods rain down exquisite fragrances, adorned with various kinds of miscellaneous flowers;
the Nirmāṇarati gods rain down tāla flowers, māndārava flowers, and liquid perfumes;
in the Tuṣita heaven, maṇi jewels rain down, complete with all manner of precious adornments.
The jewel in his topknot is like moonlight; his exquisite garments are the color of pure gold.
In the Yāma Heaven, banners, streamers, and canopies rain down, along with flower garlands, ointments, and exquisite ornaments.
There are fine robes the color of red pearls, as well as various kinds of music and dance.
The wish-fulfilling jewels of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Hard black aloeswood and sandalwood incense,
Saffron, kīra, tamāla, and the like— A rain of these falls, intermingled with exquisite flowers and fragrant waters;
Within the cities of the World Protectors, a rain of delicious food falls, Complete in color, fragrance, and flavor, increasing one’s strength.
Furthermore, inconceivable multitudes of wondrous jewels rained down, all created by the dragon kings.
Moreover, within that great ocean, rain poured forth incessantly like chariot axles;
again, inexhaustible great treasuries of jewels rained down, as well as various kinds of ornamental gems.
In the realm of the kiṃnaras, necklaces rain down, along with lotus robes of every hue and jewels;
there are bālasīka and mālatī perfumes, and all manner of musical sounds are fully present;
in the cities of the nāgas, red pearls rain down.
Within the yakṣa cities, light-maṇi jewels [shone];
among the asuras, weapons rained down, subduing all enemies;
in Uttarakuru, necklaces rained down, and likewise immeasurable, most excellent flowers.
In the two continents of Pūrvavideha and Aparagodānīya, Various kinds of ornaments rain down everywhere;
In Jambudvīpa, pure water rains down— Subtle, refreshing, and always timely—
Nourishing all flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs, And bringing all crops to maturity.
Such immeasurable and wondrous adornments— various clouds, lightning, thunder, and rain—
the Dragon King can produce all with sovereign ease, yet his body remains unmoving and free from conceptual discrimination.
If even those who dwell within the ocean of worlds can manifest such inconceivable power,
how much more so for one who has entered the ocean of Dharma and is endowed with merit— could they not perform great spiritual transformations?
The gates of liberation of those bodhisattvas cannot be fully revealed by any analogy;
yet, through these various analogies, I shall now briefly describe their power of mastery.
The foremost wisdom, the vast wisdom, the true wisdom, and the boundless wisdom;
the supreme wisdom and the most excellent wisdom—such a Dharma gate has now been taught.
This Dharma is rare and most extraordinary; if anyone, having heard it, can accept it, believe it, receive it, and proclaim it—such an act is exceedingly difficult to perform.
Among all the ordinary beings in the world, those who have faith in this Dharma are extremely rare;
only those who have diligently cultivated pure merit can believe through the power of their past causes.
Among all the beings in every world, few desire the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha are even fewer still, and those who proceed toward the Mahāyāna are extremely rare to encounter.
To aspire toward the Mahāyāna is still easy; to be able to believe in this Dharma is twice as difficult.
How much more so to uphold and recite it for others, and to practice according to the Dharma with true understanding!
To take upon one's head the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system for an entire eon without the body moving—this which they have done is not difficult;
rather, it is difficult indeed to have faith in this Dharma.
To take up ten buddha-fields with one's hand and remain suspended in mid-air for an entire kalpa—such an act is not difficult for them;
rather, it is difficult to be able to have faith in this Dharma.
If one were to bestow all articles of pleasure upon beings as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an eon, their merit would not be supreme;
those who have faith in this Dharma are the most supreme.
If one were to serve as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an entire eon,
yet another who can recite and uphold this chapter— their merit would be far more supreme than that.
When the Bodhisattva Worthy Leader had spoken these verses, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways, the palaces of Māra were obscured, and the evil realms were stilled.
The Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before him, each stroking his crown with their right hand and praising him in unison:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Please speak this Dharma!
We all rejoice in it with one accord.
— *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Fifteen.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Thirteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. Chapter Thirteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru.

At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, within every Jambudvīpa of the four continents, the Tathāgata was seen sitting beneath a tree; in each place, there were bodhisattvas who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual strength, expounded the Dharma, each of whom felt as though they were always in the presence of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, without departing from beneath the Bodhi tree, ascended Mount Sumeru and proceeded toward the palace of Śakra.

Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar before the Palace of Sublime Victory, immediately used his supernormal powers to adorn this palace and prepared a lion throne called the Universal Radiance Treasury.

This throne was composed entirely of exquisite jewels: it had ten thousand tiers of steps, most magnificently adorned; ten thousand golden nets covered its surface; ten thousand kinds of curtains and ten thousand kinds of canopies were arranged in rows around it; ten thousand silken fabrics served as hanging streamers; ten thousand pearl necklaces were interlaced throughout; ten thousand garments were spread upon the seat; and ten thousand devaputras and ten thousand Brahmā kings surrounded it from front and back, while ten thousand rays of light shone brilliantly upon it.
At that time, Śakra, having prepared and arranged a seat for the Tathāgata, bowed with palms joined and addressed the Buddha with reverence, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
Welcome, Sugata! Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
We pray only that you will have compassion for us and dwell in this palace.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted his invitation and entered the Palace of Sublime Victory;
likewise, it was so throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the sounds of music within the various palaces naturally ceased. Śakra then recollected the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke these verses:
“Kāśyapa Tathāgata was endowed with great compassion, The most unsurpassed among all auspicious things.
That Buddha once entered this palace; Therefore, this place is most auspicious.”
Kanakamuni’s vision is unimpeded; he is the most supreme among all auspicious ones.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Kara-kaṇḍu is like a mountain of gold; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
That Buddha once entered this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was free from the three stains, the most supreme among all that is auspicious;
since that Buddha once entered this hall, this place is therefore the most auspicious.
Śikhin Tathāgata, free from conceptual discrimination, is the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this palace, and for this reason, this place is most auspicious.
Vipaśyin Buddha was like the full moon, the most supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
Puṣya has realized the ultimate truth, the most supreme among all that is auspicious;
since that Buddha once entered this hall, this place is therefore most auspicious.
The Tathāgata Tiṣya possesses unimpeded eloquence, The most supreme among all auspicious things;
That Buddha once entered this hall, Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
Padmottara Buddha, pure and stainless, supreme among all that is auspicious—
since that Buddha once entered this hall, this place is therefore most auspicious.
The great radiance of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara is supreme among all auspicious things;
that Buddha once entered this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
"In this world-system, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by means of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, praised the merits of ten Buddhas with verses;
likewise, the Śakra-devānām-indras of all the world-systems in the ten directions also praised the merits of the Buddhas in this same manner."
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Palace of Sublime Victory and sat cross-legged.
Suddenly, this palace became vast and spacious, just like the dwellings of the celestial hosts;
and so it was throughout all the worlds of the ten directions.

Chapter Fourteen: Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, there came from worlds beyond as many lands as atoms in a hundred buddha-fields one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions, each accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field. They assembled together, their names being:

Bodhisattva Dharma Wisdom, Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom, Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, Bodhisattva Merit Wisdom, Bodhisattva Diligence Wisdom, Bodhisattva Skillful Wisdom, Bodhisattva Wisdom, Bodhisattva True Wisdom, Bodhisattva Unsurpassed Wisdom, and Bodhisattva Firm Wisdom.
The lands from which they have come are as follows:

the world Indrahāsa, the world Padmahāsa, the world Ratnahāsa, the world Utpalahāsa, the world Vajrahāsa, the world Sugandhahāsa, the world Manojñahāsa, the world Aruṇahāsa, the world Nārada-hāsa, and the world Gaganahāsa.
Each of them practiced the pure conduct of brahmacarya under various Buddhas, namely:

the Buddha Viśiṣṭacandra, the Buddha Akṣayacandra, the Buddha Acalacandra, the Buddha Vāyucandra, the Buddha Jala-candra, the Buddha Vimukticandra, the Buddha Anuttaracandra, the Buddha Nakṣatracandra, the Buddha Viśuddhicandra, and the Buddha Vibhakticandra.
When these bodhisattvas had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves at his feet;
then, according to the direction from which each had come, they each magically manifested a lion throne of the Vairocana-treasury and sat upon those thrones in the full lotus posture.
Just as in this world, bodhisattvas have gathered upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, so it is in all worlds;
the names of those bodhisattvas, their worlds, and the names of their Buddhas are all identical and without distinction.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of wondrously colored light from his two big toes, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions, including the palaces of Śakra, Lord of Devas, atop Mount Sumeru; the Buddha and the great assembly were all clearly manifested therein.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Buddha emits pure radiance, Universally revealing the Guide of the World,
Abiding within the Palace of Sublime Victory Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains.”
All the Śakra-devānām-indras invited the Buddha into their palaces,
and with ten sublime verses each, they praised all the Tathāgatas.
Within those great assemblies, all the hosts of bodhisattvas likewise offered praise.
All have arrived from the ten directions and sit peacefully upon transformed seats.
All the bodhisattvas in that assembly bear names identical to our own;
the worlds from which they come likewise bear such names.
The World-Honored Ones of their own lands all share these same names;
each, in the presence of their respective Buddhas, has purely cultivated the supreme practice.
Son of the Buddha, you should observe the Tathāgata’s power of mastery.
Throughout all of Jambudvīpa, everyone says the Buddha is among them;
yet we now see the Buddha dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
It is likewise in all ten directions—such is the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
In each and every world, they resolve their minds to seek the Buddha-way;
relying upon such vows, they cultivate the practices of enlightenment.
With various bodies, the Buddhas travel throughout all worlds.
The Dharma-realm is without obstruction; none can measure it.
The light of wisdom shines eternally and universally, extinguishing all darkness in the world.
Being peerless among all things, how could it ever be measured or known?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvajñāna, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to constantly behold the Tathāgata for hundreds of thousands of eons,
If one does not rely on the meaning of ultimate reality while contemplating the Savior of the World,"
Such people grasp at various signs, increasing the net of delusion and confusion;
bound within the prison of birth and death, they remain blind and do not see the Buddha.
When they observe all phenomena, they find their intrinsic nature to be non-existent.
Just as their characteristics of arising and ceasing Are merely spoken of by way of provisional names,
All phenomena are without arising, And all phenomena are without ceasing;
If one can understand in this way, The Buddhas will always be manifest before them.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
Without grasping and without seeing, the empty nature itself is the Buddha, Which cannot be grasped through thought or deliberation.
If one knows that the essential nature of all phenomena Is in every way like this, [one realizes the truth].
Such a person does not act thus, being defiled and attached by afflictions.
When ordinary beings perceive all phenomena, they merely follow after their marks;
failing to understand that phenomena are markless, they do not see the Buddha.
The Muni transcends the three times, Fully endowed with all marks;
Abiding in non-abiding, Pervasive yet unmoving.
I contemplate all phenomena And have attained complete clarity regarding them.
Now that I behold the Tathāgata, I am certain and free from doubt.
The Wisdom of Dharma has already previously explained the true nature of the Tathāgata;
through him I have come to understand that Bodhi is inconceivable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s great wisdom is rare and without equal;
throughout all worlds, no one can fathom it through thought.”
Ordinary beings observe falsely, grasping at signs in an irrational manner;
the Buddha is free from all signs and cannot be seen by them.
Those who are deluded and ignorant falsely grasp at the characteristics of the five aggregates.
Those who do not understand that true nature do not see the Buddha.
When one thoroughly knows that all phenomena have no inherent existence,
and thus understands the nature of dharmas in this way, then one sees Vairocana.
Due to the preceding five aggregates, the subsequent aggregates arise in succession;
by understanding this nature, one beholds the inconceivable Buddha.
It is like a jewel in the darkness, which cannot be seen without a lamp.
If the Buddha-dharma is not expounded by someone, though one possesses wisdom, one cannot comprehend it.
Just as when the eyes are clouded by cataracts, one does not see pure and wondrous forms;
so too, with an impure mind, one does not perceive the teachings of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, just as the bright, pure sun cannot be seen by one who is blind,
those who lack a mind of wisdom will never see the Buddhas.
If one can remove the cataracts from the eyes and abandon the perception of forms, [one shall see them].
When one does not perceive any phenomena, Then one attains the vision of the Tathāgata.
All-Wise One, you previously taught The Dharma of the Bodhi of all Buddhas;
Having heard it from you, I have attained the vision of Vairocana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All phenomena lack true reality, yet sentient beings falsely grasp at the appearance of reality;
for this reason, all ordinary worldlings wander in the prison of birth and death."
The teachings expressed through words are falsely discriminated by those of small intelligence;
therefore, obstacles arise, and they do not understand their own minds.
If one cannot understand one's own mind, how can one know the true path?
Due to their perverted wisdom, they increase all evils;
not seeing that all phenomena are empty, they constantly undergo the suffering of birth and death.
Such people have not yet attained the pure Dharma-eye.
In the past, I underwent manifold sufferings because I did not see the Buddha;
therefore, one should purify the eye of Dharma and behold that which ought to be seen.
If one attains the vision of the Buddha, the mind will have nothing to grasp.
Such a person is able to see the Dharma as the Buddha knows it.
If one sees the true Dharma of the Buddha, they are called a person of great wisdom;
such a person possesses the pure eye and is able to observe the world.
Non-viewing is itself viewing; it is able to see all phenomena.
If there were a view regarding phenomena, this would be non-seeing.
The nature of all phenomena is neither born nor extinguished.
How marvelous is the Great Teacher, Who has awakened himself and can awaken others!
The Sublime Wisdom has already proclaimed The Dharma realized by the Tathāgata;
Having heard it from him, we are now able To know the true nature of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīramatī, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“If one dwells in conceptual discrimination, Then the pure eye is destroyed;
Ignorance and false views increase, And one shall never see the Buddhas.”
If one can thoroughly understand false dharmas, According to reality and without inversion, Knowing that delusion is fundamentally true, Then seeing the Buddha is purity.
To have a view is defilement; This is not yet true seeing.
Far removed from all views, one thus beholds the Buddha.
The phenomena of worldly speech are the false conceptualizations of sentient beings;
to know that the world is entirely unborn is to truly see the world.
If one sees the world as it is seen, seeing is then the characteristic of the world;
when this is seen as equal and without distinction according to reality, one is called a true seer.
When one sees them as equal and without distinction, one does not conceptualize objects.
This vision is free from all delusions; being untainted, it attains mastery.
That which is revealed by all Buddhas—every conceptualized phenomenon—is entirely ungraspable, for its nature is pure.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally pure, Like space, it is devoid of characteristics;
Nothing can be predicated of it— Thus do the wise contemplate.
Free from the conceptualization of phenomena, They take no delight in any phenomena.
This too is without anything to be cultivated, yet one is able to see the Great Muni.
As Guṇamati has said: "One who sees thus is called a seer of the Buddha;
all conditioned phenomena are by their very nature quiescent."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Suprajñā, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"How marvelous! The great heroes, the immeasurable Tathāgatas, Whose minds are free from defilement and liberated, Having crossed over themselves, are able to deliver others."
I behold the Lamp of the World as it truly is, without inversion,
just as it is seen by those who have accumulated wisdom over immeasurable eons.
All the activities of ordinary beings inevitably and swiftly return to exhaustion.
Its nature is like space, therefore it is said to be inexhaustible.
The wise speak of inexhaustibility, yet even this is nothing that can be spoken;
because its intrinsic nature is inexhaustible, one attains an inconceivable exhaustion.
Within this inexhaustible discourse, no sentient being can be found;
knowing the nature of sentient beings to be thus, one then beholds the One of Great Renown.
To speak of seeing while there is no seeing is called "seeing"; to speak of sentient beings where there is no birth is called "sentient beings."
Whether seeing sentient beings, One understands them to be without intrinsic nature.
The seer, the seen, and the act of seeing— All these are completely dispelled.
Without destroying the true Dharma, Such a person thoroughly understands the Buddha.
If a person understands the Buddha And the Dharma taught by the Buddha,
They shall be able to illuminate the world Like the Buddha Vairocana.
The Perfectly Awakened One has skillfully revealed The single path of pure Dharma.
The Great Being Vīryamati expounds the immeasurable Dharma.
Whether existence or non-existence, all such conceptualizations are extinguished;
thus one is able to see the Buddha and abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Hearing the most supreme teaching, The light of wisdom was immediately born;
It shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, And I see all Buddhas everywhere."
In this, there is not the slightest thing; there is only a provisional name.
If one calculates that there is a self or a person, then one enters a perilous path.
All ordinary people who grasp at things falsely calculate the body to be substantially existent.
The Tathāgata is not an object to be grasped; those who seek him in such a way will never see him.
Such people lack the eye of wisdom and are unable to perceive the Buddha;
for immeasurable eons, they shall wander through the ocean of birth and death.
Where there is contention, one speaks of birth and death; where there is no contention, that is nirvāṇa.
Yet both birth and death and nirvāṇa are unattainable.
If one pursues provisional names and becomes attached to these two dharmas, [one remains bound].
Such a person is not in accordance with reality; they do not know the sublime path of the noble ones.
If they should give rise to such a thought as:
"This is the Buddha; this one is the most supreme."
"Inversion is not the true meaning; One cannot see the Perfectly Awakened One through it.
If one can know this actual reality— The mark of quiescent *tathatā*— Then one sees the Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened, Who transcends the path of language."
Language describes all phenomena, yet it cannot manifest their true nature;
only through equanimity can one see them as they are—just as the Dharma is, so too is the Buddha.
The Perfectly Awakened One has transcended the past, as well as the future and the present.
"Having forever severed the root of conceptual discrimination, for this reason they are called Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Real Wisdom (Tattvabuddhi), receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"It would be better to undergo the sufferings of hell than not to hear the names of the Buddhas."
Though they experience immeasurable bliss, they do not hear the name of the Buddha.
Therefore, in the past, for countless kalpas, they have suffered and transmigrated within birth and death because they did not hear the name of the Buddha.
Not being inverted regarding phenomena, one realizes them as they truly are;
free from all characteristics of combination, this is called unsurpassed awakening.
The present is not a combination, and the past and future are likewise so.
All phenomena are signless; this is the true essence of the Buddha.
If one can contemplate the profound meaning of all phenomena in this way, then one will see all Buddhas and the true aspect of the Dharma-body.
Seeing reality as it truly is, and seeing the unreal as unreal—such ultimate understanding is why one is called a Buddha.
The Buddha-dharma cannot be awakened to; realizing this is what is called awakening to the Dharma.
The Buddhas cultivate in this way: not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Knowing that through the one there is the many, and knowing that through the many there is the one;
all dharmas have no basis, arising only from combination.
There is no agent nor anything to be done; it arises solely from the perception of karma.
How is this known to be so?
Because nothing else exists apart from this.
"All phenomena are without abiding; A fixed location cannot be found.
The Buddhas dwell herein, Ultimately unmoving.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Unsurpassed Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Mahāsattva, Far removed from the notion of sentient beings, None can surpass him; Therefore he is called 'Unsurpassed.
The state attained by all Buddhas Is without action and without discrimination."
The coarse does not exist, and the subtle is likewise so.
This is the sphere of activity of all Buddhas; within it there are no numbers.
Perfect Awakening is far removed from number—this is the true Dharma of the Buddha.
The light of the Tathāgata shines universally, extinguishing all darkness and obscurity;
this light is not something that illuminates, nor is it something that does not illuminate.
It is without attachment to phenomena, free from thought, and untainted.
Without abiding and without location, one does not destroy the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Within this, there is no duality, nor is there even unity;
those of great wisdom who see well abide skillfully in accordance with reality.
In non-existence there is no duality, and even duality is further absent;
all that exists in the three realms is empty—this is the vision of the Buddhas.
Ordinary beings lack awakening and understanding, so the Buddhas cause them to abide in the True Dharma.
All phenomena abide nowhere; realizing this, one sees one's own body.
Though not a body, it is spoken of as a body; though not arising, it manifests as arising.
Without body and without seeing—this is the Buddha’s unsurpassed body.
"Thus has the true wisdom explained the wondrous nature of the Buddhas' Dharma;
whoever hears this teaching shall obtain the pure eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Firm Wisdom, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“Magnificent is the Great Radiance, the valiant and unsurpassed being;
for the sake of benefiting the deluded multitudes, he has arisen in the world.
With a heart of great compassion, the Buddha universally observes all sentient beings.”
