Beholding those currently within the three realms of existence, Cycling through saṃsāra and undergoing manifold sufferings—
Except for the Perfectly Awakened One, The Honored and Virtuous Guide,
Among all devas and humans, There is none who can provide protection and refuge.
If Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the like did not appear in the world,
there would be no sentient being at all who could attain peace and happiness.
It is through the Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, as well as the assembly of worthy sages, [that this is possible].
Appearing in the world, they are able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings.
Those who behold the Tathāgata obtain great and wholesome benefit;
those who hear the Buddha’s name and give rise to faith are, in this world, true reliquaries.
Having beheld the World-Honored One, we have attained great benefit;
having heard such a sublime Dharma, we shall all attain the path of Buddhahood.
All the bodhisattvas of the past, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, [have likewise attained it].
Having attained the eye of pure wisdom, I have thoroughly understood the realm of all Buddhas.
Now beholding Vairocana, my pure faith increases further;
the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless, and its exposition can never be exhausted.
"Even if Bodhisattvas such as Jñānavatī and I, Dṛḍhamati, were to speak for countless billions of kalpas, we could not exhaustively describe them. Chapter Fifteen:
The Ten Abodes (Daśabhūmika) At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, entered the Bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means.

By the power of samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms within a thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name, Dharmamati. They addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying: "Excellent!
Excellent! Son of good family,
you are able to enter this bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means.
"Good son! Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions all empower you together through their spiritual powers.

Furthermore, by virtue of the power of the past vows and majestic spiritual authority of the Tathāgata Vairocana, as well as the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, you have entered this samādhi and are enabled to preach the Dharma."

In order to increase Buddha-wisdom, to enter deeply into the Dharma-realm, to thoroughly understand the realm of sentient beings, to achieve unimpeded entry, to practice without obstruction, to attain peerless skillful means, to enter the nature of all-knowledge, to awaken to all phenomena, to know all faculties, and to be able to uphold and expound all teachings— namely,
to initiate the ten stages of dwelling of all Bodhisattvas.
“Good son! You should expound this Dharma by relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.

At that time, all the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dharmamati unimpeded wisdom, unattached wisdom, uninterrupted wisdom, non-deluded wisdom, non-differentiated wisdom, unfailing wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unsurpassed wisdom, untiring wisdom, and unassailable wisdom.
Why is this? It is because the power of this samādhi is such that the nature of dharmas is thus.
At that time, each of the Buddhas extended his right hand and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati.
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati arose from that samādhi and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
The dwelling place of a bodhisattva is vast, equal to the dharma-realm and space."
O Sons of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattvas dwell in the house of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; I shall now explain how those Bodhisattvas so dwell.
O Sons of the Buddha!
There are ten abodes of bodhisattvas, which have been taught, will be taught, and are now being taught by all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
What are these ten?

They are: the stage of initial resolve, the stage of purifying the ground, the stage of practice, the stage of noble birth, the stage of perfecting skillful means, the stage of right mind, the stage of non-retrogression, the stage of youthful truth, the stage of the prince, and the stage of consecration.
This is called the ten abodes of bodhisattvas, as taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva’s abode of the initial resolve?"

This bodhisattva beholds the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose physical appearance is upright and majestic, whose marks and signs are perfect, who is a joy for all to behold, who is difficult to encounter, and who possesses great majestic power;
or they behold his supernormal powers;
or they hear his prophetic declarations.
Either they listen to the instructions and admonitions;
or they see sentient beings undergoing various intense sufferings;
or they hear of the vast Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata, thereby giving rise to the bodhicitta and seeking omniscience.
This bodhisattva generates the mind by taking ten kinds of rare dharmas as objects.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

The knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the retribution of good and evil karma; the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings; the knowledge of the differences in various inclinations; the knowledge of the differences in various elements; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the knowledge of the meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis; the unimpeded knowledge of past lives; the unimpeded knowledge of the divine eye; and the knowledge of the universal exhaustion of outflows throughout the three periods of time.
These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are: diligently making offerings to the Buddhas;

delighting in dwelling within birth and death; acting as a leader for the world to cause them to eliminate evil karma; constantly practicing instruction through the supreme and wondrous Dharma; praising the unsurpassed Dharma; studying the merits of the Buddhas; being born before all Buddhas and always receiving their protection; skillfully expounding the samādhi of tranquility; praising the distancing from the cycle of birth and death; and acting as a place of refuge for suffering sentient beings.
Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause the Bodhisattva’s mind to expand further within the Buddha-dharma;
so that whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves, without relying on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground?
In this dwelling, the Bodhisattva gives rise to ten kinds of mind toward all sentient beings.”
What are these ten? They are:

the mind of benefit, the mind of great compassion, the mind of peace and happiness, the mind of abiding securely, the mind of pity, the mind of gathering [beings], the mind of protection, the mind of regarding others as oneself, the mind of a teacher, and the mind of a guide.
These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are: reciting and practicing what one has heard;

dwelling in empty leisure and tranquility; associating with virtuous friends; speaking with harmony and joy; always knowing the proper time for speech; having no timidity or fear in the mind; thoroughly understanding the meaning; practicing in accordance with the Dharma; remaining far removed from delusion and confusion; and abiding securely without wavering.
Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause the bodhisattva to increase great compassion toward all sentient beings;
so that whatever Dharma they hear, they will immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s dwelling of cultivation?
This Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena through ten kinds of practices.”
What are these ten? They are as follows:

contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are empty; all phenomena are selfless; all phenomena are without agency; all phenomena are without flavor; all phenomena do not correspond to their names; all phenomena have no location; all phenomena are free from conceptual discrimination; and all phenomena lack solidity.
These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be exhorted to study ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are:

observing the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, and the realm of worlds; observing the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element; and observing the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause the bodhisattva’s wisdom to be clear and lucid;
so that whatever Dharma he hears, he immediately understands it for himself, without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of Noble Birth?
This Bodhisattva is born from the holy teaching and accomplishes ten dharmas.”
What are these ten? They are as follows:

never regressing from the presence of all Buddhas; generating profound pure faith; skillfully observing the Dharma; and thoroughly understanding sentient beings, lands, worlds, karmic actions, retributions, birth and death, and nirvana.
These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are:

to fully comprehend all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present; to cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present; to bring to perfection all Buddha-dharmas of the past, future, and present; and to realize the equality of all Buddhas.
Why is this? It is because they desire to advance so that their minds may attain equanimity throughout the three periods of time;
and whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s dwelling that is fully endowed with skillful means?

This Bodhisattva cultivates all roots of goodness for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, benefiting all sentient beings, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, having compassion for all sentient beings, delivering all sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to be free from all calamities, causing all sentient beings to emerge from the suffering of birth and death, causing all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith, causing all sentient beings to be completely tamed, and causing all sentient beings to realize nirvana.”
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas. What are these ten?

That is to say: knowing that sentient beings are boundless; knowing that sentient beings are immeasurable; knowing that sentient beings are innumerable; knowing that sentient beings are inconceivable; knowing that sentient beings have immeasurable forms; knowing that sentient beings are unfathomable; knowing that sentient beings are empty; knowing that sentient beings are without activity; knowing that sentient beings possess nothing; and knowing that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature.
Why is this? It is because he desires to cause his mind to become further increased and superior, remaining free from all attachments;
so that whatever Dharma he hears, he immediately understands it for himself without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of the Rectified Mind?
This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, and their mind remains settled and unshakable.”
What are these ten? They are as follows:
whether hearing praise of the Buddha or disparagement of the Buddha, one’s mind remains fixed and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma, their mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing praise or disparagement of bodhisattvas, their mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing praise or disparagement of the practices performed by bodhisattvas, their mind remains steadfast and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing it said that sentient beings are finite or infinite, their minds remain settled and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing it said that sentient beings are defiled or undefiled, their minds remain settled and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing it said that sentient beings are easy to deliver or difficult to deliver, their minds remain settled and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing it said that the dharma-realm is finite or infinite, his mind remains settled and immovable within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing it said that the dharma-realm has formation or disintegration, his mind remains settled and immovable within the Buddha-dharma;
hearing it said that the dharma-realm exists or does not exist, his mind remains settled and immovable within the Buddha-dharma.
These are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten dharmas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

all phenomena are signless; all phenomena are without substance; all phenomena cannot be cultivated; all phenomena are non-existent; all phenomena lack reality; all phenomena are empty; all phenomena are without intrinsic nature; all phenomena are like illusions; all phenomena are like dreams; all phenomena are without discrimination.

Why is this? It is because he wishes to cause their minds to advance even further, so that they may attain the non-retrogressive patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
such that whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Non-retrogression?
This Bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings and becomes firm and non-retrogressive.”
What are the ten? They are as follows:
hearing that there are Buddhas or that there are no Buddhas, one’s mind does not regress from within the Buddha-dharma;
Hearing that dharmas exist or do not exist, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there are bodhisattvas or no bodhisattvas, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there are bodhisattva practices or no bodhisattva practices, one’s mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing that there are bodhisattvas who practice for transcendence and those who do not practice for transcendence, their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there were Buddhas in the past or that there were no Buddhas in the past, their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there will be Buddhas in the future or that there will be no Buddhas in the future, their minds do not regress from the Buddha-dharma.
Hearing that there is a Buddha in the present or that there is no Buddha in the present, their mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that the Buddha’s wisdom is finite or that the Buddha’s wisdom is infinite, their mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that the three periods of time are of one single characteristic or that the three periods of time are not of one single characteristic, their mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma.
These are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten kinds of vast dharmas.

What are these ten? They are as follows: explaining the one as the many; explaining the many as the one; the phrasing following the meaning; the meaning following the phrasing; the non-existent as existent; the existent as non-existent; the signless as having signs; that which has signs as being signless; the absence of intrinsic nature as having intrinsic nature; and that which has intrinsic nature as being without intrinsic nature.
Why is this? It is because they desire to advance further, being well able to transcend all phenomena;
whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Abode of Youthful Truth?
This Bodhisattva abides in ten kinds of activities.”

What are these ten? They are: faultless conduct of body, faultless conduct of speech, and faultless conduct of mind; taking birth at will; knowing the various desires of sentient beings; knowing the various inclinations of sentient beings; knowing the various elements of sentient beings; knowing the various karmas of sentient beings; knowing the formation and destruction of worlds; mastery over the supernormal powers; and unimpeded movement wherever one goes.
These are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten kinds of dharmas.

What are these ten? They are: knowing all buddha-fields; shaking all buddha-fields; sustaining all buddha-fields; observing all buddha-fields; traveling to all buddha-fields; roaming through countless worlds; receiving countless buddha-dharmas; manifesting transformation bodies with sovereign mastery; emitting vast sounds that pervade everywhere; and serving and making offerings to countless Buddhas in a single kṣaṇa.
Why is this? It is because they wish to cause [the practitioner] to progress further, so that they may attain skillfulness regarding all phenomena;
whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling of the Prince?
This Bodhisattva skillfully knows ten kinds of dharmas.”

What are these ten? They are: skillfully knowing the births of all sentient beings; skillfully knowing the manifestation of all afflictions; skillfully knowing the continuity of habitual tendencies; skillfully knowing the expedient means of practice; skillfully knowing immeasurable dharmas; skillfully understanding all modes of conduct; skillfully knowing the distinctions between worlds; skillfully knowing the events of the past and future limits; skillfully knowing how to expound upon conventional truth; and skillfully knowing how to expound upon the ultimate truth.
These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study ten kinds of dharmas.
What are these ten? They are:

skillfulness in the station of the Dharma King, the regulations of the station of the Dharma King, the palace of the station of the Dharma King, the entry into the station of the Dharma King, the observation of the station of the Dharma King, the consecration of the Dharma King, the empowerment of the Dharma King, the fearlessness of the Dharma King, the repose of the Dharma King, and the praise of the Dharma King.
Why is this? It is because they desire to progress with minds free from hindrance;
whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Empowerment?
This Bodhisattva attains the accomplishment of ten kinds of knowledge.”
What are these ten? They are: shaking countless worlds;

illuminating countless worlds; sustaining countless worlds; traveling to countless worlds; purifying countless worlds; revealing the teachings to countless sentient beings; observing countless sentient beings; knowing the faculties of countless sentient beings; causing countless sentient beings to enter [the path]; and causing countless sentient beings to be disciplined.
These are the ten.
O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva’s body and bodily actions, his miraculous manifestations, and his accomplishment of Buddha-lands through wisdom of the past, future, and present—his mental sphere and sphere of wisdom are both unknowable, such that even Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-princes cannot know them.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva should be encouraged to study the ten kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas. What are these ten?

That is to say: knowledge of the three periods of time; knowledge of the Buddha-dharma; unimpeded knowledge of the dharma-realm; boundless knowledge of the dharma-realm; knowledge that fills all worlds; knowledge that universally illumines all worlds; knowledge that sustains all worlds; knowledge of all sentient beings; knowledge of all phenomena; and knowledge of the infinite Buddhas.
Why is this? It is because they desire to increase all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
whatever Dharma they hear, they immediately understand it for themselves without depending on the instruction of others.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.

That is to say: they moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; they rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; they surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; they quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; they roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; they crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed equally everywhere.

Heavenly exquisite flowers, heavenly powdered incense, heavenly flower garlands, heavenly blended perfumes, heavenly precious robes, heavenly clouds of jewels, and heavenly ornaments rained down; the various celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, emitting great radiance and sublime sounds.
Thus, upon the summit of Mount Sumeru in this world-system of four continents, above the palace of Śakra, he preached the Dharma of the Ten Abodes and manifested various supernatural transformations;
likewise, it was so in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from each of the ten directions, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, there came ten times the number of bodhisattvas as the atoms in a buddha-field; they filled the ten directions and spoke these words:
"Excellent!..."
Excellent! Son of the Buddha, you have well expounded this Dharma!
We all share the same name:
Dharmamati; the lands from which they have come are all named Dharmamegha;
The Tathāgatas in those lands are all named Wondrous Dharma (Miaofa).
In the presence of our Buddhas as well, the Ten Abodes are likewise taught.
The assembly and its retinue, as well as the words and their meanings, are all likewise, without increase or decrease.
O Son of the Buddha!
We have come to this assembly by the Buddha’s spiritual power to bear witness for you.
"Just as it is in this assembly, so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm, and spoke in verse:
"I behold the most supreme wisdom and the subtle, wondrous body, Whose marks and signs are perfectly complete and dignified; ... (the rest of the verses follow)"
Thus, with such profound respect and recognizing how difficult it is to encounter [a Buddha], the Bodhisattva courageously first resolves their mind.
Seeing peerless great supernormal powers, hearing the explanations of the reading of minds and the instructions,
and perceiving the immeasurable sufferings of sentient beings in the various realms of existence, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves their mind.
Having heard that the Tathāgatas, the Universally Victorious Honored Ones, have accomplished all merits and virtues,
being like space and free from discrimination, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
The causality of the three periods of time is called the possible; our own self-nature is the impossible.
Desiring to fully understand this true meaning, the bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
All wholesome and unwholesome karmas throughout the past, future, and present worlds—
desiring to know them all completely and without exception, the bodhisattva thus first resolves upon the mind of enlightenment.
Regarding all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis— whether defiled, pure, or of infinite varieties—
if they wish to fully understand their entry, abiding, and emergence, bodhisattvas therefore first resolve their minds on enlightenment.
According to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, and their various powers of diligence—
desiring to fully comprehend and discern them all— the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
All sentient beings have various understandings, And their inclinations and preferences differ;
To fully know such infinite desires, The Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
The various realms of sentient beings are each distinct, and all worlds are immeasurable;
wishing to fully comprehend their essential nature, the bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
All conditioned paths of practice, each having its own destination—
desiring to fully understand their true nature, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
All sentient beings in all worlds, drifting with their karma without a moment's rest, desire to obtain the divine eye to see clearly;
for this reason, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
Whatever existed in past lives, with such a nature and such characteristics—
desiring to fully know those former abodes, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind.
All sentient beings' various fetters and delusions, their continuous manifestation and their latent tendencies—
if they wish to fully understand these and bring them to ultimate exhaustion, the Bodhisattva, for this reason, first generates the mind of enlightenment.
In accordance with the various ways sentient beings are established, and through all manner of discourses and linguistic paths,
desiring to know them exactly as they are according to worldly convention— by this, the Bodhisattva first resolves their mind upon enlightenment.
All phenomena are beyond verbal expression; their nature is empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.
Desiring to fully comprehend this true meaning, the Bodhisattva thus first generates the mind of enlightenment.
Wishing to cause all lands in the ten directions to tremble, To overturn all the great oceans,
And to be fully endowed with the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas— For these reasons, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
Wishing to emit light from a single pore To universally illuminate the infinite lands of the ten directions,
And within each ray of light to awaken all beings— It is for this that the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind.
Wishing to place all inconceivable Buddha-fields within the palm of one's hand without causing them to move,
and understanding that all things are like illusions and transformations— by this, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment.
Wishing to place the sentient beings of immeasurable lands upon the tip of a single hair without any crowding,
knowing fully that there is no person and no self— the Bodhisattva generates the initial resolve by means of this.
Wishing to take a drop of seawater with a single hair and cause all great oceans to be completely exhausted,
while knowing their respective quantities— one such is the bodhisattva’s first production of the mind of enlightenment.
All inconceivable world-systems, reduced to dust until not a single remnant remains—
if one wishes to discern and know their total number, it is for this that the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past and future, Regarding all the signs of the formation and destruction of every world,
Desiring to fully comprehend them and exhaust their limits, The Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
To know, without exception, the Dharma of all Tathāgatas of the three times, as well as that of all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—
for this purpose, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment.
If one wished to lift up with a single hair all the infinite and boundless worlds,
and to fully comprehend their essential nature and characteristics, it is for this reason that the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
Countless and immeasurable Cakravāḍa mountains, He wishes to cause them all to enter into a single pore;
Knowing each according to its size, The Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
Wishing to employ a single, wondrous, tranquil voice, To universally respond to all beings throughout the ten directions according to their kind,
Causing them all to understand with pure clarity— For this reason, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
Regarding all the linguistic expressions of sentient beings, there is not a single word they proclaim that is not fully exhausted;
desiring to thoroughly understand their intrinsic nature, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
They produce every kind of worldly speech and sound, causing all beings to understand and realize nirvana;
desiring such a wondrous faculty of the tongue, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves their mind on enlightenment.
Desiring to cause all worlds throughout the ten directions— both those in the process of formation and destruction— to be seen,
and knowing that they all arise from conceptual discrimination, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, immeasurable Tathāgatas completely fill them;
desiring to fully understand the Buddha-dharma of them all, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves his mind.
With various transformations of immeasurable bodies, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds,
desiring to fully comprehend that they arise from the mind, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves upon the path.
To fully comprehend in a single thought-moment all the Tathāgatas— immeasurable and innumerable— of the past, future,
and present worlds, for this reason the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
If one were to fully expound upon a single phrase of the Dharma for incalculable eons without exhaustion,
yet cause both its words and meanings to appear distinct in each instance— for this reason, the Bodhisattva first resolves his mind on enlightenment.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions, with their characteristics of flowing, turning, arising, and ceasing—
desiring to clearly comprehend them all in a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind upon enlightenment.
With body, speech, and mental actions, they go everywhere throughout the ten directions without obstruction;
realizing that the three periods of time are all empty and quiescent, the Bodhisattva thus first resolves their mind.
Once the bodhisattva has thus resolved their mind, they should be sent to the lands of the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Tathāgatas, thereby ensuring that they never regress.
The Bodhisattva seeks the Buddha-way with valor, dwelling within birth and death without weariness;
for their sake, he offers praise so that they may practice accordingly, thus causing them never to regress.
In the immeasurable lands of the worlds of the ten directions, he acts as the honored lord within them all;
for the sake of all bodhisattvas, he speaks thus, thereby causing them to never regress.
The most excellent, supreme, and foremost, profound, subtle, and pure Dharma—
exhorting all bodhisattvas to explain it to others, thus teaching them to be free from afflictions.
Peerless throughout all worlds, a state that cannot be shaken or overcome,
he is constantly praised by those bodhisattvas, who thus instruct him so that he does not regress.
The Buddha is the Great Powerful Lord of the world, Fully endowed with all merits and virtues;
Causing all bodhisattvas to dwell therein, He is the Supreme Man by virtue of this teaching.
To the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, they go to all and draw near;
always sustained by the Buddhas, they are thus instructed so as not to regress.
All the various samādhis of tranquility, He expounds and elucidates them all without exception;
For the sake of those bodhisattvas he speaks thus, Thereby causing them never to regress.
Having crushed the wheel of birth and death within all realms of existence, you turn the pure and wondrous wheel of Dharma;
unattached to anything in all the worlds, you speak thus for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
All sentient beings have fallen into evil realms, Bound and oppressed by immeasurable, heavy sufferings;
To act as their protection and place of refuge, He speaks thus for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
This is the Bodhisattva’s stage of generating the mind of awakening, Resolutely seeking the unsurpassed path;
Just as I have taught these instructions, So too do all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in the second stage, the Stage of Refining the Ground, should give rise to this thought:
"May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions be made to follow entirely the teachings of the Tathāgata."
A mind of great compassion for the benefit and peace of others, A mind abiding in loving-kindness that gathers and protects,
A mind that guards all sentient beings as oneself, A mind that regards them as teachers and guides.
Having already abided in such a supreme and wondrous mind, one should next practice recitation and study to seek extensive learning;
always delighting in tranquility and right reflection, one should draw near to all spiritual friends.
His speech is harmonious and pleasant, free from coarseness; he speaks with certainty of the right time and without fear.
He thoroughly understands the meaning and acts in accordance with the Dharma, remaining unmoved by delusion or ignorance.
This is the initial training in the conduct of awakening; those who can practice this conduct are true children of the Buddha.
I shall now explain what they ought to practice; thus should the children of the Buddha train with diligence.
The third stage, the Bodhisattva’s Abiding in Practice, Should diligently observe, in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching,
That all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty, Devoid of self or person, and lacking any activity.

All phenomena are not to be delighted in; they are without names, without location, without conceptual differentiation, and without reality. One who contemplates in this manner is called a bodhisattva.
Next, one should cause them to observe the realm of sentient beings, and likewise encourage the observation of the dharma-realm;
as for the distinctions of all worlds without exception, one should encourage the observation of them all.
The worlds of the ten directions and empty space, All earth, water, fire, and wind,
The realms of desire, form, and formlessness— Exhort them all to observe these until they are fully exhausted.
Observing the various distinctions of those realms and thoroughly exhausting their essential natures,
one who attains such teachings and practices them with diligence is called a true son of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva in the fourth stage, Dwelling in Noble Birth, is born from the teachings of all the sages;
having thoroughly realized that all realms of existence are non-existent, they transcend those phenomena and give birth to the Dharma-realm.
Faith in the Buddha is firm and indestructible; contemplating the quiescence of phenomena, the mind dwells in peace.
One thoroughly understands all sentient beings, knowing that their essential nature is illusory and lacks any reality.
The worlds, lands, karma, and its retribution, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana—all are thus.
A son of the Buddha contemplates phenomena in this way; born directly from the Buddha, they are called sons of the Buddha.

Regarding all the Buddha-dharmas existing within the past, future, and present ages, he thoroughly understands their accumulation and perfection; thus he trains until reaching the ultimate consummation.
All Tathāgatas of the three periods of time can observe them all as equal;
since no various distinctions can be found, those who observe in this way penetrate the three periods of time.
That which I have thus extolled and praised Is the merit of those dwelling in the four stages;
If one can practice diligently according to the Dharma, One will swiftly attain the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.
From this, the fifth stage of all Bodhisattvas is called the "Abode Endowed with Skillful Means";
having deeply entered immeasurable skillful means, they give rise to the ultimate karma of merit.
The manifold merits cultivated by Bodhisattvas are all for the sake of rescuing and protecting all living beings;
with single-minded intent they provide benefit and peace, and with constant compassion they cause them to attain liberation.
For the sake of all worlds, he eliminates manifold hardships, drawing forth those in the realms of existence and causing them joy;
he tames each and every being without exception, leading them all to possess virtue and turn toward Nirvana.
All sentient beings are without limit— Immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, And beyond all measure; They listen to and receive such a Dharma as this from the Tathāgata.
This fifth stage belongs to the true sons of the Buddha, who accomplish skillful means to deliver sentient beings;
these Honored Ones of Great Wisdom and all virtues reveal the Dharma in this manner.

The sixth is the dwelling of the perfection of right mind: Unconfused regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena, One contemplates with right mindfulness, free from conceptualization; Neither gods nor humans can cause such a one to waver.
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma, Of bodhisattvas and their various practices, Whether sentient beings are finite or infinite,
Whether they are defiled or undefiled, easy or difficult to deliver, Whether the dharma-realm is large or small, or subject to formation and destruction—
If the mind remains unmoved whether [these things] exist or do not exist, [one attains non-regression].
Past, future, and present—contemplate and reflect upon these with constant certainty.
All phenomena are devoid of marks; they have no substance, no intrinsic nature, and are empty and unreal.
Like illusions and dreams, they are free from conceptual discrimination; always delight in hearing such meanings.
The seventh is the non-regressing bodhisattva, who, regarding the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the bodhisattva practices— whether they exist or do not exist, whether they emerge or do not emerge— hears these teachings and yet does not regress.
In the past, future, and present worlds, whether all Buddhas exist or do not exist, whether the Buddha’s wisdom is finite or infinite, the three times are of one mark yet possess manifold marks;
the one is many, and the many are one. The letter follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the letter.
All these things are established through mutual dependence; this should be explained to those who do not regress.

Whether phenomena possess marks or are markless, whether phenomena possess intrinsic nature or lack it—having heard how these various distinctions are mutually interconnected, such a person attains the ultimate.
The eighth bodhisattva stage, the Abode of Youthful Innocence, Is fully perfected in the conduct of body, speech, and mind;
All is pure and free from all faults, Attaining mastery over taking birth according to one's will.
He knows the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, The various differences in their modes of understanding,
As well as all phenomena, And the signs of formation and destruction of the lands in the ten directions.
Having attained swift and wondrous supernormal powers, they travel to all places at will;
in the presence of all Buddhas they listen to the Dharma, praising its practice without weariness.
They thoroughly know all Buddha-fields, shaking them and sustaining them through their empowerment;
transcending immeasurable buddha-lands, they travel through worlds of infinite number.
They inquire about all incalculable dharmas; they possess complete mastery over the bodies they wish to assume;
their skillful speech and tones reach everywhere; and they serve all the countless Buddhas.
The ninth stage of the Bodhisattva Prince: He is able to perceive the differences in the births of sentient beings;
There is no affliction, whether manifest or habitual, that he does not know; And all the skillful means he employs, he thoroughly understands.
The various dharmas differ in their modes of conduct, and the worlds vary across the limits of past and future;
whether in terms of worldly convention or ultimate truth, he understands them all perfectly and without exception.
The Dharma King skillfully establishes various abodes; according to each such place, there are its respective dharmas.
If one enters the palace of the Dharma King, one beholds all that is seen therein.
The empowerment rites possessed by the Dharma King, Empowered by his spiritual power and free from fear,
Along with instructions on the palace chambers and eulogies— By these he instructs the Dharma Prince.
Thus he taught them exhaustively, causing their minds to be free from attachment;
by understanding this and practicing right mindfulness, all Buddhas appear before them.
The tenth consecration, for the true sons of the Buddha, brings to fulfillment the supreme, foremost Dharma;
throughout the countless worlds of the ten directions, they are able to cause them all to tremble as their light shines everywhere.
The Abbot proceeds without any remainder; pure and adorned, he is fully complete.
He reveals the teachings to countless sentient beings, observing and knowing their faculties entirely.
Their resolve to subdue beings is likewise boundless, Causing all to advance toward great enlightenment;
They observe the entirety of the Dharma-realm And travel to every land throughout the ten directions.
The body therein and its activities, And the manifestations of supernatural powers, are difficult to fathom;
The realms of all Buddha-lands throughout the three periods of time— Even the Prince was unable to comprehend them.
The wisdom that perceives all as the knower of the three times, The wisdom that clearly understands all Buddha-dharmas,
The unimpeded and boundless wisdom regarding the dharma-realm, The wisdom that fills all worlds,
The wisdom that illuminates and sustains the worlds, And the wisdom that thoroughly knows all phenomena of sentient beings.
And knowing the boundless wisdom of perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata explains it all so that they may fully comprehend it.
Thus, these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are all born through transformation from the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
according to their respective meritorious practices, no devas or humans can fathom them.
In the past, future, and present ages, those who have resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood are boundless;
they fill all the lands of the ten directions, and there are none who shall not attain omniscience.
All lands are without limit; so too are the worlds, sentient beings, and phenomena.
With their various distinctions of delusion, karma, mind, and inclinations, they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment based upon those very conditions.

Even the single thought-moment with which one first seeks the Buddha-way is something that worldly beings and those of the two vehicles cannot know; how much more so, then, the remaining meritorious practices!
All the worlds throughout the ten directions, one could lift up entirely with a single hair;
such a person can know this son of the Buddha, who proceeds toward the conduct of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
All the great oceans throughout the ten directions, Could be made to vanish drop by drop with the tip of a hair;
Yet such a person can know the meritorious deeds Cultivated in a single thought-moment by this Son of the Buddha.
If all worlds were ground into dust, one could distinguish and know their total number;
only such a person as this can perceive the path traversed by these Bodhisattvas.
The Buddhas of the ten directions— past, future, and present— as well as all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, have all,
through various kinds of wondrous eloquence, revealed and taught the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
The merit of generating the mind of enlightenment is immeasurable; it fills the entire realm of sentient beings.
Even if all wisdom were to speak together, they could not exhaustively describe it—how much less so the other various sublime practices!
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Sixteen;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 16: On the Holy Life (Brahmacarya).
At that time, the Devaputra Samyaksmṛti addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
All the assemblies of bodhisattvas in all worlds, relying on the teachings of the Tathāgata, dye their robes and leave the household life.
How do they attain the purity of the brahmacarya, and proceed from the stage of a bodhisattva to the path of unsurpassed bodhi?
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates the pure conduct (brahmacarya), they should take ten dharmas as their objects of focus and observe them with mental attention."
That is to say:
the body, bodily action; speech, verbal action; the mind, mental action; the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts.
One should contemplate them in this way:
Is the body itself the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
or even is it the precepts that constitute the holy life?

If the body were the holy life, one should know that the holy life would then be non-virtuous, contrary to the Dharma, turbid, foul-smelling, impure, loathsome, antagonistic, defiled, like a corpse, and a gathering place for worms.

If bodily action were the holy life (*brahmacarya*), then the holy life would consist of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; looking to the left and right; bending and stretching; and bowing and raising the head.

If speech were the holy life, then the holy life would consist of sounds and breaths; the lips, tongue, throat, and palate; the exhaling and inhaling, the restraining and releasing, and the high and low, the clear and the turbid tones.

If vocal action were the holy life (*brahmacarya*), then the holy life would consist of rising from one's seat, greeting others, brief explanations, detailed explanations, indirect explanations, direct explanations, praising explanations, disparaging explanations, formal expositions, conventional explanations, and clarifying explanations.

If the mind were the holy life (*brahmacarya*), then the holy life would be awakening, contemplation, discrimination, various forms of discrimination, mindfulness, various forms of mindfulness, reflection, various forms of reflection, illusion, and dreaming.
If mental action were the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should know that the holy life would then consist of thought, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, suffering and pleasure, sorrow and joy.

"Is right livelihood the precepts?
Having contemplated thus, one has nothing to grasp in the body, nothing to cling to in cultivation, and nothing to dwell upon in phenomena;
the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present is empty and quiescent.
There is no doer of deeds, nor is there one who experiences their retribution;
this world does not shift, and the next world does not change.
Among these, what dharma is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
From where does the holy life come?
To whom does it belong?
What is its essential nature?
By whom is it made?
Is it existent, or is it non-existent?
Is it form, or is it non-form?
Is this feeling, or is it not feeling?
Is this perception, or is it not perception?
Is this volitional formation, or is it not volitional formation?

Is this consciousness, or is it not consciousness? Observing in this way, because the dharmas of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) cannot be apprehended; because the dharmas of the three periods of time are all empty and quiescent; because the mind has no grasping or attachment; because the heart has no hindrance; because one's conduct is non-dual; because skillful means are sovereign; because one receives the dharma of signlessness; because one contemplates the dharma of signlessness; because one knows the equality of the Buddha-dharmas; and because one is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas—this is called the pure holy life.
"Furthermore, one should cultivate ten kinds of dharmas.
What are these ten? They are as follows: "

The knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the retribution of karma in the past, present, and future; the knowledge of all meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis; the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings; the knowledge of their various inclinations; the knowledge of their various elements; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the unimpeded knowledge of the divine eye; the unimpeded knowledge of past lives; and the knowledge of the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies.
One should examine each of the Tathāgata’s ten powers one by one;
within each power, there are immeasurable meanings, all of which should be inquired about.
Having heard them, one should give rise to great compassion and observe sentient beings without abandoning them.
They contemplate all phenomena without ceasing;
they perform unsurpassed deeds without seeking their karmic rewards;
and they thoroughly understand that all realms are like illusions and dreams, like shadows and echoes, and like magical transformations.

If bodhisattvas can accord with such contemplative practice, they will not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena; all Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before them, and at the very moment of their first resolve, they will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Knowing that all phenomena are the very nature of mind, they will accomplish the body of wisdom, awakening through no other.

“O Son of the Buddha!

“O Son of the Buddha!

If one compares the merit of this person to the merit of a Bodhisattva’s initial resolve to attain enlightenment, it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part; indeed, it does not even equal a fraction of an *upaniṣad*.”
Why is this? Sons of the Buddha!

When all Buddhas first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, it is not merely for the sake of providing all manner of articles of pleasure to all sentient beings throughout ten *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the ten directions for a hundred kalpas, or even for a hundred thousand *nayuta* of billions of kalpas, that they resolve upon bodhicitta.

It is not merely for the sake of teaching so many sentient beings to cultivate the five precepts and the path of ten wholesome actions, to teach them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments, or to teach them to realize the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and the path of pratyekabuddha that one generates the bodhicitta; rather,
it is for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is never interrupted,
for the sake of pervading all worlds, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings in all worlds, and for the sake of fully knowing the formation and destruction of all worlds.
In order to fully know the defilement and purity of sentient beings in all worlds; in order to fully know the intrinsic purity of all worlds;
in order to fully know the mental inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
in order to fully know the death here and birth there of all sentient beings; in order to fully know the one...
They resolve their minds upon unexcelled bodhi for the sake of skillful means regarding the faculties of all sentient beings;
for the sake of fully knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings; for the sake of fully knowing the wisdom of all sentient beings across the three periods of time;
and for the sake of fully knowing the equality of the realms of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment.
Suppose there were a person who, in a single instant, could pass through incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*) to the east;”
If one were to continue thinking in this manner for as many *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as there are, no one would be able to know the limit of these worlds.
Furthermore, suppose a second person were able, in a single moment of thought, to pass through all the worlds that the former person passed through during those *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
and if he were to do so for just as many *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as well.
Proceeding in succession from one to the next, up to the tenth direction—
namely, the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below— it is likewise so. O Son of the Buddha!
Within these ten directions, suppose there were a hundred people, each of whom traversed as many worlds as described above;

Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

It is not that Bodhisattvas set a limit, thinking they will resolve their minds on enlightenment merely to go to so many worlds and attain knowledge therein; rather, they do so for the sake of [universal] realization.
They resolve their minds on enlightenment in order to know the worlds of the ten directions.
That is to say:
they wish to thoroughly understand that a sublime world is itself a coarse world, and a coarse world is itself a sublime world;
The upward-facing world is the inverted world, and the inverted world is the upward-facing world;
the small world is the great world, and the great world is the small world;
the broad world is the narrow world, and the narrow world is the broad world.
A single world is an ineffable world, and an ineffable world is a single world;
an ineffable world enters into a single world, and a single world enters into an ineffable world.
A defiled world is a pure world, and a pure world is a defiled world.
If you wish to know the differentiated nature of all worlds within a single hair-tip,
and the unitary nature of a single hair-tip within all worlds;
if you wish to know how all worlds arise from within a single world, and that all worlds are devoid of intrinsic substance.
Desiring to know all vast worlds in their entirety with a single thought-moment without obstruction, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment.

If one were to continue contemplating in this manner for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are, no one would be able to know the limit of the number of those kalpas.

Thus it is explained in detail, up to the tenth direction.

O Son of the Buddha!
The limits of the number of kalpas of formation and destruction in these incalculable worlds of the ten directions may be known;
however, no one is able to know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness from a bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? It is not because a bodhisattva limits themselves to knowing the number of kalpas of formation and destruction for only so many worlds that they resolve their mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
rather, it is because they resolve their mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to know exhaustively, without remainder, the kalpas of formation and destruction of all worlds.
That is to say:
knowing that long eons and short eons are equal, and short eons and long eons are equal;
that one eon and countless eons are equal, and countless eons and one eon are equal.
Eons with Buddhas are equal to eons without Buddhas; eons without Buddhas are equal to eons with Buddhas.
Within a single eon of one Buddha there are unspeakably many Buddhas, and within unspeakably many eons there is but one Buddha.
Eons that are finite are equal to eons that are infinite; eons that are infinite are equal to eons that are finite.
Finite eons are equal to infinite eons, and infinite eons are equal to finite eons;
unspeakable eons are equal to a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is equal to unspeakable eons;
all eons enter into non-eons, and non-eons enter into all eons.

Desiring to fully know, within a single thought-moment, all the kalpas of formation and destruction of all worlds throughout the past, the future, and the present, one resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this is called the "Great Vow Ornamentation of the First Resolve: the Supernormal Wisdom that Knows All Kalpas."
“O Son of the Buddha!

because they wish to fully know the various immeasurable understandings—both wholesome and unwholesome—of the past, present, and future;

Desiring to fully know the profound and secret understanding, the understanding of skillful means, the analytical understanding, the spontaneous understanding, the understanding arising from causes, and the understanding arising from conditions—so that there may be no remainder in the entire web of understandings—they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the merit and roots of goodness from a bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, no one is able to know its limit. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha!

Bodhisattvas do not set limits; they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* not merely for the sake of knowing the various skillful means of sentient beings in such-and-such worlds, but rather to fully know the various skillful means of all sentient beings in all worlds—extensively explained up to—the desire to fully know the entire web of all skillful means; for this reason, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment.
Suppose there were someone who, in a single instant, could know the various and diverse minds of all sentient beings within countless worlds in the eastern direction.

To speak at length, even up to this point: while it may be possible to know the limits of the various and diverse minds of all sentient beings within these worlds of the ten directions, there is no one who can know the limit of the merit and roots of goodness from a bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

It is not for the sake of knowing the minds of only a limited number of sentient beings that a bodhisattva resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; rather, it is for the sake of knowing the minds of all sentient beings.

In order to fully know the various minds of infinite sentient beings throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, and even to exhaustively know the entire web of all minds, they resolve their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Let this analogy be set aside for a moment.
Suppose there were someone who, in a single instant, could know all the various and distinct karmas of all sentient beings within countless worlds in the eastern direction."

To speak at length, up to this point: while it may be possible to know the limits of the various differentiated karmas of sentient beings throughout these ten directions, the limit of the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be known.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

It is not because a bodhisattva limits himself to knowing only so many sentient beings' karma that he resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; rather, it is for the sake of knowing the karma of all sentient beings.

Desiring to fully know the karma of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, and even desiring to fully know the entire web of all karma, they resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment.
Suppose there were someone who, in a single instant, could know the various afflictions of all sentient beings in countless worlds in the eastern direction;”

If one were to contemplate in this manner for as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are thoughts, no one would be able to know the limit of these various distinctions among the afflictions of all beings.
Suppose there were a second person who, in a single moment of thought, could know the distinctions among the afflictions of all beings known by that first person over those asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
and suppose this were repeated until another asaṃkhyeya kalpas had passed.
This is explained in detail in successive order up to the tenth.
It is likewise so for the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
O Son of the Buddha!
The limits of the distinctions among the afflictions of sentient beings throughout these ten directions may be known;
however, the limits of the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be known.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!
It is not for the sake of knowing the afflictions of sentient beings in only so many worlds that a bodhisattva resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; rather, it is without such limitation.
They resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to fully know all the distinctions among the afflictions of all sentient beings throughout all worlds.
That is to say:

they wish to fully know light afflictions, heavy afflictions, dormant afflictions, and active afflictions—the immeasurable distinctions and various types of discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) of each and every sentient being—in order to purify all manner of defilements.
He wishes to fully know the afflictions based on ignorance and those associated with craving, in order to sever all fetters of affliction within the various realms of existence;

he wishes to fully know the afflictions categorized as greed, the afflictions categorized as hatred, the afflictions categorized as delusion, and the afflictions categorized as equal-parts, in order to sever the root of all afflictions;
he wishes to fully know the afflictions of "I," the afflictions of "mine," and the afflictions of "I-conceit," in order to awaken to the total exhaustion of all afflictions without remainder.

Desiring to fully know the root afflictions and secondary afflictions that arise from inverted discrimination, and the sixty-two views that arise from the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), in order to subdue all afflictions;

and desiring to fully know the afflictions of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the afflictions of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), so as to give rise to a mind of great compassion for rescue and protection, sever the net of all afflictions, and cause the nature of omniscience to be pure—one resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment.

Suppose there were someone who, in a single instant, offered all kinds of exquisite foods and drinks, fragrant flowers, garments, banners, flags, and parasols, as well as monasteries, magnificent palaces, jeweled canopies, latticed curtains, variously adorned lion-thrones, and many wonderful gems, to the countless Buddhas of the eastern direction and to all sentient beings within countless worlds; and suppose they continued to honor, revere, prostrate to, praise, and gaze upon them with bowed bodies without interruption for countless eons.”
Furthermore, they exhort those sentient beings, causing them all to likewise make offerings to the Buddha.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, each of them erects a stūpa for him.
Those stūpas are tall and vast, composed of various precious jewels from countless worlds and adorned in manifold ways.
Within each and every stupa, there were countless images of Tathāgatas, whose radiance shone throughout countless worlds for countless kalpas.
It was likewise so in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What do you think? Is the merit of this person not indeed great?
The Deva King said:
“The merit of this person is known only by the Buddha; none others are able to fathom it.
Son of the Buddha!

Compared to the merit of a Bodhisattva’s initial resolve for enlightenment, this person’s merit does not equal even one hundredth part, one thousandth part, one hundred-thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) fraction.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Let us set aside this analogy for a moment.

Suppose there were a second person who, in a single thought-moment, could perform all the acts of making offerings—over the course of countless eons—by both that former person and all sentient beings within countless worlds;”

Maintaining such thoughts in every moment, they offer immeasurable varieties of offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and all sentient beings throughout immeasurable worlds, for immeasurable kalpas.
The third person, and so on up to the tenth person, all likewise do so; in a single thought-moment they are able to perform all the offerings made by the preceding persons.

Moment after moment they continue in this way, using boundless, peerless, incalculable, incomparable, inconceivable, immeasurable, ineffable, and even ineffably ineffable articles of offering to make offerings to boundless—even to ineffably ineffable—Buddhas, as well as to all sentient beings in that many worlds, for boundless—even to ineffably ineffable—aeons.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas were erected for each of them, those stupas being high and vast.
This shall remain so throughout the entire kalpa of abiding.
O Son of the Buddha!

Compared to the merit of a bodhisattva’s initial resolve for enlightenment, these prior merits do not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part; indeed, they do not equal even a single *upaniṣad* (fraction) thereof.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!
It is not for the sake of making offerings to only so many Buddhas that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas resolve their minds on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; rather, they do so without such limitation.

In order to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the unspeakably unspeakable ten directions, as many as exist within the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, they resolve their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having generated this mind, one is able to know the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment and the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas of the past; one is able to have faith in all the roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the future; and one is able to know all the wisdom of all Buddhas of the present.

All the merits possessed by those Buddhas, this bodhisattva is able to believe in, accept, cultivate, attain, know, realize, and accomplish them; they are able to be of one identical nature with all Buddhas.
Why is this? This bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment in order to ensure that the lineage of all Tathāgatas is never interrupted;
he generates the mind of enlightenment in order to pervade all worlds.
They resolve their minds for the sake of liberating all sentient beings in all worlds;
they resolve their minds for the sake of fully knowing the formation and destruction of all worlds;
they resolve their minds for the sake of fully knowing the defilement and purity of all sentient beings.
They resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the purity of the three realms of existence in all worlds;
they resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the mental inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds for the sake of thoroughly knowing the death and rebirth of all sentient beings in this life and the next.
They resolve their minds for the sake of fully knowing the skillful means regarding the faculties of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds for the sake of fully knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings;
they resolve their minds for the sake of fully knowing the wisdom regarding the three periods of time of all sentient beings.

Because of having resolved the mind [for enlightenment], one is constantly remembered by all Buddhas of the three periods of time and shall attain the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
one immediately receives the sublime Dharma from all Buddhas of the three periods of time and becomes equal in essence to all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
having cultivated the auxiliary paths of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one accomplishes the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

They adorn all the unique Buddha-dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and fully attain the wisdom for expounding the Dharma of all Buddhas throughout the entire dharma-realm. Why is this?

Because by generating this mind one shall attain Buddhahood, it should be known that such a person is equal to all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they are equal to the realm of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; they are equal to the merits of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; and they attain the ultimate, equal, and true wisdom of the single body and infinite bodies of a Tathāgata.

At the very moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they are praised together by all the Buddhas of the ten directions; they are able to preach the Dharma to teach and transform all sentient beings in all worlds; they are able to shake all worlds; they are able to illuminate all worlds; they are able to extinguish the sufferings of the evil realms in all worlds; they are able to adorn and purify all lands; they are able to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood within all worlds; they are able to cause all sentient beings to attain joy; they are able to enter the nature of all dharma-realms; they are able to uphold the lineage of all Buddhas; and they are able to obtain the light of wisdom of all Buddhas.
This bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind does not obtain even the slightest thing within the three periods of time— namely,
whether it be the Buddhas or the Buddha-dharmas.
Whether it be a bodhisattva or the qualities of a bodhisattva;
whether it be a pratyekabuddha or the qualities of a pratyekabuddha;
whether it be a śrāvaka or the qualities of a śrāvaka.
Whether it be the mundane or mundane phenomena;
whether it be the supramundane or supramundane phenomena;
whether it be sentient beings or the phenomena of sentient beings.
"Seeking only all-knowledge;
within the dharma-realm, the mind has no attachments.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.

That is to say: it shook, shook everywhere, and shook equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed equally everywhere.

They rained down celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial powdered incense, celestial flower garlands, celestial robes, celestial jewels, and celestial ornaments; they performed celestial music and released celestial light and celestial sounds.

At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, all sharing the same name:
Dharmamati. Each manifested their own body before the Bodhisattva Dharmamati and spoke these words: "Excellent!
Excellent, Dharmamati! That you are now able to expound this Dharma.
We, the Buddhas of ten directions, each as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-lands, also preach this Dharma; all Buddhas speak thus.
When you preached this Dharma, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-lands resolved their minds upon Bodhi.

We now bestow upon them all their predictions: in a future age, after passing through more than a thousand unspeakably many infinite kalpas, they shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood within a single kalpa and appear in the world, all bearing the name Tathāgata Pure Mind, though the worlds in which they dwell shall each be distinct.
We shall all protect and uphold this Dharma, so that all Bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it may hear it in its entirety.
Just as this Dharma is being taught here upon the summit of Mount Sumeru in the four continents of this Sahā world, causing all sentient beings to receive transformation upon hearing it;

so too shall this Dharma be taught in worlds throughout the ten directions—in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas, in numbers infinite, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable—extending to the end of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, teaching and transforming sentient beings therein.
The preachers of the Dharma all share the same name: Dharmamati.

By the spiritual power of the Buddhas, by the power of the World-Honored One’s original vows, and for the purpose of manifesting the Buddha-dharma; for the purpose of universally illuminating with the light of wisdom; for the purpose of expounding the true meaning; for the purpose of causing the realization of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); for the purpose of causing the entire assembly to rejoice; for the purpose of revealing the causes of the Buddha-dharma; for the purpose of attaining equality with all Buddhas; and for the purpose of understanding that the dharma-realm is non-dual—they preach this Dharma in such a manner.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati surveyed all the assemblies in the lands of the ten directions throughout the entirety of space. Desiring to bring all sentient beings to full accomplishment; desiring to completely purify the retributions of all karmic actions; desiring to fully reveal and manifest the pure *dharmadhātu*; desiring to completely uproot the foundations of all defilements; desiring to cause all vast faith and understanding to increase; desiring to cause all to know the faculties of immeasurable sentient beings; desiring to cause all to know the equality of phenomena across the three periods of time; desiring to cause all to observe the realm of *nirvāṇa*;

and desiring to increase his own pure roots of goodness, he received the Buddha’s majestic power and spoke these verses: "To benefit the world, they give rise to the Great Mind, A mind that pervades the ten directions."
Sentient beings, lands, and the phenomena of the three periods of time, The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, that most supreme ocean—
Reaching the ultimate limit of space and equaling the Dharma-realm, To all that exists within every world,
They approach in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas; Thus they resolve their minds, never to regress.
Compassionately mindful of sentient beings, never forsaking them for even a moment, Free from all affliction and harm, universally bestowing benefit;
His radiance illuminates the world as a refuge, And his protection through the Ten Powers is inconceivable.
Entering all lands throughout the ten directions, manifesting every form and appearance,
like the Buddha’s merit and wisdom which are vast and boundless, they cultivate the causes accordingly without attachment.
There are lands situated upright or lying sideways or inverted, Coarse, subtle, vast, and of infinite kinds;
As soon as a Bodhisattva gives rise to the supreme mind, They are able to travel to them all without any hindrance.
The supreme practices of Bodhisattvas are ineffable; they diligently cultivate them all while abiding nowhere.
Seeing all Buddhas, they are ever joyful, universally entering the profound ocean of their Dharma.
Out of compassion for all beings in the five realms of existence, you cause them to remove defilements and become universally pure;
you perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas so that it is never severed, and you utterly destroy the palaces of Māra until nothing remains.
Having already abided in the equanimity of the Tathāgata, And having skillfully cultivated the subtle path of expedient means,
They give rise to faith in the realm of the Buddha, Attaining the Buddha’s consecration with a mind free from attachment.
Mindful of repaying the debt of gratitude owed to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, their resolve is as indestructible as a vajra;
they are able to clearly illuminate the Buddha’s conduct and naturally cultivate the practices of bodhi.
The various distinctions among the realms of existence are immeasurable; the fruits of karma and the mind are likewise not one.
Even the diverse differences in faculties and natures are all clearly perceived by the single arousal of the Great Mind.
His mind is vast and equal to the dharma-realm; Without dependence or change, it is like space.
He advances toward buddha-wisdom without grasping, Thoroughly realizing the limit of reality and free from discrimination.
Knowing the minds of sentient beings, they have no notion of birth; Thoroughly understanding all phenomena, they have no notion of phenomena.
Though they universally discern, there is no discernment; They travel to billions of nayutas of lands.
The wondrous Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable Buddhas, he follows and contemplates, entering them all;
he knows the faculties and conduct of sentient beings without exception, having reached such a state as the World-Honored One.
Always in accord with pure great vows, they joyfully make offerings to the Tathāgatas without ever regressing;
those among humans and devas who behold them can never tire of doing so, and they are constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Their minds are pure and free from dependence; though they contemplate the profound Dharma, they do not grasp it.
Contemplating in this manner for immeasurable eons, they remain unattached throughout the three periods of time.
Their minds are firm and difficult to restrain or discourage; they advance toward the Buddha’s Bodhi without hindrance.
Resolutely seeking the wondrous Way, they eliminate delusion and confusion, traveling throughout the Dharma-realm without complaint of weariness.
Knowing that the nature of all speech and language is utterly quiescent, they enter into True Suchness, transcending all divergent interpretations;
they contemplate all the realms of the Buddhas in accordance with reality, attaining unimpeded minds regarding the three periods of time.
As soon as a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the vast mind, they are able to travel everywhere to the lands of the ten directions;
the Dharma gates are immeasurable and ineffable, and the light of wisdom shines universally, making all clearly understood.
Great compassion that widely delivers others is most peerless;
