The One of All-Knowledge and All-Vision Spoke these words himself:
"The Tathāgata knows all; Therefore, he is inconceivable."
Wisdom does not arise from the absence of wisdom;
the world remains perpetually in darkness, and for this reason, [wisdom] cannot be produced.
Just as form and non-form—these two are not one.
Wisdom and non-wisdom are likewise; their natures are each distinct and different.
Just as with the characterized and the uncharacterized, or birth-and-death and nirvana, their distinctions are each different—so it is with wisdom and non-wisdom.
When the world first comes into being, it possesses no characteristic of decay;
likewise, wisdom and non-wisdom do not exist as two characteristics simultaneously.
Just as the initial thought of a bodhisattva does not coexist with a subsequent thought, [so too are these states].
Wisdom and non-wisdom are likewise; these two minds do not exist simultaneously.
Just as the various groups of consciousnesses are each without mutual conjunction, so it is with wisdom and non-wisdom: ultimately, there is no conjunction between them.
Just as the agada medicine can extinguish all poisons,
so too is the wise person able to extinguish ignorance.
The Tathāgata is unsurpassed, and there is none equal to him.
"Nothing can be compared to it; therefore, it is difficult to encounter.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Diligence, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are without distinction, and there is no one who can know them."
Only Buddhas and Buddhas know this, for their wisdom is ultimate.
Just as gold and the color of gold are in their nature without distinction, so too are phenomena and non-phenomena; in their essential nature, there is no difference.
Sentient beings and non-sentient beings—both lack true reality;
such is the nature of all phenomena: in their ultimate sense, neither exists.
Just as in the future age there is no characteristic of the past, so too is it with these things.
All phenomena are likewise thus; they possess no marks whatsoever.
Just as the marks of arising and ceasing—though manifold—are all unreal, so too are all phenomena: their intrinsic nature is non-existent.
Nirvāṇa cannot be grasped; when explained, it is of two kinds.
All phenomena are likewise so, distinguished by their various differences.
Just as there is that which is counted based on the objects being counted, so too exists the act of counting.
That nature is non-existent; thus one understands phenomena.
Just as in the method of calculation, where one increases from one to the infinite, the numerical phenomena have no intrinsic essence, yet they are distinguished by means of wisdom.
Just as in all worlds, the kalpa-fire has an end, yet space remains undamaged and unimpaired,
so too is the Buddha’s wisdom. Just as sentient beings throughout the ten directions each grasp at the characteristics of space, [so do they perceive the Buddha].
"The Buddhas are also like this; The world merely engages in false discrimination.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Power Forest (Balavana), empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"All realms of sentient beings Are entirely within the three periods of time."
All sentient beings of the three periods of time Dwell entirely within the five aggregates.
The aggregates have karma as their basis; Karma has the mind as its basis.
Mental phenomena are like illusions, And the world is likewise so.
The world is not made by itself, nor is it made by another;
yet its formation occurs, and likewise its destruction occurs.
Although the world has its formation, and although the world has its destruction,
For one who has thoroughly realized the world, these two should not be spoken of:
what constitutes the world, and what does not constitute the world?
The world and the non-world are merely distinctions of names.
The phenomena of the five aggregates throughout the three times are called the "world";
their cessation is the "non-world"—thus they are but provisional designations.
How are the aggregates (skandhas) explained?
What is the nature of the aggregates?
Since the nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished, they are therefore said to be unarisen.
When these aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished—this is the meaning of non-arising.
Since sentient beings are thus, so too are all Buddhas.
The Buddha and all the Buddha-dharmas Have no self-nature whatsoever.
One who can know these dharmas As they truly are, without inversion—
To such a person of universal knowledge and vision, The Buddha is always present before them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest-Walker, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as throughout the worlds of the ten directions, All the various elements of the earth Are devoid of intrinsic nature, Yet there is nowhere they do not pervade."
The Buddha-body is likewise: it pervades all worlds with various forms and appearances, yet has no master and no place of origin.
It is only because of various karmas that it is designated as "sentient beings."
Nor is there any karma to be found apart from sentient beings.

The nature of karma is fundamentally empty and quiescent; it is that upon which sentient beings rely, universally manifesting all manner of forms and appearances, yet having no place from which it comes.
Such are these various forms and marks; the power of karma is inconceivable.
Having thoroughly understood their root, one perceives nothing therein.
The Buddha-body is likewise; it cannot be conceived.
Various forms and appearances universally manifest throughout the lands of the ten directions.
The body is not the Buddha, nor is the Buddha the body;
rather, the Dharma is taken as the body, for one has thoroughly realized all phenomena.
If one can see the Buddha-body, pure as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
this person will have no doubts whatsoever regarding the Buddha’s teachings.
If one sees all phenomena, their intrinsic nature as being like nirvāṇa, [they shall likewise be free from doubt].
This is seeing the Tathāgata, who ultimately abides nowhere.
If one cultivates right mindfulness, one will clearly perceive the Perfectly Awakened One;
being signless and non-conceptual, such a person is called a Dharma Prince.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Awakening, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as a skilled painter Applies various pigments,
Which falsely produce diverse appearances, While the primary elements remain without distinction."
Within the primary elements there is no form; within form there are no primary elements.
Yet, without being separate from the primary elements, form can be apprehended.
Within the mind there is no painting; within the painting there is no mind.
Yet, without departing from the mind, painted images can be obtained.
That mind is ever-abidingly unstable, immeasurable and inconceivable;
it manifests all forms, each of which is unaware of the others.
For example, like a skilled painter, who does not know his own mind,
yet paints by means of that very mind— such is the nature of all phenomena.
The mind is like a skilled painter, capable of painting all worlds.
The five aggregates all arise from it; there is no phenomenon that is not created by it.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.
One should know that both the Buddha and the mind are, in their essential nature, inexhaustible.
If one knows that the movements of the mind universally create all worlds,
such a person sees the Buddha and realizes the true nature of the Buddha.
The mind does not abide in the body, nor does the body abide in the mind.
Yet they are able to perform Buddha-works, with a mastery never before seen.
If one wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Wisdom, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“That which is grasped cannot be grasped; that which is seen cannot be seen;
that which is heard cannot be heard— the single mind is inconceivable.”
The finite and the infinite—neither can be grasped.
If anyone seeks to grasp them, ultimately nothing will be found.
To speak what should not be spoken is to deceive oneself.
If one’s own task is not accomplished, one cannot cause the multitude to rejoice.
Should anyone wish to praise the Tathāgata’s boundlessly wondrous form-body,
even throughout countless eons, none could fully describe it.
Just as a wish-fulfilling gem can manifest all colors,
appearing with color though it is itself colorless, so too are the Buddhas.
Furthermore, like the pure void, they are not material and cannot be seen.
Though manifesting all forms, there is no one who can see their emptiness.
So it is with the Buddhas: they universally manifest immeasurable forms, yet these are beyond the reach of the mind; none at all can behold them.
Although one hears the voice of the Tathāgata, the sound is not the Tathāgata;
yet, without being apart from the sound, one can know the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Awakening has no coming or going, for it is free from all conceptual discrimination.
How can one say that within this, one is able to see?
The Buddhas have no dharma; how could there be any teaching by the Buddha?
It is merely according to their own minds that they say such a dharma is taught.
Chapter 21: The Ten Practices, Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi called "Excellent Contemplation."

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him ten thousand buddhas— each as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields—
all named Guṇakūṭa (Forest of Merit), who addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa, saying: "Excellent!
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to enter this Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation. O Good Man!

This is because all the Buddhas, who are equal in name and as numerous as the atoms within ten thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions, together empower you; it is also due to the power of the past vows and majestic spiritual authority of Vairocana Tathāgata, as well as the power of the roots of goodness of the assembly of Bodhisattvas, which cause you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma.

For the sake of increasing the Buddha-wisdom; for the sake of deeply entering the Dharma-realm; for the sake of thoroughly understanding the realm of sentient beings; because that which is entered is unimpeded; because that which is practiced is without obstruction; because of attaining immeasurable skillful means; because of encompassing the nature of all-knowledge; because of awakening to all phenomena; because of knowing all faculties;
and because of being able to uphold and expound all teachings—namely, the ten kinds of practices initiated by all bodhisattvas.
"Good son! You should expound this Dharma by relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.

At that time, all the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit unimpeded wisdom, unattached wisdom, uninterrupted wisdom, teacherless wisdom, non-deluded wisdom, non-differentiated wisdom, non-failing wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unsurpassed wisdom, untiring wisdom, and unassailable wisdom.
Why is this? It is because of the power of this samādhi; such is the nature of dharmas.
At that time, each of the Buddhas extended his right hand and rubbed the crown of the head of Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit arose from his concentration and addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
The conduct of bodhisattvas is inconceivable; it is equal to the realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space."
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice by training in the way of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as proclaimed by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
What are the ten? First is the practice of joy;

second is the practice of benefiting others; third is the practice of non-opposition; fourth is the practice of non-deflection; fifth is the practice of non-delusion; sixth is the practice of excellent manifestation; seventh is the practice of non-attachment; eighth is the practice that is difficult to attain; ninth is the practice of wholesome dharmas; tenth is the practice of reality. These are the ten.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the joyous practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This bodhisattva acts as a great donor, capable of bestowing all things they possess;
their mind is impartial, free from regret or stinginess, and they do not look for karmic retribution, seek fame, or crave gain and offerings;
they act solely to rescue and protect all sentient beings, to gather in all sentient beings, and to benefit all sentient beings.

To study the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, to recollect the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, to cherish the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, to purify the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, to increase the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, to uphold the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, to manifest the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, and to expound the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas, thereby causing all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate this practice, they cause all sentient beings to feel joy, affection, and delight.
By the power of their vows, wherever there are lands with poverty and deprivation, they take birth there; they become noble, wealthy, and affluent, possessing inexhaustible treasures and riches.
Suppose that in every moment of thought, immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings were to come to the Bodhisattva and say:
"O Benevolent One!
We are destitute and have nothing to sustain us; we are famished, emaciated, and suffering so greatly that our lives are on the verge of ending."
"I only pray that you will take pity on me and grant me your own flesh, so that I may eat it and preserve my life!
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately gave it to him, causing him to rejoice and his heart to be fully satisfied.

When immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings come to beg for alms, the bodhisattva never feels discouraged or intimidated by them; rather, their heart of compassion increases all the more.
Because these sentient beings all come to beg and request, when the bodhisattva sees them, he becomes even more joyful and thinks:
"I have obtained a great benefit!"
"These sentient beings are my field of merit and my virtuous friends; they have come to teach me to enter the Buddha-dharma without being sought or requested.
I should now practice and train in this way, never contravening the minds of all sentient beings."
Furthermore, he formed this thought:

"May all roots of goodness that I have performed, am currently performing, or shall perform in the future cause me to receive a vast body within all worlds and among all sentient beings in the future; with the flesh of this body, may I satisfy all sentient beings suffering from hunger."
"Even if there were but a single small creature that had not yet been fully satiated, may I not relinquish my life; and may the flesh of my body, though being cut away, never be exhausted.
By these roots of goodness, I vow to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and realize Great Nirvana.

I vow that all sentient beings who eat my flesh shall likewise attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, obtain equalizing wisdom, be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, extensively perform the work of a Buddha, and even enter into Nirvana without remainder."
"If even a single sentient being’s mind is not satisfied, I shall never realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this way, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of existence, the notion of a life-force, the notion of diversity, the notion of a person (pudgala), the notion of a human, the notion of a manava, the notion of an agent, and the notion of a recipient.

One should contemplate only the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings as boundless dharmas, empty dharmas, non-existent dharmas, signless dharmas, essence-less dharmas, locationless dharmas, supportless dharmas, and unconditioned dharmas.

When practicing this contemplation, one does not perceive oneself, nor the object given, nor the recipient; one does not perceive the field of merit, nor karma, nor retribution, nor fruit, nor great fruit, nor small fruit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva observed that the bodies received by all sentient beings of the past, future, and present are immediately subject to destruction and dissolution, and he then thought:
"How marvelous!
Sentient beings are deluded and lack wisdom; within the cycle of birth and death, they undergo countless bodies that are precarious and unstable, swiftly returning to destruction.
Whether these bodies have already been destroyed, are currently being destroyed, or are yet to be destroyed, they are unable to seek a stable body by means of this unstable body.

I shall fully learn all that the Buddhas have learned, realize all-knowledge, and know all phenomena, so as to expound for all sentient beings the equality of the three periods of time, the accord with tranquility, and the indestructible nature of reality (dharmatā), causing them to forever attain peace and happiness.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the first practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Practice of Joy.
O Son of the Buddha!"
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of benefiting others?
This bodhisattva upholds pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), remaining mentally unattached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and likewise proclaims this to sentient beings.

He seeks neither power, nor noble lineage, nor wealth, nor physical beauty, nor royal status; being thus entirely without attachment, he steadfastly maintains pure ethical discipline and reflects as follows:

"By upholding the pure precepts, I shall surely abandon all fetters, cravings, torments, hardships, oppressions, slanders, and turbidities, and attain the equal and true Dharma praised by the Buddha."
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva maintains pure precepts in this manner, even if, within a single day, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great and wicked Māras were to come to the bodhisattva’s dwelling, each bringing immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of celestial maidens—all skilled in the arts of the five desires, beautiful and lovely enough to bewitch the human heart—and carrying various kinds of precious playthings, intending to come and disturb the bodhisattva’s resolve for the Path."
At that time, the Bodhisattva formed this thought:
"These five desires are dharmas that obstruct the Path, even hindering unsurpassed Bodhi."
Therefore, they do not give rise to even a single thought of desire; their minds are as pure as the Buddha’s.
They act solely through skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, yet they never abandon the mind of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva does not, for the sake of desire, afflict even a single sentient being; rather, they would sooner sacrifice their own body and life than ever perform an act that afflicts sentient beings.
Since the Bodhisattva first attained the vision of the Buddha, he has never given rise to even a single thought of desire;
how much less would he engage in sexual acts? Were he ever to engage in such acts, it would be impossible.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought only this:
"All sentient beings, throughout the long night, conceive thoughts of the five desires, incline toward the five desires, and are greedily attached to the five desires;
their minds are resolutely immersed and submerged in them, following along with their currents and flowing away, unable to attain mastery."
I should now cause these Māras and all these celestial maidens, as well as all sentient beings, to abide in the unsurpassed precepts;
having abided in the pure precepts, their minds shall never regress from omniscience, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even unto entry into nirvana without remainder.
Why is this? This is the task we ought to perform; we should follow the Buddhas and train in this manner.

Having completed such training, we shall abandon all evil conduct, the conception of a self, and ignorance. Entering into all Buddha-dharmas through wisdom, we shall preach them for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to eliminate their inverted views.
Yet one knows that there are no inversions apart from sentient beings, and no sentient beings apart from inversions;
there are no sentient beings within inversions, nor are there inversions within sentient beings;
furthermore, inversions are not sentient beings, and sentient beings are not inversions.
Perversion is not an internal dharma; perversion is not an external dharma.
Sentient beings are not internal dharmas; sentient beings are not external dharmas.
All phenomena are false and unreal; they arise and perish swiftly, lacking any solidity. They are like dreams, like shadows, like illusions, like transformations—deceiving and deluding the foolish.
One who understands in this way is able to awaken to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), penetrate both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and realize the Bodhi of the Buddha;
having attained deliverance themselves, they cause others to attain deliverance; having attained liberation themselves, they cause others to attain liberation.
Having disciplined oneself, one disciplines others;
having attained tranquility oneself, one brings others to tranquility;
having attained peace oneself, one brings others to peace.
Having become free from defilement oneself, one causes others to be free from defilement;
having become pure oneself, one causes others to be pure;
having attained nirvāṇa oneself, one causes others to attain nirvāṇa.
"I shall bring happiness to myself and cause others to be happy.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva further reflects thus:

"I shall follow all Tathāgatas, depart from all worldly conduct, and be endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas. Abiding in the state of supreme equanimity, I shall regard all sentient beings with equality, clearly penetrate their realms, remain free from all faults, sever all conceptual discriminations, abandon all attachments, and skillfully effect transcendence. My mind shall always dwell securely in the profound wisdom that is supreme, ineffable, non-reliant, immovable, immeasurable, boundless, inexhaustible, and formless."
“O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the second beneficial practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
O Son of the Buddha!”
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of non-opposition?
This bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dharma of patience, remaining humble and respectful;
they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, and do not harm both.
Not taking for oneself, not taking from others, and not taking from both;
not being attached to oneself, not being attached to others, and not being attached to both;
nor seeking fame, reputation, profit, or offerings, but rather forming this thought:

"I shall constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to leave behind all evils, severing greed, hatred, delusion, arrogance, concealment, stinginess, envy, flattery, and deception, and causing them to dwell perpetually in patience and gentleness."
"O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva has accomplished such a dharma of patience,

even if there were hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of sentient beings who came to his presence, and each of those beings were to manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of mouths, and each mouth were to utter hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of words, namely:"

With words that are unpleasant, not in accordance with the wholesome Dharma, disagreeable, unlovely, lacking in nobility and virtue, not in accord with noble wisdom, not associated with the noble ones, not frequented by the noble ones, deeply loathsome, and unfit to be heard—by such speech they revile and insult the bodhisattva.

Furthermore, each and every one of these sentient beings possesses hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of hands; with each hand, they each grasp hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of weapons to oppress and harm the Bodhisattva.
Thus he passed through incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) without ever ceasing.
Encountering such extreme agony and torment, the hair on his body stood on end and his life was nearly extinguished; he thought to himself:

"If my mind were to become agitated by this suffering, I would not be self-subdued, I would not be self-guarded, I would not be self-clarified, I would not be self-cultivated, I would not be self-composed, I would not be self-peaceful, I would not be self-reverent, and I would give rise to attachment; how then could I cause the minds of others to attain purity?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva further thought:
"Since beginningless kalpas, I have dwelt in birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Reflecting thus, he again exhorted himself, causing his mind to become pure and attaining joy.
He skillfully disciplines and restrains himself, being able to abide securely within the Buddha-dharma, and causes all sentient beings likewise to attain this Dharma.
He further reflects:
"This body is empty and quiescent; it is without self or what belongs to a self, lacks any reality, and is by nature empty and non-dual."
Whether it be suffering or pleasure, both are non-existent because all phenomena are empty.
I shall understand this and explain it extensively for others, so that all sentient beings may eliminate this view.
Therefore, although I now encounter bitter suffering, I should endure it;

for the sake of compassionately regarding sentient beings, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, for the sake of pitying sentient beings, for the sake of gathering in sentient beings, for the sake of not abandoning sentient beings, for the sake of attaining awakening myself, for the sake of causing others to attain awakening, so that my mind does not regress, and so that I may advance toward the Buddha-way.
"This is called the third practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the practice of non-opposition.
'O Son of the Buddha!
What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s practice of being unyielding and undaunted?'"
This bodhisattva cultivates various forms of diligence, namely:

foremost diligence, great diligence, superior diligence, distinguished diligence, most excellent diligence, most wondrous diligence, supreme diligence, unsurpassed diligence, unequaled diligence, and universal diligence.
By nature they are free from the three poisons; by nature they are free from arrogance; by nature they do not conceal their faults; by nature they are free from stinginess and envy;
by nature they are free from flattery and deception; and by nature they possess self-reproach and shame.

They never practice diligence for the sake of troubling even a single sentient being, but practice diligence solely for the sake of severing all afflictions, and solely for the sake of uprooting [even] one...
They practice diligence because it is the root of severing all delusions; they practice diligence solely for the sake of eliminating all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the realms of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the death and rebirth of all sentient beings; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing all sentient beings...
They practice diligence because of afflictions; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the mental inclinations of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the spheres of experience of all sentient beings;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing all...
They practice diligence because of the mental activities of sentient beings; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the entire dharma-realm;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the fundamental nature of all Buddha-dharmas;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the equality of all Buddha-dharmas; and they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the three periods of time.
They practice diligence because of the nature of equality; they practice diligence solely for the sake of attaining the light of wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of realizing the wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas;
they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing the single true mark of all Buddha-dharmas; they practice diligence solely for the sake of knowing all...
One practices diligence because the Buddha-dharma is boundless; one practices diligence solely for the sake of attaining the vast, definitive, and skillful wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas;
and one practices diligence solely for the sake of attaining the wisdom that discerns and explains the words and meanings of all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has accomplished such diligent practice, suppose someone were to say:
"Could you, for the sake of every single sentient being in all the countless worlds, endure all manner of sufferings within the Avīci Hell for countless kalpas?"

May each and every one of those sentient beings encounter countless Buddhas appearing in the world; by virtue of seeing these Buddhas, may they fully experience all forms of happiness until they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and only then shall you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Is it so? Or not? He replied:
"I can. Furthermore, suppose someone were to say:
"There are immeasurable, incalculable great oceans; you should exhaust them by dripping from them with the tip of a single hair."
There are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds;
were they all ground into dust, one could count each drop [of water] and each grain of dust, knowing their number exactly.
For the sake of sentient beings, one would undergo uninterrupted suffering in every thought-moment for that many eons.

The Bodhisattva, upon hearing these words, did not give rise to even a single thought of regret; rather, he felt an even greater increase of joy and exultation, deeply congratulating himself on having attained such great and wholesome benefit:
"By my power, I shall cause those sentient beings to be forever liberated from all suffering."
By means of these skillful practices, the Bodhisattva causes all sentient beings throughout all worlds to ultimately attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
This is called the fourth practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: the practice of being unyielding and undaunted.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of being free from delusion and confusion?"
This bodhisattva achieves right mindfulness; his mind is undistracted, firm and immovable, supremely pure, vast and immeasurable, and free from delusion.
By virtue of this right mindfulness, they skillfully understand all worldly languages and are able to maintain the verbal expressions of supramundane dharmas.
That is to say:

they are able to maintain the verbal expressions of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*); they are able to maintain the verbal expressions establishing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of material phenomena, and even the verbal expressions establishing the intrinsic natures of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), their minds free from delusion and confusion.
Within the world, as they die here and are born there, their minds are free from delusion and confusion;
entering the womb and emerging from the womb, their minds are free from delusion and confusion;
and when they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), their minds are free from delusion and confusion.
Serving spiritual friends with a mind free from delusion and confusion;
diligently practicing the Buddha-dharma with a mind free from delusion and confusion;
recognizing the works of Māra with a mind free from delusion and confusion;
Free from all demonic activities, their minds are without delusion or confusion;
throughout unspeakable eons, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices with minds free from delusion or confusion.

Having accomplished such immeasurable right mindfulness, these bodhisattvas, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, have heard the true Dharma from all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends.

That is to say: the profound Dharma; the vast Dharma; the adorned Dharma; the Dharma of various adornments; the Dharma of expounding various bodies of names, phrases, and syllables; the Dharma of the bodhisattva’s adornments; the unsurpassed Dharma of the light of the Buddha’s spiritual power; the Dharma of the purity of right aspiration and resolute understanding; the Dharma of non-attachment to all worldly phenomena; the Dharma of discerning all worldly phenomena; the exceedingly vast Dharma; the Dharma that illuminates all sentient beings by removing the cataracts of delusion; the Dharma common to and uncommon from all worlds; the unsurpassed Dharma of bodhisattva wisdom; and the Dharma of mastery over all-knowledge.
Having heard such a Dharma as this, the Bodhisattva, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), does not forget it nor lose it; his mind constantly recollects it without interruption.

Why is this? Because when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate various practices throughout immeasurable eons, they never disturb or confuse a single sentient being, causing them to lose right mindfulness;
they do not destroy the True Dharma nor sever roots of goodness, for their minds constantly increase and expand in great wisdom.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be deluded or disturbed by various sounds.
These include:

loud and high-pitched sounds, coarse and turbid sounds, sounds that cause extreme terror, pleasant sounds, unpleasant sounds, sounds that clamor and disturb the auditory consciousness, and sounds that impair the six sense faculties.

When this bodhisattva hears such immeasurable and innumerable sounds, whether pleasant or unpleasant, even if they were to fill incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka-dhātu*), his mind never for a single thought-moment becomes distracted.

That is to say: non-distraction in right mindfulness; non-distraction regarding objective realms; non-distraction in samādhi; non-distraction in entering the profound Dharma; non-distraction in practicing the conduct of enlightenment; non-distraction in generating the bodhicitta; non-distraction in recollecting all Buddhas; non-distraction in contemplating the true Dharma; non-distraction in the wisdom that transforms sentient beings; non-distraction in the wisdom that purifies sentient beings; and non-distraction in definitively understanding the profound meaning.
Because they do not commit evil deeds, they have no obstruction of karma;
because they do not give rise to afflictions, they have no obstruction of afflictions;
because they do not treat the Dharma with contempt, they have no obstruction of dharmas.
Because they do not slander the True Dharma, they are free from any obstruction to their karmic retribution.
O Son of the Buddha!

These aforementioned sounds, such as these, each fill incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka-dhātu*) and continue without interruption for immeasurable and innumerable eons (*kalpa*). While they are able to disrupt all the faculties (*indriya*) of the body and mind of sentient beings, they cannot disturb the mind of this Bodhisattva.

When a bodhisattva enters into samādhi and abides in the noble Dharma, they contemplate and examine all sounds, skillfully knowing the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of sounds, and skillfully knowing the nature of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of sounds.
Having heard this, they do not give rise to greed, do not arouse anger, and do not lose mindfulness; they skillfully grasp their characteristics without becoming stained by attachment.
They know that all sounds are non-existent and truly unobtainable, having no creator and no fundamental limit, being equal to the dharma-realm and without distinction.
When a bodhisattva thus accomplishes the tranquil conduct of body, speech, and mind, they reach omniscience and never regress;

they skillfully enter all gateways of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), know that all samādhis share a single essential nature, and comprehend that all phenomena are without limit. They attain the true wisdom of all phenomena, achieve the profound samādhi that is free from sound, obtain incalculable gateways of samādhi, and increase their immeasurable and vast heart of compassion.

At that time, within a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva attained countless hundreds of thousands of samādhis; hearing such sounds, his mind was not confused or disturbed, causing those samādhis to gradually increase and expand further.
They form this thought:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to abide securely in unsurpassed, pure mindfulness; to attain non-retrogression regarding omniscience; and to ultimately achieve nirvana without remainder."
"This is called the fifth practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva: being free from delusion and confusion.
'O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of excellent manifestation?'"

This Bodhisattva’s physical karma is pure, verbal karma is pure, and mental karma is pure; abiding in non-apprehension, they manifest physical, verbal, and mental karma as non-apprehensible. Because they know that these three karmas are all non-existent and devoid of falsehood, they are free from bondage.
Whatever they manifest is without intrinsic nature and without dependence.

Abiding in the mind of suchness, they know the self-nature of immeasurable minds and the self-nature of all phenomena; these are without attainment and without marks, profoundly deep and difficult to enter.
Abiding in the true suchness and dharma-nature of the stage of certainty, they manifest through skillful means yet remain free from karmic retribution;
being neither born nor extinguished, they dwell in the realm of nirvana and abide in the nature of quiescence;
abiding in the nature of reality which is devoid of intrinsic nature, they transcend the path of language, surpass all worlds, and possess no basis for dependence.

They enter the dharma that is free from conceptual discrimination and devoid of bondage and attachment; they enter the dharma of supreme wisdom and ultimate reality; they enter the supramundane dharma that cannot be comprehended by any worldly beings.
This is the skillful means of the bodhisattva, manifesting the appearance of birth.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva forms this thought:
"All sentient beings have non-nature as their nature;
all dharmas have the unconditioned as their nature;
all lands have the signless as their characteristic."
All that exists throughout the three periods of time is merely verbal expression; all verbal expressions have no basis within all phenomena;
and all phenomena likewise have no basis within verbal expressions.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are utterly profound, that all worlds are entirely quiescent, and that there is no augmentation whatsoever in all Buddha-dharmas."
The Buddha-dharma is not different from worldly dharmas, and worldly dharmas are not different from the Buddha-dharma;
the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas are neither confused nor distinct.

Having realized that the essence and nature of the dharma-realm are equal, they universally enter the three periods of time; they never abandon the great bodhicitta, their resolve to transform sentient beings never regresses, and their great compassion increases ever further as they become a place of reliance for all sentient beings.
At that time, the bodhisattva further reflects:
"If I do not bring sentient beings to maturity, who shall?
If I do not discipline sentient beings, who shall?"
If I do not transform sentient beings, who shall transform them?
If I do not awaken sentient beings, who shall awaken them?
If I do not purify sentient beings, who shall purify them?
"This is what is appropriate for me; this is what I ought to do. He further thought:
"If I were to understand this profound Dharma by myself alone, then I would be the only one to attain liberation in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Yet all sentient beings are blind and sightless, entering great perilous paths, bound and fettered by various afflictions (*kleśa*).

Like those with severe illnesses who constantly suffer pain, they dwell in the prison of craving and cannot escape on their own. They do not leave behind the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and the domain of King Yama; they cannot extinguish suffering nor abandon evil karma. Constantly dwelling in the darkness of ignorance, they do not see reality, transmigrating through birth and death without finding liberation. Abiding in the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), they are stained by manifold defilements; various afflictions shroud and obstruct their minds, and deluded by false views, they do not practice the Right Path.
When the Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings in this way, he reflects:
"If these sentient beings have not yet been matured or tamed, it would be improper for me to abandon them and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
I shall first transform sentient beings, practicing the bodhisattva path for unspeakably unspeakable eons;
those who are not yet matured, I shall first cause to reach maturity;
those who are not yet tamed, I shall first cause to be tamed.

"When this bodhisattva dwells in this practice, if any among the devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or all the world’s gandharvas, asuras, and so forth, should see him, dwell with him even for a moment, revere and honor him, serve and make offerings to him, or even briefly hear his name and have it once enter their minds—such deeds shall not be in vain;
they will certainly and surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This is called the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage of Good Appearance (*sādhumatī*).
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Nineteen, Part Two;
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-one, Part Two: The Ten Practices.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the unattached practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
O Son of the Buddha!
With an unattached mind, in every thought-moment, this bodhisattva is able to enter incalculable worlds and adorn and purify incalculable worlds.
In all worlds, their minds are free from attachment; they go to the presence of incalculable Tathāgatas, paying them respectful homage, serving them, and making offerings to them.

With incalculable flowers, incalculable perfumes, incalculable garlands, incalculable ointments, powdered incenses, robes, precious jewels, banners, pennants, and exquisite parasols—each of these various ornaments being incalculable—they made offerings;
they did so for the sake of the ultimate unconditioned dharma and for the sake of abiding in the inconceivable dharma.
In every thought-moment, they see countless Buddhas;
in the presence of these Buddhas, their minds are without attachment;
and toward all Buddha-lands, they likewise have no attachment.
One has no attachment even to the marks and signs of a Buddha;
one has no attachment when seeing the Buddha’s radiance or hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma;
and one has no attachment to the worlds of the ten directions, nor to any assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Having heard the Buddha-dharma, their hearts give rise to joy; their resolve and power become vast, enabling them to embrace and practice all the bodhisattva deeds, yet they remain without attachment even toward the Buddha-dharma.

Throughout unspeakable eons, this bodhisattva beholds unspeakable Buddhas appearing in the world; at the site of each Buddha, he serves and makes offerings for the entirety of those unspeakable eons, his mind never weary or satiated.
Upon seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and witnessing the majestic adornments of the assemblies of bodhisattvas, he remains entirely free from attachment.
Even when seeing impure worlds, he feels no aversion.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva observes in accordance with the Dharma of all Buddhas.

Within the Dharma of all Buddhas, there is neither defilement nor purity, neither darkness nor light; there is neither difference nor unity, neither reality nor falsehood, neither security nor peril, and neither the right path nor the wrong path.
In this way, the bodhisattva deeply penetrates the dharma-realm to transform sentient beings, yet does not give rise to attachment toward sentient beings;
they uphold all dharmas, yet do not give rise to attachment toward those dharmas;
they resolve upon the mind of enlightenment and abide in the abode of the Buddhas, yet do not give rise to attachment toward the abode of the Buddhas.
Although there is verbal expression, the mind has no attachment to verbal expression;
entering the realms of sentient beings, the mind has no attachment to those realms;
thoroughly understanding samādhi, being able to enter and abide within it, yet the mind has no attachment to samādhi.

They travel to immeasurable Buddha-lands, whether entering them, beholding them, or dwelling within them; yet their minds have no attachment to these lands, nor do they feel any lingering regret or longing when departing.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is thus able to be without attachment, their mind is free from obstacles within the Buddha-dharma; they fully comprehend the Buddha’s bodhi, realize the dharma-vinaya, abide in the Buddha’s true teaching, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, dwell in the bodhisattva mind, contemplate the dharma of bodhisattva liberation, remain unstained by the bodhisattva’s dwelling places, and are likewise unattached to the bodhisattva’s conduct. They purify the bodhisattva path and receive the bodhisattva prediction.
Having received this prediction, they form this thought:

"Ordinary people are foolish and ignorant, lacking knowledge and vision, lacking faith and understanding, lacking wise and skillful conduct; they are stubborn, dull, and greedily attached, wandering through the cycle of birth and death."
They do not seek to see the Buddha, do not follow the enlightened guide, and do not trust the Tamer; deluded and erring, they enter perilous paths;
they do not revere the King of Ten Powers, do not recognize the kindness of the Bodhisattvas, and remain attached to their dwelling places;
upon hearing that all phenomena are empty, their hearts are filled with great terror.
They distance themselves from the True Dharma and abide in false teachings;
they abandon the level and easy path and enter dangerous and difficult ways;
they turn their backs on the Buddha’s intent and follow the will of Māra.
"Within all states of existence, they cling tenaciously and refuse to let go.
Thus the Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings, increasing great compassion and giving rise to various roots of goodness without attachment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflects:

"For the sake of even a single sentient being, I shall, throughout every single land in the worlds of the ten directions, spend unspeakably unspeakable eons to teach, transform, and bring them to maturity."
As one acts for the sake of a single sentient being, so too does one act for the sake of all sentient beings;
one never becomes weary or disheartened by this, nor does one abandon them to depart elsewhere.

Furthermore, using the tip of a single hair to measure the entirety of the Dharma-realm, they teach and discipline all sentient beings throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons at the location of that single hair-tip;
as it is at one hair-tip, so it is at every single hair-tip.
Even for as little as the snap of a finger, they do not cling to a self, nor give rise to notions of "I" or "mine.
At the tip of every single hair, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva throughout all kalpas until the end of the future;

yet they do not cling to the body, do not cling to phenomena, do not cling to mindfulness, do not cling to vows, do not cling to samādhi, do not cling to contemplation, do not cling to tranquil concentration, do not cling to realms, do not cling to the teaching and taming of sentient beings, and furthermore, they do not cling to entering the dharma-realm.
Why is this? The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"I should contemplate the entire dharma-realm as like an illusion; all Buddhas as like reflections; the Bodhisattva's practices as like a dream; the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma as like an echo; and all worlds as like transformations, because they are sustained by the retribution of karma."
Diverse bodies are like illusions, for they arise through the power of conditioned activity;
all sentient beings are like the mind, for they are subject to various defilements;
all phenomena are like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for they are immutable.
Again, he formed this thought:

"I shall, throughout the entirety of space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm, practice the bodhisattva path within the lands of the ten directions; in every thought-moment I shall attain clear realization, so that all Buddha-dharmas appear before me through right mindfulness, free from any grasping or attachment."

Thus, the Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being without self and perceives the Buddha without obstruction. For the sake of transforming sentient beings, he expounds all dharmas, causing them to give rise to immeasurable joy and pure faith in the Buddha-dharma, protecting and rescuing all beings with a mind free from weariness.
Because they are free from weariness, they go to all worlds where there are sentient beings who have not yet been matured or tamed, and there they employ skillful means to transform and deliver them.

Among those beings, with their various sounds, various karmas, various attachments, various designations, various combinations, various cycles of rebirth, various actions, various realms, various births, and various deaths, he dwells within them through his great vows to teach and transform them, ensuring that their minds do not waver or regress, nor does he give rise to a single thought of defiled attachment.
Why is this? Because they have attained non-attachment and non-reliance, their self-benefit and benefit for others are pure and fulfilled.
This is called the seventh practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the Practice of Non-Attachment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice that is difficult to attain?

It is when this bodhisattva accomplishes roots of goodness that are difficult to attain, roots of goodness that are difficult to subdue, most excellent roots of goodness, indestructible roots of goodness, unsurpassed roots of goodness, inconceivable roots of goodness, inexhaustible roots of goodness, roots of goodness of sovereign power, roots of goodness of great majestic virtue, and roots of goodness that share the same single nature as all Buddhas.”

When this Bodhisattva practices these various deeds, they attain the most supreme understanding within the Buddha-dharma, and they attain a vast understanding regarding the Bodhi of the Buddhas. They never cease from their Bodhisattva vows; throughout all kalpas, their minds know no weariness; they do not give rise to revulsion toward any suffering; they cannot be moved by any demons; they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; they fully practice all the ascetic austerities of Bodhisattvas; they cultivate the Bodhisattva path with diligence and without indolence; and they never regress from their Mahāyāna vows.

Once this bodhisattva is securely established in this difficult-to-attain practice, in every moment of thought, they are able to transform the birth and death of incalculable eons, yet they do not abandon their great bodhisattva vows.
If there are sentient beings who serve and make offerings [to them], or even those who merely see or hear [of them], they shall all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Although this bodhisattva realizes that sentient beings do not exist, they do not abandon the realm of all sentient beings.

They are like a boatman who does not dwell on this shore, nor on the far shore, nor in the middle of the stream, yet is able to ferry sentient beings from this shore to the far shore because they travel back and forth without rest.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he does not abide in saṃsāra, nor does he abide in nirvāṇa, nor does he abide within the current of saṃsāra; yet he is able to transport sentient beings from this shore and establish them on the other shore, in a place that is secure, fearless, and free from sorrow and affliction.

Furthermore, one does not become attached to the enumeration of sentient beings; one does not abandon one sentient being to become attached to many, nor abandon many sentient beings to become attached to one.
One does not increase the realm of sentient beings, nor decrease the realm of sentient beings;
one does not give rise to the realm of sentient beings, nor extinguish the realm of sentient beings.
The realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, nor is it increased;
the realm of sentient beings is not differentiated, nor is it dualistic. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva enters deeply into the realm of sentient beings as he does the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena are not two.
Within this non-dual dharma, there is no increase and no decrease, no arising and no ceasing, no existence and no non-existence, no grasping and no reliance, and no attachment and no duality.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena (*dharma*) and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are non-dual.

Thus, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the Bodhisattva enters the profound realm of phenomena and dwells in the signless (*animitta*). Adorning his body with pure marks, he realizes that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) yet is able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena. Without grasping at sentient beings, he is able to know their number; without clinging to worlds, he manifests in Buddha-fields; without discriminating phenomena, he skillfully enters the Buddha-dharma. Having deeply penetrated the principles of meaning, he extensively expounds verbal teachings. Realizing that all phenomena are the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) free from desire, he does not sever the Bodhisattva path nor retreat from Bodhisattva conduct. Constantly and diligently practicing inexhaustible deeds, he enters with mastery the pure realm of phenomena.
It is like drilling wood to produce fire; although the work of fire is immeasurable, the fire does not go out.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva’s work of transforming sentient beings is inexhaustible, yet he remains constantly present in the world without ceasing.
It is neither ultimate, nor is it non-ultimate.
Neither grasping nor non-grasping;
neither relying nor non-relying;
neither worldly dharmas nor Buddha-dharmas.
They are neither ordinary beings nor those who have attained the fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
When Bodhisattvas achieve such an inconceivable mind and practice the Bodhisattva conduct, they do not speak of the Dharma of the Two Vehicles, nor do they speak of the Buddha-Dharma;
they do not speak of the mundane world, nor do they speak of mundane dharmas.
One does not speak of sentient beings, nor does one speak of the absence of sentient beings;
one does not speak of defilement, nor does one speak of purity. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are unstained, ungraspable, non-evolving, and non-retrogressive.
When the Bodhisattva practices within such quiescent, subtle, profound, and supreme dharmas, he does not give rise to the thought:
"I am currently practicing this path, I have already practiced this path, or I shall practice this path."

They do not cling to the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; nor to the internal world, the external world, or the internal-external world. They remain entirely without attachment toward the great vows they have generated, the various perfections, and all phenomena.
Why is this? Within the dharma-realm, there is no phenomenon named "tending toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas" or "tending toward the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas"; there is no phenomenon named:
There is no dharma named "tending toward the bodhisattva vehicle" or "tending toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi";
there is no dharma named "tending toward the realm of ordinary beings," nor "tending toward defilement," "tending toward purity," "tending toward saṃsāra," or "tending toward nirvāṇa."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are neither dual nor non-dual.
For example, like space, if one seeks it throughout the ten directions—whether in the past, future, or present—it cannot be found; yet, it is not that space does not exist.
The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena in this way as being ungraspable, yet it is not that all phenomena do not exist;
as they truly are, without deviation, he does not lose what must be done, universally demonstrating the practice of all bodhisattva deeds;
without abandoning his great vows, he tames sentient beings and turns the wheel of the true Dharma.
Without destroying cause and effect, nor contradicting the sublime Dharma of equality, they are universally equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas and do not destroy the true mark;
they penetrate deeply into the Dharma, and their eloquence is inexhaustible.
Hearing the Dharma without attachment, they reach the bottom of the ocean of Dharma;
they are skillfully able to expound it with a mind free from fear;
they do not abandon the dwelling of the Buddhas, yet they do not contravene worldly laws, manifesting throughout the world without being attached to the world.

When a bodhisattva has thus accomplished this rare mind of wisdom and cultivates all practices, they deliver sentient beings from the three evil realms, teaching and taming them, and establishing them within the path of the Buddhas of the three periods of time so that they remain unshakable.
Again, he reflects:

"The sentient beings of the world do not know how to repay kindness; they harbor mutual enmity, cling to false views, are deluded and inverted, are ignorant and lacking wisdom, lack faith, follow evil companions, give rise to various forms of unwholesome intelligence, and are entirely filled with craving, ignorance, and all manner of afflictions—this is the sphere of practice for me as a bodhisattva."

Even if there were those who recognize kindness, who are clever and possessed of wisdom, and if good spiritual friends were to fill the world, I would not practice the bodhisattva path therein. Why is this?
Toward sentient beings, I harbor neither favoritism nor aversion, nor do I harbor any expectations; I seek not even a single thread, a single hair, or a single word of praise.
Throughout all kalpas of the future, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, never for even a single thought-moment acting for their own sake;
they desire only to deliver and liberate all sentient beings, causing them to become pure and forever attain transcendence.
Why is this? For one who acts as a guide for sentient beings, it is the natural law that they should neither grasp nor seek;
rather, they cultivate the bodhisattva path solely for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may reach the secure further shore and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the eighth difficult-to-attain practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Sons of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of wholesome dharmas?"

This Bodhisattva acts as a pond of the Dharma for all the world—including its devas, humans, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, and others—upholding the True Dharma and ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted.
Because he has attained the *dhāraṇī* of pure radiance, his eloquence is inexhaustible as he expounds the Dharma and bestows predictions of enlightenment;
because he has attained the *dhāraṇī* of complete meaning, his analytical power regarding meaning is inexhaustible.
Because they have attained the dhāraṇī of awakening to the true dharma, their analytical eloquence regarding phenomena (dharmapratibhāna) is inexhaustible;
because they have attained the dhāraṇī of explaining words and phrases, their analytical eloquence regarding language (niruktipratibhāna) is inexhaustible;

because they have attained the dhāraṇī of the unimpeded gateway to infinite syllables and inexhaustible meanings, their analytical eloquence regarding non-obstruction (anāvaraṇapratibhāna) is inexhaustible.
Because they receive the empowerment of the Buddha’s *dhāraṇī* upon their crowns, their eloquence of joy is inexhaustible;
because they have attained the *dhāraṇī-gate* of awakening not through others, their eloquence of light is inexhaustible;
because they have attained the *dhāraṇī-gate* of identical eloquence, their identical eloquence is inexhaustible.

Because they have attained the dhāraṇī-door of etymological interpretation within the various bodies of meaning, phrases, and syllables, their eloquence in etymological interpretation is inexhaustible;
because they have attained the boundless revolving dhāraṇī, their boundless eloquence is inexhaustible.

This Bodhisattva possesses firm and steadfast great compassion, universally gathering in all sentient beings; throughout the trichiliocosm, they manifest bodies of golden hue and perform the works of a Buddha.

According to the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all beings, they employ their broad and long tongue to manifest infinite voices within a single sound, preaching the Dharma at the appropriate time and causing all to rejoice.

Suppose there were unspeakably many sentient beings with various karmic retributions, gathered together in one place; that assembly being so vast as to fill unspeakably many worlds, and a bodhisattva were seated within that gathering.

Within this assembly, every single sentient being possesses unspeakably many *asaṃkhyeya* mouths; each mouth can produce hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* sounds, all sounding forth simultaneously, each with distinct speech and distinct questions.
In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva is able to receive them all and respond to each one, causing their doubts and delusions to be eliminated.
As it is with one assembly, so it is with all unspeakably many assemblies.
Furthermore, suppose that from every single hair-tip, in every moment of thought, there emerge unspeakably unspeakable numbers of assemblies at sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
this is likewise true for all hair-tips.
Though the kalpas of the future may come to an end, this assembly shall never be exhausted.
Within every thought-moment, these members of the assembly each pose their questions using distinct languages and diverse expressions;
yet the Bodhisattva, within a single thought-moment, is able to receive them all—without fear or timidity, without doubt or error—and reflects thus:

"Suppose all sentient beings were to come together and question me with such verbal actions; I would preach the Dharma for them without interruption or exhaustion, causing them all to rejoice and abide in the wholesome paths.

Furthermore, I would cause them to skillfully understand all forms of speech, enabling them to expound various teachings for sentient beings while remaining free from any discrimination regarding words."

Even if unspeakably many varieties of words and phrases were used to pose difficult questions, one would comprehend them all in a single thought-moment and respond to them all with a single voice, universally causing awakening without exception.

Because they have attained the consecration of omniscience, because they have attained the treasury of non-obstruction, because they have attained the perfect radiance of all dharmas, and because they are fully endowed with the wisdom of omniscience.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in the practice of wholesome dharmas, they are able to purify themselves and, through the skillful means of non-attachment, universally benefit all sentient beings, yet they do not perceive any sentient being who attains liberation."

Just as in this trichiliocosm, so too, even throughout unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms, they manifest bodies of golden hue, endowed with sublime voices, and perform the Buddha-work without any obstruction regarding all phenomena.
O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes ten kinds of bodies.
They are as follows:
Entering the boundless realm of phenomena with a body that is not subject to rebirth, for it extinguishes all worlds;
entering the boundless realm of phenomena with bodies of all realms of existence, for it gives rise to all worlds;
the non-arising body, for it abides in the equality of the dharma of non-arising.
It is not an extinguished body, because all things are extinguished and verbal expression is unattainable;
it is not a substantial body, because it attains suchness;
it is not a false body, because it manifests in accordance with conditions.
It is the non-transmigrating body, because it is free from dying here and being born there;
it is the indestructible body, because the nature of the dharma-realm is indestructible;
it is the single-characteristic body, because the pathways of speech and language are severed throughout the three periods of time.
The signless body, because it is well able to observe the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
When Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of bodies, they become a shelter for all sentient beings, because they nurture all roots of goodness;
they become a rescue for all sentient beings, because they cause them to attain great peace and security.
They are a refuge for all sentient beings, because they provide them with a great place of reliance;
they are guides for all sentient beings, because they cause them to attain unsurpassed deliverance;
they are teachers for all sentient beings, because they cause them to enter into the true Dharma.
They act as lamps for all sentient beings, so that they may clearly perceive the retribution of karma;
they act as light for all sentient beings, so that they may illuminate the profound and wondrous Dharma;
they act as torches for all three periods of time, so that they may awaken to the reality of phenomena.
To serve as an illumination for all worlds, so that beings may enter the stage of Radiance;
and to serve as light for all realms of existence, manifesting the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the ninth practice of wholesome dharmas of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
When a Bodhisattva dwells securely in this practice, they act as a pool of the cooling Dharma for all sentient beings, because they are able to exhaustively reach the source of all Buddha-dharmas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the true practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
This bodhisattva accomplishes the foremost speech of truth: they act according to what they say, and they speak according to how they act.”

This bodhisattva studies the true speech of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, enters the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, becomes equal in roots of goodness to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, attains the non-dual speech of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and achieves the wisdom of training in accordance with the Tathāgata.

This bodhisattva accomplishes the knowledge of what is possible and impossible regarding sentient beings; the knowledge of the retribution of karma in the past, future, and present; the knowledge of the sharpness and dullness of the faculties; the knowledge of various elements; the knowledge of various inclinations; the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the knowledge of the times and non-times for the arising of the defilement and purity of the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; the knowledge of recollecting former abodes in all worlds; the knowledge of the divine eye; and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, yet without abandoning any of the bodhisattva practices.
Why is this? It is because they desire to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to become pure.
This bodhisattva further gives rise to such a superior resolve:
"If I were to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before causing all sentient beings to abide in the path of unsurpassed liberation, I would be violating my original vow; this is what ought not to be."
Therefore, one must first cause all sentient beings to attain unsurpassed bodhi and nirvana without remainder, and only then become a Buddha. Why is this?

It was not at the request of sentient beings that I resolved to attain enlightenment; rather, I have become an uninvited friend to sentient beings myself, desiring first to cause all sentient beings to fulfill their roots of goodness and achieve all-knowledge.
Therefore, I am the most excellent, for I am unattached to all worlds;
I am the supreme, for I abide in the stage of the unsurpassed tamer;
I am free from obscuration, for I understand that sentient beings have no limit.
I have accomplished what was to be done, because my original vow has been fulfilled;
I am a skillful transformer, because I am adorned with the merits of a bodhisattva;
I am a worthy refuge, because I am sustained by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not abandon their original vow, they attain entry into the adornment of unsurpassed wisdom, benefiting sentient beings and causing them all to be fully satisfied;
according to their original vows, they all attain the ultimate;
possessing mastery of wisdom within all dharmas, they cause all sentient beings to universally attain purity.

In every thought-moment, they travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions; in every thought-moment, they go universally to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands; in every thought-moment, they see all unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas and their pure lands adorned by the Buddhas, manifesting the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgatas.
Throughout the universal dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, these bodhisattvas manifest immeasurable bodies, universally entering all worlds without any dependence;
within their own bodies, they manifest all lands, all sentient beings, all dharmas, and all buddhas.

This Bodhisattva knows the various perceptions, various desires, various understandings, various karmic retributions, and various roots of goodness of sentient beings; according to what is appropriate for each, he manifests his body to discipline them.

He contemplates all Bodhisattvas as being like illusions, all phenomena as being like transformations, the appearance of Buddhas in the world as being like shadows, and all worlds as being like dreams. He attains the inexhaustible treasury of the body of meaning and the body of words;
with mastery in right mindfulness, he definitively and thoroughly understands all dharmas.
With supreme wisdom, they enter the true mark of all samādhis and abide in the stage of non-dual singleness.

Because all sentient beings are attached to duality, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in great compassion and practices such a dharma of quiescence. They attain the ten powers of a Buddha, enter the Indra-net Dharma-realm, and achieve the Tathāgata’s unimpeded liberation and the great lion’s roar among men.
Attaining fearlessness, they are able to turn the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma.
Attaining wisdom and liberation, they thoroughly understand all worldly realms;
severing the revolving currents of birth and death, they enter the great ocean of wisdom;

for the sake of all sentient beings, they protect and uphold the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, reaching the ultimate source and bottom of the ocean of the true reality of all Buddha-dharmas.

Once the Bodhisattva abides in this practice of reality, all those among the devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, asuras, and others in the entire world who draw near to him, are all caused to attain awakening, becoming joyful and pure.
"This is called the tenth true practice of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, worlds as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways:

namely, they moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; they rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; they surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; they quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; they roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; they crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed equally everywhere.

It rained down exquisite celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial powdered incense, celestial garlands, celestial robes, celestial jewels, and celestial ornaments; celestial music was played, celestial light was emitted, and the subtle, wondrous voices of the devas were proclaimed.
Just as these divine transformations were manifested through the teaching of the Ten Practices in the Yāma Heaven palace of this world, so it was in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, bodhisattvas—as many as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields—arrived in this land, filling the ten directions. They addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma-vyūha, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
Excellent, excellent!”
They are well able to expound all the practices of bodhisattvas.
We are all of the same name: Forest of Merit, and the worlds in which we dwell are all named:
Guṇaketurāja, the Tathāgatas in those lands are all named Samantaguṇa.
In our Buddha-fields as well, we preach this Dharma;
The assembly and its retinue, as well as their speech and the principles of their meaning, are all likewise without increase or decrease.
O Son of the Buddha!
We have all come to this assembly by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power to bear witness for you:

"In all worlds of the ten directions, it is likewise thus. At that time, the Bodhisattva Forest of Merit, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed universally the entire assembly in the ten directions as far as the Dharma-realm. Desiring to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas would never be interrupted; desiring to purify the lineage of Bodhisattvas; desiring to prevent the lineage of vows from regressing; desiring to cause the lineage of practices to continue perpetually; desiring to make the lineages of the three periods of time entirely equal; desiring to encompass the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; desiring to reveal and expound upon the various roots of goodness that have been planted; desiring to observe all faculties, inclinations, afflictions, habitual tendencies, mental activities, and deeds; and desiring to illumine the enlightenment of all Buddhas, he spoke these verses:
"With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Honored One of Ten Powers, whose stainless and pure vision is unimpeded;
his sphere of activity is profound and far-reaching, beyond compare, as he abides upon the path that is like space."
Those most supreme among humans in the past, whose merit was immeasurable and unattached,
who were foremost in valor and without equal— they, the ones free from dust, have practiced this path.
Now, throughout the lands of the ten directions, you skillfully expound the primary truth;
free from all faults and evils, most pure, those who have no other reliance practice this path.
All future lion-like teachers of humanity, who traverse everywhere throughout the dharma-realm,
having already resolved upon the great compassion of all Buddhas— those benefactors shall walk this path.
The peerless Honored Ones of the three periods of time naturally eliminate the darkness of ignorance;
they are equal toward all phenomena—those of great power practice this path.

Universally beholding immeasurable and boundless realms, all states of existence and all destinies, having seen them, their minds do not engage in discrimination; those who are immovable practice this path.
All that exists within the dharma-realm is clearly understood; In the ultimate truth, one is most pure.
Having forever destroyed anger, pride, and delusion— Such a person of merit walks this path.
Skillfully discerning all sentient beings, they enter entirely into the true nature of the Dharma-realm;
awakening spontaneously without depending on others, those who are empty practice this path.
Throughout all the lands as vast as empty space, he travels everywhere to preach the Dharma and provide extensive instruction;
what he teaches is pure and indestructible—this is the path traversed by that supreme Muni.
Endowed with steadfastness and non-retrogression, Accomplishing the most supreme and honored Dharma,
With inexhaustible power of aspiration reaching the further shore— This is the path traveled by those who have practiced well.
The infinite and boundless stages, the vast and profound, wondrous realms—all he can know and see without exception; such is the path traversed by that Lion of Debaters.
All meanings of every phrase are clearly understood, and all opposing arguments are utterly subdued;
having attained certainty regarding the Dharma and being free from doubt, that Great Muni follows this path.
