one hundred trillion devas who had lived together in the past praised him with sublime voices;
and one hundred trillion Brahmakāyika devas prostrated themselves in reverence.
One hundred trillion Brahmā-purohita devas joined their palms above their heads;
one hundred trillion Brahmakāyika devas surrounded and attended him;
and one hundred trillion Mahābrahmā devas praised and extolled his immeasurable merits.
One hundred trillion Ābhāsvara devas prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground;
one hundred trillion Parīttābhā devas proclaimed and praised how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha in the world;
and one hundred trillion Apramāṇābhā devas paid homage to the Buddha from afar.
A hundred trillion Ābhāsvara devas praised how difficult it is to behold the Tathāgata;
a hundred trillion Śuddhāvāsa devas came to this place together with their palaces;
and a hundred trillion Parīttābha devas, with pure minds, bowed their heads in prostration.

one hundred trillion Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas, with reverence and respect, drew near to make offerings;
and one hundred trillion Bṛhatphala devas recollected their past roots of goodness.
One hundred trillion Śuddhāvāsa-devas conceived a sense of wonder before the Tathāgata;
one hundred trillion Apramāṇaśubha-devas, with resolute reverence, gave rise to various roots of goodness;
and one hundred trillion Bṛhatphala-devas bowed their bodies in respectful homage.
One hundred trillion Avṛha devas, their roots of faith firm and steadfast, paid homage with deep reverence;
one hundred trillion Atapa devas, with palms joined in mindfulness of the Buddha, felt no satiety in their devotion;
and one hundred trillion Sudarśana devas prostrated themselves, touching their heads to the ground in salutation.
One hundred trillion Suyāma devas maintained mindfulness of making offerings to the Buddha, their minds never flagging;
one hundred trillion Akaniṣṭha devas paid reverent homage;
and one hundred trillion various other devas were all filled with great joy, raising their voices in praise.
A hundred trillion devas each contemplated with skillful thought, providing adornment;
a hundred trillion bodhisattva-devas protected and sustained the Buddha’s seat, their adornments never ceasing.
One hundred trillion Puṣpahasta Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of flowers;
one hundred trillion Gandhahasta Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of incense;
one hundred trillion Mālāhasta Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of garlands.
A hundred trillion Cūrṇahasta Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of powdered incense;
a hundred trillion Vilepanahasta Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of unguents;
a hundred trillion Vastrahasta Bodhisattvas rained down all kinds of garments.
The Bodhisattva Hundred Million Trillion Canopy-Hand rained down all canopies;
the Bodhisattva Hundred Million Trillion Banner-Hand rained down all banners;
the Bodhisattva Hundred Million Trillion Pennant-Hand rained down all pennants.
A hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Jewel Hands rained down all kinds of jewels;
a hundred trillion Bodhisattvas with Ornamented Hands rained down all kinds of ornaments.
A hundred trillion sons of gods emerged from their celestial palaces and arrived at the place where the seat was located.
One hundred trillion sons of gods, with pure faith, together with their palaces;
one hundred trillion nobly born sons of gods, supporting the seat with their bodies;
and one hundred trillion consecrated sons of gods, supporting the seat with their entire bodies.
One hundred trillion contemplative bodhisattvas contemplated with reverence;
one hundred trillion nobly born bodhisattvas gave rise to pure minds;
and one hundred trillion bodhisattvas experienced joy in their faculties.
A hundred trillion bodhisattvas possessed pure profound resolve;
a hundred trillion bodhisattvas possessed pure faith and understanding;
a hundred trillion bodhisattvas possessed pure karma.
One hundred trillion bodhisattvas possess mastery over rebirth;
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas illuminate with the light of the Dharma;
one hundred trillion bodhisattvas have perfected the stages.
There were a hundred trillion bodhisattvas, who were skillfully able to teach and transform all sentient beings.

They were born from a hundred trillion roots of goodness; they were protected and sustained by a hundred trillion Buddhas; they were perfected by a hundred trillion merits; they were purified by a hundred trillion sublime minds; they were adorned and cleansed by a hundred trillion great vows; they were brought forth by a hundred trillion virtuous deeds; they were made firm by a hundred trillion wholesome dharmas; they were manifested through a hundred trillion spiritual powers; they were accomplished by a hundred trillion virtues; and they were praised with a hundred trillion methods of praise.
Just as the King of Tuṣita Heaven in this world has prepared a high seat for the Tathāgata, so too do the Kings of Tuṣita Heaven in all worlds prepare seats for the Buddha;

their adornments, their protocols, their faith and joy, their purity of mind, their delight, their gladness, their reverence, their sense of wonder, their exultation, and their yearning are all exactly the same.

At that time, after the King of the Tuṣita Heaven had prepared a seat for the Tathāgata, he conceived a heart of deep respect and, together with ten trillion asaṃkhyeya sons of the Tuṣita Heaven, went out to welcome the Tathāgata.

With pure minds, they rained down clouds of flowers of asaṃkhyeya colors; they rained down clouds of inconceivable colors and fragrances; they rained down clouds of garlands of various colors; they rained down clouds of vast and pure sandalwood; they rained down clouds of immeasurable and various canopies; they rained down clouds of subtle and exquisite celestial garments; they rained down clouds of boundless and manifold wonderful jewels; they rained down clouds of celestial ornaments; they rained down clouds of immeasurable and various burning incenses; and they rained down clouds of all kinds of sandalwood, aloeswood, and solid powdered incense.

When these clouds issued forth from the bodies of the various hosts of devaputras, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of Tuṣita devaputras, as well as the other devaputras present in the assembly, felt great joy in their hearts and paid homage with reverent prostrations;
meanwhile, asaṃkhyeyas of celestial maidens leaped for joy and, filled with longing admiration, gazed intently upon the Tathāgata.

In the Tuṣita Palace, an unspeakable multitude of bodhisattvas remained in mid-air, single-mindedly and with diligent effort, making offerings to the Buddha with ritual implements surpassing those of all the devas, and paying him respectful homage.
Innumerable musical instruments played simultaneously.

At that time, through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, the outflow of his past roots of goodness, and his inconceivable power of mastery, all the devas and devakanyās in the Tuṣita Palace saw the Buddha from afar as if he were right before their eyes; they all thought to themselves:
"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter; we have now seen the One Possessed of All-Knowledge, the Unobstructed in Dharma, the Perfectly Awakened One."
Reflecting thus and observing thus, they all together at that same time went forth to welcome the Tathāgata;

each using celestial robes to hold all kinds of flowers, all kinds of incense, all kinds of jewels, all kinds of ornaments, all kinds of celestial sandalwood powder, all kinds of celestial aloeswood powder, all kinds of celestial exquisite jewel powder, all kinds of celestial fragrant flowers, and all kinds of celestial māndārava flowers, which they all scattered as offerings to the Buddha.

Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of Tushita devaputras dwelt in the midst of space; all of them gave rise to a mind directed toward the realm of wisdom regarding the Buddha, burning all manner of incense so that the fragrance formed clouds that adorned the void.
Furthermore, they gave rise to a heart of joy toward the Buddha, raining down clouds of all celestial flowers to adorn the void.
Moreover, they gave rise to a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, raining down clouds of all celestial parasols to adorn the void.
Furthermore, giving rise to a mind of making offerings toward the Buddha, they scattered clouds of all celestial garlands to adorn the void;

furthermore, giving rise to a mind of faith and understanding toward the Buddha, they spread asaṃkhyeya golden nets to cover the void, from which all jeweled bells constantly produced wondrous sounds;

furthermore, giving rise to a mind regarding the Buddha as the most supreme field of merit, they adorned the void with asaṃkhyeya canopies and rained down clouds of all manner of necklaces without interruption.

Furthermore, conceiving a heart of profound faith toward the Buddha, they adorned the void with incalculable celestial palaces, from which all manner of divine music issued forth in subtle and wondrous tones;

furthermore, conceiving a heart that the Buddha is most supreme and difficult to encounter, they adorned the void with clouds of celestial garments of various colors and incalculable varieties, raining down incomparable and diverse exquisite robes;

furthermore, conceiving a heart of immeasurable joy and exultation toward the Buddha, they adorned the void with incalculable celestial jeweled crowns, raining down immeasurable heavenly crowns that spread out to form vast clouds.

Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of joy toward the Buddha, they adorned the void with incalculable varieties of multicolored jewels and rained down clouds of every kind of necklace without interruption.

Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeyas of devaputras all conceived pure faith toward the Buddha; they scattered countless celestial flowers of various colors and burned countless celestial incenses of various colors as offerings to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, conceiving minds of great adornment and transformation toward the Buddha, they held countless celestial sandalwood powders of various colors and offered them by scattering them over the Tathāgata.
Moreover, conceiving hearts of joy and exultation toward the Buddha, they followed after the Tathāgata holding countless parasols of various colors.

Furthermore, conceiving a superior mind toward the Buddha, they held countless celestial robes of various colors made of precious jewels, spreading them along the road as an offering to the Tathāgata;
furthermore, conceiving a pure mind toward the Buddha, they held countless celestial banners of various colors made of precious jewels, welcoming the Tathāgata;
furthermore, conceiving a mind of superior joy toward the Buddha, they held countless celestial ornaments of various colors made of precious jewels, making offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they conceived indestructible faith toward the Buddha and offered countless celestial jewel garlands to the Tathāgata;
moreover, they conceived incomparable joy toward the Buddha and offered countless celestial jewel banners of various colors to the Tathāgata.

Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of devaputras, with minds that were disciplined, tranquil, and free from negligence, held countless celestial musical instruments of various colors and produced sublime sounds to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

There were hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas who had previously dwelt in the Tuṣita palace. They were born from the dharma that transcends the three realms; born from conduct free from all afflictions; born from a mind that is all-pervading and unimpeded; born from the dharma of profound skillful means; born from immeasurable and vast wisdom; increased by firm and pure faith; born from inconceivable roots of goodness; accomplished through the arousal of incalculable skillful transformations; manifested from the mind of making offerings to the Buddha; and sealed by the dharma-gate of non-action.
With offering materials surpassing those of all the devas, they made offerings to the Buddha; and with all jeweled canopies born from the *pāramitās*, they purified all the spheres of the Buddhas.
It manifests all canopies of flowers born from the realization of non-arising; it manifests all garments born from the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
it manifests all nets of bells born from the unimpeded mind of the adamantine dharma; it manifests all solid fragrances born from the mind that realizes all phenomena are like illusions;
and it manifests [all things] pervading the Tathāgata-throne throughout all Buddha-realms, born from the mind itself.
All the wonderful jewel thrones of the Buddhas’ assemblies; all the jewel banners produced by a tireless mind in making offerings to the Buddhas;
all the jewel palaces where the Buddhas dwell, produced by a joyful mind that understands all phenomena to be like dreams;
and all clouds of jewel lotuses produced by roots of goodness free from attachment and roots of goodness of non-arising—all these were made firm.
Clouds of solid fragrance; clouds of all boundless colored flowers; clouds of all various colored exquisite garments;
clouds of all boundless pure sandalwood incense; clouds of all exquisitely adorned jeweled canopies;
clouds of all burning incense; clouds of all exquisite garlands; and clouds of all pure ornaments.
Clouds, all pervading the Dharma-realm, surpassing all the offerings of the various devas, made offerings to the Buddha.

From each of the bodies of those bodhisattvas, there emerged unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, who completely filled the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space. Their minds were equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, having arisen from the non-perverted Dharma and being empowered by the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgatas. They revealed to sentient beings the path of peace and security, possessing unspeakable numbers of names, phrases, and syllables, and universally entering immeasurable dharmas. Born from the seeds of all dhāraṇīs, they produced inexhaustible treasuries of eloquence; their minds were free from fear, and they gave rise to great joy, praising the Tathāgata with unspeakably immeasurable and inexhaustible praises of reality without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
At that time, all the devas and the assembly of bodhisattvas beheld the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the inconceivable hero among men.
His body is immeasurable and beyond calculation;
he manifests inconceivable and manifold supernatural transformations, causing the hearts of countless sentient beings to rejoice greatly;
he pervades all realms of empty space and all dharma-realms, adorning them with the adornments of a Buddha.

Causing all sentient beings to dwell securely in roots of goodness; manifesting the immeasurable spiritual powers of all Buddhas; transcending all paths of speech; being mutually revered by all great Bodhisattvas;
causing all to rejoice according to their needs for transformation;
abiding in the vast bodies of all Buddhas; and having rendered all merits and roots of goodness completely pure.
His physical form is foremost, such that none can outshine it;
the realm of his wisdom is inexhaustible, born from incomparable samādhi.

His body is boundless, dwelling pervasively within the bodies of all sentient beings, causing immeasurable beings to experience great joy and ensuring that the lineage of omniscience is never severed.
Abiding in the ultimate dwelling of all Buddhas, they are born into the family of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they cause incalculable sentient beings to attain pure faith and understanding, and they bring to fulfillment the wisdom of all Bodhisattvas and gladden their faculties;
the clouds of Dharma universally cover the void of the Dharma-realm, teaching and subduing all without exception.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, they cause all to be fully satisfied and lead them to abide in non-conceptual wisdom;
surpassing all sentient beings, they attain omniscience, radiate great light, and cause all roots of goodness from past lives to manifest;
they universally cause all to give rise to the vast mind and lead all sentient beings to abide in the indestructible wisdom of Samantabhadra.

Pervading the lands of all sentient beings, they are born from the non-retrogressive True Dharma and abide within the entirely equal Dharma-realm. Clearly understanding what is appropriate for the minds of sentient beings, they manifest unspeakably unspeakable varieties of Tathāgata bodies that cannot be fully extolled by worldly speech.
They cause all beings to constantly mindfully recollect the Buddha, filling the Dharma-realm and extensively delivering all living beings;
according to the benefits desired by those who have first resolved their minds, they bestow the gift of the Dharma to subdue them and purify their faith and understanding.
He manifests an inconceivable physical body, observing all sentient beings with a mind free from attachment;
he dwells in unimpeded abiding, attaining the ten powers of a Buddha without obstruction;
his mind is always tranquil and concentrated, never becoming distracted.

Abiding in omniscience, they are skillfully able to expound the true meaning of various phrases and sentences; they are able to penetrate deeply into the boundless ocean of wisdom and give birth to an immeasurable treasury of merit and insight;
they constantly illuminate the Dharma-realm with the sun of the Buddha, always appearing without setting through the power of their original vows;
they dwell eternally in the Dharma-realm, abiding where the Buddhas abide, without any change or variation.
They are entirely unattached to both "self" and "what belongs to self," dwelling in supramundane dharmas and remaining unstained by worldly dharmas.
They raise the banner of wisdom over all worlds; their wisdom is vast and transcends the world, free from any defilement or attachment.
They uproot all sentient beings and cause them to emerge from the mire, establishing them on the ground of supreme wisdom. All their merit benefits sentient beings without ever being exhausted.
Having fully understood all the wisdom of the bodhisattvas, they possess resolute faith and shall attain perfect enlightenment;
through great compassion, they manifest unspeakably many and infinite Buddha-bodies with various adornments;
and with wondrous voices, they expound immeasurable teachings, satisfying the intentions of all sentient beings according to their needs.
In the past, future, and present, their minds are always pure, causing all sentient beings not to become attached to sensory realms;

they constantly bestow predictions of enlightenment upon all bodhisattvas, causing them all to enter the lineage of the Buddhas, to be born into the Buddha-family, and to receive the Buddha’s consecration;
they constantly travel throughout the ten directions without ever resting, yet remain without attachment or delight toward anything whatsoever.
They are able to travel everywhere throughout the dharma-realm and all Buddha-lands, and there is no mind of any sentient being that they do not fully know;
their merit is pure and transcends the world;
they do not abide in birth and death, yet they appear universally throughout the world like reflections.
With the moon of wisdom, they universally illumine the Dharma-realm, thoroughly understanding that all things are ultimately ungraspable;
constantly through wisdom, they know that all worlds are like illusions, like shadows, like dreams, and like transformations, and that all have the mind as their own nature, abiding thus;

according to the differences in the karmic retributions of sentient beings, the distinctions in their mental inclinations, and the various differences in their faculties, they manifest the body of a Buddha.

The Tathāgata constantly takes countless sentient beings as his object of focus, teaching them that all worlds arise from conditions; he knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are entirely without marks, being only the single mark that is the foundation of wisdom.
Desiring to cause sentient beings to leave behind attachment to marks, he manifests within the world according to the nature and characteristics of all worlds, and reveals to them unsurpassed bodhi.

Wishing to rescue and protect all sentient beings, he appears in the world to reveal the Buddha-way, enabling them to behold the physical marks of the Tathāgata, to take them as objects of mindfulness and recollection, and to practice with diligent effort.

Having eliminated the characteristics of worldly afflictions and cultivated the practices of enlightenment, their minds remained undisturbed; they attained perfection in all gates of the Mahāyāna and accomplished the benefit and welfare of all Buddhas. They were able to observe the roots of goodness in sentient beings without destroying the retribution of their pure karma;
their wisdom was clear and penetrating, universally entering the three periods of time, forever free from all worldly discrimination;
they emitted nets of light that shone throughout the ten directions, filling every world without exception.
His physical body is exquisitely beautiful, such that those who behold it never tire;
through great merit, wisdom, and supernormal powers, he brings forth the various practices of a bodhisattva;
his faculties and their respective objects are sovereign and perfectly complete.
They perform all the works of a Buddha, and having performed them, they vanish;

they are skillfully able to reveal the path of omniscience throughout the past, present, and future, universally raining down immeasurable *dhāraṇīs* for the sake of all bodhisattvas, causing them to give rise to vast aspiration and joy, so that they may uphold and practice them, and accomplish all the merits of the Buddhas;
their bodies are adorned with perfect, blazing, and boundless sublime colors, such that there is no one in any world who does not behold them.
Forever free from all obstructing dharmas, having attained purity regarding the true meaning of all phenomena, and having achieved mastery over qualities of merit;
he is a great Dharma King who shines universally like the sun,
and is a field of merit for the world, endowed with great majestic power.
He universally manifests transformation bodies throughout all worlds, emitting the light of wisdom to bring all beings to enlightenment;

desiring to let sentient beings know that the Buddha is endowed with boundless merit, he receives his consecration by binding an unimpeded silken ribbon upon his crown, guiding them through skillful means in accordance with the world;

with the hand of wisdom he comforts sentient beings, acting as a great king of physicians who skillfully cures all ailments, and he is able to travel everywhere to immeasurable lands throughout all worlds without ever resting.
With the pure eye of wisdom, free from all obscurations and veils, they are able to see clearly;
they employ various means to subdue those sentient beings who commit unwholesome and evil deeds, causing them to enter the Path;
they skillfully grasp the appropriate timing, never ceasing their efforts.

If sentient beings give rise to a mind of equanimity, he immediately manifests for them the karmic retribution of equanimity; according to their inclinations and according to their karmic fruits, he manifests the Buddha-body and various supernatural transformations to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to awaken to understanding and attain the wisdom of the Dharma. Their hearts are filled with great joy, their faculties leap with vigor, they behold immeasurable Buddhas, and they give rise to profound faith.

They produce all roots of goodness and never regress. All sentient beings, bound by their karma, sleep long in birth and death; when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he is able to awaken them, comforting their minds so that they are free from sorrow and fear. If they are able to see him, he causes them all to realize and enter the wisdom of the meaning of non-reliance.
His skillful wisdom thoroughly penetrates the adornments of the realms, which are so wondrous and excellent that nothing can eclipse them.
The Dharma-sprouts of Mount Wisdom are all completely purified;
appearing sometimes as bodhisattvas and sometimes as the body of a Buddha, they cause all sentient beings to reach the stage free from affliction;
adorned with immeasurable merits, they manifest in the world through the accomplishment of karmic actions.
The adornments and purity of all Buddhas are entirely accomplished through the karma of omniscience;
they constantly maintain their original vows and do not abandon the world, acting as steadfast and virtuous friends to all sentient beings;
being supremely pure, with stainless radiance, they cause all sentient beings to behold them directly.
The sentient beings of the six realms are immeasurable and boundless, yet the Buddha, through his spiritual power, constantly follows them and never abandons them;
if there are those who have planted roots of goodness together with him in the past, he causes them all to become pure.

Toward all sentient beings in the six realms, he does not forsake his original vow nor does he deceive them, but gathers them in entirely through skillful means of wholesome dharmas, causing them to cultivate pure karma, to destroy all demons and strife, and to emerge from the limit of non-obstruction with vast power—the most supreme Sun-Treasury, free from all hindrance.
Manifesting images within the realm of the pure mind, there is no one in all the worlds who does not behold them; through various dharmas, they extensively bestow gifts upon sentient beings.
The Buddha is a treasury of boundless radiance, with all powers and wisdom fully perfected.

Constantly illuminating sentient beings with great light, he fulfills their aspirations according to their wishes. Free from all enemies, he is the supreme field of merit and the common refuge for all living beings.
May all that is given be rendered entirely pure;
may even a small virtuous deed bring forth immeasurable merit, leading all to enter the ground of inexhaustible wisdom;
may [this person] become the master who plants roots of goodness and purifies the minds of all sentient beings, and the supreme fertile field for generating merit for all sentient beings.
With profound wisdom and skillful means, they are able to rescue all beings from the suffering of the three evil realms. Thus they believe and understand; thus they observe;

thus they enter the abyss of wisdom; thus they roam the ocean of merit; thus they universally reach the wisdom of space; thus they know the field of blessings for sentient beings; thus they observe with present mindfulness; thus they contemplate the various marks and signs of the Buddha’s deeds; thus they contemplate the Buddha’s universal manifestation throughout the world; thus they contemplate the Buddha’s sovereign spiritual powers.

At that time, the great assembly beheld the body of the Tathāgata, from each and every pore of which issued hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya rays of light. Each ray possessed asaṃkhyeya colors, asaṃkhyeya purities, and asaṃkhyeya illuminations, causing asaṃkhyeya beings to observe, asaṃkhyeya beings to rejoice, asaṃkhyeya beings to experience happiness, asaṃkhyeya beings to increase their profound faith, asaṃkhyeya beings to purify their aspirations, asaṃkhyeya beings to attain coolness in their faculties, and asaṃkhyeya beings to feel reverence and respect.

At that time, the great assembly all beheld the Buddha’s body emitting hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable great radiances; each and every radiance possessed inconceivable colors and inconceivable lights, illuminating the inconceivable and boundless Dharma-realm.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, a great and wondrous sound issued forth;

this sound proclaimed hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable hymns of praise, surpassing all the verbal expressions of the world and accomplished through supramundane roots of goodness.

Furthermore, he manifested hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable, subtle, and exquisite adornments, which could not be fully extolled even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable eons; all were produced from the inexhaustible sovereignty of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, they manifest unspeakably many Buddhas and Tathāgatas appearing in the world, causing all sentient beings to enter the gate of wisdom and understand the most profound meaning.
They also manifest the transformations of unspeakably many Buddhas and Tathāgatas, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, causing all worlds to be equally pure.
Thus, all these arise from the unobstructed omniscience in which the Tathāgata dwells, and they also arise from the inconceivable, supreme virtues cultivated by the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, he manifested hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of inconceivable, wondrous jewel-flames, which arose from the roots of goodness of his past great vows. This was because he had once made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas and cultivated pure conduct without negligence; because the roots of goodness born from his unobstructed mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) had arisen; to manifest the vast pervasiveness of the Tathāgata’s power; to sever the doubts of all sentient beings; to cause all to behold the Tathāgata; to cause immeasurable sentient beings to abide in roots of goodness; to display the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers as being beyond eclipsing; to desire that sentient beings everywhere enter the ultimate ocean; to cause the bodhisattva assemblies of all Buddha-lands to gather together; and to reveal the inconceivable Dharma-gates of the Buddhas.

At that time, the Tathāgata’s great compassion universally covers all, manifesting all the adornments of omniscience. He desires to cause sentient beings in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya worlds who have not yet developed faith to do so; those who have already developed faith to increase it; those whose faith has increased to become purified; those who are already purified to reach maturity; and those who are already matured to bring their minds under control.
He contemplates the profound Dharma, is fully endowed with the light of immeasurable wisdom, gives rise to an immeasurably vast mind, and never regresses from the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).

He does not contravene the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), does not fear the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), realizes the principle of truth, fulfills all practices of the *pāramitās*, and brings all supramundane roots of goodness to complete purity.

Just as Samantabhadra has attained the sovereign mastery of a Buddha, departed from the realm of Māra, and entered the realm of all Buddhas; having thoroughly understood the profound Dharma and obtained inconceivable wisdom, his vows for the Mahāyāna never regress;
he constantly beholds all Buddhas without ever being separated from them;

he has accomplished realized knowledge and witnessed immeasurable dharmas; endowed with the power of the treasury of boundless merit, he gives rise to a heart of joy and enters the stage of non-doubt.

Free from evil and pure, relying upon all-knowledge, seeing the Dharma without wavering, they enter the assemblies of all Bodhisattvas and are constantly born into the family of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
This array manifested by the World-Honored One is entirely accomplished by the roots of goodness accumulated in the past;
it is for the purpose of taming all sentient beings, for the purpose of revealing the great majestic virtue of the Tathāgata,
for the purpose of illuminating the treasury of unimpeded wisdom, and to manifest the boundless, supreme virtues of the Tathāgata in their most blazing splendor.
Therefore, it is to manifest the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great supernormal transformations;

because by means of his power of spiritual penetrations he manifests the Buddha-body in all realms of existence; to demonstrate that the Tathāgata’s supernatural transformations and manifestations are boundless;
because his original vows have been entirely fulfilled; and to display the Tathāgata’s courageous wisdom which is able to pervade everywhere.
Because he has gone forth from the past; because he has attained sovereignty over all phenomena and become a Dharma King;
because he gives birth to all gateways of wisdom; because he manifests the purity of the Tathāgata’s body; because he further manifests his own body as most sublime and wondrous;
because he displays the realization of the equal Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; and because he reveals the treasury of pure roots of goodness.
It manifests the supreme and wondrous form that nothing in the world can compare to it;
it manifests the marks of one endowed with the ten powers, such that those who behold them never tire of doing so; and it acts as the sun for the world, illuminating the three periods of time.
The Sovereign Dharma King’s all-encompassing merits are all manifested from his past roots of goodness;
even if all bodhisattvas were to praise and extol them throughout all kalpas, they could never reach their end.

At that time, after the King of the Tuṣita Heaven had prepared such various offerings for the Tathāgata, he, together with hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of Tuṣita devaputras, joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
Welcome, Well-Gone One!
Welcome, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
Pray, out of compassion for us, remain in this palace!
At that time, the World-Honored One adorned himself with the adornments of a Buddha, possessing great majesty and virtue;

In order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to great joy; so that all bodhisattvas may develop profound awakening and understanding; so that all the sons of the Tuṣita Heaven may increase their desire for the Dharma; so that the King of the Tuṣita Heaven may never tire of making offerings and serving him; so that immeasurable sentient beings who contemplate the Buddha may resolve their minds upon enlightenment; so that immeasurable sentient beings may plant roots of goodness and merit through seeing the Buddha, which shall be inexhaustible; so that they may constantly be able to give rise to pure faith; so that they may see the Buddha and make offerings without seeking anything for themselves; so that all their aspirations and vows may be purified; and so that they may diligently accumulate roots of goodness without weariness—having thus resolved to seek all-knowledge through the issuance of great vows, he accepted the invitation of the heavenly king and entered the Palace Adorned with All Jewels.
As it is with this world, so it is with all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the Palace Adorned with All Jewels was spontaneously and exquisitely adorned, surpassing the adornments of all the devas. It was completely covered on all sides by nets of every kind of jewel, raining down everywhere clouds of all the most sublime jewels, clouds of all kinds of ornaments, clouds of all kinds of precious garments, clouds of all kinds of sandalwood incense, clouds of all kinds of solid fragrances, clouds of all kinds of jeweled parasols, and clouds of inconceivable masses of flowers. It also universally produced the sounds of inconceivable music, praising the Tathāgata’s omniscience in every respect, all of which were in perfect accord with the wondrous Dharma.
All these various articles of offering surpassed those of the devas.
At that time, within the Tuṣita Palace, music and song were performed with unceasing fervor; yet, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the mind of the King of Tuṣita remained undisturbed.

All his past roots of goodness attained fulfillment, his immeasurable wholesome dharmas became even more firm, and his pure faith increased. He gave rise to great diligence and great joy, purified his profound aspirations, and resolved upon bodhicitta. His mindfulness of the Dharma was uninterrupted, and he maintained total retention without forgetfulness.
At that time, the Deva King of Tuṣita, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, recollected the roots of goodness he had planted in the presence of past Buddhas and spoke these verses:
"In the past there was a Tathāgata named Unobstructed Moon, The most supreme among all auspicious things.
He once entered this Hall of Adornments; Therefore, this place is the most auspicious."
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Vistīrṇamati, the most excellent among all auspicious things;
he once entered this Golden Hall, and for this reason this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Universal Eye, The most preeminent among all auspicious things;
He once entered this Lotus Palace, Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Coral, The most excellent among all that is auspicious;
He once entered this Jewel-Treasury Hall, And for this reason, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata, the Lion of Debaters, most preeminent among all that is auspicious;
he once entered this palace of the King of Mountains, and for this reason, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Sūryaprabha, the most excellent among all that is auspicious;
he once entered this Hall of Many Flowers, and for this reason this place is the most auspicious.
In the past there was a Buddha named Boundless Light, the most excellent among all auspicious things;
he once entered this palace adorned with trees, and for this reason this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Tathāgata named Dharma Banner, the most excellent among all auspicious things.
He once entered this precious palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Jñānapradīpa, the most excellent among all that is auspicious;
he once entered this Gandhamādana palace; therefore, this place is most auspicious.
In the past there was a Buddha named Guṇaprabha, the most preeminent among all auspicious things;
he once entered this maṇi palace, and for this reason this place is most auspicious.
Thus, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven in this world, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, praised the Buddhas of the past with these verses;
likewise, the Kings of the Tuṣita Heavens in all worlds throughout the ten directions also praised the Buddha’s merits in this same manner.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon a lion throne within the Mani-jewel treasury of the Palace Adorned with All Jewels; his Dharma-body was pure, his wondrous functions were sovereign, and he shared the same realm as the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Abiding in all-knowledge, he entered into the same single nature as all Buddhas;
his Buddha-eye was clear and lucid, seeing all phenomena without any obstruction.
Possessing great majestic power, they travel throughout the entire Dharma-realm without ever resting;
endowed with great supernormal powers, they are able to go everywhere to wherever there are sentient beings who can be transformed;
adorning their bodies with the unimpeded adornments of all Buddhas, they skillfully know the proper time to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
Inconceivable multitudes of bodhisattvas, each having come together from various lands in other directions, have assembled;
this assembly is pure, their dharma-bodies are non-dual, they are without dependence, yet they are able to act with mastery, manifesting the conduct of the Buddha-body.

Having sat upon this seat, there spontaneously appeared within that palace immeasurable and innumerable extraordinary, exquisite, and magnificent articles of offering surpassing those of the devas, namely:
flower garlands, robes, ointments, powdered incense, jeweled parasols, banners and streamers, music, and songs of praise.
Such matters as these are each beyond measure and calculation.
With a vast mind of reverence and respect, they made offerings to the Buddha;
and it was likewise so for all the Tuṣita heavens throughout the ten directions.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-Two;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, by Imperial Command.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, there was one great bodhisattva from each of the ten directions. Each was accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields. From worlds beyond as many lands as there are atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, they came to where the Buddha was.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, Bodhisattva Sthiradhvaja, Bodhisattva Vikramadhvaja, Bodhisattva Prabhādhvaja, Bodhisattva Jñānadhvaja, Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja, Bodhisattva Vīryadhvaja, Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, Bodhisattva Jyotirdhvaja, and Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja.
The lands from which they came were:

the World of Exquisite Jewels, the World of Exquisite Joy, the World of Exquisite Silver, the World of Exquisite Gold, the World of Exquisite Maṇi, the World of Exquisite Vajra, the World of Exquisite Padma, the World of Exquisite Utpala, the World of Exquisite Sandalwood, and the World of Exquisite Fragrance.
Each of them, in the presence of a Buddha, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring; namely:

the Buddha Inexhaustible Banner, Wind Banner, Liberation Banner, Dignified Manner Banner, Radiant Appearance Banner, Constant Banner, Most Victorious Banner, Sovereign Banner, Brahma Banner, and Contemplation Banner.
When those bodhisattvas had arrived at the Buddha’s abode, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, there were immediately manifested wonderful lion thrones of precious treasuries, covered with jeweled nets that spread out and filled the area on all sides;
the assembly of bodhisattvas, according to the direction from which each had come, sat cross-legged upon them.

From his body, he emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of pure radiances; these immeasurable lights all arose from the jewel of the Bodhisattva’s pure mind, which is free from all faults and evils and is produced by great vows. They manifest the sovereign and pure dharmas of all Buddhas.

By the power of the Bodhisattvas’ impartial vows, they are able to universally rescue and protect all sentient beings; they are a joy for all worlds to behold, and those who see them do so not in vain, for all are brought to subdual.
The assembly of those bodhisattvas had all already accomplished immeasurable merits.
That is to say:
they traveled everywhere through all buddha-lands without obstruction, perceiving the pure dharma-body which is without dependence;
With the body of wisdom, they manifest infinite bodies, traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions to serve all Buddhas;

they enter the infinite, boundless, and inconceivable dharmas of mastery of the Buddhas, abide in the gateways of infinite omniscience, and through the light of wisdom, skillfully comprehend all phenomena;
having attained fearlessness regarding all dharmas, they continue their exposition of the Dharma until the end of the future.

His eloquence is inexhaustible; with great wisdom he opens the gate of *dhāraṇī*, and with the pure eye of insight he enters the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). The sphere of his wisdom is boundless, ultimately pure like empty space.

Just as the assembly of bodhisattvas has thus gathered in the Tuṣita Heaven palace of this world, so too do bodhisattvas bearing these same names gather in all the Tuṣita Heaven palaces throughout the ten directions; the lands from which they have come and the names of their respective Buddhas are likewise identical, without any difference.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his two kneecaps hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of rays of light, which universally illuminated all worlds throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Those bodhisattvas all beheld these manifestations of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations;
likewise, these bodhisattvas also beheld those manifestations of the spiritual transformations of all the Tathāgatas.
These bodhisattvas all planted roots of goodness together with Vairocana Tathāgata in the past and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva;

they have all awakened to and entered the profound liberation of the sovereign power of all Buddhas, attained a body that is the undifferentiated dharma-realm, and enter all lands without dwelling anywhere;
they behold immeasurable Buddhas and go to serve them all.
In a single thought-moment, they traverse the entire dharma-realm with sovereign non-obstruction;
their minds and intentions are pure like priceless jewels;
and they are constantly protected and mindful of by immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, who together bestow their power upon them so that they reach the ultimate, foremost shore.
Constantly abiding in pure mindfulness, they dwell in supreme enlightenment; in every thought-moment, they perpetually enter the sphere of all-knowledge.
Entering the small into the large and the large into the small, they attain mastery and achieve unimpeded penetration;
having already attained the Buddha-body, they cohabit with the Buddhas.
They have attained all-knowledge, and their bodies are born from all-knowledge;
they are able to enter into every sphere traversed by all Tathāgatas;
they expound immeasurable gateways of wisdom-dharma, reach the further shore of the great wisdom of the Vajra Banner, attain the Vajra Samādhi, and sever all doubts.

Having attained the sovereign supernormal powers of all Buddhas, they universally teach and discipline hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless sentient beings throughout all lands in the ten directions;
though they are entirely unattached to any numerical measure, they are skillfully able to practice and study until achieving ultimate perfection, establishing all dharmas through expedient means.

In this manner, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakably infinite, pure assemblies of all Bodhisattvas—the treasuries of immeasurable merit throughout the three periods of time—all gathered together at the place where the Buddha was;
and by virtue of what was seen through the light, it was exactly the same at the abodes of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, Nor is there any parinirvāṇa;
By the power of his original great vows, He manifests the dharma of sovereign mastery.”
This Dharma is difficult to conceive; it is not within the sphere of the mind.
Only when wisdom reaches the other shore can one behold the realm of the Buddhas.
The form-body is not the Buddha, and the same is true for the voice.
Nor are they apart from form and sound; one beholds the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
Those of little wisdom cannot know the true realm of all Buddhas;
only those who have long cultivated pure deeds can understand this.
Perfectly Awakened Ones have no place from which they come, nor do they go anywhere;
this pure and wondrous form-body appears through the power of spiritual transformations.
Within immeasurable worlds, they manifest the body of the Tathāgata.
He extensively expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, his mind free from all attachment.
His wisdom is boundless, thoroughly penetrating all phenomena;
he universally enters the Dharma-realm, manifesting the power of sovereign mastery.
Sentient beings and all phenomena— He understands them all without obstruction;
Universally manifesting all forms and images, Pervading throughout all lands.
Desiring to seek all-knowledge And swiftly achieve unsurpassed enlightenment,
One should cultivate the practices of enlightenment with a pure and sublime mind.
If one beholds the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power in this way,
one should make offerings to the Most Victorious Honored One without giving rise to doubt.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata is supreme and peerless; Profoundly deep, he is ineffable.
Transcending the path of language, He is as pure as space.”
Behold the Lion among Men, whose sovereign power of supernatural faculties has already transcended all conceptual discrimination, yet causes beings to perceive through discrimination.
The Guide expounds for them the most profound and subtle Dharma.
For these reasons, this incomparable body is manifested.
This is the great wisdom, the sphere of practice of all Buddhas;
those who wish to understand it should always draw near to the Buddha.
With mental karma always pure, making offerings to all Tathāgatas without ever wearying of heart, one is able to enter the Buddha-way;
possessing inexhaustible merit, one remains steadfastly established in the bodhicitta.
With this, the net of doubt is removed; one contemplates the Buddha without weariness.
Having attained mastery over all dharmas, such a person is a true son of the Buddha;
they are able to fully comprehend the sovereign power of all Buddhas.
As taught by the one of vast wisdom, desire is the root of all phenomena;
one should give rise to sublime aspiration and resolve to seek unsurpassed enlightenment.
If there are those who revere the Buddha and wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness, [they should do so].
That person shall never be parted from the dwelling place of all Buddhas.
How could a person of wisdom, having seen and heard the Buddhas,
fail to cultivate pure vows and tread the path walked by the Buddhas?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Valorous Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
"Just as with clear and pure eyes, One perceives all forms through the power of the sun;
So too is it with the pure mind: Through the Buddha's power, one beholds the Tathāgata."
Just as by the power of diligence one can reach the very bottom of the ocean’s source, so too is the power of wisdom: through it, one beholds immeasurable Buddhas.
Like a fertile and rich field, whatever is sown therein will surely grow and flourish.
Thus, from this ground of pure mind, all Buddha-dharmas are born.
Just as a person who discovers a treasure trove is forever freed from the suffering of poverty,
so too the Bodhisattva, having attained the Buddha-dharma, is free from defilement and possesses a pure mind.
Just as the *gadhā* medicine can eliminate all poisons,
so too is the Buddha-dharma, which extinguishes the affliction of all defilements.
A true spiritual friend is one praised by the Tathāgata.
By virtue of that majestic power, one is able to hear the teachings of all Buddhas.
Even if one were to bestow wealth and treasures upon the Buddhas for countless eons,
if one does not know the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha, this cannot even be called giving.
Infinite varieties of forms and marks adorn the Buddha’s body,
yet it is not within these forms and marks that one can see the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is tranquil and eternally unmoving.
Yet they are able to manifest bodies everywhere, filling the realms of the ten directions.
Just as the realm of empty space is neither born nor extinguished, so too are the Buddhas’ dharmas; ultimately, they are without birth or extinction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Light Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“In the human realm and the heavens, Throughout all worlds,
Everywhere one beholds the Tathāgata, With his pure and wondrous form-body.”
Just as the power of a single mind can give rise to various minds,
so too does the body of one Buddha universally manifest as all Buddhas.
Awakening is a non-dual reality, and it is likewise devoid of all marks.
Yet within these two dharmas, he manifests a body adorned with marks;
realizing that the nature of phenomena is empty and quiescent, arising like an illusion,
his conduct is inexhaustible— thus does the Guide manifest.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, Their Dharma-bodies are entirely pure;
According to those who should be transformed, They universally manifest wondrous form-bodies.
The Tathāgata does not think: "I have created such a body."
Manifesting spontaneously, they never give rise to conceptual discrimination.
The Dharma-realm is without differentiation and has no point of dependence;
yet, within the world, they manifest infinite bodies.
The Buddha’s body is not a transformation, nor is it not a transformation;
within the state of non-transformation, he manifests a transformed form.
Perfect Awakening is immeasurable, equal to the dharma-realm and empty space.
Profound and vast, without limit or bottom, where the path of speech is entirely cut off;
the Tathāgata has skillfully mastered it, traversing the path in all places—
through the Dharma-realm and all lands— proceeding everywhere without obstruction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“If there is one who can believe and accept The unimpeded wisdom of all-knowledge,
And cultivate the practices of enlightenment, Their mind is immeasurable.”
Throughout all lands, they universally manifest immeasurable bodies;
yet these bodies do not abide in any place, nor do they dwell within phenomena.
Each and every Tathāgata manifests their form through the power of spiritual sovereignty.
Inconceivable eons cannot be exhausted by calculation;
though the number of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time may be known,
the number of those manifested by the Tathāgata cannot be grasped.
At times they manifest as one or two, even unto immeasurable bodies, appearing universally throughout the lands of the ten directions; yet in reality, there are not two kinds.
Just as the pure full moon appears universally in all waters, so too does the Buddha appear everywhere.
Though reflections are immeasurable, the original moon has never been two.
So too, this unimpeded wisdom that achieves perfect enlightenment manifests universally in all lands, yet the Buddha-body remains non-dual.
Neither one nor two, and yet not infinite;
according to those who are to be transformed, he manifests infinite bodies.
The Buddha-body is not of the past, nor is it of the future.
In a single thought-moment, birth is manifested, as well as the attainment of enlightenment and nirvana.
Like forms produced by illusion, they are without birth and without arising;
the Buddha-body is likewise, manifesting itself without birth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Buddha-body is immeasurable, yet it can manifest a measurable body;
according to what each beholds as appropriate, the Guide thus appears.”
The Buddha-body has no location, yet it pervades all places;
like space, it is without limit, and thus it is inconceivable.
It is not a sphere where the mind operates, nor does the mind arise within it.
Within the realm of all Buddhas, there is ultimately no arising or ceasing.
Just as that which is seen by a person with cataracts is neither internal nor external,
one should know that the way the world perceives the Buddhas is likewise so.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Tathāgata appears in the world;
though sentient beings perceive his appearance, in reality, he does not arise in the world.
One cannot see the Buddha through lands, nor by means of day and night.
A single moment is but a fraction of time; know that all things are thus.
Though sentient beings say, "On such a day the Buddha attained enlightenment," and that the Tathāgata realized bodhi on that very date, in truth, it is not bound to any specific day.
The Tathāgata is free from conceptual construction; He is not of this world and transcends all numerical categories.
All the Teachers of the three times appear in this very way.
Just as the pure orb of the sun Never coincides with the darkness of night,
Yet it is said that on a certain day and night, the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus.
All kalpas of the three periods of time do not coincide with the Tathāgata;
yet it is said that there are Buddhas of the three periods—such is the Dharma of the Guide.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryaketu, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Guides of all beings, Their bodies are identical and their meaning is likewise so;
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, They manifest in various ways according to what is appropriate.”
Behold the Honored Muni: his deeds are most extraordinary;
he fills the entire dharma-realm, leaving nothing whatsoever untouched.
The Buddha-body is not within, nor is it without.
Manifested through spiritual power, such is the Dharma of the Guide.
According to the various classes of sentient beings and the karma accumulated in previous lives,
he manifests these various bodies, each appearing differently.
The bodies of all Buddhas are thus: immeasurable and beyond counting;
except for the Great Awakened Honored One, none can conceive of them.
Just as my own inconceivability cannot be grasped by the activities of the mind, so too is it with the Buddhas.
The Buddha, inconceivable, is likewise; he is not manifested by the activity of the mind.
Just as the lands are inconceivable, yet they are seen adorned with purity, so too is the Buddha inconceivable, and his wondrous marks appear without exception.
Just as all phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions, so too is the vision of the Buddha;
it must necessarily rely upon manifold wholesome karmas.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem can satisfy the hearts of sentient beings, [so too does the vision of the Buddha fulfill their aspirations].
Such is the nature of all Buddhas’ Dharma: they fulfill every aspiration.
Within immeasurable lands, the Guides arise in the world;
by virtue of their power of vows, they respond universally throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The light of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom Universally purifies all worlds;
Once the worlds have been purified, He reveals all the Buddha-dharmas.”
Suppose there were someone who wished to see Buddhas as numerous as all sentient beings;
though none fail to respond to their mind, in truth there is no place from which they come.
Taking the Buddha as one's object of focus, one should maintain this exclusive mindfulness without ceasing.
This person shall behold the Buddhas, as many as there are thoughts in their mind.
Having accomplished pure and white dharmas and being fully endowed with all merits,
they will focus their minds single-mindedly upon omniscience, never letting it go.
The Teacher, for the sake of sentient beings, expounds the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
wherever there are those capable of being transformed, he universally manifests his most supreme body.
Both the Buddha-body and the world are entirely devoid of self.
Awakening to this, one attains perfect enlightenment, And further preaches it for the sake of sentient beings.
All those lions among men, Possessing immeasurable powers of mastery, Manifest bodies such as the body of mindfulness; Each of these bodies is distinct.
The body of the world is thus, and the bodies of all Buddhas are likewise;
one who thoroughly understands their intrinsic nature is called a Buddha.
The Tathāgata perceives universally and clearly comprehends all phenomena.
The Buddha-dharma and bodhi—both are unattainable.
The Teacher has neither coming nor going, nor does he abide anywhere;
being far removed from all perversions, this is called Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Constellation Banner, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata has no abode, yet he dwells universally in all lands;
He goes to every realm and is seen in every place.”
The Buddha, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, Universally manifests all manner of bodies:
Attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, And entering parinirvāṇa.
The Buddhas are inconceivable; Who could possibly conceive of the Buddhas?
Who can perceive the Perfectly Awakened One?
Who can manifest the Most Supreme?
All phenomena are suchness, and the realm of all Buddhas is likewise so.
There is not even a single dharma that undergoes arising and ceasing as it does in the intermediate state.
Sentient beings falsely discriminate, [thinking] "this is a Buddha" and "this is a world";
those who thoroughly understand the nature of dharmas perceive neither Buddha nor world.
The Tathāgata appears universally before them, causing sentient beings to have faith and joy;
yet the Buddha-body cannot be apprehended, for there is nothing therein to be seen.
If one can, within this world, remain far removed from all attachments, [one realizes the truth].
With an unimpeded mind, one rejoices and attains awakening to the Dharma.
That which is manifested through spiritual power is what is called a Buddha;
throughout all times of the three periods, when sought, it is found to be utterly non-existent.
If one can know in this way the mind, the mental factors, and all phenomena,
perceiving and seeing them all completely, one will swiftly attain the state of a Tathāgata.
Within these words, the sovereign mastery of all Buddhas is revealed.
“Perfect Awakening transcends language; it is expressed only by means of language.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmadhvaja, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the ten directions and spoke in verse:
“It would be better to constantly endure all the sufferings of the world, rather than [forsake] the Dharma.”
They shall never be far from the Tathāgata, nor fail to behold his sovereign power.
If there are sentient beings who have not yet resolved their minds toward Bodhi,
as soon as they hear the Buddha’s name, they will certainly attain enlightenment.
If there is a person of wisdom who, in a single thought, gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they will surely become a Supreme Honored One; do not harbor doubt or hesitation.
The sovereign power of the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter even in immeasurable kalpas.
If one gives rise to a single thought of faith, one will swiftly ascend the unsurpassed path.
Even if, in every moment of thought, one were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas,
if one does not know the true Dharma, it cannot be called making an offering.
If one hears such a Dharma, from which all Buddhas are born,
though they undergo immeasurable suffering, they do not abandon the practice of Bodhi.
Upon hearing once of this great wisdom, the Dharma entered by all Buddhas—
Throughout the entire Dharma-realm, they become guides of the three periods of time.
Though they travel extensively through all Buddha-fields until the end of the future,
if they do not seek this wondrous Dharma, they will ultimately not attain Bodhi.
Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have long wandered through birth and death;
because they do not understand the true Dharma, the Buddhas appear in the world.
All dharmas are indestructible, and there is no one who can destroy them.
"Through sovereign great radiance, it is universally revealed throughout the world. Chapter 25:
The Ten Dedications. At that time, Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields, all bearing the same name:
Vajradhvaja. They all spoke in praise, saying: "Excellent!
Excellent, noble son! You are indeed able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.

"Good son! This is because the spiritual powers of the Buddhas of the ten directions—equal in number to the atoms within one hundred thousand Buddha-fields—have collectively empowered you; it is also due to the power of the vows and the majestic spiritual authority of Vairocana Tathāgata in the past, as well as the purity of your own wisdom and the increasing excellence of the roots of goodness of all Bodhisattvas. It is for these reasons that you have been enabled to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma;
so that all Bodhisattvas may attain pure fearlessness and be endowed with unimpeded eloquence, they shall enter..."
Because they abide on the stage of unimpeded wisdom; because they dwell in the great mind of omniscience;
because they have accomplished inexhaustible roots of goodness; because they have fulfilled the unimpeded pure dharmas; because they have entered the universal gateway of the dharma-realm;

because they manifest the spiritual powers of all Buddhas; because their mindfulness and wisdom regarding the past are uninterrupted; and because they have obtained the protection and sustenance of all Buddhas.
Because of the various faculties; because of the extensive exposition of manifold dharmas through immeasurable gateways;
because of hearing, fully understanding, receiving, and upholding them without forgetting; because of gathering all the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas;
because of accomplishing the aids to the supramundane path; because of not severing the wisdom of omniscience; because of developing great vows; and because of explaining the true meaning.
Therefore, because they thoroughly understand the dharma-realm, because they cause all bodhisattvas to rejoice,
because they cultivate the roots of goodness that are equal to all buddhas, and because they protect and maintain the lineage of all Tathāgatas— namely:
He expounded the ten dedications of all bodhisattvas.
"O Son of the Buddha!

You should expound this Dharma by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, because you have received the Buddha’s protective mindfulness, because you dwell securely in the household of the Buddhas, because you increase supramundane merit, because you have attained the light of dhāraṇī, because you enter the unobstructed Buddha-Dharmas, because the great light universally illumines the dharma-realm, because you gather the pure Dharmas free from fault, because you abide in the sphere of vast wisdom, and because you have attained the light of the unobstructed Dharma."

At that time, the Buddhas bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja immeasurable wisdom; they bestowed unimpeded eloquence; they bestowed skillful means for discerning the meanings of phrases; they bestowed the light of the unobstructed Dharma; they bestowed a body equal to that of the Tathāgatas; they bestowed infinite and diverse pure vocal sounds; they bestowed the bodhisattva samādhi of inconceivable skillful observation; they bestowed the wisdom of dedicating all indestructible roots of goodness; they bestowed the skillful means of accomplishing the observation of all phenomena; and they bestowed uninterrupted eloquence for expounding all dharmas in all places.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the roots of goodness from entering this samādhi.
At that time, each of the Buddhas stroked the crown of the head of Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva with his right hand.
After the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja had received the empowerment of the touching of the crown, he arose from his meditative concentration and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess inconceivable great vows that fill the Dharma-realm and are universally able to rescue and protect all sentient beings. They are as follows:"
One practices the dedication of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
O Son of the Buddha!
How many kinds of dedication are there for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas?
O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of dedication by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have collectively expounded. What are these ten?

First is the dedication for rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being"; second is the indestructible dedication; third is the dedication equal to all Buddhas; fourth is the dedication reaching all places; fifth is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; sixth is the dedication entering all impartial roots of goodness; seventh is the dedication equally conforming to all sentient beings; eighth is the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*); ninth is the dedication of liberation without bondage or attachment; tenth is the dedication entering the infinite Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of dedication of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, which have been taught, will be taught, and are now being taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s dedication of merit for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a ‘sentient being’?
O Son of the Buddha!”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, purifies the perfection of ethical discipline, cultivates the perfection of patience, arouses the perfection of diligence, enters the perfection of meditative concentration, and dwells in the perfection of wisdom; with great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, they cultivate such immeasurable roots of goodness.
When cultivating roots of goodness, one should form this thought:

"May these roots of goodness universally benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to attain purity and reach the ultimate state, forever departing from the immeasurable sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama."
"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva plants roots of goodness, he dedicates his own roots of goodness in this way:
'I shall act as a shelter for all sentient beings, so that they may be freed from all causes of suffering;
I shall act as a protector for all sentient beings, so that they may be completely liberated from all afflictions.'"
They act as a refuge for all sentient beings, so that all may be freed from every fear;
they act as a destination for all sentient beings, so that all may reach omniscience;
they act as a peace for all sentient beings, so that all may attain the state of ultimate security.
They act as a light for all sentient beings, so that they may attain the radiance of wisdom and extinguish the darkness of delusion;
they act as a torch for all sentient beings, to shatter all the darkness of ignorance;
they act as a lamp for all sentient beings, so that they may abide in the state of ultimate purity.
They act as guides for all sentient beings, leading them to enter the true Dharma;
they act as great guides for all sentient beings, bestowing upon them unimpeded great wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of goodness in this manner, they impartially benefit all sentient beings, ultimately causing them all to attain omniscience."
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the dedication of protection toward those who are not their friends, they do so without any distinction from how they treat their own friends. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have entered into the equality of all phenomena, they do not give rise to even a single thought of regarding sentient beings as anything other than friends.
Even if there are sentient beings who harbor thoughts of enmity or harm toward a Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva gazes upon them with eyes of loving-kindness and never feels anger or resentment.
Universally acting as a virtuous friend for all sentient beings, he expounds the True Dharma and causes them to practice it.
He is like the great ocean, which cannot be altered or corrupted by any poison.

The Bodhisattva is likewise; all those evil beings who are ignorant and deluded, devoid of wisdom, ungrateful for kindness and virtue, wrathful, cruel, and malicious, arrogant and conceited, whose minds are blind and sightless, and who do not recognize wholesome dharmas—though such beings may afflict him in various ways, they are unable to disturb or unsettle him.
For example, when the Sun Deity appears in the world, he does not remain hidden and fail to appear because those born blind cannot see him;

nor does he remain hidden and fail to appear because he is obscured by such things as a city of Gandharvas, the hands of an Asura, the Jambu tree of Jambudvīpa, lofty cliffs, deep valleys, dust, mist, smoke, or clouds;
nor does he remain hidden and fail to appear because of the changing of the seasons.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: possessing great merit and virtue, with a mind that is profound and vast, he observes with right mindfulness and never retreats;
desiring to bring to ultimate completion his merit and wisdom, he gives rise to a resolute aspiration for the supreme Dharma;
the light of the Dharma shines everywhere, and he perceives all meanings.
They possess sovereign wisdom regarding all dharma-gates;
they constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas for the benefit of all sentient beings, never erringly giving rise to a mind that abandons them;

nor do they abandon sentient beings simply because their natures are depraved, their views are perverse, they are turbid with anger, or they are difficult to subdue, thereby failing to practice dedication.
They adorn themselves solely with the armor of the great vows of a bodhisattva to rescue and protect sentient beings, never regressing;
they do not withdraw from the bodhisattva practice or abandon the path to enlightenment because sentient beings fail to repay their kindness;
nor do they abandon all roots of goodness that accord with reality simply because they dwell together with the foolish and ignorant.
One should not give rise to weariness or aversion toward sentient beings because their faults and evils are numerous and difficult to endure.
Why is this? It is, for example, like the Sun Deity, who does not appear in the world for the sake of a single purpose alone.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: they do not cultivate various roots of goodness and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of a single sentient being alone;
rather, they cultivate roots of goodness and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of universally rescuing and protecting all sentient beings.

In this way, they do not merely give rise to great vows of wisdom and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of purifying a single buddha-field, nor for the sake of placing faith in a single Buddha, nor for the sake of seeing a single Buddha, nor for the sake of understanding a single Dharma.

Rather, for the sake of universally purifying all buddha-fields, for the sake of universally placing faith in all Buddhas, for the sake of universally serving and making offerings to all Buddhas, and for the sake of universally understanding all Buddha-dharmas, they initiate great vows, cultivate all roots of goodness, and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes the teachings of all Buddhas as their object of focus, giving rise to a vast mind and a non-retrogressive mind. Throughout immeasurable eons, they cultivate and accumulate this rare and difficult-to-attain jewel of a mind, which is entirely equal to that of all Buddhas.”

When a bodhisattva contemplates all roots of goodness in this way, their faith becomes pure and their great compassion firm. With a profound mind, a joyful mind, a pure mind, a most excellent mind, a supple mind, a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of protection, a mind of benefit, and a mind of peace and happiness, they universally dedicate these roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings in accordance with reality, rather than merely speaking with words.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates their various roots of goodness, they form this thought:
"By means of my roots of goodness, may all beings born in any realm of existence and all sentient beings attain complete purity."
Their merit is perfected, indestructible, and inexhaustible;
they are always honored, their right mindfulness is never lost,
they attain decisive wisdom, and are endowed with immeasurable knowledge.
"May my actions of body, speech, and mind, and all my merits, be perfectly adorned and fulfilled.
Furthermore, he forms this thought:
"By means of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings serve and make offerings to all Buddhas, so that none do so in vain."
Toward all Buddhas, they possess indestructible pure faith;
having heard the True Dharma, they sever all doubts and delusions, retain it in memory without forgetting, and practice according to the teachings;
toward the Tathāgatas, they give rise to a mind of reverence, purify their physical actions, and abide securely in immeasurable and vast roots of goodness.
Forever free from poverty, they are fully endowed with the seven riches;

they constantly follow and study under all Buddhas, accomplishing immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous roots of goodness; they attain impartial realization and abide in omniscience, regarding all sentient beings with an unobstructed eye;
their bodies are adorned with the various marks, free from any flaw or deficiency.
His speech and tones are pure and sublime; his merits are perfected; his faculties are subdued; he has accomplished the ten powers; his virtuous mind is fulfilled; and he abides nowhere.
"May all sentient beings universally attain the bliss of the Buddhas, attain immeasurable abodes, and dwell where the Buddhas dwell.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see sentient beings who have committed evil deeds and undergo various heavy sufferings;
Because of these obstacles, they do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, and do not recognize the Sangha.
They then form this thought:
"I shall, within those various evil realms, undergo all manner of sufferings on behalf of all sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation."
