If there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, who have skillfully cultivated all practices, skillfully accumulated the aids to the Path, skillfully made offerings to all Buddhas, skillfully gathered pure and white dharmas, who have been guided by spiritual friends, who have skillfully gathered and purified their profound resolve, who have established vast aspirations and given rise to vast understanding, for whom compassion is manifest before them; who do so for the sake of seeking Buddha-wisdom, for the sake of attaining the ten powers, for the sake of attaining the great fearlessnesses, for the sake of attaining the equal Dharma of the Buddhas, for the sake of rescuing all worlds, for the sake of purifying great compassion, for the sake of attaining the knowledge that leaves nothing remaining throughout the ten directions, for the sake of purifying all Buddha-lands without obstruction, for the sake of knowing all three periods of time in a single thought-moment, and for the sake of turning the Great Wheel of Dharma without fear.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind—headed by great compassion, preeminent in wisdom, embraced by skillful means, sustained by the most supreme profound resolve, possessing the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgata, and endowed with the power of courageous discernment and the power of knowledge; when unimpeded wisdom is manifest before them, they accord with spontaneous wisdom, are able to receive all Buddha-dharmas, and teach through wisdom that is as vast as the dharma-realm, as ultimate as space, and extending to the end of the future.
O Son of the Buddha!

As soon as a bodhisattva first gives rise to such a mind, they immediately transcend the stage of ordinary beings and enter the rank of bodhisattvas; they are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and no one can speak of any flaw in their lineage. They leave behind the worldly realms and enter the supramundane path; they attain the bodhisattva-dharma, abide in the station of bodhisattvas, and enter into the equality of the three periods of time. Within the lineage of the Tathāgatas, they are certain to attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
When a bodhisattva abides in such dharmas,
it is called "abiding in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy," because of the correspondence with immovability.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells on the Stage of Joy, they achieve abundant joy, abundant pure faith, abundant affection, abundant serenity, abundant celebration, abundant exultation, abundant valor, abundant freedom from strife, abundant freedom from malice, and abundant freedom from resentment.

O Son of the Buddha! When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to joy by recollecting all Buddhas; they give rise to joy by recollecting all Buddha-dharmas; they give rise to joy by recollecting all bodhisattvas; they give rise to joy by recollecting all bodhisattva practices; they give rise to joy by recollecting the purity of all *pāramitās*; they give rise to joy by recollecting the excellence of the bodhisattva stages; they give rise to joy by recollecting the indestructibility of the bodhisattvas; they give rise to joy by recollecting the Tathāgatas’ teaching and transforming of sentient beings; they give rise to joy by recollecting their ability to bring benefit to sentient beings; and they give rise to joy by recollecting their entry into the skillful means of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas. Furthermore, they form this thought:

"I give rise to joy because I have turned away from all worldly spheres; I give rise to joy because I draw near to all Buddhas; I give rise to joy because I am far removed from the stage of ordinary beings; I give rise to joy because I approach the stage of wisdom; I give rise to joy because I have forever severed all evil destinies; I give rise to joy because I act as a place of refuge for all sentient beings; I give rise to joy because I behold all Tathāgatas; I give rise to joy because I am born within the realm of the Buddhas; I give rise to joy because I enter into the equality of all Bodhisattvas; and I give rise to joy because I am far removed from all terrors, such as the bristling of body hair."
Why is this? Once this bodhisattva has attained the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), all fears are entirely left behind—namely:
the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of the evil realms, and the fear of the majesty of great assemblies. Such fears as these are forever abandoned.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has abandoned the notion of a self, he does not even cherish his own body, let alone material wealth; therefore, he has no fear of being unable to sustain himself.
He does not seek offerings from others, but devotes himself solely to giving and bestowing upon all sentient beings; therefore, he has no fear of ill repute.
Being far removed from the view of self and devoid of the notion of a self, they have no fear of death;
knowing for themselves that after death they will certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they have no fear of the evil realms;
as for their aspirations and delights, there is no one equal to them in all the world, much less anyone superior!
Therefore, there is no fear regarding the majesty and power of the great assembly.
In this way, the Bodhisattva remains far removed from such things as alarm, terror, and the bristling of body hair.
"O Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, possesses a vast resolve that cannot be thwarted or destroyed; he further diligently cultivates all roots of goodness until they reach fulfillment, namely:

because his faith is preeminent, because he has abundant pure faith, because his understanding is purified, because his faith is resolute, because he gives rise to pity and sympathy, because he accomplishes great loving-kindness, because his mind is free from weariness or indolence, and because of shame and remorse.
Because they are adorned; because they have achieved gentleness and flexibility; because they reverently accord with and respect the Buddha’s teachings;
because they cultivate and accumulate roots of goodness day and night without weariness; because they draw near to spiritual friends; because they always delight in the Dharma;
because they seek out extensive learning without weariness; and because they correctly contemplate the Dharma as it has been heard.
Because the mind is free from dependence and attachment; because one does not crave gain, fame, or honor;
because one does not seek any material requisites for life; because one gives rise to a jewel-like mind that knows no satiety;
because one seeks the ground of all-knowledge; and because one seeks the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Tathāgata.
Because they seek the various pāramitās and factors conducive to enlightenment; because they are free from all flattery and deception; because they are able to practice according to their words;
because they constantly protect truthful speech; because they do not defile the family of the Tathāgata; because they do not abandon the bodhisattva precepts;
because they give rise to the mind of omniscience that is as immovable as the king of mountains; and because they do not forsake any world.
Because they accomplish the supramundane path; because they never tire of gathering the factors conducive to enlightenment;
and because they constantly seek the ever-higher, most excellent path.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes such dharmas for purifying the stages,
they are said to be "dwelling securely in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they are able to accomplish such great vows, such great courage, and such great activities as these:
"I shall give rise to vast, pure, and resolute understanding, and with all manner of offerings, I shall reverently serve and honor all Buddhas without exception;
as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing through all kalpas until the end of the future without rest."
Furthermore, he made this great vow:
"May I receive the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas; may I encompass the Bodhi of all Buddhas; may I protect the teachings of all Buddhas; may I uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas;
as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing without rest through all kalpas until the end of the future."
Furthermore, he made this great vow:

"May I go before all Buddhas who arise in all worlds—from their descent from the Tuṣita heaven, their entry into the womb, their dwelling in the womb, their birth, their renunciation, their attainment of enlightenment, their teaching of the Dharma, and their manifestation of *parinirvāṇa*—to attend upon them, serve them, and act as a leader among the assembly. May I receive and practice the True Dharma, turning the wheel of the Dharma simultaneously in all places;
vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."
Furthermore, he made this great vow:

"May all bodhisattva practices be vast and immeasurable, indestructible and unmixed, encompassing all the pāramitās and purifying all the stages (bhūmis). May I explain all bodhisattva practices—whether in their general characteristics, specific characteristics, common characteristics, distinct characteristics, characteristics of formation, or characteristics of disintegration—as they truly are. May I teach and transform all beings, causing them to accept and practice these teachings so that their minds may increase;
may they be as vast as the dharma-realm and as ultimate as space, continuing without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."
Furthermore, he made this great vow:

"May I teach and transform all beings within the realm of sentient beings—those with form and those without form, those with perception, those without perception, and those with neither perception nor non-perception; those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those bound by the three realms and entering all places of birth within the six destinies; those comprised of name-and-form—and all such classes of beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-dharma, to forever sever all worldly destinies, and to abide securely on the path of the knowledge of all-knowledge;
as vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as space, and without ceasing throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."
He further made this great vow:

"May all worlds—vast and immeasurable, whether coarse or subtle, abiding in disorder, inverted, or upright; whether entering, moving, or departing; differentiated like the net of Indra, with infinite varieties throughout the ten directions—be clearly understood by my wisdom, perceived directly, and known before me.
May this be as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as space, continuing without ceasing through all kalpas until the end of the future."
He further made this great vow:

"May all lands enter into a single land, and a single land enter into all lands; may immeasurable Buddha-lands be universally pure, adorned with arrays of radiant light and various requisites; may they be free from all afflictions and achieve the path of purity; may they be filled with sentient beings of immeasurable wisdom who universally enter the vast realms of all Buddhas, manifesting according to the minds of sentient beings to bring them all joy;
may they be as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as space, continuing without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."

Furthermore, he made this great vow: "May I share the same will and conduct as all Bodhisattvas, free from resentment or envy, gathering all roots of goodness. May I share the same single object of focus as all Bodhisattvas, always meeting together and never being separated. May I, at will, manifest various Buddha-bodies; may I, according to my own mind, be able to know the power, majesty, and wisdom of the realms of all Tathāgatas; may I attain non-retrogressive *ṛddhi* (supernormal powers) and travel through all worlds, manifesting forms in all assemblies and universally entering all places of birth.

May I accomplish the inconceivable Mahāyāna and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva—vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, continuing without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."

Furthermore, he made this great vow: "May I ride upon the wheel of non-retrogression to practice the bodhisattva path; may my actions of body, speech, and mind never be in vain. May those who see me even for a moment be certain of the Buddha-dharma; may those who hear my voice even briefly attain true wisdom; and may those who give rise to pure faith even momentarily forever sever their afflictions.

May I obtain a body like that of the Great King of Medicine Tree, and a body like that of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, to cultivate all bodhisattva practices—vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate as space, without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."
Furthermore, he made this great vow:
"May I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment in all worlds without ever departing from a single hair-tip;
may I manifest birth, renunciation, [enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and parinirvāṇa] upon every hair-tip."
They proceed to the site of enlightenment, attain perfect awakening, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter nirvana;

having attained the power of great wisdom within the realm of the Buddhas, in every thought-moment they manifest the attainment of Buddhahood according to the minds of all sentient beings to lead them to tranquility.
By means of a single moment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, they know that the entire dharma-realm is itself the characteristic of nirvana. Through this...
With a single voice they preach the Dharma so that the minds of all sentient beings are filled with joy;
they manifest entry into Great Nirvana while never ceasing their bodhisattva practices; they manifest the ground of great wisdom to establish all dharmas;

and through the supernormal power of dharma-knowledge, the supernormal power of psychic travel, and the supernormal power of illusion, they manifest sovereign transformations that fill the entire dharma-realm.
“Vast as the Dharma-realm, ultimate as empty space, it shall continue without rest throughout all kalpas until the end of the future.
“O Son of the Buddha!”

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy, they give rise to such great vows, such great valor, and such great activities; with these ten gates of vows as the foremost, they fulfill one million asaṃkhyeya great vows.
O Son of the Buddha!
This great vow is accomplished through ten phrases of totality. What are these ten?

That is to say: the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings; the exhaustion of the realm of worlds; the exhaustion of the realm of space; the exhaustion of the realm of phenomena; the exhaustion of the realm of nirvana; the exhaustion of the realm of the appearance of Buddhas; the exhaustion of the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; the exhaustion of the realm of the objects perceived by the mind; the exhaustion of the realm of the objective spheres entered by the Buddha’s wisdom; and the exhaustion of the realms of the revolution of the world, the revolution of phenomena, and the revolution of wisdom.
"If the realm of sentient beings were to be exhausted, my vow would then be exhausted;
if the worlds, and even the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, the turning of wisdom, and the turning of the realms were to be exhausted, my vow would then be exhausted."

Yet the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible; because even the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom-realm are inexhaustible, these roots of goodness from my great vow shall never come to an end.
“O Son of the Buddha!

Once a bodhisattva has made such great vows as these, they will attain a mind of benefit, a supple mind, a compliant mind, a tranquil mind, a disciplined mind, a mind of cessation, a humble mind, a moistening mind, an immovable mind, and an unclouded mind.”

One who has perfected pure faith possesses the functional power of faith: they are able to believe in the entry into the original practices of the Tathāgata; they believe in the accomplishment of the various pāramitās; they believe in the entry into the various supreme stages (bhūmis); they believe in the accomplishment of the powers (balas); they believe in the fulfillment of the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradyas); they believe in the growth of the indestructible, unique Buddha-dharmas; they believe in the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas; they believe in the emergence of the Buddha-realm which is neither middle nor extreme; they believe in the successive entry into the immeasurable realms of the Tathāgata; and they believe in the accomplishment of the fruit.
To state the essentials: it is because of the power of the teaching that one has faith in all bodhisattva practices, up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva further reflects thus:"
“The true Dharma of all Buddhas is thus profound, thus tranquil, thus quiescent, thus empty, thus signless, thus wishless, thus unstained, thus immeasurable, and thus vast.”

Yet ordinary beings have minds fallen into false views, shrouded by ignorance, and they plant the tall banner of arrogance. Entering the net of craving and thirst, they wander through the dense forest of flattery and deception, unable to emerge from it. Their minds are conjoined with stinginess and envy, which they do not relinquish; they constantly create the causes and conditions for rebirth in the various realms of existence. Greed, hatred, and delusion accumulate all manner of karma, which grows and increases day and night. Blown by the winds of resentment and anger, the fire of their consciousness burns fiercely without ceasing. Whatever actions they perform are all associated with perversion; through the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of ignorance, and the flow of views, they continuously produce the seeds of mind, intellect, and consciousness, which sprout as the buds of suffering once again within the field of the three realms.

That is to say: name-and-form arise together and are inseparable; as this name-and-form grows, the village of the six sense bases arises. Within them, contact arises through mutual opposition; because of contact, feeling arises; because of feeling, craving arises; because craving increases, grasping arises; because grasping increases, becoming arises; because there is becoming, there is birth, and with birth come old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

Thus, these sentient beings grow within a mass of suffering; herein all is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self, without cognition or awareness, without agency or experience, like grass, wood, stones, or walls, and like reflected images;
yet all sentient beings neither perceive nor know this.
"Seeing that all sentient beings cannot escape from such a mass of suffering, the Bodhisattva gives rise to the wisdom of great compassion.
He further reflects:
'I must rescue these sentient beings and establish them in the state of ultimate peace and happiness.'"
"Therefore, the wisdom of the light of great compassion arises immediately.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in accordance with such great compassion and great kindness, dwells in the first stage (*bhūmi*) with a profound and heavy mind, they have no stinginess regarding any object; seeking the great wisdom of the Buddha, they practice great relinquishment (*mahātyāga*), giving away everything they possess."

That is to say: wealth and grain, storehouses, gold and silver, *maṇi* gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and other such objects; precious jewels, necklaces, and ornaments for adorning the body; elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, subjects, cities, villages, gardens, groves, towers, and pavilions; wives, concubines, sons, daughters, and all internal and external kinsmen, as well as all other articles of luxury; even one’s head, eyes, hands, feet, flesh, blood, marrow, and every part of the body—none of these are begrudged in the pursuit of the vast wisdom of all Buddhas.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of great equanimity while dwelling in the first stage.
"O Son of the Buddha!

By means of this mind of loving-kindness, compassion, and great generosity, because the Bodhisattva seeks further and further after all mundane and supramundane beneficial matters for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings without weariness or fatigue, they immediately achieve the accomplishment of a tireless mind.
Having attained a mind free from weariness and fatigue, one’s mind will have no timidity regarding any sūtras or śāstras;
because there is no timidity, one immediately achieves the wisdom of all sūtras and śāstras.

Having attained this wisdom, they are well able to deliberate upon what should and should not be done; toward all sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—they act accordingly, according to their capacity, and in accordance with what each has practiced. Thus, the bodhisattva achieves worldly knowledge.

Having attained worldly wisdom, one knows the proper time and the proper measure; adorned with shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), one diligently cultivates the path of self-benefit and the benefit of others. Therefore, having achieved the adornment of shame and dread of blame, one diligently cultivates renunciation within this practice, remaining non-retrogressive and non-regressive, thereby accomplishing steadfast power.
Having attained firm power, they diligently make offerings to all Buddhas and are able to practice the Buddha’s teachings exactly as they have been taught.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Thus do Bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas that purify the stages, namely:

Faith, compassion, loving-kindness, equanimity, freedom from weariness, knowledge of the various sūtras and śāstras, skillful understanding of worldly dharmas, shame and remorse, firm strength, making offerings to all Buddhas, and practicing in accordance with the teachings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Having dwelled in this Stage of Joy, the Bodhisattva, through the power of great vows, comes to see many Buddhas.
They are as follows:”

He beheld many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of quadrillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of quintillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of sextillions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of septillions of Buddhas.

With a universal mind and a profound mind, they reverently honored and respected them, serving and making offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life; they also made offerings to the entire Sangha, dedicating all these roots of goodness toward unexcelled bodhi.
O Son of the Buddha!

Because this bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, they attain the method for maturing sentient beings. They gather in sentient beings through the first two means of integration—namely, generosity and kind speech;
however, regarding the latter two means of integration, they practice them only by the power of faith and understanding, as their conduct has not yet been fully mastered.
Among the ten pāramitās, this bodhisattva excels in the dāna-pāramitā;
it is not that they do not practice the remaining pāramitās, but they do so according to their power and capacity.

As this bodhisattva diligently practices, making offerings to all Buddhas and teaching and transforming sentient beings, they do so entirely by cultivating the dharmas of the pure stages. All roots of goodness are dedicated toward the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), becoming increasingly bright and pure, harmonious and supple, and fully perfected so that they may be employed at will.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a goldsmith who skillfully refines gold; by repeatedly placing it in the fire, it becomes increasingly bright and pure, becoming pliant and perfected so that it may be used according to one's will.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: making offerings to all Buddhas and teaching and transforming sentient beings are all for the sake of practicing the dharmas of the pure stages; all roots of goodness are dedicated toward the stage of omniscience, becoming increasingly bright and pure, harmonious and supple, and fully perfected so as to be fit for use according to one's will.
“O Son of the Buddha!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the First Ground should seek out and inquire of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends regarding the characteristics and the fruits attained within this ground, never becoming weary or satisfied, for the sake of accomplishing the dharmas of this ground.

Furthermore, they should seek out and inquire of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends regarding the characteristics and the fruits attained in the Second Ground, never becoming weary or satisfied, for the sake of accomplishing the dharmas of that ground.”

One should likewise investigate and inquire in this manner regarding the characteristics and the attainment of the fruits within the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, never becoming weary or satisfied, for the purpose of accomplishing the dharmas of those stages.

This bodhisattva skillfully knows the obstacles to the stages and their remedies; skillfully knows the formation and destruction of the stages; skillfully knows the characteristics and fruits of the stages; skillfully knows the attainment and cultivation of the stages; skillfully knows the purification of the dharmas of the stages; skillfully knows the progression from stage to stage; skillfully knows what is possible and impossible regarding each stage; skillfully knows the superior wisdom of each stage; skillfully knows the non-retrogression of each stage; and skillfully knows how to purify all bodhisattva stages and even transition into the stage of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus skillfully knows the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*), they initiate practice in the first stage without interruption, continuing in this manner until entering the tenth stage without any cessation.
By means of the light of wisdom of these various stages, they achieve the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a caravan leader who is skilled in expedient means and wishes to lead his merchants to a great city. Before setting out, he first inquires about the virtues and faults along the way, as well as whether the places where they will stay are secure or not; only then does he prepare the provisions for the journey and perform what is required to be done.
O Son of the Buddha!

Although that great caravan leader has not yet set out, he is able to know all matters of safety and peril within the journey. Skillfully weighing and observing with wisdom, he provides all that is required so that there is no lack; leading the multitude of merchants, he brings them safely to that great city, ensuring that both himself and the people are entirely freed from suffering and distress.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva Caravan Leader is also like this: dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), he skillfully knows the obstacles and their remedies for all stages, up to skillfully knowing the purification of all Bodhisattva stages and entering the stage of the Tathāgata. Only then does he fully possess the provisions of merit and wisdom, leading all sentient beings through the perilous wilderness of birth and death to safely reach the city of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), such that neither his own person nor the sentient beings undergo any hardship or distress.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should always cultivate with tireless diligence the sublime pure deeds of the various stages, until they enter the stage of a Tathāgata’s wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!

This is called a brief explanation of the gate for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas entering the first stage of a Bodhisattva; were it explained in detail, there would be immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya varieties of matters.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this first stage, they frequently become kings of Jambudvīpa, possessing noble status and sovereign power. They constantly protect the True Dharma and are able to gather in sentient beings through great giving. They skillfully remove the defilement of stinginess and greed from sentient beings, and they constantly practice great giving without end.”

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—all such activities as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the Saṃgha, never apart from mindfulness of fellow bodhisattvas, never apart from mindfulness of bodhisattva practices, never apart from mindfulness of the pāramitās, never apart from mindfulness of the stages, never apart from mindfulness of the powers, never apart from mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, never apart from mindfulness of the unique buddha-qualities, and even never apart from mindfulness of the perfection of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes.
Again, he forms this thought:

"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, the commander, and even the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes of knowledge relies."

If this bodhisattva wishes to leave the household life to practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, they will then be able to renounce their home, wife, children, and the five desires, and go forth from home to study the Way according to the Tathāgata’s teaching.

Having gone forth, he practiced with diligent vigor; in a single moment of thought, he attained a hundred samādhis, beheld a hundred buddhas, and knew the spiritual powers of a hundred buddhas. He could shake a hundred buddha-worlds, traverse a hundred buddha-worlds, illuminate a hundred buddha-worlds, and transform sentient beings in a hundred worlds. He could maintain a lifespan for a hundred kalpas, know the events of a hundred kalpas each in the past and future, enter a hundred dharma-gates, and manifest a hundred bodies, with each body manifesting a hundred bodhisattvas as its retinue.

If he manifests through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s supreme vows, it exceeds these numbers; even in a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand kalpas, or even a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, one could not calculate or know them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"If a person accumulates manifold virtues, Is fully endowed with pure and white dharmas, Makes offerings to the Honored One of Gods and Humans, And follows the path of compassion, ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
Their faith and understanding are most vast, and their aspirations are likewise pure;
seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, they have resolved upon this unsurpassed mind.
They purify the power of all-knowledge as well as the fearlessnesses.
To accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, to rescue and gather the multitudes of sentient beings,
to attain great compassion, and to turn the supreme wheel of Dharma,
to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields— for these reasons, they give rise to this most excellent mind.
In a single thought-moment, one knows the three periods of time, yet remains free from discrimination;
though times are diverse and distinct, this is demonstrated to the world.
Briefly stated, seeking all Buddhas and all supreme merits—
One gives rise to the vast mind, its measure equal to the realm of empty space.
With compassion as the precursor and wisdom as the sovereign, it is conjoined with skillful means.
Through a mind of pure faith and understanding, one attains the immeasurable power of the Tathāgata.
Unimpeded wisdom manifests before them; self-awakened and not dependent on another, they become fully equal to the Tathāgatas as they give rise to this most supreme mind.
As soon as these children of the Buddha first produce such a wondrous jewel-mind, it is born.
Thus transcending the stage of ordinary beings, one enters the sphere of the Buddhas' activity;
born into the family of the Tathāgatas, one’s lineage is free from blemish;
equal to the Buddhas themselves, one is destined to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
As soon as such a mind arises, one immediately enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
One’s resolve and delight are unshakable, like the king of mountains;
one possesses abundant joy and love, and likewise abundant pure faith.
With a mind of supreme courage and a heart of joyful exultation,
one remains far removed from strife, harm, and malice; possessing a sense of shame and reverence,
being upright and straightforward, one skillfully guards all the sense faculties.
The peerless Savior of the world—may I attain all his wisdom in this very place; remembering this, joy arises.
Having first entered the first stage, one immediately transcends the five fears.
Neither loss of livelihood, death, ill repute, nor the terrors of the miserable realms—
because they do not cling to "I" or "mine," these sons of the Buddhas are far removed from all fears.
Always practicing great compassion, Constantly possessing faith and respect,
Endowed with the virtues of shame and remorse, One increases wholesome dharmas day and night.
Delighting in the true benefit of the Dharma, One does not crave or accept various sensual desires.
Contemplating the Dharma as it has been heard, one remains far removed from the practice of grasping and attachment.
Not coveting gain or offerings, one delights solely in the Buddha’s bodhi;
with a single mind seeking the Buddha’s wisdom, one applies oneself with diligence and without distraction.
Cultivating the perfections, they remain far removed from flattery, vanity, and deception;
practicing exactly as they have taught, they abide in truthful speech.
They do not defile the family of the Buddhas, nor do they forsake the bodhisattva precepts.
Taking no pleasure in worldly affairs, one constantly benefits the world.
Cultivating virtue without weariness, one seeks ever more excellent paths;
thus delighting in the Dharma, one’s merit accords with its true meaning.
Constantly giving rise to the mind of great aspiration, may I behold all Buddhas,
uphold the teachings of all Buddhas, and embrace the path of the Great Sages.
Always generating such vows, one practices the most supreme conduct.
Maturing all sentient beings and adorning and purifying the Buddha-lands,
the sons of the Buddha fill all the buddha-fields;
with equal and unified minds, their deeds are never in vain.
Upon every single tip of a hair, they simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment.
Such great vows as these are immeasurable and boundless.
As are space and sentient beings, the dharma-realm and nirvana.
When a Buddha appears in the world, it is the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom-mind.
"That which the Tathāgata’s wisdom enters, and that which is exhausted through the three turnings—
if those things were to come to an end, only then would my vows come to an end."
"As that [world] has no end, so too shall my vow.
Having thus made this great vow, his mind became supple and well-disciplined.
He was able to believe in the Buddha’s merits and observed all sentient beings."
Knowing that all arises from causes and conditions, one gives rise to a mind of compassion, thinking:
"Such suffering beings—I must now rescue and liberate them.
For the sake of these beings, I shall practice various kinds of giving."
The royal throne and precious jewels, even elephants, horses, and chariots;
the head, eyes, hands, and feet, even the flesh and blood of one’s own body—
one is able to relinquish all of these, and the mind remains free from sorrow or regret.
Seeking various scriptures, their minds never weary;
Skillfully understanding their meanings and purports, they are able to act in accordance with worldly ways;
Adorned with a sense of shame and remorse, their practice becomes ever more firm and steadfast.
Making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Honoring and respecting them with reverence;
Thus constantly practicing and training, Without weariness day or night,
One's roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure, Like true gold refined by fire.
The Bodhisattva dwelling herein, Purely cultivates the ten stages;
His actions are without obstruction, Fully perfected and never interrupted.
He is like a great caravan leader, Acting for the benefit of the merchant host.
Question: Just as one who knows the dangers and ease of the road reaches the great city in safety, so too should it be known for the Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage:
through courageous vigor and without obstruction, they reach the tenth stage.
Abiding in this first stage, he acts as a great king of merit,
transforming sentient beings through the Dharma with a compassionate heart free from harm.
Ruling over Jambudvīpa, his transformative conduct reaches everywhere.
Causing all to abide in great equanimity and achieve the wisdom of the Buddha;
desiring to seek the most supreme path, he relinquished his own royal throne and was able,
within the Buddha’s teaching, to practice with courageous diligence.
Then one attains a hundred samādhis, And beholds a hundred Buddhas;
One causes a hundred worlds to tremble, And likewise radiates light through their activities;
One transforms sentient beings in a hundred lands, And enters into a hundred Dharma-gates.
They can know the events of a hundred kalpas, manifest a hundred bodies,
and appear as a hundred bodhisattvas to serve as their retinue;
yet by the power of their sovereign vows, they may exceed these numbers beyond measure.
Within the meaning of the stages, I have briefly described but a small portion;
were one to wish to analyze them extensively, even ten million eons would not suffice.
This is the supreme path of the Bodhisattvas, which brings benefit to all living beings.
Thus have I now finished explaining the dharmas of the first stage.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Four;
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-Six, Part Two: The Second Stage. Regarding the Second Stage:
When the bodhisattvas heard of this most supreme and subtle stage, they were filled with joy.
Their minds were entirely pure, and all were filled with joy.
Rising from their seats, they leaped into the midst of the air and scattered exquisite flowers above, simultaneously offering praise together:
“Excellent, Vajragarbha! O possessor of great wisdom and fearlessness!
You have well explained this stage, the dharma practiced by bodhisattvas.”
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing that the minds of the assembly were pure and that they delighted in hearing about the characteristics of all practices pertaining to the second bhūmi,
immediately requested Vajragarbha:
“O Mahāmati, please expound upon this; the sons of the Buddha all delight in hearing it—the description of the second stage wherein they dwell!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
“Sons of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already cultivated the first stage and wishes to enter the second stage, they should give rise to ten kinds of profound resolve.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
A mind that is upright, supple, workable, disciplined, tranquil, purely virtuous, unadulterated, free from attachment, expansive, and great.
By means of these ten mental states, the Bodhisattva attains entry into the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*).
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stainless Stage, their very nature is spontaneously remote from all killing; they do not keep weapons or staves, harbor no resentment, possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, and are fully endowed with benevolence and forbearance. Toward all sentient beings who possess life, they constantly give rise to thoughts of compassion and the intent to benefit them."
This bodhisattva does not even harbor ill will or cause distress to sentient beings, much less give rise to the perception of them as "sentient beings" and intentionally commit acts of killing!

By nature he does not steal; regarding his own resources, the bodhisattva always knows contentment, and regarding others, he is compassionate and forgiving, having no desire to encroach upon or damage them.

If an object belongs to another, he perceives it as belonging to another and never gives rise to a thieving mind toward it; he would not take even a blade of grass if it were not given, let alone other articles of livelihood!

By nature he refrains from sexual misconduct; the bodhisattva is content with his own wife and does not seek the wives of others. Toward the wives and concubines of others, women protected by their kin, those betrothed through family mediation, and those protected by the Dharma, he does not even give rise to a mind of lustful attachment, let alone engage in such acts.
How much more so regarding what is not the Path!

By nature he does not engage in false speech; the Bodhisattva always utters truthful speech, genuine speech, and timely speech, such that even in his dreams he would not bear to utter words of concealment, nor would he have the intention to do so, let alone intentionally commit such an offense!

By nature, he does not engage in double-tongued speech; toward all sentient beings, the bodhisattva has no mind of divisiveness and no mind of malice or harm. He does not repeat these words to others for the sake of breaking them apart, nor does he repeat those words to this person for the sake of breaking this person apart. He does not cause what is not yet divided to be divided, nor does he increase what is already divided. He does not delight in division, nor does he take pleasure in division. He does not engage in divisive speech, nor does he utter divisive speech, whether it be true or untrue.
By nature, he does not engage in harsh speech, which is to say:

One should completely abandon all such speech as: poisonous words, harsh words, words that cause suffering to others, words that incite hatred in others, words spoken in their presence, words spoken in their absence, base and evil words, vulgar and lowly words, words unpleasant to hear, words that do not please those who hear them, words of anger and resentment, words that burn the heart like fire, words of enmity and bondage, words of feverish affliction, unlovely words, disagreeable words, and words capable of destroying one's own and others' welfare. Instead, one should always employ speech that is moistening, gentle, pleasing to the mind, delightful to hear, words that bring joy to those who hear them, words that penetrate the hearts of people, words of elegant style and principle, words loved by many, words that delight many, and words that cause both body and mind to leap with joy.

By nature, he does not engage in frivolous speech; rather, the bodhisattva always delights in speech that is well-considered, timely, truthful, meaningful, in accordance with the Dharma, consistent with reason, skillfully disciplining, and decisive after due deliberation according to the occasion. This bodhisattva maintains such careful reflection even during mere jesting, let alone when intentionally uttering distracted or idle words!
By nature free from greed, the bodhisattva does not give rise to covetous thoughts toward the wealth or resources of others, nor do they desire or seek them.

By nature free from anger, the bodhisattva constantly gives rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of harmony and moisture, and a mind of embracing care; they forever abandon resentment, malice, and affliction, always intending to act with accord, benevolence, kindness, and assistance.

Furthermore, being free from wrong views, the bodhisattva abides in the right path; he does not practice divination, does not adopt evil precepts, maintains a straightforward mind and vision, is without deceit or flattery, and gives rise to resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus upholds the ten paths of wholesome action, doing so constantly and without interruption, they further reflect:
‘Among all sentient beings who fall into the evil destinies, there are none who do not do so because of the ten unwholesome actions.’”
Therefore, I shall cultivate right practice myself and also exhort others to cultivate right practice.
Why is this? It is impossible for one who cannot practice right conduct themselves to cause others to do so.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
‘The ten unwholesome paths of action are the causes for rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;’”
The ten paths of wholesome action are the cause for rebirth among humans, devas, and even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Furthermore, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are practiced with wisdom—yet because the mind is narrow and inferior, because there is fear of the three realms, because of the absence of great compassion, and because understanding is derived from hearing the voice of another—they result in the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

Furthermore, when these superior ten paths of wholesome action are cultivated and purified, because one awakens to them through self-realization rather than following the instructions of others, and because one lacks the full complement of great compassion and skillful means, yet realizes the profound law of dependent origination, one accomplishes the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, these superior ten paths of wholesome action, when cultivated to purity, constitute the vast conduct of a bodhisattva because the mind is immeasurably expansive; because they are endowed with compassion and pity; because they are embraced by skillful means; because they give rise to great vows; because they do not abandon sentient beings; because they seek the great wisdom of all Buddhas; because they purify the various stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; and because they purely cultivate all the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Furthermore, because these superior ten paths of wholesome action are pure in every respect, and because they lead even to the realization of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, all the Buddha-dharmas are fully accomplished.
"Therefore, I shall now practice the ten wholesome paths of action equally, so as to cause all beings to be fully endowed with purity;
such skillful means, a bodhisattva should learn.
"O Son of the Buddha!"
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva further reflects:

"The ten unwholesome paths of action—those of the highest degree are causes for rebirth in hell; those of the middle degree are causes for rebirth as an animal; and those of the lowest degree are causes for rebirth as a hungry ghost."
Among these, the transgression of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits: first, a short lifespan; second, much illness.
The sin of stealing also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, poverty; second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
The sin of sexual misconduct likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their wife will not be chaste and virtuous; second, they will not obtain companions as they desire.
The sin of false speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they are frequently slandered; second, they are deceived by others.
The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their retinue will be estranged and separated; second, their kinsmen will be wicked and malicious.
The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they constantly hear unpleasant sounds; second, their speech is full of contention and litigation.
The sin of frivolous speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their words will not be accepted by others; second, their speech will be unclear.
The sin of covetousness also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, their minds know no contentment; second, they have many desires and never feel satiety.
The sin of anger also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they are constantly sought out by others for their faults; second, they are perpetually afflicted and harmed by others.
The sin of wrong view also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, being born into a family of wrong views, and second, having a mind that is deceitful and crooked.
“O Son of the Buddha!
These ten unwholesome paths of action can give rise to such immeasurable and boundless masses of great suffering. Therefore, the Bodhisattva forms this thought:

‘I shall distance myself from the ten unwholesome paths and take the ten wholesome paths as my dharma-garden; I shall delight in dwelling there peacefully, abide therein myself, and likewise exhort others to dwell therein.’”
“O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further gives rise toward all sentient beings a mind of benefit, a mind of peace and happiness, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of gathering them in, a mind of protection, a mind of regarding them as oneself, a mind of regarding them as a teacher, and a mind of regarding them as a great teacher. He forms this thought:
‘Sentient beings are to be pitied; they have fallen into the dense forest of wrong views, evil wisdom, evil desires, and evil paths.’”
"I should cause them to abide in right view and practice the path of truth. He further thought:
"All sentient beings differentiate between 'self' and 'other,' destroying one another, engaging in strife and resentment that burn without ceasing."
"I shall cause them to abide in unsurpassed great compassion.
He further thought: "All sentient beings greedily grasp at things without satiety, seeking only wealth and profit, and sustaining themselves through wrong livelihoods."
"I shall cause them to abide in the dharma of right livelihood, which consists of pure actions of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, he reflects:

"All sentient beings are constantly pursued by the three poisons; because of these, their various afflictions blaze intensely, and they do not understand how to seek the skillful means for the essential way of deliverance."
"I shall cause them to extinguish the great fires of all afflictions and establish them in the cool place of nirvana.
Furthermore, he thought:

"Because all sentient beings are covered by the heavy darkness of ignorance and the thick film of false views, they enter the dense forest of obscurity, lose the light of wisdom, wander upon the perilous paths of the wilderness, and give rise to various evil views."
"I shall cause them to obtain the unobstructed, pure eye of wisdom, so that they may know the true nature of all phenomena as it really is, without following the teachings of others.
Furthermore, he thought:

"All sentient beings are within the perilous paths of birth and death; they are on the verge of falling into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; they have entered the net of evil views and are bewildered by the dense forest of ignorance; they follow false paths and practice perverted conduct."

For example, it is like a blind person who lacks a guide; taking what is not the path of deliverance to be the path of deliverance, they enter the realm of Māra, are seized by evil bandits, follow the mind of Māra, and remain far removed from the Buddha's intention.
"I shall pull them out from such perilous difficulties and cause them to dwell in the fearless city of omniscience. He further thought:

"All sentient beings are submerged by the waves of a great torrent; they have entered the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of ignorance, and the flow of views. They are caught in the eddies of birth and death, drifting and turning upon the river of craving, rushing and surging with such force that they have no leisure to observe."
Being pursued and never abandoned by thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty, the rākṣasa of the view of a self seizes them therein and leads them forever into the dense forest of craving;
they develop deep attachment to what they covet, dwell upon the high ground of egoism, and settle in the village of the six sense bases;
there is no one to rescue them well, and no one capable of delivering them.

I shall arouse great compassion for them and provide salvation through all roots of goodness, so that they may be free from calamity and affliction, depart from defilement and attain tranquility, and dwell upon the jewel-island of all-encompassing wisdom.
Furthermore, he reflected:

"All sentient beings dwell in the prison of the world, beset by manifold sufferings and afflictions; they constantly harbor love and hatred, giving rise to anxiety and fear of their own accord. Bound by the heavy shackles of craving and desire, and obscured by the dense forest of ignorance, they are unable to emerge from within the three realms."
"I shall cause them to forever leave the three realms of existence behind and abide in the great nirvana that is free from all obstructions.
He further thought: "All sentient beings are attached to a self;

they do not seek to escape from the cave-dwelling of the aggregates. Relying on the empty village of the six sense bases, they give rise to the four inverted views. They are afflicted by the venomous snakes of the four great elements and slain by the murderous bandits of the five aggregates, undergoing immeasurable suffering."
"I shall cause them to abide in the most supreme state of non-attachment, namely:
the unsurpassed nirvana in which all obstacles are extinguished. He further thought:

"All sentient beings possess minds that are narrow and inferior; they do not practice the path of supreme universal wisdom (sarvajñatā). Although they desire liberation, they take pleasure only in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"I shall cause them to abide in the vast Buddha-dharma and vast wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva guards and upholds the precepts in this way, they are well able to increase the mind of compassion.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi), by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas. Namely:”

He sees many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas; indeed, he sees as many as this, up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

Toward all Buddhas, with a vast mind and a profound mind, they revere, respect, serve, and make offerings, presenting them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life; they likewise make offerings to the entire Sangha, dedicating these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Toward all Buddhas, with a heart of deep respect, they further receive and practice the ten paths of wholesome action; according to what they have received, they shall never forget or lose them until they reach Bodhi.

Because this bodhisattva has, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, remained far removed from the stains of stinginess, envy, and broken precepts, his generosity and observance of the precepts are pure and fully perfected.
For example, when genuine gold is placed in alum and refined according to the proper method, it becomes free from all impurities and becomes even more brilliant and pure.

It is just so for a Bodhisattva dwelling in this Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*): because they have remained far removed from the stains of stinginess, envy, and breaking the precepts for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* eons, their generosity and ethical discipline are pure and fully perfected.
O Son of the Buddha!
Among the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva predominantly practices kind speech;
among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), they predominantly practice ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It is not that they do not practice other [virtues], but rather they act according to their strength and capacity.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is called:
A brief explanation of the second stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin-rāja*), acting as a great master of the Dharma. Possessing the seven jewels and sovereign power, they are able to eliminate the defilements of stinginess and broken precepts in all sentient beings, employing skillful means to establish them securely within the ten paths of wholesome action.
As a great donor, they provide for all exhaustively and without end.

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—all such activities as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha, and even never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, he forms this thought:

"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, and even the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) relies."
If this bodhisattva wishes to leave the household life to practice with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma, they are able to renounce their home, wife, children, and the five desires.

Having gone forth, they practice with diligent vigor and, in a single thought-moment, attain a thousand samādhis, behold a thousand Buddhas, and know the spiritual power of a thousand Buddhas. They can shake a thousand worlds, and even manifest a thousand bodies; in each individual body, they can manifest a thousand bodhisattvas as their retinue.

If they manifest through the sovereign power of the bodhisattva’s superior vows, it exceeds these numbers, such that even in hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not count or know them.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Honesty, flexibility, and adaptability; Subduing, tranquility, and pure goodness;
The vast mind that swiftly brings forth liberation from birth and death— By means of these ten mental states, one enters the second stage.”
Abiding here, one accomplishes the merit of ethical discipline: One stays far removed from taking life and does no harm;
One also abstains from stealing, sexual misconduct, And from lying, slander, divisive speech, and idle chatter.
Not coveting wealth or goods, always compassionate and kind; with a straightforward mind on the right path, free from flattery and hypocrisy;
leaving behind peril and abandoning pride, being exceedingly gentle and pliant; acting according to the teachings without negligence.

In the hells and among animals they undergo manifold sufferings; as hungry ghosts, they are scorched by blazing, fierce flames—all of which are brought about by their own transgressions. I shall depart from those states and abide in the True Dharma.
One may take birth at will among human beings, And even attain the bliss of dhyāna in the Peak-of-Existence Heaven;
The paths of the Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and the Buddha Vehicle— All are accomplished by means of the ten wholesome actions.
Reflecting thus with heedfulness, he maintains the pure precepts himself and teaches others to protect them;
seeing further that sentient beings undergo manifold sufferings, his great compassion increases all the more.
Ordinary fools, with their perverse wisdom and incorrect understanding, constantly harbor resentment and engage in much contention;
they greedily pursue sensory objects without limit—I shall cause them to eliminate the three poisons.
Enveloped and shrouded by the great darkness of ignorance, they have entered the treacherous path of the net of false views;
confined within the cage of birth and death and bound by enemies, I shall cause them to destroy the mara-thieves.
Swept away by the four currents, my mind is submerged; The three realms burn like fire, their suffering immeasurable.
Regarding the aggregates as a house with "I" dwelling within, I practice the Path with diligence in order to deliver them.
If, while seeking liberation, their resolve becomes inferior and they abandon the supreme wisdom of the Buddha,
I desire to establish them in the Mahāyāna, inciting them to diligent effort without weariness.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here accumulates merit, Beholding immeasurable Buddhas, he makes offerings to them all;
Cultivating and refining goodness for billions of eons, it becomes even more radiant, Like pure gold refined with excellent medicinal elixirs.
The Buddha’s heirs dwelling here act as wheel-turning kings, Universally transforming sentient beings through the practice of the ten wholesome paths.
They cultivate all virtuous dharmas To perfect the ten powers and rescue the world.
Desiring to relinquish his royal throne and treasures, he immediately abandoned the household life to rely upon the Buddha’s teaching;
through courageous diligence in a single thought-moment, he attained a thousand samādhis and beheld a thousand Buddhas.
All the various supernormal powers, The bodhisattvas of this stage can all manifest;
Yet what is accomplished through their power of vows exceeds even this, As they liberate sentient beings with immeasurable mastery.
The supreme conduct of Bodhisattvas practiced by those who benefit all worlds—
such are the merits of the second stage, which have been expounded for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas.
The sons of the Buddha, having heard of the practices of this stage— the inconceivable realm of the Bodhisattvas—
were all filled with reverence and joy; scattering flowers into the air as an offering,
they praised, saying:

“Excellent, Great Mountain King! Out of a compassionate heart, you take pity on all sentient beings and have well explained the dharmas of the wise’s discipline—the characteristics of practice within the second stage.”
These subtle and wondrous practices of the bodhisattvas are true, without variation or distinction;
desiring to benefit all living beings, they thus proclaim them with supreme purity.

O you who are honored by all gods and humans, we pray that you will expound upon the third stage, the various activities of wisdom that accord with the Dharma; may you reveal them in detail according to their true scope!
The Great Sage’s teachings on generosity and morality, Patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom,
As well as the path of skillful means, compassion, and loving-kindness— May the Buddha explain all his pure practices and vows!
Then, Vimukticandra again requested, saying:
"O Vajragarbha, Great Being free from fear, pray explain the entry into the third stage and the merits of those with gentle minds!"
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already purified the second stage and wishes to enter the third stage, they should give rise to ten kinds of profound resolve."
What are the ten? They are:

the pure mind, the settled mind, the mind of weary detachment, the mind free from greed, the non-retrogressive mind, the firm mind, the luminous and flourishing mind, the courageous mind, the expansive mind, and the great mind.
By means of these ten mental states, the bodhisattva enters the third stage.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Having dwelled in the third stage, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) according to their true nature."
That is to say:

they are impermanent, suffering, impure, and unstable; they are subject to decay, do not endure for long, and arise and perish in every moment; they do not arise from a prior limit, they do not go toward a subsequent limit, and they do not abide in the present.

Furthermore, one contemplates that these phenomena offer no refuge and no reliance; they are accompanied by sorrow and lamentation, coexisting with suffering and affliction, bound by love and hatred, and filled with ever-increasing grief. They do not remain stationary, but like the fires of greed, anger, and delusion, burn fiercely without ceasing; entangled by manifold calamities, they increase day and night, being as unreal as an illusion.

Having seen this, they develop an ever-deepening revulsion for all conditioned phenomena and turn toward the wisdom of the Buddha. They perceive that the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable, peerless, immeasurable, difficult to attain, unadulterated, free from affliction, and free from sorrow; having reached the city of fearlessness, they never again regress and are able to rescue sentient beings from immeasurable suffering and hardship.

When a bodhisattva thus perceives the immeasurable benefit of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and perceives the immeasurable faults and afflictions of all conditioned phenomena, they give rise to ten kinds of compassionate mind toward all sentient beings.
What are the ten? They are:
seeing that sentient beings are solitary and without reliance, one gives rise to a heart of compassion;
Seeing all sentient beings impoverished and destitute, he gives rise to a heart of compassion;
seeing all sentient beings burning with the fires of the three poisons, he gives rise to a heart of compassion;
seeing all sentient beings imprisoned and confined within the jails of the various realms of existence, he gives rise to a heart of compassion.
Seeing all sentient beings constantly shrouded and obstructed by the dense forest of afflictions, he gives rise to a heart of compassion;
seeing all sentient beings failing to observe with skillful discernment, he gives rise to a heart of compassion;
seeing all sentient beings lacking the desire for wholesome dharmas, he gives rise to a heart of compassion.
Seeing all sentient beings lose the Buddha-dharmas, he gives rise to a mind of compassion;
seeing all sentient beings follow the stream of birth and death, he gives rise to a mind of compassion;
seeing all sentient beings lose the skillful means for liberation, he gives rise to a mind of compassion.
These are the ten.
Thus perceiving the immeasurable suffering and affliction of the realm of sentient beings, the bodhisattva arouses great diligence and forms this thought:
"I should rescue these sentient beings; I should liberate them; I should purify them; I should deliver them."

They should be established in wholesome states; they should be made to dwell securely; they should be made to rejoice; they should be made to know and see; they should be made to be disciplined; and they should be made to attain nirvāṇa.

Thus, the Bodhisattva becomes weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and feels compassion for all sentient beings. Knowing that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) possesses supreme benefit, and desiring to rescue and deliver sentient beings by relying upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata, he reflects:

"These sentient beings have fallen into the midst of the great suffering of afflictions (*kleśa*); by what skillful means can I extricate them and cause them to abide in the bliss of ultimate *nirvāṇa*?"
Then he thought: "To deliver sentient beings and cause them to abide in nirvana is not apart from the wisdom of unobstructed liberation;
the wisdom of unobstructed liberation is not apart from the realization of all phenomena as they truly are."
The awakening to all phenomena as they truly are does not depart from the light of wisdom regarding non-action and non-arising action;
the light of wisdom regarding non-action and non-arising action does not depart from the analytical wisdom of skillful mastery in dhyāna;
and the analytical wisdom of skillful mastery in dhyāna does not depart from skillful mastery in extensive learning.

Having thus observed and fully understood, the Bodhisattva redoubled his diligent pursuit and cultivation of the True Dharma; day and night, he aspired solely to hear the Dharma, to rejoice in the Dharma, to delight in the Dharma, to rely upon the Dharma, to follow the Dharma, to understand the Dharma, to accord with the Dharma, to arrive at the Dharma, to abide in the Dharma, and to practice the Dharma.

When a bodhisattva thus diligently seeks the Buddha-dharma, they have no stinginess regarding any precious wealth; they perceive no object as difficult to obtain or particularly valuable, but regard only those who can expound the Buddha-dharma with the thought that such persons are difficult to encounter.
Therefore, regarding internal and external wealth, a bodhisattva is able to relinquish it all in order to seek the Buddha-dharma.
There is no act of reverence that they cannot perform, no pride that they cannot abandon, no service that they cannot provide, and no hardship that they cannot endure.
If one hears a single phrase of the Dharma never heard before, the great joy that arises surpasses obtaining a trichiliocosm filled with precious jewels;
if one hears a single verse of the true Dharma never heard before, the great joy that arises surpasses attaining the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King;

if one obtains a single verse of the Dharma never heard before that can purify the bodhisattva practice, it surpasses attaining the rank of Śakra or Brahmā and dwelling therein for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
If someone were to say:
"I possess a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha that can purify the bodhisattva practice;
if you can now enter a great pit of fire and undergo extreme suffering, I shall give it to you."
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"For the sake of purifying my bodhisattva practice through even a single word of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, I would willingly cast myself down from the height of the Brahma Heaven into a great trichiliocosm filled with raging fire to receive it in person; how much more so, then, could I not enter a small pit of fire!"
"However, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, I should now endure all the various sufferings of the hells, let alone the minor afflictions among human beings!
Thus the Bodhisattva rouses diligent vigor to seek the Buddha-dharma, observing and practicing according to what he has heard.
Having heard the Dharma, this bodhisattva collects his mind and dwells in composure, reflecting thus in a secluded place:
"One attains the Buddha-dharma by practicing according to what has been taught; it cannot be purified through mere words alone."
“O Son of the Buddha!

When this Bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Ground (Prabhākarī-bhūmi), he immediately becomes detached from desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and with the joy and happiness born of detachment, he dwells in the first dhyāna.

With the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, and with internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, he dwells in the second dhyāna.”

Detached from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; that which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and happy," he enters and abides in the third dhyāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the prior elimination of pain, and with the disappearance of both joy and sorrow, he enters a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, where mindfulness and equanimity are purified; he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna.

Transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters the sphere of infinite space and abides in the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness;
transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;
transcending the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"However, because they accord with the Dharma, they act without attachment or delight.
'O Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva’s mind accords with loving-kindness—vast, immeasurable, non-dual, without enmity or opposition, unobstructed and undisturbed, reaching everywhere throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of space, pervading all worlds.'"
It is likewise for abiding in compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva attains immeasurable powers of supernormal knowledge, capable of shaking the great earth;
They manifest many bodies from a single body and a single body from many bodies; they may appear or disappear at will.
They pass through stone walls and mountain barriers without obstruction, as if moving through empty space.
They travel through the air in the lotus posture, just like flying birds.
Entering the earth as if it were water, treading upon water as if it were earth;
his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire,
yet he again rains down water like a massive cloud.
The sun and moon dwell in the sky with great majestic power, yet one can reach out with one's hand to stroke and touch them;
their physical mastery extends even as far as the Brahma world.
This Bodhisattva’s divine ear is pure and surpasses that of human ears; they hear all sounds of humans and devas, whether near or far, and can even hear the sounds of mosquitoes, gadflies, and flies.

This bodhisattva, by means of the knowledge of others' minds, knows the minds of other sentient beings as they truly are. That is to say: when there is a mind with attachment, he knows it as a mind with attachment;
when there is no mind with attachment, he knows it as a mind without attachment.
He knows, as it truly is, a mind free from greed as a mind free from greed; he knows a mind with hatred and a mind free from hatred;

a mind with delusion and a mind free from delusion; a mind with afflictions and a mind without afflictions; a narrow mind and a broad mind; a great mind and an immeasurable mind; a contracted mind and a non-contracted mind; a distracted mind and a non-distracted mind; a concentrated mind and a non-concentrated mind; a liberated mind and a non-liberated mind; a surpassable mind and an unsurpassable mind; a defiled mind and a non-defiled mind; and a broad mind and a non-broad mind—all of these he knows as they truly are.
In this way, the bodhisattva knows the minds of sentient beings through the knowledge of others' minds.
This bodhisattva recollects and knows the distinctions of immeasurable past lives, namely: "I recollect one life;

I recollect two lives, three lives, four lives, and even ten lives, twenty, thirty, and even a hundred lives, immeasurable hundreds of lives, immeasurable thousands of lives, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lives; [I recollect] eons of formation, eons of destruction, eons of both formation and destruction, and immeasurable eons of formation and destruction. I was once in such-and-such a place, with such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage, such-and-such food and drink, such-and-such a lifespan, such-and-such a duration of stay, and such-and-such suffering and pleasure."
"I died there and was born in such-and-such a place; from that place I died and was born here, with such a form, such a appearance, and such a voice."
"In this way, he can recollect all such immeasurable distinctions of the past.

This Bodhisattva’s divine eye is pure and surpasses that of the human eye; he sees sentient beings at the time of birth and the time of death, their beautiful and ugly forms, their rebirths in happy or miserable realms, as they depart according to their karma."
If those sentient beings accomplish misconduct of body, accomplish misconduct of speech, and accomplish misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones;

and if they are possessed of wrong views and the causes and conditions of the karma of wrong views—then at the breaking up of the body after death, they will inevitably fall into the evil destinies and be born in hell.

If those sentient beings accomplish wholesome conduct of body, accomplish wholesome conduct of speech, and accomplish wholesome conduct of mind; if they do not revile the noble ones and are endowed with right view;
and by reason of the karma of right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly be reborn among the gods in the happy realms.
The Bodhisattva knows all divine eyes as they truly are.

This Bodhisattva is able to enter and emerge from all dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis; yet, he does not take birth according to their power, but rather takes birth within those places where the factors of enlightenment can be fulfilled, through the power of his aspirational vow.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When this bodhisattva dwells in this Ground of Radiance, by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas. Namely:”
They see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
