With a vast mind and a profound mind, they revere, respect, serve, and make offerings to them all, providing clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life. They also make offerings to the entire Saṃgha, dedicating these roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In the presence of that Buddha, they listen to the Dharma with reverence; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to their capacity.
This bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, existing only through causes and conditions;
seeing the bonds of the past extinguished, all bonds of desire, form, existence, and ignorance become increasingly subtle and thin.

Because they have not accumulated [karmic obstructions] for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, their false greed, false anger, and false delusion are all completely severed, and all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like pure gold that has been skillfully refined and smelted; it does not lose a single *liang* in weight, yet it becomes increasingly bright and pure.

So too is it with the Bodhisattva who dwells in this Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*): because they do not accumulate [unwholesome states], wrong greed, wrong hatred, and wrong delusion are all severed and eliminated, and all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.

This bodhisattva’s mind of patience, pliancy, harmony, joyfulness, non-anger, immovability, lack of turbidity, absence of high and low [pride], lack of expectation for reward, gratitude, lack of flattery, lack of deception, and freedom from crookedness all become increasingly pure.
Among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva excels particularly in beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*);
among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), he excels particularly in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
He does not fail to cultivate the others, but does so according to his strength and capacity.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s third stage, the Luminous (Prabhākari).
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and through skillful means, they cause all sentient beings to abandon and leave behind desire.”

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—whatever actions are performed in this way, none are apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha, up to and including mindfulness of the possession of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Again, he forms this thought:

"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, and even the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) relies."

If one practices with diligent vigor, in a single moment of thought, one attains hundreds of thousands of samādhis, beholds hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and knows the spiritual powers of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; one can shake hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, each body accompanied by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.

If one manifests through the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s sublime vows, it exceeds these numbers, such that even in hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, it could not be fully counted or known.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"With a mind pure, settled, and radiant; With a mind weary of saṃsāra, free from greed, and free from harm;
With a firm, courageous, and vast mind— By these, the wise enter the third stage."
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Stage, they contemplate all conditioned phenomena as suffering, impermanent, impure, decaying, and swiftly subject to extinction;
they are without solidity, without abiding, and without coming or going.
Contemplate all conditioned phenomena as a grave illness, entangled by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;
the fierce fires of the three poisons constantly blaze, never ceasing since beginningless time.

Weary of and detached from the three realms of existence, they do not cling; They seek exclusively for the Buddha-wisdom without divergent thoughts— Wisdom that is unfathomable, inconceivable, and peerless, Infinite, boundless, and free from affliction.
Having perceived the Buddha’s wisdom, he takes pity on sentient beings who are solitary, without refuge, and without protection;
who are constantly exhausted by the blazing fires of the three poisons; who dwell in the prisons of existence and perpetually suffer;
who are shrouded and blinded by the afflictions; and whose aspirations are base and inferior, having lost the treasure of the Dharma.
Following the cycle of birth and death and fearing nirvāṇa, I should diligently strive to rescue them.
Seeking wisdom to benefit sentient beings, I contemplate what skillful means will lead them to liberation.
Not departing from the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom, that [wisdom] further arises from the insight of non-arising.
Contemplating that this insight is obtained through hearing, one thus reflects and exerts oneself diligently;
listening and practicing day and night without interruption, one honors only the True Dharma.
Kingdoms, cities, wealth, shells, and various rare jewels, wives, children, retinues, and royal thrones—
out of reverence for the Dharma, the Bodhisattva is able to relinquish all such things.
Head, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, hands, feet, marrow, bones, heart, blood, and flesh—giving up all these is not difficult;
it is only the hearing of the Dharma that is most difficult.
Suppose someone were to come and say to a bodhisattva:
"Whoever can cast their body into a great mass of fire, I shall give you the treasure of the Buddha-dharma.
Having heard this, they would cast themselves into it without fear or dread.

Even if fire were to fill the three thousandfold world system, and one were to cast one's body from the Brahma-world into it, this would not be considered difficult for the sake of seeking the Dharma; how much less so the various minor sufferings of the human realm!

From the first resolution until the attainment of Buddhahood, whatever sufferings of Avīci hell may arise in that interval, one is able to endure them all for the sake of hearing the Dharma; how much more so the various sufferings of the human realm!

Having heard this, he reflected correctly and with right attention; he attained the four dhyānas and the formless absorptions, and the four immeasurables and five supernormal powers arose in succession, yet he did not take birth according to their power.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here beholds many Buddhas; Making offerings and hearing the Dharma, their mind becomes resolute.
Severing all false delusions, they become increasingly pure, Like refined true gold, whose essence never diminishes.
Dwelling here, he frequently acts as the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Transforming and guiding immeasurable hosts of devas,
Causing them to abandon greed and abide in the wholesome path, Single-mindedly and exclusively seeking the merits of the Buddha.
When the Sons of the Buddha dwell here and apply themselves with diligent vigor, they are fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
they behold hundreds of thousands of Buddhas with bodies adorned by the marks, and by the power of their vows, they may even exceed this.
Universally benefiting all sentient beings—such is the supreme conduct of those Bodhisattvas;
thus have I explained the meaning of this third stage.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Five;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Command.
Chapter Twenty-Six, Part Three: The Thirty Grounds; The Fourth Ground.

When the sons of the Buddha hear of this vast practice—this delightful, profound, subtle, and supreme ground—their hearts leap with great joy and delight, scattering many flowers everywhere as an offering to the Buddha.
When this sublime Dharma was thus expounded, the great earth and the waters of the ocean all trembled;
all the celestial maidens were filled with joy, and they all uttered wondrous sounds in unison to offer praise.
The Sovereign King of Gods was greatly filled with joy; raining down mani-jewels as an offering to the Buddha, he praised him, saying:
"For my sake the Buddha has appeared in the world, expounding the foremost practice of merit."
Such meanings of the stages for the wise are extremely difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of eons;
yet now, all at once, I have heard this sublime sound of the Dharma regarding the supreme practices of the Bodhisattvas.
May the Wise One further expound upon the stages beyond this, the definitive path without remainder, for the benefit of all devas and humans; these sons of the Buddhas all delight in hearing it!
The one of courageous and great mind, Vimukticandra, requested Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
From this point on, you shall enter the fourth stage; please proclaim all its characteristics and practices!"
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has thoroughly purified the third stage and wishes to enter the fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), they should practice ten gateways of the light of Dharma."
What are the ten? They are:

observing the realm of sentient beings, observing the realm of phenomena, observing the realm of worlds, observing the realm of space, observing the realm of consciousness, observing the realm of desire, observing the realm of form, observing the realm of formlessness, observing the realm of vast mental resolve and inclination, and observing the realm of great mental resolve and inclination.
By means of these ten gates of the illumination of dharmas, the bodhisattva enters the fourth stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom, they are able to mature the teachings through ten kinds of knowledge; thus they attain those internal dharmas and are born into the family of the Tathāgata."
What are the ten? They are:
because the profound resolve does not regress;
Because they give rise to pure faith in the Triple Gem that is ultimately indestructible;
because they contemplate the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); and because they contemplate the non-arising nature of the intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas.
By contemplating the formation and destruction of the world;
by contemplating that birth arises from causes and karma;
and by contemplating saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
By observing the karma of sentient beings and their lands;
by observing the prior limit and the subsequent limit;
and by observing the exhaustion of non-existence.
These are the ten.
Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this fourth stage, they contemplate the internal body as a body, practicing with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
Contemplating the external body, he dwells observing the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow;
contemplating both the internal and external body, he dwells observing the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.

Likewise, he contemplates internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings, dwelling in the observation of feelings as feelings; he contemplates the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external mind, dwelling in the observation of the mind as the mind; he contemplates internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena, dwelling in the observation of phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva, for the sake of preventing the arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, generates the will, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment;
for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, he generates the will, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment;
for the sake of bringing about the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he generates the will, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right practice.

In order that wholesome states already arisen may remain and not be lost, and so that they may be cultivated and further increased, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies his mind with right practice.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and the volitional formations of abandonment; he relies on disenchantment, relies on detachment, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment.

He cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation and the volitional formations of abandonment; he relies on disenchantment, relies on detachment, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices the faculty of faith, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;
he practices the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices the power of faith, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;
he practices the powers of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;

he practices the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva practices right view, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;

he practices right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.

The Bodhisattva practices such meritorious virtues for the following reasons: because they do not abandon any sentient being; because they are sustained by their original vows; because they take great compassion as their foremost priority; because they have perfected great loving-kindness; because they contemplate the wisdom of all-knowledge; because they accomplish the adornment of Buddha-fields; because they perfect the powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities of a Buddha, and the physical marks, signs, and voice of a Tathāgata; because they seek the most supreme and excellent path; because they accord with the profound liberation of the Buddhas as they have heard it; and because they contemplate great wisdom and skillful means.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), they abandon all attachments arising toward the view of a self-body as the foremost, as well as toward the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields;

they abandon all such things through the contemplation of their emergence and subsidence, by means of observation and remediation, by way of ‘mine-ness,’ by way of material possessions, and by way of points of attachment. They are entirely free from all such [notions].”
If this bodhisattva sees that an action is censured by the Tathāgata or defiled by afflictions, he completely abandons it;
if he sees that an action accords with the bodhisattva path and is praised by the Tathāgata, he practices it entirely.
“O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva, according to the skillful means and wisdom he gives rise to, cultivates the Path and the factors conducive to enlightenment. In this way, he attains a moistened mind, a supple mind, a disciplined mind, a mind intent on benefit and peace, an undefiled mind, a mind seeking the most supreme and excellent dharmas, a mind seeking sublime wisdom, a mind that rescues all worlds, a mind that reveres the honored and virtuous and does not disobey their instructions, and a mind that practices well whatever Dharma he hears.”

This bodhisattva knows kindness and knows how to repay it; his mind is exceedingly harmonious and gentle, and he dwells in peace and happiness with others. He is upright and supple, free from the conduct of dense thickets, and devoid of self-conceit. He readily accepts instruction and grasps the intent of the teacher.

When this bodhisattva thus achieves patience, thus achieves pliancy, thus achieves tranquility— having achieved such patience, pliancy, and tranquility— and while purifying the karma of the subsequent stage and practicing with focused attention,

they attain unceasing diligence, untainted diligence, non-retrogressive diligence, vast diligence, boundless diligence, blazing diligence, unequaled diligence, indestructible diligence, diligence that brings all sentient beings to maturity, and diligence that skillfully discriminates between the path and what is not the path.

The mind-realm of this bodhisattva is pure; his profound resolve remains unimpaired, his awakening and understanding are clear and sharp, and his roots of goodness increase. He is free from worldly defilement and has severed all doubts; he is fully endowed with clear discernment, filled with joy and bliss, personally protected by the Buddhas, and has completely accomplished immeasurable aspirations and delights.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Ground of Blazing Wisdom, by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas.
They are as follows:”
They see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

To all of them they pay homage, revere, serve, and make offerings, providing robes, bedding, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and all necessities of life. They also make offerings to the entire Sangha, dedicating all these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
In the presence of those Buddhas, he reverently listened to the Dharma; having heard it, he received and upheld it, practicing it fully.

Furthermore, within the teachings of those Buddhas, he left the household life to cultivate the Way, and again cultivated and refined his profound faith and understanding for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, causing all his roots of goodness to become increasingly bright and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as a goldsmith refines pure gold to create ornaments that no other gold can equal, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
all the roots of goodness residing in this stage cannot be equaled by the roots of goodness of the lower stages.
Just as the pure circle of light of a maṇi jewel can emit radiance that no other jewels can equal, and which cannot be destroyed by conditions such as wind or rain;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: dwelling in this stage, he cannot be surpassed by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages, and all Māras and afflictions cannot destroy him.
Among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva predominantly practices "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*);
among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), he predominantly practices "diligence" (*vīrya*).
He does not fail to cultivate the others, but does so according to his strength and capacity.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the fourth stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom.”

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a king of the Suyāma heaven; through skillful means, they are able to eliminate the delusions of sentient beings, such as the view of a self-identity, and cause them to abide in right view.

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—all such activities as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha, and even never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Furthermore, he forms this thought:

"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, and even the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) relies."

If this bodhisattva exerts diligent effort, in a single moment of thought they can enter billions of samādhis, see billions of buddhas, and know the spiritual powers of billions of buddhas; they can shake billions of worlds, and even manifest billions of bodies, with each body having billions of bodhisattvas as its retinue.

If they manifest through the sovereign power of their superior bodhisattva vows, it exceeds these numbers, such that even in hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know them.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The Bodhisattva, having already purified the third stage, Next contemplates the world of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena, The realm of space, the realm of consciousness, and the three realms;
With a mind of liberation, fully understanding them all, he is able to enter."
Upon first ascending the Stage of Flames, one increases in power; born into the family of the Tathāgata, one never again falls back.
One’s faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha remains indestructible, as one contemplates that all phenomena are impermanent and without arising.
Contemplating the world’s formation and destruction, the karma that gives rise to birth, and the karmas of saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, and the buddha-fields;
contemplating the past and future limits as well as their exhaustion—by practicing in this way, one is born into the family of the Buddhas.
Having attained this Dharma, his compassion increased; he further applied himself diligently to the four foundations of mindfulness.
Contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena internally and externally, he completely eliminated all worldly craving and attachment.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the four right efforts, eliminating unwholesome dharmas and increasing the wholesome;
he thoroughly cultivates the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers, and likewise the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path.
To deliver sentient beings, they cultivate those practices; protected by their original vows, they take compassion as their foremost guide.

They seek all-encompassing wisdom and Buddha-lands, and likewise contemplate the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the extraordinary marks and signs, and the profound, beautiful voice.
They also seek the sublime path and the state of liberation, practicing it through great skillful means. The sixty-two views,
headed by the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the manifold notions of "I" and "mine," and all attachments to the aggregates (*skandha*),
elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*)— all these are abandoned within these four stages.
The Tathāgata has censured those courses of affliction; all that is without benefit is completely severed.
The wise practice pure deeds, and for the sake of delivering sentient beings, there is nothing they will not do.
The Bodhisattva practices with diligence and without indolence, thereby attaining the ten mental states in their full perfection;
single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way without weariness, he aspires in his resolve to receive his office and deliver all sentient beings.
Reverencing the virtuous and practicing the Dharma, Knowing gratitude, being easy to instruct, and free from resentment or violence;
Abandoning pride and departing from flattery with a harmonious and gentle mind, One becomes increasingly diligent and never regresses.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom, their mind is pure and never regresses;
their realization is certain and their virtues increase, as they are entirely freed from the defilements of the net of doubt.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage are the most excellent among men;
having made offerings to immeasurable nayutas of Buddhas, they hear the True Dharma and likewise renounce the world, remaining as indestructible as genuine gold.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here, endowed with all virtues, practices the Path through wisdom and skillful means;
his mind does not regress before the various māras, for he is like a wondrous jewel that nothing can destroy.
Dwelling here, one mostly becomes the King of the Yama Heaven, Master of the Dharma and honored by the multitude;
Universally transforming all beings to eliminate evil views, One single-mindedly seeks Buddha-wisdom and cultivates wholesome deeds.
Through the power of diligent and intense effort, the Bodhisattva attains hundreds of millions of samādhis and the like;
yet what is accomplished through the power of his vows and wisdom exceeds these numbers beyond measure.
Thus have I, for the sake of the Buddha’s sons, proclaimed this fourth stage of the Bodhisattva—
the pure and subtle path of practice, which is fully conjoined with merit, meaning, and wisdom.
When the Bodhisattvas heard this practice of the sublime ground, they attained realization of the Dharma with joyful hearts;
flowers rained down from the sky as they praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Great Being Vajragarbha!"
The Sovereign Lord of Devas and his celestial hosts, having heard the Dharma, leaped for joy as they dwelt in the void;
they universally emitted clouds of various wondrous lights, making offerings to the Tathāgata until joy filled them completely.
The celestial maidens played heavenly music and also praised the Buddha with their voices;
through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, they uttered these words within that sound:
"The Buddha’s vow, made long ago, is now fulfilled; the Way of the Buddha, sought for a long time, is now attained."
Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived at the celestial palace; those who benefit devas and humans have seen him only after a long time.
The great ocean, after a vast eon, has now begun to stir; the Buddha’s light, after a vast eon, is now emitted.
Sentient beings, after a vast eon, have finally attained peace and joy; the voice of Great Compassion is heard only after a long time.
Having reached the further shore of all merit, With the darkness of pride entirely extinguished,
Utterly pure like space, Unstained by worldly dharmas like a lotus flower.
The Great Muni has appeared in the world, Like Mount Sumeru rising from the vast ocean;
To make offerings to him can exhaust all suffering, And through such offerings, one will surely attain the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This field of merit is worthy of peerless offerings; Therefore, with a joyful heart, I offer to the Buddha.
When these immeasurable celestial maidens had thus uttered these words of praise, all were filled with reverence and joy; gazing up at the Tathāgata, they remained silent.
At that time, the Great Being Vimukticandra again requested Vajragarbha, who is fearless:
"Regarding the characteristics of all practices in the fifth stage, I pray that the Son of the Buddha will proclaim them for us!"
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has fully perfected the practices of the fourth stage and wishes to enter the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), they should enter it by means of ten kinds of pure, equanimous minds."

What are these ten? They are: a mind of equal purity regarding the Buddha-dharma of the past; a mind of equal purity regarding the Buddha-dharma of the future; a mind of equal purity regarding the Buddha-dharma of the present; a mind of equal purity regarding ethical discipline; a mind of equal purity regarding the mind; a mind of equal purity regarding the removal of views, doubt, and regret; a mind of equal purity regarding the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path; a mind of equal purity regarding the knowledge and vision of practice; a mind of equal purity regarding the superior observation of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); and a mind of equal purity regarding the teaching and transforming of all sentient beings.
By means of these ten kinds of impartial and pure minds, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the fifth stage of a Bodhisattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this fifth stage, because they have well-cultivated the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), because their profound mind is well-purified, because they further seek the superior and victorious path, because they accord with *tathatā*, because they are sustained by the power of their vows, because they do not abandon compassion for all sentient beings, because they accumulate the merit and wisdom that assist the path, because they practice with diligent effort without ceasing, because they give rise to skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), because they observe and illuminate the higher and higher stages, because they receive the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, and because they are sustained by the power of mindfulness and wisdom, they attain a non-retrogressive mind."
“O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows as it truly is: ‘This is the Noble Truth of Suffering,’ ‘This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering,’ ‘This is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering,’ and ‘This is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. He skillfully knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), skillfully knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of differentiation (*prabheda-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of establishment (*siddhi-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of things (*vastu-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of arising (*utpāda-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of the wisdom that enters the path (*mārgāvatāra-jñāna-satya*), skillfully knows the truth of the successive accomplishment of all Bodhisattva stages, and even skillfully knows the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.”
Because this bodhisattva causes sentient beings to rejoice according to their mental inclinations, he knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
because he penetrates the single true mark (eka-lakṣaṇa), he knows the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
and because he awakens to the specific and general characteristics of phenomena, he knows the truth of marks (lakṣaṇa-satya).
Because they have thoroughly understood the distinctions among the various states of all phenomena, they know the truth of differentiation;
because they skillfully discern the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, they know the truth of establishment;
and because they have awakened to the suffering and affliction of body and mind, they know the truth of phenomena.
Because one awakens to the continuity of birth in the various realms of existence, one knows the truth of arising;
because all feverish afflictions are ultimately extinguished, one knows the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising;
because the non-dual is brought forth, one knows the truth of the knowledge of entering the path.

Because he has perfectly awakened to all modes of conduct, he thoroughly knows the sequential continuity and accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages, up to the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This is known through the power of the wisdom of faith and understanding, not through the power of ultimate wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Having attained such knowledge of the truths, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows, in accordance with reality, that all conditioned phenomena are false, deceptive, and delusive to the foolish."
At that time, the bodhisattva further increases their great compassion for all sentient beings and gives rise to the radiance of great loving-kindness.
O Son of the Buddha!

Having attained such power of wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon any sentient being, constantly seeks the wisdom of the Buddhas, and contemplates the past and future limits of all conditioned phenomena as they truly are.

He understands that from beginningless time, due to ignorance and craving for existence, there arises the cycle of birth and death; one cannot move beyond or emerge from the dwelling of the aggregates, thereby increasing the mass of suffering.
Therein, there is no self, no life-principle, no nourisher, and no one who takes up a further body in future states of existence; it is devoid of "I" and "mine."
As it was with the past limit, so it is with the future limit; all are non-existent.
Through the exhaustion of falsehood and attachment, one attains liberation;
whether things exist or do not exist, one knows them all as they truly are.
O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
"These ordinary worldlings are foolish and devoid of wisdom; they are truly to be pitied."

There have been, are now, and will be countless bodies that have perished, are perishing, and shall perish; yet though they are thus utterly extinguished, one cannot conceive a sense of revulsion toward the body. Instead, one further increases the mechanical suffering of conditioned existence, following the flow of birth and death without turning back. One seeks no escape from the house of the aggregates (*skandha*), fails to recognize the dread of the four great poisonous snakes, and is unable to extract the arrows of pride and views. One cannot extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor destroy the darkness of ignorance, nor dry up the great ocean of craving. One does not seek the Great Sage Teacher endowed with the ten powers;
rather, one enters the dense forest of Māra’s intent and is swept away and drowned by the waves of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) within the ocean of birth and death.
"O Son of the Buddha! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:

'These sentient beings undergo such suffering; they are destitute, impoverished, and oppressed; they have no rescue and no refuge; they have no island and no shelter; they have no guide and no eyes; they are shrouded by ignorance and enveloped in darkness.'"
I now, for the sake of all sentient beings, practice the dharmas that assist the path of merit and wisdom; alone I resolve my mind, seeking no companion.
By means of these merits, I shall cause all sentient beings to attain ultimate purity, even unto the attainment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and unimpeded wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with such wisdom, contemplates all the roots of goodness he cultivates as being for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, benefiting all sentient beings, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, feeling compassion for all sentient beings, bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, liberating all sentient beings, and gathering in all sentient beings;

so that all sentient beings may be freed from all suffering and affliction, so that all sentient beings may universally attain purity, so that all sentient beings may be fully tamed, and so that all sentient beings may enter parinirvāṇa."
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā),
they are called ‘the mindful one,’ because they do not forget any dharmas.”
He is called "the Wise One" because he is able to skillfully discern and understand;
he is called:
One who is "skilled in the marvelous" is so called because they understand the intended meaning of the sutras and their sequential connections;
one is called "possessed of shame and remorse" because they protect themselves and protect others.
He is named "The Firm," because he does not abandon his practice of the precepts;
he is named:
One who awakens is so called because they are able to discern what is possible and what is impossible;
one is called "one who follows wisdom" because they do not follow others.
He is named "One Who Follows Wisdom" because he skillfully knows the distinction between words that signify meaning and those that do not;
he is named:
They are called those with supernormal powers because they have skillfully cultivated meditative concentration;
they are called those with skillful means because they are able to act in accordance with the world.
He is named "The Insatiable" because he skillfully accumulates merit;
he is named:
They are "unresting" because they constantly seek wisdom;
they are called "untiring" because they accumulate great compassion.
He is named "One Who Diligently Practices for the Sake of Others," because he desires to lead all sentient beings into nirvana;
he is named:
Those who seek with tireless diligence do so for the sake of attaining the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Tathāgata;
they are called "those who can practice after having resolved their minds" because they accomplish the adornment of Buddha-lands.
He is named "One Who Diligently Cultivates Various Kinds of Wholesome Deeds," because he is able to be fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks;
he is named:
"One who constantly and diligently practices" does so because they seek to adorn the Buddha’s body, speech,
and mind; they are called "one who holds the Dharma in great esteem and reverence" because they act according to the instructions at the feet of all Bodhisattva Dharma-teachers.
He is named "One Whose Mind Is Without Obstruction," because he constantly acts within the world through great skillful means;
he is named:
"Day and night remaining far removed from other thoughts" means they constantly delight in teaching and transforming all sentient beings.

"O Son of the Buddha! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus diligently practice, they teach and transform sentient beings through giving; they teach and transform sentient beings through kind words, beneficial actions, and cooperation; they teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting physical bodies; they teach and transform sentient beings by expounding all dharmas; they teach and transform sentient beings by revealing the practices of Bodhisattvas; they teach and transform sentient beings by displaying the great majestic power of the Tathāgata; they teach and transform sentient beings by showing the faults and sufferings of birth and death; they teach and transform sentient beings by praising the wisdom and benefits of the Tathāgata; they teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting great supernormal powers; and they teach and transform sentient beings through various skillful means."
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to thus diligently employ skillful means to transform sentient beings, with a mind that is constantly continuous as it advances toward the wisdom of the Buddha;
regarding the roots of goodness they perform, there is no regression, and they always diligently cultivate and study the supreme dharmas of practice.
“O Son of the Buddha!
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices and masters all worldly arts and crafts.
That is to say:”
He thoroughly mastered writing, arithmetic, divination, and seals;
he was proficient in all treatises concerning earth, water, fire, and wind;
furthermore, he was skilled in medicinal prescriptions, capable of curing all ailments—including insanity, consumption, demonic possession, and malevolent poisons—and could completely eliminate them.
He was skilled in all matters of composition, eulogy, song, dance, music, jesting, and conversation;
he arranged cities, towns, villages, palaces, residences, gardens, groves, springs, streams, ponds, pools, grasses, trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs with perfect appropriateness;
and regarding treasuries of gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and the like, he knew their locations and brought them forth to show them to others.

He skillfully observes the sun, moon, and stars; the cries of birds, earthquakes, and auspicious or inauspicious dreams; and the physical signs of fortune or misfortune, all of which he perceives without a single error.

Upholding the precepts and entering meditative concentration, his supernormal powers are immeasurable. Regarding the four formless attainments and all other worldly matters, he reveals them all for the sake of benefiting sentient beings without causing them any harm or distress, gradually leading them to dwell securely in the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Ground of Difficult to Conquer, by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas. Namely:”
They see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

They revere, respect, serve, and make offerings to them all, presenting robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life; they also make offerings to the entire Saṃgha, dedicating these roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In the presence of all Buddhas, they listen to the Dharma with reverence; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to their capacity.
Furthermore, within the teachings of those Buddhas, they go forth into homelessness;
once ordained, they again hear the Dharma and attain dhāraṇīs, becoming Dharma masters who preserve what they have heard.

Abiding in this stage, for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, and even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as genuine gold becomes increasingly bright and pure when polished with mother-of-pearl, so too are all the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva on this stage;
through contemplation and observation by means of skillful wisdom, they become increasingly bright and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage, they accomplish meritorious qualities through the wisdom of skillful means, such that the roots of goodness of the lower stages cannot equal them.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as the sun, moon, stars, palaces, and their radiance are sustained by the power of the wind and cannot be destroyed, nor can they be shaken by any other winds;

so too are all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas on this stage. Sustained by the wisdom of skillful means and observed accordingly, they cannot be destroyed, nor can they be shaken by any of the roots of goodness of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or worldly beings.
Among the ten pāramitās, this bodhisattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā most predominantly;
it is not that they do not cultivate the others, but rather they do so according to their strength and capacity.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the fifth stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, exercising sovereign mastery over all sentient beings; they subdue all externalists and false views, and are able to establish sentient beings within the realm of the True Truth (satya).

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—all such actions as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha, and even never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Again, he forms this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most preeminent, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, and even the one who is the basis for the knowledge of all modes."

If this bodhisattva exerts diligent vigor, in a single thought-moment they attain ten trillion samādhis, see ten trillion buddhas, and know the spiritual powers of ten trillion buddhas; they can shake ten trillion buddha-worlds and even manifest ten trillion bodies, with each body surrounded by a retinue of ten trillion bodhisattvas.

If they manifest through the sovereign power of their superior bodhisattva vows, it exceeds these numbers, such that even in hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, or even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could not calculate or know them.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva’s fourth stage is already purified; He contemplates the equality of the Buddhas of the three times.
With precepts and mind, he eliminates doubt regarding the path and what is not the path; Observing in this way, he enters the fifth stage."
The foundations of mindfulness are the bow, the faculties are the sharp arrows; the right efforts are the horses, the divine bases are the chariot.
The five powers are the sturdy armor that crushes the enemy; courageous and unretreating, one enters the fifth stage.
Taking shame and remorse as their garment and the factors of enlightenment as their wreath, with pure precepts as their incense and dhyāna as their unguent,
they are exquisitely adorned with wisdom and skillful means, entering the forest of dhāraṇīs and the garden of samādhis.
With the wish-fulfilling gem as its feet and right mindfulness as its neck, with compassion as its eyes and wisdom as its tusks,
this lion among men roars the cry of non-self, destroying the enemies of affliction and entering the fifth stage.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this fifth stage, they further cultivate the supreme and pure path;
with a resolve to seek the Buddha-dharma that never regresses, they contemplate compassion without weariness.
Having accumulated the supreme merit of wisdom and virtue, Diligently applying skillful means, they contemplate the higher stages;
Empowered by the Buddha’s strength and endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, They understand the Four Noble Truths exactly as they truly are.
They well know the conventional truth and the ultimate truth, The truth of characteristics, the truth of distinctions, and the truth of establishment, The truth of phenomena,
the truths of arising and cessation, as well as the truth of the path, And even the unimpeded truth of the Tathāgata.
Although such contemplation of the truths is subtle, one has not yet attained unimpeded, supreme liberation;
nevertheless, because it can generate great merit, it surpasses worldly wisdom.
Having contemplated the truths and known that conditioned phenomena are illusory in nature and devoid of solidity,
they receive a portion of the Buddha’s compassionate light and seek the Buddha-wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings.

Contemplating the past and future limits of all conditioned phenomena, Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance and bound by craving, they wander and revolve within this mass of suffering; Therein, there is no self, no person, and no life-span.
With craving and grasping as causes, one undergoes the suffering of future births; though one seeks their limit, it cannot be found.
Drifting in delusion with no time for return—these pitiable ones I must deliver.
The aggregates are a house, the elements are serpents, and the various views are arrows;

the fire of the mind blazes fiercely, the darkness of ignorance is heavy, and one is swept away by the river of craving, having no leisure for observation; sinking into the ocean of suffering, one lacks a guide of light.
Having known this, one exerts diligent effort; all that is done is for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Such a person is called one possessed of mindfulness and wisdom, and even one who has realized the skillful means.
Practicing merit and wisdom without weariness, Revering the learned without fatigue,
Adorning both the lands and the marks of excellence— All such things are for the sake of sentient beings.
Desiring to transform and edify all the worlds, he was well-versed in the arts of writing, calculation, and seals;
he was likewise skilled in various prescriptions and medicines, treating all manner of illnesses until they were entirely healed.
His literary style, song, and dance are all exquisite; his palaces, residences, gardens, and ponds are entirely peaceful and secure;
he reveals many kinds of precious treasuries to others for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
The sun, moon, and constellations, as well as earthquakes, And even the physical marks of the body are observed;
The four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the supernormal powers— All are manifested for the benefit of the world.
The wise one dwelling on this Ground Difficult to Conquer makes offerings to nayutas of Buddhas and listens to the Dharma;
like fine jewels polishing pure gold, all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
Just as the stars in the void, sustained by the power of the wind, remain unharmed and unmoved;
and just as the lotus flower is not defiled by water—so does this Great Being move through the world.
Dwelling here, one often becomes a King of Tuṣita, Able to crush the various heterodox views;
All the virtues cultivated are for the sake of Buddha-wisdom, Vowing to attain the Ten Powers to save all sentient beings.
He further practices great diligence, immediately making offerings to a thousand billion Buddhas;
his attainment of meditative concentration and the shaking of world-systems is likewise so, yet what is accomplished through the power of his vows exceeds even this.
Thus, this fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer, the most supreme and true path among men,
I have now fully proclaimed for the sake of all the Buddha-sons through various powers of skillful means.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume 36; The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume 37.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Chapter on the Forty Stages, Part Four. The Sixth Stage.
Having heard these supreme practices, the Bodhisattva of the Sixth Stage rejoices in his heart;
he rains down exquisite flowers, emits pure radiance, scatters precious jewels, and makes offerings to the Tathāgata while praising his excellent teaching.
Hundreds of thousands of devas all rejoice, together scattering various jewels in the air—flower garlands, necklaces, banners, and streamers;
with precious parasols and fragrant ointments, they all make offerings to the Buddha.
The Sovereign King of the Heaven of Mastery, together with his retinue, gave rise to joy and dwelt in mid-air;
scattering jewels that formed clouds, they made offerings and praised him, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, please proclaim it swiftly!"
Immeasurable celestial maidens dwelling in the air together praised the Buddha with the sounds of music,
their voices all uttering these words:
“The Buddha’s speech can eliminate the disease of afflictions.”
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of all marks; Like space, it is free from discrimination;
Transcending all grasping and attachment, it is beyond the path of words; It is truly equal and eternally pure.
If one can penetrate the nature of all phenomena, The mind remains unmoved by existence or non-existence.
Diligently practicing for the sake of saving the world— Such a person is a true son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth.
They practice giving without grasping at signs; they fundamentally sever all evils and firmly uphold the precepts;
understanding that phenomena are non-harming, they are ever patient; knowing that the nature of phenomena is detached, they possess diligence;
having exhausted all afflictions, they enter the various dhyānas; and they skillfully penetrate the emptiness of nature while discerning all dharmas.
"Endowed with the power of wisdom, you are able to provide universal salvation; by extinguishing all evils, you are called a Great Being.
With thousands of millions of such wondrous voices, they offered praise and then fell silent, gazing up at the Buddha.
Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"By what characteristics does one enter the subsequent stage?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha spoke to the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra:
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already fulfilled the fifth stage and wishes to enter the sixth, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they should contemplate ten dharmas of equality.”
What are these ten? They are: the equality of all phenomena because they are signless;

the equality because they lack substantiality; the equality because they are unarisen; the equality because they are unestablished; the equality because they are primordially pure; the equality because they are free from conceptual proliferation; the equality because they are without grasping or abandoning; the equality because they are quiescent; the equality because they are like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, an echo, the moon reflected in water, an image in a mirror, a mirage, and a magical transformation; and the equality because existence and non-existence are non-dual.

When a bodhisattva thus contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, and accords with this reality without contradiction, they enter the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), attaining the sharp and clear "patience of accord" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), though they have not yet attained the "patience of the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
“O Son of the Buddha!

Having observed in this way, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with great compassion as his foremost priority, great compassion as his preeminent motive, and great compassion as his fulfillment, contemplates the arising and ceasing of the world, and forms this thought:
‘The taking of birth in the world arises entirely from attachment to a self; if one is free from this attachment, there will be no place for birth.’”

Again, he reflected: "Ordinary worldlings lack wisdom and cling to a self; they constantly seek existence and non-existence, engage in improper reflection, and give rise to deluded conduct, thereby walking upon wrong paths.

Through their actions of demerit, merit, and the imperturbable, these accumulate and increase; within these formations, they plant the seeds of the mind—leaky and with grasping—which again give rise to future birth, as well as old age and death."

That is to say: karma is the field, consciousness is the seed, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; moistened by the water of craving, irrigated by the sprinkling of self-conceit, and increased by the net of views, it produces the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). As name-and-form increases, the five sense-faculties arise; through the mutual encounter of the faculties, contact (*sparśa*) arises; from the encounter of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises; following feeling, there is the craving for rebirth (*tṛṣṇā*); as craving increases, grasping (*upādāna*) arises; as grasping increases, becoming (*bhava*) arises.
Once becoming has arisen, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arise as a body within the various realms of existence; this is called birth (*jāti*).
Once born, there is decay and transformation, which is aging; and finally, there is cessation, which is death.
At the time of aging and death, various fevers and afflictions arise;
because of these fevers and afflictions, one experiences sorrow, lamentation, and all manner of suffering.
"For this reason, there is arising, yet no one who arises; there is cessation, yet no one who ceases, occurring spontaneously.
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates the characteristics of dependent origination in accordance with reality.
O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further reflects:
"Because one does not understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is called [ignorance]:..."

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition for the karma that is performed, which is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Volitional formations depend upon the initial moment of consciousness, which is consciousness (*vijñāna*). That which arises simultaneously with consciousness—the four appropriated aggregates—is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form constitutes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of the three factors—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness—is contact (*sparśa*). Arising simultaneously with contact is feeling (*vedanā*). Attachment to feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The intensification of craving is grasping (*upādāna*). The outflowing karma produced by grasping is becoming (*bhava*). The arising of the aggregates from that karma is birth (*jāti*). The maturation of the aggregates is aging (*jarā*).

The disintegration of the aggregates is death (*maraṇa*). At the time of death, there is separation; the deluded and confused mind’s greedy attachment and mental distress is sorrow (*śoka*). Weeping, lamentation, and sighing are wailing (*parideva*). That which dwells in the five sense faculties is pain (*duḥkha*), while that which dwells in the mental ground is grief (*daurmanasya*). The further increase of this grief and pain is despair (*upāyāsa*).
"In this way, there is only the growth of the tree of suffering; there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, no agent and no experiencer.
He further thought: "If there were an agent, then there would be an action."
"If there is no agent, there is also no action; in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), both are unobtainable.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva further reflects as follows:
"All that exists within the three realms is but this single mind.
It is upon this single mind that the Tathāgata distinguishes and expounds the twelve links of existence; it is thus that they are established."

Why is this? Craving arises with the mind in accordance with its objects. The mind is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the object is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); delusion regarding these formations is ignorance (*avidyā*). That which arises together with ignorance and the mind is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of the three factors of the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*). That which arises together with contact is feeling (*vedanā*). Lack of satiety in feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Clinging and not relinquishing craving is grasping (*upādāna*). The arising of those various links of existence is becoming (*bhava*). What is called "arising" from becoming is birth (*jāti*).
The maturation of birth is aging (*jarā*), and the decay of aging is death (*maraṇa*).
“O Son of the Buddha!

Within this, ignorance has two kinds of functions: first, it causes sentient beings to become deluded regarding their objects of perception; second, it acts as the causal condition for the arising of formative activities (*saṃskāra*).”
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) also have two kinds of functions: first, they can produce future retribution; second, they act as the cause for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the continuity of all states of existence (*bhava*); second, it acts as the cause for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Name-and-form also has two kinds of functions: first, they mutually assist and complete one another; second, they act as the cause for the arising of the six sense bases.
The six sense bases also have two kinds of functions: first, each takes its own respective object; second, they act as the cause for the arising of contact.
Contact also has two kinds of functions: first, it can contact the object; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of sensation.
Sensation also has two kinds of functions: first, it can experience things such as the beloved and the hated; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of craving.
Craving also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes attachment to desirable objects; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of grasping.
Grasping also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the various afflictions to continue in succession; second, it acts as the cause for the arising of existence.
Existence (*bhava*) also has two kinds of functions: first, it can cause rebirth in other realms of existence; second, it acts as the generative cause for birth (*jāti*).
Birth also has two kinds of functions: first, it can give rise to the aggregates (*skandha*); second, it acts as the generative cause for aging (*jarā*).
Old age also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the sense faculties to undergo transformation; second, it acts as the generative cause for death. Death also has two kinds of functions:
first, it is able to destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); second, because there is no conscious awareness, the continuity of existence remains unbroken.
“O Son of the Buddha!

Regarding ‘ignorance conditions volitional formations,’ up to ‘birth conditions aging and death’: because ignorance through birth act as conditions, they cause volitional formations through aging and death to be uninterrupted, thereby assisting in their formation.”

Regarding the statement that "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease," and so on up to "with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease": because ignorance through birth do not act as conditions, they cause the cessation of all formations through aging and death, since they no longer provide assistance for their formation.
O Son of the Buddha!

Herein, the non-interruption of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitutes the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*); the non-interruption of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) constitutes the path of karma (*karma-mārga*); and the non-interruption of the remaining factors constitutes the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*).

By severing the conceptualization of the prior and posterior limits, these three paths are abandoned. Thus, these three paths are devoid of self (*ātman*) and what belongs to self (*ātmīya*); they possess only arising and ceasing, like a bundle of reeds.
Furthermore, "ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to observing the past;
"consciousness through feeling" refers to observing the present;
and "craving through existence" refers to observing the future.
From that point onward, they continue in succession.
As for "the cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of formations," this refers to cessation through dependent observation (*apekṣā-prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, the twelve links of existence are termed the three types of suffering: herein, ignorance, formations, up to the six sense bases, constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); contact and feeling constitute the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); and the remaining links constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Regarding "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease": this is the severance of the three types of suffering.
Furthermore, regarding "conditioned by ignorance, formations arise": through the causal condition of ignorance, various formations are produced;
when ignorance ceases, formations cease, because in the absence of ignorance, formations also do not exist—the same applies to the rest.
Furthermore, "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise" refers to the arising of bondage;
"with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" refers to the cessation of bondage.
The same applies to the rest.
Furthermore, "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" refers to the contemplation of non-existence;
"with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" refers to the contemplation of total extinction.
The same applies to the remaining [links].
“O Son of the Buddha!
Thus do Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate dependent origination in ten ways through both retrograde and progressive order. Namely:”

Because of the continuity of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), because they are subsumed within a single mind, because of the differentiation of one's own karma, because they are not mutually separable, because the three paths are uninterrupted, because of observing the past, present, and future, because of the accumulation of the three types of suffering, because of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, because of being bound by arising and ceasing, and because of the contemplation of non-existence and exhaustion:

"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates dependent origination through these ten aspects, they know there is no self, no person, no life-span, that it is empty of intrinsic nature, and that there is no agent and no experiencer; thus, the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before them."

Contemplating that all links of existence are by nature extinguished and ultimately liberated, such that not even the slightest dharma arises, one immediately attains the gateway to liberation of signlessness, which manifests before them.

Having thus entered into emptiness and signlessness, one has no further aspiration or seeking, except for taking great compassion as the foremost principle to transform and teach sentient beings; at that very moment, the liberation door of wishlessness manifests before them.

When a bodhisattva thus cultivates the three gates of liberation, they are free from the notion of self and other, free from the notion of an agent or a recipient, and free from the notions of existence and non-existence.
“O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s great compassion increases further, and he practices with diligent effort so that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) which are not yet fulfilled may become complete. He forms this thought:
‘All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) proceed when there is a combination [of conditions], and do not proceed when there is no combination;’”
When conditions assemble, there is turning; when conditions do not assemble, there is no turning.
Thus I know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) abound in manifold faults and afflictions, and I shall sever these causes and conditions of conjunction;
yet, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment, I shall not ultimately extinguish all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus contemplates how conditioned phenomena abound in faults and afflictions, lack intrinsic nature, and are neither born nor extinguished, yet constantly gives rise to great compassion and does not abandon sentient beings, they immediately attain the manifestation of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
which is named 'the Radiance of Unobstructed Wisdom.'"

Having accomplished such light of wisdom, although they cultivate the causes and conditions of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they do not abide within the conditioned; and although they contemplate that the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena is quiescent, they do not abide in quiescence, because the factors of enlightenment have not yet been perfected.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence, they attain the entry into the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the samādhi of supreme emptiness, the samādhi of great emptiness, the samādhi of combined emptiness, the samādhi of arising emptiness, the samādhi of emptiness that is non-conceptual as it truly is, the samādhi of non-abandoning emptiness, and the samādhi of emptiness that is neither detached nor non-detached.”
With these ten gates of emptiness samādhi as the foremost, hundreds of thousands of emptiness samādhis all manifest before him;
likewise, with these ten gates of signlessness and ten gates of wishlessness samādhi as the foremost, hundreds of thousands of signlessness and wishlessness samādhi gates all manifest before him.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence, they further cultivate and bring to fulfillment an indestructible mind, a resolute mind, a purely virtuous mind, a profoundly deep mind, a non-retrogressive mind, an unceasing mind, a vast mind, a boundless mind, a mind seeking wisdom, and a mind conjoined with skillful means and insight; all of these are made perfectly complete.”

“O Son of the Buddha! By means of this mind, the Bodhisattva accords with the Bodhi of the Buddhas; he does not fear heterodox arguments, enters the stages of wisdom, and leaves behind the paths of the two vehicles to advance toward the wisdom of the Buddhas. No afflictions or Māras can obstruct or destroy him. Abiding in the light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, he skillfully cultivates all dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; skillful means and wisdom are always in harmonious accord, and he constantly practices and never abandons the factors of enlightenment.”
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain the supremacy of the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and attain the third kind of sharp and compliant patience (*kṣānti*). This is because they accord with and do not contradict the true nature (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Having dwelled in this Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī*), the Bodhisattva, by the power of his vows, comes to see many Buddhas. Namely:”
They see many hundreds of Buddhas, even up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

With a vast mind and a profound mind, they make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise; they present all necessities of life—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—and also make offerings to the entire Saṃgha, dedicating these roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In the presence of all Buddhas, they listen to the Dharma with reverence; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, attaining the light of wisdom of the samādhi of reality as it is, practicing in accordance with it, and remembering it without forsaking it.

Furthermore, having attained the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure after passing through a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, and even through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
Just as genuine gold becomes increasingly bright and pure when repeatedly polished with lapis lazuli, so too are all the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva on this stage;
through skillful means and wisdom, they are observed accordingly, becoming increasingly bright and pure, increasingly tranquil and extinguished, such that nothing can obscure them.
Just as the moonlight shines upon the bodies of sentient beings, bringing them refreshing coolness that cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of wind-circles;

so too are all the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattvas on this stage, for they can extinguish the blazing fires of affliction of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, and cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of demonic paths.
Among the ten pāramitās, this bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā predominantly;
it is not that they do not cultivate the others, but rather they do so according to their strength and capacity.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the sixth stage of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the Stage of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the celestial king Śubhakṛtsna, exercising sovereign mastery. They cannot be defeated or intimidated by any questions or challenges posed by śrāvakas, and they are able to cause sentient beings to eliminate their pride (*asmimāna*) and penetrate deeply into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—all such actions as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, and so on, up to being never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, and even the one upon whom the wisdom of omniscience relies."

If this bodhisattva practices with diligent vigor, in a single moment of thought they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of samādhis, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas as their retinue;
yet if they manifest through the sovereign power of their vows, it exceeds these numbers, such that even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas one could not count or know them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“When a bodhisattva has perfected the fifth stage, They contemplate phenomena as signless and devoid of intrinsic nature;
Unborn and unoriginated, they are primordially pure, Free from conceptual proliferation, without grasping or rejecting.”
The essential nature and characteristics are quiescent, like illusions and the like; existence and non-existence are non-dual and free from conceptual discrimination.
Observing in accordance with the dharma-nature in this way, one attains this wisdom and enters the sixth stage.
Possessing sharp, penetrating, and compliant patience, and endowed with wisdom, he observes the marks of arising and ceasing in the world:
that the world arises through the power of the darkness of ignorance; if that darkness of ignorance is extinguished, the world does not exist.
Contemplating that the true meaning of all causes and conditions is emptiness, yet not destroying the functional utility of conventional designations;
there is no agent, no recipient, and no volition—conditioned phenomena arise everywhere like clouds.
Not knowing the ultimate truth is called ignorance; the volitional karma produced thereby is the fruit of delusion.
Consciousness arises together with these as name-and-form, and in this manner, it leads all the way to the mass of suffering.
One thoroughly understands that the three realms exist in dependence upon the mind; the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so.
Birth and death are all produced by the mind; if the mind is extinguished, birth and death are ended.
The functions of ignorance are twofold: failing to understand within the conditions of dependent origination serves as the cause for volitional formations;
thus it continues until old age and death, from which this suffering arises without end.
With ignorance as a condition, it cannot be severed; when those conditions are exhausted, they all cease.
Delusion, craving, and grasping are the factors of affliction; volitional formations and existence are karma; the rest are suffering.
From ignorance up to the six sense bases is the suffering of conditioned existence; contact and feeling are the suffering of suffering;
the remaining links of existence are the suffering of change. If one perceives non-self, these three sufferings are extinguished.
Ignorance and formations belong to the past; consciousness through feeling revolve in the present;
craving, grasping, and becoming constitute future suffering. When these conditions are severed, the limit of existence is exhausted.
Ignorance as a condition gives rise to bondage; by attaining liberation from conditions, bondage is exhausted.
From causes fruits arise; through liberation, they are severed. Contemplating this, one knows that their nature is empty.
Following along with ignorance gives rise to all states of existence; if one does not follow along, all states of existence are severed.
This existence and that existence are likewise non-existent; through these ten kinds of reflection, the mind is freed from attachment.
The continuity of the links of existence is subsumed within a single mind; it is not divorced from one’s own karma and consists of the three paths.
Arising through the causes and conditions of the three periods of time and the three types of suffering, this bondage of arising and ceasing proceeds without end.
Thus one universally contemplates the process of dependent origination: It is without agent, without recipient, and without reality;
Like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection of light, And like a fool chasing a mirage.
Observing in this way, one enters into emptiness; Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached, one attains signlessness;
Realizing their falsity, one has no aspirations, Except for compassion toward sentient beings.
The Great Being practices the gates of liberation, Increasing his great compassion as he seeks the Buddha-dharma;
Knowing that all conditioned things arise from collective action, He resolves with determination to diligently practice the Path.
The gate of the samādhi of emptiness possesses hundreds of thousands [of aspects], and the same is true for signlessness and wishlessness;
through the progressive patience of prajñā, all are further enhanced, and the wisdom of liberation is brought to full perfection.
Furthermore, with a profound mind, they made extensive offerings to the Buddhas;
practicing the Path within the Buddha’s teachings, they attained the treasury of the Dharma and increased their roots of goodness, like gold and lapis lazuli polished and refined.
Just as the moon’s coolness pervades all things, And the four winds cannot destroy it when they strike;
so too this Bodhisattva on the Ground transcends the path of Māra, and likewise cools the fever of afflictions for all living beings.
In this stage, they mostly become kings of the Heaven of Making-Everything-Appropriate, transforming and guiding sentient beings to eliminate their pride;
whatever they do, they seek only all-knowledge, having already completely surpassed the path of the śrāvakas.
