The Bodhisattvas on this stage exert diligent vigor, attaining hundreds of billions of samādhis;
they also behold countless Buddhas, like the sun in the sky during the height of summer.
Profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive or know, beyond the comprehension of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—
thus have I, for the sake of the Buddha’s sons, proclaimed this sixth stage of the Bodhisattva.

At that time, the hosts of devas rejoiced in their hearts; They scattered jewels that formed clouds abiding in the sky, And universally produced all manner of wondrous sounds, Addressing the Most Victorious and Pure One:
“You have realized the wisdom that masters ultimate truth, And have accomplished hundreds of thousands of millions of virtues.”
A lotus among men, free from all attachment, he expounds profound practices for the benefit of all beings.
The Sovereign King of Devas, stationed in the air, emits great radiance that illuminates the Buddha’s body;
he also scatters clouds of the most sublime and wondrous incense, universally making offerings to the One who has removed sorrow and affliction.
At that time, the hosts of devas were all filled with joy, and they all raised beautiful voices to praise him in unison:
"Having heard these merits of this ground, we have already obtained great and wholesome benefit."
At that time, the heavenly maidens were filled with joy in their hearts; competing with one another, they played tens of millions of kinds of musical sounds.
All of this was through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, and within those sounds, they spoke these words together:
“Your majestic demeanor is tranquil and most peerless; You are the World-Honored One who can tame the untamable.”
Having transcended all worlds, they traverse the world to reveal the wondrous Way.
Though they manifest various infinite bodies, they know that each body is devoid of self-nature.
Skillfully using words and speech to expound all dharmas, they do not grasp at the marks of letters or sounds.
They travel to hundreds of thousands of lands, making offerings to the Buddhas with all manner of supreme gifts;
possessing sovereign wisdom and free from attachment, they do not give rise to the notion of "my Buddha-land."
Though they diligently teach and transform all sentient beings, they harbor no thoughts of self or other;
though they have already cultivated and perfected vast goodness, they do not give rise to attachment toward those wholesome dharmas.
Seeing that all worlds are constantly ablaze with the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
they become entirely detached from all conceptual notions and give rise to the power of great compassion and diligence.
All the devas and devīs, having offered various kinds of worship and praise,
remained silent together for a time, gazing up at the Honored One among Men, wishing to hear the Dharma.
Then Vimukticandra again requested, saying:
"The minds of this great assembly are pure; regarding the characteristics of all practices within the seventh stage, we pray that the Son of the Buddha will proclaim them for us!"
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has fulfilled the practices of the sixth stage and wishes to enter the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), they should cultivate ten kinds of paths arising from skillful means and wisdom."
What are these ten? They are as follows:

although they skillfully cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not abandon sentient beings through their compassion; although they have attained the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, they delight in constantly making offerings to the Buddhas.
Although they have entered the gateway of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, they diligently accumulate merit;
although they are far removed from the triple world, they adorn the triple world;

although they have ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions, they are able to give rise to the extinction of the flames of greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings.

Although they know that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, shadows, echoes, mirages, transformations, the moon reflected in water, and images in a mirror—being non-dual in their intrinsic nature—they nevertheless perform immeasurable varieties of karmic actions according to the mind;
although they know that all lands are like empty space, they nonetheless adorn Buddha-fields with pure and wondrous conduct;
and although they know that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is by nature bodiless, they nonetheless adorn their bodies with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
Although they know that the nature of the Buddhas' voices is empty, quiescent, and ineffable, they are nonetheless able to produce various distinct pure sounds according to all sentient beings;

although they follow the Buddhas in realizing that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment, they nevertheless cultivate various practices through various characteristics, various times, and various kalpas, in accordance with the mental inclinations and conceptual distinctions of sentient beings.
By means of these ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom, the bodhisattva initiates sublime practices and enters the seventh stage from the sixth stage;
having entered it, these practices are constantly present before him,
which is called "abiding in the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching."
“O Son of the Buddha!
Having dwelt in this seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the infinite realms of sentient beings,
enters the infinite activities of the Buddhas in teaching and transforming sentient beings, and enters the infinite networks of worlds.”
They enter the pure lands of all Buddhas; they enter immeasurable varieties of differentiated dharmas; they enter the immeasurable wisdom of the manifest enlightenment of all Buddhas;
they enter immeasurable numbers of kalpas; they enter the immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas that fully awakens to the three periods of time;
they enter the immeasurable differences in the faith and understanding of sentient beings; and they enter the immeasurable manifestations of all Buddhas.
They enter into the various bodies of name-and-form; they enter into the differences in the inclinations, pleasures, and faculties of immeasurable sentient beings;
they enter into the immeasurable languages and sounds of all Buddhas to bring joy to sentient beings; they enter into the various mental activities of immeasurable sentient beings;
they enter into the immeasurable vast wisdom of all Buddhas that brings complete understanding; and they enter into the faith of the immeasurable Śrāvaka vehicle.
Understanding, one enters the path of wisdom taught by immeasurable Buddhas to inspire faith and comprehension;
one enters that which is accomplished by immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas; one enters the gates of profound wisdom taught by immeasurable Buddhas to lead others toward them;
one enters the skillful practices of immeasurable Bodhisattvas; and one enters the Great Vehicle compendium taught by immeasurable Buddhas.
This enables the bodhisattva to enter therein.
This bodhisattva forms this thought:

"Such immeasurable realms of the Tathāgatas—even those that could not be known even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas—I must fully accomplish with a mind that is effortless and non-conceptual."
“O Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva, observing in this way with profound wisdom, constantly and diligently cultivates the wisdom of skillful means to give rise to the sublime path. Abiding therein immovably, there is not a single thought-moment of rest, abandonment, or neglect;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, even in sleep and dreams, they never for a moment associate with hindrances or obstructions, and they never cease such contemplation.”
In every thought-moment, this bodhisattva is always able to fulfill the ten pāramitās.
Why is this? Because in every thought-moment they take great compassion as the foremost principle, practicing the Buddha-dharma in order to advance toward Buddha-wisdom.
To bestow all roots of goodness upon sentient beings for the sake of seeking Buddha-wisdom is called the *dānapāramitā*;
to be able to extinguish the heat of all afflictions is called the [śīlapāramitā].
The perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
having compassion as its foremost principle and not harming sentient beings,
this is called the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Seeking the supreme wholesome dharmas without ever becoming weary or satisfied is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*;
that the path to omniscience is always present before one and never becomes distracted is called:
The dhyāna-pāramitā;
being able to endure that all phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished is called the prajñā-pāramitā.
To be able to give birth to immeasurable wisdom is called the perfection of skillful means;
to be able to seek the most supreme and excellent wisdom is called:
The perfection of aspiration;
being incapable of being thwarted or destroyed by any heterodox disputants or hosts of Māras—
this is called the perfection of power.
To know all phenomena as they truly are is called the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*),
O Son of the Buddha!
These ten perfections, the Bodhisattva attains in their entirety within every moment of thought;

likewise, the four means of integration, the four foundations, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation—and briefly stated, even all factors conducive to awakening—are fully perfected within every moment of thought.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Do Bodhisattvas fulfill all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) only in this seventh stage, or are they also able to fulfill them in all the stages?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
While bodhisattvas are able to fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment throughout all ten stages, the seventh stage is the most preeminent."
Why is this? Because in this seventh stage, the practice of effortful application is fulfilled, and one attains entry into the practice of mastery over wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), because the bodhisattva aspires to and seeks all Buddha-dharmas, they fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

In the second stage, because they are free from the stains of the mind; in the third stage, because their aspirations increase further and they attain the light of the Dharma; in the fourth stage, because they enter the Path; in the fifth stage, because they accord with worldly activities; in the sixth stage, because they enter the profound gateways of the Dharma; and in the seventh stage, because they give rise to all Buddha-dharmas—they likewise fulfill the factors of enlightenment in each case.
Why is this? Because from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva accomplishes the portion of wisdom involving effortful application.
By the power of this, from the eighth stage through the tenth stage, all effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) is fully accomplished.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like two worlds, one defiled and one purely pure; the space between these two is difficult to traverse, except for Bodhisattvas who possess great skillful means, supernormal powers, and the power of their vows.
O Son of the Buddha!

The stages of the bodhisattvas are likewise thus: there are practices of defilement and practices of purity; it is difficult to pass between these two, except for those bodhisattvas who possess the power of great vows, skillful means, and wisdom, who are then able to pass through them.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Is this seventh-stage bodhisattva one who acts with defilement?"
"Is this pure conduct?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied,
"O Son of the Buddha!"

From the first stage through the seventh stage, all practices undertaken are free from the karma of afflictions because they are dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi and because one partially attains the path of equality; nevertheless, this is not yet termed "transcending the practice of afflictions."
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a wheel-turning sage king who, riding upon the celestial elephant-treasure, travels through the four continents. Though he perceives those who are poor, destitute, and suffering, he is not defiled by their manifold afflictions; yet, he is not yet said to have transcended the human realm.

If, however, he relinquishes his royal body and is reborn in the Brahma world, riding upon a celestial palace, beholding a thousand worlds and traveling through a thousand worlds, manifesting the radiance and majestic virtue of a Brahma—he is then said to have transcended the human realm.

O Son of the Buddha! It is the same for the bodhisattva: from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, they travel through the world mounted upon the vehicle of the perfections (*pāramitā-yāna*). Although they know the faults and afflictions of all worlds, because they ride the path of rightness, they are not defiled by the faults of those afflictions; yet, this is not yet called "transcending the course of afflictions.

When they relinquish all effortful practices and enter the eighth stage from the seventh, riding the pure vehicle of the bodhisattva to travel through the world, they know the faults of affliction and are no longer defiled by them; only then is it called "transcending the course of afflictions," because they have attained the complete transcendence of all [afflictions].
O Son of the Buddha!

This seventh stage is where Bodhisattvas completely transcend the multitude of afflictions such as excessive greed; while dwelling in this stage, they are neither called "those with afflictions" nor "those without afflictions."
Why is this? Because all afflictions do not manifest, they are not called "existent";
because the mind seeking the wisdom of the Tathāgata is not yet fulfilled, they are not called "non-existent."
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, through a profoundly pure mind, they accomplish physical action, accomplish verbal action, and accomplish mental action.”
All unwholesome courses of action—which are censured by the Tathāgata—have been completely abandoned;
all wholesome actions—which are praised by the Tathāgata—are constantly and skillfully practiced.
All the scriptures and technical arts existing in the world, as described in the context of the fifth stage, proceed spontaneously for this bodhisattva without requiring effort.

Within the trichiliocosm, this bodhisattva serves as a great illuminating teacher; with the exception of the Tathāgatas and those bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward, there are none whose profound resolve and wondrous conduct equal theirs. All dhyānas, samādhis, samāpattis, supernormal powers, and liberations manifest before them.
However, this is achieved through cultivation and is not like the attainment through karmic retribution found in the eighth stage.

In this stage, the bodhisattva fully cultivates the power of skillful means and wisdom, as well as all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), within every thought-moment, becoming increasingly superior and perfect.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they enter the bodhisattva samādhi of skillful observation and discernment, the samādhi of skillfully discerning meaning, the samādhi of supreme wisdom, the samādhi of the treasury of analyzed meanings, the samādhi of analyzing meanings as they truly are, the samādhi of the firm root of skillful abiding, the samādhi of the gateway to the supernormal powers of wisdom, the samādhi of the activity of the dharma-realm, the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s victory, and the samādhi of the various treasuries of meanings regarding the gateways of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. By entering such a million samādhis that are endowed with the gateways to great wisdom and supernormal powers, they purify and cultivate this stage.”

Because this bodhisattva has attained this samādhi, through skillfully cultivating the wisdom of pure means and by the power of great compassion, they transcend the stages of the two vehicles and attain the stage of investigative wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, because they have perfected the immeasurable, pure, signless conduct of body-karma; perfected the immeasurable, pure, signless conduct of speech-karma; and perfected the immeasurable, pure, signless conduct of mind-karma, they attain the light of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Do not the immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva from the first ground onward indeed surpass those of the two vehicles?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
They have all transcended them; however, this is solely because they seek all the Buddha-dharmas through their vows, and not by the power of their own wisdom and contemplation."
Now, in the seventh stage, by virtue of their own power of wisdom, they cannot be surpassed by any of those of the two vehicles.

It is like a prince born into a royal house, begotten by the queen, who possesses the marks of royalty; from the moment of his birth, he surpasses all the ministers, yet this is due only to the king's power and not his own strength.
When he has grown up and perfected his arts and skills, he then transcends all others through his own power.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: at the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment, because of his resolve to seek the Great Dharma, he surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
now, dwelling in this stage, by the power of the wisdom practiced by himself, he transcends all those of the two vehicles.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, they attain the profound state of being far removed from activity yet constantly engaged in the activities of body, speech, and mind; they diligently seek the supreme path without ever abandoning it. Therefore, although the bodhisattva practices within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they do not realize it as a final cessation.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
From which stage does a bodhisattva come to be able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
From the sixth bhūmi onward, a bodhisattva is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation."
Now, dwelling in this stage, they are able to enter into it moment by moment and emerge from it moment by moment,

yet they do not realize [the ultimate] as a finality. For this reason, this bodhisattva is called one who has accomplished inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind, and who courses in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without realizing it.
For example, it is like a person who boards a ship and enters the ocean; by the power of skillful means, they do not encounter the perils of the water.

The Bodhisattvas on this stage are likewise: riding the ship of the *pāramitās*, they travel upon the ocean of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet by the power of their vows, they do not realize extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
“O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva, having attained such power of the wisdom of samādhi, through great skillful means, although manifests birth and death, yet constantly dwells in nirvāṇa;
although surrounded by a retinue, he always delights in solitude.”
Although they take birth within the three realms by the power of their vows, they are not defiled by worldly dharmas;
although they are eternally in a state of quiescent extinction, they manifest blazing flames through the power of skillful means, yet they are not burned;
although they accord with the wisdom of the Buddhas, they demonstrate entry into the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Although they have attained the treasury of the Buddha-realm, they manifest as dwelling within the realm of Māra;
although they have transcended the path of Māra, they manifest the practice of Māra’s arts;
although they manifest conduct identical to that of non-Buddhists, they do not abandon the Buddha-dharma.
Although he manifests conformity with all worldly ways, he constantly practices all supramundane dharmas;

and while his every adornment surpasses those possessed by all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, he never abandons his mind that delights in the Dharma.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom and dwells in the Ground of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*), by the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas. Namely:”
They see many hundreds of Buddhas, even up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

In the presence of those Buddhas, with a vast mind and a superior mind, they make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise; they present all necessities of life—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and also make offerings to the entire Saṃgha, dedicating these roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, they reverently listen to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, attaining the light of wisdom of the *yathābhūta-samādhi* and practicing in accordance with it.

They protect and maintain the True Dharma in the presence of all Buddhas, are constantly praised and rejoiced in by the Tathāgatas, and cannot be intimidated or defeated by any challenges posed by those of the two vehicles. They benefit sentient beings, and their patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) is pure.
Thus, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, all his roots of goodness become increasingly superior.
Just as pure gold, when interspersed and adorned with various exquisite jewels, becomes even more excellent, its radiance doubling and increasing beyond the reach of any other ornaments;

so too it is with the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva dwelling in this seventh stage—they become increasingly bright and pure through the power of skillful means and wisdom, surpassing what can be attained by those of the two vehicles.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as the light of the sun cannot be rivaled by the light of the stars or the moon, and can completely dry up all the mud and mire upon the land of Jambudvīpa;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva on this Stage of Far-Reaching Travel: no followers of the Two Vehicles can rival him, and he is able to completely dry up the mud and mire of all the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Among the ten pāramitās, this bodhisattva’s pāramitā of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) is predominant;
it is not that they do not practice the others, but rather they do so according to their power and capacity.
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
This is called a brief explanation of the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (The Far-Reaching).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a sovereign king of the gods (Śakradevendra), skillfully teaching sentient beings the Dharma of realized wisdom so that they may realize and enter it.

Generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—all such actions as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, and so on, until they are never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes.
He further forms this thought:
"I shall become the foremost and the most excellent among all sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) relies."

If this bodhisattva exerts diligent effort, in a single moment they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas as their retinue;

yet if they manifest through the sovereign power of the bodhisattva’s sublime vows, it exceeds these numbers, such that even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas one could not count or know them.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The path of samādhi of the wisdom of the ultimate truth, Through the practice of the sixth stage, the mind becomes fulfilled;
Immediately one accomplishes skillful means and wisdom, And by this, the bodhisattva enters the seventh stage."
Though clear in the three liberations, they give rise to compassion; though equal to the Tathāgatas, they diligently make offerings to the Buddhas;
though contemplating emptiness, they accumulate merit. By these means, the Bodhisattva ascends to the seventh stage.
Distant from the three realms yet adorned with splendor, extinguishing the fires of delusion while emitting flames;
knowing that phenomena are non-dual yet diligently performing deeds, realizing that lands are all empty yet delighting in adorning the soil;
understanding that the body is unmoving yet endowed with all marks, and penetrating that the nature of sound is detached yet skillfully expounding it.
Entering into a single thought-moment, the various phenomena are distinct; by this, the wise ascend to the seventh stage.
Observing these dharmas with clarity, they extensively bring benefit to the deluded masses.
Entering the realms of sentient beings without end, the Buddha’s work of transformation is likewise immeasurable.
Regarding the lands, all phenomena, and the number of eons, they understand the inclinations and mental activities [of beings] and can enter them all;
their exposition of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles is likewise limitless, and in this way they transform and guide all living beings.
The Bodhisattva diligently seeks the most supreme path; whether moving or resting, they do not abandon skillful means and wisdom.
Each and every action is dedicated toward the Buddha’s bodhi, and in every thought-moment, they accomplish the pāramitās.
Arousing the mind and dedicating merit is generosity; Extinguishing delusions constitutes precepts, non-harming, and patience;
Seeking the good without weariness is diligence; Remaining unmoved on the Path is meditative concentration;
Enduring the non-arising of phenomena is named wisdom; Dedicating through skillful means is the aspiration for vows.
With the power that cannot be crushed and the wisdom of thorough understanding, all these things are brought to fulfillment.
On the first bhūmi, the objects of focus and merit are perfected; on the second, one is free from defilement and the three disputes are stilled;
on the fourth, one enters the path; on the fifth, one acts in accordance with it; and on the sixth, the light of the wisdom of non-arising shines forth.
In the seventh stage, the merit of awakening is fulfilled and all various great vows are fully realized;
by means of this, everything performed within the eighth stage is rendered entirely pure.
This stage is difficult to traverse; only through wisdom can one transcend it.
It is like the space between two worlds, or like a noble cakravartin king who remains free from attachment; yet, this is not yet called "complete transcendence."
If one dwells within the eighth stage of wisdom, Only then does one transcend the realm of the mind;
Like Brahmā surveying the world from beyond the human station, Like a lotus in water, remaining unstained by attachment.
Although this stage transcends the multitude of afflictions, it is neither called "having afflictions" nor "being without afflictions";
for while one acts therein without afflictions, the mind seeking Buddha-wisdom is not yet satisfied.
All the various arts and crafts in the world, The scriptures, rhetoric, and treatises—[he] understands them all thoroughly;
Dhyāna-concentrations, samādhis, and supernormal powers— Through such practice, he has fully accomplished them all.
The Bodhisattva cultivates and perfects the path of the seventh stage, Transcending all practices of the two vehicles;
This arises from wisdom rooted in the vows of the first stage, Just like a prince who is fully endowed with power.
Having accomplished the profound, they continue to advance on the path; though their minds are tranquil and extinguished, they do not realize [nirvana] prematurely.
They are like those who board a ship to enter the ocean: though they are in the water, they are not drowned by it.
Endowed with the merit of skillful means, wisdom, and practice, they cannot be fully understood by anyone in all the worlds;
having made offerings to many Buddhas, their minds become increasingly luminous, like gold adorned with exquisite jewels.

The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas on this stage is most luminous; Like the sun spreading its light to dry the waters of craving, They further act as sovereign lords among the devas, Transforming and guiding all living beings to cultivate right wisdom.

If, through the power of courageous diligence, one attains many samādhis and beholds many Buddhas numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, the mastery of one’s vows will exceed even this.
This is the Bodhisattva’s stage of Far-Going, The pure path of skillful means and wisdom;
Neither gods nor humans of all the worlds, Nor śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, can know it.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Seven;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, by Imperial Command.
Chapter Twenty-Six, Part Five: The Fifty Stages, Section Eight: The Eighth Stage.
At that time, the celestial kings and their hosts, Hearing of these supreme practices, were all filled with joy.
Desiring to make offerings to the Tathāgata, As well as to the boundless great Bodhisattvas, they gathered.
They rained down exquisite flowers, banners, pennants, and canopies, Fragrant garlands, necklaces,
and precious robes— Infinite, boundless, and of thousands of millions of kinds, All exquisitely adorned with mani-jewels.

The celestial maidens simultaneously played heavenly music, universally producing all manner of wondrous sounds to make offerings to the Buddha and his sons, while together uttering these words of praise:
"O All-Seeing One, Honored Among Two-Legged Beings, out of compassion for sentient beings, you manifest your supernatural powers."
May these various celestial music, emitting sublime sounds everywhere, be heard by all.
Within a single hair-tip, there are hundreds of thousands of billions of lands, as numerous as the atoms of a *nayuta*;
within these, immeasurable Tathāgatas dwell and proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
Within a single pore are immeasurable lands, Each with its four continents and great oceans;
Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains are likewise there, All seen within it without any crowding.
Upon the tip of a single hair there are the six realms of existence:
the three evil paths, as well as humans, devas, the hosts of nāgas and spirits, and asuras, each receiving their retribution according to their own karma.
In all those buddha-fields, the Tathāgatas everywhere proclaim wondrous sounds;
in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings, they turn the most supreme and pure wheel of Dharma.
Within the lands are the various bodies of sentient beings, and within those bodies are again various lands;
the realms of humans, devas, and all other destinies are each distinct, yet the Buddha, having known them all, preaches the Dharma for them.
Great lands may, at will, transform into small ones; small lands, likewise, may transform into large ones.
Such supernormal powers are immeasurable; the world’s common speech cannot exhaustively describe them.
Having universally emitted these wondrous sounds and praised the merits of the Tathāgata,
the assembly remained silent in joy, gazing with single-minded devotion, desiring to hear his teaching.
Then Vimukticandra again requested, saying:
"This assembly is now entirely tranquil; we pray that you will explain, in due order, the various characteristics of the practices within the eighth stage."
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
In the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully cultivates the wisdom of skillful means, thoroughly purifies all paths, and skillfully accumulates the factors conducive to enlightenment."

Empowered by the force of great vows, sustained by the power of the Tathāgata, and supported by one’s own roots of goodness, they constantly contemplate the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-qualities of the Tathāgata.
With well-purified and profound mental reflection, they are able to accomplish merit and wisdom;
possessing great loving-kindness and great compassion, they do not abandon sentient beings and enter into the [unconditioned].
The wisdom of measure enters into all phenomena, which from the beginning are without birth,
without arising, without marks, without formation, without destruction, without exhaustion, without transformation, and have non-nature as their nature;
they are entirely equal throughout the prior, middle, and subsequent limits, and are the sphere entered by non-conceptual suchness-wisdom, free from—
All conceptualizations of mind, intellect, and consciousness are without grasping or attachment, being like empty space;
entering into all phenomena as having the nature of empty space— this is called attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva accomplishes this patience, they immediately enter the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*). As a bodhisattva of profound practice, they become difficult to discern and indistinguishable [from others], free from all signs (*nimitta*), all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*), and all attachments. They are immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they are free from all clamor and strife, and quiescence (*śānti*) manifests before them.”

For example, it is like a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with supernormal powers and has attained mastery over the mind; proceeding through the stages until he enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), all movement of the mind, recollections, and conceptual discriminations completely cease.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), they immediately relinquish all effortful practices and attain the practice of non-effort; the mental activities of their body, speech, and mind all cease, and they abide in the practice of fruition.
It is, for example, like a person who, in a dream, sees his body falling into a great river; desiring to cross it, he exerts great courage and employs skillful means.
Because of that great courage and the application of skillful means, he immediately awakens; once awakened, all that he was doing ceases.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: seeing sentient beings within the four currents, for the sake of their rescue and deliverance, he gives rise to great courage and exerts great diligence;
by means of this courage and diligence, he reaches the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*);
having reached it, all functional efforts cease entirely, and both dualistic practice and the practice of signs no longer manifest before him.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as when one is born into the Brahma world, the afflictions of the desire realm no longer manifest;
so it is likewise for one who dwells in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), wherein all activities of mind, mentation, and consciousness no longer manifest.
For this bodhisattva mahāsattva, even the mind of a bodhisattva, the mind of a buddha, the mind of enlightenment, and the mind of nirvāṇa do not yet manifest, let alone give rise to a worldly mind!
“O Son of the Buddha!

By the power of the original vows of this stage’s bodhisattva, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, personally appear before them and bestow Tathāgata-knowledge, causing them to enter the gateway of the stream of Dharma, and speak these words:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
"Noble son! This patience is foremost; it accords with all the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, noble son!"

"We possess all the dharmas of a Buddha—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—which you have not yet attained. You should now apply yourself with diligent effort to achieve these dharmas; do not again abandon this gate of patience."
Furthermore, son of good family!

Although you have attained this liberation of quiescence, ordinary beings have not yet realized it; all manner of afflictions manifest before them, and various discursive thoughts constantly assail them. You should take pity upon such sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should recall your original vow to universally and greatly benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the gate of inconceivable wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family!

This dharma-nature of all phenomena remains eternally constant and unchanging, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear. It is not because of attaining this dharma that the Buddhas are called Tathāgatas; even all followers of the two vehicles are able to attain this non-conceptual dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Observe that our physical forms are immeasurable, our wisdom is immeasurable, our buddha-lands are immeasurable, our skillful means are immeasurable, our radiance is immeasurable, and our pure voices are likewise immeasurable;
you should now bring these matters to fulfillment.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You have now just attained this one illumination of the Dharma, namely:
that all phenomena are unborn and without discrimination.

"Good son! The illumination of the Dharma of the Tathāgata has immeasurable entries, immeasurable functions, and immeasurable transformations; even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, it cannot be fully known.
You should practice and bring this Dharma to fulfillment."
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should observe the infinite lands, infinite sentient beings, and infinite dharmas of the ten directions, with all their various distinctions, and you should thoroughly comprehend these matters exactly as they are.
“O Son of the Buddha!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, grant this Bodhisattva such immeasurable gateways for the arising of wisdom, enabling him to give rise to immeasurable and boundless activities of differentiated wisdom.”
O Son of the Buddha!
If the Buddhas did not grant this Bodhisattva the gateway to the arising of wisdom, he would at that time enter ultimate *nirvāṇa* and abandon all activities for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because the Buddhas have bestowed such immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of wisdom, the karmic activity of wisdom produced in a single thought-moment surpasses all the practices cultivated from the first aspiration up to the seventh stage;

even a hundredth part does not equal it, nor do a hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta parts. Likewise, even an asaṃkhyeya part, a kalā part, a numerical part, a metaphorical part, or an upaniṣad part does not equal it.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva previously practiced with a single body; now, dwelling in this stage, he attains immeasurable bodies, immeasurable voices, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable births, and immeasurable pure lands. He teaches and transforms immeasurable sentient beings, makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, enters immeasurable Dharma-gates, and possesses immeasurable supernormal powers. There are immeasurable distinctions among his assemblies and sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Dwelling in immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions, he accumulates all the practices of a Bodhisattva by virtue of the dharma of immovability.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like one who boards a ship intending to enter the great ocean: before reaching the sea, much effort and labor are required;

but once the sea has been reached, one simply follows the wind, needing no human exertion to reach the great ocean. The distance traveled in a single day after reaching it cannot be matched by the time spent before reaching it, even if one were to continue for a hundred years during that prior period.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: having accumulated the vast provisions of roots of goodness, they board the ship of the Mahāyāna and reach the ocean of bodhisattva practices. In a single thought-moment, through non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), they enter the realm of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). This is something that their original conceptual practices (*sābhoga-caryā*), even over the course of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of eons, could not attain.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this eighth stage, by means of the effortless wisdom of awakening arising from the skillful knowledge of great expedient means, they contemplate the sphere of activity of the knowledge of all-knowledge.”
That is to say:
observing the formation of the world and observing the destruction of the world;
it is formed because of the accumulation of this karma, and it is destroyed because of the exhaustion of this karma.
How long does it take for formation?
How long does it take for destruction? And how long does it take for the period of formation and abiding?
He knows, exactly as they are, for how long they abide and when they disintegrate.

Furthermore, he knows the minor characteristics, major characteristics, immeasurable characteristics, and differentiated characteristics of the earth element; he knows the minor, major, immeasurable, and differentiated characteristics of the water, fire, and wind elements; and he knows the subtle characteristics, differentiated characteristics, and immeasurably differentiated characteristics of atoms.
In whatever world-system there may be, he knows as they truly are all the aggregates of atoms and the distinct characteristics of those atoms;

in whatever world-system there may be, he knows as they truly are how many atoms constitute each of the elements of earth, water, fire, and air, how many atoms constitute all precious objects, how many atoms constitute the bodies of sentient beings, and how many atoms constitute the bodies of lands.

They know that the large bodies and small bodies of sentient beings are each composed of a certain number of atoms; they know that the bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, devas, and humans are each composed of a certain number of atoms, thereby attaining such wisdom that discerns the distinctions among atoms.

Furthermore, he knows the formation of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; he knows the destruction of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; and he knows the small characteristics, the great characteristics, the immeasurable characteristics, and the differentiated characteristics of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Thus, he attains the wisdom that contemplates the distinctions among the three realms.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva further gives rise to the illumination of wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings.
That is to say:”
They skillfully know the differences among the bodies of sentient beings, skillfully discern the bodies of sentient beings, and skillfully observe the places of their birth;
according to what is appropriate for each, they manifest their own bodies to teach, transform, and bring them to maturity.
In a single trichiliocosm, this bodhisattva universally manifests birth through the light of wisdom, according to the differences in the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings;

likewise, in two, three, or even hundreds of thousands, up to unspeakably many trichiliocosms, they universally manifest birth therein, according to the differences in the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings.

Because this bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, while his body remains unmoved within a single buddha-field, he manifests his form in the assemblies of as many buddha-fields as are unspeakably numerous.
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva manifests his body within the assemblies of those buddha-fields according to the various differences in the faith and understanding of the bodies and minds of sentient beings.
That is to say:

among the assembly of śramaṇas, he manifests the form of a śramaṇa; among the assembly of brāhmaṇas, he manifests the form of a brāhmaṇa; among the assembly of kṣatriyas, he manifests the form of a kṣatriya.

Likewise, among the assemblies of vaiśyas, śūdras, householders, the four heavenly kings, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the māras, the brahmās, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha devas, he manifests his form according to each of their respective classes.
Furthermore, for those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a śrāvaka, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka;
for those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha;
and for those who are to be delivered by means of the body of a bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a bodhisattva.
To those who are to be liberated by the body of a Tathāgata, he manifests the form of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
In this manner, throughout all unspeakably many Buddha-lands, the Bodhisattva manifests his body in whatever way corresponds to the differences in the faith and inclinations of sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva remains far removed from all conceptualizations and discriminations regarding the body, abiding in equanimity.

This bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, the body of the land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of śrāvakas, the body of pratyekabuddhas, the body of bodhisattvas, the body of Tathāgatas, the body of wisdom, the body of Dharma, and the body of space.”

This bodhisattva knows the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings; he is able to take the bodies of sentient beings as his own body, and likewise manifests the bodies of lands, the bodies of karmic retribution, and even the bodies of empty space.

Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, they are able to manifest the body of a buddha-field as their own body, and likewise manifest the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of karmic retribution, and even the body of empty space.

Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, they are able to manifest their own body as a body of karmic retribution, and likewise manifest it as the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, and even as the body of empty space.
Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, he is able to manifest his own body as the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, and even the bodies of empty space.
According to the different inclinations of sentient beings, he manifests such forms within these bodies.
This bodhisattva knows the body of accumulated karma, the retribution body, the affliction body, the form body,
and the formless body of sentient beings; furthermore, they know the bodies of lands with small characteristics,
large characteristics, immeasurable characteristics, defiled characteristics, pure characteristics, expansive characteristics, inverted orientation, upright orientation, and universal penetration.
Regarding the characteristics of the distinctions within the square net: one knows the conventional designations for the differences among bodies of karmic retribution;
one knows the conventional designations for the differences among the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;

and one knows that the body of a Tathāgata consists of the body of awakening, the body of vows, the transformation body, the body of sustaining power, the body adorned with the marks and signs, and the body of majestic authority.
The mind-made body, the merit-body, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body; the characteristics of the wisdom-body as skillful reflection, the characteristics of its determination according to reality,
the characteristics of being subsumed within the practice of the fruit, the characteristics of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane,
the characteristics of the distinctions among the three vehicles, the common characteristics, the uncommon characteristics, and the characteristics of transcendence.
He knows the signless nature that is neither the sign of renunciation, nor the sign of training, nor the sign of no-more-training;

he knows the equal nature of the Dharma-body, its indestructible nature, its nature of conventional differentiation according to time and worldly custom, the differentiation between the dharmas of sentient beings and non-sentient beings, and the differentiation between the dharmas of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha; and he knows the immeasurable nature of the space-body.
...the mark of pervasiveness, the mark of formlessness, the mark of non-differentiation, the mark of boundlessness, and the mark of manifesting the physical body.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva has accomplished such bodily wisdom, they attain mastery over life, mastery over the mind, mastery over wealth, mastery over karma, mastery over birth, mastery over vows, mastery over liberation, mastery over the miraculous, mastery over wisdom, and mastery over the Dharma.
Because they have attained these ten masteries, they are possessors of inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, vast wisdom, and indestructible wisdom.
"Once this bodhisattva has entered in this way and accomplished in this way, they attain ultimately faultless bodily action, faultless verbal action, and faultless mental action."

Their physical, verbal, and mental actions proceed in accordance with wisdom; they are preeminent in the perfection of prajñā, led by great compassion, and endowed with skillful means. They are adept at discernment, skilled in generating great vows, protected by the power of the Buddhas, and constantly and diligently cultivate the wisdom that benefits sentient beings, dwelling universally throughout infinite and diverse worlds.
O Son of the Buddha!
To state it in brief:
when a bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage, all actions performed through body, speech, and mind are capable of accumulating all the Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they attain the power of well-established profound resolve, because all afflictions do not arise;
they attain the power of well-established superior resolve, because they do not depart from the Path.
They attain firm abiding in the power of great compassion, because they do not abandon the benefit of sentient beings;
they attain firm abiding in the power of great loving-kindness, because they rescue and protect all the world;
they attain firm abiding in the power of dhāraṇī, because they do not forget the Dharma.
They attain the power of eloquence through which they skillfully observe and discern all phenomena;
they attain the power of supernormal knowledges through which they travel universally to boundless worlds;
and they attain the power of great vows through which they never abandon the deeds performed by all bodhisattvas.
They attain the power of the perfection of skillful abiding, because they accomplish all Buddha-dharmas;
they attain the power of the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness, because all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge manifest before them.
Having attained such power of wisdom, this bodhisattva is able to manifest all manner of activities, and among all these deeds, there is no fault or transgression.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This stage of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is named the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), because it cannot be obstructed or destroyed;
it is named:
It is called the "Non-retrogressive Stage" because wisdom never regresses;
it is called the "Difficult-to-attain Stage" because no one in any world can fathom it.
It is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*), because it is free from all faults;
it is called:
It is called the Ground of Birth (*janma-bhūmi*), because one has mastery over all that is desired;
it is called the Ground of Accomplishment (*niṣpanna-bhūmi*), because there is nothing further to be done.
It is called the Ground of Ultimate Perfection, because wisdom is definitive;
it is called:
It is called the Stage of Transformation, because it accomplishes all according to one's vows;
it is called the Stage of Sustained Power, because others cannot move it.
It is named the Stage of Effortless Mastery, because it has already been accomplished beforehand.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such wisdom, they enter the realm of the Buddha, are illuminated by the Buddha’s merits, and accord with the Buddha’s majestic deportment. As the Buddha-realm manifests before them, they are constantly protected and remembered by the Tathāgata; Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vajrapāṇi spirits always follow and guard them. They never abandon the various great samādhis and are able to manifest infinite varieties of bodies, each possessing great power. Having attained mastery over supernatural powers and samādhis as a result of their retribution, they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment wherever there are sentient beings capable of being transformed.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva thus enters the assembly of the Great Vehicle, attains great supernormal powers, radiates great light, and enters the unobstructed Dharma-realm; when they know the distinctions of worlds, manifest all manner of great merits, and act with sovereign mastery according to their will; when they are well able to penetrate the past and the future, universally subduing all demonic and heterodox paths, and deeply entering the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice; and when they cultivate the Bodhisattva path in immeasurable lands by attaining the dharma of non-retrogression—for these reasons, they are said to dwell in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
“O Son of the Buddha!

Once a bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), by the power of samādhi, they constantly perceive immeasurable Buddhas face-to-face, never ceasing to serve and make offerings to them.”

In each and every eon and in each and every world, this bodhisattva sees immeasurable hundreds of buddhas, immeasurable thousands of buddhas, and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddhas; he reveres, honors, serves, and makes offerings to them, presenting all necessities of life as gifts.
Having attained the profound Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas from all Buddhas, they receive immeasurable clarifications of the Dharma, such as the distinctions between worlds;
if anyone should pose difficult questions regarding such matters as the distinctions between worlds, there is no one who can defeat them.

In this manner, throughout immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of kalpas, and even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.

For example, just as a crown fashioned from refined gold, when placed upon the head of a noble Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) who rules Jambudvīpa, has no equal among all the ornaments of his ministers and subjects;

so too are the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva on this stage. No roots of goodness belonging to any of the followers of the Two Vehicles, nor even those of Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage, can equal them. This is because, by abiding in this stage, they possess the light of great wisdom that universally extinguishes the darkness of afflictions in sentient beings and is well able to open wide the gates of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as Mahābrahmā, the lord of a thousand worlds, can universally exercise a mind of compassion and universally radiate light that fills a thousand worlds;

so too is it with the Bodhisattvas on this stage, who can emit light that illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms within a million buddha-fields, causing all sentient beings to extinguish the fires of affliction and attain refreshing coolness.
Among the ten pāramitās, this bodhisattva’s pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) is predominant;
it is not that they do not practice the remaining pāramitās, but they do so according to their strength and capacity.
This is called a brief explanation of the eighth stage, the Immovable Bhūmi, of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in the course of immeasurable kalpas.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently become Great Brahmā Kings, presiding over a thousand worlds with supreme sovereignty. They skillfully expound all meanings and are able to bestow upon Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas the path of the pāramitās.
Should anyone pose difficult questions regarding the distinctions between worlds, none can cause them to falter or be overcome.”

Generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and cooperation—all such actions as these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, and so on, up to being never apart from mindfulness of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I shall become the foremost among all sentient beings, the most excellent, and even the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) relies."

If this bodhisattva, by exerting the power of great diligence, in a single thought-moment attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, and even manifests as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems to serve as his retinue;

yet if he were to manifest through the sovereign power of the bodhisattva’s sublime vows, it would exceed such numbers, such that even in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas one could not calculate or know them.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Having cultivated the wisdom of skillful means in the seventh stage, And having well accumulated the power of great vows that aid the path,
Furthermore, being sustained by the Honored One among Men, One ascends to the eighth dwelling in pursuit of supreme knowledge."
Accomplished in merit, ever compassionate, With wisdom vast as space, One who hears the Dharma can give rise to the power of certainty; This is the patient acceptance of quiescence and non-arising.
Knowing that phenomena have no birth and no arising, No formation, no destruction, and no revolving;
Detached from existence, equal, and beyond discrimination, They transcend all mental activities and abide like space.
Having accomplished patience that transcends conceptual proliferation, Profoundly immovable and eternally quiescent, It cannot be known by any in the world;
All mental characteristics and attachments are utterly abandoned.

Abiding in this stage, one does not engage in conceptual discrimination; it is like a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), or like dreaming of crossing a river which vanishes upon waking, or like being born in the Brahma-heaven, having severed all lower desires.
Inspired by the power of their original vows, they exhorted him, praising his supreme patience and conferring upon him empowerment, saying:
"We possess all the teachings of the Buddhas; you have not yet attained them, so you must now exert yourself with diligence."
Although you have already extinguished the fire of afflictions, the flames of delusion in the world still burn fiercely;
you should now mind your original vow to deliver sentient beings, causing them all to cultivate the causes that lead to liberation.
The nature of phenomena is truly eternal and transcends mental conception; even those of the two vehicles can attain this.
It is not on account of this that one is called the World-Honored One, but solely because of profound and unimpeded wisdom.
Such a person is worthy of offerings from devas and humans;
by being granted this wisdom for contemplation, they shall fully accomplish all boundless Buddha-dharmas, surpassing all former practices in a single thought-moment.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage of wondrous wisdom, They then attain vast and great supernormal powers;
In a single thought, their bodies manifest throughout the ten directions, Like a ship entering the sea, carried across by the wind.
With a mind free from effort, relying on the power of wisdom, they fully know the formation, destruction, and abiding of all lands;
they can comprehend the various and distinct differences among all realms, whether small, large, or immeasurable.
The four great elements of the three thousandfold world system, the distinct bodies of sentient beings in the six realms of existence,
and even the number of atoms within all manner of jewels— these he observes with wisdom without exception.
The Bodhisattva is able to know all bodies, assuming forms identical to theirs to transform sentient beings;
though lands are infinite and of various distinctions, he manifests his form in them all without exception.
Just as the sun and moon dwell in the void, And their reflections appear in all waters;
So too, while dwelling unmoved within the dharma-realm, They manifest reflections according to the mind.
According to the diverse inclinations of their minds, he manifests his body within all assemblies;
whether as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas, or even as the body of a Buddha, there is none in which he does not appear.
The bodies of sentient beings, lands, and karmic retribution, And the various wisdom-dharmakāyas of the sages—
The characteristics of these bodies of space are all equal, Universally manifested for the sake of sentient beings.
Universally observing with the ten kinds of noble wisdom, they further perform various deeds in accordance with compassion;
all the Buddha-dharmas are thus accomplished, and their upholding of the precepts is as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
Having accomplished the ten powers, he is unshakable; None among the hosts of Māras can turn him back.
Protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and honored by the heavenly kings, The Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi constantly attends and guards him.
The merits of this stage are boundless; even in hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*, they could not be fully described.
Furthermore, through the excellence of making offerings to the Buddhas, they become even more radiant, like the ornaments upon a king’s crown.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this eighth stage, they frequently become Brahma-kings, lords of a thousand worlds;
they expound the Three Vehicles without end, and their compassionate light shines universally to eliminate all delusions.
In a single thought-moment, one attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in a million worlds;
all such deeds performed are likewise so, yet through the power of vows, their manifestations exceed even this.
I have already briefly explained for you the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva, the Immovable;
if one were to analyze it in detail and in successive order, even after ten million eons, one could not exhaust it.
While this eighth stage of the Bodhisattva was being expounded, the Tathāgata manifested great supernormal powers,
shaking all the lands throughout the ten directions in inconceivable numbers of billions.
The Unsurpassed Honored One, possessing all-knowing vision, Emanates great radiance from his body,
Illuminating those immeasurable lands, Causing all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas simultaneously leaped up and remained in the air,
offering supreme celestial delicacies as offerings to the Most Victorious One among speakers.
Maheśvara and Īśvara, all with one mind, rejoiced immeasurably;
each, with various kinds of manifold offerings, made worship to the ocean of profound merit.
Furthermore, there were ten trillion celestial maidens, their bodies and minds filled with pervasive joy;
each played countless varieties of musical instruments as an offering to the Great Teacher among men.

At that time, various musical instruments were played simultaneously—hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of different kinds—all through the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata, producing wondrous sounds in praise:
"Tranquil, gentle, stainless, and free from harm, You have skillfully cultivated each stage you entered; [The Buddhas] praise you with such voices."
With a mind like space, they travel to the ten directions, Extensively expounding the Buddha-way to awaken all living beings.
In every place, whether in heavens or among humans, They manifest peerless and wondrous adornments;
Born from the merit of the Tathāgata, They cause all who see them to delight in the Buddha’s wisdom.
Without leaving a single land, they reach all realms, Like the moon appearing everywhere to illuminate the world;
Vocal sounds and mental thoughts are entirely extinguished, Just as an echo responds to everything without exception.
If there are sentient beings whose minds are inferior, for them he expounds the practice of the Śrāvakas;
if their minds are clear and sharp and they delight in the Pratyekabuddha path, then for them he teaches the way of the Middle Vehicle.
If there is one who possesses compassion and delights in benefiting others, for them they explain the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas;
if there is one with the mind of supreme wisdom, then they reveal the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Just as a magician performs various feats, Whose diverse forms and appearances are all unreal, So too is the magical illusion of a Bodhisattva’s wisdom:
Though it manifests all things, it is free from existence and non-existence.
Thus, with millions of such beautiful sounds, they sang praises to the Buddha and then remained silent.
Vimukticandra said:
"The assembly is now pure; I pray that you will speak of the practices of the ninth stage!"
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed Vimukticandra Bodhisattva, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has thus contemplated and investigated with immeasurable wisdom, desiring to further seek a more supreme, tranquil liberation, and again practicing the wisdom of the Tathāgata, entering the secret Dharma of the Tathāgata, observing the nature of inconceivable great wisdom, purifying all *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* gates, possessing vast supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), entering differentiated worlds, cultivating the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), following the Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma, and not abandoning the power of the original vow of great compassion, he attains entry into the ninth Bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).”
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this Stage of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), they know, as they truly are, the courses of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena; the courses of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena; the courses of mundane and supramundane phenomena; the courses of conceivable and inconceivable phenomena; the courses of determinate and indeterminate phenomena; the courses of the phenomena of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the courses of the phenomena of Bodhisattva practices; the courses of the phenomena of the Tathāgata stages; and the courses of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.”

By means of such wisdom, this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the dense forest of the minds of sentient beings, the dense forest of afflictions, the dense forest of karma, the dense forest of faculties, the dense forest of understandings, the dense forest of natures, the dense forest of inclinations, the dense forest of latent tendencies, the dense forest of births, the dense forest of the continuity of habitual tendencies, and the dense forest of the distinctions among the three groups.
This Bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the various characteristics of the minds of sentient beings, namely:

the characteristic of arising in a mixture, the characteristic of rapid transformation, the characteristic of decay and non-decay, the characteristic of formlessness, the characteristic of being without boundaries, the characteristic of purity, the characteristic of being stained or stainless, the characteristic of bondage and non-bondage, the characteristic of being produced by illusion, and the characteristic of following birth in the various realms of existence;
he knows all such [characteristics], numbering in the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and even infinitely, exactly as they are.
Furthermore, he knows the various characteristics of all afflictions (*kleśa*), namely: the characteristic of persisting for a long duration; the characteristic of initiating boundless [rebirth];

the characteristic of arising simultaneously and not being abandoned; the characteristic of the single meaning of dormancy and manifestation; the characteristic of being associated with or dissociated from the mind; the characteristic of abiding according to the birth one receives in the various realms of existence; the characteristic of the distinctions within the three realms; the characteristic of the faults of craving, views, delusion, and pride penetrating deeply like arrows;

and the characteristic of the causal conditions of the three types of action (*karma*) being uninterrupted. Briefly stated, up to eighty-four thousand [afflictions], he knows them all as they truly are.

Furthermore, he knows the various characteristics of all karmas, namely: the characteristics of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the characteristics of informative and non-informative; the characteristics of arising simultaneously with the mind and being inseparable from it; the characteristics of accumulating fruits in succession despite the momentary destruction of their causal nature; the characteristics of having retribution or being without retribution; the characteristics of receiving various retributions such as black-for-black; the characteristics of being immeasurable like a field; the characteristics of the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages; the characteristics of being experienced in the present life, in the next life, or in subsequent lives;
and the characteristics of belonging to the vehicles or not, and being fixed or unfixed. Briefly stated, even up to eighty-four thousand types, he knows them all as they truly are.

Furthermore, he knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of the faculties being dull, medium, or superior; the characteristics of distinction and non-distinction between the past limit and the future limit; the characteristics of superior, middling, and inferior; the characteristics of afflictions arising simultaneously and being inseparable from them; the characteristics of those belonging to a vehicle or not a vehicle, and those who are fixed or unfixed; the characteristics of being matured and pliant; the characteristics of following the net of the faculties, being light, shifting, and subject to decay; the characteristics of being dominant and incapable of being destroyed; the characteristics of falling back or not falling back;
and the characteristics of distant, following, co-arising, or dissimilar. Briefly stated, up to eighty-four thousand such types, he knows them all as they truly are.
Furthermore, he knows the various degrees of understanding—soft, medium, and superior—the various dispositions—soft, medium, and superior—and the various inclinations—soft, medium, and superior;
all of these are briefly explained as numbering up to eighty-four thousand.

Furthermore, one knows the various characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely: the characteristic of arising together with the profound mind; the characteristic of arising together with the mind; the characteristic of the distinction between being associated with or dissociated from the mind; the characteristic of persisting for a long duration; the characteristic of being unextracted since beginningless time; the characteristic of being contrary to all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the characteristic of the bondage of continuous rebirth within the three realms; the characteristic of causing the succession of infinite mental states to manifest; the characteristic of opening the gates to the sense bases; the characteristic of being solid and difficult to treat; the characteristic of being established or not established in specific stages and locations; and the characteristic of being extracted solely by the Noble Path.

Furthermore, one knows the various characteristics of taking birth, namely: the characteristic of taking birth according to karma; the characteristic of the distinctions among the six destinies; the characteristic of the distinctions between the form and formless realms; the characteristic of the distinctions between those with perception and those without perception; the characteristic of the sprout of future existence arising from karma as the field, craving-water as the moisture, and ignorance-darkness as the covering, with consciousness as the seed; the characteristic of name-and-form arising together and being inseparable; the characteristic of the continuity of existence through delusion, craving, and longing; the characteristic of beginningless attachment to the desire for sensation and the desire for birth; and the characteristic of falsely claiming to transcend the three realms while still greedily seeking them.

Furthermore, one knows the various characteristics of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), namely: the characteristic of the distinction between practice and non-practice; the characteristic of perfuming according to the realms of existence (*gati*); the characteristic of perfuming according to the conduct of sentient beings; the characteristic of perfuming according to karma and afflictions (*kleśa*); the characteristic of perfuming as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; the characteristic of perfuming according to entry into future existence; the characteristic of sequential perfuming; the characteristic of perfuming that does not abandon even while traveling far without severing the afflictions; the characteristic of perfuming as real or unreal; and the characteristic of perfuming through seeing, hearing, and associating with śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.

Furthermore, one knows the characteristics of sentient beings who are fixed in the right, fixed in the wrong, or not yet fixed, namely: the characteristic of being fixed in the right through right view; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong through wrong view; the characteristic of being unfixed in both; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong due to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); the characteristic of being fixed in the right due to the five faculties (*indriya*); the characteristic of being unfixed in both; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong due to the eightfold wrong path; the characteristic of being fixed in the right due to the state of right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*); the characteristic of being unfixed in both by virtue of neither acting nor refraining; the characteristic of being fixed in the wrong due to deep attachment to false dharmas; the characteristic of being fixed in the right due to practicing the noble path (*āryamārga*); and the characteristic of being unfixed in both due to abandoning both.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva accords with such wisdom, it is called "abiding in the Stage of Good Intelligence."
Having dwelt in this stage, they thoroughly understand the distinctions among the various conducts of sentient beings, and through teaching and taming them, cause them to attain liberation.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva is well able to expound the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the Dharma of the Bodhisattva vehicle, and the Dharma of the Tathāgata stage."

Because wisdom follows along with all spheres of activity, he is able to accord with the differences in the faculties, dispositions, inclinations, and practices of sentient beings, as well as the distinctions among their various groups; furthermore, he preaches the Dharma according to their births, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, and the habitual energies of their karma, causing them to give rise to faith and understanding, increasing their wisdom, and enabling each to attain liberation within their respective vehicle.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), they act as a great Dharma-preacher, possessing the conduct of a Dharma-preacher, and are well able to protect the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma. By means of immeasurable skillful wisdom, they give rise to the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) and expound the Dharma using the language of bodhisattvas.”
This bodhisattva constantly follows and turns with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, never abandoning them for even a moment.

What are these four? They are: the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
This bodhisattva, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), knows the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), knows the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), speaks without error or confusion.
The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid) consists of uninterrupted and inexhaustible speech.
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), one knows the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), one knows the arising and ceasing of all phenomena.
The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence is the uninterrupted teaching that establishes all phenomena;
the unimpeded knowledge of inspired speech is the indestructible and boundless discourse that follows whatever has been established.
