All Buddhas together embrace and protect them; they have already entered the ranks of future Buddhas; they are born from virtuous friends, and none of their aspirations fail to bear fruit.

Possessing great majestic power, they abide in the superior resolve and are able to skillfully explain all that they have heard; they also reveal the roots of goodness derived from hearing the Dharma.
Abiding in the wheel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), their minds encounter no obstacles regarding any phenomena;
they do not abandon various practices, yet remain free from all conceptual discrimination, their minds unmoved by thought toward any phenomenon.

Attaining the light of wisdom, they extinguish all darkness of delusion and are able to clearly illuminate all Buddha-dharmas; they enter into the midst of all realms of existence without being destroyed by them, thoroughly understanding the spheres of all such existences.

From the very beginning, there has been no activity; the actions of body, speech, and mind are all entirely boundless. Although one follows worldly convention to expound various and immeasurable syllables, one never destroys or departs from the Dharma that is beyond words.
Deeply entering the ocean of the Buddhas, they know that all phenomena possess only provisional names, remaining unbound and unattached amidst all objective realms;
they realize that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, and that the various practices they cultivate arise from the Dharma-realm, being like space—without characteristics and without form.

They enter deeply into the Dharma-realm and expound it in accordance with its nature; within a single gateway of objects, they give rise to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Observing the stage of the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), they cultivate and study through wisdom, using wisdom as a bridge to reach omniscience (*sarvajña*). With the eye of wisdom, they see all phenomena without obstruction; they skillfully enter the various stages (*bhūmi*) and understand their manifold meanings. They attain complete clarity regarding every single Dharma-gateway, and there are no great vows that they do not fulfill.

“O Son of the Buddha! By this, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reveals the non-differentiated nature of all Tathāgatas. This is the gateway of unimpeded skillful means; this is that which can give birth to the assemblies of Bodhisattvas; this Dharma is exclusively the realm of samādhi; this is that which can courageously enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); this is that which can open and manifest the gates of all samādhis; this is that which can unimpededly and universally enter all lands (*kṣetra*); this is that which can subdue all sentient beings; this is that which can abide in the limit of the non-existence of sentient beings; this is that which can reveal all Buddha-Dharmas; and this is that which finds nothing to be attained within any realm.”
Although they expound and reveal [the Dharma] at all times, they are always far removed from conceptual discrimination;
although they know that all phenomena are devoid of activity, they are able to manifest all manner of deeds;
although they know that all Buddhas have no dual characteristics, they are able to manifest all Buddhas.
Although they know there is no form, they expound upon all forms;
although they know there is no sensation, they expound upon all sensations;
although they know there is no perception, they expound upon all perceptions.
Although they know there is no activity, they expound all activities;
although they know there is no consciousness, they expound all consciousnesses, constantly revealing and instructing all beings with the Wheel of Dharma;
although they know dharmas are unarisen, they constantly turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Although they know that phenomena are without distinction, they speak of various doors of differentiation;
although they know that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, they speak of all characteristics of arising and ceasing;
although they know that all phenomena are neither coarse nor subtle, they speak of the coarse and subtle characteristics of phenomena.
Although they know that all phenomena have no superior, middling, or inferior, they are able to proclaim the most supreme Dharma;
although they know that all phenomena are ineffable, they are able to expound pure speech;
although they know that all phenomena have neither interior nor exterior, they speak of all internal and external phenomena.
Although they know that all phenomena cannot be fully comprehended, they speak of various forms of wisdom and observation;
although they know that all phenomena lack any true reality, they speak of the true path to liberation;
although they know that all phenomena are ultimately inexhaustible, they are able to expound the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they know that all phenomena are without conflict or dispute, they do not disregard the distinction between self and others;
although they know that all phenomena ultimately have no teacher, they always revere all teachers and elders;
although they know that all phenomena are realized without depending on another, they always revere all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Although they know that dharmas do not revolve, they turn the wheel of Dharma;
although they know that dharmas have no arising, they demonstrate all causes and conditions;
although they know that all dharmas have no prior limit, they extensively explain the past.
Although they know that all phenomena have no future limit, they extensively explain the future;
although they know that all phenomena have no middle limit, they extensively explain the present;
although they know that all phenomena have no agent, they speak of various actions.
Although they know that all phenomena have no causes or conditions, they speak of the causes of all accumulations;
although they know that all phenomena have no analogies, they speak of the paths of equality and inequality;
although they know that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression, they definitively explain the dharmas of the three periods of time.
Although they know that all phenomena have no basis, they teach that liberation is attained by relying on wholesome dharmas;
although they know that dharmas have no body, they extensively teach the Dharma-body;
although they know that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are boundless, they are able to proclaim that there is but one Buddha.
Although they know that dharmas are formless, they manifest various forms;
although they know that dharmas are without views, they extensively explain all views;
although they know that dharmas are without marks, they speak of various marks.
Although they know that all phenomena have no objective realm, they extensively proclaim the realm of wisdom;
although they know that all phenomena have no distinctions, they speak of the various distinctions among practices and their fruits;
although they know that all phenomena have no transcendence, they speak of the pure practices of transcendence.
Although they know that all phenomena are primordially and eternally abiding, they speak of all phenomena of saṃsāric flux;
although they know that all phenomena have no illumination, they constantly and extensively expound the Dharma of illumination.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters this Great Majestic Virtue Samādhi Wheel of Wisdom, they are able to realize all Buddha-dharmas, enter into all Buddha-dharmas, accomplish them, fulfill them, accumulate them, purify them, abide in them, and thoroughly comprehend them; they accord with the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Yet, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not form such a thought:”

"There are various bodhisattvas, various bodhisattva-dharmas, various culminations of bodhisattvahood, various culminations of illusion, various culminations of transformation, various accomplishments of supernormal powers, various accomplishments of wisdom, various modes of reflection, various modes of realization, various directions of inclination, and various spheres of experience."
Why is this? Because the samādhi of a bodhisattva has such a nature, is thus boundless, and is thus preeminent.
This samādhi possesses various spheres of experience, various powers, and various profound penetrations, namely:
They enter the gateway of ineffable wisdom; they enter the various adornments free from conceptual discrimination;
they enter the boundless and supreme pāramitās; they enter countless dhyāna-samādhis; they enter the unspeakably vast wisdom of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas;
they enter the vision of the infinite, sublime treasury of Buddhas; and they enter into realms without ceasing.
Entering the factors conducive to the path of pure faith and resolve; entering the sharpness of the faculties and great supernormal powers;
entering the state where the mind is unimpeded regarding all objects; entering the impartial eye that beholds all Buddhas;
entering the accumulation of Samantabhadra’s supreme vows and practices; entering the body of wondrous wisdom like that of Nārāyaṇa; and entering the exposition of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The Ocean enters into the arising of immeasurable kinds of sovereign spiritual transformations; enters into the birth of all Buddhas' inexhaustible gates of wisdom;
enters into and dwells within the manifest realm of all Buddhas; enters into the purified sovereign wisdom of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
enters into the revelation of the incomparable wisdom of the universal gate; and enters into the universal knowledge of all subtle details within the Dharma-realm.
Entering the realm of all subtle spheres that universally manifest throughout the dharma-realm; entering the light of all supreme wisdom;
entering the limit of all sovereign powers; entering the limit of all dharma-gates of eloquence;
entering the body of wisdom that pervades the entire dharma-realm; entering the accomplishment of the path that traverses everywhere; entering...
They skillfully abide in the samādhi of all distinctions and enter the knowledge of the minds of all Buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!

These Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra, enter ten billion unspeakable numbers of samādhis in every thought-moment; yet they do not perceive the limit of the beginning of the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, nor the adornments of the realm of the Buddhas."

Why is this? Because they know that all phenomena are ultimately inexhaustible; because they know that all Buddha-fields are boundless; because they know that the realm of all sentient beings is inconceivable; because they know that the past has no beginning; because they know that the future is infinite; because they know that the present pervades all of space and the entire Dharma-realm without limit; because they know that the spheres of activity of all Buddhas are inconceivable; because they know that the practices of all Bodhisattvas are innumerable; because they know that the spheres described by the eloquence of all Buddhas are ineffable and boundless; and because they know that the phenomena perceived by the illusory mind are immeasurable.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel: whatever is sought is entirely obtained; though those who seek it are inexhaustible and their intentions are all satisfied, the power of the jewel never fails or ceases.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering this samādhi, they know that the mind is like an illusion, giving rise to the spheres of all phenomena, which are pervasive and inexhaustible, neither depleted nor ceasing.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the unimpeded wisdom of Samantabhadra’s conduct; they observe immeasurable and vast illusory manifestations as being like reflections, neither increasing nor decreasing.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like ordinary beings, each of whom gives rise to thoughts—those already arisen, those currently arising, and those yet to arise—which are without limit, uninterrupted, and inexhaustible;
the flow of their minds continues in succession without ceasing, being inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having entered this Samādhi of the Universal Door of Illusion, it is without limit and cannot be measured. Why is this?
Because they have thoroughly realized the infinite dharmas of the universal illusory gate of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like when the dragon kings Nanda, Upananda, and Manasvi, along with other great dragons, send down rain; the drops are as large as axle-trees and are without limit.
Although it rains in this manner, the clouds are never exhausted; this is the effortless realm of the nāgas.

So too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: dwelling in this samādhi, they enter the gates of all samādhis, gates of wisdom, gates of Dharma, gates of beholding all Buddhas, and gates of proceeding to all directions of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
The gate of mastery over the mind, the gate of empowerment, the gate of spiritual transformations, the gate of supernormal powers, the gate of illusory manifestations,
the gate of all phenomena being like illusions, the gate of being filled by unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas,
and the gate of approaching Tathāgatas, perfectly awakened ones, as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
They enter the gateway of the unspeakably unspeakable vast net of illusions; they know the gateway of the unspeakably unspeakable distinctions of vast Buddha-fields;
they know the gateway of the unspeakably unspeakable worlds that possess intrinsic nature and those that lack intrinsic nature;
they know the gateway of the unspeakably unspeakable perceptions of sentient beings; they know the [gateway of] non-...
They know, as they truly are, the distinctions between times that can be described and those that cannot;

the formation and destruction of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds; and the downward-facing and upward-facing Buddha-fields of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of realms—all within a single thought-moment.
Thus, upon entering [this state], there is no boundary and no exhaustion; one is neither weary nor disheartened, neither ceasing nor resting, neither regressing nor losing ground.
Among all phenomena, one does not abide in improper places, but constantly engages in right reflection, neither sinking nor becoming agitated.
Seeking omniscience, one never retreats or abandons it, acting as a world-illuminating lamp for all Buddha-fields, turning the wheel of Dharma that is unspeakably unspeakable.

With wondrous eloquence, he interrogated the Tathāgata without end; he demonstrated that the realization of the Buddha-way is boundless, and that his subduing of sentient beings is never abandoned or neglected; he constantly and diligently cultivates the practices and vows of Samantabhadra without ever resting, manifesting immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable forms and bodies without interruption.
Why is this? It is like lighting a fire: as long as there are conditions present, the fire will continue to burn without ceasing for that duration.

So it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: observing the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, and the world-realm as being like space, without limit or boundary, they are able, in a single moment of thought, to travel to as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
In the presence of each and every Buddha, they enter into unspeakably unspeakable varieties of all-knowledge;
they cause unspeakably unspeakable realms of sentient beings to leave the household life for the sake of the Way, diligently cultivating roots of goodness until they reach ultimate purity;

and they cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattvas who have not yet attained certainty regarding the practices and vows of Samantabhadra to attain such certainty, establishing them in the gateway of Samantabhadra’s wisdom.

By means of immeasurable skillful means, they enter into unspeakably unspeakable numbers of vast and diverse eons of formation, endurance, and destruction throughout the three periods of time; and within unspeakably unspeakable realms of the world’s diverse states of formation, endurance, and destruction, they give rise to as many great compassionate vows as there are beings, taming all infinite sentient beings without exception.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to deliver and liberate all sentient beings, cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, give rise to the wisdom of Samantabhadra, and fulfill all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.

Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should diligently practice within this kind of samādhi—of such a nature, such a sphere, such majesty, such vastness, such immeasurability, such inconceivability, such universal illumination, wherein all Buddhas dwell before them, wherein they are protected and remembered by all Tathāgatas, wherein they have accomplished past roots of goodness, and wherein their minds are unimpeded and immovable; doing so without feverish distress or weariness, with a mind that does not regress, establishing deep resolve and joy, being courageous and fearless, they shall accord with the realm of this samādhi and enter the ground of inconceivable wisdom.

One should not rely on words, not be attached to the world, not grasp at phenomena, not give rise to discrimination, not be defiled by worldly affairs, and not differentiate between objective spheres; regarding the wisdom of all phenomena, one should simply abide therein and not engage in measurement or evaluation.
That is to say:
drawing near to all-knowledge, awakening to and understanding the Buddha’s bodhi, accomplishing the radiance of the Dharma, and bestowing roots of goodness upon all sentient beings.

They rescue sentient beings from within the realm of Māra, causing them to enter the sphere of the Buddha-dharma; they cause them not to abandon their great vows, to diligently contemplate the path of transcendence, to expand the pure realms, to accomplish the various perfections, and to give rise to profound faith and understanding in all Buddhas.
One should constantly observe the nature of all phenomena, never abandoning this for even a moment;
one should know that one's own self and the nature of all phenomena are universally equal;
and one should clearly understand worldly activities, demonstrating the wisdom and skillful means that accord with the Dharma.
One should always be diligent and tireless;
one should observe that one's own roots of goodness are meager;
and one should diligently increase the various roots of goodness in others.
One should personally cultivate the path to omniscience;
one should diligently increase the bodhisattva realm;
and one should joyfully draw near to all spiritual friends.
One should dwell together with fellow practitioners;
one should not discriminate against the Buddha;
and one should not abandon mindfulness.
One should always abide peacefully in the equal dharma-realm;
one should know that all consciousnesses are like illusions;
one should know that the various formations of the world are like dreams.
One should know that the manifestation of the Buddhas through the power of their vows is like a reflected image;
one should know that all vast karmic activities are like magical transformations;
and one should know that all speech is entirely like an echo.
One should contemplate all phenomena as being entirely like illusions;
one should know that all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing are like sounds;
and one should know that all Buddha-fields to which one goes are devoid of intrinsic nature.
One should inquire after the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata without ever becoming weary;
one should diligently provide instruction in order to awaken all the world, never abandoning them;
and one should subdue all sentient beings by preaching the Dharma at the appropriate time, without ceasing.

O Son of the Buddha! Thus do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the conduct of Samantabhadra; thus do they perfect the realm of Bodhisattvas; thus do they penetrate the path of transcendence; thus do they uphold the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time; thus do they observe the gates of all-knowledge; thus do they contemplate the unchanging Dharma; thus do they purify their superior aspirations and inclinations; thus do they have faith and understanding in all Tathāgatas; thus do they comprehend the vast power of the Buddhas; thus do they attain a resolute mind free from obstruction; and thus do they gather in and sustain all sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters this Great Wisdom Samādhi in which the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra abides, in each of the ten directions there are unspeakably unspeakable numbers of lands. In each of these lands, there are as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, and before each and every name of these Tathāgatas, there appear as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. These Buddhas bestow upon him the power of mindfulness of the Tathāgatas, so that he may not forget the realm of the Tathāgatas;
they bestow upon him the ultimate wisdom of all dharmas, so that he may enter into omniscience.”
Grant them the definitive wisdom that discerns the various meanings of all phenomena, enabling them to uphold all Buddha-dharma and enter into it without obstruction;
grant them the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddhas, enabling them to enter all-knowledge and awaken to the Dharma-realm;
and grant them the ultimate wisdom of Bodhisattvas, enabling them to attain the radiance of all phenomena and be free from all darkness.
I grant them the non-retrogressive wisdom of Bodhisattvas, enabling them to discern the timely and the untimely, and to skillfully subdue sentient beings through expedient means;
I grant them the unimpeded eloquence of Bodhisattvas, enabling them to realize and understand boundless dharmas and to expound them exhaustlessly;

I grant them the power of spiritual transformations, enabling them to manifest unspeakably unspeakable varieties of bodies with infinite physical forms, each distinct from the other, to awaken sentient beings.
He is endowed with perfect speech and sound, enabling him to manifest unspeakably unspeakable varieties of voices and diverse expressions to awaken sentient beings;
he is endowed with the power of non-wastefulness, ensuring that all sentient beings who see his form or hear his Dharma shall achieve their goals, none passing by in vain.
O Son of the Buddha!

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus fulfills the conduct of Samantabhadra, he attains the powers of the Tathāgata, purifies the path of renunciation, and fulfills all-knowledge. By means of unimpeded eloquence, supernormal powers, and transformations, he ultimately tames all sentient beings;

endowed with the majestic virtue of a Buddha, he purifies the conduct of Samantabhadra, abides in the path of Samantabhadra, and until the end of the future, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, he turns the subtle and wondrous wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!

Because these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have accomplished such sublime and great vows and bodhisattva practices, they become Dharma-teachers for all the world, suns of Dharma for all the world, and moons of wisdom for all the world.
They become the King of Mountains, Sumeru, for all the world, towering loftily, firm and immovable;
they become a shoreless ocean of wisdom for all the world;
they become a bright lamp of the True Dharma for all the world, illuminating boundlessly and continuing without interruption.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they reveal boundless pure merits, causing them all to dwell securely in roots of goodness and merit;

they accord with omniscience and maintain great vows of equality, practicing the vast conduct of Samantabhadra, and are always able to exhort and inspire immeasurable sentient beings to abide in the samādhi of vast conduct that is ineffably ineffable, manifesting great sovereignty.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained such wisdom, realized such dharmas, and dwells with clear vision and firm stability in such dharmas;
he has acquired such supernormal powers, abides in such realms, manifests such miraculous transformations, and exercises such spiritual penetrations.”
Always dwelling securely in great compassion, constantly benefiting sentient beings, revealing to them the secure and correct path, and establishing the great banner of light of merit and wisdom;

having realized inconceivable liberation, abiding in the liberation of all-knowledge, and reaching the further shore of the liberation of all Buddhas; having already attained mastery in training in the gates of inconceivable liberation-expedients, entering the gates of the distinctions of the Dharma-realm without confusion, sporting with sovereign ease in the unspeakably unspeakable samādhis of Samantabhadra, and abiding in the lion’s-leap wisdom with unimpeded mind and intellect.
Their minds constantly abide in ten great treasuries of Dharma. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
Abiding in the recollection of all Buddhas; abiding in the recollection of all Buddha-dharmas;
abiding in the great compassion that subdues all sentient beings; abiding in the wisdom that manifests inconceivable, pure buddha-lands;
abiding in the resolute understanding that deeply penetrates the realm of all Buddhas; and abiding in the equality of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The equality-marked bodhi abides at the limit of non-obstruction and non-attachment; it abides in the signless nature of all phenomena;
it abides in the equal roots of goodness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
and it abides in the wisdom that precedes the undifferentiated body, speech, and mental activities of the dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present.
He dwells in the contemplation that the birth, renunciation, journey to the site of enlightenment,
attainment of perfect awakening, turning of the wheel of Dharma, and parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely contained within a single momentary limit (*kṣaṇa*).
O Son of the Buddha!

These ten great treasuries of Dharma are vast and immeasurable; they are incalculable, incomparable, inconceivable, ineffable, inexhaustible, and difficult to endure, such that no worldly wisdom can describe them.
“O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has reached the further shore of all practices of Samantabhadra and realized the pure Dharma. With vast power of resolve, he reveals immeasurable roots of goodness to sentient beings, increases all the powers of Bodhisattvas, fulfills all the merits of a Bodhisattva in every thought-moment, and accomplishes all the practices of a Bodhisattva. He attains all the dhāraṇī-dharmas of the Buddhas and upholds all that is spoken by all the Buddhas.
Although he constantly dwells in the reality-limit of *tathatā*, he conforms to all worldly conventions to manifest the taming of all sentient beings.”
For what reason?
Because when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this samādhi, such is the nature of dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha!

By means of this samādhi, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the vast wisdom of all Buddhas; attains the sovereign eloquence that skillfully expounds all vast dharmas; attains the most supreme, pure, and fearless dharma within all worlds; attains entry into the wisdom of all samādhis; attains the skillful means of all bodhisattvas; attains the gate of illumination for all dharmas; reaches the further shore of the dharma that comforts all worlds; knows the proper and improper times for all sentient beings; illuminates every place throughout the worlds of the ten directions; causes all sentient beings to attain superior wisdom; acts as the unsurpassed teacher of all worlds; abides securely in all merits; reveals the pure samādhi to all sentient beings; and leads them into the highest wisdom.

Why is this? When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice in this way, they benefit sentient beings; they increase their great compassion; they draw near to spiritual friends; they behold all Buddhas; they comprehend all dharmas; they travel to all lands; they enter all directions; they enter all worlds; they awaken to the equality of all dharmas; they know the equality of all Buddhas; and they abide in the equality of omniscience.
Within this Dharma, one performs such actions and not other actions;

one dwells with a mind that is not yet satisfied, dwells with an undistracted mind, dwells with a concentrated mind, dwells with a mind of diligent cultivation, dwells with a resolute mind, and dwells with an unchanging mind;
thus one reflects, thus one acts, and thus one reaches the ultimate goal.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no discrepancy between speech and action; his speech accords with his action, and his action accords with his speech. Why is this?
For example, just as a vajra receives its name because it is indestructible and never at any time departs from that indestructibility, so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
he receives his name through the phenomena of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-dharma) and never at any time departs from those phenomena of conditioned formations.
For example, just as genuine gold receives its name because of its exquisite color and never at any time departs from that exquisite color;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who receives his name because of his various wholesome deeds and never at any time departs from those various wholesome deeds.
For example, the Sun Deva Prince receives his name from his wheel of radiance, and there is never a time when he is separated from that wheel of radiance;
likewise, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva receives his name from the light of wisdom, and there is never a time when he is separated from that light of wisdom.

For example, just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, stands upon the great ocean with its four jewel peaks, rising loftily so as to receive its name and never at any time being separated from those four peaks;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who dwells in the world by means of various roots of goodness, rising loftily so as to receive his name and never at any time being separated from those roots of goodness.
Just as the great earth receives its name from supporting all things and never at any time abandons that capacity to support;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who receives his name from delivering all beings and never at any time abandons great compassion.
For example, the great ocean derives its name from containing all waters and never at any time abandons them;
likewise, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva derives his name from his various great vows and never for a moment forsakes the vow to deliver sentient beings.
For example, just as a military general acquires his reputation through mastery in the arts of combat and never at any time abandons that proficiency;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who acquires his name through mastery in this samādhi and, until the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), never at any time abandons this practice.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King governs the four continents, constantly and diligently protecting all sentient beings so that none suffer untimely death and always experience happiness;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: entering such great samādhis, he constantly and diligently transforms and delivers all sentient beings, even leading them to ultimate purity.
Just as when a seed is planted in the earth, it can cause the stems and leaves to grow;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who, by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra, can cause the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings to increase.
It is like a great cloud that, during the hot months of summer, pours down heavy rain, thereby causing all seeds to grow and flourish.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering such great samādhis as these, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and rain down the great rain of Dharma, even unto the point of enabling all sentient beings to attain ultimate purity, ultimate nirvāṇa, ultimate peace and security, ultimate arrival at the other shore, ultimate joy, and ultimate severance of doubt; acting as the ultimate field of merit for all sentient beings, causing their meritorious acts of giving to become entirely pure, causing them all to abide in the path of non-retrogression, causing them to collectively attain the wisdom of all-knowledge, causing them all to achieve transcendence from the triple world, causing them all to attain ultimate wisdom, and causing them all to attain the ultimate Dharma of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, establishing all sentient beings in the state of all-knowledge.

Why is this? Because when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish these dharmas, their wisdom becomes clear and penetrating; they enter the gateway of the Dharma-realm and are able to purify the inconceivable and immeasurable practices of a bodhisattva.
That is to say:
being able to purify all forms of knowledge for the sake of seeking omniscience;
and being able to purify sentient beings so that they may be tamed.
They can purify buddha-fields because they constantly dedicate [their merit];
they can purify all dharmas because they universally understand them;
they can purify fearlessness because they are free from timidity.
They can purify unimpeded eloquence by skillfully expounding the teachings;
they can purify dhāraṇīs by attaining mastery over all phenomena;
and they can purify the practice of intimacy by constantly beholding all Buddhas appearing in the world.

O Son of the Buddha! When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in this samādhi, they attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of unspeakably unspeakable pure merits. This is because they have attained mastery over the spheres of such samādhis; because they are empowered by all Buddhas; because they flow from the power of their own roots of goodness; because they enter the stage of wisdom with great majesty; because of the guiding power of spiritual friends; because they have subdued all the powers of Māra; because of the power of the purity of their shared roots of goodness; because of the power of their vast vows and aspirations; because of the power of the fulfillment of the roots of goodness they have planted; and because they possess an incomparable power of inexhaustible merit that transcends all worlds.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they attain ten kinds of dharmas that are identical to those of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”
What are these ten? They are:
attaining the various marks and signs, with all their manifold adornments, identical to those of all Buddhas;
They are able to emit great nets of pure light, identical to all Buddhas;
their supernormal powers and transformations that subdue sentient beings are identical to those of all Buddhas;
and their boundless physical bodies and pure, perfect voices are identical to those of all Buddhas.
Manifesting pure buddha-lands according to the karma of sentient beings, they are equal to all Buddhas;
being able to retain and never forget any speech uttered by all sentient beings, they are equal to all Buddhas;
possessing inexhaustible eloquence, they turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the minds of sentient beings to give rise to wisdom, and are thus equal to all Buddhas.
He utters the great lion’s roar without any fear or timidity, awakening all sentient beings through immeasurable teachings, equaling the Buddhas;
in a single thought-moment, he universally enters the three periods of time through great supernormal powers, equaling the Buddhas;
and he is able to manifest for all sentient beings the adornments of all Buddhas, the majestic power of all Buddhas, and the realms of all Buddhas, equaling the Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"Son of the Buddha!
Since these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have attained such dharmas and are equal to all Tathāgatas, for what reason are they not called: [Tathāgatas]?"
"Buddha"?
For what reason is he not called "The One with Ten Powers" (Daśabala)?
For what reason is he not called "Omniscient"?
For what reason is he not called...?
Regarding those who attain bodhi within all dharmas:
for what reason can they not be called "Universal Eye"?
For what reason is he not called "the one who sees without obstruction within all objects"?
For what reason is he not called...?
Having awakened to all dharmas,
for what reason is he not called "One Who Dwells Non-dually with the Buddhas of the Three Times"?
For what reason are you not called "one who abides in the limit of reality"?
For what reason do you continue to practice the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra without ceasing?
"For what reason would one be unable to exhaustively penetrate the dharma-realm and abandon the bodhisattva path?
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed Pūrvapradarśana Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, O Son of the Buddha!"
As you have said, if this bodhisattva mahāsattva is identical to all buddhas, for what reason is he not called a "buddha"?
Until when will he be unable to relinquish the bodhisattva path?
O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already been able to cultivate the various practices and vows of all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present; having entered the realm of wisdom, he is then named a Buddha.
One who practices the bodhisattva conduct in the presence of the Tathāgata without ceasing is called a "bodhisattva.
One who has fully entered into all the powers of the Tathāgata is then called:
Although they have attained the ten powers, they practice the conduct of Samantabhadra without rest; this is called a bodhisattva.
To know all phenomena and be able to expound them is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*);
although one is able to expound all phenomena, to skillfully contemplate each and every phenomenon without ever ceasing is called:
A bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are without dual characteristics; this is what is called "awakening to all phenomena."
One who skillfully observes the paths of differentiation among all phenomena— both dual and non-dual— and progresses ever further toward excellence without ceasing,
is called a bodhisattva.
Having already been able to clearly perceive the realm of the Universal Eye, it is called the "Universal Eye";
although one has attained the realm of the Universal Eye, because it increases moment by moment without ever ceasing, it is called:
A Bodhisattva is able to clearly illuminate all phenomena and is free from all obscurations of darkness;
this is called "unimpeded vision."
One who constantly and diligently recollects the one with unimpeded vision is called a bodhisattva.
Having already attained the eye of wisdom of all buddhas, this is what is called:
Awakened to all phenomena;
observing the eye of the Tathāgatas’ perfect awakening wisdom without negligence— this is called a bodhisattva.
Dwelling where the Buddha dwells, being non-dual with the Buddha, is called "dwelling in non-duality with the Buddha";
being sustained by the Buddha and cultivating all forms of wisdom is called:
A bodhisattva constantly contemplates the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all worlds; this is what is called "one who dwells in the reality-limit."
Although they constantly observe the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, they neither realize it nor abandon it; this is called a "bodhisattva.
Without coming or going, without similarity or difference—all such conceptual discriminations are forever stilled; this is what is called:
Those who have rested their vows;
those who, through vast cultivation, have attained perfection and non-retrogression, are called:
those whose Universal Wishes of Samantabhadra are Unresting.
To thoroughly know that the Dharma-realm has no boundaries, and that all phenomena are of a single mark which is markless—
this is called the Bodhisattva path of ultimate relinquishment of the Dharma-realm.

Yet, while knowing the Dharma-realm has no boundaries, to know all its various distinct marks and give rise to great compassion to deliver all sentient beings, without weariness until the end of the future— this is called:
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the elephant king Elāpattra, who dwells within a cave of seven treasures on Mount Suvarṇakakṣa. The perimeter of that cave is entirely enclosed by railings made of the seven treasures, with rows of precious tārā trees standing in succession, and a net of pure gold completely covering them from above."

The elephant’s body was as pure white as jade or snow; atop it stood a golden banner, adorned with golden necklaces. A jeweled net covered its trunk, and precious bells hung down. Its seven limbs were perfectly formed and its six tusks complete; it was upright and full, bringing joy to all who saw it. It was well-trained and docile, its mind free from any contrary intent.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was about to go forth on a journey, the Elephant King immediately discerned his intention; he then vanished from his precious cave and appeared before Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. By means of his supernormal powers, he manifested various transformations, causing his body to have thirty-three heads. From each head, he produced seven tusks; from each tusk, he produced seven ponds; within each pond were seven lotus flowers; and within each flower were seven celestial maidens, all simultaneously performing hundreds of thousands of divine musical performances.
At that time, Śakra, riding this precious elephant, departed from the Sudarśana Palace and proceeded to the Flower Garden, which was filled everywhere with puṇḍarīka lotuses.

Having arrived at the Flower Garden, Śakra descended from the elephant and entered the Palace Adorned with All Jewels; there, surrounded by an immeasurable retinue of celestial maidens, he enjoyed various pleasures through song and music.

At that time, the Elephant King again used his supernormal powers to conceal his elephant form and manifest as a celestial being. Together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and their various handmaidens, he enjoyed himself and sported within the Puṇḍarīka Lotus Garden. His manifested physical appearance, radiance, garments, movements, comings and goings, speech, laughter, and manner of looking were all identical to those of the gods; there was no difference between them, and none could distinguish them.
One could not tell which was the elephant and which was the god, for the elephant and the god resembled one another in every respect.
O Son of the Buddha!

That Elephant King Elāpattra, while remaining within a cave of the seven treasures on Mount Suvarṇakukṣi without undergoing any transformation, ascends to the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa devas. Desiring to make offerings to Śakra Devānām Indra, he manifests various delightful objects and enjoys celestial pleasures, no different from the gods themselves.

O Son of the Buddha! It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: they cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and various samādhis as ornaments of manifold jewels; the seven factors of enlightenment serve as the Bodhisattva’s body; the radiance they emit serves as their net; they erect the great Dharma banner and ring the great Dharma bell; they take great compassion as their cave-dwelling; they take firm and steadfast great vows as their tusks; their wisdom and fearlessness are like those of a lion; they bind the Dharma silken ribbon upon their heads; they reveal the secrets; and they reach the further shore of all Bodhisattva practices and vows.

Desiring to establish oneself upon the seat of enlightenment, to achieve all-knowledge, and to attain supreme perfect awakening; to increase the vast practices and vows of Samantabhadra, never retreating or resting, never ceasing or abandoning them; with great compassion and diligence, to deliver all suffering beings throughout the limits of the future.

Without abandoning the path of Samantabhadra, they manifest the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment; they manifest unspeakably unspeakable gateways to attaining perfect enlightenment, manifest unspeakably unspeakable gateways to turning the wheel of Dharma, and manifest unspeakably unspeakable gateways to abiding in the profound mind.
Within unspeakably unspeakable vast lands, they manifest the gateways of nirvana and transformation;
within unspeakably unspeakable differentiated worlds, they manifest birth and the cultivation of the practices of Samantabhadra, appearing as unspeakably unspeakable Tathāgatas.
In unspeakably, unspeakably vast lands, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment beneath bodhi trees, surrounded by an assembly of unspeakably, unspeakably many bodhisattvas who drew near to him.

In some cases, one may attain perfect enlightenment by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra in a single moment of thought; in others, in a brief instant, or at a certain time, or for a day, or for half a month, or for a month, or for a year, or for countless years, or for a single kalpa, and so on, even unto unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra and attaining perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, he became the foremost among all the Buddha-fields, drawing near to the Buddhas to prostrate, make offerings, and inquire about the observation of the illusory realm, as well as the pure cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable practices, immeasurable wisdoms, various spiritual transformations, various majestic virtues, various insights, various spheres, various supernormal powers, various masteries, various liberations, various lights of Dharma, and various methods for teaching and taming sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
The original body of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perish; through the power of their practices and vows, they manifest themselves in this way in all places. Why is this?

It is because they wish to subdue all sentient beings through the sovereign spiritual powers of Samantabhadra; to cause unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings to attain purity; to cause them to forever sever the wheel of birth and death; to adorn and purify vast and great worlds; to constantly behold all Tathāgatas; to enter deeply into the flow of all Buddha-dharmas; to recollect the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; to recollect all Buddha-dharmas and the Dharma-body throughout the ten directions; to universally cultivate all Bodhisattva practices until they are perfected; and to enter the flow of Samantabhadra so as to be able to realize all-knowledge with mastery.
O Son of the Buddha!

You should observe this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who does not abandon the practices of Samantabhadra, does not sever the path of the Bodhisattvas, beholds all Buddhas, realizes all-knowledge, and freely enjoys the dharmas of all-knowledge.

Just as the elephant king Airāvaṇa, without relinquishing his elephant body, goes to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to be mounted by the devas, experiencing celestial bliss, engaging in divine play, serving the Lord of Devas, and sporting with celestial nymphs, being no different from the other devas.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: they do not abandon the various practices of the Great Vehicle of Samantabhadra, they do not retreat from their vows, they attain the sovereignty of a Buddha, they are endowed with all-knowledge, they realize the liberation of a Buddha, they are unobstructed and unhindered, they achieve purity, they are unstained by any lands, and they make no distinctions within the Buddha-dharma;
although they know that all phenomena are universally equal and devoid of dual characteristics, they constantly perceive clearly all Buddha-lands.
Although they have already become equal to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they continue to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva without interruption.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in such vast dharmas of the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra, you should know that this person’s mind has attained purity.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the vast wisdom of the sublime mind of the tenth Great Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!"
"This is the Great Wheel of the Ten Samādhis of the Universal Worthy Conduct in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell.
*The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Teachings*, Scroll 43;
*The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Teachings*, Scroll 44.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Pervasive Powers (Daśa-vyāhāra-parivarta).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What are the ten?
“O Son of the Buddha!
By means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows the distinctions among the minds of sentient beings within a single trichiliocosm, namely:”

He fully discerns and knows all the various and immeasurable distinctions among the minds of sentient beings: wholesome minds, unwholesome minds; expansive minds, narrow minds; great minds, small minds; minds that follow the cycle of birth and death, minds that turn away from the cycle of birth and death; the minds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the minds engaged in the practices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; the minds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, hell-beings, animals, those in the realm of King Yama, hungry ghosts, and sentient beings in the various states of hardship. Thus, he thoroughly distinguishes and knows all such diverse mentalities of sentient beings.

Just as with one world, so too does he discern and know the minds of all sentient beings within a hundred worlds, a thousand worlds, a hundred thousand worlds, a hundred thousand billion nayuta worlds, and even throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
This is called the first supernormal power of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: skillfully knowing the minds of others.
"O Son of the Buddha!

By means of the unimpeded, pure supernormal knowledge of the divine eye, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives sentient beings within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields—beings dying here and being born there, in happy realms or miserable realms, possessing the marks of merit or the marks of transgression, whether handsome or ugly, or defiled or pure.
In this manner, he clearly perceives with unobstructed vision all such immeasurable classes of sentient beings—namely:

the hosts of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, beings with subtle bodies, beings with vast bodies, small groups, and large groups. Within these various multitudes of beings, he sees them all clearly:

according to the karma they have accumulated, the suffering and pleasure they experience, their minds, their conceptualizations, their views, their speech, their causes, their actions, their objects of perception, and their arising—all of which he perceives without error.
This is called the second unimpeded supernormal knowledge of the divine eye of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"O Son of the Buddha!

By means of the supernormal power of the recollection of past lives, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to know the events of their own past lives and those of all sentient beings within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields, throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
That is to say:
born in such-and-such a place, with such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage, such-and-such food and drink, and such-and-such suffering and pleasure.

From beginningless time, within the various realms of existence, through causes and conditions, they have grown and increased in succession, continuing in an unbroken cycle of saṃsāra. He fully understands all such matters as the various categories, various lands, various modes of rebirth, various forms, various karmic actions, various fetters and afflictions, various mental states, various causes and conditions, and the distinctions in taking birth.
Furthermore, I recall as many eons ago as there are atoms in those buddha-fields, within as many worlds as there are atoms in those buddha-fields,
there were as many Buddhas as there are atoms in those buddha-fields;
for each Buddha, there was such a name, such an appearance in the world, such an assembly, and such parents.
"Attendant, such was the śrāvaka; such were these two most eminent great disciples;
in such a city they went forth; beneath such a bodhi tree they attained supreme perfect enlightenment;
in such a place, seated upon such a seat, they expounded such various sūtras."
He can fully recollect all such things as: how many sentient beings he benefited; for how long a duration he remained in his life span;
how many such Buddha-activities he performed; how he entered parinirvāṇa by relying on the realm of nirvana without remainder;
and, after his parinirvāṇa, how long the Dharma remained in the world. All such matters he is able to remember.

Furthermore, I remember the names of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; for each and every name, there are Buddhas as numerous as atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. From their first aspiration, through the arousal of vows and the practice of cultivation, their making offerings to all Buddhas, their taming of sentient beings, their preaching the Dharma within assemblies, the duration of their lifespans, their supernatural transformations, up to their entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the length of time their teachings remain after their *parinirvāṇa*, and the various adornments of the stupas and temples they establish to cause all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness—all these I am able to know.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s third supernormal knowledge: the power of knowing past lives throughout kalpas of the past.
"O Son of the Buddha!
By means of the supernormal power of knowledge that knows the exhaustion of all kalpas until the end of the future,
the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows all the kalpas within as many world-systems as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; and within each and every kalpa,
he knows all sentient beings— their deaths and rebirths, the continuity of their various states of existence, their karmic actions, and their retributive fruits, whether virtuous or otherwise.
Whether unwholesome, or leading to transcendence, or not leading to transcendence; whether determinate, or indeterminate;
whether wrongly determined, or rightly determined; whether wholesome roots are accompanied by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), or wholesome roots are not accompanied by latent tendencies;
whether wholesome roots are complete, or wholesome roots are incomplete; or...
Whether they have grasped roots of goodness or not, whether they have accumulated roots of goodness or not,
or whether they have accumulated unwholesome dharmas or not—
he is able to understand all such things as these.
Furthermore, one knows that in worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, throughout the entirety of the future,
there are eons as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; in each and every eon,
there are Buddhas with names as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, and for each and every name, there are [infinite]...
One may speak of as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields; for each and every Tathāgata,

from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, their arising of vows and establishment of practices, their making offerings to all Buddhas, their teaching and transforming of sentient beings,
their assemblies and preaching of the Dharma, the length of their lifespans, their supernormal powers and transformations, and even their entry into [nirvāṇa]...
He fully understands all such matters as the remaining nirvana, the duration for which the Dharma will abide after his parinirvāṇa,
and the construction of stūpas and temples with various adornments to enable all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s fourth supernormal knowledge of wisdom: knowing all kalpas to the end of the future.
"O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes the unimpeded, pure divine ear, which is perfected and vast, acute and free from obstructions, penetrating and unhindered; having fully achieved this, regarding all sounds whatsoever, whether he wishes to hear them or not, he possesses sovereign mastery according to his will.
O Son of the Buddha!

In the eastern direction, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. All the profound and vast teachings—those spoken, demonstrated, revealed, expounded, established, taught, disciplined, recollected, and analyzed by those Buddhas; those which are of various distinctions and immeasurable skillful means and immeasurable ingenuity and purity—he is able to receive and uphold them all.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning or the phrasing therein—whether concerning a single person or a great assembly—he is able to retain and uphold all of it according to their respective sounds and words, their respective wisdoms, their respective realizations, their respective manifestations, their respective modes of discipline, their respective spheres, their respective bases, and their respective paths of departure; he forgets nothing and loses nothing, neither halting nor regressing, without confusion or delusion.
He expounds it for others, causing them to attain awakening and understanding, never forgetting or losing a single word or a single phrase.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
This is called the fifth unimpeded, pure superknowledge of the divine ear of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“O Son of the Buddha!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the supernatural power of the absence of intrinsic nature, the supernatural power of non-action, the supernatural power of equality, the supernatural power of vastness, the supernatural power of immeasurability, the supernatural power of non-reliance, the supernatural power of accordance with thought, the supernatural power of arising, the supernatural power of non-arising, the supernatural power of non-retrogression, the supernatural power of non-interruption, the supernatural power of indestructibility, the supernatural power of increase, and the supernatural power of going wherever one intends.”
This bodhisattva hears the names of all Buddhas in worlds extremely far away—
namely, the names of the Buddhas in countless worlds, immeasurable worlds, and even in worlds as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
having heard their names, they immediately perceive themselves present before those Buddhas.
Those worlds are some upright and some inverted; each has its own shape, its own location, and its own distinctions, being boundless and unimpeded.
With their various lands and various eons, they are each adorned with immeasurable merits.
Those various Tathāgatas appear therein, manifesting spiritual transformations and proclaiming their names—immeasurable, innumerable, and each distinct.

As soon as this bodhisattva hears the names of those Tathāgatas, without moving from his original location, he perceives his own body at the presence of those Buddhas, where he pays homage with reverence, serves and makes offerings, inquires about the bodhisattva-dharmas, and enters into the wisdom of the Buddhas. He is able to fully comprehend the buddha-fields, the sites of enlightenment, the assemblies, and the teachings proclaimed by those Buddhas, reaching the ultimate limit without any grasping or attachment.

In this manner, throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields, they reach everywhere throughout the ten directions without actually going anywhere;

yet they visit Buddha-fields to behold the Buddhas, listen to the Dharma, and request the Path, never ceasing, never abandoning, never resting, and never becoming weary, as they cultivate the practices of Bodhisattvas and fulfill their great vows in their entirety, never regressing, in order that the vast lineage of the Tathāgatas may never be interrupted.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s sixth abiding: the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom that proceeds to all Buddha-fields without intrinsic nature and without activity.
"O Son of the Buddha!

By means of the supernormal knowledge of skillfully discerning the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the various modes of expression of sentient beings within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
That is to say:

the speech of the noble ones, the speech of those who are not noble, the speech of devas, the speech of nāgas, the speech of yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and even the speech of all beings—unspeakably unspeakable in number—each expressed with its various distinctions; all such speech he is able to fully comprehend.

In whatever world-system this bodhisattva enters, they are able to know all the inclinations and dispositions of the sentient beings therein; according to those inclinations and dispositions, they produce speech such that all may understand it clearly and without any doubt.
Just as when the sunlight appears, it universally illuminates all forms, enabling those with eyes to see them clearly;

so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: by means of the wisdom that skillfully discriminates all speech, they enter deeply into the clouds of all speech, causing all the wise and intelligent in the world to fully understand every word.
This is called the seventh supernormal knowledge of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the wisdom of skillfully discerning all speech and terminology.
"O Son of the Buddha!

By means of the supernormal power of wisdom that produces the adornment of immeasurable, incalculable physical bodies (*rūpakāya*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are far removed from the characteristics of form; they possess no characteristic of differentiation, no characteristic of variety, no characteristic of immeasurability, no characteristic of conceptual discrimination, and no characteristics of blue, yellow, red, or white.
In this way, the bodhisattva enters the dharma-realm and is able to manifest their body, assuming various forms. These are:
boundless forms, immeasurable forms, pure forms, adorned forms, and pervasive forms.
Incomparable form, universally illuminating form, surpassing form, non-opposing form, form endowed with all marks,
form free from all evils, form of great majesty, form worthy of reverence, inexhaustible form,
manifold and exquisite form, extremely majestic form, immeasurable form, and well-guarded form.
Form, the form that can mature, the form that accords with transformation, the form without obstruction,
the form of extreme clarity and penetration, the form free from defilement and turbidity, the form of ultimate purity, the form of great courage and vigor,
the form of inconceivable skillful means, the indestructible form, the form free from blemish and obscuration, the form without hindrance or darkness, and the virtuous form.
The color of abiding in peace; the color of exquisite adornment; the color of features that are dignified and majestic; the color of various secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*);
the color of great nobility; the color of sublime objects; the color of being well-polished and refined; the color of a pure and profound mind;
the color of blazing and magnificent brilliance; the color of supreme vastness; the color of uninterrupted continuity; the color of non-...
The color of the basis; the color of the peerless and incomparable; the color that fills unspeakable Buddha-fields;
the color of growth; the color of firm grasping; the color of supreme merit; the color that accords with the inclinations of all minds;
the color of pure understanding; the color of the accumulation of manifold wonders; the color of skillful certainty; and the color of non-existence.
The color of unobstructed space; the color of the luminous purity of empty space; the color of pure and delightful beauty; the color free from all dust and defilement; the color that is immeasurable;
the color of wondrous vision; the color of universal vision; the color manifested according to the occasion;
the color of tranquility; the color free from craving; the color of the true field of merit; and the color capable of producing peace and security.
The form that is free from all fears; the form that is free from the conduct of ignorance;
the form of courageous wisdom; the form of unimpeded physical characteristics; the form that travels everywhere; the form upon which the mind does not rely;
the form arising from great loving-kindness; the form manifested by great compassion; the form of impartial renunciation; and the form endowed with merit.
The color of form; the color of form recollected according to the mind; the color of infinite wonderful jewels; the color of the radiance of jewel-treasuries;
the color of sentient beings' faith and delight; the color of the manifestation of all-knowledge;
the color of eyes of joy; the foremost color adorned with various jewels; the color that has no location; the color manifested through sovereign power; and various [other colors].
The color of supernormal powers; the color of being born into the family of the Tathāgata; the color that transcends all analogies; the color that pervades the entire dharma-realm;
the color to which all beings approach; the color of various kinds; the color of accomplishment; the color of renunciation;
the color of the deportment according to those to be converted; the color that one never tires of beholding; and the color of various pure luminosities.
It can emit countless nets of light; the variously differentiated colors of ineffable radiance;
the colors of inconceivable fragrant light that transcend the three realms; the colors of immeasurable solar orbs illuminating all;
the manifestation of incomparable lunar bodies; and the emergence of clouds of immeasurable, delightful flowers.
The color adorned by clouds of various lotus garlands; the color of fragrant flames surpassing all worlds that universally permeate;
the color from which the treasury of all Tathāgatas is produced; the color that reveals and expounds all dharmas through ineffable sounds;
and the color endowed with all the practices of Samantabhadra.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters deeply into such formless *dharmadhātu* and is able to manifest these various types of physical bodies (*rūpakāya*), causing those to be transformed to see them, causing those to be transformed to remember them, and turning the wheel of Dharma for those to be transformed;

according to the timing of those to be transformed and according to the characteristics of those to be transformed, causing those to be transformed to draw near, causing those to be transformed to attain awakening, giving rise to various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) for those to be transformed, manifesting various masteries (*vibhutva*) for those to be transformed, and bestowing various efficacious deeds upon those to be transformed.
This is called:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s diligent cultivation and accomplishment of the eighth immeasurable knowledge of physical bodies and supernormal powers for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
By means of the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of all phenomena, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all phenomena have no names and no intrinsic nature;
they neither come nor go; they are neither different nor not different;
they are neither manifold nor not manifold; they are neither dual nor non-dual; they are without self and without peer.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither moving nor decaying, neither real nor unreal, a single mark yet markless, neither non-existent nor existent, neither dharma nor non-dharma,
not following the conventional yet not not following the conventional, neither karma nor non-karma, neither retribution nor non-retribution.
Retribution is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither the ultimate truth nor not the ultimate truth;
neither the path nor not the path; neither transcendence nor non-transcendence;
neither measurable nor immeasurable; neither mundane nor supramundane; neither born from causes nor not born from causes.
Arising from causes, it is neither determinate nor indeterminate; neither accomplished nor unaccomplished;
neither emerging nor non-emerging; neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized;
neither according to principle nor not according to principle.

This bodhisattva does not grasp at conventional truth, does not dwell in the ultimate meaning, does not discriminate among phenomena, and does not establish verbal designations. They accord with the nature of quiescence, yet do not abandon any vows; seeing the significance and knowing the Dharma, they spread the clouds of Dharma and pour down the rain of Dharma.

Although he knows that the true nature of reality (dharmatā) is ineffable, through skillful means and inexhaustible eloquence, he expounds it in successive order according to the phenomena and their meanings.

Because he has attained mastery in the verbal expression and discourse of all dharmas, and because his great loving-kindness and great compassion are entirely purified, he is able to produce words from within all wordless dharmas. In accordance with and without contradicting either the phenomena or their meanings, he teaches that all dharmas arise from conditions; thus, although there is verbal expression, there is no attachment.

They manifest all dharmas with inexhaustible eloquence, analyzing and establishing them, developing and guiding others so that the nature of all phenomena becomes fully apparent, severing the web of doubts and bringing all to complete purity.

Although they gather in sentient beings, they do not abandon ultimate reality; they never regress from the non-dual Dharma and are always able to expound the unimpeded Dharma-gate. With various wondrous voices, they accord with the minds of sentient beings, universally raining down the rain of Dharma without missing its proper time.
This is called the ninth supernormal power of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas: the wisdom of all dharmas.
"O Son of the Buddha!

By means of the supernormal power of the wisdom of the samādhi of the extinction of all dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the samādhi of the extinction of all dharmas in every thought-moment; yet they do not regress from the bodhisattva path, do not abandon the bodhisattva’s tasks, and do not relinquish the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion. They practice the pāramitās without ever resting, observing all buddha-lands without weariness, not abandoning the vow to deliver sentient beings, not interrupting the work of turning the wheel of Dharma, not neglecting the activity of teaching and transforming sentient beings, not ceasing the practice of making offerings to all buddhas, not relinquishing the gate of mastery over all dharmas, not ceasing the constant vision of all buddhas, and not ceasing the constant hearing of all dharmas.

They know that all phenomena are equal and unimpeded, freely accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas, and fulfilling all their supreme vows. They thoroughly understand the distinctions between all lands, enter the lineage of the Buddhas, and reach the further shore.

They are able to study all dharmas within each and every world, realizing that phenomena are signless; they know that all phenomena arise from conditions and possess no intrinsic nature, yet they expound them according to worldly conventions and skillful means.
Although their minds do not dwell upon any phenomena, they accord with the faculties, inclinations, and desires of sentient beings, skillfully teaching them various dharmas.

When this bodhisattva dwells in samādhi, according to his mental inclination, he may dwell for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or ten billion kalpas, or a hundred billion kalpas, or a thousand billion kalpas, or a hundred thousand billion kalpas, or ten billion nayutas of kalpas, or a hundred billion nayutas of kalpas, or a thousand billion nayutas of kalpas, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of kalpas, or for incalculable kalpas, or for immeasurable kalpas, or even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas.

When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi of the extinction of all dharmas, although they remain within it for that many eons, their body does not disintegrate, does not wither, and does not undergo transformation; it is neither seen nor unseen, neither extinguished nor destroyed, neither fatigued nor weary, and it can never be exhausted.
Although they perform no action regarding either existence or non-existence, they are nevertheless able to accomplish all the works of Bodhisattvas.
That is to say:

they never abandon any sentient beings, teaching and taming them without ever missing the proper time, causing them to increase in all Buddha-dharmas, and bringing all Bodhisattva practices to complete fulfillment.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, his supernormal transformations never cease; like light and shadows appearing everywhere, he remains tranquil and unmoving within samādhi.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom-superknowledge of entering the samādhi of the extinction of all phenomena.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in these ten kinds of superknowledges, they cannot be conceived by any gods or humans, nor can they be conceived by any sentient beings."
All śrāvakas, all pratyekabuddhas, and all other bodhisattvas are likewise unable to conceive of this. The physical karma of this bodhisattva is inconceivable;

his verbal karma is inconceivable; his mental karma is inconceivable; his mastery over samādhi is inconceivable; and the sphere of his wisdom is inconceivable. Except for the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have attained these same supernormal powers, no one else is able to describe, extol, or praise the merits of this person.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of supernormal powers of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in these supernormal powers, they will fully attain the supernormal power of unimpeded knowledge throughout all three periods of time.
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Ten Endurances. At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of patience; if they attain these patiences, they will reach the stage of all bodhisattvas' unimpeded patience, wherein all Buddha-dharmas are unimpeded and inexhaustible.
What are these ten? They are:

the patience of sound, the patience of conformity, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, the patience of being like an illusion, the patience of being like a flame, the patience of being like a dream, the patience of being like an echo, the patience of being like a shadow, the patience of being like a transformation, and the patience of being like space.
These ten kinds of patience have been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those who have taught them in the past, those who teach them now, and those who will teach them in the future.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding sounds?"

That is to say, upon hearing the Dharma spoken by the Buddhas, one is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; one deeply believes and realizes it, takes delight in and inclines toward it, recollects it with single-minded focus, and cultivates it until one abides therein.
This is called the first patience regarding sounds of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformative patience)?

It refers to the contemplation and observation of all phenomena with equanimity and without contradiction; it is the thorough understanding through conformity, which purifies the mind, establishes one correctly in practice, and leads to entry and accomplishment.
This is called the second conformative patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon arising, nor does he perceive even the slightest phenomenon ceasing.

Why is this? If there is no arising, then there is no ceasing; if there is no ceasing, then there is no exhaustion; if there is no exhaustion, then one is free from defilement; if one is free from defilement, then there is no differentiation; if there is no differentiation, then there is no location; if there is no location, then there is tranquility; if there is tranquility, then one is free from desire; if one is free from desire, then there is no activity; if there is no activity, then there is no aspiration; if there is no aspiration, then there is no abiding; and if there is no abiding, then there is neither going nor coming.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s third patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience that is like an illusion?
Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are entirely like illusions, arising from causes and conditions; within a single phenomenon they understand many phenomena, and within many phenomena they understand a single phenomenon.
