Having realized that all phenomena are like illusions, this bodhisattva thoroughly understands lands, thoroughly understands sentient beings, thoroughly understands the dharma-realm, thoroughly understands the equality of the world, thoroughly understands the equality of the appearance of Buddhas, and thoroughly understands the equality of the three periods of time, thereby accomplishing various supernatural powers and transformations.

For example, an illusion is not an elephant, nor a horse; not a chariot, nor infantry; not a man, nor a woman; not a boy, nor a girl; not a tree, nor a leaf, nor a flower, nor a fruit; not earth, nor water, nor fire, nor wind; not day, nor night; not the sun, nor the moon; not a half-month, nor a month; not a year, nor a hundred years; not one eon, nor many eons; not fixed, nor chaotic; not pure, nor mixed; not one, nor different; not broad, nor narrow; not many, nor few; not measurable, nor immeasurable; not coarse, nor subtle; it is none of these various kinds of things.
The various phenomena are not the illusion, nor is the illusion the various phenomena; nevertheless, by means of illusion, the various differentiated things are manifested.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, contemplating all worlds as being like illusions; namely:

the world of karma, the world of afflictions, the world of lands, the world of phenomena, the world of time, the world of destinies, the world of formation, the world of destruction, the world of movement, and the world of conditioned activity.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all worlds as being like an illusion, they do not perceive the birth of sentient beings, nor do they perceive the cessation of sentient beings;
they do not perceive the birth of lands, nor do they perceive the cessation of lands;
they do not perceive the birth of phenomena, nor do they perceive the cessation of phenomena.
One does not perceive a past that can be differentiated, nor does one perceive a future with arising activity, nor does one perceive the present abiding for even a single thought-moment;
one does not contemplate enlightenment, nor does one differentiate enlightenment;
one does not perceive the appearance of a Buddha, nor does one perceive the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha.
They do not perceive abiding in great vows, nor do they perceive entering into right abiding; they do not emerge from the state of equality.
Although these bodhisattvas accomplish buddha-fields, they know that fields are without differentiation;
although they accomplish the realm of sentient beings, they know that sentient beings are without differentiation.
Although they universally contemplate the dharma-realm, they abide peacefully in the nature of phenomena, serene and unmoving;
although they realize the equality of the three periods of time, they do not contradict the differentiation of dharmas across the three periods;
although they accomplish the aggregates and sense bases, they have forever severed their basis.
Although they liberate sentient beings, they thoroughly understand that the dharma-realm is equal and devoid of any distinctions;
although they know that all phenomena are remote from words and ineffable, they constantly teach the Dharma with inexhaustible eloquence;
although they do not grasp at or cling to the task of transforming sentient beings, they do not abandon great compassion, turning the wheel of Dharma to deliver all beings.
Although they reveal past causes and conditions, they know that the nature of causes and conditions is devoid of movement or change.
This is called the fourth *māyopama-kṣānti* (patience like an illusion) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like a mirage?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all worlds are identical to a mirage.

Just as a mirage has no location, being neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither of a single color nor of various colors, nor even colorless, it is merely displayed through worldly conventional discourse.
When a bodhisattva thus observes according to reality, understands all phenomena, realizes them directly, and brings them to perfection,
this is called the fifth patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva: the patience like a mirage.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience regarding dreams?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all worlds are like dreams.

Just as a dream is neither the world nor apart from the world, neither the desire realm, the form realm, nor the formless realm; neither arising nor passing away, neither defiled nor pure, yet it manifests—so too are all worlds.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: they know that all worlds are entirely identical to dreams, because they are without change, because their self-nature is like a dream, because attachment to them is like a dream, because their nature is devoid [of intrinsic reality] like a dream, because their fundamental nature is like a dream, because what is manifested is like a dream, because they are without distinction from a dream, because they are conceptualized through mental construction like a dream, and because they are like the state upon waking from a dream.
This is called the sixth patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is like a dream.
O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like an echo?
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears the Buddha preach the Dharma, contemplates the nature of all phenomena, cultivates and masters them, and reaches the other shore.
They know that all sounds are identical to echoes, neither coming nor going, and thus they manifest them.
O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the voice of the Tathāgata as not emerging from within, not emerging from without, and not emerging from both within and without.

Although they understand that this sound is neither internal, nor external, nor emerging from both internal and external, they are nevertheless able to manifest skillful names and phrases to accomplish their exposition.

Like an echo arising from conditions, it does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), enabling all sentient beings to understand according to their own kind and thereby engage in cultivation and study.
It is like the wife of Śakra, the daughter of an asura named Śacī,
who produces a thousand kinds of sounds within a single voice, yet does not even mentally intend for them to be produced in such a way.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering the realm of non-discrimination, he achieves skillful sounds that accord with the various classes of beings, and constantly turns the wheel of Dharma throughout boundless worlds.

This Bodhisattva is skillfully able to observe all sentient beings and expounds the Dharma for them with the mark of a broad and long tongue; his voice is unimpeded, pervading the lands of the ten directions, so that according to what is appropriate for each, they hear the Dharma differently.
Although he knows that sound has no arising, he universally manifests voices; although he knows there is nothing to be said, he extensively expounds all dharmas.
His wondrous voice is impartial, and each type of being understands it according to their own kind; he is able to comprehend all this through his wisdom.
This is called the seventh patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is like an echo.
"O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like a shadow?
O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is neither born in the world nor does he perish in the world.
Neither within the world nor outside the world;
neither moving through the world nor not moving through the world;
neither identical to the world nor different from the world.
Neither going to the world nor not going to the world;
neither abiding in the world nor not abiding in the world;
neither being the world nor transcending the world.
It is neither the cultivation of bodhisattva practices nor the abandonment of great vows;
it is neither real nor unreal.
Although one constantly practices all Buddha-dharmas, one is able to accomplish all worldly affairs; yet one does not follow the flow of the world, nor does one dwell in the flow of dharmas.

For example, objects such as the sun and moon, men and women, houses, mountains and forests, rivers and springs, manifest their reflections within pure substances such as oil, water, the body, jewels, and bright mirrors.

The reflection and the oil, etc., are neither identical nor different; they are neither separate nor joined. Within the flowing stream it does not drift away, and within the pond or well it does not sink; though it appears therein, it remains unstained by attachment.
Nevertheless, sentient beings know that such reflections appear in this place, and they also know that such reflections do not exist in that place;
although distant objects and near objects both manifest as reflections, the reflections themselves do not possess proximity or distance according to the objects.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he is able to know that both his own body and the bodies of others are entirely within the realm of wisdom, without forming a dualistic understanding that distinguishes between self and other; yet, within his own lands and the lands of others, they appear simultaneously and universally in all their respective differences.
Just as within a seed there are no roots, sprouts, stalks, nodes, branches, or leaves, yet it is able to give rise to such things;
so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva: within the non-dual dharma, they discern dual characteristics through skillful means, attaining unimpeded penetration.
This is called the eighth patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, known as "Patience Like a Reflection.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this patience, although they do not personally travel to the lands of the ten directions, they are nevertheless able to manifest universally in all buddha-fields.
Neither departing from this nor arriving at that, they manifest universally like shadows; their movements are unimpeded.

They cause all sentient beings to perceive distinct bodies as having the same solid and substantial characteristics as worldly phenomena; yet these distinctions are themselves non-distinct, for there is no obstruction between distinction and non-distinction.
This bodhisattva is born from the lineage of the Tathāgatas; because his body, speech, and mind are pure and unimpeded, he is able to attain a body of infinite, pure forms and characteristics.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s acceptance of the illusory nature of phenomena?
O Son of the Buddha!”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all worlds are entirely like transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
That is to say:
the mental karma of all sentient beings is a transformation, because it arises from conceptualization and perception;
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the world are transformations arising from conceptual discrimination;
all suffering and pleasure are transformations of inversion arising from false grasping;
and all unreal phenomena in the world are transformations manifested through verbal expression.
All afflictions are transformations of discrimination, for they arise from conceptual thought;
furthermore, there are transformations of pure subduing, which manifest through non-discrimination;
and there are transformations that do not shift across the three periods of time, for they are equal in their lack of arising.
The transformation through the power of the Bodhisattva’s vows is due to vast cultivation;
the transformation through the Tathāgata’s great compassion is due to the manifestation of skillful means;
and the transformation through the skillful means of turning the wheel of Dharma is that which is spoken by wisdom, fearlessness, and eloquence.

In this way, the bodhisattva thoroughly understands worldly and world-transcending transformations; he realizes them through direct perception, knows them extensively, knows them boundlessly, knows them as they truly are, knows them with mastery, and knows them with reality. He cannot be shaken by false views, and even while following the ways of the world, he does not lose or destroy his realization.
For example, it is like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*): it does not arise from the mind, nor does it arise from mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*);
it does not arise from karma, nor does it undergo karmic retribution; it is neither born in the world nor does it perish in the world;
it cannot be pursued, nor can it be grasped or touched; it does not abide for long, nor does it abide for even a moment; it does not travel through the world, nor...
It transcends the world; it is not bound exclusively to one direction, nor is it universally attached to all directions;
it is neither finite nor infinite; it does not weary nor does it cease, yet it is neither non-wearying nor non-ceasing;
it is neither ordinary nor noble; it is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither birth nor death; it is neither wise nor foolish; it is not a view.
It is not non-seeing; it does not rely on the mundane world, nor does it enter the Dharma-realm;
it is neither sharp wisdom nor dullness; it is neither grasping nor non-grasping; it is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana;
it is neither existence nor non-existence.
Through such skillful means, the bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path within the world and thoroughly understands worldly phenomena;
they manifest emanations to travel about, yet remain unattached to the world and do not grasp at a self, making no conceptual distinctions between the world and the body;
they neither abide in the world nor depart from the world.
They do not abide in phenomena, nor do they depart from phenomena;
by virtue of their original vows, they do not abandon a single realm of sentient beings, nor do they fail to subdue even the slightest realm of sentient beings.
They do not discriminate among phenomena;

yet it is not that they do not discriminate. They know that the nature of all phenomena neither comes nor goes, and although they possess nothing, they fulfill the Buddha-dharma, realizing that phenomena are like illusions—neither existent nor non-existent.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus dwells in the patience regarding the illusory nature of phenomena, they are able to fully fulfill the path to enlightenment of all Buddhas and bring benefit to sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s ninth patience, that of being like a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*).

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has accomplished this patience, whatever they do is entirely like a magical creation. Just as a magically created being, they have no place of dependence or dwelling in any Buddha-field; they have no grasping or attachment toward any world; they do not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding any Buddha-dharma; yet they proceed toward the Buddha-enlightenment without weariness, cultivating the Bodhisattva practices free from all inversions. Although they have no body, they manifest all bodies; although they have no dwelling, they abide in all lands; although they have no form, they universally manifest all forms; and although they do not cling to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they clearly illuminate the equality and perfection of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no dependence upon any phenomena;
he is named "The Liberated One."
One who has completely abandoned all faults is named "The Subduer";
one who is immovable and unswerving, universally entering the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, is named:
One who possesses supernormal powers;
one who has attained skillfulness regarding the non-arising of phenomena,
and is thus named "The Non-regressive";
"Endowed with all powers, neither Mount Sumeru nor the Iron Ring Mountains can obstruct them; they are named 'The Unobstructed.
O Son of the Buddha! "
What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s patience like space?
Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands that all dharma-realms are like empty space because they are without marks.
All worlds are like space, because they are without arising;
all phenomena are like space, because they are non-dual;
the conduct of all sentient beings is like space, because there is no place for it to proceed.
All Buddhas are like space, because they are free from discrimination;
all powers of the Buddhas are like space, because they are without distinction;
all meditative concentrations are like space, because they are equal throughout the three periods of time.
All dharmas that are taught are like space, because they are ineffable;
all Buddha-bodies are like space, because they are unattached and unimpeded.
In this way, the bodhisattva, through skillful means that are like space, realizes that all phenomena are utterly non-existent.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realizes all phenomena through the patient wisdom that is like space, they attain a body and bodily actions like space; they attain speech and verbal actions like space; and they attain a mind and mental actions like space.
Just as all phenomena rely upon space, which is neither born nor perishes;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the entire Dharma-body is neither born nor perishes.
Just as space cannot be destroyed, so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: their wisdom and powers cannot be destroyed.
Just as space is that upon which all worlds depend, yet depends on nothing itself;
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he is the basis upon which all dharmas rely, yet he has no basis of his own.
Just as space is without birth and without cessation, yet can sustain the birth and cessation of all worlds;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: without direction and without attainment, yet able to demonstrate direction and attainment, universally causing the world to practice with purity.
Just as space has no directions and no corners, yet can manifest infinite directions and corners;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: though they have no karma and no retribution, they are able to manifest all manner of karmas and retributions.
Just as space neither moves nor abides, yet can manifest various modes of conduct;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: neither moving nor abiding, yet able to discern all conditioned activities.
Just as space is neither form nor non-form, yet can manifest all manner of forms;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who is neither worldly form nor supramundane form, yet can manifest all forms.
Just as space is neither distant nor near, yet abides for eternity and manifests all things;
so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: neither distant nor near, yet able to abide for eternity, manifesting all the practices performed by a Bodhisattva.
Just as space is neither pure nor defiled, yet is not separate from purity or defilement;
so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva: neither obstructed nor unobstructed, yet not separate from obstruction or non-obstruction.
For example, just as space appears before all worlds, yet does not appear before all worlds;
so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: all dharmas appear before him, yet he does not appear before all dharmas.

Just as space universally enters into all things yet has no boundary, so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: they universally enter into all dharmas, yet the bodhisattva’s mind has no boundary.
Why is this? Because that which is performed by a bodhisattva is like space.
That is to say, all cultivation, all purification, and all accomplishment are entirely equal—of one substance, one flavor, and one kind—with a magnitude like space, pure and pervasive in all places.

Thus, they realize and know all dharmas; they are without discrimination regarding any dharma; they adorn and purify all Buddha-lands; they perfect all bodies that are without dependence; they understand all directions without confusion; they possess all powers that cannot be destroyed; they fulfill all boundless merits; they have reached the realm of all profound dharmas; they penetrate the path of all pāramitās; they sit universally upon all vajra-thrones; they universally emit voices according to the various types of beings; and for all worlds, they turn the wheel of Dharma without ever missing the proper time.

This is called the tenth patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is like space. When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this patience, they attain a body that does not come, because it does not go; and a body that does not go, because it does not come. It is neither born nor extinguished, neither comes nor goes, and is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is called the patience of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva that is like space. They attain the body of non-arising, because it is without cessation;
they attain the immovable body, because it is without decay;
they attain the unreal body, because it is free from falsehood.
One attains the body of a single characteristic, because it is without characteristics;
one attains the immeasurable body, because the power of the Buddha is immeasurable;
one attains the equal body, because it is identical to the characteristic of suchness.
They attain the body of non-differentiation, because they observe the three periods of time with equality;
they attain the body that reaches all places, because their pure eyes illuminate everything without obstruction;
they attain the body of the limit of detachment from desire, because they know that all phenomena have neither conjunction nor dispersion.
They attain a body with infinite boundaries like space, because their treasury of merit is inexhaustible like space;

they attain a body of unceasing and inexhaustible eloquence in the equality of the dharma-nature, because they know that the characteristics of all phenomena are but a single characteristic, having non-substantiality as their substance, just like space;
they attain a body of immeasurable and unimpeded sound, because it is without obstruction like space.
They attain a body of Bodhisattva practice that is fully perfected in all skillful means and pure, because it is unobstructed in all places like space;
they attain a body that is the continuous succession of the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas, because it is indestructible like space;
they attain a body that manifests infinite Buddha-fields within all Buddha-fields, because it is free from all attachment like the boundlessness of space.
They attain a body that manifests all sovereign dharmas without cessation, for it is as boundless as the great ocean of empty space;
they attain a body of indestructible, firm power, for it sustains all worlds like empty space;
they attain a body with faculties as sharp and clear as a vajra, firm and indestructible, for it cannot be burned by the fires at the end of any kalpa, just as empty space cannot be consumed.
They attain a body endowed with the power to sustain all worlds, for their power of wisdom is like space.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are called the ten kinds of patience of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as there may be people in the world Who hear of a place where a treasure-trove lies;
Because it can be obtained, Their hearts give rise to great joy."
Such is their great wisdom; these Bodhisattvas, true children of the Buddha, hear all the teachings of the Buddhas regarding the profound and quiescent nature of phenomena.
When they hear this deep Dharma, their minds attain peace and stability.
Neither startled nor terrified, nor giving rise to fear,
the Great Being seeking bodhi, upon hearing this vast sound,
maintains a pure mind and is able to endure it, remaining free from doubt or hesitation.
Reflecting that by hearing this most profound and subtle Dharma,
he shall attain all-encompassing wisdom and become a great teacher of gods and humans,
the Bodhisattva, upon hearing these sounds, felt great joy in his heart.
Generating a firm resolve, they aspire to seek all Buddha-dharmas.
Because they delight in bodhi, their minds gradually become subdued;
their faith increases further, and they neither oppose nor slander the Dharma.
Therefore, upon hearing this sound, their minds attain endurance;
dwelling in peace without wavering, they practice the bodhisattva deeds.
For the sake of seeking enlightenment, they single-mindedly proceed along that path.
With diligence that never regresses, they do not abandon the yoke of manifold virtues.
For the sake of seeking bodhi, their minds are free from fear;
hearing the Dharma increases their valor, as they make offerings to the Buddhas to bring them joy.
Just as a person of great merit, having discovered a treasury of pure gold,
fashions ornaments from whatever clothing they require;
so too is the Bodhisattva, who, upon hearing this most profound meaning, [acts accordingly].
By contemplating this, one increases the ocean of wisdom and practices in accordance with the Dharma.
One understands in accordance that phenomena exist, and understands in accordance that phenomena do not exist;
following those phenomena as they are, one thus knows all dharmas.
Having accomplished a pure mind, With clarity and great joy,
Knowing that phenomena arise from conditions, One practices with courageous diligence.
Observing all phenomena with equanimity, One thoroughly understands their intrinsic nature.
Not contradicting the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, universally awakening to all phenomena;
their resolve and joy ever firm and steadfast, they adorn and purify the Buddha’s bodhi;
as immovable as Mount Sumeru, they single-mindedly seek perfect enlightenment.
Having aroused the mind of diligence, they further cultivate the path of samādhi;
practicing with effort for immeasurable eons, they have never experienced any decline.
The dharmas entered by the Bodhisattvas are the sphere of action of the Buddhas.
One who can understand this, whose mind knows no weariness or indolence,
and who observes all phenomena with equanimity as taught by the Peerless One,
possesses an impartial patience that is able to accomplish equalizing wisdom.
In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, they accomplish this gateway of patience;
they understand things according to the Dharma, yet do not discriminate among phenomena.
Among all the sons of the gods within the Heaven of the Thirty-three, [they are preeminent].
They eat together from a single vessel, yet what they consume differs for each.
These various kinds of food do not come from the ten directions;
according to the karma they have cultivated, it appears naturally within the vessel.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: observing that all phenomena arise entirely from causes and conditions, they are without birth and thus without cessation;
because there is no cessation, there is no exhaustion; and because there is no exhaustion, there is no defilement.
Regarding the phenomena of worldly change, he understands them to be without change;
where there is no change, there is no location; where there is no location, there is quiescent extinction.
His mind is free from defilement and attachment, and he vows to deliver all living beings.
Single-mindedly focused on the Buddha-dharma, never allowing for distraction or agitation,
yet with a heart of compassionate vows, they employ skillful means to act within the world.
Diligently seeking the Ten Powers, they dwell in the world without being attached to it.
Neither going nor coming, he skillfully teaches the Dharma through expedient means.
This patience is the most supreme; realizing that phenomena are inexhaustible, he enters the true realm of reality, yet in truth there is nothing entered.

When a bodhisattva abides in this patience, they universally behold all Tathāgatas, who simultaneously bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment; this is called receiving the office of a Buddha.
They thoroughly comprehend the phenomena of the three periods of time, which possess the characteristics of quiescence and purity.
Yet they are able to transform sentient beings, Establishing them within the paths of goodness.
The various phenomena of the world— All are like illusions;
If one can know them thus, One’s mind remains unmoved.
All karmas arise from the mind; therefore, it is said that the mind is like an illusion.
If one is free from this discrimination, all realms of existence are universally extinguished.
Just as a skilled illusionist manifests all manner of forms and images, so too does the mind appear in various ways.
It merely causes the multitude to crave pleasure, yet in the end, nothing is obtained.
The world is likewise thus: everything is like an illusion;
it has no intrinsic nature and no arising, yet it manifests in various forms.
To deliver all sentient beings, causing them to know that dharmas are like illusions;
that sentient beings are no different from illusions, and that within illusion there are no sentient beings.
Sentient beings and their lands, and all dharmas throughout the three periods of time—
Thus, without exception, all things are like illusions.
Like illusions they manifest the forms of men and women, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep;
houses, ponds, and springs; and gardens, groves, flowers, and fruits.
Illusory objects have no cognition, nor do they have any place of abiding;
their ultimate nature is that of quiescent extinction, appearing only in accordance with conceptual discrimination.
When Bodhisattvas can perceive in this way, they universally behold all worlds.
All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are thoroughly understood to be like illusions.
Sentient beings and their lands are all fashioned by various karmas;
having entered the realm of illusion, one has no dependence or attachment therein.
Having thus attained such skillfulness, they abide in the stage of non-obstruction—
quiescent and free from conceptual proliferation— manifesting great majestic power everywhere.
These courageous sons of the Buddha follow and enter the sublime Dharma.
He skillfully observes all perceptions, which entangle the world like a net.
All perceptions are like a mirage, causing sentient beings to misunderstand;
the Bodhisattva, knowing perceptions well, abandons all such perversions.
Sentient beings are each distinct and diverse, their forms and types not of a single kind;
yet one who fully understands them knows they are all merely conceptual constructions, and that none possess any true reality.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions are shrouded by these very conceptions.
If one abandons inverted views, Then the perception of the world is extinguished.
The world is like a mirage; Because of conceptualization, there are distinctions.
Knowing that the world dwells in conceptualization, One remains far removed from the three inversions.
Just as a mirage in the heat, which people in the world perceive as water, yet in reality no water exists there—so the wise should not seek it;
so too it is with sentient beings: the realms of worldly existence do not exist at all.
Like a mirage abiding in perception, it is the unobstructed realm of the mind.
If one is free from all perceptions and likewise free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
those who are deluded and attached to perceptions shall all attain liberation.
Far removed from the mind of pride, Having eliminated worldly perceptions,
Abiding in the state where exhaustion is inexhaustible— This is the skillful means of a bodhisattva.
The bodhisattva understands that all worldly phenomena Are entirely like a dream.
Neither non-place nor absence of place, their essential nature is eternally quiescent.
All phenomena are without discrimination; like a dream, they do not differ from the mind.
Throughout the three times and all worlds, everything is exactly thus.
The essence of a dream is without arising or ceasing, And it has no location or direction;
All three realms are likewise so— One who sees this attains liberation of mind.
A dream does not exist within the world, Nor does it exist outside the world.
When these two are not discriminated, one attains entry into the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Just as various diverse appearances are seen within a dream, so too is the world; it is no different from a dream.
One who dwells in the meditative concentration of dreams understands that all worlds are like dreams:
neither identical nor different, neither one nor manifold.
So too are the karmas of sentient beings and their lands, whether defiled or pure.
Thus they fully understand that these are all equal to a dream.
The practices performed by Bodhisattvas, as well as their great vows,
they clearly perceive as being like dreams, no different from the world itself.
Realizing that all worlds are empty and quiescent, yet not destroying worldly phenomena—
just like the various forms seen in a dream, such as long and short—
this is called "patience like a dream. By means of this, one thoroughly understands worldly phenomena.
Swiftly accomplishing unimpeded wisdom, They extensively deliver all living beings.
Practicing such conduct, they give rise to vast understanding;
Skillfully knowing the nature of all phenomena, Their minds have no attachment to dharmas.
All the various sounds within all the worlds, Are neither internal nor external; realize them all to be like echoes.
Just as when hearing various echoes, The mind gives rise to no discrimination.
When a bodhisattva hears sounds, their mind is just like this:
gazing up at all the Tathāgatas and listening to the sound of their preaching the Dharma,
they hear the immeasurable sūtras being expounded, yet though they hear them, they remain unattached.
Like an echo, there is no place from which it comes; so too is the sound that is heard.
Yet one is able to discern phenomena without contradicting the nature of phenomena.
Thoroughly understanding all sounds and voices, one does not conceptually differentiate within sound.
Knowing that all sounds are empty and quiescent, they universally produce pure voices.
Understanding that phenomena do not reside in words, they skillfully enter the realm of wordlessness,
yet are able to manifest verbal teachings, like echoes pervading the world.
Thoroughly understanding the path of speech and being fully endowed with the components of sound,
one knows that the nature of sound is empty and quiescent, yet speaks by means of worldly vocal expressions.
Just as all sounds exist in the world, one demonstrates them as being identical to the phenomena of conceptual discrimination.
That sound pervades everywhere, awakening all living beings.
Having attained this patience, the Bodhisattva purifies their voice to transform the world;
skillfully explaining the three periods of time, they remain unattached to the world.
Desiring to benefit the world, he focuses his mind on seeking enlightenment;
yet constantly entering the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he remains free from conceptual discrimination regarding them.
He universally contemplates all worlds as being quiescent and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Yet they constantly act for the benefit of others, their resolve unshakable as they practice.
They do not abide in the world, nor are they apart from the world;
they have no dependence upon the world, for no place of dependence can be found.
Having thoroughly understood the nature of the world, they are unstained by that very nature;
though not dependent upon the world, they transform the world so that it may transcend it.
Regarding all phenomena within the world, they fully know their inherent nature.
Realizing that phenomena are without duality, Even non-duality is without attachment.
The mind does not depart from the world, Nor does it abide within the world;
Neither outside of the world, Does one cultivate all-knowledge.
Just as a reflection in water is neither internal nor external,
so the Bodhisattva seeking awakening realizes that the world is not the mundane.
He does not abide in or depart from the world, for the world is inexpressible.
Nor does it abide within or without; like a shadow appearing in the world, one enters this profound meaning.
Free from defilement and entirely lucid, one does not forsake the mind of original vows, universally illuminating the lamp of wisdom.
The world is boundless, yet wisdom enters it all with perfect equality;
universally transforming all living beings, causing them to relinquish their manifold attachments.
Contemplating the profoundly deep Dharma, he brings benefit to the multitudes of sentient beings.
From this one enters into wisdom, practicing all paths.
The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, clearly understanding them all to be like illusions;
yet they perform illusory deeds, never ultimately abandoning them.
In accordance with the nature of transformation, one cultivates the path to enlightenment;
all phenomena are like transformations, and so too is the conduct of the bodhisattva.
All worlds, as well as immeasurable karmas, [are likewise].
All are equal and like transformations, ultimately abiding in quiescent extinction.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise entirely like transformations;
through the cultivation of various practices via their original vows, they manifest as Tathāgatas.
The Buddha, with great compassion, delivers and transforms sentient beings;
yet that which is delivered is also like an illusion. By the power of transformation, he preaches the Dharma.
Knowing that all worlds are like illusions, he does not discriminate among them.
The various distinctions of transformative deeds all arise from the differences in karma.
Cultivating the practices of bodhi adorns the treasury of transformations;
with immeasurable virtuous adornments, it is like karma creating the world.
The transformative dharma is free from conceptualization, And yet it does not conceptualize phenomena;
Both of these are utterly quiescent— Such is the practice of the Bodhisattva.
The ocean of transformations is realized through wisdom, And the nature of transformation seals the world.
Transformation is not a phenomenon of arising and ceasing; wisdom is likewise so.
The tenth stage of patience clearly contemplates that the essential nature of sentient beings and all phenomena is entirely quiescent, like space, having no fixed location.
Having attained this wisdom that is like space, one is forever free from all grasping and attachment;
like space, it is devoid of manifoldness, and thus there is no obstruction in the world.
Having accomplished the power of the patience of emptiness, it is like space, without exhaustion.
The objective sphere is like space; one does not form conceptual discriminations regarding it as empty.
Space has no intrinsic nature, nor is it subject to annihilation;
it possesses no manifold distinctions, and the power of wisdom is likewise so.
Space has no beginning, nor does it have a middle or an end;
its measure cannot be apprehended, and the wisdom of the Bodhisattva is likewise.
Observing the nature of phenomena in this way, all things are like space.
Neither arising nor ceasing—this is what the Bodhisattva has attained.
Abiding spontaneously in the dharma that is like space, he further preaches it for the sake of sentient beings;
subduing all Māras—all this is the skillful means of this patience.
The various distinctions of worldly characteristics are all empty and devoid of marks;
entering the state where no marks exist, all characteristics are entirely equal.
By means of this single expedient, one universally enters all worlds.
It means that one knows the dharmas of the three periods of time are all equal to the nature of empty space.
Wisdom and sound, as well as the bodies of bodhisattvas, have a nature like empty space; all are utterly quiescent.
These ten kinds of patience are what the sons of the Buddha practice;
with their minds well-established therein, they explain them extensively for the sake of sentient beings.
By training well in this, they achieve vast and great power.
The power of the Dharma and the power of wisdom are the skillful means for bodhi.
By penetrating this gate of patience, one achieves unimpeded knowledge,
surpasses all multitudes, and turns the unsurpassed wheel.
The vast conduct he has cultivated is immeasurable;
only the Ocean of Wisdom of the Tamer of Men can discern and know it.
Having relinquished the self to practice, he has entered the profound nature of phenomena.
The mind constantly abides in pure dharmas, and thus bestows them upon all living beings.
Though the number of sentient beings and the atoms of all lands may still be known,
the various merits of the Bodhisattvas can never have their limit measured.
The Bodhisattvas are able to accomplish these ten kinds of patience;
their wisdom and their conduct are such that no sentient beings can fathom them.
— *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Teachings*, Scroll 44.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Forty-five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree. Chapter Thirty:
The Chapter on the Incalculable (Asaṃkhyeya). Chapter Thirty: The Chapter on the Incalculable.
At that time, Bodhisattva Mind-King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, expound upon that which is incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, uncountable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, unspeakable, and unspeakably unspeakable."
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘incalculable’ (asaṃkhyeya) up to ‘unspeakably unspeakable’?
The Buddha addressed Mind-King Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
You now ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desiring to cause all the worlds to enter into the meaning of the measure of what is known by the Buddha.”
"Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!"
"I shall now explain it for you.
At that time, Bodhisattva Mind-King (Cittarāja) responded, "So be it," and received the instruction.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! One hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi; one koṭi multiplied by itself constitutes one ayuta;
one ayuta multiplied by itself constitutes one nayuta; one nayuta multiplied by itself constitutes one bimbara...”
One *prabhedana* makes one *vibhedana*; one *vibhedana* makes one *kaṅkara*;
one *kaṅkara* makes one *agāra*; one *agāra* makes one *parama*;
one *parama* makes one *mabhāra*; one *mabhāra* makes one *ā*.
One *bharā* is equal to one *abharā*; two *abharās* make one *tambharā*;
two *tambharās* make one *khaṇḍa*; two *khaṇḍas* make one *pramā*; two *pramās* make one *nemā*;
two *nemās* make one *apahelā*; two *apahelās* make one *helā*.
One *apahkṣa* makes one *miga-upabha*; one *miga-miga* makes one *vilaga*;
one *vilaga-vilaga* makes one *vigā-upabha*; one *vigā-upabha-vigā-upabha* makes one *saṃkhyāma*; one *saṃkhyāma-saṃkhyāma* makes one *visā*.
One *la* makes one *visāra*; one *visāra* makes one *viṃśatibhāga*;
one *viṃśatibhāga* makes one *viṃśatikaga*; one *viṃśatikaga* makes one *viṃśatidha*;
one *viṃśatidha* makes one *vibhava*; one *vibhava* makes one *vibhava*.
One *tala* makes one *vitāla*; one *vitāla* makes one *vikhaṇḍa*;
one *vikhaṇḍa* makes one *tulita*; one *tulita* makes one *dhṛti*; one *dhṛti* makes one *viloma*;
one *viloma* makes one *viparyāsa*; one *viparyāsa* makes one *triṃśat*.
Three *māyā* and three *māyā* make one *vidhura*; two *vidhura* make one *khepara*;
two *khepara* make one *vicāra*; two *vicāra* make one *parivarta*;
two *parivarta* make one *udvaha*; two *udvaha*... [and so on].
One *eka* is the most excellent; one most excellent is one *parama-eka*;
one *parama-eka* is one *nirava*; one *nirava* is one *ahura*; one *ahura* is one *vivara*;
one *vivara* is one *ahuruga*; one *ahuruga* is one *ahuruga-saṃ*.
Three *hāri* make one *kharu-ga*; two *kharu-gas* make one *dharā-pota*; two *dharā-potas* make one *haruṇa*;
two *haruṇas* make one *maruta*; two *marutas* make one...
Two *saṃmudā* make one *cīradā*; two *cīradās* make one *marumama*;
two *marumamas* make one *dānta*; two *dāntas* make one *vigatamāna*; two *vigatamānas* make one *akampya*.
One *acala* makes one *paramāṇu*; one *paramāṇu* makes one *amatra*; one *amatra* makes one *bhamatra*;
one *bhamatra* makes one *gamatra*; one *gamatra* makes one [unit].
Thus, *tāla*, *tāla*, *tāla* makes one *kha-mā-tala*; *kha-mā-tala*, *kha-mā-tala* makes one *vi-mā-tala*;
*vi-mā-tala*, *vi-mā-tala* makes one *pra-mā-tala*; *pra-mā-tala*, *pra-mā-tala*...
Ten *la* make one *śivamatra*; ten *śivamatras* make one *elā*;
ten *elās* make one *velā*; ten *velās* make one *telā*; ten *telās* make one *gelā*; ten *gelās* make one *sopala*.
Two *sūbhra* make one *nīla*; two *nīla* make one *kīla*;
two *kīla* make one *sūkṣma*; two *sūkṣma* make one *pīla*;
two *pīla* make one *mīla*; two *mīla* make one *sālada*.
One *tuśala-tu* makes one *meruta*; one *meruta-meruta* makes one *kheruta*;
one *kheruta-kheruta* makes one *madhura*; one *madhura-madhura* makes one *samura*; one *samura-samura* makes one *ayasa*. One *ayasa*...
One *sāya* makes one *kāmla*; one *kāmla-kāmla* makes one *maghava*;
one *maghava-maghava* makes one *atula*; one *atula-atula* makes one *heluya*; one *heluya-heluya* makes one *veluva*; one *veluva*...
One *baviluba* makes one *karaba*; one *karaba-karaba* makes one *hahabha*;
one *hahabha-hahabha* makes one *vibhara*; one *vibhara-vibhara* makes one *nabhara*; one *nabhara-nabhara* makes one *mālara*.
Mala-mala makes one sa-bha-śara; sa-bha-ra-sa-bha-ra makes one mi-la-pu; mi-la-pu-mi-la-pu makes one ca-ma-ra;
ca-ma-ra-ca-ma-ra makes one dha-ma-ra; dha-ma-ra-dha-ma-ra makes one pa-la-ma.
Da, bala-māda-bala-māda is one vigama; vigama-vigama is one upabaddha;
upabaddha-upabaddha is one vyākhyāna; vyākhyāna-vyākhyāna is one akṣaya; akṣaya-akṣaya is one utpāda.
One *jāti* (birth) makes one *ajāti* (non-birth); one *ajāti* makes one *apada* (footless);
one *apada* makes one *utpala* (blue lotus); one *utpala* makes one *padma* (lotus);
one *padma* makes one *saṃkhyā* (count); and one *saṃkhyā* makes one [great] *saṃkhyā*.
A *gati* (course), ten *gatis* make one *eka-gati*; ten *eka-gatis* make one *asaṃkhyeya*;
ten *asaṃkhyeyas* make one *asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*; ten *asaṃkhyeya-parivartas* make one *aprameya*;
ten *aprameyas* make one *aprameya-parivarta*; ten *aprameya-parivartas* make one... [etc., as above].
The infinite, the infinite, and the infinite constitute one "infinite-turn"; the infinite-turn, the infinite-turn, and the infinite-turn constitute one "unequaled";
the unequaled, the unequaled, and the unequaled constitute one "unequaled-turn"; the unequaled-turn, the unequaled-turn, and the unequaled-turn constitute one "incalculable";
the incalculable, the incalculable, and the incalculable constitute one "incalculable-turn. Not...
Countable revolutions and uncountable revolutions constitute one "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*); incalculables and incalculables constitute one "incalculable revolution" (*asaṃkhyeyaparivarta*);
incalculable revolutions and incalculable revolutions constitute one "inconceivable" (*acintya*);
inconceivables and inconceivables constitute one "inconceivable revolution" (*acintyaparivarta*); inconceivable revolutions and inconceivable... [revolutions constitute one... *acintya*.
One *aprameya* becomes one *aprameyāprameya*; one *aprameyāprameya* becomes one *aprameyaparivarta*;
one *aprameyaparivarta* becomes one *anabhilāpya*; one *anabhilāpyānabhilāpya* becomes one *anabhilāpyaparivarta*; and one *anabhilāpyaparivarta* becomes one *anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*.
"It is unspeakable; furthermore, this unspeakable-unspeakable constitutes one unspeakable-unspeakable revolution.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse for the sake of Cittarāja Bodhisattva:
"Inexpressible and beyond expression, Pervading all that is inexpressible,
Throughout inexpressible eons, One could never exhaustively speak of what is inexpressible."
Inconceivable Buddha-fields, all ground down into fine dust—within a single mote of dust are fields beyond description; as it is for one, so it is for all.
These unspeakable Buddha-fields, in a single thought-moment, are reduced to unspeakably many atoms;
in every successive thought-moment they are likewise reduced, continuing thus for all unspeakable eons.
The lands contained within this atom are unspeakable; it is even more difficult to speak of the atoms within those lands.
By means of the method of calculation for the unspeakable, one may count unspeakable eons in this manner.
Using these atoms as the number of kalpas— where one atom represents one hundred thousand unspeakable numbers—
for that many kalpas to praise a single Samantabhadra, one could never exhaust the measure of his merit.
Upon a single, minute hair-tip, there are unspeakably many Samantabhadras;
so it is upon every hair-tip, and thus throughout the entire dharma-realm.
All the lands upon a single hair-tip, Their number is immeasurable and beyond description;
Throughout all hair-tips as vast as the limits of space, Every single location contains lands exactly like this.
Within those lands upon the tip of a hair, there dwell infinite varieties of distinct types;
there are unspeakably many realms of different kinds, and unspeakably many realms of the same kind.
Upon every tip of a hair, which is itself ineffable, there are unspeakably many pure lands;
their various adornments are unspeakable, and their manifold wonders are unspeakable.
Within each and every tip of a hair, they proclaim the names of unspeakably many Buddhas;
within each and every name are Tathāgatas, all of whom are unspeakably, unspeakably many.
Upon the bodies of each and every Buddha, there appear unspeakably many pores;
within each and every one of those pores, unspeakably many varieties of forms and appearances are manifested.
Ineffable numbers of pores all emit ineffable rays of light;
within each and every ray of light, ineffable lotus flowers are fully manifested.
Within each and every one of those lotuses, there are unspeakably many petals;
within the unspeakably many petals of each unspeakable flower, unspeakably many forms and appearances manifest.
Within those unspeakably many forms, there further appear unspeakably many petals;
within the petals, the radiance is unspeakable, and within the radiance, the forms and characteristics are unspeakable.
Within these ineffable forms and appearances, Each manifests ineffable rays of light;
Within those lights, ineffable moons appear, And from those moons, further ineffable moons manifest.
Within unspeakably many moons, each manifests unspeakably many rays of light;
within each of those individual rays of light, there again appear unspeakably many suns.
Within unspeakably many suns, each manifests unspeakably many forms;
within each of those forms, again, unspeakably many radiances appear.
Within each and every one of those rays of light, there appear unspeakably many lion thrones;
each ornamental feature is unspeakable, and each ray of light is unspeakable.
The wondrous colors within the light are ineffable; The pure light within those colors is ineffable.
Within each and every one of those pure lights, Various kinds of wondrous radiances further appear.
This light further manifests various lights, Inexpressible and beyond expression;
Within each of these various radiances, A wondrous jewel appears, like Mount Sumeru.
Within each and every ray of light, there appear jewels that are unspeakably unspeakable;
even as a single exquisite jewel like Mount Sumeru manifests unspeakably many buddha-lands.
Exhausting all the jewels of Mount Sumeru without remainder, he manifests all buddha-fields in this same way;
taking a single field and reducing it to dust, the color and form of a single mote of dust are ineffable.
The multitude of lands becomes dust, and each mote of dust has its own form;
Inexpressible and beyond expression are such various forms of dust, All of which emit inexpressible rays of light.
Buddhas appearing within the light are unspeakable; The Dharma taught by those Buddhas is unspeakable;
The sublime verses within that Dharma are unspeakable; Attaining understanding upon hearing those verses is unspeakable.
Ineffable understanding within every thought-moment, The ineffable manifestation of the ultimate truth,
Revealing all future Buddhas, Constantly expounding the Dharma without end.
Each and every Buddha-dharma is unspeakable; The various purities are unspeakable;
The utterance of wondrous sounds is unspeakable; The turning of the wheel of the true Dharma is unspeakable.
Within each and every wheel of Dharma, he expounds unspeakable numbers of sūtras;
within each and every sūtra, he analyzes unspeakable numbers of dharma-gates;
within each and every dharma-gate, he further explains unspeakable numbers of dharmas.
Within each and every one of those dharmas, Inconceivable numbers of sentient beings are tamed.
Or again, upon the tip of a single hair, They dwell for inconceivable eons;
As it is with one hair-tip, so it is with all others, And the number of eons they dwell is likewise.
Their minds are unimpeded and ineffable; the manifestations of the Buddhas are ineffable.
Each and every manifested Tathāgata further manifests further manifestations that are ineffable.
That Buddha’s Dharma-body is ineffable; That Buddha’s emanated bodies are ineffable;
His immeasurable adornments are ineffable; His journeys to the ten directions are ineffable;
His travels through all lands are ineffable; His observation of sentient beings is ineffable.
The purification of sentient beings is unspeakable; The taming of sentient beings is unspeakable.
Their various adornments are unspeakable; Their various spiritual powers are unspeakable;
Their various masteries are unspeakable; Their various miraculous transformations are unspeakable.
All spiritual powers are ineffable; all realms are ineffable;
all empowerments are ineffable; all worlds in which they dwell are ineffable.
The pure true nature is ineffable; the teaching of the sūtras is ineffable.
Within each and every sūtra, the exposition of dharma-gates is ineffable;
within each and every dharma-gate, the further explanation of all dharmas is ineffable.
Within each and every one of those dharmas, all that is determinate is ineffable;
within each and every one of those determinates, the taming of sentient beings is ineffable.
Inexpressible are dharmas of the same class; Inexpressible is the mind of the same class;
Inexpressible are dharmas of different classes; Inexpressible is the mind of different classes;
Inexpressible are the faculties of different classes; Inexpressible are the languages of different classes.
In every thought-moment, throughout all places of practice, Taming sentient beings is unspeakable;
All spiritual transformations are unspeakable, All manifestations are unspeakable;
The eons within them are unspeakable, The distinctions within them are unspeakable.
The Bodhisattva is able to analyze and explain them all, such that even the most skilled mathematicians cannot discern them.
Within the tip of a single hair, there are buddha-lands of great and small extent;
lands that are defiled or pure, coarse or subtle—all such things are ineffable, yet each is clearly understood and can be distinguished.
If one were to grind a single land into dust, the number of those particles would be immeasurable and beyond description;
as many boundless lands as there are such particles all come together and gather upon the tip of a single hair.
These unspeakably many lands gather together upon the tip of a single hair without any crowding;
yet the tip of the hair does not expand, even as all those lands assemble there.
Within them, all the various lands, Their forms remain as they were, without confusion;
As one land does not interfere with another, So it is with all lands.
The realm of empty space is boundless; He can cause every hair-tip to be filled with it.
Within all such lands upon those hair-tips, A Bodhisattva can describe them all in a single thought-moment.
Within a single subtle pore, unspeakably many lands enter in succession;
the pore can contain all those lands, yet the lands cannot pervade the pore.
The number of kalpas for entering is unspeakable; The number of kalpas for receiving is unspeakable;
And while abiding in this array, All kalpas are beyond description.
Having thus embraced and settled therein, The realms of experience are ineffable;
The skillful means of entry are ineffable; What is done after entering is ineffable;
The clarity of the mental faculty is ineffable; Wandering through all directions is ineffable.
Their courageous diligence is unspeakable; their sovereign spiritual transformations are unspeakable;
all their reflections are unspeakable; all their great vows are unspeakable;
all their spheres of experience are unspeakable; and their universal penetration of all things is unspeakable.
The purity of physical action is unspeakable; The purity of verbal action is unspeakable;
The purity of mental action is unspeakable; The purity of faith and understanding is unspeakable;
The purity of sublime wisdom is unspeakable; The purity of sublime insight is unspeakable.
The realization of all true realities is ineffable; The severing of all doubts and delusions is ineffable;
Transcending birth and death is ineffable; Ascending to the stage of certainty is ineffable;
The profound samādhi is ineffable; The thorough penetration of all things is ineffable.
All sentient beings are ineffable; all Buddha-fields are ineffable.
Knowing the bodies of sentient beings is ineffable; knowing their mental inclinations is ineffable;
knowing the fruits of their karma is ineffable; and knowing the resolutions of their minds is ineffable.
Knowing that their categories are ineffable; knowing that their spiritual lineages are ineffable;
knowing that their assumption of bodies is ineffable; knowing that their places of birth are ineffable;
knowing that their actual birth is ineffable; knowing that their having been born is ineffable.
Knowing that their understanding is ineffable, knowing that their inclinations are ineffable,
knowing that their speech is ineffable, and knowing that their activities are ineffable.
The Bodhisattva possesses such great compassion, Benefiting all worlds throughout the universe.
Their manifestations are everywhere, beyond words; They enter Buddha-fields, beyond words;
They behold Bodhisattvas, beyond words; They give rise to wisdom, beyond words.
It is unspeakable how they inquire about the True Dharma; It is unspeakable how they propagate the Buddha’s teachings;
It is unspeakable how they manifest various bodies; It is unspeakable how they travel to all lands;
It is unspeakable how they display supernatural powers; It is unspeakable how they pervade the ten directions.
Manifesting bodies everywhere, unspeakably many; Approaching all Buddhas, unspeakably many;
Creating various articles of offering, unspeakably many; Of every kind and measureless variety, unspeakably many;
Pure and exquisite jewels, unspeakably many; Supremely wondrous lotus flowers, unspeakably many.
Inexpressible are the most excellent fragrant garlands; Inexpressible is the making of offerings to the Tathāgatas;
Inexpressible is pure faith; Inexpressible is the most excellent realization;
Inexpressible is the superior aspiration and delight; Inexpressible is the honoring of all Buddhas.
The practice of giving is ineffable; That mind of the past is ineffable;
Giving to all who seek is ineffable; Giving everything away is ineffable;
The purity of ethical discipline is ineffable; The purity of the mental faculty is ineffable.
Praising all Buddhas is unspeakable; Delighting in the True Dharma is unspeakable;
Accomplishing all patiences is unspeakable; The patience of the non-arising of dharmas is unspeakable;
Being fully endowed with tranquility is unspeakable; Abiding in the stage of tranquility is unspeakable.
The arousal of great diligence is unspeakable; His mind in the past is unspeakable;
The mind of non-retrogression is unspeakable; The unshakable mind is unspeakable;
The treasury of all concentrations is unspeakable; The contemplation of all phenomena is unspeakable.
Tranquil in meditative concentration, it is ineffable; Thoroughly penetrating all dhyānas, it is ineffable;
Wisdom that penetrates all things, it is ineffable; Mastery over samādhi, it is ineffable;
Thoroughly penetrating all dharmas, it is ineffable; Clearly beholding all Buddhas, it is ineffable.
The cultivation of immeasurable practices is unspeakable; The arousal of vast vows is unspeakable;
The most profound realm is unspeakable; The pure Dharma-gates are unspeakable;
The power of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma is unspeakable; The abiding of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma is unspeakable.
Those various states of right mindfulness are ineffable; those various dharma-realms are ineffable;
the cultivation of the wisdom of skillful means is ineffable; the study of profound wisdom is ineffable;
immeasurable wisdom is ineffable; ultimate wisdom is ineffable.
Those various knowledges of phenomena are ineffable; that pure wheel of Dharma is ineffable;
that great cloud of Dharma is ineffable; that great rain of Dharma is ineffable;
those various supernormal powers are ineffable; and those various skillful means are ineffable.
Entering the wisdom of emptiness and stillness is ineffable; The continuous succession of every thought-moment is ineffable;
Infinite gateways of practice are ineffable; Constant abiding in every thought-moment is ineffable;
The ocean of all Buddha-lands is ineffable; Being able to travel to them all is ineffable.
The distinctions among all lands are unspeakable; Their various purities are unspeakable;
Their distinct adornments are unspeakable; Their boundless forms and signs are unspeakable;
Their various interlacing patterns are unspeakable; Their various exquisite beauties are unspeakable.
Pure buddha-fields are unspeakable; Defiled worlds are unspeakable.
Knowing sentient beings is unspeakable; Knowing their spiritual lineages is unspeakable;
Knowing their karmic retributions is unspeakable; Knowing their mental activities is unspeakable.
Knowing their faculties and natures is ineffable; knowing their understandings and inclinations is ineffable;
their defilement and purification are ineffable; observing and subduing them is ineffable;
their mastery of transformations is ineffable; manifesting various bodies is ineffable.
The cultivation of diligence is ineffable; The liberation of sentient beings is ineffable;
The manifestation of spiritual transformations is ineffable; The emission of great radiance is ineffable;
The various forms and appearances are ineffable; Causing sentient beings to attain purity is ineffable.
Each and every pore is unspeakable; The emission of nets of light is unspeakable;
The manifestation of colors by those nets of light is unspeakable; The universal illumination of Buddha-fields is unspeakable;
Courageous fearlessness is unspeakable; Skillful means and expedients are unspeakable.
Taming sentient beings is ineffable; Causing them to transcend birth and death is ineffable;
Purifying physical action is ineffable; Purifying verbal action is ineffable;
Boundless mental action is ineffable; Excellently sublime conduct is ineffable.
The accomplishment of the jewel of wisdom is unspeakable; Deep entry into the dharma-realm is unspeakable;
The bodhisattvas' dhāraṇīs are unspeakable; Their skillful cultivation and study are unspeakable;
The voices of the wise are unspeakable; The purity of those voices is unspeakable.
Right mindfulness is truly ineffable; awakening sentient beings is ineffable;
being endowed with dignified deportment is ineffable; pure cultivation is ineffable;
achieving fearlessness is ineffable; taming the world is ineffable.
The assemblies of all Buddha-sons are unspeakable; Their pure and supreme practices are unspeakable;
Praising all Buddhas is unspeakable; Extolling them inexhaustibly is unspeakable;
The Guides of the World are unspeakable; Expounding and praising them is unspeakable.
Those bodhisattvas are ineffable; their pure merits are ineffable; their limits are ineffable;
their ability to dwell therein is ineffable; the wisdom of dwelling therein is ineffable;
and even if one were to dwell there for all kalpas, it could not be fully described.
Delighting in all Buddhas is unspeakable; Wisdom that is equal is unspeakable;
Skillfully entering all phenomena is unspeakable; Being unimpeded regarding phenomena is unspeakable;
The three times being like space is unspeakable; The wisdom of the three times is unspeakable.
Thoroughly comprehending the three periods of time is ineffable; Abiding in wisdom is ineffable;
Excellently sublime conduct is ineffable; Immeasurable great vows are ineffable;
Pure great vows are ineffable; The accomplishment of bodhi is ineffable.
The Bodhi of all Buddhas is ineffable; the arising of wisdom is ineffable;
the discernment of principles is ineffable; the knowledge of all phenomena is ineffable;
the adornment and purification of Buddha-fields is ineffable; the cultivation of the various powers is ineffable.
The long-term cultivation of practice is ineffable; Awakening and understanding in a single thought-moment is ineffable;
The sovereign mastery of all Buddhas is ineffable; The extensive proclamation of the True Dharma is ineffable;
The various supernormal powers are ineffable; The manifestations within the world are ineffable.
The pure wheel of Dharma is unspeakable; The courageous ability to turn it is unspeakable;
Its various expositions are unspeakable; Its compassion for the world is unspeakable.
Though one were to spend unspeakable eons praising unspeakable virtues,
those unspeakable eons might yet come to an end, but the unspeakable virtues can never be exhausted.
Inexpressible Tathāgatas, with inexpressible tongues, Praise the Buddha’s inexpressible virtues; Even in inexpressible eons, they could never reach the end.
All sentient beings throughout the ten directions, May all simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment;
Within them, a single Buddha can universally manifest Inexpressibly many bodies.
Within one body among these unspeakable [bodies], he manifests unspeakable heads;
within one head among these unspeakable [heads], he manifests unspeakable tongues;
within one tongue among these unspeakable [tongues], he manifests unspeakable voices.
Within this ineffable single sound, it remains for an ineffable number of kalpas.
As it is with one such [sound], so it is with all Buddhas; as it is with one such [sound], so it is with all bodies, all heads, and all tongues.
If one were to use every single sound in this way, praising the Buddha for unspeakable eons,
those unspeakable eons might yet come to an end, but the praise of the Buddha’s virtues could never be exhausted.
Within a single atom there are entirely present, unspeakably many lotus worlds;
within each and every lotus world, unspeakably many Tathāgatas named Bhadramukha reside.
Even unto the entire pervasion of the dharma-realm, All the atoms contained therein—
Whether worlds are forming, abiding, or decaying, Their number is immeasurable and beyond description.
Within the space of a single atom, there are infinite boundaries; Immeasurable lands enter therein from all directions.
The distinctions of the ten directions are ineffable, And the distribution of the ocean of lands is ineffable.
In each and every land there is a Tathāgata, Whose lifespan in kalpas is ineffable;
The conduct of all Buddhas is ineffable, The profound and wondrous Dharma is ineffable,
Their supernormal powers and great strength are ineffable, And their unobstructed wisdom is ineffable.
Entering into the pores is ineffable; The causal conditions of the pores are ineffable;
Accomplishing the ten powers is ineffable; Awakening to bodhi is ineffable;
Entering the pure dharma-realm is ineffable; Attaining the treasury of profound wisdom is ineffable.
The various quantities are unspeakable, yet they know them all completely;
The various forms and measures are unspeakable, yet there is nothing therein they do not thoroughly penetrate.
The various samādhis are unspeakable; they are all able to abide therein for the duration of kalpas.
At the abodes of unspeakably many Buddhas, their pure conduct is unspeakable.
They attain an ineffable, unimpeded mind; They travel to ineffable lands in the ten directions;
They manifest ineffable displays of spiritual power; Their conduct is boundless and ineffable;
They visit ineffable multitudes of buddha-fields; They fully comprehend the ineffable Buddhas.
Their diligent vigor is unspeakable; their wisdom and penetration are unspeakable.
Regarding phenomena, they neither act nor refrain from acting; their entry into all realms is unspeakable.
Throughout unspeakably many great eons, they constantly travel throughout the ten directions—this too is unspeakable.
The wisdom of skillful means is ineffable; the wisdom of reality is ineffable;
the wisdom of supernormal powers is ineffable; the manifestations in every thought-moment are ineffable.
Regarding the ineffable dharmas of all Buddhas, Knowing each and every one to be ineffable,
They may realize enlightenment in a single moment, Or enter into realization at various times.
Buddha-fields on the tips of hairs are unspeakable; Buddha-fields within atoms are unspeakable.
Thus he visits all such Buddha-fields, And beholds unspeakably many Tathāgatas.
Penetrating the ineffable single reality, skillfully entering the ineffable Buddha-lineage,
and traversing all ineffable Buddha-lands, they are able to go forth everywhere to achieve enlightenment.
The lands, sentient beings, and all Buddhas— Their essential natures and distinctions are ineffable;
Thus, throughout the three periods of time without end, The Bodhisattva clearly perceives them all.
Chapter 31: On Lifespan At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mind-King (Cittarāja), amidst the great assembly, addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
One kalpa in the realm of Śākyamuni Buddha, this Sahā world, constitutes one day and night in the realm of Amitābha Buddha, the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
one kalpa in the Land of Ultimate Bliss constitutes one day and night in the realm of Vajradṛḍha Buddha in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja;
and one kalpa in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja constitutes one day and night in the realm of Supuṣpitaśrīpadmavikrāntarāja Buddha in the world of Avaivartikasvaracakranirghoṣa.
One eon in the world-system of Avivartyasvaracakrā is a single day and night in the Dharmanetrabuddhakṣetra of Vimalā;
one eon in the world-system of Vimalā is a single day and night in the Siṃhabuddhakṣetra of Supradīpā;
one eon in the world-system of Supradīpā is a single day and night in the Prabhāgarbhabuddhakṣetra of Sūryaprabhā.
One eon in the world-system *Sudarśanaprabhā* is a single day and night in the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata *Dharmaprabhā-saṃkusumita-padma* in the world-system *Duratikrama*;
one eon in the world-system *Duratikrama* is a single day and night in the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata *Sarvābhijñāprabha* in the world-system *Vyūhamati*;
and one eon in the world-system *Vyūhamati* is a single day and night in the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata *Candrājñāna* in the world-system *Ādarśaprabhā*.
O Son of the Buddha!

Following this sequence, even passing through as many as a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, the one *kalpa* of the final world constitutes a single day and night in the world-system of the Victorious Lotus (*Vijayapadma*) within the Buddha-field of Worthy Victory (*Bhadrottama*). This realm is filled with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all his fellow great bodhisattvas.

there currently resides a bodhisattva named:

Chapter Thirty-Three: The Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddhas, Part One.
At that time, among the great assembly, there were bodhisattvas who thought to themselves:
"In what way are the buddha-fields of the Buddhas inconceivable?"
How inconceivable are the original vows of all Buddhas?
How inconceivable is the spiritual lineage of all Buddhas?
How inconceivable is the manifestation of all Buddhas?
How is the body of the Buddhas inconceivable?
How is the voice of the Buddhas inconceivable?
How is the wisdom of the Buddhas inconceivable?
How is the sovereign mastery of the Buddhas inconceivable?
How is the unimpeded nature of the Buddhas inconceivable?
How is the liberation of the Buddhas inconceivable?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, empowered them with his spiritual power, sustained them with his wisdom, illuminated them with his radiance, and filled them with his majestic presence. He caused the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury to abide in the fearlessness of the Buddhas, enter the Buddha-dharmadhātu, attain the Buddha’s majesty and virtue, achieve mastery in supernormal powers, obtain the unimpeded and vast observation of a Buddha, know the sequential order of all Buddha-lineages, and dwell in the inconceivable skillful means of the Buddha-dharmas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury was able to penetrate the unobstructed Dharma-realm; he was able to abide securely in profound practices free from hindrances; he was able to fulfill the great vows of Samantabhadra; and he was able to know and see all Buddha-dharmas. Observing sentient beings with a heart of great compassion, he desired to lead them to purity through diligent cultivation without weariness or indolence. He received and practiced all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, giving birth to Buddha-wisdom in a single thought-moment, understanding all inexhaustible gates of wisdom, and being fully endowed with dharanis and eloquence.
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he addressed the Bodhisattva Lotus Treasury, saying: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have immeasurable abodes, namely: they abide in great compassion;

they abide in manifesting various bodies to perform the works of Buddhas; they abide in turning the pure wheel of Dharma with an impartial mind; they abide in expounding immeasurable teachings through the four analytical knowledges; they abide in all inconceivable Buddha-dharmas; they abide in pure voices pervading immeasurable lands; they abide in the ineffable and profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*); they abide in manifesting all supreme supernatural powers; and they abide in being able to reveal the ultimate dharma that is without obstruction.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of dharmas that pervade the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-realm. What are these ten?
That is to say:
all Buddhas possess boundless bodies, whose physical forms are pure, entering universally into all realms of existence without defilement or attachment;
all Buddhas possess boundless, unobstructed eyes, which are able to clearly perceive all phenomena.
All Buddhas possess boundless and unobstructed ears, capable of fully understanding all sounds;
all Buddhas possess boundless noses, able to reach the shore of mastery of all Buddhas;
all Buddhas possess broad and long tongues, emitting wondrous sounds that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
All Buddhas possess boundless bodies that manifest in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, enabling all to behold them;
all Buddhas possess boundless intentions, abiding in the unimpeded and equal Dharma-body;
all Buddhas possess boundless and unimpeded liberation, manifesting inexhaustible and great supernormal powers.

All Buddhas possess boundless, pure worlds; according to the inclinations of sentient beings, they manifest various Buddha-lands, fully endowed with immeasurable and manifold adornments, yet they remain free from any defiled attachment therein.
All Buddhas possess boundless bodhisattva practices and vows; having attained perfect wisdom, they sport with sovereign ease and are able to thoroughly penetrate all Buddha-dharmas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which pervade the dharma-realm without limit.
O Son of the Buddha!"
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of wisdom that arise in every thought-moment. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest their descent from heaven in immeasurable worlds;
all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the birth of Bodhisattvas in immeasurable worlds;
all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest their renunciation of home life and study of the Way in immeasurable worlds.
All Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi trees in immeasurable worlds;
all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the turning of the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in immeasurable worlds;
all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment, are able to manifest the teaching and transformation of sentient beings and the making of offerings to all Buddhas in immeasurable worlds.
In a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest within immeasurable worlds various Buddha-bodies that are ineffable;
in a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest within immeasurable worlds various adornments, countless adornments, and the treasury of all-knowledge of the Tathāgatas’ sovereign power;
in a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest within immeasurable worlds immeasurable and innumerable pure sentient beings.

In a single thought-moment, all Buddhas are able to manifest the various faculties, various degrees of diligence, and various modes of practice and understanding of the Buddhas of the three periods of time throughout immeasurable worlds, as well as their attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment within those three periods.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of non-misplaced timing."
What are these ten? They are:
all Buddhas attain equal and perfect enlightenment without missing the proper time;
All Buddhas bring those with whom they have a karmic connection to maturity without missing the proper time;
all Buddhas bestow predictions of enlightenment upon Bodhisattvas without missing the proper time;
all Buddhas manifest spiritual powers in accordance with the minds of sentient beings without missing the proper time.
All Buddhas manifest Buddha-bodies according to the understanding of sentient beings without missing the proper time;
all Buddhas abide in great equanimity without missing the proper time;
all Buddhas enter various villages without missing the proper time.
All Buddhas gather in those of pure faith without missing the proper time;
all Buddhas discipline evil sentient beings without missing the proper time;
all Buddhas manifest the inconceivable spiritual powers of a Buddha without missing the proper time.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
