They are as follows: not abandoning any sentient being; conceiving the thought of a Tathāgata toward all bodhisattvas; never slandering any Buddha-dharma; knowing that all buddha-lands are inexhaustible; generating profound faith and joy in the practices of bodhisattvas; not forsaking the mind of enlightenment that is equal to space and the dharma-realm; observing enlightenment and entering the powers of a Tathāgata; diligently cultivating unimpeded eloquence; teaching and transforming sentient beings without weariness; and dwelling in all worlds with a mind free from attachment.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide securely in these ten dharmas, they are then able to fulfill ten kinds of purity."
What are these ten? They are: purity through penetrating the profound Dharma;

purity through attending upon spiritual friends; purity through upholding the teachings of all Buddhas; purity through thoroughly understanding the realm of space; purity through deeply entering the Dharma-realm; purity through observing the boundless mind; purity through sharing the same roots of goodness as all bodhisattvas; purity through non-attachment to all eons; purity through observing the three periods of time; and purity through practicing all the teachings of the Buddhas.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these ten dharmas, they become fully endowed with ten kinds of vast wisdom."

What are these ten? They are: the wisdom that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings; the wisdom that knows the karmic retributions of all sentient beings; the wisdom that knows all Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom that knows the profound and secret principles of all Buddha-dharmas; the wisdom that knows all *dhāraṇī* gates; the wisdom that knows the eloquence of all written characters; the wisdom that possesses skill in the languages, sounds, and expressions of all sentient beings; the wisdom that universally manifests its body in all worlds; the wisdom that universally manifests its image within all assemblies; and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) complete within all places of rebirth.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these ten knowledges, they then attain entry into ten kinds of universal penetration."
What are these ten? They are:
all worlds entering into a single hair-pore, and a single hair-pore entering into all worlds;
The bodies of all sentient beings enter into one body, and one body enters into the bodies of all sentient beings;
unspeakable eons enter into a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment enters into unspeakable eons;
all Buddha-dharmas enter into a single dharma, and a single dharma enters into all Buddha-dharmas.
The unspeakable enters a single place, and a single place enters the unspeakable;
the unspeakable faculties enter a single faculty, and a single faculty enters the unspeakable faculties;
all faculties enter the non-faculty, and the non-faculty enters all faculties.
All perceptions enter into a single perception, and a single perception enters into all perceptions;
all speech and sounds enter into a single speech and sound, and a single speech and sound enters into all speech and sounds;
all three periods of time enter into a single period of time, and a single period of time enters into all three periods of time.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have observed in this manner, they abide in ten kinds of sublime and wondrous minds."

What are these ten? They are: the sublime mind that abides in the speech and non-speech of all worlds; the sublime mind that abides in the mental conceptions of all sentient beings without any basis; the sublime mind that abides in the ultimate realm of empty space; the sublime mind that abides in the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); the sublime mind that abides in all profound and secret Buddha-dharmas; the sublime mind that abides in the extremely deep and undifferentiated Dharma; the sublime mind that abides in the eradication of all doubts and delusions; the sublime mind that abides in the equality and non-differentiation of all worlds; the sublime mind that abides in the equality of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; and the sublime mind that abides in the immeasurable powers of all Buddhas.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas abide in these ten kinds of sublime and wondrous minds, they then attain ten kinds of skillful knowledge regarding the Buddha-dharma."

What are these ten? They are: the skillful wisdom that thoroughly understands the profound Buddha-dharma; the skillful wisdom that gives birth to the vast Buddha-dharma; the skillful wisdom that proclaims the various Buddha-dharmas; the skillful wisdom that realizes the equality of the Buddha-dharma; the skillful wisdom that clearly discerns the distinctions within the Buddha-dharma; the skillful wisdom that awakens to and understands the non-distinction of the Buddha-dharma; the skillful wisdom that deeply enters the adornments of the Buddha-dharma; the skillful wisdom that enters the Buddha-dharma through a single expedient means; the skillful wisdom that enters the Buddha-dharma through immeasurable expedient means; the skillful wisdom that knows the non-distinction of the boundless Buddha-dharmas; and the skillful wisdom that, by the power of one’s own mind and one’s own strength, does not regress from any of the Buddha-dharmas.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Having heard this Dharma, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should all resolve their minds to respectfully receive and uphold it."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds this Dharma will, with little exertion, swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they shall fully possess all Buddha-dharmas, which are entirely equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma,
worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.
There fell clouds of flowers, clouds of incense, clouds of powdered incense, and clouds of robes and parasols, all surpassing those of all the devas.
Clouds of banners, pennants, mani-jewels, and all manner of ornaments; clouds raining various musical performances;
clouds raining bodhisattvas; clouds raining the unspeakable physical marks and signs of the Tathāgatas;
clouds raining unspeakable praises of "Excellent! to the Tathāgatas; and clouds raining the voices of the Tathāgatas that fill all phenomena.
From the clouds of realms, they rain down clouds of unspeakably adorned worlds; they rain down clouds of unspeakably increasing bodhi;
they rain down clouds of unspeakably radiant illumination; they rain down clouds of unspeakably teaching the Dharma through spiritual powers.

Just as in this world, beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment within the Bodhisattva palace of the four continents, one sees the Tathāgata attaining perfect enlightenment and expounding this Dharma, so it is likewise in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because the nature of phenomena is thus, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there came to this land bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, filling the ten directions and speaking these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to expound this profound Dharma of the prediction of great vows of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
O Son of the Buddha!

We are all named Samantabhadra, each having come from the world called Universal Excellence to this land from the presence of the Tathāgata Universal Banner Sovereignty. By the spiritual power of the Buddha, we have expounded this Dharma in all places;
just as in this assembly and just as it has been spoken here, it is entirely equal everywhere, without increase or decrease.
We all, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, have come to this site of enlightenment to bear witness for you.
Just as we, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, have come to bear witness here, so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and the power of his own roots of goodness, surveyed the ten directions throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Desiring to reveal the conduct of Bodhisattvas, desiring to proclaim the realm of the Tathāgata’s enlightenment, desiring to speak of the realm of great vows, desiring to explain the number of kalpas in all worlds, desiring to clarify how the Buddhas appear according to the times, desiring to explain how the Tathāgata appears before sentient beings whose faculties have matured so that they may make offerings, desiring to clarify that the merit of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is never in vain, desiring to clarify that the roots of goodness one plants will surely yield their fruit, and desiring to clarify how Bodhisattvas of great majesty manifest forms and preach the Dharma for all sentient beings to bring them to awakening, he spoke these verses:
“You all should rejoice, And cast off all hindrances.”
Listen with single-minded reverence to the various vows and practices of the Bodhisattvas.
I shall now explain in due order the practices cultivated by the bodhisattvas of the past, those most excellent lions among men;
I shall also describe the number of kalpas, the worlds, and all their karmic deeds.
And the Peerless Honored One appeared therein.
Such were the Buddhas of the past who arose in the world through great vows;
how did they extinguish all suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings?
All the lions among teachers, whose conduct was continuous and perfected,
attained the Buddha’s equal Dharma, the realm of omniscience.
They beheld all the lions among men of the past.
Emitting a great net of light rays, they universally illumine the realms of the ten directions.
Contemplating thus, they make this vow:
"I shall become a lamp for the world, fully endowed with the merits of a Buddha, the ten powers, and all-encompassing wisdom."
All sentient beings are ablaze with greed, hatred, and delusion;
I shall rescue and liberate them all, causing them to extinguish the sufferings of the evil realms.
Having made such a vow, may it be firm and irreversible.
Fully cultivating the bodhisattva practices, he attains the ten unimpeded powers.
Having made such vows, he practices without retreat or fear;
his deeds are all unfailing, and he is called a Lion among Teachers.
Within a single Bhadrakalpa, a thousand Buddhas appear in the world;
I shall now explain their Universal Eye in due order.
As it is within one Bhadrakalpa, so it is throughout immeasurable kalpas.
I shall now explain in detail the future practices of those Buddhas;
as it is with one Buddha-field system, so it is with immeasurable fields.
I shall now describe all the deeds of the future Honored Ones of Ten Powers.
As the various Buddhas arise in succession within the world, according to their vows and their names,
according to the predictions they receive, according to the length of their lifespans,
and according to the True Dharma they practice, they single-mindedly seek the unimpeded path.
According to the beings to be transformed, the True Dharma abides in the world;
according to the Buddha-fields purified, so too do the sentient beings and the Wheel of Dharma.
Expounding at the proper and improper times, they gradually purify the multitudes of living beings.
In accordance with the karma of sentient beings, their conduct, and their inclinations—
whether superior, middling, or inferior— he transforms them to lead them in practice.
Entering into such wisdom, he cultivates the most supreme conduct.
Constantly performing the deeds of Samantabhadra, Universally delivering all sentient beings.
With unobstructed physical karma, And speech-karma entirely pure, The mental conduct is likewise so;
Throughout the three periods of time, it is no otherwise.
When Bodhisattvas practice in this way, they ultimately fulfill the path of Samantabhadra;
they give rise to the sun of pure wisdom, which shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm.
Throughout all kalpas of future ages, there will be unspeakable numbers of lands.
In a single thought, one fully understands them, yet remains without discrimination therein.
The practitioner is able to enter this most supreme stage;
I shall now briefly explain these dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
With wisdom that has no limit, they penetrate the realm of the Buddhas;
they enter skillfully into all things, and their practice never regresses.
Endowed with the wisdom of Samantabhadra, they fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra.
Entering into peerless wisdom, I shall now explain that practice:
within a single atom, all worlds are clearly seen;
were sentient beings to hear this, their minds would become confused and they would go mad.
As it is with a single atom, so it is with all atoms;
the entire world enters within them, in a manner thus inconceivable.
Within each and every atom, there exist the phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The realms of all destinies are infinite, yet he can discern and know them all.
Within every single atom there are infinite kinds of Buddha-fields;
though these various fields are all immeasurable, there is not one that he does not know.
All that exists within the dharma-realm, The various and diverse characteristics,
And the distinct differences among the classes of beings— He is able to discern and know them all.
Deeply entering subtle wisdom, He distinguishes all worlds.
The formation and destruction of all kalpas, he can explain with complete clarity.
Knowing the length and brevity of all kalpas, he realizes that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment.
Whether various practices are identical or different, he is able to discern and know them all.
They enter deeply into all worlds— those vast and those not vast—
wherein a single body pervades immeasurable lands, and a single land contains immeasurable bodies.
Throughout the ten directions, there exist all the various kinds of worlds.
The vast and immeasurable marks, they are able to know them all.
Within all the three periods of time, throughout immeasurable lands,
possessing profound and perfect wisdom, they fully comprehend their formation and destruction.
In the worlds of the ten directions, some are forming and some are decaying;
such things are ineffable, yet those of noble virtue understand them all profoundly.
There are also various lands, adorned with diverse kinds of ground.
The various realms of existence are likewise so, arising from the purity of one's karma.
There are some worlds that possess immeasurable varieties of defilement;
these arise from the karmic retribution of sentient beings, all according to their own conduct.
Immeasurable and boundless lands, one knows them all to be a single land;
thus entering into all lands, their number is unknowable.
All worlds without exception enter entirely within a single land.
The worlds are not one, yet they are neither confused nor disordered;
some worlds face upward, others face downward, some are high and others are low—
all these are the perceptions of sentient beings, which [the Buddha] can discern and know completely.
Throughout vast and expansive worlds, immeasurable and boundless,
they know the manifold as one, and know the one as manifold.
O Samantabhadra, sons of the Buddhas, you who are able to employ the wisdom of Samantabhadra—
They thoroughly know the number of all lands, a number that is without limit.
They know the transformations of all worlds— the transformation of lands, the transformation of sentient beings,
the transformation of dharmas, and the transformation of all Buddhas— all of which reach ultimate perfection.
All worlds throughout the ten directions, Subtle and vast lands,
With their various and diverse adornments, Arise entirely from karma.
Innumerable sons of the Buddha, Skillfully training to enter the Dharma-realm,
With sovereign power of supernormal knowledges, pervading the ten directions,
even if one were to speak the names of those worlds for as many eons as there are sentient beings,
one could not exhaust them, except through the revelation of a Buddha.
The worlds and the Tathāgatas, with all their various names and titles,
could not be fully described even after passing through immeasurable eons;
how much less so the most supreme wisdom and the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time!
Born from the dharma-realm, they fill the stage of the Tathāgata!
With pure and unimpeded mindfulness and boundless, unobstructed wisdom,
they discern and expound the dharma-realm, having reached the further shore.
All worlds of the past, whether vast or minute,
adorned by their cultivation, he can know them all in a single thought.
Among them, those lions among men who have practiced the various deeds of a Buddha—
Having attained perfect enlightenment, they manifest all sovereign powers;
likewise, throughout the future ages, over successive immeasurable kalpas,
the Bodhisattvas are able to know all those who are the Honored Ones among men.
All vows and practices, all realms and spheres—
By diligently cultivating these, one attains perfect enlightenment therein.
One also knows those assemblies, their lifespans, and how they transform sentient beings.
By means of these various Dharma-gates, they turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
Bodhisattvas who know thus abide on the stage of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
their wisdom is fully clear and lucid, giving birth to all Buddhas.
Comprising all the Buddha-fields of the present age,
they enter deeply into these lands and penetrate the Dharma-realm.
Within those worlds, they perceive all the Buddhas currently residing there.
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, their discourse is unimpeded.
They also know the assemblies of beings, the power of their pure lands, and their transformative manifestations;
throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, they constantly contemplate these matters.
The Honored One who tames the world, with all his majestic spiritual power and inexhaustible treasury of wisdom, is able to know everything.
He gives birth to unimpeded eyes, and unimpeded ears, nose, and body.
With an unimpeded, broad, and long tongue, he is able to bring joy to all beings.
Possessing the most supreme and unimpeded mind, vast and universally pure,
his wisdom fills everywhere as he fully knows the dharmas of the three periods of time.
Skillfully training in all transformations— the transformation of lands, the transformation of sentient beings,
the transformation of worlds, and the transformation of discipline— one reaches the ultimate shore of transformation.
The manifold distinctions of the world all arise from abiding in conceptualization.
Entering the Buddha’s wisdom of skillful means, they understand all of this with complete clarity.
To the unspeakably vast assemblies, he manifests his body for each and every one,
causing them all to behold the Tathāgata and leading countless beings to liberation.
The profound wisdom of all Buddhas is like the sun rising upon the world;
throughout all lands, it manifests everywhere without ceasing.
It fully comprehends that all worlds are merely provisional names and possess no substantial reality.
Sentient beings and the world are like dreams and like reflections of light;
regarding all worldly phenomena, one does not give rise to discriminative views.
One who is well-detached from discrimination likewise does not perceive discrimination.
Immeasurable and incalculable eons, when understood, are but a single thought-moment;
knowing that this thought-moment is itself without thought—thus one perceives the world.
Immeasurable lands, in a single thought-moment, are all transcended.
Passing through immeasurable eons, they do not move from their original place.
Unspeakable eons are but a single moment; do not perceive length or brevity, for all is ultimately the dharma of the *kṣaṇa*.
The mind dwells in the world, and the world dwells in the mind;
regarding these, do not give rise to false conceptions, nor to the dualistic discrimination of "two" or "not-two.
Sentient beings, worlds, and eons, as well as all Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma—[all are thus].
All things are like illusions and transformations; the Dharma-realm is entirely equal.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, they manifest infinite bodies;
knowing that these bodies arise from conditions, they ultimately remain unattached.
Relying upon non-dual wisdom, the Lion among Men appears;
Unattached to the dharma of non-duality, he knows that non-duality is not dual.
He thoroughly understands all worlds To be like a mirage, like a shadow, or like a reflection.
Like an echo and like a dream, like a magical illusion and like a transformation;
entering thus in accordance with these, one reaches the sphere of action of all Buddhas,
accomplishes the wisdom of Samantabhadra, and universally illumines the profound Dharma-realm.
Sentient beings are stained by attachments; having relinquished them all, they give rise to the mind of great compassion and universally purify all worlds.
The Bodhisattva always maintains right mindfulness, discoursing upon the lion-like sublime Dharma.
Pure as space, they give rise to great skillful means.
Seeing that the world is constantly deluded and inverted, they resolve to save all beings;
their practices are entirely pure, pervading the entire realm of phenomena.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the Buddha-dharma and the worldly dharma—
if one perceives their true reality, there is no distinction between them at all.
The Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya-treasury universally pervades the world.
Though dwelling in the world, one has no attachment to the world.
Just as in pure water, reflections neither come nor go;
know that the Dharma-body pervading the world is likewise so.
Thus, free from defilement and attachment, body and world are both pure;
serene as empty space, all things are without arising.
Knowing that the body is inexhaustible, it neither arises nor ceases.
Neither eternal nor impermanent, it manifests throughout all worlds.
It eradicates all false views and reveals right view;
the nature of phenomena neither comes nor goes, and it is free from attachment to self and what belongs to self.
Just as a skilled illusionist manifests various phenomena,
which come from nowhere and go nowhere;
the nature of illusion is neither finite nor infinite.
Within that great assembly, he manifests both the measurable and the immeasurable.
By means of this mind of tranquil concentration, he cultivates all roots of goodness;
from these arise all Buddhas, who are neither measurable nor immeasurable.
The finite and the infinite are both entirely false imaginings;
having thoroughly understood all realms of existence, one does not cling to the finite or the infinite.
The profound Dharma of the Buddhas is vast, deep, and utterly tranquil.
With profound and immeasurable wisdom, they know the depths of all realms of existence.
Free from delusion and inversion, their pure minds flow in constant succession;
through their skillful exercise of supernormal powers, they deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
They bring peace to those who are not yet at peace, and to those already at peace, they reveal the site of enlightenment;
thus pervading the entire dharma-realm, their minds remain without attachment.
They do not abide in the limit of reality, nor do they enter into nirvana.
Thus throughout the entire world, he awakens all living beings.
Knowing the number of dharmas and the number of sentient beings, he understands them without attachment;
he rains down the rain of Dharma everywhere, saturating all worlds.
Throughout all worlds, in every thought-moment,
they attain perfect enlightenment and cultivate the bodhisattva practices, never once turning back.
They fully comprehend all the various bodies within the world.
Knowing the nature of the body in this way, one attains the body of all Buddhas.
Universally knowing all sentient beings, all kalpas,
and all lands throughout the ten directions without limit, there is no ocean of wisdom into which they do not enter.
The bodies of sentient beings are immeasurable, yet he manifests a body for each and every one;
the Buddha’s body is boundless, and the wise perceive it all.
Within a single thought-moment, he brings forth the appearance of all Tathāgatas.
Even throughout immeasurable eons, their praises could not be fully extolled.
The Buddhas are able to manifest their bodies and enter parinirvāṇa in every place;
within a single thought-moment, they appear in infinite numbers, each with distinct relics.
Likewise, in future ages, those who seek the fruit of Buddhahood and possess the immeasurable bodhicitta— all these the Wisdom of Certainty knows fully.
Thus, throughout the three times, all the Tathāgatas—
One who can know all things in their entirety is said to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Discerning and knowing in this way the immeasurable stages of practice,
one enters the realm of wisdom, where the wheel never regresses.
Subtle, wondrous, and vast wisdom, Deeply entering the realm of the Tathāgata;
Having entered, never to regress— This is called the wisdom of Samantabhadra.
The Most Victorious Honored One of all Universally enters the Buddha-realm.
Practicing without regression, they attain unsurpassed bodhi.
With immeasurable and boundless minds, each with its distinct karma—all are accumulated through conceptualization; these they fully understand with equanimity.
Defiled and undefiled, The minds of those in training and those beyond training—
All these unspeakable states of mind, He knows fully in every single thought-moment.
He understands them as neither one nor two, Neither defiled nor pure.
Nor is there any confusion; all arise from one's own perceptions.
Thus one clearly sees that for all sentient beings, the mental conceptions differ, giving rise to the various worlds.
By means of such skillful expedients, Cultivating all supreme practices,
Born through transformation from the Buddha-dharma, One is named Samantabhadra.
Sentient beings all falsely give rise to The perceptions of good and evil realms;
Because of this, some are born in heaven, while others fall into hell.
When Bodhisattvas contemplate the world, they see it arises from the karma of false conceptualization;
because false conceptualization is boundless, the world is likewise immeasurable.
All lands throughout the ten directions Are manifested by the web of conceptualization;
By means of the skillful methods of the net of illusion, One can enter them all in a single thought-moment.
The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, And the faculty of mind are likewise so.
The world’s perceptions are diverse, yet one can enter them all with equanimity.
Within each and every realm of the eye, infinite eyes all enter;
though their various natures are distinct, they are infinite and ineffable.
What is seen is without distinction, nor is there any confusion;
each, according to their own karma, experiences its respective retribution.
The power of Samantabhadra is immeasurable, for he knows them all completely.
All objects within the realm of the eye, great wisdom is able to enter them all.
Thus, all worlds can be discerned and known;
while practicing all deeds, there is likewise no regression.
The Buddha’s teaching, the teaching of sentient beings, And the teaching of lands—such teachings of the three periods of time, He fully understands them all in their various forms.
Within the past, there is the future; Within the future, there is the present.
The three periods of time see one another, each and every one clearly understood.
In such infinite ways, he awakens all worlds;
the skillful means of the Omniscient One are beyond the reach of limits.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Forty-nine;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 37: The Appearance of the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a great radiance named "Appearance of the Tathāgata," with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of light rays as its retinue.

That light shone universally throughout all worlds in the ten directions, as far as the void of the Dharma-realm; it circled to the right ten times, manifesting the infinite sovereignty of the Tathāgata, awakening countless multitudes of bodhisattvas, shaking all worlds in the ten directions, extinguishing the sufferings of all evil realms, eclipsing all the palaces of Māras, and revealing all Buddhas and Tathāgatas seated upon the Bodhi throne, attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, together with all their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment.
Having performed these deeds, it returned and circled to the right the assembly of bodhisattvas, then entered the crown of the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagotrasamudgataruciraguṇa.
At that time, the entire great assembly at this site of enlightenment leaped for joy in body and mind, giving rise to great rapture, and thought to themselves:
"How marvelous and extraordinary!
"Now that the Tathāgata has emitted this great radiance, he will surely proclaim the most profound Great Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Nature-Arising Subtle Virtue, seated upon a lotus throne, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and with single-minded devotion toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:
"The Great Wisdom born of the merits of Perfect Enlightenment, Universally penetrating all realms and reaching the further shore."
Equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, I now pay respectful homage to you.
Having ascended to the shore of the signless realm, you manifest a body adorned with wondrous marks.
Emitting a thousand stainless rays of light, you utterly destroy the hosts of Māra.
All worlds throughout the ten directions, He is able to shake them all without exception;
Yet he never causes even a single sentient being to feel fear— Such is the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata.
The nature of the void and the dharma-realm is equal; having been able to abide thus, may all sentient beings, however infinite in number, cause all evils to cease and all defilements to be removed.
Having practiced asceticism and exerted effort for countless eons, you have accomplished the supreme path of Bodhi;
your wisdom is unimpeded regarding all spheres of experience, and your nature is identical to that of all Buddhas.
The Teacher has emitted this great radiance, Shaking all worlds throughout the ten directions;
Having manifested immeasurable supernormal powers, It now returns once more and enters my body.

Those who have well trained in the definitive Dharma, And all the immeasurable bodhisattvas who have gathered here, Have inspired in me the resolve to inquire about the Dharma; Therefore, I now entreat the King of Dharma.
This present assembly is entirely pure, Able to skillfully deliver all the worlds;
With boundless wisdom and free from attachment, Such noble and excellent ones have all gathered here.

Honored Teacher who benefits the world, whose wisdom and diligence are both immeasurable, you now illuminate the great assembly with light; I pray that you allow me to inquire about the unsurpassed Dharma.
Who is able to truly and fully expound the profound realm of the Great Seer?
Who is the eldest son of the Tathāgata’s Dharma?
O Honored Guide of the World, please reveal this!
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted from his mouth a great radiance named "Unobstructed and Fearless," with hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeya rays of light as its retinue.

It universally illumined all worlds throughout the ten directions, as vast as empty space and equal to the Dharma-realm, circling them ten times to the right. It manifested the various sovereign powers of the Tathāgata, awakening immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas, shaking all worlds in the ten directions, extinguishing the sufferings of all evil realms, eclipsing all the palaces of Māras, and revealing all Buddhas and Tathāgatas seated upon the Bodhi throne, attaining perfect enlightenment, along with all their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment.
Having performed these deeds, it came and circled the assembly of bodhisattvas to the right, entering the mouth of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.

Once that light had entered, the body and lion throne of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva became a hundred times greater than they were before, as did the bodies and thrones of all the other bodhisattvas, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata’s lion throne.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-vyuha-guṇa asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

This vast display of great supernormal transformations manifested by the Buddha causes all Bodhisattvas to give rise to joy; it is inconceivable and cannot be known by the world. What auspicious sign is this?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

In the past, I beheld all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones manifesting such vast and great supernatural transformations, and thereupon they expounded the Dharma-gate of the Appearance of the Tathāgata."
"As I contemplate it, since this sign has now appeared, you shall preach that Dharma.
When these words were spoken, the entire great earth shook in its entirety, and immeasurable light illuminating the questions of the Dharma emerged.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nature-Arising Subtle Virtue asked the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:
"Son of the Buddha!
How should a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understand the manner in which the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear?"
"May the Buddha explain this for me!
Son of the Buddha!

This assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas has all long cultivated pure deeds and perfected mindfulness and wisdom; they have reached the ultimate shore of great adornment, possess the conduct and dignified bearing of all Buddhas, maintain right mindfulness of all Buddhas without ever forgetting, observe all sentient beings with great compassion, definitively understand the spheres of supernatural power of the great bodhisattvas, have already received the empowerment of the spiritual power of all Buddhas, and are able to receive the sublime Dharma of all Tathāgatas."
Endowed with such immeasurable merits as these, they have all gathered here. O Son of the Buddha!

You have already served and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas; you have accomplished the most supreme and wondrous practices of a Bodhisattva; you have attained mastery over all gates of samādhi; you have entered the secret realms of all Buddhas; you know the teachings of all Buddhas; you have severed all doubts and delusions; you are empowered by the spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas; you know the faculties of sentient beings and preach the Dharma of true liberation according to their inclinations; you follow the wisdom of the Buddhas to expound the Buddha-Dharma and reach the other shore. You possess such immeasurable merits as these.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!

We pray that you will explain the manner in which the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears: his physical marks, his speech and sounds, the sphere of his mind, the practices he performs, his attainment of the Way and turning of the Dharma, up to his manifestation of entry into parinirvāṇa; and the roots of goodness produced by seeing, hearing, and drawing near to him—such matters as these, we pray that you will explain them all for us!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-vyūha-śrī, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra with these verses:
"Excellent is your unimpeded great wisdom; You have well awakened to the boundless realm of equality.
I pray you will speak of the infinite conduct of the Buddhas, That the sons of the Buddha, having heard it, may all rejoice!"
How do Bodhisattvas accord with and enter [the truth] regarding the appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world?
What are the spheres of their body, speech, and mind, and their spheres of activity? Please explain all of this!
How do the Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment?
How does the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma?
How does the Sugata enter parinirvāṇa?
Having heard this, the great assembly rejoiced in their hearts.

If there are those who behold the Buddha, the Great Dharma King, and draw near to him to increase all roots of goodness, I pray you will explain that treasury of merits: what do sentient beings obtain upon seeing him?

If there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata, whether he is in the present world or has entered parinirvāṇa, and give rise to deep faith in that treasury of merit—what benefits will they obtain? Please proclaim this!
All these bodhisattvas join their palms and gaze upon the Tathāgata, upon you, and upon me—the realm of the ocean of great merit. O Purifier of sentient beings, we pray that you will speak!
I pray that you will, by means of causes, conditions, and parables, expound the meaning corresponding to the sublime Dharma;
having heard it, may sentient beings give rise to the Great Mind, their doubts exhausted and their wisdom purified like space.
Just as throughout all lands, the adorned bodies manifested by all Buddhas exist,
may you likewise reveal the Buddha’s Bodhi through wondrous sounds and causal analogies.
In the thousands of millions of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, across billions of nayutas of immeasurable eons,
such an assembly of bodhisattvas gathered as now is difficult to encounter anywhere among them all.
All these bodhisattvas pay reverent homage, And give rise to a yearning thirst for the subtle and wondrous meaning.
We pray that you will fully expound with a pure mind The vast Dharma of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world!
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Tathāgatagotraśrī and others, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This place is inconceivable; that is to say, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared by means of immeasurable dharmas. Why is this?
The appearance of a Tathāgata is not accomplished through a single condition nor through a single matter;
rather, it is accomplished through ten immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya matters.
What are these ten?
They are as follows:

It is because it is formed by the bodhicitta that has encompassed all sentient beings throughout immeasurable past eons; because it is formed by immeasurable past pure and sublime aspirations; because it is formed by immeasurable past great loving-kindness and great compassion that rescue and protect all sentient beings; because it is formed by immeasurable past continuous practices and vows; because it is formed by immeasurable past cultivation of merit and wisdom with a mind never weary or satisfied; because it is formed by immeasurable past offerings to the Buddhas and the teaching and transforming of sentient beings; because it is formed by immeasurable past paths of wisdom and skillful means that are utterly pure; because it is formed by immeasurable past treasuries of pure merit; because it is formed by immeasurable past knowledge of the path of adornment; and because it is formed by immeasurable past thorough penetration of the meaning of the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!
Thus, through the perfection of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya dharma-gates, one becomes a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!

For example, a trichiliocosm is not accomplished through a single condition nor through a single matter; it is only through immeasurable conditions and immeasurable matters that it is finally brought into being.
That is to say:
great clouds arise and spread, pouring down heavy rain, sustained by a succession of four kinds of wind-circles as their support.
What are these four?
The first name is:
Able to Sustain, because it can sustain great waters;
the second name is:
It is called "Able to Eliminate," because it can eliminate great floods;
its third name is "Establishment," because it establishes all locations.
The four names are:
Adornment, and Skillfulness in the Distribution of Adornments.

All of these arise from the collective karma of sentient beings and the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas, causing all sentient beings therein to receive and enjoy them each according to their own suitability.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is through such immeasurable causes and conditions that a trichiliocosm is formed. Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): there is no one who gives birth to it, no one who creates it, no one who knows it, and no one who accomplishes it; yet, that world is nonetheless brought into existence.

The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise so: it is not accomplished by a single condition nor by a single matter, but is accomplished through immeasurable causes and conditions and immeasurable phenomena.
That is to say:

having in the past heard and upheld the great rain-clouds of the Dharma from the presence of former Buddhas, they are thereby able to give rise to the four kinds of great wisdom-wind-circles of the Tathāgata.
What are these four?
First is the great wisdom wind-wheel of the dhāraṇī of mindful retention without forgetfulness, which can sustain the great dharma-cloud rains of all Tathāgatas;
second is the great wisdom wind-wheel that gives birth to śamatha and vipaśyanā, which can exhaust and dry up all afflictions.
Third is the great wisdom wind-wheel of skillful dedication, which is able to accomplish all roots of goodness;

fourth is the great wisdom wind-wheel of birth through stainless, distinct adornments, which purifies the roots of goodness of all sentient beings previously transformed, thereby accomplishing the power of the Tathāgata’s untainted roots of goodness.
The Tathāgata thus attains equal and perfect enlightenment; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is accomplished through being unborn and unconditioned.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like when the trichiliocosm is about to be formed, a great cloud sends down rain called 'The Great Downpour.
No place whatsoever can receive it or sustain it, except for those locations within the trichiliocosm that are about to be formed."
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: he raises a great cloud of Dharma and pours down a great rain of Dharma called "The Accomplishment of the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

This cannot be received or sustained by any of the followers of the two vehicles whose mental dispositions are narrow and inferior; it can only be sustained by the power of the continuous mental stream of the great Bodhisattvas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, by the power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds send down rain; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise, through the power of the roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas, raises the great cloud of Dharma and sends down the great rain of Dharma; it also comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, when a great cloud pours down heavy rain, no sentient being within the great trichiliocosm can know its measure; were one to attempt to calculate it, it would only drive them to madness.
Only Maheśvara, the Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm, by virtue of the power of the roots of goodness cultivated in the past, understands every single drop without exception.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: he raises the great cloud of Dharma and pours down the great rain of Dharma, which all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas cannot know; should they attempt to fathom it, their minds would surely become deranged.

With the sole exception of the Lords of all worlds—the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—who, by virtue of the power of the wisdom cultivated in the past, can penetrate even a single word or phrase into the minds of sentient beings, understanding them all clearly.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, when a great cloud sends down rain, there is a great cloud-rain called "The Extinguisher," which can extinguish the calamity of fire;
there is another great cloud-rain called:
There is the ability to cause [rain] to arise;
there is the great cloud-rain named "Able to Cease," which is able to cease the great waters.
There is a great cloud-rain named "Able to Accomplish," which is able to accomplish all mani-jewels;
there is a great cloud-rain named:
Discrimination; one discriminates the trichiliocosm.
Son of the Buddha!
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: he raises great clouds of Dharma and rains down great rain of Dharma. There is a great rain of Dharma, named:
It can extinguish; it can extinguish the afflictions of all sentient beings.
It possesses a great rain of Dharma, named:
"Able to Arouse," which can arouse the roots of goodness in all sentient beings.
There is a great rain of Dharma called "The Able to Cease," which is able to cease all the delusions of view of sentient beings;
there is a great rain of Dharma called:
It is capable of accomplishment; it can accomplish the jewel-treasury of all wisdom-dharmas.
It possesses a great rain of Dharma called "Discrimination," which discriminates the inclinations and joys of the minds of all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, a great cloud rains water of a single flavor, yet according to where it falls, there are immeasurable distinctions.
The appearance of a Tathāgata is likewise: he rains the dharma-water of a single flavor of great compassion, yet according to what is appropriate, his teachings have immeasurable distinctions.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the trichiliocosm is first formed, first the palaces of the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are formed, next the palaces of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are formed, and finally the dwellings of humans and other sentient beings are formed.

O Son of the Buddha! The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise so: first he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of bodhisattvas; next, he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of pratyekabuddhas; next, he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of the roots of goodness of śrāvakas; and finally, he gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of the conditioned roots of goodness of all other sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a great cloud that rains water of a single flavor, yet the palaces that arise are variously different according to the differences in the roots of goodness of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s rain of the Dharma, which is of a single flavor through great compassion, manifests distinctions according to the capacities of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
For example, when a world system is first about to be formed, a great body of water arises, filling the trichiliocosm;
from it grows a great lotus flower named:
The jewel-adorned merit of the Tathāgata’s appearance covered the surface of the water, its light illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, Maheśvara, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others, having seen these flowers, immediately knew with certainty that in this kalpa there would be so many Buddhas appearing in the world.
"O Son of the Buddha!
At that time, a wind-circle arose therein,
named 'Pure Radiance,' which was able to form the celestial palaces of the various devas of the Form Realm."
A wind-circle arises, named Pure Light Adornment,
which is able to form the palaces of the various heavens in the desire realm.
A wind-circle arises, named:
Solid and dense, it cannot be destroyed; it can form the various Great and Small Cakravāḍa mountains as well as the Vajra Mountains.
A wind-circle arises, named "Supremely High," which can form Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
A wind-circle arises, named "Immovable," which is able to form ten great mountain kings. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
Mount Khadiraka, Mount Ṛṣigiri, Mount Māra-vinardita, Mount Mahā-māra-vinardita, Mount Yugandhara, Mount Nimindhara, Mount Munindara, Mount Mahāmunindara, Mount Gandhamādana, and Mount Himavat.
A wind-circle arises, named "Abiding," which is able to form the great earth.
A wind-circle arises, named:
Adorned with splendor, it can produce the palaces of the earth-dwelling devas, the palaces of the nāgas,
and the palaces of the gandharvas. A wind-circle arises,
named "Inexhaustible Treasury," which can produce all the great oceans of the trichiliocosm.
A wind-circle arises, named Universal Radiance Treasury, which is able to form all the mani-jewels of the trichiliocosm.
A wind-circle arises, named:
With firm roots, they can bring all wish-fulfilling trees to fruition.
O Son of the Buddha!
The single-flavored water rained down by the great clouds makes no distinctions;
Because the roots of goodness of sentient beings differ, the wind-circles differ;
because the wind-circles are differentiated, the worlds are differentiated.
O Son of the Buddha!

The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: fully endowed with all roots of goodness and merit, he emits the light of supreme great wisdom called "Inconceivable Wisdom that Never Breaks the Lineage of the Tathāgatas," which universally illumines all worlds throughout the ten directions and bestows upon all bodhisattvas the consecration and prediction of all Tathāgatas:
"You shall attain perfect enlightenment and appear in the world."
O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears, there is another light of supreme great wisdom called "Pure and Stainless," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s untainted and inexhaustible wisdom.
Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named "Universal Illumination," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom that universally enters the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there is a light of supreme great wisdom named:
Sustaining the lineage of the Buddhas, they are able to accomplish the Tathāgata’s unshakable power.
Furthermore, there is the light of supreme great wisdom called "Transcending the Indestructible," which is able to accomplish the Tathāgata’s fearless and indestructible wisdom.
Furthermore, there is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom called "All Spiritual Powers," which is able to accomplish all the unique qualities of a Tathāgata and the knowledge of all-knowledge.

Furthermore, there is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom called "Birth of Transformations," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s wisdom that ensures the roots of goodness produced by seeing, hearing, and drawing near to him are never lost or destroyed.

Furthermore, there is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom named "Universal Accordance," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s body of inexhaustible merit and wisdom, bringing benefit to all sentient beings.

Furthermore, there is the light of supreme great wisdom called "Inexhaustible," which can accomplish the profound and wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata; according to those it awakens, it causes the lineage of the Triple Gem to never be severed.

Furthermore, there is the light of unsurpassed great wisdom called "Various Adornments," which can perfect the Tathāgata’s marks and signs that adorn the body, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, there is a light of unsurpassed great wisdom named "Indestructible," which can accomplish the Tathāgata’s supreme lifespan—
equal to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*)— which is inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!

The water of the Tathāgata’s great compassion is of a single flavor and free from discrimination; yet, because the desires and inclinations of sentient beings differ and their faculties and natures are each distinct, he gives rise to various wind-circles of great wisdom, causing all Bodhisattvas to accomplish the dharma of the Tathāgata’s manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha!
All Tathāgatas share one and the same essential nature, from within which the wheel of great wisdom gives rise to various radiances of insight.
O Son of the Buddha!
"You should know that from a single taste of liberation, the Tathāgata gives rise to immeasurable and inconceivable varieties of merit. Sentient beings think to themselves:
'This is created by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.'"
"O Son of the Buddha!
This was not created by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!"
It is impossible for even a single bodhisattva who has not previously planted roots of goodness under a Buddha to attain even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

It is solely by the power of the majestic virtue of all Buddhas that all sentient beings are enabled to possess the merits of a Buddha; yet the Buddha-Tathāgata is without discrimination, without formation or destruction, without an agent, and without any created phenomena.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
Just as four wind-wheels arise depending upon space and are able to support the water-wheel, what are these four?
The first is named:
Abiding; secondly, named "Ever-Abiding"; thirdly, named "Ultimate"; fourthly, named:
Firm. These four wind-wheels are able to support the water-wheel, and the water-wheel is able to support the great earth so that it does not disintegrate.
Therefore it is said:
The earth wheel rests upon the water wheel; the water wheel rests upon the wind wheel; the wind wheel rests upon space;
and space has nothing upon which it rests. Although it has no support, it enables the trichiliocosm to abide securely.
O Son of the Buddha!

The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: relying upon the light of unimpeded wisdom, he gives rise to the four kinds of great wisdom-wind-circles of a Buddha, which are able to sustain the roots of goodness of all sentient beings.
What are these four? They are:

the great wisdom wind-wheel that universally gathers all sentient beings and causes them all to rejoice; the great wisdom wind-wheel that establishes the true Dharma and causes all sentient beings to give rise to love and joy; the great wisdom wind-wheel that protects the roots of goodness of all sentient beings; and the great wisdom wind-wheel that possesses all skillful means and penetrates the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
These are the four.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, protect all sentient beings with great kindness, deliver all sentient beings through great compassion, and universally benefit them with both great kindness and great compassion.

Great loving-kindness and great compassion depend upon great skillful means; great skillful means depends upon the appearance of the Tathāgata; the appearance of the Tathāgata depends upon the light of unimpeded wisdom; and the light of unimpeded wisdom has no basis upon which it depends.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, once the trichiliocosm has been fully formed, it brings benefit to immeasurable and diverse sentient beings.
That is to say:

aquatic beings receive the benefit of water; terrestrial beings receive the benefit of land; beings dwelling in palaces receive the benefit of palaces; and beings dwelling in space receive the benefit of space.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise thus, providing manifold benefits to immeasurable sentient beings.
That is to say:
those who see the Buddha and give rise to joy obtain the benefit of joy;
Those who abide in pure ethical discipline obtain the benefit of pure ethical discipline;
those who abide in the various meditative concentrations and the immeasurables obtain the benefit of the great supranormal powers that are noble and transcend the world;
and those who abide in the illumination of the Dharma-gates obtain the benefit of the non-destruction of cause and effect.
Those who abide in the radiance of non-existence attain the indestructible benefit of all dharmas.
Therefore it is said:
"The Tathāgata appears in the world to bring benefit to all immeasurable sentient beings."
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth sign of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know it thus."
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows the appearance of the Tathāgata, they know him as immeasurable, because they know he has accomplished immeasurable practices;
they know him as vast, because they know he pervades the ten directions.”
Then one knows there is no coming or going, because one knows it is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing;
then one knows there is no movement and no place of movement, because one knows it is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness;
then one knows there is no body, because one knows it is like empty space.
Then one knows equality, because one knows that all sentient beings are without self;
then one knows inexhaustibility, because one knows that throughout all lands there is no end;
then one knows non-retrogression, because one knows that until the end of time there shall be no interruption.
Thus one knows there is no destruction, because one knows that the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no opposition;
thus one knows there is no duality, because one knows that he observes the conditioned and the unconditioned with equality;
thus one knows that all sentient beings obtain benefit, because his original vows and dedications are spontaneously and perfectly fulfilled.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The Great Hero of Ten Powers is most unsurpassed; Like space, he is peerless and beyond compare.
His sphere of activity is vast and immeasurable; His merit is supreme, transcending the world."
The merit of the Ten Powers is boundless and immeasurable, beyond the reach of mental calculation;
this single Dharma-door of the Lion among Men cannot be known by sentient beings even in hundreds of millions of eons.
The lands of the ten directions may be ground into dust, and some might calculate and know their number;
yet the measure of the merit of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata cannot be described even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
As if a person were to take a measuring rod to measure empty space, and another followed along to calculate its extent—the limits of empty space cannot be found; such is the realm of the Tathāgata.
There may be those who, in a single kṣaṇa, can fully know the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time;
yet even if they were to pass through kalpas equal in number to all those sentient beings, they could not know the nature of a single thought-moment of a Buddha.
Just as the dharma-realm pervades all things, yet cannot be seen or grasped as being "all," so too is the sphere of the Ten Powers: it pervades all, yet is not "all."
True Suchness is free from delusion and eternally quiescent; Without birth and without cessation, it is universally pervasive.
The realm of all Buddhas is likewise so; Its essential nature is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Just as the limit of reality is not a limit, and though it pervades the three times, it is not pervasive;
so too is the realm of the Guide: it extends throughout the three times without any obstruction.
The nature of phenomena is without action and without change, Just as empty space is fundamentally pure;
The nature of all Buddhas is likewise pure, Its original nature being neither a "nature" nor a "non-nature," transcending existence and non-existence.
The nature of phenomena does not reside in speech; it is beyond expression, transcends all talk, and is eternally quiescent.
The nature of the realm of the Ten Powers is likewise; no words or phrases can ever fully describe it.
Knowing that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent, like a bird flying through the sky leaving no trace,
he manifests a physical body through the power of his original vows, causing beings to behold the Tathāgata’s great spiritual transformations.
If there are those who wish to know the realm of the Buddha, They should purify their minds like empty space;
By remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all grasping, They cause the mind to be unimpeded wherever it turns.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, listen well: I shall clarify the realm of the Buddha through a few similes.
The merit of the Ten Powers is immeasurable; I now speak briefly for the sake of awakening sentient beings.
The physical, verbal, and mental activities manifested by the Teacher,
His turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma and his parinirvāṇa— I shall now describe all these roots of virtue.
Just as when the world was first established, it could not have been formed by a single cause and condition;
rather, through immeasurable skillful means and various causes and conditions, this trichiliocosm was brought into being.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise so: it is accomplished through immeasurable merit;
while the thoughts within a single moment of mind across the atoms of all lands may still be known, the causes for the birth of the Ten Powers cannot be fathomed.
Just as when clouds pour down rain at the beginning of a kalpa, And four kinds of great wind-wheels arise,
Through the roots of goodness of sentient beings and the power of Bodhisattvas, This trichiliocosm is formed and each abides in peace.

The Dharma-cloud of the Ten Powers is likewise: it raises the wind-circle of wisdom from a pure mind, universally guiding all sentient beings toward whom it was formerly dedicated, so that they may achieve the unsurpassed fruit.
Just as there is a great rain called "the vast downpour," for which no place exists that can contain it,
except for the power of the pure void and the great wind-force at the time when the world is about to be formed.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise: he rains down the rain of Dharma everywhere, filling the entire Dharmadhātu;
yet none with inferior intent can uphold it, except for those with pure and vast minds.
Just as when great rain pours from the sky, It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
There is neither an agent nor a recipient, Yet it naturally and universally saturates all.
The Dharma rain of the Ten Powers is likewise: without going, without coming, and without fabrication.
With past conduct as its cause and the power of the Bodhisattvas, all those of great resolve listen and receive it.
Just as when empty clouds pour down a great rain, no one is able to count its drops,
except for the Sovereign Kings of the Three Thousandfold World, who possess the power of merit and understand them all completely.

The Dharma rain of the Sugata is likewise; no sentient beings can fathom it, except for those who have attained mastery over the world, who see it clearly as if beholding a jewel in the palm of their hand.
Just as empty clouds pour down great rain, Which can extinguish, can arise, and can sever,
All precious jewels it can fully produce, And all that exists within the three thousandfold world-system it discerns.
The Dharma rain of the Ten Powers is likewise: it extinguishes delusions, gives rise to goodness, and severs all views;
it causes all jewels of omniscience to be perfected, and it fully discerns the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.
For example, when rain of a single flavor falls from the sky, it differs according to what it falls upon;
how could there be any differentiation in the nature of that rain? Yet, the phenomena [it encounters] differ according to the objects—such is the way of things.
The Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is neither one nor many; it is equal, tranquil, and free from discrimination.
Yet, according to the various differences among those to be transformed, its natural manifestations appear thus in boundless ways.
For example, when the world is first formed, the palaces of the gods of the Form Realm are formed first;
next come those of the Desire Realm gods, then the human abodes, and finally the palaces of the gandharvas are formed last.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is likewise: first he initiates the boundless practices of bodhisattvas;
next he transforms the pratyekabuddhas who delight in tranquility; then the assembly of śrāvakas; and finally all sentient beings.
When the devas first beheld the auspicious omen of the lotus, they knew the Buddha was about to be born and were filled with joy;
through the power of wind acting upon the element of water, the palaces, mountains, and rivers of the world were all established.
The Tathāgata’s great radiance of past virtues skillfully distinguishes bodhisattvas and bestows their predictions;
the essence of all their wheels of wisdom is pure, each capable of revealing all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as forests exist depending on the earth, and the earth remains unbroken by depending on water,
the water-mass depends on wind, and wind depends on space, yet that space has nothing upon which it depends.
All Buddha-dharmas rely upon compassion; Compassion, in turn, is established upon skillful means.
Skillful means rely upon wisdom, and wisdom relies upon insight; The body of unimpeded wisdom has no dependence.
Just as when the world is established, all sentient beings obtain its benefits—
those dwelling on earth or water, those living in the sky, and those with two or four legs— all receive its grace.
The appearance of the Dharma King is likewise: all sentient beings obtain its benefit;
if they see, hear, or draw near to him, he causes them all to extinguish every delusion and affliction.
The appearance of the Tathāgata is the boundless Dharma, which the deluded of the world are unable to know;
desiring to awaken all sentient beings, he speaks metaphors for that which is beyond metaphor.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive the body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Son of the Buddha!”
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive the body of the Tathāgata in immeasurable locations. Why is this?

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not perceive the Tathāgata in a single dharma, a single matter, a single body, a single land, or a single sentient being; rather, they should perceive the Tathāgata pervading all places.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like space, which pervades all places—both those with form and those without form—yet it neither arrives nor does it not arrive. Why is this?
Because space has no body, the body of the Tathāgata is likewise: it pervades all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, and all lands; it neither arrives nor does it not arrive.
Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is no-body, he manifests that body for the sake of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first mark of the Tathāgata’s body; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive it in this way.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
It is like space, which is vast and non-material, yet is able to manifest all forms, while that space itself is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation."

The body of the Tathāgata is likewise thus; because it universally illuminates with the light of wisdom, it causes all the roots of goodness and karmic deeds of worldly and world-transcending nature belonging to all sentient beings to reach fulfillment, yet the body of the Tathāgata remains free from discrimination and free from conceptual proliferation.
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, all attachments and all conceptual proliferations have been eternally severed.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second mark of the Tathāgata’s body, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the rising of the sun over Jambudvīpa, whereby immeasurable sentient beings all receive benefit.
That is to say:

it dispels darkness to create light, transforms moisture into dryness, causes plants and trees to grow, brings grain crops to maturity, makes the void clear and transparent, causes lotus flowers to bloom, enables the practitioner to see the Path, and allows the dweller to accomplish their tasks.
Why is this? Because the solar orb universally emits immeasurable light.
O Son of the Buddha!
The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise thus, universally benefiting sentient beings through immeasurable means.
That is to say:

it extinguishes evil and gives rise to goodness; it shatters ignorance to produce wisdom; it provides rescue and protection through great kindness; and it effects deliverance through great compassion.
To cause them to increase their faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment;
to cause them to give rise to deep faith and abandon turbid minds;
and to enable them to see and hear so that they do not destroy the law of cause and effect.
May they attain the divine eye to see the places of death and rebirth;
may their minds be unimpeded so that their roots of goodness are not destroyed;
and may their wisdom be cultivated and clarified, causing the flowers of awakening to bloom.
They cause them to resolve their minds and bring their fundamental practices to fulfillment. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s vast sun-body of wisdom radiates immeasurable light that shines everywhere.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, it first illuminates all the great kings of mountains such as Mount Sumeru; next it illuminates the Black Mountains; then it illuminates the high plateaus; and finally, it shines universally upon the entire earth.
The sun does not form the thought:
"I shall first illuminate this, and later illuminate that.
It is simply because mountains and lands have elevations and depressions that the illumination occurs earlier or later.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: having accomplished the wheel of wisdom of the boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), he constantly emits the light of unimpeded wisdom. First, it illuminates the great mountain kings such as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; next, it illuminates the Pratyekabuddhas; next, it illuminates the Śrāvakas; and next, it illuminates those sentient beings with resolute roots of goodness, manifesting vast wisdom according to their mental capacities. Thereafter, it universally illuminates all sentient beings, even reaching those fixed in the wrong path, in order to act as the causal conditions for their future benefit and to bring them to maturity.
Yet that Tathāgata, the Sun of Great Wisdom, does not form such a thought:
"I shall first illumine the great practices of Bodhisattvas, and only later illumine sentient beings fixed in wrong views."
"Yet it merely emits light that shines equally and universally, without obstruction, without hindrance, and without discrimination.
Son of the Buddha!
It is like the sun and moon appearing according to the seasons, shining impartially upon great mountains and deep valleys."

The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: it universally illumines all things without discrimination, yet the radiance of its wisdom appears in various ways according to the differing faculties and inclinations of sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, when the sun rises, sentient beings who are blind from birth cannot see it because they lack the faculty of sight;
yet, even though they have never seen it, they are nonetheless benefited by its light.

Why is this? Because by means of this, one knows the divisions of day and night and the seasons, thereby enjoying various garments and food and drink to keep the body in harmony and free from all ailments.

The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: those who lack faith, lack understanding, violate the precepts, hold wrong views, and live by wrong livelihood—these who are like those born blind because they lack the eye of faith—do not see the solar orb of the Buddhas’ wisdom.
Although they do not see the sun-disk of the Buddha’s wisdom, they are nonetheless benefited by that sun of wisdom. Why is this?
Because through the Buddha’s majestic power, all physical suffering, afflictions, and the causes of future suffering belonging to those sentient beings are completely extinguished.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata has a light named "Accumulation of All Meritorious Virtues."
There is a light named "Universally Illuminating All";
there is a light named:
Pure and Sovereign Illumination;
there is a light named:
Producing Great Sublime Sounds;
There is a light named "Universally Understanding All Languages and Dharmas to Delight Others";
there is a light named:
There is a manifestation of the sovereign realm of eternally severing all doubts;
there is a light named "Universal Illumination of the Sovereignty of Non-abiding Wisdom."
There is a light named Sovereign Wisdom that Permanently Severs All Proliferations;
there is a light named:
They emit wondrous sounds according to what is appropriate;
there is a light called "Adorning the Realm with the Emanation of Pure, Sovereign Sounds to Mature Sentient Beings."
O Son of the Buddha!

From each and every pore of the Tathāgata, such thousands of kinds of light rays are emitted; five hundred light rays universally illumine the regions below, and five hundred light rays universally illumine the regions above.

The assemblies of bodhisattvas from various buddha-fields, in the presence of various Buddhas, upon seeing this light, all simultaneously attained the realm of the Tathāgata; their ten heads, ten eyes, ten ears, ten noses, ten tongues, ten bodies, ten hands, ten feet, ten stages, and ten wisdoms were all rendered completely pure.

Those bodhisattvas who had previously attained various stages and levels saw that light become even more pure; all their roots of goodness reached full maturity, and they were directed toward omniscience.
Those dwelling in the two vehicles extinguished all defilements.

Furthermore, a certain portion of sentient beings born blind experienced physical happiness and mental purity; becoming supple and disciplined, they became capable of cultivating mindfulness and wisdom.

All sentient beings in the various realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals shall attain happiness and be liberated from all sufferings; at the end of their lives, they shall all be reborn in the heavens or among human beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Those sentient beings do not perceive or know by what causes and conditions, or by what spiritual power, they have come to be born here.
Those who were born blind think to themselves:"
"I am Brahmā! I am the emanation of Brahmā!
At that time, the Tathāgata entered the Samādhi of Universal Sovereignty and uttered sixty kinds of wondrous sounds, addressing him thus:
"You are not Brahmā, nor are you created by Brahmā, nor were you made by Śakra or the World-Protectors; all this is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata."
When those sentient beings heard these words, through the Buddha’s spiritual power they all came to know their past lives and were filled with great joy.

Because their hearts were joyful, there spontaneously emerged clouds of *udumbara* flowers, clouds of incense, clouds of music, clouds of robes, clouds of parasols, clouds of banners, clouds of pennants, clouds of powdered incense, clouds of jewels, clouds of lion-pennant crescent-shaped pavilions, clouds of songs and praises, and clouds of various adornments; all of these they offered to the Tathāgata with a heart of deep reverence.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings have attained the pure eye, the Tathāgata bestows upon them the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Son of the Buddha!
In this way, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom benefits sentient beings who are blind from birth, enabling them to acquire roots of goodness and reach full maturity.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive in this manner.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!
For example, the lunar disc possesses four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities. What are these four?
First, it eclipses the radiance of all the stars;
second, it manifests its waning and waxing in accordance with the seasons;
third, its reflection appears without exception within the clear and pure waters of Jambudvīpa.
"Fourth, although all who behold it have it directly before their eyes, this lunar disc is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation.
Son of the Buddha!
The moon-like body of the Tathāgata is likewise; it possesses four marvelous and unprecedented qualities."
What are these four? They are:
eclipsing all the assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, those in training, and those beyond training;
According to what is appropriate for each, the Tathāgata manifests lifespans of varying lengths—long or short—yet the body of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
Within the vessels of bodhi among all sentient beings of pure mind in every world, his reflection appears without exception.
