All sentient beings who behold him each think that the Tathāgata has appeared before them alone; he preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations, brings them liberation according to their spiritual stages, and causes them to see the Buddha-body according to their needs for transformation. Yet the body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation; all the benefits he brings to fruition reach ultimate perfection.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, it is like the Great Brahmā King of the trichiliocosm, who, through a slight expedient means, manifests his body throughout the great trichiliocosm so that all sentient beings perceive the Brahmā King appearing before them; yet this Brahmā King does not divide his body, nor does he possess various distinct bodies.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: they are without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation; they do not divide their bodies, nor do they have various bodies, yet they manifest their bodies in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, without forming the thought that they are manifesting various bodies.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a king of physicians who is well-versed in all medicines and various incantations; there is no medicinal substance in Jambudvīpa that he does not fully utilize. Furthermore, by means of the power of his roots of goodness from past lives and the power of great vidyā-mantras as skillful means, no sentient being who sees him fails to be cured of their illness.
That Great King of Physicians, knowing his life was about to end, thought to himself:
"After my death, all sentient beings will have no one to rely upon; I should now manifest skillful means for their sake."

At that time, the King of Physicians compounded a medicine and applied it to his body; sustained by the power of a mystic mantra, after his death his body did not disintegrate, nor did it wither or dry up. His deportment, vision, and hearing were no different from when he was alive, and all those he treated for illness were completely cured.

O Son of the Buddha! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Physicians, is likewise so. Over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, he has refined and prepared the medicinal drugs of the Dharma until they are perfected; he has studied all the skillful means and the power of the Great Mantra of Radiance until he has reached the other shore. He is well able to eliminate the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings and to sustain their life-span.

Having passed through immeasurable kalpas, his body is pure, free from discursive thought, and free from active exertion; yet the various works of a Buddha have never ceased. Any sentient being who beholds him finds that all their diseases of affliction are completely extinguished.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
For example, within the great ocean there is a great maṇi-jewel named Vairocana-garbha that Collects All Radiance;
if any sentient beings touch its light, they all become identical in color to it.
If there are those who behold it, their eyes will attain purity.
Wherever that radiance shines, mani-jewels named "Peace and Bliss" rain down,
causing all sentient beings to be free from suffering and become harmonious and at ease.
O Son of the Buddha!
The bodies of all Tathāgatas are likewise thus: they are great accumulations of jewels, treasuries of all merit and great wisdom.
If there are sentient beings who touch the jewel-like body of a Buddha or its light of wisdom, they become identical in color to the Buddha’s body.
If there are those who see it, their Dharma-eye will become pure.
Wherever that light shines, it shall cause all sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of poverty and, ultimately, to be fully endowed with the bliss of Buddha-enlightenment.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and free from conceptual proliferation, yet it is able to universally perform great Buddha-works for all sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth mark of the Tathāgata’s body; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should view it in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the great ocean, which possesses a great sovereign *maṇi* jewel-king named:

This treasury of adornments for all worlds is fully endowed with and has accomplished a million merits; wherever it dwells, it causes all calamities and afflictions of sentient beings to be eliminated and their aspirations to be fulfilled.
Yet, this sovereign wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel cannot be seen by sentient beings of meager merit.
The body of the Tathāgata, like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, is also thus;

it is named "That Which Causes All Sentient Beings to Be Utterly Joyful. Should any behold his body, hear his name, or praise his virtues, he causes them all to forever leave behind the suffering and afflictions of birth and death.

Even if all sentient beings in all worlds were to simultaneously focus their minds on desiring to see the Tathāgata, he would cause them all to behold him, so that their aspirations are entirely fulfilled.
O Son of the Buddha!
The body of the Buddha cannot be seen by sentient beings with meager merit, except for those who are to be tamed by the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata;

if there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha’s body, plant roots of goodness and even reach maturity, it is for the sake of their maturation that they are enabled to see the body of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha! This is the tenth mark of the Tathāgata’s body, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should perceive in this way:

because his mind is immeasurable and pervades the ten directions; because his conduct is unimpeded like space; because he universally enters the Dharma-realm; because he dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); because he is without birth or cessation; because he dwells equally throughout the three periods of time; because he is forever free from all conceptual discrimination; because he dwells in vows that extend to the end of the future; because he purifies all worlds; and because he adorns each and every Buddha-body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Just as space pervades the ten directions, Whether form or non-form, existence or non-existence,
The bodies and lands of sentient beings throughout the three times— Thus it is universally present, without limit."
The true body of all Buddhas is likewise: it pervades the entire dharma-realm without exception;
it cannot be seen and cannot be grasped, yet it manifests forms in order to transform sentient beings.
Just as space cannot be grasped, yet it universally causes sentient beings to perform all manner of karmic deeds, so too one does not think:
"What am I doing now? How is it that I act, and for whom do I act?"
The physical actions of all Buddhas are likewise: they cause all living beings everywhere to cultivate wholesome dharmas, yet the Tathāgata never entertains the discrimination:
"I am now performing various deeds for them."
Just as when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, its radiance destroys all darkness without exception;
the mountains, trees, ponds, lotuses, the earth, and all things—every variety of species—receive its benefit.
The emergence of the Buddhas as the rising sun is likewise: it causes the wholesome deeds of the multitudes of humans and devas to grow;
it forever eliminates the darkness of ignorance so that the light of wisdom is attained; and one constantly enjoys honor, dignity, and all forms of bliss.

For example, when the sun’s light appears, it first illuminates the King of Mountains, then the other mountains, and finally the high plateaus and the great earth; yet the sun never engages in discrimination.

The radiance of the Sugata is likewise: first it illuminates the Bodhisattvas, then the Pratyekabuddhas, and finally it shines upon the Śrāvakas and all sentient beings, yet from the very beginning, the Buddha has been free from any movement of thought.
Just as one born blind does not see the sun, yet the sunlight still brings them benefit,
enabling them to know the seasons and partake of food and drink, thereby forever leaving behind all ailments and remaining secure in body.
Sentient beings lacking faith do not see the Buddha, yet the Buddha still brings about their benefit and welfare;
by hearing his name or being touched by his light, they may thereby attain even Bodhi.
Just as the pure moon in the void Can eclipse the multitude of stars and manifest its waxing and waning,
Its reflection appears in all waters, And for all who gaze upon it, it stands before them.
The Tathāgata’s pure moon is likewise; it can obscure other vehicles to manifest long and short durations.
It appears universally within the water of the pure minds of devas and humans, such that all believe it stands before them.
Just as the Brahma King, dwelling in his own palace, Manifests himself universally in all the Brahma abodes of the three thousandfold world-system,
Such that all humans and devas are able to see him, Yet in reality he does not divide his body and go toward them.
The manifestation of bodies by all Buddhas is likewise: they pervade all the ten directions without exception;
their bodies are innumerable and beyond measure, yet they neither divide their bodies nor engage in conceptual discrimination.
Just as there is a king of physicians skilled in medical arts, whom all who see have their illnesses cured—
even if one's life has already come to an end, by applying medicine to the body, it enables them to perform all tasks just as before.

The Supreme King of Physicians is likewise so: Possessing all-encompassing wisdom and skillful means, He manifests the Buddha-body through his past sublime practices; Those sentient beings who behold him have their afflictions extinguished.
Just as there is a king of jewels within the ocean, Which universally emits immeasurable rays of light;
Sentient beings who touch it take on its color, And those who behold it gain purity of eye.
The Supreme King of Jewels is likewise: those who touch its light all become the same color;
if anyone should behold it, their five eyes open, they shatter the darkness of all defilements, and abide on the stage of a Buddha.
Just as the wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel satisfies all that is sought,
yet beings with little merit cannot see it, it is not that the king of jewels possesses any discrimination.
The Sugata, the King of Jewels, is likewise: he fulfills all sought-after desires and pleasures;
yet sentient beings lacking faith do not see the Buddha—it is not that the Sugata’s mind has abandoned them.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty-one.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan under Imperial Order.
Part Two of Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Appearance of the Tathāgatas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the voice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
“O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that the voice of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere, because it pervades all immeasurable sounds;
they should know that the voice of the Tathāgata brings joy to all according to their mental inclinations, because its teaching of the Dharma is clear and lucid.”
One should know that the voice of the Tathāgata brings joy to all according to their faith and understanding, for it causes the mind to attain coolness;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata transforms beings without missing the proper time, for there is none among those who ought to hear it who does not hear it;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is without arising or ceasing, being like an echo.
One should know that the voice of the Tathāgata has no master, for it arises from the cultivation of all karmas;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep, for it is difficult to measure;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is without crookedness, for it is born of the dharma-realm.
One should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is uninterrupted, for it universally enters the dharma-realm;
one should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is unchanging, for it reaches ultimate consummation.
O Son of the Buddha!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know that the voice of the Tathāgata is neither measurable nor immeasurable, neither having a master nor lacking a master, and neither indicative nor non-indicative.
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!
For example, when a world is about to be destroyed, though there is no master and no agent, four kinds of sounds naturally emerge by the very nature of things.
What are these four? First:
"You should know that the first dhyāna is peaceful and blissful; it is free from all desires and evils, and transcends the realm of desire."
"Once the sentient beings have heard this, they naturally achieve the first dhyāna, cast off their bodies in the desire realm, and are reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Second: 'You should know that the second dhyāna is peaceful and blissful; being without vitarka and without vicāra, it transcends the Brahma Heaven.'"
Upon hearing this, the sentient beings spontaneously achieved the second dhyāna; they relinquished their bodies as Brahmā gods and were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Thirdly, [the Buddha said]:
"You should all know that the bliss of the third dhyāna is free from fault and transcends the Ābhāsvara Heaven."
Upon hearing this, sentient beings spontaneously attained the accomplishment of the third dhyāna; they cast off their bodies of Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
The fourth [instruction] was:
"You should know that the fourth dhyāna is tranquil; transcend the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven."
Upon hearing this, sentient beings spontaneously achieve the four dhyānas, cast off their bodies of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and are reborn in the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
This is the fourth.
O Son of the Buddha!
These various sounds have no master and no agent; they arise solely from the power of the various wholesome karmas of sentient beings.
Son of the Buddha!

The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: it has no master and no agent, it is without discrimination, neither entering nor exiting, yet it issues forth the four kinds of vast sounds solely from the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and dharmas.
What are these four?
The first is:
"You should all know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely suffering, namely:"

There is the suffering of the hells, the suffering of animals, the suffering of hungry ghosts, the suffering of lacking merit, the suffering of clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," and the suffering of committing various evil deeds.
Those who wish to be born among humans or devas should plant roots of goodness;
by being born among humans or devas, they will be free from the states of woe.
"Having heard this, sentient beings abandon their perversions, cultivate various wholesome deeds, leave behind all places of hardship, and are reborn among humans and devas.
Second: 'You should know that all conditioned phenomena are ablaze with manifold sufferings, like glowing iron balls.'"
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to decay and destruction.
Nirvāṇa is tranquil, unconditioned, and blissful; it is far removed from the burning fires of existence and extinguishes all feverish afflictions.
Having heard this, sentient beings diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and attain the patience that accords with sounds within the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Third: "You should know that those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle understand according to the words of others; their wisdom is narrow and inferior."
"Furthermore, there is a superior vehicle called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, which is realized without a teacher; you all should train in it.
Having heard these words, those who delighted in the supreme path abandoned the Śrāvaka path and cultivated the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
The fourth is:
"You should know that beyond the stages of the two vehicles there is a further, superior path, which is called the Mahāyāna."

The conduct of a bodhisattva accords with the six pāramitās; they do not interrupt the bodhisattva practice and do not abandon the bodhicitta. Dwelling amidst immeasurable births and deaths without weariness or fatigue, they surpass the two vehicles. This is called:
the Great Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle, the Victorious Vehicle, the Most Victorious Vehicle, the Superior Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, and the Vehicle that Benefits All Sentient Beings.

If there are sentient beings whose faith and understanding are vast, whose faculties are sharp and keen, who have planted roots of goodness in the past, who are empowered by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, and who possess superior aspirations and seek the fruit of Buddhahood;
upon hearing this sound, they shall give rise to the bodhicitta.
O Son of the Buddha!
The voice of the Tathāgata does not issue from the body, nor does it issue from the mind, yet it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it in this way.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is like an echo, which arises due to mountains and valleys and sound; it has no form and cannot be seen, nor does it possess discrimination, yet it can follow after all speech."
The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: it has no form and cannot be seen; it is neither localized nor non-localized.
It issues forth only in accordance with the inclinations and understandings of sentient beings as conditions; its nature is ultimate, beyond words and demonstration, and cannot be proclaimed.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, the devas possess a great Dharma drum named "Awakening.
Whenever the sons of the gods act with negligence, a voice issues from the midst of space, proclaiming:
"You all should know that all sensual pleasures are entirely impermanent, false and inverted, subject to momentary change and decay; they merely deceive the foolish, causing them to become attached."
"Do not be negligent; if you are negligent, you will fall into the various evil realms, and it will be too late for regrets.

Having heard these words, the negligent devas were struck with great anxiety and fear. They abandoned all the sensual pleasures within their own palaces and went to the presence of the Heavenly King to seek the Dharma and practice the Path.
O Son of the Buddha!
That sound of the celestial drum has no master and no creator; it neither arises nor ceases, yet it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
You should know that the Tathāgata is likewise: desiring to awaken sentient beings who are heedless, he produces the sounds of immeasurable sublime Dharma, namely:

The sound of non-attachment, the sound of heedfulness, the sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, the sound of non-self, the sound of impurity, the sound of tranquility, the sound of nirvāṇa, the sound of immeasurable spontaneous wisdom, the sound of the indestructible bodhisattva practice, and the sound of the Tathāgata’s effortless ground of wisdom that reaches all places—with these sounds, they awaken beings throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Upon hearing this sound, countless sentient beings were all filled with joy; they diligently cultivated wholesome dharmas and each sought liberation through their respective vehicles—namely, some practiced the Śrāvaka vehicle, some practiced the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and others studied the unsurpassed Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the voice of the Tathāgata does not abide in any location and is beyond verbal expression.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha!
It is like the divine consort of the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereign Power, named Good Mouth (Suvaktrā).

From within her mouth she utters a single sound, and that sound resonates in harmony with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music; within each of these musical instruments, there are again hundreds of thousands of distinct tones."
O Son of the Buddha!
From a single sound from the mouth of that woman of virtuous speech, such immeasurable sounds were produced.

You should know that the Tathāgata is likewise: from within a single voice, he produces immeasurable sounds, which reach everywhere according to the differences in the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, causing them all to attain understanding.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
It is like the Great Brahmā King, who, while dwelling in his Brahma palace, utters a Brahma voice that all the Brahma hosts hear, yet that sound does not go beyond their assembly.
All the hosts of Brahmā deities conceived this thought:
"The Great Brahmā King is speaking with me alone.
It was the same with the Tathāgata’s wondrous voice: the entire assembly at the site of enlightenment heard it, yet its sound did not issue beyond the gathering.
Why is this? Because those whose faculties are not yet mature should not hear it.
Those who hear the sound all think to themselves:
“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has spoken this for me alone.
O Son of the Buddha!
The voice of the Tathāgata neither issues forth nor abides, yet it is able to accomplish all activities.
This is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

It is like all waters, which are of one single taste; yet because they follow the differences of their vessels, the water appears to have distinctions. The water has no thoughts and no discrimination."

The vocal sounds of the Tathāgata are likewise thus: they are of but a single flavor, namely the flavor of liberation; yet, because the mental capacities of sentient beings differ, they manifest in immeasurable distinctions, while remaining free from thought and devoid of discrimination.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the Dragon King Anavatapta raises great dense clouds and pours down sweet rain everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa, the hundred grains and all crops grow and flourish, and all rivers, streams, springs, and ponds become completely full.
This great rain does not emerge from the body or mind of the dragon king, yet it is able to provide manifold benefits to sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: he raises the clouds of great compassion that pervade the worlds of the ten directions, universally raining down the supreme nectar-rain of the Dharma, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy, increasing their wholesome dharmas, and fulfilling all vehicles.
"O Son of the Buddha!
The voice of the Tathāgata does not come from without, nor does it issue from within, yet it is able to benefit all sentient beings.
This is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know in this way."
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the Dragon King Manasvin, who, when he intends to send down rain, does not do so immediately; first, he raises a great cloud that covers the void and remains suspended for seven days, waiting for all sentient beings to complete their labors."
Why is this? Because that Great Dragon King possesses a heart of compassion and does not wish to disturb or trouble sentient beings.
After seven days have passed, he sends down a fine rain that universally moistens the great earth.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is the same with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. When he is about to let fall the rain of Dharma, he does not do so immediately; first, he raises the clouds of Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity, desiring that their minds be free from alarm and fear.

Once they have matured, he then universally lets fall the nectar-like rain of Dharma, expounding the most profound, subtle, and wondrous wholesome teachings, gradually causing them to be satisfied with the unsurpassed flavor of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, within the ocean there is a great dragon king named Great Adornment;
when he sends down rain upon the great sea, he may send down ten kinds of adorned rain, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand kinds of adorned rain.
O Son of the Buddha!
Water is without discrimination; it is merely through the inconceivable power of the dragon kings that it is made magnificent, even unto hundreds of thousands of immeasurable varieties.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: when he teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, he may speak using ten distinct tones, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand; or he may speak using eighty-four thousand sounds to explain the eighty-four thousand practices, even up to using immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sounds to teach the Dharma individually, causing all who hear it to give rise to joy.

The voice of the Tathāgata is without discrimination; rather, because the Buddhas are perfectly pure within the profound realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), they are able to produce various vocal sounds according to what is appropriate for the faculties of sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, when the Dragon King Sāgara wishes to manifest the great sovereign power of a dragon king to benefit sentient beings and cause them all to rejoice, he raises a vast network of clouds that completely covers everything from the four continents up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations.

The colors and characteristics of those clouds were of infinite variety: some had the radiant color of Jāmbūnada gold, some the radiant color of vaidūrya, some the radiant color of white silver, some the radiant color of crystal, some the radiant color of musāragalva, some the radiant color of agate, some the radiant color of the supreme treasury, some the radiant color of red pearls, some the radiant color of immeasurable fragrance, some the radiant color of stainless garments, some the radiant color of pure water, and some the radiant color of various ornaments; such nets of clouds spread out and pervaded everywhere.
Once it had spread everywhere, it emitted flashes of lightning of various colors. Namely:

From clouds the color of Jāmbūnada gold, lightning the color of lapis lazuli issued forth; from clouds the color of lapis lazuli, lightning the color of gold issued forth; from clouds the color of silver, lightning the color of crystal issued forth; from clouds the color of crystal, lightning the color of silver issued forth; from clouds the color of musāragalva, lightning the color of agate issued forth; from clouds the color of agate, lightning the color of musāragalva issued forth; from clouds the color of the supreme treasury jewel, lightning the color of red pearls issued forth; from clouds the color of red pearls, lightning the color of the supreme treasury jewel issued forth; from clouds the color of immeasurable fragrance, lightning the color of stainless garments issued forth; from clouds the color of stainless garments, lightning the color of immeasurable fragrance issued forth; from clouds the color of pure water, lightning the color of various ornaments issued forth; from clouds the color of various ornaments, lightning the color of pure water issued forth.
Even unto clouds of various colors emitting lightning of a single color, and clouds of a single color emitting lightning of various colors.
Furthermore, from within those clouds, various kinds of thunderous sounds issued forth, causing all sentient beings to rejoice according to their own inclinations.

These were as follows: some were like the singing voices of celestial maidens; some were like the sounds of the musical instruments of the devas; some were like the singing voices of nāga maidens; some were like the singing voices of gandharva maidens; some were like the singing voices of kinnara maidens; some were like the sound of the great earth quaking; some were like the sound of the waves and tides of the ocean; some were like the roaring of the king of beasts; some were like the warbling of beautiful birds; and there were other such immeasurable varieties of sounds.

Once the thunder has struck, a cool breeze arises, causing all sentient beings to feel joy in their hearts; thereafter, various rains descend, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
From the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations down to the earth, the rain that falls in each place is different.
That is to say:
in the great ocean, it rains clear, cool water, which is named:
It is uninterrupted;
among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the rain of various musical sounds such as flutes and pipes is called "exquisite."
In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, there falls a rain of great maṇi jewels named "Emitting Great Radiance";
in the Tuṣita Heaven, there falls a rain of great ornaments named:
In the Yāma Heaven, there falls a rain of great, wondrous flowers called "Various Adornments."
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, a rain of various exquisite fragrances fell,
named "Delightful";
in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, a rain of celestial jewel-garments fell, named:
It covers [the realm];
in the palaces of the dragon kings, it rains red pearls named "Emanating Radiance."
In the palaces of the asuras, they rain down various weapons,
named "Subduing Enemies";
in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, they rain down various flowers, named:
It blooms; the other three continents are all likewise, yet the rain that falls differs according to each respective location.
Although the mind of that dragon king is impartial and free from the distinction of "self" and "other," there are differences in the rain solely because the roots of goodness of sentient beings vary.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, is likewise: wishing to transform sentient beings through the True Dharma, he first spreads clouds of his body to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting different forms according to their inclinations and desires.

That is to say: for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of birth-bodies; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of transformation-bodies; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of bodies sustained by power; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of form-bodies; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of bodies with the primary and secondary marks; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of merit-bodies; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of wisdom-bodies; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of indestructible bodies of the various powers; for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of fearlessness-bodies; and for some sentient beings he manifests clouds of dharma-realm-bodies.
"O Son of the Buddha!

With such immeasurable clouds of bodies, the Tathāgata universally covers all worlds throughout the ten directions, manifesting various kinds of radiant lightning flashes individually according to the inclinations of all sentient beings."
That is to say:
for the sake of sentient beings, they may manifest the light of lightning, called "Reaching Everywhere."
Or they manifest for sentient beings a flash of light called "Boundless Radiance";
or they manifest for sentient beings a flash of light called:
They enter the secret dharma of the Buddhas;
or they manifest light like flashes of lightning for the sake of sentient beings, named "Manifesting Radiance."
Or they manifest for sentient beings a lightning-flash of light named "Radiant Illumination";
or they manifest for sentient beings a lightning-flash of light named:
They enter the gate of the inexhaustible dhāraṇī;
or they manifest for sentient beings the light of lightning,
named "Right Mindfulness Without Distraction."
For some sentient beings, they manifest a lightning-flash of light named "Ultimately Indestructible";
for other sentient beings, they manifest a lightning-flash of light named:
They enter all realms of existence in accordance with their conditions; or they manifest for sentient beings the light of lightning,
named "Fulfilling All Vows and Causing All to Rejoice."
O Son of the Buddha!

After the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has manifested such immeasurable flashes of light as these, he further produces the thunderous sound of immeasurable samādhis, in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.

They are: the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of Skillful Awakening Wisdom; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Radiant, Stainless Ocean; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of Sovereignty over All Dharmas; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Vajra Wheel; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Sumeru Banner; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Sun Lamp; the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Treasury; and the thunderous sound of the Samādhi of the Indestructible Power of Liberation.
O Son of the Buddha!

After the Tathāgata’s cloud-like body has emitted such immeasurable and diverse thunderous sounds of samādhi, he is about to let fall the rain of Dharma; first, he manifests auspicious signs to awaken sentient beings.
That is to say:
from the unobstructed mind of great compassion, there appears the wind-circle of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom,
named "Able to Cause All Sentient Beings to Give Rise to Inconceivable Joy and Delight."
Once these signs had appeared, the bodies and minds of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings attained refreshing clarity.

Thereafter, from the Tathāgata’s great cloud of the Dharma-body, the great cloud of compassion, and the great inconceivable cloud, there fell the inconceivable rain of the vast Dharma, causing the bodies and minds of all sentient beings to become pure.
That is to say:
for the Bodhisattvas seated at the site of enlightenment, there falls a great rain of Dharma called "The Non-differentiation of the Dharma-realm."
For Bodhisattvas in their final existence, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called "The Bodhisattva’s Playful Secret Teaching of the Tathāgata";
for Bodhisattvas bound by only one more birth, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called:
Pure Universal Radiance;
for the sake of the Bodhisattvas receiving consecration, it rains a great Dharma rain called "Adorned with the Ornamentations of the Tathāgata."

For Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of Patience, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called "The Uninterrupted Practice of the Great Compassion of Bodhisattvas, Named the Blooming Flower of Wisdom-Jewels of Merit";
for Bodhisattvas who abide in the stage of Approaching Practice, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called:
They enter the profound gateway of manifesting transformations and practice the bodhisattva path without rest or weariness;

for the sake of bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, they rain down a great Dharma rain called "Giving Birth to the Tathāgata’s Practice of Great Compassion to Rescue and Protect Sentient Beings."
For those sentient beings seeking the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called "Deeply Understanding the Law of Dependent Origination,
Remaining Far Removed from the Two Extremes, and Attaining the Fruit of Indestructible Liberation";
for those sentient beings seeking the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, he rains down a great rain of Dharma called:
With the great sword of wisdom, they sever all enemies that are the afflictions;

for the sake of sentient beings— both those whose roots of goodness are fixed and those who are not— they rain down the great Dharma rain called "Causing the Accomplishment of Various Dharma Gates and Producing Great Joy."
O Son of the Buddha!
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, rain down such vast rains of Dharma, filling all infinite worlds.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a mind of equanimity and is without stinginess regarding the Dharma; yet, because the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings differ, the rain of Dharma he showers forth appears to have distinctions.
This is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha,
you should know that the voice of the Tathāgata possesses ten kinds of immeasurability.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
being immeasurable like the realm of space, because it reaches all places;
As the dharma-realm is immeasurable, because there is nowhere it does not pervade;
as the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable, because it causes all minds to rejoice;
as all karmas are immeasurable, because their retributions are explained;
Just as afflictions are immeasurable, so too does he cause them all to be extinguished;
just as the speech and sounds of sentient beings are immeasurable, so too does he enable them to hear according to their understanding;
just as the desires and inclinations of sentient beings are immeasurable, so too does he universally observe and deliver them.
It is as immeasurable as the three periods of time, for it has no boundaries;
it is as immeasurable as wisdom, for it discerns all things;
it is as immeasurable as the realm of the Buddhas, for it enters the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s vocal qualities are accomplished with such incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and immeasurable attributes; all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand them in this way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"When the trichiliocosm is about to be destroyed, The power of the merit of sentient beings issues forth a voice, proclaiming:
'The four dhyānas are tranquil and free from all suffering. Having heard this, they all become detached from desire."

The World-Honored One of Ten Powers is likewise; emitting sublime sounds that pervade the Dharma-realm, he proclaims for all that conditioned phenomena are suffering and impermanent, causing them to forever cross the sea of birth and death.
Just as in the deep mountains and vast valleys, every sound that arises is echoed;
though the echo follows the words of others, it ultimately possesses no discrimination.
The speech and sounds of the One Possessing Ten Powers are likewise thus:
manifesting according to the ripening of their faculties, causing them to be tamed and to give rise to joy, yet without thinking, "I am now able to expound this."

Just as there is a celestial drum named "The Awakener," which constantly resounds with the sound of Dharma in the sky to admonish those negligent sons of gods, causing them to hear it and thereby become free from attachment.
The Dharma drum of the Ten Powers is likewise; it emits various wondrous sounds, awakening all sentient beings and causing them all to realize the fruit of Bodhi.
The Celestial King Vaśavartin has a precious consort, Who skillfully plays all manner of music from her mouth;
From a single sound she can produce a hundred thousand tones, And within each of those sounds, yet another hundred thousand.
The voice of the Sugata is likewise: from a single sound, all sounds emerge;
according to the inclinations and faculties of beings, they differ, yet each, upon hearing it, brings their afflictions to an end.
Just as when the Brahmā King utters a single sound, He is able to cause all the Brahma-multitudes to rejoice;
The sound reaches only the Brahma-heaven and does not go beyond, Yet each one says, "I alone have heard it."

The Brahmā King Daśabala is likewise; though he utters a single sound that fills the entire Dharma-realm, it reaches only those within the assembly and does not extend far beyond, for they are unable to receive it due to a lack of faith.
Just as all waters share a single nature, And their eight meritorious qualities are without distinction,
Yet because they rest upon different grounds and are contained in different vessels, They thus become various and diverse.
The voice of omniscience is likewise: the nature of phenomena is of a single flavor and without distinction;
yet, according to the differing conducts of sentient beings, it causes what is heard to appear in various ways.
Just as the great Nāga King Anavatapta sends down rain that universally moistens the land of Jambudvīpa,
causing all grasses and trees to grow, yet this rain does not issue forth from his body or mind.

The sublime voices of all Buddhas are likewise; they rain down universally upon the entire Dharma-realm, completely saturating it, enabling the birth of goodness and the extinction of all evils, yet these do not arise from within or without.
For example, when the Naga King Manasvin raises clouds for seven days without first raining,
he waits until all sentient beings have finished their labors, and only then does he let fall the rain to bring about benefit.

The exposition of the meanings by the One of Ten Powers is likewise: first he transforms sentient beings so that they reach maturity, and only then does he preach the most profound Dharma, ensuring that those who hear it are not struck with fear.

The Great Adorned Dragon, within the ocean, Pours down ten kinds of adorned rain— Whether in hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of varieties; Though the water is of a single taste, the adornments differ.
Ultimate eloquence is likewise: when expounding ten, twenty, a hundred, a thousand, or even immeasurable Dharma-gates, no thought of distinction arises in the mind.
The most supreme Dragon King Sāgara raises clouds that universally cover the four continents;
though the rain falls differently in every place, the dragon’s mind harbors no dual thoughts.
The Buddhas, Kings of Dharma, are likewise; their great compassionate clouds of bodies pervade the ten directions.
They rain down diverse teachings for those who practice, yet they remain without discrimination toward any of them.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Son of the Buddha!”
The Tathāgata’s mind, thought, and consciousness are all unapprehendable; one should know the Tathāgata’s mind only by means of the immeasurability of wisdom.
"For example, just as space is that upon which all things depend, yet space itself has nothing upon which it depends."
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: it is the basis upon which all mundane and supramundane wisdoms rely, yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata has no basis of its own.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, although the dharma-realm constantly gives rise to the liberations of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, the dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: it constantly gives rise to all kinds of mundane and supramundane wisdom, yet the wisdom of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the second characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, it is like the great ocean, whose waters flow secretly beneath the lands of the four continents and the eighty billion minor islands; those who dig there will invariably find water, yet that great ocean makes no such discrimination as, "I am producing this water."

The ocean-water of the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it flows into the hearts of all sentient beings. If these sentient beings observe their spheres of experience and cultivate the Dharma-gates, they will attain a wisdom that is pure and lucid; yet the Tathāgata’s wisdom is equal and non-dual, without differentiation. It is only because the mental activities of sentient beings differ that the wisdom they obtain varies from one to another.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the third characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, the great ocean possesses four precious jewels that are endowed with immeasurable virtues and are able to produce all the rare treasures within the sea;
if these jewels were not in the great ocean, not even a single treasure could be found.
What are the four?
The first is named Accumulated Jewels; the second is named:
The Inexhaustible Treasury has three names:
the third is "Far Removed from Blazing Heat," and the fourth is "Endowed with Complete Adornments."
O Son of the Buddha!
These four precious jewels cannot be seen by any ordinary beings, nāgas, devas, or others. Why is this?
Because the Naga King Sagara places this precious jewel, which is magnificent, upright, and square, in a deep and secret place within his palace;
so it is, O Son of the Buddha!

The great ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise. Within it are four great jewels of wisdom, fully endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom. By means of these, the jewels of wisdom for all sentient beings—those in the stages of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and all Bodhisattvas—are produced.
What are these four? They are:

the great wisdom-jewel of skillful means that is free from attachment; the great wisdom-jewel of skillfully discerning conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; the great wisdom-jewel of discerningly expounding immeasurable teachings without violating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); and the great wisdom-jewel of knowing the proper and improper time without ever erring.
If these four jewels did not exist within the great ocean of the Tathāgatas’ wisdom, it would be impossible for even a single sentient being to enter the Mahāyāna.
These four jewels of wisdom cannot be seen by sentient beings of meager merit.
Why is this? Because they are placed within the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.

These four jewels of wisdom are balanced and upright, pure and exquisitely beautiful; they are universally able to benefit the assembly of bodhisattvas, causing them all to attain the radiance of wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fourth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, in the great ocean there are four great jewels of blazing radiance spread across its floor; their nature is extremely fierce and hot, and they are constantly able to drink up and contract the immeasurable waters poured into it by the hundred rivers. For this reason, the great ocean neither increases nor decreases.
What are the four? The first is named Sūryagarbha; the second is named...
Free from moisture, it has three names:
Flame Light; fourth, Exhaustion Without Remainder.
O Son of the Buddha!
If these four jewels did not exist within the great ocean, everything from the four continents up to the Summit of Existence would all be swept away and submerged.
O Son of the Buddha!
When the light of the Great Jewel Radiance of the Sun-Treasury shines upon it, the waters of the ocean all transform into milk;
when the light of the Great Jewel Radiance of Separation from Moisture shines upon it, that milk all transforms into curd.
When the great jewel radiates light and its brilliance touches it, that curd is entirely transformed into ghee;
when the great jewel radiates light and its brilliance touches it until nothing remains, that ghee is transformed into clarified butter (maṇḍa),
just as a fire blazes until it is completely extinguished without remainder.
O Son of the Buddha!

The ocean of great wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise; it possesses four kinds of jewels of great wisdom, fully endowed with immeasurable majesty, virtue, and radiance.
When the light of these wisdom-jewels touches the bodhisattvas, it even causes them to attain the great wisdom of a Tathāgata.
What are these four? They are:

the great wisdom-jewel that extinguishes all waves of dispersed goodness; the great wisdom-jewel that removes all craving for dharmas; the great wisdom-jewel whose light of insight shines everywhere; and the great wisdom-jewel of equality with the Tathāgata, which is boundless and effortless.
O Son of the Buddha!

When all Bodhisattvas practice all the factors conducive to enlightenment, they give rise to immeasurable waves of distracted virtue that cannot be destroyed by any gods, humans, or asuras in the world.

The Tathāgata, with the light of the jewel of great wisdom that extinguishes all waves of distracted virtue, touches those Bodhisattvas, causing them to abandon all waves of distracted virtue, to hold their minds in a single object, and to abide in samādhi.

Furthermore, the light of the great wisdom-jewel that removes craving for all phenomena touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish attachment to the taste of samādhi and to give rise to vast supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Furthermore, the light of the great wisdom-jewel that universally illumines with the radiance of wisdom touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish the vast supernormal powers they have produced and to abide in the practice of the function of great illumination.

Furthermore, the light of the great wisdom-jewel that is equal to the Tathāgata’s boundless and effortless nature touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish the practice of the function of great illumination and even attain the stage of equality with the Tathāgata, wherein all functions are stilled so that nothing remains.
O Son of the Buddha!
If there were not the great light of touch from these four jewels of wisdom of the Tathāgata, it would be impossible for even a single bodhisattva to attain the stage of a Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

From the surface of the waters up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, all that exists within these great trichiliocosm worlds—the abodes of sentient beings in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—none of them arise apart from space, nor do they abide apart from space.
Why is this? Because space is all-pervasive;
although that space universally contains the triple world, it is devoid of discrimination.
O Son of the Buddha!

The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: whether it be the wisdom of śrāvakas, the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of bodhisattvas, the wisdom of conditioned practices, or the wisdom of unconditioned practices—all arise from the wisdom of the Tathāgata and abide in the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom pervades all things;
although it universally accommodates immeasurable wisdom, it remains free from discrimination.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the sixth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
On the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a king of medicinal trees named Inexhaustible Root.
The roots of that medicinal tree grow from sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas below, reaching all the way down to the adamantine ground at the limit of the water-circle.
When that medicinal king-tree takes root, it causes all the roots of the trees in Jambudvīpa to grow;
when its trunk grows, it causes all the trunks of the trees in Jambudvīpa to grow;
and it is likewise for its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
In this medicinal king tree, the roots can produce stems, and the stems can produce roots; the roots are inexhaustible, and are thus named "Inexhaustible Roots.
O Son of the Buddha!
That medicinal king-tree causes growth in all places, yet it is unable to provide the benefit of growth in only two locations:
namely, within the deep pits of hell and within the water-circle;
nevertheless, it never feels weary or abandons them.

O Son of the Buddha! The Great Medicine King Tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: it takes as its roots the vast vows of great compassion—vows made in the past to accomplish all wholesome dharmas of wisdom, to universally cover all realms of sentient beings, and to eliminate the sufferings of all evil destinies; it takes as its trunk the firm and immovable skillful means born from the lineage of the true wisdom of all Tathāgatas; it takes as its branches the wisdom that pervades the Dharma-realm and the various *pāramitās*; it takes as its leaves the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the great samādhis; it takes as its flowers the dhāraṇīs, eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); and it takes as its fruit the ultimate, unchanging liberation of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
For what reason is the Tathāgata’s wisdom, this great medicinal king tree,
named "Inexhaustible Root"?
Because it is ultimately without rest and because it does not interrupt the bodhisattva practice—
since the bodhisattva practice is the Tathāgata-nature and the Tathāgata-nature is the bodhisattva practice— it is therefore named the "Inexhaustible Root."
O Son of the Buddha!
When the roots of the Tathāgata’s great medicinal king tree emerge, they cause all bodhisattvas to produce the root of great compassion that never abandons sentient beings;
when its trunk emerges, it causes all bodhisattvas to increase the trunk of a deep resolve characterized by firm diligence.
When its branches grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to increase the branches of all the pāramitās;
when its leaves grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to grow the leaves of pure ethical discipline, dhūta virtues, fewness of desires, and contentment;
when its flowers grow, they cause all bodhisattvas to possess the flowers of the marks and signs that adorn their roots of goodness.
When its fruit ripens, it causes all bodhisattvas to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the fruit of the empowerment of all Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
The great medicinal king tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom can only fail to provide growth and benefit in two places, namely:

The followers of the two vehicles fall into the vast and deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while those sentient beings who have destroyed their roots of goodness and are unfit vessels drown in the waters of great false views and craving;
yet, he never feels weary of or abandons them.
O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom of the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases, for it is well-established in the faculties and arises without cessation.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the seventh characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is like when the kalpa-fire arises in a trichiliocosm, burning away all grasses, trees, and forests, until even the Iron Ring Mountains and Great Iron Ring Mountains are completely incinerated without remainder.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Suppose there were someone who took dry grass in their hand and threw it into that fire; what do you think—would it not be burned? He replied:
"No, it would not. "Son of the Buddha!
That grass thrown there might perhaps not burn; however—"
The wisdom of the Tathāgata discerns all sentient beings, all lands, all kalpas, and all dharmas throughout the three periods of time; there is nothing he does not know.
To say that he does not know is impossible.
Why is this? Because their wisdom is equal and they have attained complete and clear penetration.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is the eighth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
For example, when the world-system is destroyed by the calamity of wind, a great wind arises, named:
The Wind of Dispersion and Destruction can shatter the trichiliocosm, reducing even the Iron Ring Mountains and all else to fine dust.
Furthermore, there is a great wind named "The Obstructing," which surrounds the trichiliocosm and obstructs the winds of dispersion and destruction, preventing them from reaching other world-systems.
O Son of the Buddha!
If this great obstructing wind did not exist, there would be no world in the ten directions that would not be utterly destroyed.
It is the same with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: he possesses a great wind of wisdom, which is named:
It is capable of extinguishing; it can extinguish the habitual tendencies of affliction of all great bodhisattvas.

There is a wind of great wisdom called "Skillful Sustenance," which skillfully sustains those bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature, preventing the wheel of the wind of great wisdom from extinguishing their habitual tendencies of affliction.
O Son of the Buddha!
If there were not the wind of the Tathāgata’s skillful sustaining wisdom, immeasurable bodhisattvas would all fall to the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
by virtue of this wisdom, it causes all bodhisattvas to transcend the stages of the two vehicles and dwell securely in the ultimate position of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the ninth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind, which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
The wisdom of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere. Why is this?
There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts, inversions, and attachments that they do not realize it.
If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will manifest before one.
Son of the Buddha!

It is like a great scripture, equal in size to the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, upon which all matters within that triple-thousand great thousandfold world system have been written in their entirety.
That is to say:
writing down the events within the Great Iron Ring Mountains, their extent would equal that of the Great Iron Ring Mountains;
writing down the events within the great earth, their extent would equal that of the great earth.
If one were to write down the events within a medium chiliocosm, the volume would equal that of a medium chiliocosm;
if one were to write down the events within a small chiliocosm, the volume would equal that of a small chiliocosm.

Likewise, whether it be the four continents, the great oceans, Mount Sumeru, the palaces of the terrestrial devas, the palaces of the space-dwelling devas of the desire realm, the palaces of the form realm, or the palaces of the formless realm—if one were to write down each of these, their volume would all be exactly equal.
Although this great sutra scroll is equal in measure to the great trichiliocosm, it dwells entirely within a single minute atom;
as it is with one minute atom, so it is with all minute atoms.

At that time, there was a person of wise and penetrating insight who had fully perfected the pure divine eye. Seeing this sutra scroll within a mote of dust, providing no benefit whatsoever to sentient beings, he thought to himself:
"I shall, by the power of diligence, shatter that mote of dust, bring forth this sutra scroll, and cause all sentient beings to obtain abundant benefit."
Having formed this thought, he immediately applied skillful means to break those atoms and bring forth this great sutra, so that all sentient beings might universally obtain benefit.
Just as it is with one atom, so should it be known for all atoms.
O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: immeasurable and unimpeded, it is able to universally benefit all sentient beings, being fully present within the bodies of all sentient beings.
However, all ordinary and ignorant people, through their deluded thoughts and attachments, neither know nor perceive this, and thus fail to obtain benefit.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure eye of wisdom, universally surveyed all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm and spoke these words:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
"How marvelous!
How is it that these sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet, being deluded and ignorant, neither know nor see it?

I shall instruct them in the Noble Path so that they may forever leave behind false conceptualizations and attachments, and perceive within their own bodies the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, no different from that of the Buddha."
He then instructs those sentient beings to cultivate the Noble Path so that they may leave behind false conceptualization;
having left behind false conceptualization, they realize the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This is the tenth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it in this way.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of such immeasurable, unimpeded, and inconceivable marks of vastness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"If you wish to know the mind of all Buddhas, You should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddhas.
The wisdom of the Buddhas has no place of dependence, Just as space has nothing upon which it relies."
The various pleasures of sentient beings, as well as all skillful means and wisdom, all rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom; yet the Buddha’s wisdom has no basis of reliance.
The liberation of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas—[all arise from this].
All depend upon the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it gives birth to all-knowledge, yet it neither increases nor decreases, being neither born nor exhausted.
Just as water flows beneath the earth, Seeking it, one never fails to find it;
Without thought and without exhaustion, Its power pervades the ten directions.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: It is universally present within the minds of all sentient beings.
If one practices with diligence, one will swiftly attain the light of wisdom.
Just as a dragon possesses four jewels that produce all manner of treasures,
yet when placed in a deep and secret place, ordinary people are unable to see them.
The Buddha’s four wisdoms are likewise so: they give birth to all-encompassing knowledge, which no other person can perceive, except for the great Bodhisattvas.
Just as the ocean contains four treasures and is able to drink up all waters, [so too are the Buddha's wisdoms].
It causes the ocean not to overflow, nor does it ever increase or decrease.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise: it calms the waves and eliminates attachment to dharmas;
vast and without limit, it can give birth to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
From the lowest realm up to the Peak of Existence, throughout the realms of desire,
form, and formlessness, all things depend upon space, yet space makes no distinctions.
So it is with the wisdom of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas.
All depend upon the Buddha’s wisdom, yet that Buddha-wisdom is free from discrimination.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a king of medicines called "Inexhaustible Root," which can produce all trees— roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: born from the lineage of the Tathāgatas, once enlightenment has been attained, one further gives rise to the practices of a bodhisattva.
It is like a person holding dry grass and placing it within the conflagration at the end of an eon.
Even adamant remains ablaze; there is no principle here that is not consumed by fire.
Throughout the kalpas and lands of the three periods of time, as well as the sentient beings within them—even if those grasses were not to burn, there is nothing this Buddha does not know.
There is a wind named "Dissolution," capable of destroying the great trichiliocosm;
if there were no other winds to stop it, its destruction would extend to immeasurable realms.
So too is the wind of Great Wisdom: it extinguishes the delusions of all bodhisattvas.
There is another skillful wind that causes one to abide in the stage of the Tathāgata.
It is like a great sutra scroll, equal in size to the three-thousandfold world system, contained within a single atom; so it is with every atom.
There is a wise person whose pure eyes see all clearly;
Breaking through the dust, they bring forth a scripture to universally benefit sentient beings.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it pervades the minds of all sentient beings.
Ensnared by false imaginings, they neither perceive nor know.
Out of great compassion, the Buddhas cause them to eliminate these imaginings;
thus they appear, bringing benefit to all bodhisattvas.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Fifty-one;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Fifty-two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Thirty-Seven, Part Three: The Appearance of the Tathāgatas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
O Son of the Buddha!

By means of unobstructed and unhindered wisdom, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all worldly realms are the realm of the Tathāgata; he knows that all realms of the three periods of time, all realms of lands, all realms of phenomena, all realms of sentient beings, the realm of non-differentiated true thusness, the realm of unobstructed dharma-realm, the realm of the boundless limit of reality, the realm of space without measure, and the realm of no realm are the realm of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as the realms of all worlds are immeasurable, so too are the realms of the Tathāgata immeasurable;
just as the realms of all three periods of time are immeasurable, so too are the realms of the Tathāgata immeasurable.
Furthermore, just as the realm of non-realm is immeasurable, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata immeasurable;
just as the realm of non-realm does not exist anywhere, so too the realm of the Tathāgata likewise does not exist anywhere.
O Son of the Buddha!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know that the realm of the mind is the realm of the Tathāgata.
Just as the realm of the mind is immeasurable and boundless, neither bound nor liberated, so too the realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless, neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because through such and such conceptualization and discrimination, there is such and such immeasurable manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as a great dragon king sends down rain according to his will, yet that rain comes from neither within nor without, so too is the realm of the Tathāgata:
according to such conceptualization and discrimination, there is such an immeasurable manifestation, which has no place of origin anywhere throughout the ten directions.
O Son of the Buddha!

Just as the waters of the great ocean all arise from the mental power of the dragon kings, so too is the ocean of all-knowledge of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; it likewise arises entirely from the great vows made by the Tathāgatas in the past.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The ocean of all-knowledge is immeasurable and boundless, inconceivable and ineffable;
nevertheless, I shall now briefly provide a parable for you, which you should listen to with close attention.”
O Son of the Buddha!

In this Jambudvīpa, two thousand five hundred rivers flow into the great ocean; in Aparagoyānī in the west, five thousand rivers flow into the great ocean; in Pūrvavideha in the east, seven thousand five hundred rivers flow into the great ocean; and in Uttarakuru in the north, ten thousand rivers flow into the great ocean.
“O Son of the Buddha!
In these four continents, twenty-five thousand such rivers flow continuously and without interruption into the great ocean.
What do you think? Is this water much?”
He replied, "Very many. "O Son of the Buddha!"
Furthermore, there were ten Dragon Kings of Radiance who rained water into the great ocean twice as much as before;
the Dragon King Hundred Radiances rained water into the great ocean twice as much as the former;

the Dragon King Great Adornment, the Dragon King Mānasa, the Dragon King Thunder-Resonance, the Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda, the Dragon King Immeasurable Radiance, the Dragon King Uninterrupted Torrent, the Dragon King Great Victory, and the Dragon King Great Exertion—these and eighty billion other great dragon kings each rained into the great ocean, all successively doubling the amount of the one preceding them.
The crown prince of the Dragon King Sāgara is named Jambūdhvaja;
the water he rains down upon the great ocean is twice as much as before.
O Son of the Buddha!
The water from the palace of the Dragon King Daśaprabha flows into the great ocean, exceeding the former by a factor of ten;
the water from the palace of the Dragon King Śataprabha flows into the great ocean, exceeding the former by another factor of ten;

and the waters from the palaces of the Dragon Kings Mahāvyūha, Mānasvin, Stanayitnu, Nanda and Upananda, Amitaprabha, Avicchinnadhārā, Mahāvijaya, and Mahāvikrama—these and eighty billion other such great dragon kings, each with their own distinct palaces—the water within them all flows into the great ocean, each successively exceeding the previous by a factor of ten.
The water flowing from the palace of the Prince of the Sāgara Dragon King, Yaṃvudhvaja, into the great ocean is twice as much as before.
O Son of the Buddha!
When the Sāgara Dragon King pours down rain continuously upon the great ocean, the water is again twice as much as before.
The water that surges out from within the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara and enters the sea is twice as much as before;
the water that emerges is the color of deep lapis lazuli and flows forth at specific times, which is why the tides of the great ocean do not miss their appointed hour.
O Son of the Buddha!
Thus, this great ocean has immeasurable water, immeasurable varieties of jewels, immeasurable sentient beings, and the great earth upon which it rests is likewise immeasurable.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What do you think? Is that great ocean immeasurable? He replied:
"It is truly immeasurable and cannot be compared.
"O Son of the Buddha!
This great ocean is immeasurable, yet it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part of the immeasurable ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
I merely provide analogies in accordance with the minds of sentient beings; yet the realm of the Buddha cannot be reached by analogy.
Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable, because from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, they have cultivated all bodhisattva practices without interruption.

One should know that the accumulation of jewels is immeasurable, because it ensures that all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the lineages of the Three Jewels are never interrupted;

one should know that the sentient beings who dwell therein are immeasurable, because they are the objects of enjoyment for all those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas;

and one should know that the stages (*bhūmi*) upon which they dwell are immeasurable, because they are the abodes of all bodhisattvas from the initial Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the ultimate Stage of Non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-bhūmi*).
O Son of the Buddha!
In order to enter immeasurable wisdom and benefit all sentient beings, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
“As the realms of the mind are immeasurable, so too are the realms of all Buddhas;
as the realms of the mind arise from the intellect, one should observe the realm of the Buddha in this same way.”
Just as a dragon, without leaving its original place, pours down great rain through the power of its mind—
though the rain has no place of coming or going— it completely saturates all things in accordance with the dragon’s intention.

The Muni endowed with the ten powers is likewise: coming from nowhere and going nowhere, he manifests his body for those with pure hearts, equal in measure to the dharma-realm and entering into every pore.
As the wonders of the ocean are immeasurable, so too are sentient beings and the great earth;
the nature of water is of one single flavor, without distinction, and those born therein each receive its benefit.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: all that exists therein is immeasurable;
those in training, those beyond training, and those dwelling on the stages—all find benefit within it.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Son of the Buddha!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that unimpeded conduct is the conduct of the Tathāgata; they should know that the conduct of true suchness (*tathatā*) is the conduct of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as true suchness is not born in the past limit, does not move in the future limit, and does not arise in the present;
The practice of the Tathāgata is also like this: it is unborn, unmoving, and unarisen.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the Dharma-realm: it is neither measurable nor immeasurable, because it is formless.
The practice of the Tathāgata is also like this: it is neither measurable nor immeasurable, because it is formless.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like a bird flying through the void; even after a hundred years have passed, the distance already traversed and the distance yet to be traversed can both not be measured.
Why is this? Because the realm of space is without limit.

The practice of the Tathāgata is likewise; even if someone were to analyze and expound it for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, that which has been explained and that which remains unexplained would both be immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the practice of the Tathāgata is boundless.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha dwells in unimpeded conduct and has no fixed abode, yet he is able to universally manifest his activities for all sentient beings; having seen them, they transcend all paths of obstruction.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the King of Golden-Winged Birds, who flies through the void, circling and soaring without ceasing. With his pure eyes, he observes the various dragon palaces within the ocean; exerting fierce and courageous power, he beats the seawater with his left and right wings until it parts in two, and knowing which male or female dragons have reached the end of their lives, he seizes them.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the King of Golden-Winged Birds, is likewise. Abiding in unimpeded conduct, he observes all sentient beings within the various palaces of the dharma-realm with his pure Buddha-eye. If there are those who have previously planted roots of goodness that have already matured, the Tathāgata exerts his ten heroic powers; with the two wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā, he stirs up the great ocean of the waters of craving within saṃsāra, causing it to part so as to seize them, place them within the Buddha-dharma, cause them to sever all conceptual proliferation and idle discourse, and establish them in the Tathāgata’s non-conceptual and unimpeded conduct.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the sun and the moon, which travel alone without equal through the void, benefiting sentient beings, yet they do not form this thought:
"From where have I come, and to what place have I arrived?"

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise thus: their nature is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of discrimination. Yet, they manifest wandering throughout all realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, performing the works of a Buddha without ceasing, without giving rise to such conceptual proliferation or discrimination as:
"I come from that place, and I go toward that place."
"O Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should, by means of such immeasurable skillful means and immeasurable natures and characteristics, know and see the conduct practiced by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Just as True Suchness is neither born nor extinguished, Having no location and being invisible;
So too is the conduct of the Great Benefactor, Transcending the three periods of time and immeasurable."
The Dharma-realm is neither a realm nor a non-realm; it is neither finite nor infinite.
The conduct of those of great merit is likewise: neither finite nor infinite, for they possess no body.
As a bird flies through the air for billions of years, the space before and behind it remains equal and without distinction;
so too, though one were to expound the Tathāgata’s deeds throughout many kalpas, what has been said and what remains unsaid cannot be measured.
