As the golden-winged bird surveys the great ocean from the sky, It cleaves the waters to seize the male and female nagas;
So too, the One of Ten Powers can uproot those with wholesome roots, Causing them to emerge from the sea of existence and eliminate all delusions.
Just as the sun and moon travel through space, Illuminating all things without discrimination;
So the World-Honored One traverses the entire Dharma-realm, Teaching and transforming sentient beings without a single stirring thought.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas understand how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attains perfect enlightenment?
O Son of the Buddha!”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that when a Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he does not observe any objective referents; regarding all phenomena as equal, he is free from doubt, non-dual, and signless. He is without activity and without cessation, immeasurable and boundless, far removed from the two extremes, and abides in the Middle Way. Transcending all written characters and verbal expressions, he knows the mental activities, faculties, dispositions, inclinations, afflictions, and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings.
To state the essential point: within a single thought-moment, he fully knows all dharmas of the three periods of time.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the great ocean, which can universally reflect the forms and images of all sentient beings within the four continents; for this reason, it is collectively called the "great ocean.

The Bodhi of the Buddhas is also like this: it universally manifests the mental thoughts, faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings, yet there is nothing that is manifested. For this reason, it is named the "Bodhi of the Buddhas."
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhi of all Buddhas cannot be proclaimed by any written characters, cannot be reached by any sounds, and cannot be spoken by any speech; it is only revealed through skillful means according to what is appropriate for each being.

O Son of the Buddha! When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha attains perfect enlightenment, he attains a body equal in measure to all sentient beings; he attains a body equal in measure to all phenomena; he attains a body equal in measure to all lands; he attains a body equal in measure to all three periods of time; he attains a body equal in measure to all Buddhas; he attains a body equal in measure to all languages; he attains a body equal in measure to True Suchness; he attains a body equal in measure to the Dharma-realm; he attains a body equal in measure to the realm of empty space; he attains a body equal in measure to the unobstructed realm; he attains a body equal in measure to all vows; he attains a body equal in measure to all practices; and he attains a body equal in measure to the realm of quiescent nirvāṇa.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as with the body one has attained, so it is with speech and mind; one attains such immeasurable and innumerable purities of the three wheels.
O Son of the Buddha!

When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvana; they are all of one single nature, namely:
the nature of non-nature.
What kinds of natures are non-existent? They are:

the nature of signlessness, the nature of inexhaustibility, the nature of non-arising, the nature of non-ceasing, the nature of non-self, the nature of non-non-self, the nature of non-sentient beings, the nature of non-non-sentient beings, the nature of non-enlightenment, the nature of non-dharmadhātu, and the nature of non-space; furthermore, there is also no nature of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Because they know that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, they attain omniscience, maintain a continuous flow of great compassion, and deliver sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like space: whether all worlds are formed or destroyed, it remains forever without increase or decrease.
Why is this? Because space is without arising.
The *bodhi* of all Buddhas is likewise; whether they attain perfect enlightenment or do not attain perfect enlightenment, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because awakening is without marks and without non-marks, being neither one nor manifold.
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were someone who could manifest as many minds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each of those minds further manifested as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—all of whom were without color, without form, and without marks—and continued doing so without rest for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
O Son of the Buddha! What do you think?
How many Tathāgatas could that person’s emanated mind create through such transformations?
The Bodhisattva Tathāgata-gotra-prabhāsa-vimala said:
"As I understand the meaning of what you have said, transformation and non-transformation are equal and without distinction; why then do you ask how many there are?"
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of the Buddha!"
As you have said, even if all sentient beings were to attain perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment, it would be no different from their not attaining perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because awakening is signless;
if there are no signs, then there is neither increase nor decrease.
O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment is identical to bodhi—characterized by a single mark and yet without marks.
When a Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he enters the samādhi of the wisdom of excellent awakening through the skillful means of the single mark.
Having entered, within a single vast body of a Perfectly Enlightened One, he manifests bodies equal in number to all sentient beings and dwells within them.
Just as it is with this one vast body of a Perfectly Enlightened One, so it is with all vast bodies of Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable gateways to the attainment of perfect enlightenment; therefore, you should know that the bodies manifested by the Tathāgata are immeasurable.
Because they are immeasurable, the body of the Tathāgata is said to be an immeasurable realm, equal to the realm of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that within a single pore of the Tathāgata’s body, there are bodies of Buddhas equal in number to all sentient beings. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata’s body of perfect enlightenment is ultimately without arising or ceasing, just as a single pore pervades the entire Dharma-realm, so it is with all pores; one should know that there is not even the slightest place empty of the Buddha-body.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, reaches everywhere;

according to their capacities and according to their powers, he manifests the attainment of equal and right enlightenment upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment through various bodies.
O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that within every thought-moment of his own mind, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this mind.

Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings: within them all, the Tathāgata attains equal and right enlightenment, vast and pervasive, existing everywhere, neither departing nor ceasing, without rest, entering the inconceivable gateway of skillful means.
"O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand the Tathāgata’s attainment of perfect enlightenment in this way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
“Perfectly awakened, he realizes all phenomena: non-dual, free from duality, and entirely equal;
their intrinsic nature is pure like space, without discrimination between self and non-self.”
Just as the ocean seal manifests the bodies of sentient beings, and for this reason it is called the great ocean;
so too, Bodhi universally seals all mental activities, and for this reason it is called Perfect Enlightenment.
Just as the world undergoes formation and destruction, yet space neither increases nor decreases;
so too, though all Buddhas appear in the world, the single characteristic of bodhi is eternally signless.
Just as when a person’s emanated mind creates a Buddha, the nature of the emanation and the non-emanation are no different;
so too, when all sentient beings attain enlightenment, there is neither increase nor decrease in those who have attained it or those who have not.

The Buddha possesses a samādhi named "Good Awakening"; Entering this concentration beneath the Bodhi tree, He emits immeasurable light equal for all sentient beings, Awakening the multitudes like the blossoming of lotuses.

As many as there are eons, lands, and sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, and all their mental thoughts, faculties, and desires—bodies equal in number to these he manifests; therefore, the Perfectly Awakened One is called Immeasurable.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Son of the Buddha!”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand that the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma through the power of mastery over the mind, without arising or shifting, because he knows all phenomena are eternally without arising;
he turns the wheel of Dharma by severing what is to be severed through the three turnings, because he knows all phenomena are free from extreme views;
he turns the wheel of Dharma beyond the limit of desire and the non-limit, because he enters the limit of emptiness of all phenomena.
One turns the wheel of Dharma without verbal expression, for one knows that all phenomena are inexpressible;
one turns the wheel of Dharma through ultimate quiescence, for one knows that all phenomena have the nature of nirvana;
and one turns the wheel of Dharma by means of all letters and all speech, for the voice of the Tathāgata reaches everywhere.
One turns the wheel of Dharma knowing that sounds are like echoes, because one has realized the true nature of all phenomena;
one turns the wheel of Dharma by producing all sounds within a single sound, because ultimately there is no master;
one turns the wheel of Dharma without omission or exhaustion, because there is no attachment to the internal or external.
O Son of the Buddha!

Just as all written characters and spoken language could never be exhausted even if one were to speak them throughout all future kalpas, so too is the turning of the Wheel of Dharma by the Buddha: established and revealed through all written characters, it is without rest and without end.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma enters entirely into all speech and written characters, yet it abides nowhere.
It is like written letters, which universally enter into all things, all speech, all calculations, and all mundane and supramundane realms, yet they abide nowhere.
The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: it universally enters into all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, all karmas, and all retributions, yet abides nowhere.
The various languages of all sentient beings are entirely not apart from the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma.
Why is this? Because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of speech and sound is itself the wheel of Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand the Tathāgata’s turning of the wheel of Dharma in this way: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who wishes to know the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata should know the source from which the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma arises."
What is the source from which the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma arises?
O Son of the Buddha!
In accordance with the infinite distinctions in the mental activities, inclinations, and desires of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata produces various sounds and turns the wheel of Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses a samādhi called "Ultimate Unobstructed Fearlessness.

Having entered this samādhi, from each and every body and each and every mouth of his perfected enlightenment, he emits vocal sounds equal in number to all sentient beings. Within each and every sound, all varieties of voices are fully present, each distinct as they turn the wheel of Dharma, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
One who can know the turning of the wheel of Dharma in this way should be known as one who accords with all Buddha-dharmas;
one who does not know it in this way does not accord with them.
"O Son of the Buddha!
All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should thus know the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Buddhas, because it universally enters the infinite realms of sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma does not turn; throughout the three periods of time, there is neither arising nor attainment.
Just as written characters have no end, so too is the wheel of Dharma of the One of Ten Powers.”
Just as letters universally enter yet nowhere arrive, so too is the wheel of the True Awakening;
it enters all speech and sounds without entering anything, yet is able to cause all sentient beings to rejoice.
The Buddha possesses a samādhi named Ultimate; having entered this concentration, he then preaches the Dharma.
For all sentient beings, who are without limit, he universally emits his voice to cause them to awaken and understand.
Within each and every sound, they further manifest Infinite vocal expressions, each distinct;
Masters of the world, free from discrimination, They cause all to hear according to their inclinations and desires.
Syllables do not emerge from within or without, nor are they lost or destroyed, nor do they accumulate;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, they turn the wheel of Dharma—such sovereign mastery is most extraordinary.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
O Son of the Buddha!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to know the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata must thoroughly understand the fundamental self-nature.
As is the Nirvāṇa of True Suchness (tathatā), so too is the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;
as is the Nirvāṇa of the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), so too is the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
As is the nirvana of the dharma-realm, so too is the nirvana of the Tathāgata;
as is the nirvana of space, so too is the nirvana of the Tathāgata;
as is the nirvana of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), so too is the nirvana of the Tathāgata.
As is the limit of detachment, which is nirvana, so too is the nirvana of the Tathāgata;
as is the limit of signlessness, which is nirvana, so too is the nirvana of the Tathāgata;
as is the limit of self-nature, which is nirvana, so too is the nirvana of the Tathāgata.
Just as the limit of the nature of all phenomena is nirvāṇa, so too is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;
just as the limit of suchness is nirvāṇa, so too is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because nirvāṇa is without arising and without emergence;
if a phenomenon is without arising and without emergence, then it is without cessation.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata does not speak of the ultimate nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas for the sake of bodhisattvas, nor does he manifest that matter to them. Why is this?

Desiring to cause all Tathāgatas to appear ever-present before them, they perceive, within a single thought-moment, the physical forms and marks of all Buddhas of the past and future as being perfectly complete, just as if they were present now, yet they give rise neither to the notion of duality nor to the notion of non-duality.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are forever free from all conceptual attachments and perceptions.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgatas appear in the world in order to inspire joy in sentient beings;
they manifest parinirvāṇa in order to inspire longing and veneration in sentient beings.
Yet, in reality, there is no such thing as the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world, nor is there any parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? The Tathāgata eternally abides in the pure Dharma-realm, yet manifests nirvāṇa in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!

For example, when the sun rises and shines universally upon the world, its reflection appears in all vessels of pure water; it pervades all places without coming or going, yet if even a single vessel is broken, the reflection no longer appears.
“O Son of the Buddha!
What do you think? Is it the fault of the sun that its reflection does not appear? He replied:
"No, it is not so. It is merely because the vessel is broken; the sun is not at fault.
"O Son of the Buddha!"

The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: it manifests universally throughout the dharma-realm without before or after; there is no sentient being whose vessel of a pure mind in which the Buddha does not appear. If the vessel of the mind is constantly pure, one constantly beholds the Buddha-body; yet if the mind is turbid or the vessel is broken, one shall not see him.
O Son of the Buddha!

If there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata manifests nirvāṇa for them; yet in reality, the Tathāgata is without birth, without death, and without passing into extinction.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the element of fire, which performs the function of fire throughout all worlds; yet at times, the fire may be extinguished in a single location.
What do you think? Is the fire in all worlds thereby extinguished?
He replied, “No, Son of the Buddha!”

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: he performs the buddha-work in all worlds, yet in one world, having completed his tasks, he manifests entry into nirvāṇa; how could it be that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in all worlds have all entered parinirvāṇa?
O Son of the Buddha!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand the great parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha in this way.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

It is, for example, like a master illusionist who is highly proficient in the arts of illusion; by the power of his illusions, he manifests illusory bodies in all the lands, cities, towns, and villages throughout the trichiliocosm, remaining there for the duration of an eon sustained by his illusory power;
yet in other places, having completed his illusory display, he conceals his body and does not appear.
O Son of the Buddha!
What do you think? Does that great illusionist, by concealing his body and disappearing from one place, truly vanish and cease to exist in all places?
He replied, "No, Son of the Buddha! "Son of the Buddha! [the Buddha said.]

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise: well-versed in the various illusory arts of immeasurable wisdom and skillful means, he manifests his body throughout the entire dharma-realm, maintaining it so that it remains eternally present until the end of the future;
yet in a single location, according to the minds of sentient beings, once his work is accomplished, he manifests parinirvāṇa.
How could one say that because the Tathāgata manifests entry into *nirvāṇa* in a single location, he has therefore attained final extinction everywhere?
Son of the Buddha!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand the great *parinirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this way.
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha! When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests his entry into nirvāṇa, he enters the Immovable Samādhi (*acalā-samādhi*).

Having entered this samādhi, from each and every body he emits immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great light rays. From each light ray emerge incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lotus flowers; each lotus flower has unspeakably many exquisite jewel stamens; on each stamen is a lion throne; and upon each throne sits a Tathāgata in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). The number of these Buddhas' bodies is exactly equal to the number of all sentient beings, and they are all adorned with supreme and wondrous merits, having arisen through the power of their original vows."
If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured, upon seeing the Buddha’s body, they all receive transformation.
Yet that Buddha-body abides eternally until the end of the future, skillfully transforming and delivering all sentient beings according to their needs, never missing the proper time.
O Son of the Buddha!

The body of the Tathāgata has no fixed location; it is neither real nor unreal. It appears solely through the power of the original vows of all Buddhas, manifesting whenever sentient beings are ready to be delivered.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this way.
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgata dwells within the immeasurable, unobstructed, ultimate realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the realm of empty space, true suchness (tathatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-arising and non-ceasing, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); yet for the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests at appropriate times.
"By virtue of upholding their original vows, they never cease; they do not abandon any sentient beings, any lands, or any dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"As the sun spreads its light across the Dharma-realm, When the vessel breaks and the water leaks away, the reflection perishes along with it."
The sun of supreme wisdom is likewise: though sentient beings lack faith, they perceive it as entering nirvāṇa.

Just as fire performs its functions in the world within a single city or town before sometimes ceasing, so too the Supreme among Men, pervading the entire dharma-realm, manifests his final passing once his work of transformation is complete.
The illusionist manifests his body in all lands, yet vanishes once his task is complete;
the Tathāgata’s transformations are likewise, for while he may pass away here, the Buddha is always seen in other realms.
The Buddha possesses a samādhi named Immovable; having finished transforming sentient beings, he enters this concentration.
In a single thought-moment, his body emits immeasurable light, and from the light emerge lotus flowers, upon each of which sits a Buddha.
The Buddha’s bodies are as infinite as the Dharma-realm, visible only to sentient beings who possess merit;
each of these infinite bodies is fully endowed with a complete lifespan and majestic adornments.
As the nature of non-arising, the Buddha appears in the world; as the nature of non-extinction, the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa.
All words and metaphors are utterly transcended; he who accomplishes all meanings has no equal.
“O Son of the Buddha!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, and drawing near to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?”

O Son of the Buddha! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that all roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, and attending upon the Tathāgata are entirely not in vain. This is because they give rise to inexhaustible awakened wisdom; because they are free from all obstacles and difficulties; because they lead decisively to the ultimate goal; because they are without falsehood or deception; because all vows are fulfilled; because they do not exhaust conditioned activities; because they accord with unconditioned knowledge; because they give birth to the wisdom of all Buddhas; because they extend to the end of the future; because they accomplish all kinds of supreme practices; and because they reach the stage of effortless wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a man who eats a small piece of diamond; it is never digested, but must pass through his body and emerge from the outside. Why is this?

Because the vajra does not coexist with the impurities of the physical body, so too it is with even a small root of goodness planted toward the Tathāgata: it must pierce through the body of afflictions consisting of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and reach the state of ultimate unconditioned wisdom.
Why is this? Because these few roots of goodness do not coexist with the afflictions of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
O Son of the Buddha!
Suppose there were a pile of dry grass as large as Mount Sumeru, and one were to cast into it a spark of fire the size of a mustard seed; it would surely burn them all away. Why is this?
Because fire has the power to burn.
It is likewise with even a small root of goodness planted before the Tathāgata: it will surely burn away all afflictions and lead ultimately to nirvana without remainder.
Why is this? Because the nature of these few roots of goodness is ultimately consummate.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, on Mount Himavat there is a king of medicinal trees called Sudarśana;
if anyone sees it, their eyes attain purity.
If there are those who hear it, their ears shall attain purity;
if there are those who smell it, their noses shall attain purity;
if there are those who taste it, their tongues shall attain purity.
If there are those who touch it, their bodies will attain purity;
if there are sentient beings who take up the soil of that ground, it will likewise bring about the benefit of curing their illnesses.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed King of Medicine, is likewise able to bring about every benefit for sentient beings.
If there are those who behold the physical body of the Tathāgata, their eyes attain purity;
if there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata, their ears attain purity.
If there are those who smell the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s precepts, their sense of smell becomes purified;
if there are those who taste the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, their sense of taste becomes purified, they come to possess a broad and long tongue, and they understand the language of the Dharma;
if there are those who touch the light of the Tathāgata, their bodies become purified, and they ultimately attain the unsurpassed Dharma-body.
If one gives rise to mindfulness of the Tathāgata, one will attain the purity of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).

If there are sentient beings who make offerings to the lands traversed by the Tathāgata as well as to his stūpas and temples, they too shall possess roots of goodness, eliminate all afflictions and ailments, and attain the bliss of the noble ones (*ārya*).
"O Son of the Buddha!

I now tell you: even if there are sentient beings who, upon seeing or hearing the Buddha, have their karmic obstructions so entangling and obscuring that they do not give rise to faith or joy, yet they plant roots of goodness that shall never go to waste, until they ultimately enter into nirvana."
O Son of the Buddha!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that the roots of goodness planted through seeing, hearing, and attending upon the Tathāgata are entirely free from all unwholesome dharmas and are fully endowed with wholesome dharmas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata uses all manner of similes to explain various matters, yet there is no simile capable of explaining this Dharma. Why is this?
The path of mind and intellect is cut off because it is inconceivable.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas merely accord with the minds of sentient beings to cause them joy, employing parables for their sake; these are not the ultimate truth.
O Son of the Buddha!
This Dharma-door is named:
"The Secret Place of the Tathāgata. Its name is:
That which cannot be known by any in the world is called:
"Entering the Seal of the Tathāgata," called:
"Opening the Door of Great Wisdom," and called:
Manifesting the lineage of the Tathāgatas is named:
Accomplishing All Bodhisattvas; it is named:
That Which Cannot Be Destroyed by Any World; it is named:
Constantly conforming to the realm of the Tathāgata is called "Able";
purifying all realms of sentient beings is called:
He expounds the inconceivable, ultimate Dharma of the Tathāgata’s fundamental true nature.
O Son of the Buddha!

This Dharma gate is not taught by the Tathāgata for other sentient beings; it is taught only for Bodhisattvas who are intent upon the Mahāyāna, and only for Bodhisattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle.
This Dharma-gate does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the seven treasures possessed by a wheel-turning sage king; it is because of these treasures that he is manifested as a wheel-turning king. These treasures do not fall into the hands of other sentient beings, except for the crown prince born of the first consort, who is fully endowed with the marks of a sage king.
If a Wheel-Turning King does not have such a crown prince endowed with these many virtues, then after the king’s life has ended, these various jewels will all vanish and perish within seven days.
O Son of the Buddha!

This jewel of a sutra is likewise; it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and have planted the various roots of goodness that constitute the marks of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
If there were no such true sons of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate would soon perish and vanish. Why is this?
All followers of the two vehicles do not even hear this sutra, let alone receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or analyze and explain it!
Only bodhisattvas are capable of such things.
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear this Dharma-gate, they should feel great joy and receive it with reverence, honoring it upon the crown of their heads. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has faith and delight in this sutra will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).

If one has not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable great majesty of the Tathāgata, or if having heard it at some time, one does not believe it, understand it, accord with it, or enter into it, such a person cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

If one hears this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom, and having heard it, believes and understands it, accords with it, and enters into realization, you should know that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgatas; they accord with the realm of all Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with all the dharmas of Bodhisattvas, abide securely in the realm of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), remain far removed from all worldly dharmas, give rise to all that is practiced by the Tathāgatas, penetrate the dharma-nature of all Bodhisattvas, possess no doubt or uncertainty regarding the sovereign mind of the Buddha, dwell in the teacherless Dharma, and enter deeply into the unobstructed realm of the Tathāgatas.

O Sons of the Buddha! Having heard this Dharma, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are then able, through the wisdom of equality, to know immeasurable dharmas; through a straightforward mind, to be free from all conceptual discrimination; through the joy of supreme aspiration, to manifestly behold all Buddhas; through the power of mental attention, to enter the realm of equalized space; through the power of sovereign mindfulness, to traverse the boundless dharma-realm; through the power of wisdom, to be endowed with all merits; through natural wisdom, to be free from all worldly defilements; through the bodhicitta, to enter the net of all ten directions; through great observation, to know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time share one and the same essence; and through the wisdom of dedicating roots of goodness, to universally enter such dharmas—entering them by not entering.
One does not take any single phenomenon as an object of attachment, but constantly contemplates all phenomena through the lens of that one phenomenon.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish such merits, they attain untaught, spontaneous wisdom with little exertion.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Beholding, hearing, and making offerings to all Tathāgatas, The merit thereby obtained is immeasurable;
Within the realm of the conditioned it shall never be exhausted, But will surely extinguish afflictions and bring liberation from all suffering."
Just as when a person swallows a small piece of diamond, it will never be digested but must eventually pass through;
so too, by making offerings to the merits of the One of Ten Powers, one extinguishes delusions and shall surely reach the Diamond Wisdom.
Just as a heap of dry grass equal to Mount Sumeru Is entirely consumed when a mustard-seed fire is cast upon it;
So too, even a small merit from making offerings to the Buddhas Will surely sever all afflictions and lead to Nirvana.
In the Snowy Mountains there is a medicine named Sudarśana; seeing, hearing, smelling, or touching it dispels all ailments.
If one sees or hears of the One of Ten Powers, one attains supreme merit and reaches the wisdom of a Buddha.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and because such is the nature of the Dharma, ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways:

namely, rising in the east and sinking in the west; rising in the west and sinking in the east; rising in the south and sinking in the north; rising in the north and sinking in the south; rising at the edges and sinking in the center; and rising in the center and sinking at the edges.
There were eighteen kinds of movements, namely: shaking, shaking everywhere, shaking equally everywhere;

rising, rising everywhere, rising equally everywhere; surging, surging everywhere, surging equally everywhere; quaking, quaking everywhere, quaking equally everywhere; roaring, roaring everywhere, roaring equally everywhere; crashing, crashing everywhere, crashing equally everywhere.

They rained down clouds of all kinds of celestial flowers surpassing those of the devas; clouds of all kinds of canopies, banners, streamers, incense, garlands, ointments, ornaments, great luminous maṇi-jewel clouds, clouds of the praises of all bodhisattvas, and clouds of the distinct bodies of unspeakably many bodhisattvas. They rained down clouds of the attainment of perfect enlightenment and clouds that adorn and purify inconceivable worlds; they rained down clouds of the Tathāgata’s speech and sounds, filling the boundless dharma-realm.
In this manner, the Tathāgata’s spiritual power manifests such displays within these four continents, causing all bodhisattvas to experience great joy;
throughout all worlds in the ten directions, it is likewise in every respect.

At that time, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Tathāgatas, each equal in number to the atoms in eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields, all sharing the same name:
Samantabhadra. They all appeared before him and spoke these words: "Excellent!
O Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power and in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), to expound the inconceivable dharma of the Tathāgata’s manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha!
We, the Buddhas of the ten directions—equal in number to the atoms within eighty unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields—all preach this Dharma;
as I have spoken it, so do all the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions speak it.
O Son of the Buddha!
In this assembly, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields who have attained the samādhi of all bodhisattva supernormal powers;
we have all bestowed upon them the prediction that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a single lifetime.
Sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

we, too, bestow upon them the prediction that in a future age, after passing through kalpas as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields, they shall all attain Buddhahood, sharing the common name:
"Buddha Supreme Realm."
In order that future bodhisattvas may hear this Dharma, we shall all together protect and uphold it.

Just as with the sentient beings to be delivered within these four continents, so it is for all the sentient beings to be delivered throughout the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds in the ten directions—worlds that are innumerable, immeasurable, and even unspeakably unspeakable, equaling the entire dharma-realm and space. All are likewise to be protected.
At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, by the power of Vairocana’s original vows,
by the suchness of the Dharma, by the power of roots of goodness, because the Tathāgata gives rise to wisdom without missing a single thought,
because the Tathāgata responds to conditions without failing the proper time, and in order to awaken all bodhisattvas according to the occasion, he went forth.
Because that which was done in the past is never lost or destroyed, because it causes one to attain the vast conduct of Samantabhadra,

and because it manifests the sovereignty of all-knowledge; beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there are respectively ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas...
Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms within other Buddha-fields, have come to this place, filling all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions.
They manifest the vast adornments of bodhisattvas, radiate great nets of light, shake all worlds throughout the ten directions, shatter all the palaces of Māras, and extinguish all...
Manifesting the suffering of the evil realms, revealing the majestic power of all Tathāgatas,
singing praises of the infinite and diverse qualities of the Tathāgatas’ Dharma, raining down all manner of various showers, manifesting infinite and diverse bodies,
and receiving the infinite teachings of the Buddhas, they each spoke these words through the Buddha’s spiritual power:
“Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You are indeed able to expound this indestructible dharma of the Tathāgata.”
"O Son of the Buddha!

We are all named Samantabhadra, and we have each come here from the presence of the Tathāgata Universal Banner Sovereignty in the world Universal Radiance. In all those places, this very Dharma is also being taught—with these same words and phrases, these same principles, this same proclamation, and this same certainty—identical to what is here, neither more nor less."
"By the spiritual power of the Buddha and because we have attained the Dharma of the Tathāgata, we have come to this place to bear witness for you.
Just as we have come here, so it is in all the four continents throughout all worlds in the ten directions, equal to space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm."

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas. Desiring to further clarify the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, the indestructibility of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma, the fact that immeasurable roots of goodness are never in vain, and how the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is necessarily endowed with all supreme dharmas; and how they skillfully observe the minds of all sentient beings and teach the Dharma according to their needs without ever missing the proper time; and how they give rise to the immeasurable light of the Dharma for all bodhisattvas; and how they possess the sovereign adornments of all Buddhas;

and how all Tathāgatas are of one body without distinction, arising from the great practices of the beginningless past—he spoke these verses: “The various deeds performed by all Tathāgatas Cannot be matched by any worldly analogy. ... (The remainder of the verses follows) ...”
In order to bring sentient beings to awakening and understanding, that which is not an analogy is displayed as an analogy.
Such subtle, secret, and profound dharmas are difficult to hear even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;
only those who possess diligence, wisdom, and self-mastery can hear this secret and mysterious meaning.
If one hears this Dharma and gives rise to joy, they have previously made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas and praised by humans and devas, they shall always receive offerings.
This is the supreme wealth that transcends the world; this can deliver all classes of beings;
this can give birth to the pure path—ye should uphold it and not be negligent.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty-two;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
38. Chapter on Transcending the World.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the country of Magadha, at the site of enlightenment in the forest retreat, within the Hall of Universal Radiance. He sat upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne; his wondrous realization was fully perfected, the two paths were forever severed, and he had attained the dharma of signlessness.
Abiding in the dwelling of the Buddhas, he had attained the equality of the Buddhas and reached the unobstructed state of the irreversible dharma.
Their conduct is unimpeded, they are established in the inconceivable, and they universally perceive the three periods of time;
their bodies constantly pervade all lands, and their wisdom is eternally clear and penetrating regarding all phenomena;
they comprehend all practices, exhaust all doubts, and no one can fathom their bodies.

The wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas has reached the ultimate, non-dual shore of Buddhahood; it is fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s impartial liberation, and realizes the Buddha’s level of equality, which is without center or periphery, extending throughout the entire realm of phenomena as vast as the realm of empty space.

He was accompanied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields; all were destined to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in their final birth, having gathered together from various lands in other directions, and were fully endowed with the skillful means and wisdom of bodhisattvas.
That is to say:
they are skillfully able to observe all sentient beings and, through the power of expedient means, cause them to be tamed and established in the Dharma of Bodhisattvas;
they are skillfully able to observe all worlds and, through the power of expedient means, go to visit them all.

They are well able to observe the realm of nirvana, contemplating and deliberating upon the eternal transcendence of all conceptual proliferation and discrimination, while practicing sublime conduct without interruption;

they are well able to gather in and sustain all sentient beings, skillfully entering immeasurable methods of expedient means, knowing that all sentient beings are empty and non-existent yet not destroying the retribution of karma;
they skillfully know the various distinctions among the mental impulses, faculties, objects, and expedient means of sentient beings.
They are able to receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time; having attained understanding for themselves, they further explain them to others.
Regarding the immeasurable mundane and supramundane dharmas, they are well-established in them all and know their reality.
Regarding all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, they skillfully observe them all and know them to be non-dual.
Within a single thought-moment, they are able to fully attain all the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
in every thought-moment, they are able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, causing all sentient beings to resolve their minds toward the Way and achieve it;
and regarding the objects of a single sentient being’s mind, they fully know the realms of all sentient beings.
Although they have entered the stage of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, they do not abandon the various activities of the bodhisattva path; through wisdom and skillful means, they remain non-active.

For the sake of each and every sentient being, they abide for immeasurable kalpas, yet they are difficult to encounter even in incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. They turn the wheel of the true Dharma to subdue sentient beings without fail, and they have fully perfected the pure vows and practices of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Having accomplished such immeasurable merits, all Tathāgatas could not exhaustively describe them even in infinite kalpas.
Their names were:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantavikurvita Bodhisattva, Samantamati Bodhisattva, Samantadarśin Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantadṛṣṭi Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva, Samantadhvaja Bodhisattva, Samantabuddhi Bodhisattva, and so forth.

In this way, there were as many as ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, as numerous as atoms of dust, all of whom had fully accomplished the practices and vows of Samantabhadra; their profound resolve and great vows were entirely fulfilled;
they were able to travel to every place where any Buddha appeared in the world to request the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
and they were well able to receive and uphold the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas, ensuring that the lineage of all Buddhas was never interrupted.

They skillfully know the sequence of all Buddhas appearing in the world, their bestowal of prophecies, their names, their lands, their attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, and their turning of the wheel of Dharma;
they manifest as Buddhas in worlds where no Buddha exists, enabling all defiled sentient beings to become entirely pure;
they can extinguish all karmic obstacles of Bodhisattvas and enter the unobstructed, pure Dharma-realm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra entered a vast samādhi called "Adornment of Buddha-Flowers.
When he entered this samādhi, all worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways and eighteen manners, and a great sound issued forth that was heard by everyone without exception.
Thereupon, he arose from that samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantamati, knowing that the assembly had gathered, addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

What is the body? What is speech? What is the purification of vocal action?

For what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha manifest parinirvāṇa? Excellent,
O Son of the Buddha!
"May you, for our sake, expound upon such dharmas as these!
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the bodhisattvas, including Puhui and the others, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!..."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of reliance. What are the ten?
They are as follows:
They rely on the bodhicitta, because they never forget it;
they rely on spiritual friends, because they are in harmony with them as one;
they rely on roots of goodness, because they cultivate, accumulate, and increase them.
They rely on the *pāramitās* because they practice them to completion;
they rely on all phenomena because they lead to ultimate transcendence;
they rely on great vows because they increase awakening.
They rely on all practices because they universally accomplish them;
they rely on all bodhisattvas because their wisdom is identical;
they rely on making offerings to all buddhas because their faith is pure.
Taking all Tathāgatas as one’s reliance, because their compassionate father-like instruction is never interrupted—
this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will become the locus of reliance for the unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of extraordinary conceptions of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
regarding all roots of goodness, one conceives the thought that they are one's own roots of goodness;
regarding all roots of goodness, one conceives the thought that they are seeds of enlightenment.
One should conceive the thought of all sentient beings as vessels for awakening;
one should conceive the thought of all vows as one's own vow;
and one should conceive the thought of renunciation toward all phenomena.
One should conceive the thought of self-conduct regarding all conditioned phenomena;
conceive the thought of the Buddha-dharma regarding all dharmas;
and conceive the thought of the path of speech regarding all modes of expression.
To conceive of all Buddhas as one’s compassionate father;
and to conceive of all Tathāgatas as non-dual. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme skillful perception.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of conduct."
What are these ten? They are:
causing the conduct of all sentient beings to ripen universally;
Because they fully cultivate and study all practices for seeking the Dharma;
because they cause all roots of goodness to increase;
and because their single-mindedness remains undisturbed in all practices of samādhi.
Because there is nothing among all practices of wisdom that is not fully understood;
because there is nothing among all practices of cultivation that cannot be cultivated;
and because all practices regarding all Buddha-fields are entirely adorned.
The conduct of all spiritual friends, because of reverently making offerings;
the conduct of all Tathāgatas, because of honoring and serving them. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the practice of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of spiritual friends."
What are these ten? They are:
spiritual friends who cause one to abide in the bodhicitta;
Spiritual friends who cause one to give rise to roots of goodness;
spiritual friends who cause one to practice the various pāramitās;
and spiritual friends who explain all dharmas.
The spiritual friend who brings all sentient beings to maturity;
the spiritual friend who causes one to attain definitive eloquence;
the spiritual friend who causes one to be unattached to all worlds.
They cause one to have spiritual friends who cultivate practice without weariness throughout all kalpas;
they cause one to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra through spiritual friends;
and they cause one to enter that which is entered by the wisdom of all Buddhas through spiritual friends.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of diligent effort.
What are the ten? They are:
diligent application of effort in transforming and teaching all sentient beings;
The diligence of penetrating all dharmas;
the diligence of purifying all worlds;
the diligence of practicing all that is to be learned by bodhisattvas;
The diligent vigor that eradicates all evils of sentient beings;
the diligent vigor that brings to rest all sufferings of the three evil realms;
the diligent vigor that crushes and destroys all Māras;
May I exert diligent effort to act as the pure eye for all sentient beings;
may I exert diligent effort to make offerings to all Buddhas;
and may I exert diligent effort to cause all Tathāgatas to be fully delighted.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed perfection of diligence.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of minds that attain peace and security.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Abiding oneself in the bodhicitta, one should also cause others to abide in the bodhicitta, so that the mind attains peace and security;
having oneself ultimately abandoned anger and contention, one should also cause others to abandon anger and contention, so that the mind attains peace and security;
having oneself departed from the dharmas of the foolish and ignorant, one should also cause others to depart from the dharmas of the foolish and ignorant, so that the mind attains peace and security.
One diligently cultivates roots of goodness oneself and also encourages others to diligently cultivate roots of goodness, whereby the mind attains peace and stability;
one abides in the path of the *pāramitās* oneself and also leads others to abide in the path of the *pāramitās*, whereby the mind attains peace and stability;
one is born into the family of the Buddhas oneself and shall likewise cause others to be born into the family of the Buddhas, whereby the mind attains peace and stability.
Having personally entered deeply into the true dharma of selflessness, they also cause others to enter the true dharma of selflessness, and their minds attain peace and stability;
having personally refrained from slandering any of the Buddha-dharmas, they also cause others not to slander any of the Buddha-dharmas, and their minds attain peace and stability;
having personally fulfilled the vow for the enlightenment of omniscience, they also cause others to fulfill the vow for the enlightenment of omniscience, and their minds attain peace and stability.

Having personally entered the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, they also cause others to enter the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom of all Tathāgatas, and their minds attain peace and stability.
These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, great wisdom and peace of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten ways of bringing sentient beings to maturity.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
They bring sentient beings to maturity through giving;
they bring sentient beings to maturity through the form body;
and they bring sentient beings to maturity through the teaching of the Dharma.
They bring sentient beings to fulfillment by practicing in accord with them;
they bring sentient beings to fulfillment through non-attachment;
they bring sentient beings to fulfillment by revealing the bodhisattva practices.
They accomplish the maturation of sentient beings by manifesting all worlds in a blazing splendor;
they accomplish the maturation of sentient beings by manifesting the great majestic power of the Buddha-dharma;
and they accomplish the maturation of sentient beings through the manifestation of various supernatural transformations.
By means of various subtle, secret, and skillful expedient means, they bring sentient beings to maturity.
These are the ten.
By these, Bodhisattvas bring the realm of sentient beings to maturity.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of precepts. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the precept of not forsaking the bodhicitta;
the precept of remaining far removed from the stages of the two vehicles;
The precept of observing the benefit of all sentient beings;
the precept of causing all sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-dharma;
and the precept of cultivating all that is studied by Bodhisattvas.
The precept of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena;
the precept of dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment;
and the precept of non-attachment to the bodies of all Tathāgatas.
The precept of contemplating all phenomena as free from grasping and attachment;
the precept of restraint of the sense faculties.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and vast perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); by means of these, bodhisattvas know for themselves that they have received the prediction."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
generating the bodhicitta with a sublime intention, and knowing for oneself that one has received the prediction of enlightenment;
Never wearying of or abandoning any bodhisattva practices, they know for themselves that they have received the prediction;
dwelling through all kalpas while practicing the bodhisattva path, they know for themselves that they have received the prediction;
cultivating all Buddha-dharmas, they know for themselves that they have received the prediction.
One has deep and unwavering faith in all the Buddha’s teachings and knows that one has received the prediction;
one cultivates all roots of goodness until they are fully perfected and knows that one has received the prediction;
one establishes all sentient beings in the Bodhi of the Buddhas and knows that one has received the prediction.
One knows that one has received the prediction of enlightenment by being non-dual in harmony with all spiritual friends;
one knows that one has received the prediction of enlightenment by conceiving of all spiritual friends as Tathāgatas;
and one knows that one has received the prediction of enlightenment by constantly and diligently guarding the original vow for Bodhi.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of entries by which they enter into all bodhisattvas."
What are the ten? They are:
entering into one's original vows;
Entering into practice;
entering into the assemblies;
entering into the various pāramitās.
Entering into accomplishment;
entering into the differentiation of vows;
entering into various inclinations;
Entering the adornment of buddha-fields;
entering mastery over spiritual powers;
and entering the manifestation of taking birth.
These are the ten.
By means of these, Bodhisattvas universally enter into all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of entries by which they enter into all Tathāgatas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Entering into boundless perfect enlightenment;
entering into boundless turning of the wheel of Dharma;
entering into boundless skillful means.
Entering infinite varieties of sounds;
entering the infinite taming of sentient beings;
entering infinite mastery of spiritual powers.
They enter into infinite varieties of distinct bodies;
they enter into infinite samādhis;
they enter into infinite powers and fearlessnesses.
Entering the manifestation of infinite nirvāṇa—
this is the tenth. By means of these,
the bodhisattva universally enters all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of entry into the conduct of sentient beings for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
entering into the past conduct of all sentient beings;
entering into the future conduct of all sentient beings;
Entering into the present conduct of all sentient beings;
entering into the virtuous conduct of all sentient beings;
entering into the non-virtuous conduct of all sentient beings.
Entering into the mental activities of all sentient beings;
entering into the faculties and activities of all sentient beings;
entering into the understandings and activities of all sentient beings.
They enter into the conduct of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions of all sentient beings;
they enter into the timely and untimely conduct for the teaching and subduing of all sentient beings.
These are the ten.
By means of this, the bodhisattva universally enters into the conduct of all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter worlds."
What are the ten? They are:
entering defiled worlds;
Entering pure worlds;
entering small worlds; entering large worlds.
Entering worlds within a single minute particle; entering subtle worlds;
entering inverted worlds.
They enter worlds where [Buddhas] are being venerated; they enter worlds where there are Buddhas;
they enter worlds where there are no Buddhas.
These are the ten.
By means of these, the Bodhisattva universally enters all worlds throughout the ten directions.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten ways of entering into eons (*kalpa*).
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Entering past eons; entering future eons;
entering present eons.
Entering countable eons;
entering incalculable eons;
entering countable eons as being incalculable eons.
Entering incalculable eons is entering calculable eons;
entering all eons is entering non-eons;
entering non-eons is entering all eons.
Entering all kalpas as a single thought-moment—
this is the tenth. By means of this,
the bodhisattva universally enters all kalpas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas discourse upon the three periods of time. What are these ten?
That is to say:
speaking of the past life in terms of the past life;
speaking of the future life in terms of the past life.
Speaking of the present age regarding the past age;
speaking of the past age regarding the future age;
and speaking of the present age regarding the future age.
They speak of the future world within the present world;
they speak of the past world within the present world;
and they speak of the future world within the present world.
To speak of the present age as equality;
and to speak of the three periods of time within the present age as being but a single thought-moment—
these constitute the ten.
By means of this, the Bodhisattva universally explains the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of knowledge regarding the three periods of time."
What are the ten? They are:
knowing all established arrangements;
He knows all languages;
he knows all discourses;
he knows all rules of conduct.
He knows all designations;
he knows all established rules;
he knows all provisional names.
One knows its inexhaustibility;
one knows its quiescent extinction;
one knows that all things are empty.
These are the ten.
By means of these, the Bodhisattva universally knows all dharmas throughout the three periods of time.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to ten kinds of tireless minds.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
A mind free from weariness in making offerings to all Buddhas;
a mind free from weariness in attending upon all spiritual friends;
and a mind free from weariness in seeking all dharmas.
Listening to the true Dharma without weariness;
proclaiming the true Dharma without weariness;
and teaching and taming all sentient beings without weariness.
The mind free from weariness in establishing all sentient beings in the enlightenment of the Buddha;
the mind free from weariness in practicing the bodhisattva conduct for unspeakably unspeakable eons in each and every world-system;
and the mind free from weariness in wandering through all worlds.
To contemplate and reflect upon all Buddha-dharmas with a mind free from weariness—
this is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, great wisdom that is free from weariness.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of differentiated knowledge. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the wisdom that knows the differences among sentient beings;
the wisdom that knows the differences among their faculties; and so forth.
The wisdom that knows the distinctions among karmic retributions;
the wisdom that knows the distinctions among births;
and the wisdom that knows the distinctions among worlds.
The wisdom that knows the distinctions within the dharma-realm;
the wisdom that knows the distinctions among all Buddhas;
and the wisdom that knows the distinctions among all phenomena.
The wisdom that knows the distinctions of the three periods of time;
the wisdom that knows the distinctions of all paths of language.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, vast, and distinguished wisdom of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of dhāraṇīs."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, because it upholds all dharmas without forgetting or losing them;
The dhāraṇī of practice, because it skillfully contemplates all phenomena as they truly are;
the dhāraṇī of reflection, because it thoroughly understands the nature of all phenomena;
the dhāraṇī of the light of Dharma, because it illuminates the inconceivable teachings of all Buddhas.
The samādhi-dhāraṇī, because one hears the true Dharma from all present Buddhas with an undistracted mind;
the perfect-sound dhāraṇī, because one understands inconceivable sounds and languages;
the three-time dhāraṇī, because one expounds the inconceivable teachings of the Buddhas of the three times.
The *dhāraṇī* of various eloquences, for the purpose of expounding the boundless teachings of all Buddhas;
the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded hearing, for the purpose of being able to hear all the teachings spoken by unspeakably many Buddhas;
and the *dhāraṇī* of all Buddha-dharmas, for the purpose of abiding securely in the powers and fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas wish to attain these dharmas, they should diligently practice and study them.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas speak of ten kinds of Buddhas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
The Buddha who has attained perfect enlightenment;
the Buddha of vows;
the Buddha of karmic retribution;
The Buddha of Abiding;
the Buddha of Nirvana;
the Buddha of the Dharma-realm;
The Buddha of Mind;
the Buddha of Samādhi;
the Buddha of Original Nature;
The Buddha Anuruddha.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to ten kinds of Samantabhadra-minds.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
He gives rise to the mind of great kindness, for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings;
he gives rise to the mind of great compassion, for the sake of undergoing suffering on behalf of all sentient beings;
he gives rise to the mind of universal giving, relinquishing everything that he possesses.
They give rise to the mind that takes omniscience as its foremost priority, because they joyfully seek all Buddha-dharmas;
they give rise to the mind adorned with merit, because they study all bodhisattva practices;
they give rise to the adamantine mind, because they do not forget or lose [their resolve] throughout all places of rebirth.
They resolve upon a mind like the ocean, because all pure and white dharmas flow into it;
they resolve upon a mind like the king of great mountains, because they endure all evil words;
they resolve upon a mind of peace and security, because they bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
They give rise to the ultimate mind of the *prajñāpāramitā*, because they skillfully contemplate that all phenomena are non-existent.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these minds, they will swiftly achieve the skillful wisdom of Samantabhadra.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of Samantabhadra practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct, which aspires to abide throughout all future eons;
and the practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct, which aspires to make offerings to and reverently serve all Buddhas of the future.
May all sentient beings be established in the practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s conduct and the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
may they accumulate all roots of goodness through the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
and may they enter all the perfections through the Dharma of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
May there be the practice of Samantabhadra that fulfills all bodhisattva practices;
may there be the practice of Samantabhadra that adorns all worlds;
may there be the practice of Samantabhadra that brings forth birth in all buddha-fields.
May I skillfully observe the *samantabhadra-caryā* of all phenomena;
may I attain unexcelled bodhi in all buddha-fields through the *samantabhadra-caryā*.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas diligently cultivate this dharma, they will swiftly attain fulfillment of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
"Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to great compassion by contemplating sentient beings in ten ways."
What are these ten? They are:
observing sentient beings who are without support or protection, and giving rise to great compassion;
Observing that the nature of sentient beings is unruly and unyielding, he gives rise to great compassion;
observing that sentient beings are impoverished and lack roots of goodness, he gives rise to great compassion;
observing that sentient beings sleep through the long night, he gives rise to great compassion.
He observes sentient beings practicing unwholesome dharmas and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes sentient beings bound by the fetters of desire and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes sentient beings submerged in the ocean of birth and death and gives rise to great compassion.
He observes that sentient beings are constantly afflicted by the suffering of illness and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes that sentient beings lack the desire for wholesome dharmas and gives rise to great compassion;
he observes that sentient beings have lost all Buddha-dharmas and gives rise to great compassion.
These are the ten.
A bodhisattva constantly observes sentient beings with this mind.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten causes and conditions for generating the bodhicitta. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of teaching, transforming, and subduing all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of eliminating the mass of suffering of all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing complete peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.
One generates the bodhicitta for the sake of severing the ignorance of all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of bestowing the Buddha-wisdom upon all sentient beings;
one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of reverently making offerings to all Buddhas.
They resolve upon bodhicitta in order to follow the Tathāgata’s teachings and cause the Buddhas to rejoice;
they resolve upon bodhicitta in order to behold the physical forms and the marks and embellishments of all Buddhas;
they resolve upon bodhicitta in order to enter the vast wisdom of all Buddhas.
They resolve their minds on enlightenment in order to manifest the powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas.
This is the tenth.
"O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva has resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment and, for the sake of realizing and entering the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), approaches and makes offerings to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they should give rise to ten kinds of mental states.
What are the ten? They are:

the mind of service, the mind of joy, the mind free from opposition, the compliant mind, the mind free from seeking anything else, the single-minded mind, the mind sharing the same roots of goodness, the mind sharing the same vows, the Tathāgata-mind, and the mind sharing the same perfected conduct.
These are the ten.
“O Son of the Buddha!
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to such a mind, they will attain ten kinds of purity.”
What are the ten? They are:
the purity of the profound mind, because it reaches the ultimate and is never subject to loss or destruction;
The form-body is pure, because it manifests itself according to what is appropriate;
the voice is pure, because it thoroughly understands all languages;
and eloquence is pure, because it skillfully expounds the infinite teachings of the Buddhas.
Wisdom is pure because it abandons all the darkness of ignorance;
birth is pure because it is endowed with the sovereign power of a bodhisattva;
and retinue is pure because it accomplishes the roots of goodness of sentient beings who practiced together in the past.
The fruit of retribution is pure because all karmic obstructions are eliminated;
the great vows are pure because they are non-dual in nature with those of all bodhisattvas;
and all practices are pure because one attains liberation through the vehicle of Samantabhadra.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pāramitās."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
the perfection of giving, because of relinquishing all that one possesses;
The perfection of ethical discipline, because it purifies the Buddha’s precepts;
the perfection of patience, because it abides in the Buddha’s forbearance;
the perfection of diligence, because one does not regress in any undertaking.
The dhyāna-pāramitā is so called because of mindfulness upon a single object;
the prajñā-pāramitā is so called because of observing all phenomena as they truly are;
the jñāna-pāramitā is so called because of entering the powers of a Buddha.
The perfection of vows, because it fulfills all the great vows of Samantabhadra;
the perfection of spiritual powers, because it manifests all sovereign functions;
the perfection of Dharma, because it universally enters into all Buddha-dharmas.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed perfection of great wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of realization through wisdom. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
The wisdom that awakens to the infinite distinctions of all worlds;
the wisdom that awakens to the inconceivable realm of all sentient beings;
and the wisdom that awakens to the single entry into all phenomena and the manifold entries into the one.
They follow and awaken to the vast wisdom that penetrates the entire realm of phenomena;
they follow and awaken to the ultimate wisdom that pervades the entire realm of space;
they follow and awaken to the wisdom that enters all worlds throughout the past.
The wisdom that realizes the entry of all worlds into the future;
the wisdom that realizes the entry of all worlds into the present;
and the wisdom that realizes the fulfillment of the infinite vows and practices of all Tathāgatas within a single wisdom.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are identical in their single practice, thereby attaining liberation through the wisdom of subsequent realization;
this is the tenth.

If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the radiant mastery over all phenomena, fulfill all their vows, and in a single thought-moment, be able to comprehend all Buddha-dharmas and achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of realization for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
knowing that all dharmas have a single characteristic;
knowing that all dharmas have immeasurable characteristics.
Knowing that all phenomena are contained within a single thought-moment;
knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings without obstruction;
and knowing that the faculties of all sentient beings are equal.
They know the conduct of the afflictions and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
they know the conduct of the mental impulses of all sentient beings;
they know the conduct of the wholesome and unwholesome of all sentient beings.
They know the sovereign mastery, maintenance, and transformations of all bodhisattvas’ vows and practices;
they know that all Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the ten powers and have attained equal and perfect enlightenment. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these teachings, they will attain skillful means regarding all phenomena.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of power."
What are the ten? They are:
the power of entering into the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
The power of entering into all phenomena as being like transformations;
the power of entering into all phenomena as being like illusions;
the power of entering into all phenomena as being entirely the Buddha-dharma.
The power of non-attachment toward all phenomena;
the power of profound and clear understanding of all phenomena;
and the power of a mind that never abandons or fails to respect any spiritual friend.
The power to cause all roots of goodness to accord with and lead toward the sovereignty of unsurpassed wisdom;
the power of profound faith in all Buddha-dharmas without disparagement;
and the skillful power to ensure that the mind of omniscience never regresses.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will possess the unsurpassed powers of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of equality.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

They are equal toward all sentient beings, equal toward all phenomena, equal toward all lands, equal toward all profound intentions, equal toward all roots of goodness, equal toward all bodhisattvas, equal toward all vows, equal toward all perfections, equal toward all practices, and equal toward all buddhas.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, equal dharma of all buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of phrases regarding the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
All phenomena are merely names;
all phenomena are like illusions;
all phenomena are like reflections.
All phenomena are merely dependent origination;
all phenomena are pure in their karma;
all phenomena are merely the products of words and letters.
The reality-limit of all phenomena;
the signlessness of all phenomena;
the ultimate truth of all phenomena.
All phenomena are the dharma-realm; these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will skillfully enter the supreme, true meaning of the wisdom of all-knowledge.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas teach ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
preaching the profound Dharma;
preaching the vast Dharma;
He teaches various dharmas;
he teaches the dharma of omniscience;
he teaches the dharmas that accord with the pāramitās.
He expounds the Dharma of generating the powers of a Tathāgata;
he expounds the Dharma corresponding to the three periods of time;
