and the profound resolve to cultivate all the Buddha-dharmas. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the supreme purity of the profound mind of omniscience.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of superior profound minds."
What are these ten? They are:
the superior, profound resolve of non-retrogression, because it accumulates all roots of goodness;
The superior profound mind free from doubt and suspicion, because it understands the secret language of all Tathāgatas;
the superior profound mind of correct upholding, because it flows from great vows and great practices;
the superior profound mind of supreme excellence, because it penetrates deeply into all Buddha-dharmas.
The sovereign superior profound mind, because of mastery over all Buddha-dharmas;
the expansive superior profound mind, because of universally entering various dharma-gates;
the preeminent superior profound mind, because of the accomplishment of all that is undertaken.
The superior profound mind of mastery, because it is adorned by all samādhis, supernatural powers, and transformations;
the superior profound mind of abiding, because it upholds original vows;
and the superior profound mind of non-ceasing, because it brings all sentient beings to maturity.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, pure, and superior profound resolve of all buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of diligent cultivation.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
They diligently cultivate generosity, relinquishing everything without seeking any reward;
they diligently cultivate ethical discipline, practicing ascetic dhūta-powers, having few desires and being content, because they do not deceive others;
they diligently cultivate patience, abandoning the notions of self and other, enduring all evils, because they ultimately never give rise to thoughts of anger or malice.
They diligently cultivate vigor, so that their physical, verbal, and mental actions are never distracted, and all they do is non-regressive because it reaches ultimate perfection;

they diligently cultivate meditative concentration, so that they manifest liberations, samādhis, and supernormal powers, having departed from all desires, afflictions, strife, and worldly entanglements;
and they diligently cultivate wisdom, practicing and accumulating all merits without weariness.
They diligently cultivate great loving-kindness because they know that all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature;
they diligently cultivate great compassion because they know all phenomena are empty and universally undergo suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without weariness;
they diligently cultivate the awakening to the ten powers of the Tathāgata because they thoroughly understand them and manifest them for sentient beings without obstruction.
They diligently cultivate the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma, because they turn it until it reaches the minds of all sentient beings. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the diligent cultivation of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of resolute understanding for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the supreme and definitive resolve, because it plants roots of goodness characterized by reverence;
the adorned definitive resolve, because it gives rise to various kinds of adornments.
The resolute conviction of vastness, because the mind has never been narrow or inferior;
the resolute conviction of quiescence, because it is able to enter the profound nature of phenomena;
the resolute conviction of universality, because the generation of the mind reaches everywhere without exception.
The resolute understanding of capability, because it is able to receive the empowerment of the Buddha’s power;
the resolute understanding of firmness, because it destroys all demonic activities;
the resolute understanding of clear discernment, because it thoroughly knows all karmic retributions.
The resolute understanding of manifestation, because one is able to manifest supernormal powers at will;
the resolute understanding of succession, because one receives the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas;
and the resolute understanding of mastery, because one attains Buddhahood according to one's wish and at any time.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, definitive understanding of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of definitive understanding through which they know all worlds.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
They know how all worlds enter into a single world;
they know how a single world enters into all worlds;
they know that throughout all worlds, a single body of a Tathāgata and a single lotus seat completely pervade them all.
They know that all worlds are like empty space;
they know that all worlds are endowed with the adornments of the Buddhas;
they know that all worlds are filled with Bodhisattvas.
Knowing that all worlds enter into a single pore;
knowing that all worlds enter into the body of a single sentient being;
knowing that all worlds are entirely pervaded by a single Buddha’s bodhi tree and a single Buddha’s site of enlightenment;
To know that a single voice pervades all worlds, causing all sentient beings to understand it individually and giving rise to joy in their hearts—
this is the tenth.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and definitive resolve regarding Buddha-fields.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of definitive understandings by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know the realm of sentient beings.
What are these ten?
That is to say:
knowing that the intrinsic nature of all realms of sentient beings is without reality;
and knowing that all realms of sentient beings entirely enter into the body of a single sentient being.
They know that all realms of sentient beings entirely enter the body of a bodhisattva;
they know that all realms of sentient beings entirely enter the Tathāgatagarbha;
and they know that the body of a single sentient being universally enters all realms of sentient beings.
He knows that all realms of sentient beings are entirely capable of being vessels for the Buddha-dharma;
he knows that throughout all realms of sentient beings, he manifests the bodies of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors according to their respective desires;
and he knows that throughout all realms of sentient beings, he manifests the tranquil deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas according to their respective desires.
Knowing all realms of sentient beings, they manifest the adorned bodies of bodhisattvas’ merit;
knowing all realms of sentient beings, they manifest the Tathāgata’s marks and signs, tranquil deportment, and awaken sentient beings.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, great majestic power and definitive understanding.
*The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Fifty-Six.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty-seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree, Part Five of Chapter Thirty-eight: "Transcending the World."
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of habitual tendencies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the habitual tendencies of the bodhicitta;
the habitual tendencies of the roots of goodness;
The habitual tendencies of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
the habitual tendencies of seeing Buddhas;
and the habitual tendencies of taking birth in pure worlds.
The habitual tendencies of conduct;
the habitual tendencies of aspiration;
the habitual tendencies of the perfections;
The habitual tendencies of contemplating the equality of phenomena;
and the habitual tendencies of the distinctions among various objective realms. These are the ten.

If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will forever be free from all afflictions and habitual tendencies, attaining the Tathāgata’s great wisdom—the wisdom that knows both habitual tendencies and the absence of habitual tendencies.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of grasping by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not sever their bodhisattva practices. What are these ten?
That is to say:
taking up all realms of sentient beings for the sake of their ultimate transformation;
and taking up all worlds for the sake of their ultimate adornment and purification.
One takes up the Tathāgata for the sake of practicing the bodhisattva conduct as an offering;
one takes up roots of goodness for the sake of accumulating the merits of the Buddhas' marks and signs;
and one takes up great compassion for the sake of extinguishing the suffering of all sentient beings.
They embrace great loving-kindness, because they bestow upon all sentient beings the bliss of omniscience;
they embrace the perfections, because they accumulate all the adornments of a bodhisattva;
they embrace skillful means, because they manifest themselves in all places.
They take up enlightenment because they attain unimpeded wisdom;
in brief, Bodhisattvas take up all phenomena because they manifest and clearly realize them in all places through their brilliant wisdom.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these graspings, they will be able to continue the practices of all bodhisattvas and attain the supreme, non-grasping dharmas of all Tathāgatas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of cultivation for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
practicing the various pāramitās;
practicing and studying.
cultivating wisdom;
cultivating meaning;
cultivating phenomena;
Cultivating renunciation;
cultivating manifestation;
and cultivating diligent practice without indolence.
To cultivate and achieve perfect enlightenment;
and to cultivate and turn the wheel of the true Dharma. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the supreme cultivation that cultivates all dharmas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma."
What are the ten? They are:
not being separated from spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to accomplish the Buddha-dharma;
One accomplishes the Buddha-dharma by having deep faith in the Buddha's words;
one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma by not slandering the True Dharma;
and one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma by dedicating immeasurable and inexhaustible roots of goodness.
They achieve the Buddha-dharma by resolving with faith in the boundless realm of the Tathāgata;
they achieve the Buddha-dharma by knowing the realm of all worlds;
they achieve the Buddha-dharma by not abandoning the realm of the Dharma-realm.
They achieve the Buddha-dharma by remaining far removed from the realms of all Māras;
they achieve the Buddha-dharma by maintaining right mindfulness of the realms of all Buddhas;
they achieve the Buddha-dharma by joyfully seeking the realm of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will achieve the unexcelled, great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of retrogression from the Buddha-dharma that they should avoid.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
To treat spiritual friends with contempt is to fall away from the Buddha-dharma;
to fear the suffering of birth and death is to fall away from the Buddha-dharma;
to grow weary of practicing the bodhisattva path is to fall away from the Buddha-dharma.
Not delighting in dwelling in the world leads to the loss of the Buddha-dharma;
being attached to samādhi leads to the loss of the Buddha-dharma;
grasping at roots of goodness leads to the loss of the Buddha-dharma.
Slandering the true Dharma leads to the loss of the Buddha-dharma;
severing the bodhisattva practices leads to the loss of the Buddha-dharma;
delighting in the paths of the two vehicles leads to the loss of the Buddha-dharma.
Hating and resenting various bodhisattvas causes one to fall away from the Buddha-dharma; this is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas distance themselves from these dharmas, they enter the bodhisattva path of certainty (*niyāma*).
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten paths for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that lead away from birth. What are these ten?
That is to say:
to give birth to the *prajñāpāramitā* and constantly observe all sentient beings—this is the first;
to remain far removed from all views and liberate all sentient beings bound by views—this is the second.
Not dwelling on any signs while not abandoning sentient beings who cling to signs—this is the third;
transcending the three realms while constantly remaining in all worlds—this is the fourth;
being forever free from afflictions while dwelling together with all sentient beings—this is the fifth.
To have attained the dharma of detachment from desire, yet always to feel great compassion and pity for all sentient beings attached to desire—this is the sixth;
to always delight in stillness and solitude, yet constantly manifest the presence of a retinue—this is the seventh;
to be free from birth in the mundane world, yet to die here and be born there while initiating the bodhisattva practice—this is the eighth.
To remain unstained by all worldly dharmas while not ceasing any worldly activities—this is the ninth;
for the Bodhi of all Buddhas to be manifest before one’s eyes yet not abandoning any of the bodhisattva’s vows and practices—this is the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten paths of transcendence for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by which they emerge from the world, do not share in worldly things, and yet do not mix with the practices of the two vehicles.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the bodhisattva’s dharma of certainty.
"Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of dharma of certainty."
What are the ten? They are:
being born with certainty into the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
They are definitively established within the realm of all Buddhas;
they definitively and fully understand the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas;
and they definitively abide in the various pāramitās.
They will certainly attain entry into the assembly of the Tathāgata;
they will certainly be able to manifest the lineage of the Tathāgata;
and they will certainly abide securely in the powers of the Tathāgata.
They are certain to enter deeply into the Bodhi of the Buddhas;
they are certain to be of one and the same body with all Tathāgatas;
and they are certain to be non-dual with the dwelling place of all Tathāgatas.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give birth to the path of the Buddha-dharma."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
following virtuous friends is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because one plants roots of goodness in common with them;
Deep-seated faith and understanding is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, for it knows the sovereignty of the Buddhas;
the arousal of great vows is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, for its mind is vast and expansive;
patience toward one's own roots of goodness is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, for it knows that karma is never lost.
Practicing throughout all kalpas without weariness is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it extends to the end of the future;
manifesting in all incalculable worlds is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it brings sentient beings to maturity;
never ceasing the bodhisattva practices is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it increases great compassion.
The immeasurable minds are the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because in a single thought-moment they pervade all realms of empty space;
sublime practices are the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because what was originally practiced is never lost or destroyed;

and the lineage of the Tathāgatas is the path that gives birth to the Buddha-dharma, because it causes all sentient beings to joyfully resolve upon bodhicitta and sustains them with all wholesome dharmas.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they shall obtain the title of "Great Man.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten titles of great beings.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
He is named "Bodhisattva," because he is born from the wisdom of enlightenment;
he is named:
He is a mahāsattva because he dwells securely in the Mahāyāna;
he is called the foremost sattva because he has realized the foremost dharma.
He is named Supreme Sattva, because he has awakened to the supreme Dharma;
he is named:
He is called the Supreme Being (*sattva*) because his wisdom is supreme;
he is named the Exalted Being (*uttama-sattva*) because he gives rise to exalted diligence.
He is named the Unsurpassed Sattva, because he reveals the unsurpassed Dharma;
he is named:
He is called a *balasattva* because he extensively knows the ten powers;
he is named an *asamasattva* because he is peerless in the world.
They are named "Inconceivable Sattvas," because they attain Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas obtain these names and titles, they will then accomplish the bodhisattva path.
"Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of paths."
What are these ten? They are as follows:
the single path is the bodhisattva path, because one does not abandon the solitary mind of enlightenment.
The second path is the bodhisattva path, because it gives rise to wisdom and skillful means.
The third path is the bodhisattva path, because by practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one does not cling to the triple world.

These four practices constitute the bodhisattva path: the confession and removal of karmic obstacles, the sympathetic rejoicing in merit, the respectful veneration and invitation of the Tathāgatas, and the skillful dedication of merit without cessation.

The five faculties are the path of the bodhisattva: because they abide securely in pure faith, remaining firm and unshakable; they give rise to great diligence until all tasks are brought to completion; they maintain one-pointed right mindfulness without wandering toward other objects; they skillfully know the expedient means for entering and emerging from samādhi; and they are well able to discern the realm of wisdom.
The six supernormal powers are the path of the bodhisattva.
They are as follows:
the divine eye, by which one sees all forms existing in all worlds and knows the deaths and rebirths of all sentient beings; and so forth.
The divine ear, by which one hears the teachings of all Buddhas, upholds them in memory, and extensively expounds them to sentient beings according to their faculties;
the knowledge of others' minds, by which one knows the thoughts of others with sovereign unimpededness;
and the recollection of past lives, by which one remembers and knows the number of all past kalpas in order to increase roots of goodness.
The supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery manifests in various ways according to the needs of all sentient beings to be transformed, so that they may delight in the Dharma;
the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is the direct realization of the limit of reality, arising from the uninterrupted practice of the bodhisattva path.
The seven recollections are the path of the bodhisattva.
They are as follows:
recollection of the Buddha, wherein one perceives immeasurable Buddhas within a single pore, for the purpose of awakening the minds of all sentient beings;

He contemplates the Dharma, never departing from the assemblies of a single Tathāgata, personally receiving the sublime Dharma within the assemblies of all Tathāgatas, and expounding it according to the faculties, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings so that they may awaken and enter;
he contemplates the Sangha, constantly seeing them in uninterrupted succession without rest, beholding Bodhisattvas throughout all worlds;
he contemplates relinquishment, thoroughly understanding all the practices of relinquishment of Bodhisattvas, thereby increasing and expanding the mind of great giving.
He recollects the precepts, never forsaking the bodhicitta, because he dedicates all roots of goodness to sentient beings;
he recollects the devas, constantly mindful of the Bodhisattvas in their final birth in the Tuṣita heaven palace;
and he recollects sentient beings, teaching and taming them through wisdom and skillful means, extending universally to all without interruption.
The path of the eightfold noble way that accords with enlightenment is the bodhisattva path.
That is to say:
practicing the path of right view, because it distances one from all false views;
They give rise to right reflection, abandoning false discrimination, because their minds always accord with omniscience;
they constantly practice right speech, remaining free from the four faults of speech, because they follow the words of the sages;
and they perpetually cultivate right action, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they may be subdued.

Abiding in right livelihood, practicing *dhūta* austerities with contentment, and maintaining dignified conduct that is careful and correct, they accord with the four noble lineages by being forever free from all faults;
they give rise to right diligence, zealously cultivating all the ascetic practices of a bodhisattva, and enter the ten powers of a Buddha without obstruction;
their minds are always in right mindfulness, capable of retaining all speech and sounds, and having eliminated the distracted and agitated mind of the world.
Their minds are always in right concentration, skillfully entering the inconceivable gates of liberation of bodhisattvas, because within a single samādhi they give birth to all samādhis.
Entering the nine successive meditative absorptions is the bodhisattva path.
That is to say:
being free from desire, ill will, and harm, one expounds the Dharma through all vocal actions without obstruction;
They eliminate discursive thought and investigation, yet employ the discernment of all-knowledge to teach and transform sentient beings;
they abandon craving and delight, yet behold all Buddhas with great joy in their hearts;
they leave behind worldly pleasures, yet accord with the supramundane bliss of the Bodhisattva path.
From this state of immovability, they enter the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*), yet they do not abandon rebirth in the realms of desire or form;
although they abide in the meditative attainment that extinguishes all perceptions and feelings (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), they do not cease their bodhisattva practices.
Training in the ten powers of a Buddha is the path of a bodhisattva.
These are: the wisdom that thoroughly knows what is possible and what is impossible;
The wisdom that thoroughly knows the causes and effects of the karmic retributions of all sentient beings in the past, future, and present;
the wisdom that thoroughly knows how to preach the Dharma according to the needs of all sentient beings by discerning their superior, middling, and inferior faculties;
and the wisdom that thoroughly knows the various and immeasurable natures of all sentient beings.
The wisdom that skillfully knows the distinctions among the inferior, middling, and superior understandings of all sentient beings, thereby enabling them to enter the Dharma;

the wisdom that universally manifests the physical forms and majestic deportment of the Tathāgatas throughout all worlds, all lands, all three periods of time, and all eons, yet never abandons the practices of a bodhisattva;

and the wisdom that skillfully knows all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis—whether defiled or pure, timely or untimely—and through skillful means brings forth the gates of liberation of all bodhisattvas.
The wisdom that knows the distinctions of all sentient beings as they die here and are born there within the various realms of existence;
the wisdom that, in a single thought-moment, fully knows the number of all kalpas throughout the three periods of time;

and the wisdom that skillfully knows the inclinations, latent tendencies, afflictions, and habitual patterns of all sentient beings, along with their cessation and exhaustion, yet without ever abandoning the practices of a bodhisattva.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed path of skillful means of all Tathāgatas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have immeasurable paths, immeasurable aids to the path, immeasurable paths of cultivation, and immeasurable paths of adornment.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of immeasurable paths.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
Because space is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable;
because the dharma-realm is boundless, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable;
because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
Because the world is boundless, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable;
because the number of kalpas cannot be exhausted, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable;
because the linguistic conventions of all sentient beings are immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
Because the body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable;
because the voice of the Buddha is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable;
because the powers of the Tathāgata are immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
Because the knowledge of all-knowledge is immeasurable, the bodhisattva path is also immeasurable.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of immeasurable aids to the path.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
As the realm of empty space is immeasurable, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path immeasurable;
as the dharma-realm is boundless, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path boundless;
as the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to the path inexhaustible.
Just as the world has no limit, the bodhisattva’s accumulation of aids to the path is likewise limitless;
just as the number of eons cannot be fully described, the bodhisattva’s accumulation of aids to the path likewise cannot be fully described by all the worlds;

just as the linguistic conventions of sentient beings are immeasurable, the wisdom produced by the bodhisattva’s accumulation of aids to the path that understands these linguistic conventions is likewise immeasurable.

Just as the body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, so too is the accumulation of the bodhisattva’s aids to the path immeasurable, as it pervades all sentient beings, all lands, all worlds, and all eons;

just as the voice of the Buddha is immeasurable, so too is the accumulation of the bodhisattva’s aids to the path immeasurable, for when the bodhisattva utters a single sound, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm such that there is not a single sentient being who does not hear and know it;
just as the power of the Buddha is immeasurable, so too is the accumulation of the bodhisattva’s aids to the path immeasurable, as they are gathered by relying upon the power of the Tathāgata.
Just as the wisdom of all-knowledge is immeasurable, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of the aids to enlightenment immeasurable.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of immeasurable paths of cultivation for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
cultivation without coming or going, because there is no activity of body, speech, or mind;
cultivation without increase or decrease, because it is like its original nature.
Cultivation that is neither existent nor non-existent, because it is without intrinsic nature;
cultivation that is like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, like an echo, like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage, and like the moon in water, because it is free from all attachments;
and cultivation of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of effort, because one clearly perceives the three realms while accumulating merit without ceasing.
The cultivation that is inexpressible, beyond verbalization, and free from verbalization, because it is far removed from the establishment of conventional designations;
the cultivation that does not destroy the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because wisdom directly perceives all phenomena;

the cultivation that does not destroy true suchness (*tathatā*) or the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because it universally enters into true suchness, the limit of reality, and the limit of space (*ākāśakoṭi*).
They cultivate vast wisdom because the power of all their activities is inexhaustible;

they dwell in the cultivation of equality regarding the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and the knowledge of all modes of knowledge, because they directly perceive all phenomena without doubt.
These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme skillfulness in cultivating all-knowledge.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of adornments of the path. What are the ten?
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not depart from the desire realm, yet enters the meditative concentrations, liberations, and various samādhis of the form and formless realms; furthermore, he does not undergo rebirth therein because of them—this is the first path of adornment.
When wisdom manifests and one enters the path of the śrāvaka, yet does not seek liberation through this path alone—this is the second adornment of the path.
When wisdom manifests and one enters the path of the pratyekabuddha, yet gives rise to great compassion without ceasing—this is the third adornment of the path.

Although surrounded by a retinue of humans and devas, and attended by hundreds of thousands of maidens singing and dancing, he never for a moment abandons dhyāna, liberation, and the various samādhis; this is the fourth adornment of the path.

To enjoy all manner of sensual pleasures together with all sentient beings, yet never for even a single thought-moment depart from the bodhisattva’s samādhi of equanimity—this is the fifth adornment of the path.
Having reached the further shore of all worlds, one is entirely unattached to worldly dharmas, yet does not abandon the practice of delivering sentient beings; this is the sixth path of adornment.

Abiding securely in the right path, right knowledge, and right view, one is able to manifest entry into all deviant paths without taking them as real or grasping at them as pure, thereby causing those sentient beings to distance themselves from deviant dharmas; this is the seventh adornment of the path.

He constantly and skillfully upholds the pure precepts of the Tathāgata, such that his actions of body, speech, and mind are free from all faults. Desiring to transform sentient beings who violate the precepts, he manifests the practice of all the behaviors of the ignorant and foolish. Although he is already fully endowed with pure merit and dwells in the bodhisattva path, he manifests birth in all places of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and various perilous difficulties, poverty, and so forth, causing those sentient beings to attain liberation. Yet, in reality, the bodhisattva is not born into those realms; this is the eighth path of adornment.

Without relying on the instruction of others, he attained unimpeded eloquence; the light of his wisdom universally illumined all Buddha-dharmas; he was sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas; he shared the same Dharma-body as all Buddhas; he accomplished all firm, great-person, clear, and pure secret dharmas; he dwelt securely in all equal vehicles; the realms of all Buddhas appeared before him; he was fully endowed with the light of all worldly knowledge; he perceived the realms of all sentient beings; he was able to act as a teacher of the Dharma for sentient beings, demonstrating that his quest for the true Dharma never ceased; and while he was in truth the unsurpassed teacher of sentient beings, he demonstrated the practice of honoring and respecting his *ācāryas* and *upādhyāyas*.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), abide in the bodhisattva path and manifest themselves in accordance with what is appropriate for each being.
This is the ninth adornment of the path.

Fully endowed with roots of goodness and having perfected all practices, they have received the collective empowerment of all Tathāgatas; they have reached the further shore of mastery over all dharmas, with the unimpeded Dharma-ribbon crowning their heads.

Their bodies pervade all worlds, universally manifesting the unimpeded body of a Tathāgata; having attained the supreme perfection of mastery over the Dharma, they turn the unimpeded, pure wheel of Dharma.
Having already accomplished all the sovereign qualities of Bodhisattvas, they manifest birth in all lands for the sake of sentient beings.

They share the same realm as all Buddhas of the three periods of time, yet they do not cease their bodhisattva practices, do not abandon the bodhisattva teachings, do not slacken in their bodhisattva activities, do not depart from the bodhisattva path, do not relax their bodhisattva decorum, do not interrupt their bodhisattva aspirations, do not rest from their bodhisattva skillful means, do not terminate the tasks performed by bodhisattvas, do not grow weary of the bodhisattva’s power to produce and sustain beings, and do not halt the bodhisattva’s power of maintenance.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva who wishes to swiftly realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment observes the gateway to all-knowledge and cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva without ceasing.
This is the tenth adornment of the path.
If bodhisattvas abide in this dharma, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great adornment of the path, yet they do not abandon the bodhisattva path.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of feet. What are these ten?
These are: the foot of ethical discipline, because all supreme great vows are fully accomplished;
the foot of diligence, because one does not regress in gathering all factors conducive to enlightenment;
and the foot of supernormal powers, because one brings joy to sentient beings according to their inclinations.
The perfection of supernormal power, because one travels from a single buddha-field to all buddha-fields without leaving the former;
the perfection of the profound mind, because one aspires to seek all supreme dharmas;
the perfection of firm vows, because all that is undertaken is brought to ultimate completion.
The foot of compliance, because it does not contradict the instructions of any venerable one;
the foot of delighting in the Dharma, because it tirelessly hears and retains all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas;
the foot of the rain of Dharma, because it expounds them for the sake of the assembly without timidity.
The perfection of conduct, because all evils are completely abandoned.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and most supreme feet; with a single step, they are able to reach every world-system.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of hands. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the hand of profound faith, because it single-mindedly accepts and ultimately upholds all that has been taught by the Buddha;
and the hand of generosity, because it fulfills the desires of those who come to seek, according to their wishes.
The hand that inquires with forethought, for it extends the right palm to welcome and guide others;
the hand that makes offerings to all Buddhas, for it gathers a multitude of merits without weariness;
the hand of extensive learning and skillful means, for it completely severs the doubts of all sentient beings.
The hand that causes transcendence of the triple world, for it grants [liberation] to sentient beings and pulls them out from the mire of desire;
the hand that places [beings] on the other shore, for it rescues drowning sentient beings from within the four violent currents;
the hand that does not begrudge the true Dharma, for it reveals and expounds all sublime teachings in their entirety.
They are hands that skillfully employ various treatises to extinguish the ailments of body and mind with the medicine of wisdom;
they are hands that constantly hold the jewel of knowledge to shatter the darkness of afflictions by illuminating the light of the Dharma.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed hand of the Tathāgata, which universally covers all worlds throughout the ten directions.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of bellies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
a belly free from flattery and crookedness, because the mind is pure;
a belly free from illusion and deceit, because one's nature is straightforward.
The belly that is not false, because it is free from treachery and perversity;
the belly that does not deceive or plunder, because it has no greed for any object;
the belly that severs afflictions, because it is endowed with wisdom.
The belly of the pure mind, because it is free from all evils;
the belly that observes food and drink, because it contemplates the Dharma as it truly is;
the belly that observes non-action, because it awakens to dependent origination.
The belly that awakens to all paths of renunciation, because it thoroughly matures the profound mind;
the belly that is free from the defilement of all extremist views, because it causes all sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s belly.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, vast belly of a Tathāgata, which is fully capable of containing all sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of treasuries (*kośa*). What are these ten?
That is to say:
not severing the lineage of the Buddhas is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it reveals the immeasurable majesty and virtue of the Buddha-dharma;
increasing the seeds of the Dharma is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it gives birth to the vast radiance of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is that which sustains the lineage of the monastic community, so as to enable them to enter the wheel of non-retrogression;
it is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka that awakens sentient beings established in right concentration, for it skillfully accords with their timing without exceeding a single thought-moment;
it is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka that brings to ultimate maturity those sentient beings who are not yet fixed, ensuring that the causal continuity remains uninterrupted.
To give rise to great compassion for sentient beings who are fixed in error is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it causes all future causes to be fully accomplished;
to fulfill the indestructible cause of the Buddha’s ten powers is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it possesses the invincible roots of goodness that subdue the armies of Māra;
the most supreme, fearless Great Lion’s Roar is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because it causes all sentient beings to rejoice.
Attaining the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because wisdom universally enters all places;
universally and thoroughly knowing all sentient beings, all lands, all phenomena, and all Buddhas is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because they are clearly perceived within a single thought-moment.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme storehouse of great wisdom, which is rooted in invincible roots of goodness.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of mind.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
A mind of diligent application, because all that is undertaken is brought to ultimate completion;
a mind free from indolence, because it accumulates the merit and conduct for the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha;
a mind of great courage and strength, because it crushes and destroys all the armies of Māra.
The mind that acts in accordance with reality, because it eliminates all afflictions;
the non-retrogressive mind, because it never ceases until reaching enlightenment;
the inherently pure mind, because it knows the mind is immovable and free from attachment.
Knowing the minds of sentient beings in order to lead them toward liberation according to their inclinations;

causing them to enter the mind of the Great Brahma-abode of the Buddha-dharma by knowing the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings, rather than protecting them through separate vehicles;
and the mind of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and effortlessness, because of not grasping at or adhering to the appearances of the triple world.
With a mind adorned by the supreme treasury of the vajra-solidity of the svastika-mark, even if as many māras as there are sentient beings were to come, they could not move so much as a single hair.
These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s treasury of the heart of unsurpassed great wisdom-light.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of donning of armor.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
They don the armor of great loving-kindness, for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings;
they don the armor of great compassion, for the sake of enduring all sufferings;
they don the armor of great vows, for the sake of bringing all that is undertaken to ultimate completion.
They don the armor of dedication, for the purpose of establishing all the adornments of the Buddhas;
they don the armor of merit, for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings; they don the armor of the perfections, for the purpose of delivering all conscious beings;
they don the armor of wisdom, for the purpose of extinguishing the darkness of afflictions of all sentient beings.
They don the armor of skillful means, because they give rise to roots of goodness through the universal gateway;
they don the armor of the firm and undistracted mind of omniscience, because they take no pleasure in other vehicles;
they don the armor of single-minded resolve, because they are free from doubt regarding all phenomena.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will don the unsurpassed armor of the Tathāgata and be able to utterly crush and subdue all the armies of Māra.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of weapons. What are these ten?
That is to say:
giving is the weapon of a bodhisattva, for it destroys all stinginess;
ethical discipline is the weapon of a bodhisattva, for it abandons all transgressions.
Equanimity is the weapon of the bodhisattva, for it severs all conceptual discrimination;
wisdom is the weapon of the bodhisattva, for it extinguishes all afflictions;
right livelihood is the weapon of the bodhisattva, for it distances one from all forms of wrong livelihood.
Skillful means are the weapons of a bodhisattva, for they manifest in all places;
in brief, all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion are the weapons of a bodhisattva, for they deliver sentient beings through the gateway of affliction;
birth and death are the weapons of a bodhisattva, for they do not sever their bodhisattva practices while teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Teaching the Dharma as it truly is is the weapon of a bodhisattva, for it can shatter all attachments;
omniscience is the weapon of a bodhisattva, for it does not abandon the gateways of bodhisattva practice.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will be able to eliminate all the afflictions and fetters accumulated by sentient beings throughout the long night.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of heads for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the head of nirvana, because its crown cannot be seen;
the head of veneration, because it is honored and saluted by all humans and devas.
He is foremost in vast resolute conviction, for he is the most supreme within the trichiliocosm;
he is foremost in the primary roots of goodness, for all sentient beings of the three realms offer him worship;
he is foremost in bearing the burden of sentient beings, for he has accomplished the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance) upon his crown.
The head of not disparaging others, for it is always honored and supreme in all places;
the head of the *prajñāpāramitā*, for it nurtures all dharmas of merit;
the head of the correspondence between skillful means and wisdom, for it universally manifests bodies identical to all classes of beings.
It is the foremost for teaching and transforming all sentient beings, because it takes all sentient beings as its disciples;
it is the foremost for guarding the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas, because it ensures that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the head of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of eyes.
They are: the fleshly eye, because it sees all forms;
The divine eye, because it perceives the minds of all sentient beings;
the wisdom eye, because it perceives the faculties and spheres of all sentient beings;
the dharma eye, because it perceives the true reality of all phenomena.
The Buddha-eye, because it perceives the ten powers of the Tathāgata;
the wisdom-eye, because it knows and sees all phenomena;
the light-eye, because it beholds the radiance of the Buddha;
It is the eye of birth and death, because it perceives nirvana;
it is the unimpeded eye, because there is no obstruction to what is seen;
it is the eye of all-knowledge, because it perceives the universal gateway of the dharma-realm.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great eye of wisdom. "O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of ears."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
hearing sounds of praise, one eliminates craving and attachment;
Hearing sounds of disparagement, they eliminate anger;
hearing discourses on the Two Vehicles, they neither cling to nor seek them;
hearing of the Bodhisattva path, they rejoice and leap for joy.
Upon hearing of the various places of suffering and hardship, such as the hells, one gives rise to great compassion and makes vast vows;
upon hearing accounts of the superior and wondrous matters of humans and devas, one knows that all these are phenomena subject to impermanence;
and upon hearing the praises of the merits of the Buddhas, one applies oneself with diligent vigor so that they may be swiftly perfected.
Hearing the teachings on the six perfections, the four means of integration, and other such dharmas, they resolve to practice them, vowing to reach the other shore;
hearing all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they know them all to be like echoes, thereby entering into the ineffable, profound, and wondrous meaning.

From their initial resolve until they reach the site of enlightenment, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas constantly hear the True Dharma without a moment’s rest, yet they never abandon the work of transforming sentient beings.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom-ear.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of noses.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
Upon smelling various foul odors, they do not perceive them as foul;
upon smelling various fragrances, they do not perceive them as fragrant;
when both fragrance and stench are smelled together, their mind remains equanimous.
Neither perceiving fragrance nor stench, he dwells in equanimity;
yet if he hears the fragrances or odors of sentient beings' clothing, bedding, or their very limbs, he can discern whether their conduct is dominated by greed, hatred, or delusion.
Furthermore, if he smells the scents of hidden treasures, grasses, trees, and so forth, he clearly distinguishes them all as if they were right before his eyes.
If they smell the fragrance of sentient beings, from those as low as the Avīci Hell to those as high as the Peak of Existence, they know all the past deeds those beings have performed;
if they smell the fragrance of the generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and wisdom of the śrāvakas, they abide in the mind of omniscience without allowing it to be distracted or moved;
if they smell the fragrance of all bodhisattva practices, they enter the stage of the Tathāgata through the wisdom of equality.
They smell the fragrance of the realm of wisdom of all Buddhas, yet they do not abandon or neglect any of the bodhisattva practices.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s immeasurable and boundless pure nose.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of tongues. What are the ten?
That is to say:
the tongue that reveals and expounds the inexhaustible conduct of sentient beings;
the tongue that reveals and expounds inexhaustible Dharma-gates;
The tongue that praises the inexhaustible merits of all Buddhas;
the tongue that expounds eloquence and rhetoric without end;
the tongue that elucidates the Mahāyāna and the factors conducive to the Path.
A tongue that completely covers the void of the ten directions;
a tongue that universally illumines all Buddha-fields;
a tongue that causes all sentient beings to attain realization and understanding.
The tongue that causes all Buddhas to utter words of praise and joy;
the tongue that subdues all demons and non-Buddhists, eradicates all afflictions of birth and death, and leads beings to Nirvana.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed tongue of the Tathāgata that universally covers all buddha-lands.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of bodies.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
A human body, for the sake of teaching and transforming all humans;
a non-human body, for the sake of teaching and transforming those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;
a celestial body, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The body of one in training (*śaikṣa*), because it manifests the stage of training;
the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because it manifests the stage of an arhat;
and the body of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), because it teaches and transforms others to lead them into the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
The body of a bodhisattva, for the sake of bringing the Mahāyāna to fulfillment;
the body of a Tathāgata, for the sake of the consecration by the water of wisdom;
the mind-made body, for the sake of skillful manifestation.
The untainted Dharma-body manifests to all sentient beings through effortless spontaneity.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas accomplish these qualities, they shall attain the unsurpassed body of a Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of intention. What are these ten?
That which is called the preeminent mind, because it initiates all roots of goodness;
the abiding mind, because its profound faith is firm and immovable;
the penetrating mind, because it understands in accordance with the Buddha-dharma;
The internalized mind, because it knows the inclinations and joys of the hearts of all sentient beings;
the undisturbed mind, because it is not intermingled with any afflictions;
the luminously pure mind, because adventitious defilements cannot stain or adhere to it.
They skillfully observe the intentions of sentient beings, for they do not miss the proper moment by even a single thought;
they skillfully select their actions, for they never give rise to transgression in any situation;
they closely guard their sense faculties, subduing them so that they do not wander or scatter.
They skillfully enter the mental state of samādhi, because they have deeply entered the Buddha’s samādhi which is free from self and what belongs to a self.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed intention of all Buddhas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the practice of hearing the Dharma, because of delighting in the Dharma;
the practice of expounding the Dharma, because of benefiting sentient beings.
They practice the conduct free from greed, hatred, and delusion in order to subdue their own minds;
they practice the conduct of the desire realm in order to transform sentient beings of the desire realm;
and they practice the samādhis of the form and formless realms in order to cause them to quickly turn back [from those states].
The practice of approaching the meaning of the Dharma, because it swiftly attains wisdom;
the practice of all places of birth, because it freely teaches and transforms sentient beings;
and the practice of all Buddha-fields, because it pays homage to and makes offerings to all Buddhas.
The practice of nirvāṇa, because it does not sever the continuity of birth and death;
and the practice of bringing all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment, because it does not abandon the practices of a bodhisattva.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s practice of neither coming nor going.
"Sons of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of abodes."
What are the ten? They are:
dwelling in the bodhicitta, because it is never forgotten;
Abiding in the pāramitās because one does not weary of the factors conducive to enlightenment;
abiding in the teaching of the Dharma because it increases wisdom;
and abiding in the araṇya because it realizes great meditative concentration.
He dwells in accordance with all-knowledge through the ascetic practices (dhūta), contentment, and the four noble lineages, because he has few desires and few affairs;
he dwells in profound faith, because he bears the burden of the True Dharma;
he dwells in proximity to the Tathāgata, because he trains in the Buddha’s majestic deportment.
The dwelling of the birth of supernormal powers, because of the perfection of great wisdom;
the dwelling of patience, because of the fulfillment of receiving the prophecy;
and the dwelling of the site of enlightenment, because of the possession of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the Buddha-dharmas.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme dwelling of omniscience.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of sitting.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
The seat of the Wheel-Turning King, because it gives rise to the ten paths of wholesome action;
the seat of the Four Heavenly Kings, because they establish the Buddha-dharma with sovereign mastery throughout all worlds;
the seat of Śakra, because he acts as the supreme lord for all sentient beings.
The Brahmā-sitting, because of attaining mastery over the minds of oneself and others;
the lion’s sitting, because of being able to preach the Dharma;
the True Dharma-sitting, because of revealing and teaching through the power of dhāraṇī and eloquence.
The seat of firmness, because of the vow to reach ultimate fulfillment;
the seat of great loving-kindness, because it causes all evil sentient beings to rejoice;
the seat of great compassion, because it endures all suffering without weariness or fatigue.
The vajra posture, because it subdues all māras and non-Buddhists.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will attain the seat of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of reclining for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
lying down in tranquility, because body and mind are serene;
lying down in meditative concentration, because one practices in accordance with reality.
One sleeps in samādhi because body and mind are supple;
one sleeps like a Brahmā because one does not afflict oneself or others;
one sleeps with virtuous karma because there will be no regret hereafter.
One lies down with right faith, for it cannot be shaken;
one lies down on the right path, for virtuous friends awaken one;
one lies down with sublime vows, for they skillfully dedicate merit.
One lies down because all tasks are finished and what was to be done has been accomplished;
one lies down having relinquished all exertion because everything has become habitual. These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed great Dharma-sleep of the Tathāgata and will be able to awaken all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten places of abiding.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
They take great loving-kindness as their dwelling place, because their minds are impartial toward all sentient beings;
they take great compassion as their dwelling place, because they do not disparage those who have not yet trained;
they take great sympathetic joy as their dwelling place, because they are free from all sorrow and affliction.
They take great equanimity as their dwelling place, because they are equal toward the conditioned and the unconditioned;
they take all the perfections as their dwelling place, because the bodhicitta is their foremost priority;
they take all emptinesses as their dwelling place, because of their skillful observation.
They take signlessness as their place of abiding, because they do not depart from the state of correctness;
they take wishlessness as their place of abiding, because they observe the taking of birth;
they take mindfulness and wisdom as their place of abiding, because the dharma of patience is brought to fulfillment.
Taking the equality of all phenomena as one's place of abiding, because one attains the prediction of enlightenment—
this is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas dwell securely in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed and unimpeded place of abiding of the Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten spheres of activity for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
taking right mindfulness as the sphere of activity, because of fulfilling the foundations of mindfulness;
taking the various realms of existence as the sphere of activity, because of correctly awakening to the course of all phenomena.
They take wisdom as their sphere of practice, because they attain the Buddha’s joy;
they take the perfections as their sphere of practice, because they fulfill the knowledge of all modes of knowledge;
they take the four means of integration as their sphere of practice, because they transform and guide sentient beings.
They take birth and death as their sphere of activity in order to accumulate roots of goodness;

they take engaging in various conversations and play with all sentient beings as their sphere of activity in order to teach and transform them according to their needs so that they may be forever liberated;
and they take supernormal powers as their sphere of activity in order to know the faculties and realms of all sentient beings.
They take skillful means as their sphere of activity because they are in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
they take the site of enlightenment as their sphere of activity because they realize all-knowledge while never ceasing their bodhisattva practices.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of observation.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
The observation that knows all karmas, because it perceives them in their subtlest detail;
the observation that knows all realms of existence, because it does not grasp at sentient beings;
the observation that knows all faculties, because it thoroughly understands the absence of faculties.
The observation that knows all phenomena, because it does not destroy the dharma-realm;
the observation that sees the Buddha-dharma, because it diligently cultivates the Buddha-eye;
the observation that attains wisdom, because it expounds the Dharma according to principle.
The observation of the patience of non-arising, because it definitively realizes the Buddha-dharma;
the observation of the stage of non-retrogression, because it extinguishes all afflictions and transcends the three realms and the stages of the two vehicles;
and the observation of the stage of consecration, because one attains sovereign immovability regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
The samādhi of the observation of excellent awakening-wisdom is for the purpose of performing the buddha-deeds throughout all ten directions. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom of great observation.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of universal observation for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
universally observing all who come seeking [something], fulfilling their intentions with a mind free from contradiction;
and universally observing all sentient beings who violate the precepts, establishing them within the pure precepts of the Tathāgata.
Universally observing all sentient beings with harmful intent, they establish them within the Tathāgata’s power of patience;
universally observing all indolent sentient beings, they exhort them to be diligent so that they do not abandon their burden of carrying the Great Vehicle;
universally observing all distracted sentient beings, they cause them to abide in the stage of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, free from all agitation and movement.
Universally observing all sentient beings of evil wisdom, so as to cause them to eliminate doubt and destroy views of existence;
universally observing all impartial spiritual friends, so as to comply with their instructions and abide in the Buddha-dharma;
universally observing all teachings heard, so as to swiftly attain realization and vision of the supreme meaning.
They universally observe all boundless sentient beings, because they never abandon the power of great compassion;
they universally observe the teachings of all Buddhas, because they swiftly achieve the realization of all-knowledge.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme great wisdom of universal observation.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of prowess (*vikrīḍita*). What are these ten?
They are as follows:
The majestic display of the Bull King, because it outshines all the great assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others;
the majestic display of the Elephant King, because his mind is well-tamed and gentle as he bears the burden of all sentient beings;

and the majestic display of the Dragon King, because he raises the dense clouds of the Great Dharma, flashes the lightning of liberation, thunders the roar of the meaning of reality as it is, and pours down the nectar-rain of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis.

The Great King of Golden-Winged Birds manifests his prowess to dry up the waters of craving and destroy the shell of ignorance; he seizes the venomous dragons of affliction to bring about deliverance from the great ocean of birth-and-death suffering.
The Great Lion King manifests his prowess, dwelling securely in fearless and impartial great wisdom as his weapon to subdue all Māras and non-Buddhists.
With heroic vigor, he manifests his prowess, able to crush and annihilate all enemies of affliction within the great battle array of birth-and-death.
The prowess of great wisdom, because it knows the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and all dependent origination, and thus freely reveals all phenomena;
the prowess of dhāraṇī, because by the power of mindfulness and wisdom it upholds the Dharma without forgetting and proclaims it according to the faculties of sentient beings;
the prowess of eloquence, because it discerns all things with unimpeded swiftness, causing all to receive benefit and their hearts to rejoice.

The Tathāgata is majestic in his prowess; he has fully perfected all the dharmas that assist the path to omniscience. By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, he has attained everything that was to be attained and realized everything that was to be realized. Seated upon the lion throne, he has subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies, thereby accomplishing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme, sovereign, and powerful mastery of all Buddhas over all phenomena.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of lion’s roars.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
To proclaim,
"I shall certainly attain perfect, complete enlightenment," is the great lion's roar of the bodhicitta.

"I shall cause all sentient beings who have not yet crossed over to cross over; those who have not yet been liberated to be liberated; those who have not yet found peace to find peace; and those who have not yet attained nirvana to attain nirvana."
"This is the Great Compassionate One’s Great Lion’s Roar:
'I shall cause the lineage of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to never be severed.
This is the Great Lion’s Roar that repays the kindness of the Tathāgata."
"I shall adorn and purify all Buddha-fields"—
this is the ultimate, firm vow, the great lion's roar.
"I shall eliminate all evil realms and places of hardship."
"This is the great lion’s roar of upholding pure precepts:
'I shall fulfill the physical, verbal, and mental marks and signs that adorn the bodies of all Buddhas.'"
"This is the great lion’s roar of insatiable seeking of merit:
'I shall fully accomplish all the wisdom possessed by all Buddhas.
This is the great lion’s roar of insatiable seeking of wisdom."
"I shall eliminate all Māras and all demonic activities"—this is the great lion’s roar of one who practices correctly to sever all afflictions.
"I shall thoroughly understand that all phenomena are without self, without a sentient being, without a life-span, and without a person; they are empty, signless, wishless, and as pure as space."
"This is the great lion's roar of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When a Bodhisattva in their final birth causes all Buddha-lands to tremble and makes them entirely pure and adorned, at that time, all Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings come together to praise and entreat him, saying:
'We only pray that the Bodhisattva will manifest birth by means of the dharma of non-arising!'"
The Bodhisattva, with his unimpeded eye of wisdom, surveyed the world universally and thought:
"Among all sentient beings, there is none like me.
He then manifested his birth within the royal palace and, taking seven steps himself, let out the great lion's roar:
"I am the most supreme and foremost in the world; I shall bring an eternal end to the limits of birth and death"—this is the Great Lion’s Roar spoken according to reality.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed great lion’s roar of the Tathāgata.
*The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Great Vaipulya*, Fascicle Fifty-seven.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Fifty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
Part Six of Chapter Thirty-Eight: Leaving the World. Part Six.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure giving for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
giving with equanimity, because one does not discriminate among sentient beings;
giving according to their wishes, because one fulfills their aspirations.
Giving without distraction, so as to bring about benefit;
giving according to what is appropriate, by knowing the superior, middling, and inferior [capacities];
giving without attachment, because one does not seek karmic retribution.
The gift of relinquishment, because the mind is free from attachment;
the universal gift, because it is ultimately pure;
the gift dedicated to enlightenment, because it is far removed from both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The gift for transforming sentient beings is so called because it is not abandoned until one reaches the site of enlightenment;
the gift of the three spheres of purity is so called because one correctly observes the giver, the recipient, and the gift as being like space through right mindfulness.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, pure, and vast generosity.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure precepts.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
The precept of purity of body, because it guards against the three evils of the body;
the precept of purity of speech, because it is free from the four faults of speech;
the precept of purity of mind, because it is forever free from greed, anger, and false views.
The pure precept of not violating any training rules, because it acts as a sovereign lord among all humans and devas;
the pure precept of guarding the bodhicitta, because one does not delight in the Lesser Vehicle;
and the pure precept of guarding what was ordained by the Tathāgata, because one feels great dread even toward the commission of the most subtle offenses.
The pure precept of secret protection, because it skillfully uproots sentient beings who have transgressed the precepts;
the pure precept of non-action toward all evils, because of the vow to cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
the pure precept of distancing oneself from all views of existence, because of non-attachment to the precepts.
They guard the pure precepts of all sentient beings because they give rise to great compassion.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, faultless, and pure precepts.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure patience for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure patience of peacefully accepting insults and humiliation for the sake of protecting all sentient beings;
and the pure patience of peacefully accepting blades and staves for the sake of skillfully protecting oneself and others.
The pure patience that does not give rise to anger or malice, because the mind is unshakable;
the pure patience that does not reproach the lowly, because one is superior and capable of being magnanimous;
the pure patience that provides refuge and saves all, because one sacrifices even one's own life.
The pure patience of being far removed from self-conceit, because one does not disparage those who have not yet trained;
the pure patience of not feeling anger toward those who revile or harm, because one contemplates all things as being like illusions;
the pure patience of not seeking retribution for offenses committed, because one perceives neither self nor other.
The pure patience that does not follow afflictions, because it is detached from all objective spheres;

and the pure patience of knowing the non-arising of all phenomena through the true wisdom of a bodhisattva, because it accords with reality and enters the sphere of omniscience without depending on the instruction of others.
These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the supreme Dharma-patience that is realized by all Buddhas without depending on another.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure diligence.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Purity of physical vigor, because one serves, makes offerings to, and honors all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and teachers, never turning back from the field of merit;
purity of verbal vigor, because one extensively expounds for others whatever Dharma one has heard, praising the merits of the Buddha without weariness;
purity of mental vigor, because one is skillfully able to enter and emerge from loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity, meditative concentration, liberation, and all samādhis without rest.
The pure diligence of an upright mind, because it is free from deception, flattery, crookedness, and hypocrisy, and because it practices all things with diligence without ever turning back;
the pure diligence of an increasing and superior mind, because its resolve constantly seeks the highest of high wisdom and vows to be endowed with all pure and white dharmas;
and the pure diligence that is not in vain, because it gathers up generosity, ethical discipline, patience, learning, and heedfulness, continuing without ceasing even unto enlightenment.
The pure diligence that subdues all māras, for it is able to completely eliminate greed, hatred, delusion, false views, all afflictions, and all entanglements and hindrances;

the pure diligence that fulfills the light of wisdom, for its every action is thoroughly examined and brought to ultimate completion so as to prevent future regret, thereby attaining the unique qualities of all Buddhas;

and the pure diligence that is neither coming nor going, for it attains knowledge of reality as it is, enters the gateway of the Dharma-realm, realizes the equality of body, speech, and mind, and understands that characteristics are non-characteristics, remaining free from all attachment.

Having accomplished the pure diligence of the light of the Dharma, they transcend all stages and receive the Buddha’s consecration; through their untainted bodies, they manifest death and birth, renunciation, the attainment of enlightenment, the preaching of the Dharma, and final nirvana, thereby fulfilling such universal deeds of Samantabhadra.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, pure vigor.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). What are the ten?
They are as follows:
The pure dhyāna of always delighting in leaving the household life, because of relinquishing all that one possesses;
the pure dhyāna of attaining true spiritual friends, because of demonstrating and teaching the right path;
the pure dhyāna of dwelling in an araṇya and enduring wind, rain, and so forth, because of being free from the notions of "self" and "mine."
The pure meditation of beings who have left behind clamor and bustle, because they always delight in stillness;
the pure meditation of mental activity that is harmonious and supple, because it guards the sense faculties;
and the pure meditation of the tranquil extinction of mind and intellect, because no sounds or thorns of meditative concentration can disturb it.
The pure dhyāna of skillful means for awakening, because it directly realizes all things through observation;
the pure dhyāna free from attachment to flavors, because it does not abandon the desire realm;
the pure dhyāna that initiates clear penetration, because it knows the root-natures of all sentient beings.
They sport with mastery in pure dhyāna and enter the samādhis of the Buddhas because they realize non-self.
This is the tenth.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, great, and pure dhyāna.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure wisdom. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure wisdom that knows all causes, because it does not destroy the retribution of results;
the pure wisdom that knows all conditions, because it does not conflict with their conjunction.
The pure wisdom that knows neither annihilation nor permanence, because it thoroughly understands that all dependent origination is exactly as it is;
the pure wisdom that uproots all views, because it neither grasps nor rejects the marks of sentient beings;
the pure wisdom that contemplates the mental activities of all sentient beings, because it realizes they are like illusions;
The pure wisdom of vast eloquence, because it distinguishes all phenomena and engages in question-and-answer discourse without impediment;
the pure wisdom that cannot be known by any māras, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, because it penetrates deeply into the wisdom of all Tathāgatas;

the pure wisdom that perceives the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas, perceives the inherently pure nature of all sentient beings, perceives that all phenomena are entirely quiescent, and perceives that all lands are identical to empty space, because it knows that all marks are without obstruction.
The pure wisdom of all dhāraṇīs, eloquence, and the perfection of skillful means, because it causes one to attain all supreme knowledge;
the adamantine wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment that realizes the equality of all phenomena and their purity, because it attains the most honored knowledge of all phenomena.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the unimpeded great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
What are the ten? They are as follows:
The pure compassion of equanimity, because it universally gathers in all sentient beings without discrimination;
the pure compassion of benefit, because it causes all who encounter its actions to rejoice;
the pure compassion that regards others as oneself, because it ultimately causes all to transcend birth and death.
The pure compassion that does not abandon the world, because its mind constantly contemplates the accumulation of roots of goodness;
the pure compassion that leads to liberation, because it universally causes all sentient beings to eliminate all afflictions;
the pure compassion that gives birth to bodhi, because it universally causes all sentient beings to resolve to seek the mind of omniscience.
The unimpeded pure compassion for the world, because it emits great radiance that shines equally and universally;
the pure compassion that fills space, because it protects and delivers sentient beings without there being a place it does not reach;
and the pure compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana*), because it realizes the true reality of suchness (*tathatā*).
The objectless, pure loving-kindness, because it enters into the bodhisattva’s nature of transcendence from birth.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure loving-kindness.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure compassion for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
compassion pure through being without companions, because it arises from a solitary resolve;
