compassion pure through freedom from weariness, because one undergoes suffering on behalf of all sentient beings without regarding it as toil.
Pure compassion for taking birth in difficult realms, for the sake of delivering sentient beings;
pure compassion for taking birth in happy realms, for the sake of manifesting impermanence;
pure compassion for sentient beings fixed in error, because of never abandoning their great vows throughout kalpas.
Pure compassion that does not cling to one’s own happiness, because it universally bestows joy upon all sentient beings;
pure compassion that seeks no recompense for its kindness, because it purifies the mind through cultivation.
The pure compassion that can eliminate perversion, because it teaches the Dharma as it truly is.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, unstained, and free from feverish affliction, yet that sentient beings undergo manifold sufferings due to adventitious afflictions;
having known this, they give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, which is called:
Because they teach the Dharma of stainless, pure radiance for the sake of that which is inherently pure;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are like the tracks of birds in the sky, which sentient beings—obscured by the cataracts of ignorance—cannot perceive or understand;
observing them in this way, he gives rise to great compassion, which is named:
The wisdom of reality, because it reveals the Dharma of nirvāṇa for them. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure compassion.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of pure joy for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the pure joy of generating the bodhicitta;
the pure joy of relinquishing all that one possesses;
The pure joy of teaching and bringing to fulfillment those sentient beings who have broken their precepts without feeling aversion;
the pure joy of vowing to rescue and deliver sentient beings who commit evil while being able to endure them;
and the pure joy of sacrificing one's body to seek the Dharma without giving rise to regret.
Having personally renounced sensual pleasures, they always delight in the pure joy of the Dharma-pleasure;
they cause all sentient beings to renounce the pleasure of material sustenance and always delight in the pure joy of the Dharma-pleasure;
seeing all Buddhas, they reverently make offerings to them without ever feeling weary or satisfied, experiencing the pure joy of the equality of the Dharma-realm.
May all sentient beings love and delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and the playful mastery of entering and emerging from samādhis with pure joy;

may their hearts delight in fully practicing all ascetic disciplines in accordance with the bodhisattva path, and may they realize the pure joy of the Sage’s (*muni*) tranquil, immovable, and unsurpassed concentration and wisdom.
These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed, vast, and pure joy of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure relinquishment.
What are the ten? They are as follows:
Pure equanimity that does not give rise to attachment when all sentient beings show respect, honor, and make offerings;
pure equanimity that does not give rise to anger when all sentient beings treat one with contempt, disparage, or insult one;
and pure equanimity that remains untainted by the eight worldly concerns while constantly moving through the world.

Pure relinquishment that waits for the proper time to transform those sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma; pure relinquishment that does not give rise to aversion toward those who are not vessels for the Dharma;
pure relinquishment that does not seek the dharmas of the learners or non-learners of the two vehicles;
and pure relinquishment in which the mind is always far removed from all sensual pleasures and dharmas that accord with the afflictions.
He does not praise the two vehicles, but maintains pure equanimity through weariness with and detachment from birth and death;

he remains far removed from all worldly speech—speech that is not of nirvāṇa, not of dispassion, not in accord with principle, speech that disturbs others, or the speech of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and in brief, he maintains pure equanimity by remaining far removed from all speech that obstructs the bodhisattva path;

furthermore, regarding sentient beings whose faculties are already matured and who have generated mindfulness and wisdom but are as yet unable to know the supreme Dharma, he maintains pure equanimity while waiting for the proper time to transform them.

There may be sentient beings whom the Bodhisattva has already taught in the past, such that they can only be tamed upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood; these too await the purity of the opportune time for relinquishment (*tyāga*).

Regarding these two types of persons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is neither high nor low, neither grasping nor rejecting; remaining far removed from all various forms of conceptual discrimination, he constantly dwells in right concentration, enters the Dharma of reality as it is, and his mind attains the purity of patient endurance and relinquishment.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, vast, and pure equanimity.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of meanings.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
The meaning of "much learning" is due to firm cultivation;
the meaning of "Dharma" is due to skillful discernment;
the meaning of "emptiness" is due to the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The meaning of tranquility is because it is free from the clamor and confusion of all sentient beings;
the meaning of ineffability is because it does not cling to any speech or language;
the meaning of suchness is because it thoroughly realizes the equality of the three periods of time.
The meaning of the *dharmadhātu* is that all phenomena are of a single flavor;
the meaning of *tathatā* is that all Tathāgatas accord with and enter it;
the meaning of the *bhūtakoṭi* is the thorough knowledge of reality as it truly is to its ultimate extent.
The meaning of the Great Parinirvāṇa is that one extinguishes all suffering while cultivating the various practices of a bodhisattva.
These constitute the ten [meanings].
If bodhisattvas abide securely in these dharmas, they will attain the supreme meaning of omniscience.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of dharmas for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the Dharma of reality, because one practices according to what is taught;
the Dharma of detachment from grasping, because both the grasper and the grasped are entirely relinquished.
The dharma of non-contention, because it is free from all delusive disputes;
the dharma of quiescence, because it extinguishes all feverish afflictions;
the dharma of detachment from desire, because all craving and lust are severed.
Non-conceptual dharmas, because clinging and discrimination have forever ceased;
unarisen dharmas, because they are as immovable as space;
unconditioned dharmas, because they are free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
The dharmas of the fundamental nature are inherently undefiled and pure;
they relinquish all *upadeśa* (instructional) nirvāṇa-dharmas and are able to give rise to all bodhisattva practices, for their cultivation is uninterrupted.
These are the ten.
If Bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the unsurpassed, vast Dharma of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of requisites for merit.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Exhorting sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit,
because it ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed.
Practicing the ten kinds of dedication in accordance with them is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit;
Because they sever all unwholesome dharmas and accumulate all wholesome dharmas;
because their wisdom provides guidance and instruction, it serves as an auxiliary to the bodhisattva’s merit,
for it transcends the merit of the triple world.
A mind free from weariness is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit,
because it brings all sentient beings to ultimate liberation.
Relinquishing all that one possesses, both internal and external, is a supportive factor for a bodhisattva’s merit;
Because they are unattached to all things, they practice diligence without retreating in order to fulfill the primary and secondary marks; this is the bodhisattva’s equipment for merit.
Because they open the gates of great giving without limit, [this is their equipment for wisdom].

Dedicating all roots of goodness—whether superior, middling, or inferior—toward unsurpassed enlightenment, with a mind free from disparagement, constitutes the bodhisattva’s requisites for the accumulation of merit;
this is because they are in accord with skillful means.
To give rise to great compassion for sentient beings who are fixed in error, inferior, or unwholesome, and not to harbor contempt for them, is a factor for the bodhisattva’s equipment of merit;
this is because they constantly give rise to the heart of the great person’s vast vow.

To reverently make offerings to all Tathāgatas, to conceive the thought of a Tathāgata toward all bodhisattvas, and to cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy— these are the requisites for the merit of a bodhisattva,
because they maintain their original vows with extreme firmness.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accumulated roots of goodness over incalculable eons and desires to realize unsurpassed awakening as if it were held in the palm of his hand, yet gives it all away to all sentient beings with a mind free from distress or regret, his mind being vast and equal to the realm of empty space— this is the bodhisattva’s equipment for the accumulation of merit,
for the sake of giving rise to great wisdom and realizing the Great Dharma.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in them, they will be fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed and vast accumulation of merit.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of requisites for wisdom.
What are the ten? They are as follows:

To draw near to learned and truly virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and prostrating before them, following them in every way, and not contradicting their instructions—this is the first;
for all things are upright and free from falsehood or pretension.

Second, they are forever free from pride and arrogance, always practicing humility and respect; their physical, verbal, and mental actions are without coarseness or rudeness, being gentle, harmonious, and compliant, neither hypocritical nor crooked, because their bodies are capable of serving as vessels for the Buddha-dharma.

Mindfulness and wisdom follow awakening without ever becoming distracted; one possesses a sense of shame and propriety, is gentle and supple, and the mind remains unshakable. One constantly recollects the six remembrances (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), constantly practices the six respects, and always dwells in accordance with the six firm dharmas—these constitute three [factors].
This is for the sake of employing the ten kinds of knowledge as skillful means.

Delighting in the Dharma and delighting in its meaning, taking the Dharma as one's joy, always delighting in hearing it without weariness or satiety, abandoning worldly discourse and worldly talk, single-mindedly listening to and receiving supramundane teachings, distancing oneself from the Lesser Vehicle, and entering the wisdom of the Great Vehicle—these are the four;
because of recollecting with a single mind without distraction.

To single-mindedly bear the burden of the six *pāramitās*; to have fully matured the practice of the four *brahma-vihāras*; to skillfully cultivate all practices in accordance with the luminous Dharma; to diligently inquire of those who are wise and sagacious; to distance oneself from the evil destinies and turn toward the noble paths; to always delight the mind, observe with right mindfulness, subdue one’s own emotions, and protect the intentions of others—this constitutes the fifth [set], because it consists of firm cultivation and true practice.

Constantly delighting in renunciation, not being attached to the three realms of existence, perpetually awakening to one's own mind, never harboring evil thoughts, having severed the three types of deluded perceptions, ensuring that the three karmas are all wholesome, and definitively realizing the self-nature of the mind— these are the six [qualities],
because they can cause the minds of both oneself and others to become pure.

To observe that the five aggregates are all like magical illusions, the elements (*dhātu*) are like venomous snakes, and the sense bases (*āyatana*) are like an empty village; and that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like dreams, like shadows, like echoes, like reflections, like drawings in the sky, like whirling firebrands, like the colors of a rainbow, and like the light of the sun and moon—being without marks or form, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither coming nor going, and having no place of abiding—to observe in this way and know that all phenomena are without arising and without ceasing is the seventh [point];
for one knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears that all phenomena are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, without persons, without mind, without objects, without greed, hatred, or delusion, without body, without things, without master, without dependence, without attachment, and without activity—that all such things are non-existent and entirely return to quiescence—and having heard this, believes it deeply, neither doubting nor slandering it;
this is the eighth [perfection], because they are able to achieve and perfect understanding.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully disciplines all the sense faculties, practices in accordance with reality, and constantly abides in śamatha and vipaśyanā.
With a mind that is tranquil and still, all stirring thoughts are entirely non-arising; there is no self, no person, no agent, and no activity.
There is no conceiving of a self-concept, no conceiving of karmic deeds for a self, and there are no afflictions or wounds.
...without scars, nor is there any patience attained therein; the actions of body, speech, and mind neither come nor go; there is no diligence and no valor;
observing all sentient beings and all phenomena, the mind is entirely equal and abides nowhere, being neither this shore nor—
The "other shore" is free from the nature of this or that; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
To constantly contemplate with wisdom in this manner is the ninth [perfection], because one has reached the state of the other shore of all differentiated marks.

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives the dharma of dependent origination, he perceives the purity of dharmas; because he perceives the purity of dharmas, he perceives the purity of the buddha-fields; because he perceives the purity of the buddha-fields, he perceives the purity of space; because he perceives the purity of space, he perceives the purity of the dharma-realm; because he perceives the purity of the dharma-realm, he perceives the purity of wisdom—these are the ten [purities], for the sake of practicing and accumulating all-knowledge.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of requisites for wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s mass of all-dharmas, unobstructed, pure, and subtle wisdom.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of sufficiency of illumination for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the light-footed skillful discernment of all phenomena;
the light-footed non-attachment to all phenomena.
The foot of clarity through being free from inverted views;
the foot of clarity through the illumination of wisdom upon all faculties;
and the foot of clarity through skillfully initiating right diligence.
The perfection of the light of wisdom that can deeply penetrate the knowledge of ultimate truth;
the perfection of the light of wisdom that achieves the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising by extinguishing afflictions and karma;
and the perfection of the light of wisdom that universally observes with the divine eye.
The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, which is pure, clear, and sufficient regarding the prior limit;
and the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, which is the wisdom that severs all outflows of sentient beings, being pure, clear, and sufficient. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the unsurpassed great light regarding all Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten ways of seeking the Dharma."
What are the ten? They are:
seeking the Dharma with a straightforward mind, because one is free from flattery and deception;
One seeks the Dharma with diligence because of being far removed from indolence and pride;
one seeks the Dharma single-mindedly because of not begrudging body or life;
and one seeks the Dharma for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings, rather than for the sake of fame, profit, or honor.
One seeks the Dharma for the benefit of oneself and all sentient beings, not merely for one's own profit;
one seeks the Dharma to enter into wisdom, not out of a fondness for words and letters;
one seeks the Dharma to transcend birth and death, not out of greed for worldly pleasures.
They seek the Dharma for the sake of delivering sentient beings, because they have resolved to attain bodhicitta;
they seek the Dharma for the sake of severing the doubts of all sentient beings, so that none may remain in hesitation;
and they seek the Dharma for the sake of fulfilling the Buddha-dharma, because they take no pleasure in other vehicles.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the great wisdom of all Buddha-dharmas that does not depend on the instruction of others.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of clearly understood dharmas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
To cultivate roots of goodness in accordance with worldly conventions is the method clearly understood by ignorant ordinary beings;
to attain unimpeded and indestructible faith and awaken to the intrinsic nature of phenomena is the method clearly understood by those who follow through faith;
to diligently practice the Dharma and abide in accordance with the Dharma is the method clearly understood by those who follow through the Dharma.
To distance oneself from the eightfold wrong paths and proceed toward the eightfold right path is the Dharma clearly understood by the person of the eighth stage;
to eliminate all fetters, sever the outflows of birth and death, and perceive the true reality is the Dharma clearly understood by the *srotāpanna*;
to contemplate sensory flavors as a source of affliction and to know there is no coming or going is the Dharma clearly understood by the *sakṛdāgāmin*.

To take no delight in the three realms, to seek the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*), and to give rise to not even a single thought of attachment toward the phenomena of rebirth—this is the clear understanding of the *anāgāmin*.

To attain the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), to achieve the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and to fully accomplish the nine meditative concentrations and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—this is the clear understanding of the *arhat*.

To naturally delight in contemplating the single flavor of dependent origination, to have a mind that is ever tranquil, to be content with few affairs, to understand causes through self-attainment, to awaken without depending on others, and to accomplish various supernormal powers and wisdoms—this is the clear understanding of the *pratyekabuddha*.

With vast wisdom and keenly sharpened faculties, they constantly delight in liberating all sentient beings; they diligently cultivate the dharmas of merit and wisdom that assist the path, and they are fully endowed with all the Tathāgata’s ten powers, fearlessnesses, and merits—such is the person of the bodhisattva who clearly understands the Dharma.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the Tathāgata’s supreme, great wisdom that clearly understands all phenomena.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practices for cultivation.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
The practice of revering and honoring all spiritual friends;
the practice of being constantly awakened by the devas;
and the practice of always maintaining a sense of shame and remorse in the presence of all Buddhas.
The practice of compassionately regarding sentient beings and not abandoning the cycle of birth and death;
the practice of ensuring that all undertakings reach completion with an unchanging mind;
and the practice of diligently training by single-mindedly following the assembly of bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
The practice of diligently seeking the right path while remaining far removed from false views;
the practice of destroying all demons, afflictions, and karma;
and the practice of knowing the superior or inferior capacities of the faculties of all sentient beings and teaching the Dharma accordingly so that they may abide in the stage of Buddhahood.
The practice of dwelling in the boundlessly vast dharma-realm, eliminating afflictions, and purifying the body—
this constitutes the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will attain the unsurpassed practice of the Tathāgata.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of māras for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), because it gives rise to all forms of grasping;
the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), because it is constantly defiling.
The karma-māra, because it can create obstacles;
the mind-māra, because it gives rise to arrogance;
the death-māra, because it abandons the place of birth.
The celestial māra exists because of self-indulgence;
the root-of-goodness māra exists because of constant grasping;
the samādhi māra exists because of long-term attachment to its flavor.
The demon of virtuous friends, because of giving rise to a mind of attachment;
the demon of the wisdom of the Dharma of Bodhi, because of not wishing to relinquish it.
These are the ten.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should employ skillful means to swiftly seek to remain far removed from them.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of demonic activities for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
to cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is a work of Māra;

To give with a malicious mind, to maintain precepts with a mind of hatred, to abandon those of evil character, to distance oneself from the indolent, to treat the distracted with contempt, and to revile those of poor wisdom—these are the works of Māra.

To harbor stinginess regarding the profound Dharma, to fail to teach those who are capable of being transformed, or to insist on teaching even those who are not vessels for the Dharma when one receives wealth, profit, respect, and offerings—these are the works of Māra.

To take no pleasure in hearing the various pāramitās; even if one hears them explained, to fail to practice them; or though one does practice, to frequently give rise to indolence; and because of such indolence, to have a narrow and inferior resolve, failing to seek the unsurpassed Great Bodhi Dharma—these are the works of Māra.

To distance oneself from virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and draw near to evil associates; to delight in seeking the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and take no pleasure in taking birth; to set one’s will upon *nirvāṇa*, desiring the tranquility of detachment—these are the works of Māra.

To give rise to a mind of anger toward a bodhisattva, to look upon them with an evil eye, to seek out their faults and misdeeds, to proclaim their transgressions, and to cut off all offerings of wealth and profit they receive—these are the works of Māra.

To slander the true Dharma and take no pleasure in hearing it; even if one should hear it, to immediately produce disparagement; to see someone preaching the Dharma and fail to show respect, saying, "Only what I say is correct, while everything else is wrong"—these are the works of Māra.

To delight in studying worldly treatises, clever arts, and literary rhetoric; to expound the Two Vehicles while concealing the profound Dharma; or to transmit sublime meanings to those who are unworthy, thereby distancing oneself from Bodhi and dwelling in false paths—this is the work of Māra.

To constantly delight in associating with and making offerings to those who have already attained liberation and established themselves in peace, yet refuse to associate with or transform those who have not yet attained liberation or peace—this is the work of Māra.

To increase self-conceit and lack reverence; to inflict much harm upon sentient beings; to seek neither the True Dharma nor authentic wisdom; and for one’s mind to be so corrupt and evil that it is difficult to awaken—this is the work of Māra.
These are the ten.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should swiftly distance themselves from these and diligently seek the work of a Buddha.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten ways of abandoning the activities of Māra.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
To associate with spiritual friends and honor them with offerings is to abandon the works of Māra;
to refrain from self-exaltation and self-praise is to abandon the works of Māra;
to have faith and understanding in the profound Dharma of the Buddha without slandering it is to abandon the works of Māra.
Never forgetting the mind of omniscience is to abandon the deeds of Māra;
diligently cultivating sublime conduct while remaining ever heedful is to abandon the deeds of Māra;
constantly seeking all the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is to abandon the deeds of Māra.
Constantly expounding the Dharma with a mind free from weariness, one abandons the works of Māra;
taking refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions and conceiving the thought of their protection, one abandons the works of Māra;
faithfully accepting and recollecting all Buddhas and their empowerment through spiritual power, one abandons the works of Māra.
They plant roots of goodness identical to those of all bodhisattvas, remaining equal and non-dual, and abandon the activities of Māra.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will be able to transcend all paths of Māra.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten ways in which Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas see the Buddha. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the unattached vision of the Buddha who has attained perfect enlightenment while abiding in the world;
and the vision of the Buddha’s manifestation through aspiration.
The Buddha of karmic retribution is seen through deep faith;
the Buddha of sustaining maintenance is seen through conformity;
the Buddha of nirvāṇa is seen through profound penetration.
The Buddha of the Dharma-realm is seen as universally reaching everywhere;
the Buddha of the mind is seen as dwelling in tranquility;
the Buddha of samādhi is seen as immeasurable and non-reliant.
The Buddha of Original Nature is seen through clear realization;
the Buddha of Accordant Joy is seen through universal reception. These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will always behold the unsurpassed Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of buddha-activities."
What are the ten? They are as follows: providing guidance according to the appropriate time is the Buddha’s work;
To cause them to practice correctly, he causes them to see [the Buddha] within their dreams; this is the work of the Buddha.
To awaken them to their past roots of goodness, [he does so].
To expound for others sutras previously unheard is the work of a Buddha,
because it causes the arising of wisdom and the severing of doubt.
To teach the Dharma of liberation to those entangled by the fetters of remorse is the work of a Buddha;
It is for the purpose of causing them to be free from doubt.

If there are sentient beings who give rise to thoughts of stinginess, up to and including thoughts of malicious wisdom, the mind of the two vehicles, harmful intent, doubt, distraction, or arrogance, [the Buddha] manifests for them the Tathāgata’s body adorned with all the marks;
this is the work of a Buddha, for it causes the growth of past roots of goodness.

When the True Dharma is difficult to encounter, he extensively expounds the teachings so that, upon hearing them, beings may attain the wisdom of dhāraṇī and the wisdom of supernormal powers, thereby universally benefiting immeasurable sentient beings;
this is the Buddha-work, because his resolute conviction is pure.

If demonic activities arise, one is able to employ skillful means to manifest sounds such as those of the realm of empty space, preaching the Dharma that does not harm or afflict others as an antidote, thereby causing them to attain awakening; once the various demons have heard this, their majestic radiance subsides and vanishes—this is the work of a Buddha, for his aspiration and delight are supreme and his majestic virtue is great.

With an uninterrupted mind, he constantly guards himself so as not to allow entry into the fixed positions of the two vehicles; if there are sentient beings whose faculties are not yet mature, he never speaks of the realm of liberation for them—this is the work of a Buddha, for it is accomplished through his original vows.

To be entirely free from the fetters, outflows, and bonds of birth and death; to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva in uninterrupted succession; and to embrace sentient beings with great compassion, causing them to initiate practice for ultimate liberation—this is the work of a Buddha, because one does not cease the cultivation of bodhisattva practices.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly understands that his own body and all sentient beings are originally quiescent and extinguished;
thus, he is neither startled nor terrified, yet he diligently cultivates merit and wisdom without ever becoming weary or satisfied.

Although he knows that all phenomena are devoid of volitional construction, he does not abandon the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. Although he is forever free from craving regarding all sensory objects, he constantly...

They delight in beholding and honoring the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas; though they know that entry into the Dharma does not depend on another, they seek omniscience through various skillful means;
though they know all buddha-fields are like empty space, they constantly delight in adorning all buddha-lands;
and though they perpetually observe the non-existence of persons and the absence of self, they teach and transform sentient beings without [weariness].
There is no weariness; although one is fundamentally unmoving within the dharma-realm, one manifests various transformations through the power of supernatural penetrations and wisdom;
although one has already accomplished the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), one practices the bodhisattva deeds without rest;
although one knows that all phenomena are ineffable, one turns the pure wheel of Dharma to gladden the minds of sentient beings; although...
To be able to manifest the spiritual powers of all Buddhas without ever wearying of or abandoning the bodhisattva body, and though manifesting entry into great parinirvāṇa,
to manifest birth in all places— to be able to perform such a dharma that unifies the provisional and the real— is the work of a Buddha.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the unsurpassed, teacherless, and vast activity that does not depend on the instruction of others.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of conceited actions. What are these ten?
They are as follows:

To fail to show respect toward the Teacher, the Sangha, one’s parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—those who abide in the right path and are directed toward the right path, and who are fields of merit—is an act of pride.

Or, when there is a Dharma teacher who has attained the most supreme Dharma, who rides upon the Mahāyāna, who knows the path of deliverance, who has obtained dhāraṇīs, and who expounds the vast teachings of the sūtras without ceasing—to give rise to a heart of arrogance toward such a person and to fail to show respect for the Dharma they preach is an act of pride.
To hear the sublime Dharma being taught within an assembly and yet refuse to praise it so as to cause others to believe and accept it is an act of pride.
To take pleasure in giving rise to *māna* (pride), exalting oneself and looking down upon others, failing to see one's own faults and unaware of one's own shortcomings—this is the karma of pride.

To take pleasure in giving rise to *atimāna* (excessive pride), failing to praise those of virtue when they should be praised, and failing to feel joy when others offer praise—this is the karma of pride.

To see a Dharma teacher preaching the Dharma for others, knowing it to be the Dharma, the Vinaya, the truth, and the word of the Buddha, yet out of resentment for that person, also resenting the Dharma, personally engaging in slander and inciting others to slander it—this is the karma of pride.

Seeking a high seat for oneself, claiming to be a Dharma teacher, and receiving offerings while refusing to perform manual labor; seeing elders who have long practiced the path and failing to rise in greeting or offer service—this is the karma of pride.
Seeing those with virtue, frowning and showing displeasure, speaking with coarse and harsh words, and watching for their faults—this is the karma of pride.
Seeing those who are wise and knowledgeable in the Dharma, being unwilling to draw near, respect, or make offerings to them, and being unwilling to inquire of them—this is the karma of pride.
"What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What should be done?"
"What should not be done? What kind of karma, when performed, will bring various benefits and peace for a long night?
Being foolish and stubborn, swallowed by pride, they are ultimately unable to see the path of deliverance; this is the karma of conceit.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings shrouded by pride who, despite the appearance of Buddhas in the world, are unable to draw near, respect, or make offerings to them. They do not give rise to new roots of goodness and cause old roots of goodness to perish. They speak what should not be spoken and engage in disputes that should not be contested; consequently, they will inevitably fall into perilous and deep pits in the future, failing to encounter even a single Buddha for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, let alone hear the Dharma!
"However, because they have once given rise to the bodhicitta, they will ultimately awaken of their own accord; this is the karma of pride.
This constitutes the tenth.
If all bodhisattvas distance themselves from this karma of pride, they will attain ten kinds of karmic activities of wisdom."
What are the ten? They are:
having faith and understanding in the retribution of karma, not subverting cause and effect—this is the work of wisdom;
Not forsaking the bodhicitta and constantly recollecting all Buddhas is the work of wisdom;
drawing near to spiritual friends, honoring and making offerings to them with a mind of reverence that never grows weary or indolent is the work of wisdom;
delighting in the Dharma and delighting in its meaning without satiety, remaining far removed from wrong thoughts, and diligently cultivating right mindfulness is the work of wisdom.

To be free from the conceit of "I" toward all sentient beings; to regard all bodhisattvas as Tathāgatas; to cherish the true Dharma as one’s own body and to honor the Tathāgata as one protects one’s own life; and to conceive the thought of all Buddhas toward those who practice—this is the activity of wisdom.
To have no unwholesome deeds of body, speech, or mind; to praise the noble ones and accord with Bodhi—this is the activity of wisdom.
Not to subvert dependent origination, to be free from all false views, to destroy darkness and attain clarity, and to illuminate all phenomena—this is the activity of wisdom.

To practice in accordance with the ten kinds of dedication, regarding the perfections as one’s compassionate mother and skillful means as one’s compassionate father, and entering the abode of enlightenment with a profound and pure mind—this is the work of wisdom.

To constantly and diligently accumulate all such factors conducive to the path, including generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, tranquility and insight, merit, and wisdom, without ever becoming weary—this is the work of wisdom.

If there is a single karma praised by the Buddha, which can destroy the demons, afflictions, and strife; which can leave behind all hindrances, coverings, entanglements, and fetters; which can teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings; which can accord with wisdom and embrace the True Dharma; which can adorn and purify Buddha-fields; and which can give rise to supernormal powers and clarity—diligently cultivating all such things without weariness or retreat is the karma of wisdom.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the unsurpassed great wisdom and the karma of all skillful means of the Tathāgatas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten things that are sustained by Māra. What are these ten?
They are as follows:
A mind of indolence is possessed by Māra;
a narrow and inferior aspiration is possessed by Māra;
being satisfied with meager practice is possessed by Māra.
To accept only one thing and nothing else is to be possessed by Māra;
not to generate the great vow is to be possessed by Māra;
to delight in dwelling in quiescent extinction and severing afflictions is to be possessed by Māra.
To seek the permanent severance of birth and death is to be held by Māra;
to abandon the conduct of a bodhisattva is to be held by Māra;
to fail to transform sentient beings is to be held by Māra.
To doubt and slander the true Dharma is to be possessed by Māra. These are the ten.
"If bodhisattvas are able to abandon these states of being possessed by Māra, they will attain ten kinds of being possessed by the Buddhas."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
first, being able to initially resolve upon bodhicitta, which is sustained by the Buddhas;
In every successive birth, they maintain the bodhicitta without letting it be forgotten, being sustained by the Buddhas;
they awaken to all demonic activities and are able to remain far removed from them, being sustained by the Buddhas;
upon hearing the various pāramitās, they practice according to the teachings, being sustained by the Buddhas.
To know the suffering of birth and death yet not feel revulsion toward it is sustained by the Buddha;
to contemplate the profound Dharma and attain immeasurable fruits is sustained by the Buddha;
to preach the teachings of the Two Vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings yet not personally realize the liberation of those vehicles is sustained by the Buddha.

To contemplate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas without dwelling within them; to give rise to no dualistic thoughts regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned—this is sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment.
To reach the realm of non-arising (*anutpāda*) yet manifest birth therein—this is sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment.
Although having realized all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), to still engage in the conduct of a bodhisattva and not sever the lineage of bodhisattvas—this is sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in them, they will attain the power of the supreme sustenance of all Buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by ten kinds of dharmas.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
One knows that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, sustained by the Dharma;
one knows that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, sustained by the Dharma;
one knows that all conditioned phenomena are non-self, sustained by the Dharma.
He knows that all phenomena are quiescent and in *nirvāṇa*, sustained by the Dharma;
he knows that all phenomena arise from conditions and do not arise in the absence of conditions, sustained by the Dharma;

he knows that because of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), ignorance arises, and because ignorance arises, there is the arising of everything up to old age and death; and that through the cessation of improper mental attention, ignorance ceases, and through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of everything up to old age and death—all sustained by the Dharma.

Knowing that the three gates of liberation give rise to the Śrāvaka vehicle, which is sustained by the Dharma; knowing that the realization of the dharma of non-contention gives rise to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, which is sustained by the Dharma;
knowing that the six pāramitās and the four means of integration give rise to the Mahāyāna, which is sustained by the Dharma;
and knowing that all lands, all dharmas, all sentient beings, and all worlds are the sphere of the Buddha’s wisdom, which is sustained by the Dharma.
Knowing how to sever all thoughts, relinquishing all grasping, being free from the limits of the past and future, conforming to nirvana, and being sustained by the Dharma— these are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide therein, they will obtain the support of the supreme Dharma of all buddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven, there are ten kinds of activities they perform."
What are these ten? They are as follows:
for the sake of the devaputras of the desire realm, he teaches the Dharma of wearying detachment, saying:
"All sovereign powers are impermanent; all pleasures shall eventually fade away.
Thus he exhorted those devas to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
This was the first deed performed.

For the gods of the form realm, he teaches the entry into and emergence from the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis. If they develop attachment therein, and because of that attachment give rise to the view of a self-body, false views, ignorance, and so forth, he then teaches them the wisdom of reality as it is.

If they give rise to inverted perceptions regarding all material and immaterial phenomena, regarding them as pure, he teaches them that all things are impure and impermanent, exhorting them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
This is the second task to be performed.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, he enters a samādhi called "Adornment of Radiance.
His body emits light that shines throughout the trichiliocosm, and according to the minds of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for them using various voices.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings develop pure faith; at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he exhorts them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
This is the third deed performed.

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven, with their unobstructed eyes they universally behold all the bodhisattvas within the Tuṣita Heavens of the ten directions, and those bodhisattvas likewise see them.
Having seen one another, they discuss the sublime Dharma, namely:
the descent into the mother’s womb, the initial birth, the renunciation of home, the journey to the site of enlightenment, and the perfection of great adornments.
Furthermore, he manifests the practices performed since the distant past; by means of those practices, he has accomplished this great wisdom.
While all his meritorious qualities do not depart from their original place, he is nevertheless able to manifest such events as these.
This is the fourth task to be performed.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, all the assemblies of Bodhisattvas from the Tuṣita palaces throughout the ten directions gather together, surrounding him with reverence.

At that time, desiring to cause those Bodhisattvas to fulfill their aspirations and give rise to joy, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva expounds Dharma-gates according to the stages in which those Bodhisattvas should dwell, their practices, their abandonments, their cultivations, and their realizations.

Having heard this teaching of the Dharma, those bodhisattvas were all greatly delighted and attained what they had never experienced before; each returned to their own native land and their respective palaces.
This is the fifth deed performed.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelt in the Tuṣita Heaven, Māra Pāpīyān, the lord of the desire realm, surrounded by his retinue, approached the Bodhisattva’s abode with the intent to disrupt and confound his bodhisattva activities.

At that time, in order to subdue the demonic host, the Bodhisattva dwelt in the gateway of wisdom consisting of skillful means and the *prajñāpāramitā* encompassed by the adamantine path; he preached the Dharma using both gentle and harsh speech, ensuring that Māra Pāpīyān could find no opportunity.
When Māra beheld the sovereign power of the Bodhisattva, all of them resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the sixth task to be performed.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven and perceives that the devaputras of the desire realm do not delight in hearing the Dharma,
he then emits a great sound and proclaims to them everywhere:
"Today the Bodhisattva shall manifest rare and wondrous events within the palace; those who wish to see them should go there quickly.
When the sons of the gods heard these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of them all gathered together.
At that time, seeing that the hosts of devas had assembled, the Bodhisattva manifested various rare and wondrous events within the palace for them.
Those devaputras had never before seen or heard such things; having now beheld them, they were all filled with great joy, their hearts becoming intoxicated and overwhelmed.
Furthermore, amidst their pleasure, they raised their voices and declared: "O worthy ones!..."
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all dharmas are without self; nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction.
He further addressed them, saying:
"You all should cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and you shall all bring to perfection the knowledge of all modes of knowledge.
When those sons of the gods heard this Dharma-sound, they sighed with sorrow and lamentation, giving rise to weary detachment; there was not one among them who did not resolve to attain bodhicitta.
This is the seventh task to be performed.

While dwelling in the Tuṣita palace, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not leave his original place, yet is able to travel to the presence of all the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, where he beholds the Tathāgatas, approaches them, pays homage, and reverently listens to the Dharma.
At that time, because those Buddhas wish to cause the Bodhisattva to obtain the supreme dharma of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), they preach for him the Bodhisattva stage named:
Through all supernormal powers, by means of wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, one becomes fully endowed with all supreme merits and enters the stage of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
This is the eighth task to be accomplished.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the Tuṣita Palace, desiring to make offerings to all Tathāgatas, they employ great supernormal powers to manifest various kinds of offering articles called "Excellently Delightful.
These offerings pervade the Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and all worlds as they make offerings to all Buddhas.
When the immeasurable sentient beings within those worlds behold these offerings, they all resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the ninth task performed:

when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven, they bring forth immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates that are like illusions and like shadows, pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions. They manifest various colors, various marks, various forms, various modes of conduct, various activities, various skillful means, various parables, and various discourses, causing all sentient beings to rejoice according to their respective minds.
This is the tenth activity performed.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of activities performed by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven.
If Bodhisattvas accomplish these dharmas, they will be able to descend to be born among humans hereafter.
"Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, they manifest ten things."
What are these ten?
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven to take birth, he emits a great light from the soles of his feet, named:
Adorned with peace and bliss, it universally illumines all sentient beings in the evil realms and states of hardship throughout the trichiliocosm;
those who come into contact with this light all attain liberation from suffering and find peace and happiness.
Having attained peace and happiness, they all know that a wondrous Great Being is about to appear in the world.
This is the first matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great radiance from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, named:
Upon awakening, he universally illumined the trichiliocosm, shining upon the bodies of all those bodhisattvas who had practiced together with him in past lives.

Once those bodhisattvas were bathed in this light, they all knew that the Bodhisattva was about to descend to be born; each of them prepared immeasurable offerings and went to where the Bodhisattva was to present their worship.
This is the second matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great radiance from his right palm, named:

This pure realm is fully capable of adorning and purifying all trichiliocosms. Within them, if there are pratyekabuddhas who have attained the outflow-free state and perceive this light, they immediately relinquish their life-span;
if they do not perceive it, by the power of the radiance, they are transported to other worlds in other directions.

All māras, non-Buddhists, and sentient beings with views are likewise transported to other worlds, with the sole exception of those sentient beings sustained by the spiritual power of the Buddhas who are to be transformed through emanation.
This is the third matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great light from his two knees, named:
Pure and magnificently adorned, it universally illuminated all the celestial palaces, pervading everywhere from the World-Protectors below up to the Pure Abodes above;

all those devas, knowing that the Bodhisattva was about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, were filled with longing and affection, and lamented with grief and distress. Each holding various kinds of flower garlands, robes, ointments, powdered incense, banners, canopies, and musical instruments, they went to the Bodhisattva’s abode to pay respectful homage and offerings, following him down to his birth and even unto his parinirvāṇa.
This is the fourth matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great radiance from within the heart-treasury adorned with the *svastika* vajra; its name is:
The Invincible Banner, who universally illumines all worlds in the ten directions as a Vajrapāṇi;
at that time, ten billion Vajrapāṇis all assembled and followed him in attendance and protection, from his initial descent into birth until his entry into nirvana.
This is the fifth matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits great light from every single pore of his body, named:
Distinguishing sentient beings, it universally illumines all the great trichiliocosms, pervasively touches the bodies of all bodhisattvas, and further touches all devas and worldlings;
all these bodhisattvas then think: "I should abide here to make offerings to the Tathāgata and to transform sentient beings."
This is the sixth matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great radiance from within the Great Maṇi Jewel Treasury Palace; its name is:
Observing with skillful stability, he illuminates the royal palace where this bodhisattva is to be born;

once the light has shone, all the other bodhisattvas follow him down to Jambudvīpa, manifesting birth in his home, his village, or his city, for the purpose of teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
This is the seventh matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, they emit a great radiance from the celestial palaces, the great towers, and all the various adornments, named:
All the palaces were pure and magnificently adorned, illuminating the womb of the Bodhisattva’s mother;

having been thus illuminated by the light, they caused the Bodhisattva’s mother to be peaceful, secure, and joyful, fully accomplishing all merits. Within her womb, there spontaneously appeared a vast and lofty pavilion, adorned with great maṇi jewels, intended as a dwelling place for the Bodhisattva’s body.
This is the eighth matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great light from beneath his two feet, which is named:
It is well-established;

if any sons of the gods or Brahmās are nearing the end of their lives, they shall all obtain longevity through the touch of this light’s radiance, and they shall make offerings to the Bodhisattva from his initial descent until his parinirvāṇa.
This is the ninth matter manifested.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born, he emits a great light from his secondary marks (anuvyañjana), which is named:
The Adornment of the Eye manifests the various karmas of Bodhisattvas:

at times, humans and devas may see the Bodhisattva dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven; or see him enter the womb; or see his birth; or see him leave home; or see him attain enlightenment; or see him subdue Māra; or see him turn the wheel of Dharma; or see him enter parinirvāṇa.
This is the tenth matter of manifestation.
O Son of the Buddha!
Within their bodies, seats, palaces, and towers, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emit millions of asaṃkhyeya rays of light, all of which manifest the various deeds of bodhisattvas.
Having manifested these deeds and being fully endowed with all dharmas of merit, he descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born among humans.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fifty-eight;
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Fifty-nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree, Part Seven of Chapter Thirty-Eight: "Transcending the World.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest dwelling in the womb for ten reasons.
What are these ten?
O Son of the Buddha!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, desiring to bring to fulfillment those sentient beings of small minds and inferior understanding, does not wish for them to conceive such a thought as:
"This present bodhisattva has arisen through spontaneous transformation; his wisdom and roots of goodness were not obtained through cultivation."
For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests dwelling in the womb;
this is the first matter.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests dwelling in the womb in order to bring to maturity the roots of goodness of his parents, his kinsmen, and those sentient beings who were his companions in past lives.
Why is this? Because they must all see the maturation of all their roots of goodness while dwelling in the womb.
This is the second matter.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters his mother’s womb, he does so with right mindfulness and right awareness, free from confusion;
having entered the womb, his mind remains constantly in right mindfulness, without any derangement.
This is the third matter.

While the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva remains in the mother’s womb, he constantly expounds the Dharma; the great Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, all assemble there, causing them all to obtain immeasurable spiritual powers and boundless wisdom. Thus, while dwelling in the womb, the Bodhisattva achieves such eloquence and superior efficacy.
This is the fourth matter:
while the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is in his mother’s womb, he assembles a great congregation and, by the power of his original vows, teaches and transforms all the hosts of bodhisattvas.
This is the fifth matter:
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Buddhahood among humans, he should be endowed with the most excellent human birth; it is for this reason that he manifests dwelling within a mother’s womb.
This is the sixth matter.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is within his mother’s womb, the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm all see the Bodhisattva, as one sees the reflection of one’s own face in a clear mirror.

At that time, the great-minded devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all approach the Bodhisattva to pay homage and make offerings with reverence.
This is the seventh matter.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is in his mother’s womb, all the Bodhisattvas in other worlds who are in their final birth and are likewise in their mothers’ wombs come together to assemble, and they expound the Dharma-gate of the Great Assembly called the "Treasury of Vast Wisdom."
This is the eighth matter.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is in his mother’s womb, he enters the Samādhi of the Stainless Treasury (*vimalagarbha-samādhi*). By the power of this samādhi, he manifests within the mother’s womb a great palace, adorned with all manner of exquisite and wonderful ornaments, such that even the Tuṣita Heaven palace cannot compare to it, while ensuring the mother’s body remains peaceful, secure, and free from ailment.
This is the ninth matter.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the mother’s womb, by means of great majestic power, they manifest offering implements called "The Opening of the Great Merit and Stainless Treasury," which pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions and make offerings to all Tathāgatas. Those Tathāgatas all expound for them the Dharma-treasury of the boundless dwelling places of Bodhisattvas.
This is the tenth matter.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten matters concerning the manifestation of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dwelling in the womb.
If bodhisattvas thoroughly comprehend this Dharma, they are able to manifest extremely subtle modes of conduct.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of extremely subtle modes of conduct."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, up to and including the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka-bhūmi).
While in the mother’s womb, he manifests dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests his initial birth;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests the stage of childhood.
While in the mother’s womb, he manifests dwelling in the royal palace;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests renouncing the world;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests practicing austerities, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, and attaining perfect awakening.
While in the mother’s womb, he manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests parinirvāṇa;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifests the great subtlety, namely:
The infinite gateways of the various distinctions of the sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas and all bodhisattva practices.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten subtle modes of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva while dwelling in the mother’s womb.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the subtle course of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of births for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
What are the ten? They are:
being born with right mindfulness and right awareness, far removed from delusion;
The birth that arises from emitting a great net of light that universally illumines the trichiliocosm;
the birth that dwells in the final existence and no longer receives a subsequent body;
and the birth that is neither produced nor arisen.
The birth through knowing that the three realms arise like illusions;
the birth through manifesting bodies everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
and the birth through realizing the body of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Born from the universal awakening of all sentient beings through the radiance of all Buddhas;
born from the body of the samādhi of entering the observation of great wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!

When the Bodhisattva was born, all Buddha-fields trembled, all sentient beings were liberated, all evil realms were extinguished, and all Māras were eclipsed; immeasurable Bodhisattvas all came to assemble.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of births of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which they manifest in this way for the sake of taming sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha!"
For ten reasons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests a smile and makes a vow within his own mind.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reflects, saying:
"All the world is submerged in the mire of desire; except for me alone, there is no one capable of delivering them.
Having known this, he smiles joyfully and makes a vow within his own mind.
He further thought to himself:
"All the world is blinded by afflictions; I alone now possess perfect wisdom.
Having realized this, he smiled with joy and made a vow within his own mind.
Again, he thought:
"By means of this provisional name-body, I shall now attain the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Dharma-body that pervades the three periods of time.
Having understood this, he smiled with joy and made a vow within his own mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with his unobstructed eye, surveyed all the Brahmā heavens and even all the Maheśvara heavens throughout the ten directions, and thought to himself:
"All these sentient beings each claim for themselves to possess great power of wisdom."
Having known this, he smiled with joy and made a vow within his own mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva observed all sentient beings who, having long planted roots of goodness, were now all falling away;
having known this, he smiled with joy and made a vow within his own mind.
The Bodhisattva observes that the seeds of the world, though few when sown, yield exceedingly abundant fruit;
having understood this, he smiles with joy and makes a vow within his own mind.
The Bodhisattva observes all sentient beings and sees that, having received the Buddha's instruction, they will certainly obtain benefit;
having known this, he smiles with joy and makes a vow within his own mind.
The Bodhisattva observes that in past ages, fellow-practicing bodhisattvas became attached to other matters and failed to attain the vast merit of the Buddha-dharma;
having understood this, he smiles with joy and makes a vow within his own mind.

The Bodhisattva contemplates how the various devas and humans who gathered together in past ages have remained even until now on the level of ordinary beings, unable to abandon it and never weary of it;
having known this, he smiles with joy and makes a vow within his own mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, touched by the light of all Tathāgatas, felt redoubled joy and consolation; with a serene smile, he made a vow within his own mind.
This is the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is for the sake of taming sentient beings that the Bodhisattva manifests in such a way.
O Son of the Buddha!
For ten reasons, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests the act of walking seven steps.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
He manifested the walking of seven steps to manifest the power of a bodhisattva;
he manifested the walking of seven steps to manifest the bestowing of the seven riches;
he manifested the walking of seven steps to fulfill the vows of the earth deities.
He displays the walking of seven steps because he manifests the appearance of transcending the three realms;
he displays the walking of seven steps because he manifests the most supreme conduct of a bodhisattva, which surpasses the conduct of the elephant king, the bull king, and the lion king;
he displays the walking of seven steps because he manifests the appearance of the vajra-ground.
To manifest the power of valor for all sentient beings, he demonstrated walking seven steps;
to manifest the cultivation of the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment, he demonstrated walking seven steps;
to manifest that the Dharma he had attained was not derived from the instruction of another, he demonstrated walking seven steps.
Because he manifests as the most supreme and peerless one in the world, he demonstrates walking seven steps.
This is the tenth.
O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva manifests in this way for the sake of taming sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
For ten reasons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests as dwelling in the stage of a youth."
What are these ten? They are:
dwelling in the stage of a youth in order to manifest mastery over all worldly scripts, calculations, diagrams, seals, and various crafts;
He dwells in the stage of childhood in order to manifest mastery over all worldly arts, such as elephants, horses, chariots, bows and arrows, swords and halberds;
he dwells in the stage of childhood in order to manifest mastery over all worldly matters, such as calligraphy, rhetoric, board games, and diversions;
and he dwells in the stage of childhood in order to manifest the complete removal of all faults in the actions of body, speech, and mind.
He dwells in the stage of a youth in order to manifest the gate of entering meditative absorption and abiding in nirvāṇa throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions;

he dwells in the stage of a youth in order to manifest a power that surpasses all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, humans, and non-humans;
he dwells in the stage of a youth in order to manifest the physical form and majestic radiance of a bodhisattva that surpasses all Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protectors.
He dwells in the stage of a youth in order to cause sentient beings who are attached to sensual pleasures to rejoice in and delight in the Dharma;
he dwells in the stage of a youth in order to revere the True Dharma and diligently make offerings to the Buddhas throughout all worlds in the ten directions;
and he dwells in the stage of a youth in order to manifestly receive the empowerment of the Buddhas and be illumined by the light of the Dharma.
These are the ten.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Having manifested the stage of a youth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifests residence in a royal palace for ten reasons."
What are these ten? They are:
in order to bring to maturity the roots of goodness of those sentient beings who practiced together with him in previous lives, he manifests dwelling in the royal palace;
He manifests dwelling in the royal palace to demonstrate the power of a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness;
he manifests dwelling in the royal palace to show the great majestic splendor and requisites of pleasure to those humans and devas who are addicted to such things;
and he manifests dwelling in the royal palace to accord with the minds of sentient beings in the world of five turbidities.
He manifests dwelling in the royal palace in order to demonstrate that a Bodhisattva possesses great majestic power capable of entering samādhi within the deep inner chambers;
he manifests dwelling in the royal palace in order to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings who shared the same vows in past lives;
and he manifests dwelling in the royal palace because he wishes to fulfill the wishes of his parents, relatives, and kinsmen.
He manifests his presence in the royal palace because he wishes to provide offerings to all Tathāgatas by producing the sublime sound of the Dharma through music and song;

he manifests his presence in the royal palace because he wishes to dwell within the palace in subtle samādhis, manifesting everything from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until the final nirvāṇa;
and he manifests his presence in the royal palace in order to accord with and protect the teachings of all Buddhas.
These are the ten.
After the Bodhisattva in his final existence has thus manifested dwelling in a royal palace, he subsequently renounces the household life.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest renunciation for ten reasons.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
He manifests renunciation because he wishes to bring about weariness with the household life;
he manifests renunciation so that sentient beings attached to the household may abandon it;
and he manifests renunciation to conform to and inspire faith in the path of the noble ones.
He manifests renunciation in order to proclaim and praise the merit of leaving the household life;
he manifests renunciation in order to demonstrate the eternal departure from the views of the two extremes;
and he manifests renunciation in order to cause sentient beings to abandon the pleasure of desire and the pleasure of self.
He manifests the renunciation of the household life in order to first display the characteristics of the triple world;
he manifests the renunciation of the household life in order to demonstrate mastery that is not dependent on others;
he manifests the renunciation of the household life in order to reveal that he shall attain the ten powers and the qualities of fearlessness of a Tathāgata.
Finally, because it is the natural law for Bodhisattvas, they manifest the act of leaving the household life.
These are the ten [ways].
By means of these, Bodhisattvas discipline sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
For ten reasons, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest the practice of asceticism. What are these ten?
That is to say:
for the sake of bringing to maturity those sentient beings with inferior understanding, he manifests the practice of asceticism;
for the sake of uprooting the wrong views of sentient beings, he manifests the practice of asceticism.
He manifests the practice of asceticism in order to cause sentient beings who do not believe in karmic retribution to see it;
he manifests the practice of asceticism because it is appropriate for him to conform to the ways of a defiled world;
and he manifests the practice of asceticism to demonstrate his ability to endure toil while diligently cultivating the Path.
He manifests the practice of asceticism in order to cause sentient beings to joyfully seek the Dharma;
he manifests the practice of asceticism for the sake of those sentient beings who are attached to sensual pleasures and self-indulgence;
and he manifests the practice of asceticism to demonstrate the excellence of the Bodhisattva’s undertaking of practice, showing that even in his final birth he does not abandon diligent vigor.
He manifests the practice of asceticism in order to cause sentient beings to delight in the dharma of tranquility and to increase their roots of goodness;
he manifests the practice of asceticism because the faculties of gods and worldly people are not yet matured, and he awaits the time for them to reach maturity.
These are the ten.
By means of these skillful methods, the Bodhisattva subdues all sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten matters concerning the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s proceeding to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). What are these ten?
They are as follows:
When approaching the site of enlightenment, they illuminate all worlds;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, they cause all worlds to tremble;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, they manifest their bodies throughout all worlds.
When approaching the site of enlightenment, they awaken all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings who were their companions in past lives;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, they manifest all the adornments of the site of enlightenment;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, they manifest various physical postures according to the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, as well as all the adornments of the Bodhi tree.
When approaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they manifestly behold all Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
when approaching the site of enlightenment, with every lifting and lowering of their feet they constantly enter samādhi, attaining Buddhahood in every thought-moment without interruption;

when approaching the site of enlightenment, all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the world-protecting kings, each unaware of the others, present various kinds of supreme and wondrous offerings.

When approaching the site of enlightenment, one uses unimpeded wisdom to universally observe all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and attain perfect awakening in all worlds.
These are the ten.
By means of these, the Bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten matters concerning a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). What are these ten?
They are as follows:
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, they cause all worlds to tremble in various ways;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, they illuminate all worlds with equanimity;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, they eliminate the sufferings of all evil realms.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, he causes all worlds to be composed of vajra;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, he universally contemplates the lion-thrones of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, his mind is like space, free from all discrimination.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, he manifests physical postures and deportment according to what is appropriate;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, he dwells in accordance with the adamantine samādhi;
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, he receives a pure and wondrous place sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, one’s own power of roots of goodness is able to empower all sentient beings.
This is the tenth.
"O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, there are ten kinds of extraordinary and unprecedented events.
What are these ten?
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, all Tathāgatas of the worlds in the ten directions appear before him, all raising their right hands and praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
"O Unsurpassed Teacher! This is the first unprecedented event.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, all Tathāgatas protect and mindfully remember him, bestowing upon him their majestic power; this is the second unprecedented event.

When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, all the assemblies of Bodhisattvas who were his companions in practice throughout past lives come to surround him, honoring and making offerings with various kinds of ornaments; this is the third unprecedented event.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), all the grasses, trees, forests, and insentient things in every world bend their bodies and lower their shadows, turning toward the site of enlightenment; this is the fourth unprecedented marvel.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they enter a samādhi called "Contemplating the Dharma-realm.
By the power of this samādhi, all the practices of the Bodhisattva are brought to complete fulfillment; this is the fifth unprecedented event.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits upon the site of enlightenment, they attain a dhāraṇī named "The Supreme, Stainless, Wondrous Light Ocean-Treasury," which is able to receive the great cloud-like Dharma rain of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas; this is the sixth unprecedented event.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they employ the power of their majestic virtue to produce supreme and wondrous offerings, making them throughout all worlds as an offering to all Buddhas; this is the seventh unprecedented event.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they abide in supreme wisdom and fully perceive and understand the faculties, intentions, and mental activities of all sentient beings; this is the eighth unprecedented event.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he enters a samādhi called "Excellent Awakening.
By the power of this samādhi, his body fills all worlds throughout the three periods of time and the entirety of the realm of empty space; this is the ninth unprecedented event.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sits upon the site of enlightenment, they attain the great wisdom of stainless radiance and non-obstruction, causing their physical actions to universally enter the three periods of time; this is the tenth unprecedented event.
"O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of extraordinary and unprecedented events that occur when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment.
O Son of the Buddha!"
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he manifests the subduing of Māra for the sake of contemplating ten meanings.
What are these ten? They are as follows:
Because sentient beings in this defiled age delight in strife and combat, he manifests the subduing of Māra in order to reveal the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic virtue;
because there are gods and worldly people who harbor doubts, he manifests the subduing of Māra in order to sever those doubts;
