When I beheld this brahmin, the summit of Mount Sumeru shook in six ways; we were terrified, yet all resolved upon the bodhicitta with firm and unshakable resolve.
Furthermore, there were ten thousand dragon kings,
namely the Dragon King Airāvata, the Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda, and others, who rained down black sandalwood from the midst of the sky.
Immeasurable dragon maidens played celestial music and rained down exquisite celestial flowers and celestial perfumed water as an offering of respect, speaking these words:

“Good son! When this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of those flames universally illuminated all the palaces of the nāgas, causing the nāga hosts to be freed from the fear of hot sand and the fear of the garuḍas. Their anger was extinguished, their bodies attained coolness, and their minds became free from defilement. Hearing the Dharma, they gained faith and understanding; they came to loathe the nāga realm and, with a sincere heart, repented and removed their karmic obstructions, even resolving to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abiding in omniscience.”
Furthermore, ten thousand yakṣa kings, from within the void, venerated this brahmin and Sudhana with various kinds of offerings, speaking these words: "O noble son!

When this brahmin was performing the austerity of scorching his body with five fires, I and my retinue all gave rise to a heart of compassion for sentient beings; even all the rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others likewise conceived a heart of compassion.
Because of this compassionate mind, they came to see me without causing any harm or affliction to sentient beings.
Neither I nor they felt any attachment to our own palaces; we immediately accompanied him and went to that place.

At that time, the brahmin preached the Dharma to us according to our needs, so that all of us attained peace and happiness of body and mind, and further caused immeasurable yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kumbhāṇḍas to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta.
Furthermore, ten thousand gandharva kings, from within the void of space, spoke these words: "O noble son!

When this brahmin performed the austerity of scorching his body with five fires, the radiance of those flames illuminated our palaces, causing us all to experience inconceivable and immeasurable bliss; for this reason, we have come to his presence."
"This brahmin has preached the Dharma for us, enabling us to attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, ten thousand asura kings emerged from the great ocean and stood in the air; kneeling on their right knees and joining their palms in prostration, they spoke these words:
"O noble son!..."

"When this brahmin scorched his body with the five heats, all our asura palaces, the great ocean, and the earth shook; this caused us to abandon our arrogance and negligence, and for this reason we have come to where he is."
"By hearing the Dharma from him, they abandon flattery and deception, abide securely on the ground of patience, remain firm and unshakable, and perfect the ten powers.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand *garuḍa* kings, with the King Valiant Strength (*Vīrabala-dhara*) as their leader; they manifested in the forms of non-Buddhist youths and proclaimed these words in the sky: "O noble sons!
When this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of that fire illuminated our palace; everything shook and we were all struck with terror, which is why we have come to his place.

At that time, the brahmin immediately preached the Dharma to us as was appropriate, causing us to cultivate great loving-kindness and praising great compassion; he spoke of crossing the ocean of birth and death, of rescuing sentient beings from the mire of desire, of extolling the bodhicitta, of giving rise to the wisdom of skillful means, and of taming sentient beings according to what is suitable for them.
Furthermore, ten thousand kinnara kings, from within the void, proclaimed these words: "O noble son!

When this brahmin tormented his body with the five fires, from the many *tāla* trees, jeweled bell-nets, jeweled silk ribbons, musical trees, exquisite jewel-trees, and various musical instruments in the palaces where we dwell, there spontaneously issued forth the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of the assembly of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, and the sound of those aspiring for unexcelled bodhi, saying: "
“In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, there is a certain bodhisattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta;

in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, there is a certain bodhisattva who practices asceticism, being able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish, even unto the purification of all-knowledge conduct;
in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, there is a certain bodhisattva who proceeds to the site of enlightenment.”
"Even as far as a certain direction or a certain country, where a certain Tathāgata has performed the work of a Buddha and entered parinirvāṇa. "Good son!

Suppose there were a person who reduced all the grasses and trees of Jambudvīpa to fine dust; the limit of the number of these particles might be known, but the limits of the names of bodhisattvas, the names of Tathāgatas, the great vows they have made, and the practices they have cultivated—as spoken of by the precious tārā trees and even the musical instruments within my palace—cannot be known by anyone."
“Good son! Because we heard the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, we gave rise to great joy and came to this place.”
At that time, the brahmin immediately preached the Dharma to us as was appropriate, causing me and immeasurable other sentient beings to attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, immeasurable devas of the desire realm, from within the void, made offerings with exquisite ritual implements and paid him respectful homage, proclaiming these words: "O noble son!
When this brahmin scorched his body with the five fires, the radiance of those flames illuminated all the hells, including Avīci, causing all the sufferings endured therein to cease entirely.
Because we beheld this light of the fire, pure faith arose in our hearts;
by virtue of that faith, at the end of our lives there, we were reborn among the devas.
Out of gratitude, we have come to this place to gaze upon him with reverence, never wearying of doing so.
"At that time, the brahmin preached the Dharma for me, causing immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta.

Then, having heard this teaching, the youth Sudhana was filled with great joy; he conceived a heart of true spiritual friendship toward the brahmin, prostrated himself at his feet in reverence, and spoke these words:
"I have given rise to unwholesome thoughts toward you, O Great Sage and Spiritual Friend; I only pray that the Holy One will grant me forgiveness for my transgression!"
Then the brahmin spoke these verses for the sake of Sudhana:
“If there are bodhisattvas who follow the instructions of spiritual friends,
they will have no doubt or fear at all, remaining securely established with an unshakable mind.”
"You should know that such a person as this will surely obtain vast and great benefits;
sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, they shall achieve unsurpassed awakening.
At that time, the youth Sudhana immediately ascended the mountain of blades and threw himself into the mass of fire.
Before he had even reached the middle, he attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Excellent Abiding;
as soon as he touched the flames, he further attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Supernatural Power of Tranquil Bliss.
Sudhana said: "How marvelous!
O Noble One!"
"Thus, when my body touches this mountain of swords and this great mass of fire, it is peaceful and blissful.
Then, the brahmin said to Sudhana:
"O son of good family!
I have attained only this Bodhisattva liberation of the Inexhaustible Wheel.

As for the great flames of merit of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, which can burn away all the delusions of view among sentient beings until nothing remains; as they possess minds that are never regressive, inexhaustible, untiring, and undaunted; as they give rise to a mind like the Vajra-treasury Nārāyaṇa; as they swiftly cultivate all practices with no slackening; and as their vows are like wind-circles that universally sustain all great oaths of diligence without ever turning back—how could I possibly know or speak of their meritorious conduct?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a city named Siṃhavikrīḍita;”
Among them is a maiden named Maitrīcaryā. Go to her and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, Sudhana the youth prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and took his leave to depart.

Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Six: The Dharma Realm of the Six Entrances.

At that time, the youth Sudhana gave rise to a heart of supreme reverence toward his spiritual benefactor and produced a vast, pure understanding. He constantly kept the Mahāyāna in mind, single-mindedly seeking the wisdom of the Buddhas, and vowed to behold all Buddhas. Contemplating the realm of phenomena, the wisdom free from obstruction was ever-present before him. He decisively and fully realized the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena: the limit of eternal abiding, the limit of every moment across all three periods of time, the limit like space, the limit of non-duality, the limit of the non-differentiation of all dharmas, the limit of unobstructed meaning, the limit of the indestructibility of all eons, and the limit of the limitlessness of all Tathāgatas.

Regarding all Buddhas, their minds are free from discrimination; they have shattered the web of manifold conceptions and are detached from all clinging. They do not grasp at the assemblies or the sites of enlightenment of the Buddhas, nor do they grasp at the pure lands of the Buddhas.
They know that all sentient beings are devoid of a self, that all sounds are like echoes, and that all forms are like reflections.
Traveling south by stages, he arrived at the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita and searched everywhere for the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.

He learned that this maiden was the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja, accompanied by five hundred maidens as her attendants; she resided in the Vairocanagarbha Palace, seated upon a throne of Nāgajaya-candana feet, a golden-threaded net, and celestial garments, preaching the sublime Dharma.
Having heard this, Sudhana went to the gate of the royal palace to seek an audience with the maiden.
Seeing an immeasurable multitude entering the palace, Sudhana asked them: "Where are you all going now?"
They all replied to him, saying,
"We wish to go to the maiden Maitrīyaśas to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
Sudhana the youth then thought to himself:
"This palace gate is without obstruction; I too should enter. Once Sudhana had entered, he beheld the Vairocana-garbha Hall:

its floor was made of crystal, its pillars of lapis lazuli, its walls of diamond, and its perimeter of Jāmbūnada gold. It had hundreds of thousands of light-rays for windows and was adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) maṇi-jewels. It was surrounded by treasure-store maṇi-mirrors and decorated with the most supreme maṇi-jewels of the world. Countless jeweled nets covered it from above, and hundreds of thousands of golden bells emitted wondrous sounds. Such were the inconceivable arrays of various jewels that adorned it.
That maiden Maitrāyaṇī had skin the color of gold, eyes of deep purple, and hair of deep blue; she expounded the Dharma with a voice like that of Brahmā.
Having seen him, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood before him with palms joined, saying: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice."
"How does one cultivate the path of a bodhisattva?
I have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will explain this to me! Then, the maiden Maitrāyaṇī said to Sudhana:
“Good son! You should observe the adornments of my palace. Sudhana prostrated himself and surveyed it thoroughly.

Within every wall, every pillar, every mirror, every mark, every form, every mani-jewel, every ornament, every golden bell, every jewel-tree, every precious image, and every precious necklace, he saw all the Tathāgatas of the Dharma-realm—from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, through their cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, the fulfillment of their great vows, the perfection of their merits, their attainment of equal and right enlightenment, their turning of the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and even their manifestation of entry into nirvana.

In this way, there was no such image that did not appear, just as all the various forms of the sun, moon, and stars are universally seen within clear water; all of this was due to the power of the roots of goodness cultivated by the maiden Maitrāyaṇī in her past lives.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, recollecting the marks of all the Buddhas he had seen, joined his palms and gazed up at the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
Then the maiden said to Sudhana: "Noble son!
This is the gate of the Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā; I sought and attained this Dharma from as many Buddhas as there are sands in thirty-six Ganges Rivers.
Those Tathāgatas each, through different approaches, led me to enter this gate of the Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā;
what was expounded by one Buddha was not repeated by the others.
Sudhana said: "Noble One!
What is the scope of this 'Gate of Universal Adornment' of the Perfection of Wisdom?"
The young woman replied, "Noble son!

When I entered this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā, and followed it, inclined toward it, contemplated and observed it, and retained and analyzed it, I attained the Universal Gate Dhāraṇī, and one million asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇī gates all appeared before me."
That is to say: the dhāraṇī door of buddha-fields, the dhāraṇī door of buddhas, the dhāraṇī door of the Dharma,
the dhāraṇī door of sentient beings, the dhāraṇī door of the past, and the dhāraṇī door of the future.
The present dhāraṇī gateway; the dhāraṇī gateway of the eternally abiding limit;
the dhāraṇī gateway of merit; the dhāraṇī gateway of the requisites for merit; the dhāraṇī gateway of wisdom;
the dhāraṇī gateway of the requisites for wisdom; the dhāraṇī gateway of all vows; and the dhāraṇī gateway of the discernment of all vows.
The dharani-door of gathering all practices, the dharani-door of pure practice,
the dharani-door of perfected practice, the dharani-door of karma, the dharani-door of the non-destruction of karma,

The dharani-door of the formation of world-systems, the dharani-door of the destruction of world-systems,

The dharani-door of knowing that which dwells in dependence on conceptualization; the dharani-door of entering the subtle through the coarse;
the dharani-door of entering the coarse through the subtle; the dharani-door of beholding all Buddhas;
the dharani-door of discerning the bodies of the Buddhas; the dharani-door of the Buddha’s net of light-adornments; the Buddha’s perfection...
The dharani-door of the full sound, the dharani-door of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, the dharani-door of accomplishing the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma,
the dharani-door of differentiating the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, the dharani-door of the non-differentiation of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma,
the dharani-door of explaining the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, and the turning of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma.
The dharani-door, the dharani-door capable of performing the buddha-work, the dharani-door for discerning the assemblies of Buddhas,
the dharani-door for entering the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, the dharani-door for universally illuminating the power of the Buddhas,
the dharani-door of the samadhis of all Buddhas, and the dharani-door of the sovereign application of the samadhis of all Buddhas.
The dharanī-gate of the dhāraṇīs, the dharanī-gate in which all Buddhas abide, the dharanī-gate sustained by all Buddhas,
the dharanī-gate of the transformations of all Buddhas, the dharanī-gate through which Buddhas know the mental activities of sentient beings,
the dharanī-gate of the miraculous manifestations of the supernatural powers of all Buddhas, and [the dharanī-gates] from dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven palace...
The dhāraṇī door of manifesting entry into nirvāṇa; the dhāraṇī door of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings;
the dhāraṇī door of entering the profound Dharma; the dhāraṇī door of entering the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
the bodhicitta dhāraṇī door; the dhāraṇī door of generating the bodhicitta; and the dhāraṇī door of assisting bodhi.
The dharani-gate of the mind, the dharani-gate of all vows, the dharani-gate of all practices,
the dharani-gate of supernormal powers, the dharani-gate of renunciation, the dharani-gate of the purity of total retention,
the dharani-gate of the purity of the wheel of wisdom, and the dharani-gate of the purity of wisdom.
...the *bodhi-apramāṇa-dhāraṇī-mukha*, and the *svacitta-viśuddhi-dhāraṇī-mukha*.
"O son of good family!
I know only this *prajñāpāramitā-samantavyūha-mukha*."

Just as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have minds that are vast, equal to the realm of empty space, and enter into the Dharma-realm; their merit is fully perfected, they abide in supramundane dharmas, and they distance themselves from worldly conduct; their eye of wisdom is free from cataracts, and they universally contemplate the Dharma-realm; their heart of wisdom is as vast as empty space, clearly perceiving all spheres of experience; they have attained the ground of non-obstruction and the great treasury of radiant light; they are skillfully able to discern the meaning of all dharmas; they engage in worldly activities yet are unstained by worldly dharmas; they are able to benefit the world and cannot be destroyed by the world; they serve as a universal refuge for all worlds; they universally know the mental activities of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate; and at all times, they always attain mastery.
How then could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a land named Trayanetra;”
There is a bhikṣu there named Sudarśana. Go to him and ask:
“How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and gazing up at him with longing devotion, took his leave and departed.

At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated the profundity of the dwelling places of Bodhisattvas; he contemplated the profundity of the dharmas realized by Bodhisattvas; he contemplated the profundity of the spheres entered by Bodhisattvas; he contemplated the profundity of the subtle wisdom of sentient beings; he contemplated the profundity of the world’s abiding in conceptualization; he contemplated the profundity of the actions performed by sentient beings; he contemplated the profundity of the flow of the minds of sentient beings; he contemplated the profundity of sentient beings being like reflections and light; he contemplated the profundity of the names and titles of sentient beings; he contemplated the profundity of the speech of sentient beings; he contemplated the profundity of the adornment of the Dharma-realm; he contemplated the profundity of planting karmic deeds; and he contemplated the profundity of karma adorning the world.

Traveling by stages, he arrived at the country of Trayanī. In cities, towns, villages, hamlets, marketplaces, riversides, plains, mountains, and valleys—in every location—he searched everywhere for the bhikṣu Sudarśana.
He was seen in the forest, walking back and forth in meditation, in the prime of his youth, handsome and of pleasing appearance.

His hair was deep blue-black, curling to the right without disorder; he possessed a *uṣṇīṣa* on his crown, his skin was golden in color, and his neck bore three lines. His forehead was broad and even, and his eyes were long and wide like blue lotuses. His lips were crimson and pure like the *bimba* fruit; upon his chest was the *svastika* mark, and his seven parts were full and level. His arms were slender and long, his fingers were joined by webbing, and upon the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were *vajra*-wheels.

His body was exquisite like that of a god of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven; from top to bottom it was straight like a nyagrodha tree; all his primary marks and secondary signs were perfectly complete, like the various adornments of the King of Snowy Mountains; his eyes did not blink, and he possessed a halo one fathom in width.

His wisdom is as vast and expansive as the great ocean; amidst all sensory objects, his mind remains unmoved. Whether sinking or rising, whether it be knowledge or non-knowledge, all fluctuations and conceptual proliferations are entirely stilled.
Having attained the state of equality practiced by the Buddhas, he teaches and transforms all sentient beings with great compassion, never abandoning them for even a moment.

Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, desiring to reveal the Dharma-eye of the Tathāgata, and desiring to tread the path traveled by the Tathāgatas, he walks with neither slowness nor haste, but with careful and discerning mindfulness.
Surrounded before and behind by immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, and non-humans,
the presiding deities of the directions turned according to their respective quarters, leading the way before him. His feet...
The deity Moving Amidst All Divinities held precious lotus flowers to support his feet; the deity Boundless Light extended light to shatter the darkness;
the deity Jambū-dhvaja Forest rained down various mixed flowers; the deity Immovable Treasury Earth manifested all manner of treasure troves;
the deity Universal Radiance Space adorned the void; and the deity Ocean of Accomplished Virtues rained down maṇi jewels.
The mountain spirit Vimalagarbha-Sumeru bowed his head in prostration with palms joined;
the wind spirit Anāvaraṇabala rained down exquisite fragrant flowers; the night goddess Vasanta-pradhāna adorned her body and cast herself prostrate upon the ground;
and the day goddess Nitya-bodhana held aloft a mani-banner that universally illumines all directions, standing poised in the sky and radiating light.
Great Radiance.
At that time, the youth Sudhana went to the place of the bhikṣu, prostrated at his feet, bowed with palms joined, and said: "Noble One!
"I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Having heard that the Holy One is well able to reveal the path of all bodhisattvas, I pray that you will explain to me:
how does a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct?"
"How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? Sudarśana replied, "Noble son!
I am young in years, and my ordination is also recent.

In this life of mine, I have purified my conduct of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers. In the presence of some Buddhas, I purified my conduct for one day and one night; in the presence of others, for seven days and seven nights; in the presence of yet others, for half a month, one month, one year, a hundred years, ten thousand years, a hundred million years, a nayuta of years, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of years; or for a small kalpa, or half a great kalpa, or a full great kalpa, or a hundred great kalpas, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of great kalpas. Therein I heard the sublime Dharma, received and practiced its teachings, adorned all my vows, entered the state of realization, purified all practices, and fulfilled the ocean-like sea of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
I also see those Buddhas attaining enlightenment and preaching the Dharma, each distinct and without confusion, as they maintain the bequeathed teachings until their final passing.

I also know the original vows made by those Buddhas: how they adorned and purified all Buddha-lands through the power of samādhi and their vows; how they purified and cultivated all bodhisattva practices through the power of the samādhi that enters into all conduct; and how they purified all the perfections of the Buddhas through the power of renunciation by means of the vehicle of Samantabhadra.
"Furthermore, good son!
When I am walking in meditation, in a single thought-moment, all the ten directions appear before me, because my wisdom is pure;
in a single thought-moment, all worlds appear before me, because I traverse unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds."
In a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields are all purified and adorned, because of the fulfillment of the power of great vows;
in a single thought-moment, the diverse practices of unspeakably unspeakable sentient beings all appear before one, because of the fulfillment of the wisdom of the ten powers;
in a single thought-moment, the pure bodies of unspeakably unspeakable Buddhas all appear before one, because of the fulfillment of the power of Samantabhadra’s conduct and vows.

In a single thought-moment, they reverently make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, by virtue of their vow-power to achieve a supple mind and make offerings to the Tathāgatas;

in a single thought-moment, they receive and comprehend as many teachings of the Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, by virtue of their power of the dhāraṇī that realizes and maintains the wheel of Dharma through incalculable varieties of dharmas;

in a single thought-moment, oceans of practices of as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields all appear before them, by virtue of their vow-power to purify all practices like Indra’s net.

Within a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable oceans of samādhis all manifest before them, by virtue of the power of their vow to enter every door of samādhi through a single door of samādhi and cause them all to be purified;

within a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable oceans of faculties all manifest before them, by virtue of the power of their vow to know the limit of all faculties and perceive all faculties within a single faculty;

within a single thought-moment, moments as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields all manifest before them, by virtue of the power of their vow that the wheel of Dharma turns at all times until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, yet the wheel of Dharma itself is never exhausted.

Within a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable oceans of all three periods of time appear before one, because of having attained the light of wisdom and the power of vows that thoroughly knows all temporal states within all worlds throughout the three periods of time.
“Good son! I only know this Bodhisattva liberation door of the Lamp that Follows Accordance.

As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they are like a vajra-lamp, truly taking birth in the family of the Tathāgatas; they fully accomplish the life-faculty of immortality, constantly kindling the lamp of wisdom without exhaustion or extinction; their bodies are firm and solid, incapable of being destroyed or broken; they manifest bodies of illusory form-appearances, with infinite varieties according to the law of dependent origination, appearing individually to the minds of sentient beings; their physical features and forms are peerless in the world, incapable of being harmed by poison, blades, or fires, and indestructible like a mountain of vajra, subduing all Māras and non-Buddhists.”

His body was exquisitely beautiful like a mountain of pure gold, most preeminent among gods and humans; his fame was so vast that there were none who did not hear or know it. He beheld all worlds as if they were before his very eyes, expounding the profound treasury of Dharma inexhaustibly like the ocean, and emitting great radiance that universally illumined the ten directions.
If there are those who see it, they will surely shatter the great mountain of all obstacles, surely uproot all unwholesome roots, and surely cause vast roots of goodness to be planted.
"Such persons are difficult to encounter and difficult to appear in the world;
how then could I know or describe their meritorious conduct? 'Good son!'"
To the south of here, there is a land named Yaśas;
upon an island in a river, there is a youth named:
"Lord of Mastery, go to him and ask:
How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"

At that time, the youth Sudhana, desiring to bring to ultimate completion the courageous and pure conduct of a bodhisattva; desiring to obtain the great power and radiance of a bodhisattva; desiring to cultivate the unsurpassed and inexhaustible meritorious practices of a bodhisattva; desiring to fulfill the firm great vows of a bodhisattva; desiring to perfect the vast and profound mind of a bodhisattva; desiring to uphold the immeasurable and supreme practices of a bodhisattva; with a heart never weary of the Dharma of a bodhisattva; wishing to enter into all the virtues of a bodhisattva; wishing to constantly guide and govern all sentient beings; wishing to transcend the dense forest and wilderness of birth and death;

and always delighting in seeing, hearing, serving, and making offerings to spiritual friends without ever feeling weariness—he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, having received the instructions of the bhikṣu Sudarśana, the youth Sudhana memorized them, contemplated and practiced them, and through clear and certain understanding, attained entry into that Dharma-gate.
Surrounded before and behind by hosts of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, they headed toward the country of Yaśovatī, searching everywhere for the youth Īśvaradatta.
At that time, devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others, from the midst of the sky, addressed Sudhana, saying:
"O son of good family!
This boy is now upon an island in the river."
At that time, Sudhana went to where he was, and saw this boy surrounded by ten thousand other boys, playing at building castles out of sand.
Having seen him, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and with palms joined in reverence, stood to one side and said: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice,
nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I pray that you will explain this for me!
The Lord of Sovereignty said,
"O son of good family!

In the past, I studied the arts of writing, calculation, arithmetic, and sealing under the youth Mañjuśrī, whereby I immediately attained entry into the Dharma-gate of the wisdom of all crafts and supernormal powers.

"Good son! Because of this Dharma-gate, I have come to know the worldly arts of writing, calculation, arithmetic, seals, and the divisions of the world; I am also able to treat illnesses such as wind-disorders, epilepsy, emaciation, and possession by malevolent spirits—indeed, all such ailments. Furthermore, I can establish cities, villages, parks, terraces, towers, palaces, and various dwellings; I am skilled at refining various elixirs of the immortals; I am adept at managing all occupations such as agriculture, sericulture, and commerce, ensuring that every action of taking or rejecting, advancing or retreating, is performed with perfect propriety."

Furthermore, he skillfully discerns the physical characteristics of sentient beings—whether they perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds, whether they are destined for rebirth in a happy realm or a miserable realm—and he fully knows such matters as: "This person should attain the path of the Śrāvaka vehicle; this person should attain the path of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and this person should enter the stage of omniscience. Thus, he is able to know all such things.
I also cause sentient beings to study this Dharma, so that they may increase their certainty and attain ultimate purity.
"Good son! I am also able to know the calculations of the bodhisattvas."

That is to say: one hundred lakṣas make one koṭi; one koṭi times one koṭi makes one ayuta; one ayuta times one ayuta makes one nayuta; one nayuta times one nayuta makes one bimbara; one bimbara times one bimbara makes one kankaṇa; and so on in detail until:
one utpala times one utpala makes one padma. Padma... [and so forth].
One *paduma* constitutes one *kalpa*; one *kalpa* times one *kalpa* constitutes one *gati*; one *gati* times one *gati* constitutes one *nayuta*;
one *nayuta* times one *nayuta* constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya*; one *asaṃkhyeya* times one *asaṃkhyeya* constitutes one *asaṃkhyeyaparivarta*;
one *asaṃkhyeyaparivarta* times one *asaṃkhyeyaparivarta* constitutes one *aprameya*; and one *aprameya* times one *aprameya* constitutes one *aprameyaparivarta*.
An immeasurable transformation of immeasurable transformations constitutes one boundless; a boundless of boundless constitutes one boundless transformation;
a boundless transformation of boundless transformations constitutes one incomparable; an incomparable of incomparable constitutes one incomparable transformation;
an incomparable transformation of incomparable transformations constitutes one incalculable; an incalculable of incalculable...
One *asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* (incalculable revolution) is equal to one *asaṃkhyeya-asaṃkhyeya*;
one *asaṃkhyeya-asaṃkhyeya* is equal to one *anabhilāpya* (inexpressible); one *anabhilāpya-anabhilāpya* is equal to one *anabhilāpya-parivarta*;
one *anabhilāpya-parivarta-anabhilāpya-parivarta* is equal to one *acintya* (inconceivable); and one *acintya-acintya* is equal to one *acintya-parivarta*.
One *acintya-parivarta* (inconceivable revolution) makes one *aprameya* (immeasurable);
one *aprameya-aprameya* makes one *aprameya-parivarta*; one *aprameya-parivarta-aprameya-parivarta* makes one *anabhilāpya* (ineffable);
one *anabhilāpya-anabhilāpya* makes one *anabhilāpya-parivarta*; [one *anabhilāpya-parivarta*... does not...
It can be said that one unspeakable-unspeakable becomes an unspeakable-unspeakable; furthermore, this unspeakable-unspeakable becomes one unspeakable-unspeakable through transformation.
“Good son! By means of this bodhisattva method of calculation, I can calculate a vast heap of sand extending for immeasurable yojanas and know exactly how many grains are within it;

I am likewise able to calculate and know all the various distinctions and sequential arrangements of all worlds in the eastern direction, and so too in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.”

They are also able to calculate and know the breadth, narrowness, magnitude, and names of all worlds throughout the ten directions; they fully comprehend all the names of kalpas therein, as well as the names of all Buddhas, all dharmas, all sentient beings, all karmas, all bodhisattvas, and all truths.
“Good son! I only know this Dharma-gate of the Light of Wisdom of Great Supernatural Power in All Crafts.

As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they are able to know the number of all sentient beings; they are able to know the number of categories of all dharmas; they are able to know the number of distinctions among all dharmas; they are able to know the number of all three periods of time; they are able to know the number of names of all sentient beings; they are able to know the number of names of all dharmas; they are able to know the number of all Tathāgatas; they are able to know the number of names of all Buddhas; they are able to know the number of all Bodhisattvas; and they are able to know the number of names of all Bodhisattvas.”

How could I possibly describe their merits, demonstrate their conduct, reveal their spheres of activity, praise their supreme powers, discern their aspirations, proclaim their aids to the Path, manifest their great vows, extol their wondrous practices, expound their various perfections, elaborate upon their purity, or bring forth the light of their extraordinary wisdom?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a great city named Sāgarāvasthita;”
There is an upāsikā named Paripūrṇā; go to her and ask:
“How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?

When the youth Sudhana heard these words, the hairs on his body stood on end; he leaped for joy and attained a rare jewel-like mind of faith and delight. He accomplished a vast mind intent on benefiting sentient beings, clearly beheld the successive appearances of all Buddhas, and thoroughly penetrated the profound wisdom of the pure wheel of Dharma. He manifested his body in accordance with all realms of existence, understood the equal nature of the three periods of time, gave rise to an inexhaustible ocean of merit, emitted the great light of sovereign wisdom, and opened the locks of all cities within the three realms of existence.
He prostrated at [Mañjuśrī’s] feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave.

At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated and reflected upon the instructions of the spiritual friends; like the vast ocean that never tires of receiving the great rains from the clouds, he thought to himself:
"The instructions of the spiritual friends are like the spring sun, causing all the roots and sprouts of wholesome dharmas to grow;
the instructions of the spiritual friends are like the full moon, such that wherever they shine, everything becomes cool and refreshing."
The instruction of a spiritual friend is like the snowy mountains in summer, able to remove the heat and thirst of all wild beasts;
the instruction of a spiritual friend is like the sun over a fragrant pond, able to open the lotus flowers of all virtuous minds;
the instruction of a spiritual friend is like a great jewel island, with various jewels of the Dharma filling one’s mind.
The teaching of the spiritual friend is like the Jambu tree, which accumulates all the flowers and fruits of merit and wisdom;
the teaching of the spiritual friend is like the great dragon king, who sports with sovereign ease within the void of space;
the teaching of the spiritual friend is like Mount Sumeru, where the thirty-three gods dwell amidst immeasurable wholesome dharmas.
The instruction of a virtuous friend is like Śakra, surrounded by a vast assembly that none can eclipse; it is able to subdue the heterodox paths and the hosts of asuras.
Reflecting thus, he traveled by stages until he reached the city of Samudraprastha, searching everywhere for this upāsikā.
At that time, all the people there said to him:
“Good son! This upāsikā resides within her home in this city.
Having heard this, Sudhana went immediately to her gate and stood there with palms joined in reverence.

Her residence was vast and expansive, adorned in various ways, with walls made of many jewels encircling it on all sides; each of its four sides had a gate adorned with jewels. After Sudhana entered, he saw the upāsikā seated upon a jeweled throne;

she was in the prime of her youth and possessed a beautiful complexion, upright and lovely to behold. She wore plain white garments with her hair hanging loose, and her body was without necklaces or ornaments. Yet the color of her form, her majestic virtue, and her radiant light were such that none could equal them, save for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Within that residence, ten billion seats were arranged, surpassing all that exists among humans and devas; these were all accomplished through the karmic power of the Bodhisattva.
Inside the house, there were no garments, food, drink, or any other articles of daily life, except for a single small vessel placed before them.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand young maidens surrounding him; their deportment and physical appearance were like those of celestial nymphs. Their bodies were adorned with exquisite jewel ornaments, and their voices were so melodious that all who heard them were filled with joy. They remained constantly at his side, attending to him with reverence and gazing upon him; they contemplated and observed his every move, bowing with heads bowed low, awaiting and obeying his instructions.
From the bodies of those maidens issued a wondrous fragrance that universally perfumed all;

any sentient beings who encountered this fragrance were all rendered non-retrogressive, free from thoughts of anger or harm, free from thoughts of resentment or enmity, free from thoughts of stinginess or jealousy, free from thoughts of flattery or deception, free from thoughts of crookedness or guile, free from thoughts of hatred or attachment, free from thoughts of malice, free from thoughts of inferiority, and free from thoughts of arrogance. They gave rise to a mind of equanimity, initiated a mind of great compassion, developed a mind intent on benefiting others, dwelt in a mind of restraint, and became free from a mind of greedy seeking.
Those who hear her voice rejoice and leap for joy;
those who behold her body are entirely freed from the defilement of greed.
At that time, having seen the laywoman Guṇavatī, Sudhana prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her with reverence, and stood with palms joined, saying:
“Noble One! I have already set my mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva practice.”
"How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path?
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction;
I pray that you will explain it to me! He then replied:

“Good son! I have attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit. Within this single small vessel, I can produce all kinds of delicious food and drink according to the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings, filling them all completely.”

Suppose there were a hundred beings, a thousand beings, a hundred thousand beings, ten billion beings, a hundred billion beings, a trillion beings, a hundred thousand *nayuta* of beings, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of beings;

suppose there were beings as numerous as the atoms in Jambudvīpa, beings as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world system, in a small thousand-world system, a medium thousand-world system, or a great trichiliocosm, even up to beings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;

and suppose there were all the sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions—were one to cause them all to be fully satisfied according to their desires and inclinations, yet the food and drink would never be exhausted nor diminished.

Such food and drink, such various superior flavors, various seats, various garments, various bedding, various vehicles, various flowers, various garlands, various perfumes, various unguents, various incenses, various powdered incenses, various precious jewels, various necklaces, various banners, various pennants, various parasols, and various excellent articles of daily life—all these were made fully available according to their wishes and inclinations.
"Furthermore, noble son!

Suppose that in a single world-system in the eastern direction, all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having eaten my food, were to realize the fruits of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and abide in their final bodies; [if they were all to do so...]"

Just as it is in one world, so it is in a hundred worlds, a thousand worlds, a hundred-thousand worlds, a billion worlds, ten billion worlds, a hundred billion worlds, a trillion worlds, a hundred-trillion nayuta worlds, worlds as numerous as the dust motes of Jambudvīpa, worlds as numerous as the dust motes of a single four-continent system, worlds as numerous as the dust motes of a small chiliocosm, worlds as numerous as the dust motes of a medium chiliocosm, and worlds as numerous as the dust motes of a great trichiliocosm, even up to worlds as numerous as the dust motes of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—may all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas therein, having eaten my food, realize the fruits of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and abide in their final bodies.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Furthermore, noble son!

In one world in the eastern direction, and even throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, all those bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth who have eaten my food sit beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, subdue the armies of Māra, and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
“Good son! Do you see these ten thousand maidens who are my retinue? He replied:
“I have seen it,” the upāsikā said.
“Noble son! she continued.
With these ten thousand maidens as their leaders, there were thus a million *asaṃkhyeya* followers;
they all shared the same practice, the same vow, the same roots of goodness, the same path of renunciation,
the same pure resolve, the same pure mindfulness, the same pure destination, and the same immeasurable awakening.
They have attained the same faculties, the same vast mind, the same sphere of activity, the same principle, the same meaning,
the same clarity of dharma, the same pure physical form, the same immeasurable power, the same supreme diligence,
the same sound of the true dharma, the same sounds according to the species [of beings], the same supremely pure sound, and the same praise of the unconditioned.
They share the same purity of merit; they share the same purity of karma; they share the same purity of retribution;
they share the same great loving-kindness that universally protects and delivers all; they share the same great compassion that universally brings sentient beings to maturity;

they share the same purity of physical action that arises in accordance with conditions to bring joy to those who see them; and they share the same purity of verbal action that accords with worldly speech.
They proclaim the transformation of the Dharma; they go together to the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas;
they go together to all Buddha-fields to make offerings to all Buddhas; they are able together to manifest and behold all Dharma-gates;
and they dwell together in the pure stages of Bodhisattva conduct.

“Good son! These ten thousand maidens can take superior food and drink from this vessel and, in a single kṣaṇa, reach everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all bodhisattvas in their final birth, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, even extending to all those in the realm of hungry ghosts, causing them all to be fully satisfied.”
"Good son! These ten thousand women, by means of this vessel of mine, can provide sufficient celestial food among the gods, and even sufficient human food among humans."
"Good son! Wait but a moment, and you shall see for yourself.
As these words were spoken, Sudhana saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates; they had all been invited there by the original vows of the laywoman.
Once they had assembled, he prepared seats for them to sit upon, provided them with food and drink according to their needs, and ensured that everyone was fully satisfied.
He then addressed Sudhana, saying:
"O son of good family!
I know only this liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.

As for the merits of all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, they are as profoundly deep and inexhaustible as the great ocean; as vast and boundless as space; like wish-fulfilling jewels that fulfill the vows of sentient beings; like great villages where everything sought is obtained; like Mount Sumeru where all treasures are gathered; like a profound storehouse constantly holding the wealth of the Dharma; like a bright lamp that destroys all darkness; and like a lofty canopy that universally shelters all living beings.
How could I possibly know or speak of their meritorious conduct?
"Good son! To the south there is a city named Mahodaya;
There is a householder there named Mingzhi (Wisdom-Light).
Go to him and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazing up at him without weariness, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, having attained the light of liberation known as the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Adorned Merit," the youth Sudhana contemplated that ocean of merit, observed that space of merit, proceeded toward that mass of merit, ascended that mountain of merit, gathered that treasury of merit, entered that abyss of merit, roamed in that pool of merit, purified that wheel of merit, beheld that storehouse of merit, entered that gate of merit, traversed that path of merit, and cultivated those seeds of merit.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city of Mahāsaṃbhava and searched everywhere for the wise layman (gṛhapati).

He conceived a thirsting longing for the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and his mind was permeated by that spiritual friend. His resolve toward the spiritual friend became firm; through skillful means, his mind never turned back in its desire to meet all spiritual friends, and his aspiration to serve them was free from weariness.
He understood that by relying upon a spiritual friend, one is able to fulfill all virtues.
They know that by relying on spiritual friends, one can generate manifold blessings;
they know that by relying on spiritual friends, one can increase manifold practices;
and they know that by relying on spiritual friends, one is able to serve all virtuous friends spontaneously, without being taught by others.

When contemplating in this way, one’s roots of goodness grow, one’s profound resolve is purified, one’s spiritual faculties are enhanced, the foundation of one’s virtue is augmented, one’s great vows are strengthened, one’s great compassion is expanded, one draws near to all-knowledge, one fulfills the path of Samantabhadra, one illuminates the true Dharma of all Buddhas, and one increases the radiance of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
At that time, Sudhana saw the householder within the city, at the crossroads of the marketplace, upon a terrace of the seven precious gems, seated on a throne adorned with countless jewels.

That seat was exquisite and beautiful, its body fashioned from pure maṇi jewels and its feet from diamond and sapphire; it was interlaced with jeweled cords and adorned with five hundred wonderful gems.
Celestial precious robes were spread upon it, celestial banners and pennants were erected, a great jeweled net was stretched over it, and a great jeweled canopy was provided;
a coverlet of Jāmbūnada gold was made for it, with a staff of vaidūrya, which people held to shade it from above.
The king of geese, with his pure and immaculate plumage, serves as a fan;
he is perfumed with various exquisite incenses, and a rain of celestial flowers falls.

To his left and right, five hundred musical instruments are constantly played, their sounds more exquisite than those of the heavenly musicians, such that no sentient being who hears them fails to be filled with joy.

Surrounded by ten thousand attendants before and behind him—whose physical forms were upright and majestic, pleasing to all who beheld them, and adorned with celestial ornaments—they were preeminent and peerless among gods and humans. Having fully accomplished the aspirations of a bodhisattva and sharing the same roots of goodness from the past as the householder, they stood in attendance, gazing upon him and receiving his instructions.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying:
"Noble One! For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, and to cause all sentient beings to emerge from all sufferings and hardships..."
Therefore, it is for the sake of bringing ultimate peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abide on the island of the Dharma-treasure;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to dry up the river of craving; and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to give rise to great compassion.
Therefore, it is for the sake of causing all sentient beings to abandon desire and attachment;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to thirst for and yearn for the Buddha’s wisdom; for the sake of causing all sentient beings to emerge from the wilderness of birth and death;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to delight in the merits of all Buddhas; and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to transcend the three [realms]...
Because it is the city of the realms, and in order to cause all sentient beings to enter the city of omniscience,
he has resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet he does not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice,
how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path, or how one can act as a place of reliance for all sentient beings.
The householder said:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"You are indeed able to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family!
Such a person who resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is difficult to find."

If one can resolve their mind [toward enlightenment], such a person will be able to seek the bodhisattva practices; they will encounter spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) without ever becoming weary; they will attend upon spiritual friends without ever growing fatigued; they will make offerings to spiritual friends without ever becoming indolent; they will serve spiritual friends without giving rise to sorrow or distress; they will seek out spiritual friends without ever turning back; they will cherish spiritual friends without ever abandoning them; they will attend to spiritual friends without even a moment’s rest; they will gaze up at spiritual friends without ceasing for a single instant; they will carry out the instructions of spiritual friends without ever being negligent; and they will receive the teachings of spiritual friends without any error or omission.
“Good son! Do you see this assembly of mine? Sudhana replied:
"Yes, indeed; I have seen it.
The householder said:

“Good son! I have already caused him to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, to be born into the family of the Tathāgata, to increase the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), to dwell securely in the immeasurable *pāramitās*, to study the ten powers of a Buddha, to leave behind the seeds of the world and abide in the lineage of the Tathāgata, to cast off the wheel of birth and death, to turn the wheel of the true Dharma, to extinguish the three evil destinies, and to abide in the path of the true Dharma—just as all Bodhisattvas are able to rescue and protect all sentient beings.”
“Good son! I have attained the liberation door of the treasury of merit that arises according to one’s wishes; whatever is required, all such vows are fulfilled.
That is to say:”

Clothing, necklaces, elephants, horses, carriages, flowers, incense, banners, parasols, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, houses, dwellings, couches and seats, lamps and torches, male and female slaves, cattle, sheep, and various attendants—all such articles of daily life and whatever else may be required—were provided in full abundance; furthermore, he expounded for them the true and wondrous Dharma.
“Good son! Wait but a moment, and you shall see for yourself.

As these words were spoken, immeasurable sentient beings from various locations, various worlds, various lands, and various cities—each with distinct physical forms and differing desires—gathered together in infinite numbers by the power of the Bodhisattva’s past vows, each making requests according to their own wishes.
At that time, the householder, knowing that the assembly was gathered together, focused his mind for a moment and gazed up into the void;
whatever they required descended from the sky, and the entire assembly was fully satisfied.
Thereafter, he further expounded various teachings for them, namely:

for those who sought to be satisfied with fine food, he taught the practice of accumulating various merits, the practice of leaving poverty behind, the practice of knowing all dharmas, the practice of attaining the food of dharma-joy and the bliss of dhyāna, the practice of cultivating and perfecting the primary and secondary marks, the practice of increasing and accomplishing invincibility, the practice of skillfully understanding the unsurpassed food, and the practice of accomplishing inexhaustible great majestic power to subdue Māra and his enemies.
For those who desire to obtain excellent drink and be fully satisfied, I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to abandon attachment to birth and death and enter the flavor of the Buddha-dharma;
for those who desire to obtain various superior flavors, I preach the Dharma for them, causing them all to attain the marks of the superior flavor of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
for those who desire to obtain vehicles and be fully satisfied, I proclaim various Dharma-gates for them, causing them all to be carried by the Mahāyāna vehicle.

For those who seek to be fully provided with clothing, he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may obtain the garment of pure shame and modesty, up to and including the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous form.
In this way, he provided for everyone without exception, and thereafter preached the Dharma to each according to their needs.
Having heard the Dharma, they returned to their respective places.
At that time, after the householder had manifested for the youth Sudhana the inconceivable realm of the Bodhisattva’s liberation, he said:
“Good son! I know only this liberation door of the treasury of merit that arises according to one’s wishes.

As for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have perfected the jewel-hand, which covers all lands throughout the ten directions, they universally rain down all necessities of life through their power of mastery, namely:”

They rain down various colored jewels, various colored necklaces, various colored crowns, various colored garments, various colored music, various colored flowers, various colored perfumes, various colored powdered incenses, various colored burning incenses, and various colored jeweled parasols and banners, filling all the dwellings of sentient beings as well as the assembly grounds and *bodhimaṇḍas* of all Tathāgatas—some to bring all sentient beings to maturity, and some to make offerings to all Buddhas.
How could I possibly know or describe those meritorious powers of sovereign spiritual mastery?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a great city named Siṃhala (Lion’s Palace);”
There is a householder there named Dharmaratnaśikhin.
You should go and ask him:
"How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana was filled with joy and exultation; with reverence and respect, he paid homage as a disciple would and thought to himself:

"Because this householder has taken me under his care, I have been enabled to see the path of omniscience; my affectionate regard for the spiritual friend is uninterrupted, my heart of reverence for the spiritual friend remains unimpaired, I am always able to follow the instructions of the spiritual friend, I possess resolute and deep faith in the words of the spiritual friend, and I constantly give rise to a profound mind of service toward the spiritual friend."
He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Sixty-Five;
*The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Sixty-Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree, Chapter Thirty-nine, Part Seven: Entering the Dharma Realm.

At that time, having heard this liberation from the householder Sumati, the youth Sudhana wandered through that ocean of merit, cultivated that field of merit, gazed upon that mountain of merit, proceeded toward that ford of merit, opened that treasury of merit, contemplated those dharmas of merit, purified that wheel of merit, tasted that mass of merit, gave birth to that power of merit, and increased that momentum of merit.
Traveling by stages toward the city of Siṃhapura, he searched everywhere for the elder Ratnaśikhin.
Seeing the elder in the marketplace, he immediately approached him, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice,
nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
“Excellent, O Noble One!
I pray that you will explain to me the path of the bodhisattvas, so that by means of this path I may proceed toward omniscience!
At that time, the elder took Sudhana by the hand, led him to his residence, showed him his house, and spoke these words:
“Good son! Observe my home for a moment.

At that time, Sudhana beheld the house, pure and radiant, composed of genuine gold; its walls were of white silver, its halls of crystal, its pavilions of deep-blue lapis lazuli, and its pillars of exquisite *śaṅkha* gems, adorned throughout with hundreds of thousands of kinds of jewels.
A *lohitamukti* mani-jewel served as the lion throne;
a *maṇi* jewel formed a canopy, and a net of pearls completely covered it from above;
agate jewel-pools were filled with fragrant water, and immeasurable jewel-trees stood in rows all around.
That residence was vast and spacious, with ten stories and eight gates.
Once Sudhana had entered, he observed it in successive order.
Upon seeing the lowest story, he saw that various foods and drinks were being distributed there.
Upon seeing the second tier, he bestowed various precious garments.
Upon seeing the third tier, he gave all manner of precious ornaments.
Upon seeing the fourth tier, he bestowed various court ladies as well as all kinds of supreme and exquisite treasures.

He saw the fifth tier, where bodhisattvas from the first through the fifth stages had gathered like clouds, expounding various dharmas to benefit the world, and accomplishing all dharani-gates, the seals of all samādhis, and the light of wisdom of all samādhi-practices.

He saw the sixth tier, where there were bodhisattvas who had all already perfected profound wisdom and clearly understood and penetrated the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). They had accomplished the vast gates of *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* that are free from obstruction; their conduct was unimpeded, and they did not dwell in dualistic dharmas. Gathered together within an ineffable and wondrously adorned site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they analyzed and displayed the gates of the *prajñāpāramitā*, namely:
the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* of the treasury of tranquility; the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* of the wisdom that skillfully distinguishes all sentient beings;
the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* of immovability; and the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* of the light of detachment.
The gate of the perfections; the gate of the Perfection of Wisdom as the treasury that cannot be overcome;
the gate of the Perfection of Wisdom that illuminates the wheel of sentient beings; the gate of the Perfection of Wisdom as the ocean-treasury;
the gate of the Perfection of Wisdom of universal vision’s relinquishment and attainment; and the gate of the Perfection of Wisdom that enters the inexhaustible treasury.
The gate of Prajñāpāramitā of the ocean of all skillful means; the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of entering the ocean of all worlds;
the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of unimpeded eloquence; the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of conforming to sentient beings;
the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of unimpeded radiance; and the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of constant contemplation.
Through the power of past affinities, he spread the cloud of Dharma, [entering] the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*...
and thus spoke of one million *asaṃkhyeya* gates of *prajñāpāramitā*.

Upon seeing the seventh layer, there were bodhisattvas who had attained the patience like an echo; through the wisdom of skillful means, they discerned and observed, thereby achieving liberation, and were all able to hear, retain, and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas.

Upon seeing the eighth layer, he beheld immeasurable bodhisattvas gathered therein, all of whom had attained supernatural powers and were free from regression. They were able to pervade the lands of the ten directions with a single voice, and their bodies appeared universally in all places of enlightenment, reaching everywhere throughout the entire dharma-realm. They entered universally into the realms of the Buddhas, universally beheld the bodies of the Buddhas, and universally served as the leaders within the assemblies of all Buddhas, expounding the Dharma.
In the ninth tier, he saw an assembly of bodhisattvas bound to one more birth gathered therein.

In the tenth tier, he saw all the Tathāgatas filling it, from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, through their cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, their transcendence of birth and death, and their fulfillment of great vows and supernormal powers, as they purified buddha-lands and assemblies at sites of enlightenment, turned the wheel of the true Dharma, and tamed sentient beings.
In this way, he caused all these things to be clearly seen.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Sudhana said:
"Noble One!..."
"By what cause has this pure assembly been brought about?
What roots of goodness were planted to obtain such a reward? The elder replied:
“Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field,
there was a world named Perfect Adornment, and the Buddha’s name was:”

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, King of Universal Adornment of the Boundless Radiance of the Dharmadhātu, whose ten titles were fully perfected—when that Buddha entered the city, I played musical instruments and burned a single pellet of incense as an offering. I dedicated this merit toward three goals:

namely, to forever be free from all poverty and suffering, to always see the Buddhas and spiritual friends, and to constantly hear the True Dharma; it is for these reasons that I have obtained this retribution.
“Good son! I know only this bodhisattva liberation door of the treasury of immeasurable merit and virtue.

As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the inconceivable treasury of jewels of merit, who enter the ocean of the non-conceptual body of the Tathāgata, who receive the non-conceptual, unsurpassed cloud of Dharma, who cultivate the non-conceptual implements of meritorious qualities, who give rise to the non-conceptual net of Samantabhadra’s practices, who enter the non-conceptual realm of samādhi, who equalize the non-conceptual roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas, who dwell where the non-conceptual Tathāgatas dwell, who realize the non-conceptual equality of the three periods of time, who abide in the non-conceptual realm of the Universal Eye, and who dwell through all kalpas without weariness;”
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? "Good son!
To the south of here, there is a land named:
Its roots are wisteria;
in that land there is a city named Samantamukha.
Among them is an elder named Universal Eye.
Go to him and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, having heard this liberation from the elder Ratnacūḍa, the youth Sudhana entered deeply into the infinite knowledge and vision of all Buddhas; he dwelt securely in the infinite supreme practices of Bodhisattvas; he thoroughly understood the infinite skillful means of Bodhisattvas; he sought after the infinite Dharma-gates of Bodhisattvas; he purified the infinite faith and understanding of Bodhisattvas; he made the infinite faculties of Bodhisattvas sharp and keen; he accomplished the infinite aspirations of Bodhisattvas; he mastered the infinite gateways of Bodhisattva conduct; he increased the infinite power of the vows of Bodhisattvas; he established the invincible banner of Bodhisattvas; and he gave rise to Bodhisattva wisdom to illuminate the Bodhisattva Dharma.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Veṇu-mūla and inquired about the location of that city.

Although he encountered many hardships, he did not shrink from toil and suffering; he maintained only right mindfulness of the instructions of the spiritual friend, vowing to always remain close to him, serve and make offerings to him, and constantly exert all his faculties to remain free from negligence.
Thereafter, he beheld the city of Samantamukha, surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of villages; its battlements were lofty and steep, and its streets were broad and level.
Seeing that elder, he went to his location, prostrated before him, stood with palms joined, and said: "Noble One!"
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice,
nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
The elder said: "Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"You have already been able to resolve your mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Son of good family!
I know all the various illnesses of all sentient beings."
Whether it be ailments caused by wind, yellow phlegm, heat, malevolent spirits, or poisonous charms, or even injuries sustained by water or fire—
I can, through every possible skillful means, provide healing for all such diseases that may arise.
“Good son! All sentient beings of the ten directions who are afflicted by illness come to me; I treat them all so that they may be healed.

Furthermore, I bathe their bodies with fragrant water and adorn them with fragrant flowers, necklaces, famous garments, superior robes, and various ornaments. I provide them with food, drink, and wealth and treasures, ensuring they are fully satisfied and lack for nothing.”
Thereafter, he preached the Dharma to each according to their needs:
for those with excessive desire, he taught the contemplation of impurity;
for those with excessive hatred, he taught the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
For those with an abundance of delusion, he teaches them to discern the various characteristics of phenomena;
for those whose [afflictions] are in equal measure, he reveals to them the sublime gateways of the Dharma.
Desiring to cause them to give rise to the bodhicitta, he extols the merits of all Buddhas.
To cause them to give rise to the mind of great compassion, he reveals the immeasurable suffering and affliction of birth and death;
to cause their merits to increase, he praises the cultivation and accumulation of immeasurable merit and wisdom;
and to cause them to make great vows, he extols the subduing of all sentient beings.
In order to cause them to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra, he speaks of how all bodhisattvas dwell in all lands throughout all eons, cultivating the net of all practices;
in order to cause them to be endowed with the marks and signs of a Buddha, he extols and praises the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā);
and in order to cause them to attain the pure body of a Buddha that is able to reach everywhere, he extols and praises the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
In order to cause them to attain the Buddha’s pure and inconceivable body, he extols and praises the perfection of patience;
in order to cause them to obtain the Tathāgata’s invincible body, he extols and praises the perfection of vigor;
in order to cause them to attain a pure and peerless body, he extols and praises the perfection of meditation.
In order to cause the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya*, they extol and praise the *prajñāpāramitā*;
in order to cause the manifestation of the Buddha-Bhagavān’s pure *rūpakāya*, they extol and praise the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*;
and in order to cause him to abide for all *kalpas* for the sake of all sentient beings, they extol and praise the *praṇidhānapāramitā*.
In order to cause them to manifest a pure body that transcends all Buddha-fields, he extols and praises the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*);
in order to cause them to manifest a pure body that brings joy to all sentient beings according to their inclinations, he extols and praises the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*);
and in order to cause them to obtain a body that is ultimately pure and sublime, he extols and praises the eternal departure from all unwholesome dharmas.
Having bestowed these gifts in this manner, he sent them all back.
"Good son! Furthermore, I am well-versed in the essential methods for compounding all types of incense, namely:

He fully knows the methods for preparing and blending such incenses as Anupama-gandha (Incomparable Incense), Siṃhaparākrama-gandha (Lion’s Prowess Incense), Anabhibhūta-gandha (Unconquerable Incense), Vibodhana-gandha (Awakening Incense), Aruṇavati-gandha (Dawn Incense), Kālāguru-candana-gandha (Black Aged Sandalwood Incense), Uragasāra-candana-gandha (Snake-Heart Sandalwood Incense), Agaru-gandha (Aquilaria Incense), and Akṣobhyendriya-gandha (Unshakable Faculties Incense).
"Furthermore, noble son!
I hold this incense as an offering, and thus universally behold all Buddhas, with all my vows fulfilled—namely:
the vow to rescue and protect all sentient beings, the vow to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, and the vow to make offerings to all Tathāgatas."
"Furthermore, good son!

When this incense is burned, from each and every piece of incense emerge immeasurable fragrances that pervade all the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas throughout the entire Dharma-realm of the ten directions. These manifest as incense palaces, incense halls, and likewise as incense railings, incense walls, incense parapets, incense windows, incense multi-storied pavilions, incense crescents, incense canopies, incense banners, incense pennants, incense curtains, incense nets, incense images, incense ornaments, incense radiance, and incense clouds and rains, filling every place as a magnificent adornment."
“Good son! I know only this Dharma-door for causing all sentient beings to universally behold all Buddhas and rejoice.

As for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, who are like great medicinal kings—if one sees them, hears of them, recollects them, dwells with them, follows them on their travels, or calls upon their names—all shall obtain benefit; none shall pass by in vain.”

If there are sentient beings who even briefly encounter [this], they shall certainly cause all afflictions to be extinguished, enter the Buddha-dharma, and depart from the aggregates of suffering; they shall forever stifle all fears of birth and death, reach the state of omniscience that is free from fear, demolish the great mountain of old age and death, and abide securely in the bliss of equanimous nirvana.
How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct? "Good son!
To the south of here, there is a great city named:
Tārādhvaja; within it there was a king named Analaṃkṛta.
"Go to him and ask:
How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Samantanetra, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave.
At that time, the youth Sudhana recollected and reflected upon the instructions of the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), mindful of them thus:
"They are able to sustain me and protect me, causing me not to regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)."

Reflecting in this way, he gave rise to a mind of joy, a mind of pure faith, a vast mind, a serene and pleasant mind, a leaping-forth mind, a mind of celebration, a sublime mind, a tranquil mind, an adorned mind, an unattached mind, an unimpeded mind, an impartial mind, a sovereign mind, a mind abiding in the Dharma, a mind that travels everywhere to Buddha-fields, a mind beholding the adornments of the Buddhas, and a mind that does not forsake the ten powers.
Traveling by stages, he passed through kingdoms, villages, towns, and settlements until he reached the city of Tālaketu. There he inquired as to the whereabouts of King Anala, and the people replied:

"The king is currently in the main hall, seated upon the lion throne, proclaiming the Dharma and transforming sentient beings. He governs those who may be governed and gathers in those who may be gathered; he punishes their evils and adjudicates their disputes; he comforts the orphaned and the weak, causing them all to forever sever killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. He also causes them to prohibit false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter, and further leads them to distance themselves from greed, anger, and wrong views."
Then, following the words of the people, Sudhana immediately went to visit him.
From afar he saw the king seated upon a Nārāyaṇa-vajra throne, whose feet were made of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels and which was adorned with immeasurable jewel-images;

it was covered above by a net of golden cords. He wore a crown of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* gems adorning his head; a crescent of Jāmbūnada gold adorned his forehead; lapis lazuli *maṇi* earrings hung down from his ears; priceless *maṇi* gems formed necklaces adorning his neck; and exquisite celestial *maṇi* gems formed seals and bracelets adorning his arms.

Jambūnada gold formed its canopy; various jewels were interspersed to form the spokes of the wheel; great lapis lazuli gems formed its shaft; and *prabhāsa-rasa* mani-jewels formed its finial. Bells made of diverse gems constantly emitted sublime sounds, and they radiated great light that pervaded the ten directions. Such precious canopies covered him from above.
King Anala possessed great power and majesty, capable of subduing all other hosts and having no one able to oppose him;
