with a stainless silk cloth bound upon his crown, he was surrounded before and behind by ten thousand ministers who together administered the affairs of state.

In front of him were further one hundred thousand fierce soldiers, hideous in appearance and clad in coarse, shabby garments; brandishing their weapons, they bared their arms and glared with fury, such that no sentient being who saw them failed to be struck with terror.

Countless sentient beings violate the king’s commands—whether by stealing the property of others, taking the lives of others, violating the wives of others, giving rise to false views, harboring anger and resentment, or conceiving greed and envy. Having committed such various evil deeds, their bodies are bound with the fivefold fetters and they are led before the king to be punished according to their offenses.

Some have their hands and feet severed; some have their ears and noses cut off; some have their eyes gouged out; some have their heads lopped off; some have their skin flayed; some have their bodies dismembered; some are boiled in boiling water; some are burned with fire; some are driven up high mountains and pushed over to fall; there are such immeasurable tortures as these.
They raise their voices and wail, like those in the Saṃghāta Great Hell.
Having seen this, Sudhana thought to himself:
"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I seek the conduct of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva."

Now, this king destroys all wholesome dharmas and commits great sinful karma; he oppresses and torments sentient beings, even unto taking their lives, without ever regarding or fearing the evil realms of the future.
"How can one seek the Dharma in this regard and give rise to the mind of great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings?
While he was thinking this, a deva in the sky addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!
"You should remember the instructions of the spiritual friend, the Elder Universal Eye.
Sudhana looked up and said to him, "I constantly remember them;
I have not dared to forget from the very beginning."
The deva said: "Good son!
Do not feel weary of or turn away from the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). A spiritual friend is one who can lead you to a place of safety free from all perils."

"Noble son! The Bodhisattva’s wisdom of skillful means is inconceivable; the wisdom that gathers in sentient beings is inconceivable; the wisdom that protects and mindfulness of sentient beings is inconceivable; the wisdom that brings sentient beings to maturity is inconceivable; the wisdom that guards sentient beings is inconceivable; the wisdom that delivers sentient beings is inconceivable; and the wisdom that tames sentient beings is inconceivable."
At that time, having heard these words, the youth Sudhana went to where the king was, prostrated at his feet, and said: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the bodhisattva conduct."
"How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path?
I have heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me!
At that time, King Anala, having finished attending to his royal affairs, took Sudhana by the hand, led him into the palace, invited him to sit together with him, and said:
“Good son! You should observe the palace in which I dwell.

As he was told, Sudhana immediately looked all around and saw that the palace was incomparably vast, composed entirely of exquisite jewels. It was surrounded on all sides by walls made of the seven precious substances, with hundreds of thousands of towers and pavilions fashioned from various gems. All its diverse adornments were exquisitely beautiful, and it was covered above by inconceivable nets of mani-jewels.

He had a billion handmaidens of exquisite beauty and peerless charm; their deportment and every movement were worthy of admiration, and all their actions were skillful and artful. They rose before him and retired after him, serving his every wish with gentle hearts.
At that time, King Anala said to Sudhana:
"Son of good family,
what do you think?"
If I have truly committed such evil karma, how could I obtain such a retribution, such a physical body, such a retinue, such abundant wealth, and such sovereignty?
“Good son! I have attained the bodhisattva liberation of being like an illusion. Good son!”

In this land of mine, the sentient beings therein mostly practice killing, stealing, and even wrong views; I have employed various other skillful means, yet I am unable to cause them to abandon their evil karma.

"Good son! For the sake of subduing those sentient beings, I manifest as an evil person who commits various sinful deeds and undergoes all manner of suffering. When all those sentient beings who have committed evil see this, their hearts are filled with terror, they develop a sense of weary detachment, and they become disheartened; thus they sever all the evil karma they have created and resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Good son! By means of such skillful expedients, I cause all sentient beings to abandon the ten unwholesome actions and abide in the path of the ten wholesome actions, so that they may attain ultimate happiness, ultimate peace, and ultimately dwell upon the ground of omniscience."
"Good son! My body, speech, and mind have never harmed or afflicted even a single sentient being. Good son!"

One whose mind is like mine would rather undergo the suffering of the Avīci Hell in the future than ever give rise to a single thought of causing harm to even a mosquito or an ant, let alone a human being!
Human beings are fields of merit, for they are able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas. "Good son,
I have attained only this liberation that is like an illusion."

As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), who know that all realms of existence are entirely like illusions, that all bodhisattva practices are entirely like transformations, that all worlds are entirely like shadows, and that all phenomena are entirely like dreams; who enter the unimpeded dharma-gate of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); who cultivate all practices of the Indra-net (*indrājāla*); who traverse the spheres of objects with unimpeded wisdom; who universally enter all samādhis of equality;
and who have already attained mastery over dhāraṇīs—how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a city named Wondrous Light;”
The king's name is Mahāprabha. Go to him and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the king's feet, circumambulated him countless times, took his leave, and departed.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, with single-minded and correct mindfulness, contemplated the dharma-gate of illusory wisdom attained by that king; he reflected upon that king’s liberation as being like an illusion, observed that king’s illusory nature of phenomena, made aspirations like an illusion, purified dharmas like an illusion, and universally gave rise to various illusory transformations throughout all three times which are like an illusion—thus he reflected.
Traveling by stages, he may reach human cities, towns, and villages, or pass through wildernesses, rocky valleys, and perilous difficulties, never becoming weary or ever taking rest.
Thereafter, he proceeded until he reached the great city of Prabhāvyūha and asked the people,
"Where is the great city of Prabhāvyūha? and they all replied:
“The City of Wondrous Light is this very city; it is the dwelling place of King Mahāprabha.
At that time, the youth Sudhana leaped for joy and thought to himself:

“My spiritual friend is within this city. I shall now surely behold him in person; I shall hear of the practices performed by the Bodhisattvas, hear of the gateways to liberation of the Bodhisattvas, hear of the dharmas realized by the Bodhisattvas, hear of the inconceivable merits of the Bodhisattvas, hear of the inconceivable sovereignty of the Bodhisattvas, hear of the inconceivable equanimity of the Bodhisattvas, hear of the inconceivable valor of the Bodhisattvas, and hear of the vast, pure, and inconceivable spheres of the Bodhisattvas.”
Having formed this thought, he entered the city of *Prabhāsa*.

He beheld this great city, which was composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate; it was surrounded by sevenfold moats made of these same seven treasures.
These were filled with water possessing the eight virtues, their bottoms strewn with golden sand, and covered everywhere with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses.
The precious *tāla* trees were arranged in seven rows, and seven kinds of diamond walls surrounded them each, namely:

the diamond wall of lion-radiance, the diamond wall of unsurpassable victory, the diamond wall of indestructibility, the diamond wall of unbreakability, the diamond wall of firmness and non-obstruction, the diamond wall of the treasury of exquisite nets, and the diamond wall of dust-free purity. All were adorned with countless exquisite *maṇi* jewels interspersed throughout, and various kinds of treasures formed their battlements.

The city was ten yojanas in length and breadth, with eight sides and eight gates opening on each face; all were extensively adorned with the seven treasures, and its ground was made of lapis lazuli, decorated in various ways so as to be most delightful.
Within that city, there are ten billion thoroughfares; between each and every road, there dwell immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings.
There are countless Jambūnada gold pavilions, covered above by nets of lapis lazuli and maṇi jewels;
and countless silver pavilions, covered above by nets of red pearls and maṇi jewels.
Countless lapis lazuli pavilions were covered by nets of exquisite *maṇi* jewels from the treasury of wonders;
countless crystal pavilions were covered by nets of the stainless-treasury *maṇi* king;
countless *maṇi* jewel pavilions that illuminate the world were covered by nets of the sun-treasury *maṇi* king.
Countless celestial-blue maṇi-jewel pavilions were covered by nets of exquisite light maṇi-kings;
countless ocean-like maṇi-king pavilions of sentient beings were covered by nets of flaming radiance maṇi-kings;
countless diamond-jewel pavilions were covered by nets of invincible banner maṇi-kings.
There were countless pavilions of black sandalwood, their tops covered by nets of celestial *mandārava* flowers;
there were countless pavilions of incomparable king-of-incenses, their tops covered by various kinds of flower-nets.

That city was further covered by countless nets of mani jewels, countless nets of precious bells, countless nets of celestial incense, countless nets of celestial flowers, and countless nets of precious images; it was also overspread by countless canopies of precious garments, countless canopies of precious parasols, countless canopies of precious pavilions, and countless canopies of precious flower garlands, with precious parasols, banners, and streamers erected everywhere.

Within this city, there was a tower named Treasury of the True Dharma (*Saddharmakośa*), adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels; its radiance was brilliant and peerless, such that sentient beings who beheld it could never tire of looking upon it. King Mahāprabha constantly resided therein.

At that time, the youth Sudhana had no attachment whatsoever to any of these precious and wonderful objects, including men, women, and the six sensory realms; he focused his correct contemplation solely on the ultimate Dharma and single-mindedly aspired to see a spiritual friend.

Traveling by stages, he saw King Mahāprabha, not far from his dwelling, seated upon a vast and magnificently adorned lion throne of *cintāmaṇi* jewel lotus-essence at the crossroads. Its legs were made of deep-blue lapis lazuli, it was draped with canopies of golden silk, covered with nets of various jewels, and provided with cushions of exquisite celestial garments.
The king sat cross-legged upon it, his body adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs;
he was like a mountain of pure gold, blazing with radiant color,
and like the sun in a clear sky, resplendent with majestic light.
Like the full moon, he brings refreshing clarity to all who behold him;
like the Brahmā King, he dwells amidst the assembly of Brahmās;
and like the great ocean, his jewels of meritorious dharmas are boundless.
He is like the Snowy Mountains, adorned with the groves of the marks and embellishments;
he is like a great cloud, able to thunder forth the Dharma and awaken all classes of beings;
he is like space, manifesting the various constellations of the Dharma-gates.
Like Mount Sumeru, its four colors appear universally within the ocean of the minds of sentient beings;
it is also like a jewel island, filled with various treasures of wisdom.

Before the royal throne, there were heaps of precious gems—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, coral, amber, conch shells, and jade—as well as an immeasurable and boundless variety of clothing, necklaces, and food and drink, all filling the space.

Furthermore, he saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite jeweled chariots, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial musical performances, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial wonderful incenses, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of medicinal decoctions and requisites for sustaining life for those afflicted by illness—all of these were entirely precious and excellent.
There were immeasurable milch cows with hooves and horns of golden hue;

there were immeasurable billions of beautiful women whose bodies were anointed with the finest sandalwood, adorned with celestial garments and various necklaces, who were thoroughly proficient in all sixty-four arts and skilled in all worldly etiquette and social conventions, bestowing gifts upon sentient beings according to their inclinations.
In cities, villages, and along the sides of crossroads, they placed all manner of necessities for life.

Along each and every path, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who bestowed these various things upon sentient beings for the following purposes: to universally gather in sentient beings; to cause sentient beings to rejoice; to cause sentient beings to leap with joy; to cause the minds of sentient beings to become pure; to cause sentient beings to attain refreshing coolness; to extinguish the afflictions of sentient beings; to cause sentient beings to understand all principles and meanings; to cause sentient beings to enter the path of omniscience; to cause sentient beings to abandon the mind of enmity; to cause sentient beings to leave behind the evils of body and speech; to cause sentient beings to uproot all false views; and to cause sentient beings to purify all paths of karma.

Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, bowed at his feet, and circumambulated him to the right for immeasurable circuits. Standing with palms joined, he addressed him, saying: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice,
nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me! At that time, the King said: "Good son!..."
I have purely cultivated the bodhisattva practice of the banner of great compassion; I have fulfilled the bodhisattva practice of the banner of great compassion.
Son of good family!

At the abodes of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas, I have questioned them regarding this Dharma, contemplated and observed it, and cultivated its adornments.

“Good son! I rule as king by means of this Dharma; I issue commands by means of this Dharma; I gather and sustain beings by means of this Dharma; I follow after the world by means of this Dharma; I guide sentient beings by means of this Dharma; I cause sentient beings to practice by means of this Dharma; I cause sentient beings to enter [the path] by means of this Dharma; I provide skillful means for sentient beings by means of this Dharma; I cause sentient beings to cultivate habitual perfuming by means of this Dharma; I cause sentient beings to initiate practice by means of this Dharma; I cause sentient beings to abide in the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena by means of this Dharma; and I cause sentient beings to abide in a mind of loving-kindness, taking loving-kindness as their sovereign and being fully endowed with the power of loving-kindness.”

In this way, they cause [beings] to abide in a mind of benefit, a mind of happiness, a mind of compassion, a mind of gathering, a mind that protects sentient beings without abandoning them, and a tireless mind that uproots the suffering of sentient beings.

By means of this Dharma, I cause all sentient beings to attain ultimate happiness, remaining forever joyful themselves, with their bodies free from all suffering and their minds attaining cool serenity. They sever the craving for birth and death, delight in the joy of the True Dharma, wash away the defilements of affliction, shatter the obstructions of evil karma, cut off the flow of saṃsāra, and enter the ocean of the True Dharma. They sever all realms of existence, seek omniscience, purify the ocean of their minds, and give rise to indestructible faith.
"Noble son! I have already dwelled in this practice of the Banner of Great Compassion, and am thus able to transform the world through the True Dharma. Noble son!"
All sentient beings within my land have no fear or dread toward me.
Good son! If there are sentient beings who are poor and destitute, they come to me with their requests and searches.
I opened my treasuries for them to take from as they pleased, and spoke to them, saying:
"Commit no evil; do not harm sentient beings; do not give rise to various views; do not produce attachments."

"You who are impoverished, if you have anything you require, you should come to my place or to the crossroads; there all manner of things are fully provided, so take as you wish without harboring any doubt or hesitation."

“Good son! The sentient beings dwelling in this city of Wondrous Light are all bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Great Vehicle; according to their respective inclinations, what they perceive differs. Some see this city as being small in scale, while others see it as being vast in scale;
some see its ground as consisting of earth and sand, while others see it adorned with various jewels.”
In some places they see mounds of earth used as walls; in others, they see precious walls surrounding them on all sides.

In some places they see the ground covered with many tiles and stones, uneven and high and low; in others, they see it adorned with countless great *maṇi* jewels interspersed throughout, level as the palm of a hand.

In some places they see houses made of wood and earth; in others, they see palaces, various pavilions, courtyards, windows, gates, balconies, and casements—all of these are nothing but exquisite jewels.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings whose minds are pure, who have planted roots of goodness by making offerings to the Buddhas, who have resolved their minds to pursue the path to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) with all-knowledge as their ultimate goal, and whom I previously embraced while practicing the bodhisattva conduct in the past—these shall see this city adorned and purified with various jewels;
all others see it as defiled.”
“Good son! All sentient beings in this land, during this age of the five turbidities, delight in committing various evils.
Out of compassion for them and wishing to rescue and protect them, I have entered the gate of the Bodhisattva samādhi ‘Following Accordance with the World,’ which is headed by great loving-kindness.”
When entering this samādhi, all such states of mind as fear, malice, enmity, and contention that exist within those sentient beings are entirely extinguished of their own accord.
Why is this? Because he has entered the Bodhisattva samādhi "Compassion as the Foremost in Accordance with the World," for such is the nature of phenomena.
O son of good family!
"Wait but a moment, and you shall see it for yourself.
At that time, King Mahāprabha entered this meditative absorption.

The city, both inside and out, shook in six ways; and from all the jeweled grounds, jeweled walls, jeweled halls, jeweled palaces, towers, pavilions, balconies, steps, and windows, a wondrous sound issued forth, and they all bowed their bodies in reverent salutation toward the king.
All the inhabitants within the city of Prabhāsa simultaneously leaped for joy and rushed toward the king’s location, prostrating themselves with their whole bodies upon the ground.
The entire multitude from the villages, camps, and towns all came to see the king, greeting him with joy and reverence.
The birds and beasts dwelling near where the King resided gazed upon one another, gave rise to hearts of compassion, and all together turned before the King to pay respectful homage.
All the mountains, plains, grasses, and trees likewise turned toward the King, none failing to offer reverent salutation.
The ponds, springs, wells, rivers, and oceans all overflowed and surged forth, flowing before the King.
Ten thousand dragon kings raised great clouds of incense, flashing lightning and rolling thunder, while pouring down a fine, misty rain.
There were ten thousand celestial kings, namely:

the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the King of the Yāma Heaven, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, the King of the Sunirmita Heaven, and the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven... with these as their leaders, they performed various kinds of music in the midst of the void.

Countless celestial maidens sang praises in song, raining down countless clouds of flowers, countless clouds of incense, countless clouds of precious garlands, countless clouds of precious robes, countless clouds of precious parasols, countless clouds of precious banners, and countless clouds of precious pennants, adorning the void as they made offerings to the king.

The great elephant king Airāvaṇa, by his sovereign power, spread countless great jewel lotuses in the midst of space; he hung down countless jewel necklaces, countless jewel silk ribbons, countless jewel garlands, countless jewel ornaments, countless jewel flowers, and countless jewel incenses, using various wonderful marvels as adornments, while countless celestial maidens sang various songs of praise.

Within Jambudvīpa, there were furthermore immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *rākṣasa* kings, *yakṣa* kings, *kumbhāṇḍa* kings, and *piśāca* kings—some dwelling in the great ocean and some inhabiting the land—who drank blood and ate flesh, harming and injuring sentient beings;
yet they all gave rise to a heart of compassion, vowing to practice what is beneficial, clearly recognizing the future life and refraining from all evils;
with palms joined in reverence, they prostrated themselves before the King.

Just as it is in Jambudvīpa, so it is in the other three continents, even throughout the trichiliocosm, and even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of worlds in the ten directions—all sentient beings who are poisonous and evil are exactly like this.
At that time, King Mahāprabha arose from samādhi and said to Sudhana:
"Good man! I know only this gate of the bodhisattva samādhi called 'Following the World with Great Compassion as the Foremost.'"
Just as all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are like a high canopy, because their compassionate mind universally shades all sentient beings;
they are like a practice, because they perform the lower, middle, and superior deeds with equal conduct;
they are like the great earth, because they are able to sustain all sentient beings with a compassionate heart.
They are like the full moon, for the light of their merit manifests equally throughout the world;
they are like the pure sun, for the light of their wisdom illuminates all objects of knowledge;
they are like bright lamps, for they can dispel all darkness within the minds of sentient beings.
They are water-clearing jewels, for they can purify the turbidity of flattery and deception within the minds of all sentient beings;
they are wish-fulfilling gems, for they can completely satisfy every aspiration in the hearts of all sentient beings;
they are great winds, for they swiftly cause sentient beings to practice samādhi and enter the great city of omniscience.

How could I possibly know their conduct, describe their virtues, weigh that mountain of merit, gaze upon those stars of excellence, examine that wind-wheel of great vows, enter those profound gateways of Dharma, reveal that ocean of adornments, elucidate those practices of Samantabhadra, open up those caves of samādhi, or praise that cloud of great compassion?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a royal capital named Anvaya;”
There is a laywoman named Acalā. Go to her and ask:
"How should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
At that time, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the king's feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, the youth Sudhana emerged from the city of Suprabha and traveled along the road, contemplating with right mindfulness the instructions of King Mahāprabha; recollecting the bodhisattva’s practice-gate of the Banner of Great Compassion; reflecting on the bodhisattva’s samādhi-light gate of conforming to the world; increasing his power of mastery over inconceivable vows and merit; strengthening his inconceivable wisdom for maturing sentient beings; observing their inconceivable and unique majesty of enjoyment; recollecting those inconceivable distinct characteristics; reflecting on those inconceivable pure retinues; and reflecting on those inconceivable activities performed.

They give rise to a mind of joy, a mind of pure faith, a mind of fierce intensity, a mind of delight, a mind of exultation, a mind of auspiciousness, a mind free from turbidity, a pure mind, a firm mind, a vast mind, and an inexhaustible mind.

Reflecting thus, he wept with flowing tears, mindful that the spiritual friend is truly rare, the source from which all merits arise, the source from which all bodhisattva practices arise, the source from which all pure mindfulness of bodhisattvas arises, the source from which all wheels of dhāraṇī arise, the source from which the radiance of all samādhis arises, the source from which the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas arises, who universally rains down the Dharma-rain of all Buddhas, who reveals all gates of bodhisattva vows, who gives birth to the inconceivable radiance of wisdom, and who causes the roots and sprouts of all bodhisattvas to grow.

Furthermore, they form this thought: "A spiritual friend is one who can universally rescue and protect from all evil realms; who can universally expound all dharmas of equality; who can universally reveal all paths, whether level or perilous; who can universally elucidate the profound meanings of the Mahāyāna; who can universally exhort and inspire the various practices of Samantabhadra; who can universally lead one to the city of omniscience; who can universally cause one to enter the great ocean of the Dharma-realm; who can universally cause one to see the ocean of dharmas of the three periods of time; who can universally bestow the sites of enlightenment of all the sages; and who can universally increase all wholesome dharmas."
While the youth Sudhana was thus grieving and reflecting, the deva who constantly follows and awakens Bodhisattvas, acting as a messenger of the Tathāgata, spoke to him from the midst of the sky:
"O son of good family!
Those who practice the teachings of spiritual friends will be gladdened by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
those who comply with the words of spiritual friends will draw near to the stage of omniscience;
and those who are able to remain free from doubt regarding the words of spiritual friends will always encounter all virtuous friends.
"Whoever resolves their mind with the vow never to be separated from spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) shall attain the fulfillment of all meaningful benefits.
Son of good family!

You should go to the royal capital of Anala; there you will surely see the great spiritual friend, the laywoman (upāsikā) Acalā. At that time, the youth Sudhana arose from the light of wisdom of that samādhi and, traveling by stages, arrived at the city of Anala, where he searched everywhere for the whereabouts of the laywoman Acalā.
An immeasurable multitude of people all said to him: "Good son!
The laywoman Acalā is a maiden living in her own home, protected by her parents; she is expounding the sublime Dharma for her own kinsmen and an immeasurable multitude of people."
Having heard these words, the youth Sudhana was filled with joy, as if he had seen his own parents; he immediately went to the house of the laywoman Acalā.
Entering her residence, he beheld her hall, which was everywhere illuminated by a golden radiance; those who encountered this light felt their bodies and minds become cool and refreshed.
When the light touched the body of the youth Sudhana, he immediately attained five hundred gates of samādhi, namely:

the gate of samādhi for comprehending all rare signs; the gate of samādhi for entering tranquility; the gate of samādhi for remaining far removed from all worlds; the gate of samādhi for the universal eye’s relinquishing and attaining; and the gate of samādhi for the Tathāgatagarbha...
Having attained such five hundred gates of samādhi, his body and mind became as supple as a seven-day-old embryo.
Furthermore, he smelled a wondrous fragrance such as no deva, nāga, gandharva, human, or non-human could possess.

Sudhana approached her, joined his palms in reverence, and observed her with single-minded attention; he saw that her physical form was upright, exquisite, and sublime, such that among all the women in the worlds of the ten directions, none could equal her, let alone surpass her!
Except for the Tathāgata and all the consecrated Bodhisattvas,
whose mouths emit wondrous fragrances and whose palaces are adorned with splendor, together with their retinues— none are equal to them, much less superior!
Among all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions, there is none who gives rise to a mind of defiled attachment toward this upāsikā;
if they should behold her even for a moment, all their afflictions will spontaneously be extinguished.
Just as the hundred thousand Great Brahma Kings certainly do not give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm,
you should know that the same applies to all the afflictions of those who behold this upāsikā.
The sentient beings of the ten directions never tire of beholding this woman, except for those who possess great wisdom.

At that time, the youth Sudhana bowed with palms joined and observed her with right mindfulness; he saw that this woman’s body was sovereign and inconceivable, her physical form and countenance peerless in the world, her radiance penetrating and clear such that nothing could obstruct it, universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings. From every pore of her body, a wondrous fragrance constantly issued forth; her retinue was boundless, her palace was supreme, and the depth and breadth of her merit were beyond measure.
His heart filled with joy, he praised her in verse:
"Guarding the pure precepts, Practicing vast patience,
With diligence that never regresses, His radiance illuminates the world.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the youth Sudhana said:
“Noble One! I have already set my mind on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should train in the conduct of a bodhisattva.”
"How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path?
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me!
Then, the laywoman Acalā comforted Sudhana with gentle and pleasing words of a bodhisattva, and addressed him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
you have already been able to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

"Good son! I have attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the treasury of invincible wisdom; I have attained the bodhisattva door of firm upholding and practice; I have attained the bodhisattva door of the dhāraṇī of the level of equality of all phenomena; I have attained the bodhisattva door of eloquence that illuminates all phenomena; I have attained the bodhisattva samādhi door of seeking all phenomena without weariness."
Sudhana said, "Noble One!
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the treasury of wisdom that is difficult to subdue, up to the samādhi door of seeking all dharmas without weariness— what is its sphere?"
The maiden said,
"Noble son! This place is difficult to understand."
Sudhana said: "I only pray that the Noble One, relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, will explain this for me!

Through a spiritual friend, I shall be able to believe and accept it, to know and understand it, to enter into and observe it, to practice in accordance with it, to leave behind all conceptual discrimination, and to reach ultimate equality."
The upāsikā said: “Good son! In a past age, there was an eon named:”
In the world Free from Defilement, the Buddha’s name was Long Arms.
At that time, there was a king named:
"Elektrota, I have only one daughter, who is none other than myself.
During the night when the music has ceased, my parents, brothers, and all five hundred maidens are fast asleep."

From atop my tower, as I gazed upward at the constellations, I beheld that Tathāgata in the midst of space like a king of jewel mountains, surrounded by immeasurable and boundless devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, as well as a multitude of bodhisattvas. The Buddha’s body universally radiated a great net of light that pervaded the ten directions without obstruction, and from every pore of his body issued forth wondrous fragrances.
Upon smelling this fragrance, my body became supple and my heart was filled with joy;
I then descended from the upper story to the ground, joined my ten fingers in reverence, and prostrated before the Buddha.
Furthermore, when observing that Buddha, I could not see the crown of his head; looking at the left and right sides of his body, I could find no limit to them.
Contemplating all the primary marks and secondary signs of that Buddha, I could never tire of them, and I thought to myself:

"What kind of karma did this World-Honored Buddha perform to obtain such a supreme and wondrous body, with its perfect primary and secondary marks, complete radiance, accomplished retinue, and magnificent palace? His merit and wisdom are entirely pure, his dhāraṇīs and samādhis are inconceivable, his supernormal powers are sovereign, and his eloquence is unimpeded?"
“Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing my thoughts, addressed me, saying:
‘You should give rise to an indestructible mind and extinguish all afflictions;’”
One should give rise to an invincible mind to shatter all attachments;
one should give rise to a fearless mind to enter the profound Dharma gates;
and one should give rise to a mind of endurance to rescue sentient beings who are evil.
One should give rise to a mind free from delusion, taking birth throughout all realms of existence;
one should give rise to a mind free from weariness, seeking to behold all Buddhas without ceasing;
one should give rise to a mind free from complacency, receiving the rain of Dharma from all Tathāgatas.
One should give rise to a mind of right reflection, universally producing the light of all Buddha-dharmas;
one should give rise to a mind of great upholding, universally turning the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas;
one should give rise to a mind of extensive circulation, bestowing the treasure of the Dharma upon sentient beings according to their inclinations.

“Good son! From that Buddha, I heard such a Dharma as this: I sought all-knowledge; I sought the ten powers of a Buddha; I sought the eloquence of a Buddha; I sought the radiance of a Buddha; I sought the form-body of a Buddha; I sought the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha; I sought the assemblies of a Buddha; I sought the buddha-field of a Buddha; I sought the majestic deportment of a Buddha; and I sought the lifespan of a Buddha.”
Having generated this mind, it becomes as firm and solid as a vajra, such that all afflictions and even those of the two vehicles cannot destroy it. "Good son!
Since I first gave rise to this mind, I have passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of Jambudvīpa, yet I have not even given rise to a thought of desire, much less committed the act!
Throughout those kalpas, he did not give rise to a mind of anger even toward his own relatives, much less toward other sentient beings!
Throughout those kalpas, he did not give rise to the view of self regarding his own body, much less conceive of material possessions as "mine"!

Throughout those kalpas, at the time of death, at the time of birth, and while dwelling in the womb, he was never confused enough to give rise to the notion of a sentient being or a neutral state of mind, let alone at other times!
Throughout those kalpas, even in dreams, he never forgot the sight of a single Buddha, let alone what was seen by the ten eyes of a bodhisattva!

Throughout those kalpas, he upheld all the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas without ever forgetting a single word or phrase; he did not forget even mundane expressions, let alone that which was spoken from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata!

Throughout those kalpas, he upheld the ocean of all Tathāgatas' teachings, such that there was not a single word or phrase that he did not contemplate or examine; even all mundane dharmas were likewise treated in this manner.

Throughout all those eons, they have upheld such oceans of all dharmas; there has never been a single dharma among them in which they did not attain samādhi, even including the mundane arts and crafts—this was likewise true for every single dharma.

Throughout those kalpas, you have upheld the wheel of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas; in whatever way you have upheld it, you have never abandoned even a single word or a single phrase, nor have you ever given rise to worldly knowledge, except for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings.

Throughout those kalpas, I beheld oceans of Buddhas; at the site of not a single Buddha did I fail to accomplish my pure great vows, and this was likewise true even at the sites of all the emanation Buddhas.
Throughout those kalpas, I have seen all the bodhisattvas practicing sublime conduct; there was not a single practice that I did not accomplish.

Throughout those kalpas, among all the sentient beings I encountered, there was not a single being whom I did not encourage to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor did I ever encourage a single being to give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

Throughout all those kalpas, regarding every Buddha-dharma, even down to a single word or a single phrase, they did not give rise to doubt, did not give rise to dualistic thoughts, did not give rise to discriminatory thoughts, did not give rise to various thoughts, did not give rise to thoughts of attachment, did not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority, and did not give rise to thoughts of love or hatred.

“Good son! From that time forth, I have constantly seen all Buddhas; I have constantly seen Bodhisattvas; I have constantly seen true spiritual friends. I have constantly heard the vows of all Buddhas; I have constantly heard the practices of Bodhisattvas; I have constantly heard the gates of the Bodhisattva *pāramitās*; I have constantly heard the gates of the light of wisdom of the Bodhisattva stages; I have constantly heard the gates of the inexhaustible treasury of Bodhisattvas; I have constantly heard the gates of entering the network of boundless worlds; I have constantly heard the gates of producing the causes for the boundless realms of sentient beings. I have constantly used the light of pure wisdom to eliminate the afflictions of all sentient beings; I have constantly used wisdom to grow the roots of goodness of all sentient beings; I have constantly manifested my body according to the inclinations of all sentient beings; and I have constantly awakened all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu* with pure and sublime speech.”

“Good son! I have attained the Bodhisattva’s gateway of adornment that seeks all dharmas without weariness; I have attained the gateway of the dhāraṇī of the level of equality of all dharmas, manifesting inconceivable and sovereign spiritual transformations.”
"Do you wish to see it? Sudhana replied, "Yes!"
"I wish to see her.

At that time, the laywoman Acalā sat upon the lion throne of the Dragon Treasury and entered the gate of the samādhi called "Adornment of Insatiable Seeking for All Dharmas," the gate of the samādhi called "Adornment of the Unfailing Wheel," the gate of the samādhi called "Manifestation of the Wheel of Wisdom of the Ten Powers," and the gate of the samādhi called "Inexhaustible Treasury of the Buddha-lineage. She entered ten thousand such gates of samādhi.
When entering this gate of samādhi, worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions shook in six ways; all were composed of pure lapis lazuli.
Within each world, there were ten billion sets of four continents, and in each, ten billion Tathāgatas—some dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, others even unto their parinirvāṇa.

Each Tathāgata emitted a web of light that pervaded the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment throughout the Dharma-realm, surrounded by pure retinues, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma and awakening all living beings.
Then, the laywoman Acalā arose from samādhi and said to Sudhana,
"Son of good family, do you see this?"
Sudhana said, "Yes! I have seen them all."
The upāsikā said: "Good son!
I have only attained this Samādhi-light of Insatiable Seeking for All Dharmas, whereby I preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice."

Just as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are like golden-winged garuḍas, traveling through space without obstruction, able to enter the great ocean of all sentient beings and, upon seeing those whose roots of goodness have matured, immediately seize them and place them on the shore of Bodhi;
or like merchant travelers entering a great island of jewels to seek the treasure of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the ten powers;
or like fishermen holding the net of the True Dharma, entering the ocean of birth and death to scoop up sentient beings from the waters of craving.
Like an asura king, he is able to thoroughly agitate the ocean of afflictions within the great cities of the three realms of existence;
again, like the solar disk appearing in the void, he illuminates the mud of craving and attachment, causing it to dry up;
and again, like the full moon appearing in the void, he causes the lotus hearts of those capable of being transformed to blossom.
Furthermore, it is like the great earth, which is universally equal, upon which immeasurable sentient beings dwell, and where the roots and sprouts of all wholesome dharmas grow;
it is also like a great wind, which moves without obstruction in whatever direction and can uproot the great trees of all views;
it is like a wheel-turning monarch, who travels through the world and gathers in all sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction.
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? "Good son!
To the south of here, there is a great city named:
In the immeasurable Duṣārā,
there was a renunciant non-Buddhist practitioner named Pūrṇa.
"Go there and ask him:
'How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave to depart.
