having obtained this, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra then extended his right hand and touched the crown of his head.

Once his head had been rubbed, Sudhana immediately attained as many gateways of samādhi as there are atoms in all buddha-fields, each having as many samādhis as there are atoms in all buddha-fields as its retinue.

In each and every samādhi, they behold oceans of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields, never before seen; they gather the requisites for omniscience as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; they give rise to the supreme, wondrous dharmas of omniscience as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; they generate great vows for omniscience as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; they enter oceans of great vows as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; they abide in the paths of deliverance for omniscience as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; they cultivate the practices of all Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; they arouse great vigor for omniscience as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields; and they attain the pure light of omniscience as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.
Just as the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra touched the crown of Sudhana’s head at the place of the Buddha Vairocana in this Sahā world,

so too did the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra touch the crown of Sudhana’s head at the places of all Buddhas in every world throughout the ten directions, and within every single atom of those worlds— in all such worlds and at the abodes of all Buddhas— and the Dharma-gates he received were likewise identical in all respects.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra addressed Sudhana, saying: "Good son,
do you see this power of my spiritual transformations?"
“Yes, indeed! We have seen them,
Great Sage!”
"This matter of inconceivable great supernormal power can only be known by the Tathāgata.
Samantabhadra replied, "Good son!"
In the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, I practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva, seeking all-knowledge.
In each and every kalpa, for the sake of purifying the bodhicitta, I served Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

In each and every kalpa, for the sake of accumulating the merit and virtue necessary for all-knowledge, I established vast assemblies of giving as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, making them known to all the worlds, so that whatever was sought was entirely fulfilled.

In each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking the dharma of omniscience, he practiced giving away wealth and possessions as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;

in each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, he practiced giving away cities, villages, kingdoms, royal thrones, wives, children, retinues, eyes, ears, noses, tongues, bodies, flesh, hands, feet, and even his own life, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
in each and every kalpa, for the sake of seeking the head of omniscience, he practiced giving away heads as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

In each and every eon, for the sake of seeking all-knowledge, he reverently honored, respected, served, and made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, providing everything required—robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal requisites—and having left the household life to study the Way within their teachings, he practiced the Buddha-dharma and protected and upheld the true doctrine.

“Good son! Throughout those oceans of kalpas, I recall that never for even a single thought-moment did I fail to comply with the Buddha’s teachings; nor did I, for even a single thought-moment, give rise to a mind of anger or harm, a mind of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ a mind of distinction between self and others, a mind remote from bodhicitta, a mind of weariness or exhaustion regarding birth and death, a mind of indolence, a mind of obstruction, or a mind of confusion. Rather, I dwelt solely in the unsurpassed, indestructible bodhicitta that gathers all the auxiliary dharmas for the path to omniscience.”
“Good son! I adorn Buddha-lands, rescue and protect sentient beings with a heart of great compassion, teach and bring them to maturity, make offerings to all Buddhas, and serve spiritual friends;
for the sake of seeking the True Dharma, I propagate, uphold, and protect it, being able to relinquish everything internal and external, even my own body and life, without any stinginess.”
Though one might exhaust an ocean of eons in explaining their causes and conditions, these [causes] would never be exhausted. "Good son!

Within the ocean of my Dharma, there is not a single word or a single phrase that was not sought by relinquishing the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king, nor was there any that was not sought by relinquishing all that one possesses."
"Good son! All the Dharma I seek is for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings. With single-minded reflection, I pray: 'May all sentient beings hear this Dharma;

may the light of wisdom universally illuminate the world; may I reveal and show them supramundane wisdom; may all sentient beings attain peace and happiness; and may I universally praise all the merits of all Buddhas.'"
"Such past causes and conditions of mine as these could not be fully recounted even in an ocean of eons numbering as many atoms as there are in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields."
"Therefore, son of good family!

By means of the power of these factors conducive to enlightenment, the power of all roots of goodness, the power of great aspiration, the power of cultivating merit, the power of contemplating all phenomena as they truly are, the power of the eye of wisdom, the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the power of great compassion, the power of pure supernormal knowledges, and the power of spiritual friends, I have attained this ultimate, pure Dharma-body, which is equal throughout the three periods of time. Furthermore, I have attained a pure and unsurpassed form-body that transcends all worlds. In accordance with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, I manifest forms for them; I enter all lands and pervade all places, extensively displaying supernormal powers in all worlds, so that none who behold them fail to rejoice."
"Good son! You should observe my physical body as it is:
this physical body of mine has been accomplished over an ocean of boundless kalpas; it is difficult to see and difficult to hear of even in immeasurable thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas."

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness, or even Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas who have planted only a few roots of goodness, they cannot yet hear my name, let alone see my body!"
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who hear my name, they shall no longer regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This applies equally to those who see me or touch me, those who welcome or escort me, those who follow me for even a moment, and even those who see or hear me in their dreams."
There are sentient beings who attain maturity by recollecting me for a single day and night;

others who attain maturity by recollecting me for seven days and nights, half a month, one month, half a year, one year, a hundred years, a thousand years, or even for an incalculable number of kalpas—up to an unspeakably unspeakable number of kalpas as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields;
and others who attain maturity by recollecting me for a single lifetime, a hundred lifetimes, or even for an incalculable number of lifetimes as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields.
Some see me emitting great radiance, while others see me shaking the buddha-fields; some give rise to fear, while others give rise to joy, and all thereby attain maturity.
"Good son! By means of such skillful gates as these, numbering as many as the atoms within Buddha-fields, I cause all sentient beings to attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Good son! If there are sentient beings who see or hear of my pure land, they will certainly be born within this pure land;
if there are sentient beings who see or hear of my pure body, they will certainly be born within my pure body.”
“Good son! You should contemplate this pure body of mine.

At that time, the youth Sudhana contemplated the body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; within each of its marks and signs, limbs and joints, and every single pore, there were oceans of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
In each and every ocean of lands, there were Buddhas appearing in the world, surrounded by assemblies of great Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, I saw that all those oceans of lands were established in various ways, with various shapes, various adornments, and various great mountains encircling them; various clouds of diverse colors covered the void, and various Buddhas appeared to expound various teachings;
such matters as these were each and every one different.

Furthermore, he saw Samantabhadra, within each and every ocean of worlds, manifesting clouds of Buddha-nirmāṇakāyas as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to turn toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the youth Sudhana again saw himself within the body of Samantabhadra, teaching and transforming sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

Furthermore, compared to the roots of goodness and the light of wisdom obtained by Sudhana through attending as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, the roots of goodness obtained by him upon seeing the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra did not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor even one hundred-thousand-billionth part; indeed, they could not be reached even by calculation or analogy.

From the time the youth Sudhana first resolved his mind toward enlightenment until he beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, all the oceans of Buddha-lands he entered during that interval are now surpassed by the oceans of Buddha-lands entered in a single thought-moment within a single pore of Samantabhadra; they exceed the former by a factor of unspeakably unspeakable times the number of atoms in a Buddha-land.
As it is with one pore, so it is with every pore.

In a single step taken by the youth Sudhana within the world-systems of the pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he passes through worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

Traveling in this manner until the end of all future eons, he would still be unable to know the limits of the ocean of lands within a single pore—their sequential order, their treasury, their distinctions, their universal entry, their formation, their destruction, or their adornments;
nor could he know the limits of the ocean of Buddhas—their sequential order, their treasury, their distinctions, their universal entry, their birth, or their cessation.

Furthermore, they cannot know the limits of the ocean-like assemblies of bodhisattvas—their sequential order, their treasuries, their distinctions, their universal entry, their gathering, and their dispersal;

nor can they know the limits of such oceans as the entry into the realms of sentient beings, the knowledge of the faculties of sentient beings, the wisdom that teaches and tames all sentient beings, the profound mastery in which bodhisattvas abide, and the various stages and paths entered by bodhisattvas.

Within the pore-lands of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the youth Sudhana traveled thus for one kalpa in a single land, and continued in this manner until he had traveled for as many kalpas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands; yet he did not vanish from this land to appear in that land, but in every thought-moment pervaded the boundless ocean of lands, teaching and transforming sentient beings, leading them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the youth Sudhana successively attained the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; he became equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas. With a single body, he filled all worlds, becoming equal in buddha-lands, equal in practices, equal in perfect enlightenment, equal in spiritual powers, equal in wheels of Dharma, equal in eloquence, equal in speech, equal in voices, equal in powers and fearlessnesses, equal in the abodes of Buddhas, equal in great compassion, and equal in inconceivable liberation and mastery in every respect.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra spoke these verses:
“You should all remove the stains of delusion And listen with single-minded concentration and without distraction;
I shall speak of the Tathāgata’s possession of all perfections, The true path of universal liberation.”
The supramundane, disciplined, and sublime Great Being, whose mind is as pure as space,
constantly radiates the great light of the sun of wisdom, universally causing all living beings to extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
The Tathāgata is difficult to see or hear; only now, after immeasurable billions of kalpas, have we encountered him.
Like the udumbara flower that appears but once in an age, one should therefore listen to the Buddha’s merits.
Conforming to all the activities of the world, like a phantom person manifesting various deeds,
he acts solely to please the minds of sentient beings, never giving rise to conceptual discrimination or mental constructions.

At that time, having heard these words, all the bodhisattvas became single-mindedly thirsty for the Dharma and looked up with longing, wishing only to hear of the true merits of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One. They all thought to themselves:
"Samantabhadra Bodhisattva has fully cultivated all practices; his essential nature is pure, and all his words are entirely non-deceptive. He is praised by all the Tathāgatas."
Having formed this thought, they conceived a profound longing and veneration.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—fully adorned with merit and wisdom, like a lotus flower unsullied by any dust or defilement of the triple world—addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Listen attentively! I now wish to speak of a single drop from the ocean of the Buddha’s merits."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as space, Pervading the minds of all sentient beings;
It fully understands all the delusions of the world, Without giving rise to various distinct discriminations.”
In a single thought-moment, they fully know the phenomena of the three periods of time, And likewise comprehend the faculties of all sentient beings;
Like a skillful master of great illusion, They manifest boundless deeds in every moment of thought.
According to the various mental activities of sentient beings and the power of their past karma and vows, what they perceive each differs;
yet the Buddha is fundamentally free from any movement of thought.
In some places, one sees Buddhas seated, filling all worlds throughout the ten directions;
yet there are those whose minds are not pure, who do not see a Buddha for immeasurable eons.
Some, possessing faith and understanding and free from pride, attain the vision of the Tathāgata as soon as they resolve their minds;
others, with deceitful, hypocritical, and impure hearts, may search for him through billions of eons and yet never encounter him.
In some places, one hears the Buddha’s voice, its melody exquisite and pleasing to the heart;
yet for hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, or millions of kalpas, there are those who do not hear it because their minds are impure.
Or one may see great Bodhisattvas of pure virtue, filling the three thousandfold world-system;
having all fully perfected the practices of Samantabhadra, the Tathāgata sits majestically amidst them.
Some see this realm as peerless in its excellence, adorned and purified by the Buddha over immeasurable eons;
therein, the most supreme Honored One, Vairocana, attained awakening and realized Bodhi.
In some, he sees a supreme and wondrous lotus land, where the Tathāgata Bhadraśrī resides,
surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom diligently cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.
Some see the Buddha Amitāyus, surrounded by Avalokiteśvara and others,
all of whom abide in the stage of consecration, filling the worlds of the ten directions.
Some may see this trichiliocosm adorned in various ways like the world of Abhirati,
with the Tathāgata Akṣobhya dwelling therein, as well as bodhisattvas such as Gandhahastin.
Some behold the Greatly Renowned Candrabuddhi, together with the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja and others,
abiding in a wondrous adornment like a perfect mirror, pervading the pure lands throughout the ten directions.
Or they see the World-Honored One, Sūryagarbha, dwelling in the pure land of Auspicious Radiance,
together with all the consecrated bodhisattvas, filling the ten directions as he preaches the Dharma.
In some places he sees the Buddha Great Vajra Flame, together with the Bodhisattva Wisdom Banner,
traveling throughout all vast lands, preaching the Dharma to eliminate the cataracts of sentient beings.
On each and every tip of a hair, unspeakably many Buddhas, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
are surrounded by their assemblies of Bodhisattvas, preaching various teachings to deliver sentient beings.
Some perceive within a single pore a vast realm, perfectly adorned,
wherein dwell immeasurable Tathāgatas, and which is filled with pure sons of the Buddha.
Some may see within a single mote of dust All the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
Completely filled with immeasurable Bodhisattvas Who have cultivated all practices for unspeakable eons.
Some behold within the space of a single hair-tip Immeasurable oceans of lands as numerous as dust motes and sands;
Arising from various karmas, each distinct, Vairocana therein turns the wheel of Dharma.
Some see the world as impure, while others see it composed of pure jewels;
they behold the Tathāgata remaining for immeasurable eons, even manifesting his entry into nirvāṇa.
Pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions, He manifests various inconceivable displays;
According to the mental faculties, wisdom, and karma of sentient beings, There are none whom he does not transform and purify.
Thus the Unsurpassed Great Teacher fills all lands throughout the ten directions;
manifesting various supernormal powers, I shall speak of but a small portion—please listen.
Some see Śākyamuni having already attained the Way of Buddhahood after inconceivable kalpas;
others see him now beginning as a bodhisattva, benefiting all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Some behold this Lion of the Śākyas, practicing the path by making offerings to all Buddhas;
others behold the Most Honored One among men, manifesting various powers and supernatural feats.
Sometimes they are seen practicing giving or maintaining the precepts; sometimes patience, energy, or the various dhyānas;
through wisdom, skillful means, vows, power, and knowledge, they manifest all things in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.

Some see the ultimate perfection of the pāramitās; some see them dwelling securely in the various stages (bhūmis), with their dhāraṇīs, samādhis, supernormal powers, and wisdom—all such things appear completely and without exception.
Some manifest practicing for immeasurable eons, abiding in the bodhisattva stage of endurance;
some manifest abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, while others manifest receiving the empowerment of the Dharma-water poured upon their crowns.
Sometimes manifesting the bodies of Brahmā, Śakra, or the World-Protectors, Or manifesting as Kṣatriyas or Brahmins,
adorned with various forms and features, Just like a magician displaying a multitude of images.
Sometimes he manifests his initial descent of spirit from Tuṣita; sometimes he is seen receiving consorts within the palace;
sometimes he is seen renouncing all worldly glory and pleasure, leaving home and the secular world to practice the Way.

Some see him just born, or see him pass away; some see him leave home to practice the extraordinary path, or see him sit beneath the Bodhi tree, subduing the armies of Māra and attaining perfect enlightenment.
Some see the Buddha having just entered parinirvāṇa; some see stūpas arising throughout the world;
some see images of the Buddha installed within those stūpas—these appear in such ways because he knows the proper time.
Or one may see the Tathāgata Amitāyus bestowing the sublime prediction upon various bodhisattvas,
so that they become unsurpassed Great Teachers and succeed him as the resident of the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Some see [them], after performing buddha-works for immeasurable billions of kalpas, entering parinirvāṇa;
some see them now just beginning to attain bodhi, or see them currently practicing various wondrous deeds.
Some see the Tathāgata as a pure moon, Abiding in the Brahma world and the palace of Māra,
In the palaces of Maheśvara and Nirmāṇarati, Manifesting all manner of miraculous transformations.
Or they see him in the Tuṣita Heaven, surrounded by immeasurable devas;
for their sake he preaches the Dharma to bring them joy, and they all together resolve their minds to make offerings to the Buddha.
Or they see him dwelling in the Yāma Heaven, In the realms of the Trāyastriṃśa, the World-Protectors, and the Nāgas;
Within all such celestial palaces, There is not one in which his image does not appear.
In the presence of that World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, he scattered flowers and spread his hair as an offering;
from this, he came to understand the profound and wondrous Dharma, and has constantly transformed all living beings through this path.
Some see the Buddha long since entered parinirvāṇa; some see him first attaining bodhi.
Some see him remaining for immeasurable kalpas; some see him enter extinction in an instant.
Physical marks, radiance, and lifespan; wisdom, bodhi, and nirvana;
the assemblies, those to be transformed, majestic deportment, and voice—each and every one of these is infinite.
Sometimes he manifests a body of extreme vastness, like the great jewel mountain Sumeru;
at other times, one sees him sitting cross-legged, unmoving, filling boundless worlds.
Some see the halo extending for one fathom; some see it for thousands, tens of thousands, or millions of yojanas;
some see it illuminating immeasurable lands; and some see it filling all buddha-fields.
Some see the Buddha’s lifespan as eighty years; some as hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of years;
some see him abide for inconceivable eons, and thus it continues to increase manifold beyond this.
The Buddha’s wisdom penetrates all with purity and unimpededness; in a single thought-moment, he universally knows the phenomena of the three periods of time.
All arise from the causes and conditions of mind and consciousness; they are subject to birth and extinction, impermanent, and devoid of self-nature.
Attaining perfect enlightenment within a single land, they likewise do so in all lands;
each enters into every other, manifesting in this way according to the minds of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata abides in the unsurpassed path, Accomplishing the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses;
Possessing wisdom that is unimpeded, He turns the wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects.
Fully understanding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, they discern the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination;
with unimpeded eloquence regarding the dharma, its meaning, joyful exposition, and phrasing, they extensively expound through these four analytical knowledges.
All phenomena are without self and without marks; the nature of karma neither arises nor perishes.
All things are utterly remote like space, yet the Buddha distinguishes them through skillful means.
The Tathāgata thus turns the wheel of Dharma, universally shaking all lands throughout the ten directions;
palaces, mountains, and rivers all tremble, yet he causes no sentient beings to feel alarm or fear.
The Tathāgata universally proclaims a vast and sublime sound, causing all to understand according to their faculties and inclinations;
he causes them all to resolve their minds to eliminate the defilements of delusion, yet the Buddha never gives rise to a thought of such intention.
Some hear of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, Meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means;
Others hear of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— Each expressed through various distinct sounds and words.
Some hear of the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts, The bases of psychic power, the faculties and powers, as well as the factors of enlightenment and the path;
The various recollections, supernormal powers, calm abiding and insight, And the immeasurable skillful means of all dharma-gates.
The eight classes of nāgas and spirits, humans and non-humans, and the hosts of devas such as Brahmā, Śakra, and the World Protectors—
the Buddha preaches the Dharma for them with a single voice, causing each to understand according to their own kind.
If there be greed, hatred, and delusion, anger, concealment, stinginess, envy, as well as pride and flattery—
these eighty-four thousand diverse afflictions— he causes all to hear the teaching of their respective remedies.
If they have not yet fully cultivated pure and white dharmas, cause them to hear the exposition of the ten precepts;
for those who are already able to practice giving and self-restraint, cause them to hear the sound of quiescent nirvana.
If there are those whose resolve is weak and who lack compassion, who loathe birth and death and seek only their own escape;
cause them to hear the teaching of the three gates of liberation, so that they may attain the bliss of nirvāṇa beyond suffering.
If there are those who possess little desire by nature, who loathe the three realms of existence and seek tranquility;
cause them to hear the teaching on dependent origination, so that they may attain liberation by means of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
If there are those with pure and vast minds, Who are fully endowed with the merits of giving and precepts,
And who draw near to the Tathāgata with compassion, May they hear the sound of the Mahāyāna being proclaimed.
In some lands, they hear of the One Vehicle; in others, two, three, four, or five, and so on until there is no measure—this is entirely the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.
Nirvāṇa is eternally quiescent and never otherwise; yet there are distinctions in the excellence or inferiority of wisdom and practice.
Just as the nature of space is one, while the flight of birds—whether far or near—is each different.
The Buddha’s body and voice are likewise: they pervade the entirety of the realm of empty space;
yet according to the differences in the mental faculties and wisdom of sentient beings, what is heard and what is seen each vary.
The Buddha, having cultivated all practices in the past, is able to manifest wondrous sounds according to the inclinations of others;
he has no mental reckoning of "this" or "that," nor does he think, "To whom shall I speak, and to whom shall I not speak?"
The Tathāgata’s face emits great rays of light, Complete in number eighty-four thousand;
The Dharma-gates he teaches are likewise so, Universally illuminating the world to eliminate afflictions.
Fully endowed with pure merit and wisdom, you always accord with the three worlds;
like space, you are free from defilement, yet you appear for the sake of sentient beings.
They manifest the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, And likewise manifest dwelling in the world for a full lifespan;
Though they appear in such ways in accordance with the world, Their essential nature is pure, identical to space.
All lands are without limit, and the faculties and desires of sentient beings are likewise immeasurable;
with the eye of wisdom, the Tathāgata clearly perceives them all, manifesting the Buddha-way according to those who are to be transformed.
Throughout the ultimate void of the worlds of the ten directions, amidst all the assemblies of humans and devas,
according to their various and differing forms, the Buddha manifests his body in just such a way.
If one is among the great assembly of śramaṇas, shaving off hair and beard and donning the kāṣāya robe,
holding the robes and bowl while guarding the sense faculties, causing them to rejoice and bring their afflictions to rest.
Whenever he associates with brahmins, he manifests a frail and emaciated body;
holding a staff and carrying a water-pot, he is ever pure, endowed with wisdom, and skillful in discourse.
Exhaling the old and inhaling the new to satisfy himself, he consumed wind and dew as his food;
whether sitting or standing, he remained unmoving, manifesting these ascetic practices to subdue heterodox paths.

Some uphold those precepts and act as teachers of the world; they are well-versed in medical treatises and other sciences, including writing, mathematics, astronomy, and the various signs of the earth, as well as the auspicious and inauspicious omens pertaining to the body—all of which they understand without exception.
They enter deeply into all meditative concentrations and liberations, as well as the practices of samādhi, supernormal powers, and wisdom;
through conversation, chanting, and shared play, they employ skillful means to cause all beings to abide in the Buddha-way.
Sometimes he manifests noble garments to adorn his body, wearing a flower crown upon his head and shaded by a lofty parasol;
surrounded on all sides by the fourfold army, he assembles the multitudes, proclaims his majesty, and subdues the minor kings.
Or he may serve as a judge who hears lawsuits and adjudicates legal cases;
skillfully understanding all worldly affairs, he examines every matter of granting or withholding with clarity and precision, causing everyone to be fully satisfied and submissive.
Sometimes he acts as a great minister, solely to assist and support, skillfully employing the laws and regulations for governing kings;
his benefits to the ten directions are all-pervasive, yet no sentient beings are aware of it.
Sometimes appearing as minor kings scattered like grains of millet, or as flying universal monarchs (cakravartin),
they cause all the princes and retinues of court ladies to receive transformation, such that none can fathom it.
Sometimes he becomes one of the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, commanding the hosts of nāgas, yakṣas, and others;
for their assemblies he preaches the Dharma, causing them all to rejoice greatly.
Sometimes he becomes the Great Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, dwelling in the Sudharmā Hall and the Nandana Grove;
wearing a flower crown upon his head, he proclaims the wondrous Dharma, such that all the devas gaze up in reverence, unable to fathom him.
Abiding in the heavens of Yāma and Tuṣita, or in the realms of Nirmāṇarati and Vaśavartin,
and dwelling within palaces of maṇi jewels, he teaches the practice of truth to bring them to subdual.
Sometimes he goes into the assemblies of the Brahma-heaven, preaching the four immeasurables and the various paths of dhyāna;
causing all to rejoice, he then departs, and none can know the manner of his coming or going.
Or ascending as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, he preaches for them the precious flowers of the factors of enlightenment and other immeasurable noble virtues;
only then does he depart, leaving those who lack wisdom behind.
As seen by the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom, all sentient beings therein are taught and brought to maturity through various means by means of infinite expedient doors.
Just as a master illusionist, skilled in magical arts, manifests various illusory phenomena;
so too does the Buddha transform sentient beings, manifesting for them various bodies.
Just as the pure moon in the sky causes the beings of the world to see its waxing and waning,
appearing as reflections in all rivers and ponds, and eclipsing the radiance and color of all the stars.
The moon of the Tathāgata’s wisdom appears in the world, yet through skillful means it manifests increase and decrease;
its reflection appears in the water of the Bodhisattvas' minds, while the constellations of the Śrāvakas lack its luster and color.
Just as the great ocean is filled with jewels, pure, unturbid, and immeasurable;
all sentient beings throughout the four continents manifest their reflections therein.
The ocean of the Buddha’s physical merits is likewise: Stainless, untroubled, and without limit;
Throughout all sentient beings within the realm of phenomena, There is not one who does not see their reflection therein.
Just as the pure sun emits a thousand rays, Shining upon the ten directions without moving from its place;
The radiance of the Buddha-sun is likewise: Neither coming nor going, it dispels the darkness of the world.
Just as when a dragon king sends down a great rain, it does not emerge from his body nor from his mind,
yet it is able to moisten and saturate everywhere, washing away the scorching heat and bringing refreshing coolness.

The Dharma rain of the Tathāgata is likewise: it does not issue from the body or mind of the Buddha, yet it can awaken all sentient beings, universally causing them to extinguish the fires of the three poisons.
The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body is peerless throughout all the three realms;
for, by way of supramundane discourse, its nature is neither existent nor non-existent.
Though having no basis, there is nowhere it does not abide; though there is nothing it does not reach, it does not depart.
Like a painting in the sky or what is seen in a dream, one should contemplate the Buddha-body in this way.
All phenomena within the three realms, whether existent or non-existent, cannot serve as metaphors for the Buddha;
just as among the birds and beasts of the mountains and forests, there is none that dwells by relying upon space.
The mani-jewels of the great ocean possess infinite colors, and the distinctions of the Buddha’s body are likewise so;
the Tathāgata is neither form nor non-form, appearing according to what is appropriate without abiding anywhere.
Space, suchness, and the limit of reality, Nirvana, the dharma-nature,
and quiescence— Only such true dharmas as these Can be revealed by the Tathāgata.
The atoms within all lands may be counted, The waters within the great oceans may be drunk dry,
Space may be measured and the wind may be bound, But none can fully describe the virtues of the Buddha.

If there are those who hear of this ocean of merit and give rise to a heart of joy, faith, and understanding, they shall obtain everything as it has been extolled; be careful not to harbor doubts regarding this.
The Great Vaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sutra, Scroll Eighty.
